Kyiv Independent community helps fund 26 drone detectors for front-line journalists
The Kyiv Independent community helped raise more than $24,000 through an online store collection launched to mark World Press Freedom Day, enabling the purchase of 26 drone detectors to help protect independent journalists reporting from Ukraine’s front lines.
The “No News is Bad News” collection was launched by the Kyiv Independent ahead of World Press Freedom Day on May 3, with profits supporting the Institute of Mass Information (IMI), a Kyiv-based organization that protects journalists’ rights and safety.
Between April 21 and May 5, the campaign raised $9,182 through sales of the collection, which featured a T-shirt carrying the message “No News is Bad News” and a notebook reading “Press Freedom is Your Freedom.” The campaign also received $14,040 in additional donations, with a further $784 donated directly to IMI by Kyiv Independent supporters.
Together, these contributions enabled IMI to purchase 26 Vydun 7.5 drone detectors for independent regional journalists working near the front line. The equipment provides early warning of approaching drones, giving journalists crucial time to seek cover while reporting.
The campaign originally aimed to fund 20 detectors. The support from the Kyiv Independent community made it possible to fund six additional devices.
For journalists working in Ukraine’s front-line regions, drone attacks have become an increasingly serious threat. Natalia Chaika, a journalist with RIA Pivden, was among those who received a detector from IMI. She said the equipment is essential not only when reporting from areas close to the front line, but also when covering sites of Russian attacks and working around Zaporizhzhia.
IMI had been seeking funding for drone detectors for media workers for months before the campaign. According to the organization, many potential funders could not support the purchase of equipment intended for use in areas of active hostilities. The contributions from Kyiv Independent supporters helped make the project possible.
The campaign is one example of how the Kyiv Independent community extends beyond supporting our journalism directly. Through memberships, donations, purchases from our store, and other forms of support, our community helps us sustain independent journalism from Ukraine — and provide practical support to the people doing that work on the ground.
Our community is an essential part of the Kyiv Independent’s mission. It allows us to keep reporting from Ukraine and to support the broader ecosystem of independent journalism here. Consider joining the Kyiv Independent community and becoming part of what makes this work possible.

MOSCOW, September 28. /TASS/. The European military-industrial complex is incapable of rapidly producing and supplying weapons to troops in the event of a hypothetical conflict with Russia; consequently, the EU is seeking to prolong the conflict in Ukraine, Alexey Chadayev, an unmanned aviation expert and CEO of the Ushkuynik Research and Production Center, said.

Given its position and circumstances, it is therefore banking on one thing: that the Russia-Ukraine conflict continues for as long as possible and that Ukraine manages to hold out for some more time," he said at the 5th foresight forum, titled "The Special Military Operation and World War III."

VILNIUS - Lithuania is sticking to its original 2030 deadline for the first phase of the Rail Baltica project despite a Baltic agreement to extend the deadline to 2034, the country's transport minister said, according to business news portal Verslo Zinios.

Response to Russia's hybrid attacks should be creation of a European defense union - Stakis  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:23:53 UTC
23:23:53 KST

RIGA - The European Union (EU) should respond to Russia’s hybrid attacks by forming a European defense union, the development of which could begin with the establishment of a security council, said Martins Stakis (Progressives), a member of the European Parliament (EP), in an interview with LETA.
When asked whether the EU is providing sufficient funding for defense against hybrid threats - including in the areas of critical infrastructure, communications, and cybersecurity - Stakis replied that, in his view, the key issue is not the amount of funding but a change in mindset. In his view, a response that is too weak will not deter Russia from further attacks.
The MEP cited as an example the drone incident at the Leipzig/Halle Airport, for which Germany has blamed Russia. In Stakis’ assessment, the retaliatory measures announced by Germany - including the decision to terminate the lease agreement for the Russian House in Berlin - are not strong enough.
Stakis emphasized that the stricter response options he has proposed are, for now, merely ideas. In his view, a serious response would be an agreement among EU member state leaders to form a European defense union and jointly develop the capabilities of their armed forces.
The politician mentioned the use of Europe’s most powerful weapon - bureaucracy - as another possible response. Stakis suggested that Russia’s shadow fleet vessels could be thoroughly inspected, with up to a month devoted to inspecting each ship. In his view, this would deal a blow to the Russian economy.
The MEP believes that continuing with the current approach will not yield different results. He emphasized that Russia’s hybrid attacks have not diminished but have become more frequent.
Speaking about the possibility of creating a European defense union, Stakis noted that the EP has prepared a draft report on its institutional aspects. In his view, the formation of the union should begin with the establishment of a European Security Council.
Stakis explained that decisions in this council could be made by majority vote. According to him, the current requirement for unanimity allows a single EU member state to block decision-making.
The MEP also highlighted opportunities for practical cooperation. He noted that countries continue to develop defense innovations independently and conduct procurement on a relatively small scale. In his view, for example, the prime ministers of the Baltic and Nordic countries could agree to pool funding for innovation, jointly develop technologies, and conduct procurements. In Stakis’ view, this would reduce costs and allow for faster action.
He believes that countries need to recognize the capabilities they cannot develop on their own, as well as the opportunity to save money through cooperation. The defense industry's interest and political leadership are also necessary.

Education information listed by MP Butans raises uncertainty  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:23:50 UTC
23:23:50 KST

RIGA - Uncertainties have arisen regarding the educational background listed by Saeima member Arturs Butans (National Alliance) in the last three Saeima elections, according to information compiled by LETA and explanations provided by the politician.
In the documents for the 2018 and 2022 Saeima elections, as well as initially on his candidate profile for this year’s election, Butans had listed higher education. After LETA inquired about the qualification obtained in Australia, his higher education was changed to secondary education on his 15th Saeima election candidate form, and the Sydney Business College was removed from the list of educational institutions.
Butans explained to LETA that he had obtained a business management certificate in Australia, which he had not submitted in Latvia for recognition of educational qualifications. He later stated that he would contact the Academic Information Center (AIC) to determine the equivalence of his education.
Butans admitted that since obtaining the certificate in 2018, he had not pursued its recognition in Latvia. He explained that in 2022, upon learning of his election to the Saeima, he enrolled in a bachelor’s degree program in Latvia at the first opportunity, which he plans to complete by the end of this year. Next year, he intends to continue his studies in a part-time master’s program.
To verify the information provided by the politician, LETA contacted the AIC. The center responded that without an educational document, it cannot assess whether the qualification Butans obtained is equivalent to higher education in Latvia.
In response to LETA’s questions, Butans indicated that he had decided to seek consultation from the AIC to determine whether his studies in Australia are equivalent to professional or first-level higher education.
Currently, the candidate profile for Butans published by the Central Election Commission (CVK) lists secondary education as his highest level of education. The education section lists only the Riga Distance Learning Secondary School, the year 2012, and "general secondary education."
A reference to higher education in Butans’ election documents can be found as early as 2018. In the candidate information for the 13th Saeima elections published in Latvijas Vestnesis official bulletin, he listed Sydney Business College, graduation in 2018, his major as Business Management, and his educational level as Higher Education. The same information regarding Sydney Business College was also published in the documents for the 14th Saeima elections in 2022.
In the initial version of the 2026 candidate profile, Butans was also listed as having earned a higher education degree in business management from Sydney Business College in 2018.
Sydney’s Bridge Business College was a private vocational education and training institution. The college’s registration expired on June 30, 2020, and its current status is "withdrawn," meaning its registration has been revoked.
Sub-paragraph (f) of paragraph 4 of Article 11 of the Saeima Election Law stipulates that a candidate’s list must be accompanied by a statement, signed by the candidate, regarding their level of education, degree obtained and professional qualifications, as well as the educational institution and year of graduation. Meanwhile, Article 52 provides for liability for persons who have knowingly provided false information about themselves in these documents.
Section 272 of the Criminal Law provides for criminal liability for knowingly providing false information to a state institution, where the person is under a legal obligation to provide such information. This offence is punishable by short-term imprisonment, probation, community service or a fine.
Glorija Grevcova, who was previously convicted of providing false information to the Central Election Commission (CVK) and was elected to the 14th Saeima from For Stability party, has been sentenced. The false information she provided concerned her education and place of employment.

The court found that the agreement complied with the law, was entered into voluntarily, and approved it.
The state will confiscate 77,104.32 euros of Bessedin's assets, from which procedural costs of 3,195.80 euros will also be covered as per the agreement.
The ruling has not yet entered into force.

'Ulya' to open Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:23:15 UTC
23:23:15 KST

TALLINN - The opening film of the 30th Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (POFF) will be "Ulya," which will kick off the festival's Baltic focus.
The biographical drama by Latvian director Viesturs Kairiss received a seven-minute standing ovation at its premiere at this year's Cannes Film Festival. The film, which is breaking box-office records in Latvia and has been submitted for an Oscar, will now be screened for an Estonian audience for the first time at the POFF opening ceremony on November 6 at the Alexela Concert Hall.
The story is set in 1964 in the Latvian Old Believers' village of Paberzi. 14-year-old Ulya is a girl just like any other, except for one thing: she is already two meters tall, still growing, and constantly ridiculed for her height. The film explores whether Ulya's extraordinary stature is a curse or a blessing, and at what cost.
This emotional story of self-discovery is inspired by the life of Uljana Semjonova, once the world's best female basketball player, and features significant Estonian contribution to its production.
The film's co-producers include Pille Runk and the studio Allfilm, with Andris Feldmanis and Livia Ulman as co-screenwriters. The music was composed by the band Puuluup, with sound design by Siim Skepast and makeup by Liisi Pollumaa.
The title role is played by Latvian actor Karlis Arnolds Avots, for whom the part is a dream come true. He is also the author of the film's idea and original screenplay. Avots won the Best Actor award at the Jerusalem Film Festival for his portrayal of the Latvian basketball legend.
Semjonova, who passed away in January, was a two-time Olympic champion, a three-time world champion, and a ten-time European champion. For nearly her entire career, she played for the legendary Latvian women's basketball team TTT Riga, winning the Soviet Union championship 15 times. She was also named Latvian Athlete of the Year 12 times.
The screening of "Ulya" also marks the beginning of this year's POFF focus program, which is dedicated to Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
The three countries will also be united at the POFF opening ceremony with the premiere of "Round and Round," a production created for the anniversary festival that looks back on the past three decades. Three pianists - Hans Matthias Kari from Estonia, Karlis Gusts Zarins from Latvia, and Gabriele Agile Bajoraite from Lithuania - will perform film scores from their respective countries on three pianos.
The Black Nights Film Festival will run from November 6 to 22.

TIMELINE – 26 years since Al-Aqsa Intifada: Key events in 5 years of bloodshed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:22:28 UTC
23:22:28 KST

Twenty-six years after it erupted, the Al-Aqsa Intifada remains one of the bloodiest chapters of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, marked by deadly Israeli raids into Palestinian cities, assassinations and attacks.
The uprising, the second after the First Intifada, also known as the “Stone Intifada”, began on Sept. 28, 2000, after then-Israeli opposition leader Ariel Sharon stormed Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem.
Monday marks the 26th anniversary of the uprising, which gradually subsided before the February 2005 Sharm el-Sheikh summit in Egypt effectively brought it to an end.
According to official figures, 4,412 Palestinians were killed and 48,322 others injured during the uprising.
The First Palestinian Intifada began on Dec. 9, 1987, after four Palestinian workers were killed when they were run over by an Israeli truck. It started in the Jabalia refugee camp and spread across the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, lasting around six years.
The Al-Aqsa Intifada erupted as the Palestinian-Israeli peace process had reached an impasse following the failure of the US-sponsored Camp David summit in July 2000 to reach an agreement on final-status issues, including Jerusalem, borders, refugees and illegal settlements.
On Sept. 28 that year, Sharon stormed Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem accompanied by a large number of Israeli police and security personnel.
The incursion triggered Palestinian protests and clashes around the mosque that quickly spread to East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza Strip, developing within days into widespread confrontations.
The UN has identified Sharon’s visit as the immediate trigger for the uprising, while the stalled peace process and diminishing prospects for a political settlement were among the factors that contributed to the escalation.
The following day, Israeli forces stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound and used live fire and other means against worshippers and protesters, leaving Palestinians killed and wounded before clashes spread elsewhere.
As the violence escalated, images of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces fueled public anger and widened the protests.
Among the most prominent was the killing of 11-year-old Muhammad al-Durrah in Gaza by Israeli gunfire as he sheltered beside his father, an image that later became one of the symbols of the uprising.
As Israeli attacks intensified, the uprising gradually shifted from popular protests and street clashes to armed confrontations between Palestinians and the Israeli army.
Israel escalated military operations in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip, carrying out assassinations targeting Palestinian political and military figures, alongside mass arrests, shelling and incursions into cities and refugee camps.
On Dec. 3, 2001, the Israeli government imposed a siege on former Palestinian President Yasser Arafat at his presidential headquarters in Ramallah that continued until he died.
During the siege, Israeli forces destroyed large parts of the presidential compound and repeatedly shelled the building, where Arafat was staying with aides and associates, using tanks and aircraft.
Israeli forces also struck presidential facilities in Gaza and the occupied West Bank and destroyed Gaza International Airport and Palestinian presidential helicopters, preventing Arafat from traveling, according to the official news agency Wafa.
Arafat died in Paris on Nov. 11, 2004, after his health deteriorated, amid Palestinian suspicions that he may have been poisoned, an issue that remained subject to controversy and subsequent investigations without a definitive judicial finding.
In March 2004, Israel assassinated Hamas founder Ahmed Yassin and Abdul Aziz al-Rantisi, who succeeded him as the movement’s leader, the following month. It also killed senior Hamas figures Salah Shehadeh and Ismail Abu Shanab.
In August 2001, Israel killed Secretary General of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) Abu Ali Mustafa in an airstrike on his office in the West Bank city of Al-Bireh.
The uprising entered one of its bloodiest periods in 2002 when Israel launched a major offensive code-named “Operation Defensive Shield”, involving large-scale incursions into cities, towns and refugee camps across the occupied West Bank.
During the operation, the Israeli army redeployed inside Palestinian city centers after having partially withdrawn under arrangements stemming from the 1993 Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).
Several Palestinian cities and refugee camps witnessed major military operations, including the Jenin refugee camp in the northern West Bank. Palestinian areas also saw widespread home demolitions, the bulldozing of agricultural land and extensive damage to infrastructure.
The UN documented the return of Israeli forces during the uprising to parts of the Palestinian territories where they had not been deployed for years, including populated areas classified as Area A.
Under the 1995 Oslo II Accord, which was intended as an interim arrangement, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C.
Area A was placed under full Palestinian control, Area B under Palestinian civilian control and Israeli security control, while Area C remained under full Israeli control and accounts for around 60% of the West Bank.
During the years of the uprising, Palestinian factions carried out attacks inside Israel that killed and wounded Israelis.
In October 2001, PFLP members assassinated Israeli Tourism Minister Rehavam Ze’evi at a hotel in Jerusalem.
The uprising also saw a development in the military capabilities of Palestinian factions compared with the First Intifada, which had been primarily associated with demonstrations, strikes and the throwing of stones and Molotov cocktails.
Palestinian factions, particularly Hamas’ armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, began firing locally manufactured rockets toward Israeli towns, marking a military development that later became one of the defining features of confrontations between the two sides.
Around 1,069 Israelis were killed and 4,500 others injured in Palestinian attacks during the uprising, according to Israeli figures.
On Feb. 8, 2005, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, then-Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon, former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Jordan’s King Abdullah II met in Egypt’s resort city of Sharm el-Sheikh to discuss ways to end the crisis that began with the Al-Aqsa Intifada.
Abbas and Sharon agreed, according to statements issued at the time, to halt “acts of violence.”
The summit is widely regarded as the point at which the Al-Aqsa Intifada effectively ended, nearly five years after it began.
Months later, Israel implemented its unilateral “disengagement” plan in September 2005, evacuating illegal settlements and withdrawing forces from the Gaza Strip. The withdrawal, however, did not end Israeli control over the enclave, as Israel continued to control its borders, airspace, and territorial waters.
Israel imposed a blockade on Gaza from mid-2006, and subsequently launched several wars on the enclave, most recently its genocidal war that began in October 2023 and has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 others.
The period has also been accompanied by escalating Israeli military operations in the occupied West Bank, including killings, home demolitions, displacement of Palestinians and settlement expansion.

LIVERPOOL, England — Britain’s chief diplomat said Monday that the U.K. will not ditch its ban on directly engaging with Russian officials after Donald Trump invited Vladimir Putin to the G20 meeting in December.
Speaking in The POLITICO Pub at Labour Party conference, Ed Miliband said it is for the U.S. to “make their own decisions” on inviting the Russian president to the summit in Miami later this year — but stressed the U.K. is unlikely to take the same approach next year.
“We’ve had a long-standing policy not to have direct engagement at my level with the Russians since the invasion of Ukraine. We’re not changing that policy,” Miliband said when asked whether the greater engagement with Moscow is a good thing.

Miliband said the decision is in part about showing solidarity with the Ukrainian people, adding: “Different countries make different decisions on these things.”
The U.K. foreign secretary confirmed Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be at the Miami G20 later this year, but declined to “second guess the decisions” about who’s invited.
Elsewhere in his interview, Miliband acknowledged that disagreements with the Trump administration over the future of the Chagos Islands were discussed when Burnham met Trump at the U.N. General Assembly earlier this month.
“It’s pretty clear, as became apparent from that meeting, that the U.S. administration does not at the moment agree with the arrangement,” Miliband said, adding he and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio “talk a lot” about the way forward. Britain has agreed to cede sovereignty of the archipelago, home to the joint U.S.-U.K. Diego Garcia airbase, to Mauritius. A lease arrangement has been worked out to allow continued use of the base, but critics fear a strategic toehold risks falling into the orbit of China.

Dutch ban on West Bank, Golan imports 'outrageous, offensive,' Foreign Min. official tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:18:54 UTC
23:18:54 KST

The Dutch measure banning the entry of products from the West Bank into the Netherlands is “outrageous and offensive,” the Foreign Ministry's Political Director, Gilad Cohen, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.
Cohen argued that, in practice, it is leading to Israelis being singled out and treated differently from other travelers.
“This is a very offensive law,” Cohen said. “It allows Dutch customs officials to open the luggage of visitors from Israel and check whether they have brought products from Judea and Samaria, east Jerusalem or the Golan Heights.”
The law, which has now entered into force, prohibits the import of products from the West Bank, east Jerusalem or the Golan Heights into the Netherlands. Anyone caught importing such products could face up to six years in prison.
According to Cohen, Israel has already received reports of Israelis being stopped at airports in the Netherlands and asked to open their luggage for inspection.
“We sent our consul in The Hague to look into the matter,” he said. “There are indeed signs at the airport explaining the law and telling passengers to expect inspections.”
Cohen explained that Israeli travelers arriving in the Netherlands go through passport control, collect their luggage and then pass through customs.
“At customs, they stop passengers arriving on flights from Israel and tell them to open their luggage,” he said. “They check whether there are products from Judea and Samaria, Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and so on.”
Israel views Dutch decision as significant escalation
Cohen said Israel views the Dutch measure as a significant escalation in relations between the two countries.
“I am not familiar with a precedent for something like this, where Israelis’ luggage is opened, and they are asked where they got a particular item,” he said. “From our perspective, this is definitely an escalation.”
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar announced on Sunday that Israel was revoking the status of Dutch diplomats based in Ramallah and requiring them to return their diplomatic accreditation within seven days as a response to Dutch customs checks. At the end of that period, the immunities and privileges Israel granted them as part of that status will expire.
“The message was that if they want to operate vis-à-vis the Palestinians, there is no problem; they can do so from Ramallah,” Cohen said.
Cohen described the Israeli response as part of a broader policy of countermeasures in response to what Jerusalem views as unilateral and hostile steps.
'Israel will respond, take countermeasures, to unilateral, hostile measures'
“If someone takes unilateral and hostile measures against Israel, Israel will have to respond and take countermeasures,” he said.
According to Cohen, countries seeking to remain relevant to developments in the Middle East cannot simultaneously take steps that Israel views as unilateral actions against it.
“Unilateral measures will be met by the State of Israel,” he said. “We have no choice. We will not leave this unanswered, and we will not accept it without responding. We are responding.”
Asked whether Israel was concerned that additional European countries could adopt similar measures, Cohen said Jerusalem was working to prevent the Dutch policy from spreading.
“I very much hope that this will not happen, but we need to prepare and make sure that it does not,” he said. “We reserve the right to respond to each case individually.”
Cohen stressed that Israel is in contact with additional European governments and noted that not all EU member states support measures of this kind.
“We hope common sense will prevail,” he said, warning that the consequences of the policy are not limited to residents of the West Bank or the Golan Heights.
“These are measures that hurt all Israelis,” he said. “It hurts every Israeli, regardless of who they are.”
At the same time, Cohen stressed that Israel does not view the Netherlands as a single, unified entity, distinguishing between the Dutch government and other actors in the country.
“There are also friendly elements in the Netherlands. It is not all one monolithic bloc,” he said.
Cohen said Israel had engaged in extensive diplomatic efforts to prevent the policy from taking effect.
“There were a great many contacts with the Netherlands, especially in recent times, at every level, with the authorities there, with the Foreign Ministry and with other officials,” he said.
A local organization in the Netherlands also petitioned the court against the law, but the court rejected the petition.
“This is an outrageous and offensive measure that harms the entire Israeli public,” Cohen said. “The Israeli response is accordingly proportionate, and we view this as a hostile step, and therefore we are responding with the tools at our disposal.”

Likud candidate in the upcoming Knesset election and bereaved father Itzik Bonzel wrote in a Monday morning Facebook post that he wished "there were a way to turn back the clock and return" 88-year-old former hostage Yocheved Lifshitz "to Hamas."
Bonzel later apologized in a subsequent Facebook post.
"As a bereaved father, who lost his son in the war to return hostages, it pained me to see the harsh things that humiliated our soldiers, but in a storm of emotions, I wrote a sentence about Yocheved Lifshitz in the context of Hamas, which I did not mean, and I apologize," he wrote.
Bonzel, who was placed 29th on the Likud list for the Knesset by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and lost his son Amit early in the war in Gaza, made the remarks in response to Lifshitz's televised interview on Channel 13, in which she criticized the Netanyahu government.
Yocheved, whose husband was killed in captivity after being taken hostage alongside her from Kibbutz Nir Oz on October 7, said in the interview: "Bibi [Netanyahu] didn't bring back a single hostage; Miriam Adelson bought us from Trump. If this government remains after the elections, it will be a disaster for the country."
Bonzel responded with fury, writing, "Mrs. Yocheved, the person who rescued you from the darkness of the Gaza tunnels was not Miriam Adelson, but hundreds of heroes who entered that hell to bring you back alive - some of whom never returned. Our sons paid with their lives and with the heartbroken blood of every home in Israel so that you could sit safely in yours. How pathetic, infuriating, and out of touch your words are. In the face of such shameful statements, and the unbearable pain of losing the sons who fell for you, the rage simply knows no bounds.
"I have never written in such a manner before, but I wish there were a way to turn back the clock and return you to the hands of Hamas - because in the face of this display of ingratitude, it seems you simply did not deserve to have our precious, holy sons sacrifice their lives for you."
He concluded his controversial statement, writing, "Your hatred for Netanyahu has driven you out of your mind, shattered every trace of morality and shame, and trampled the honor of those who rescued you at the cost of their lives. Silence in the face of such a rock-bottom disgrace is an unforgivable sin."
Lifshitz: Hit sent by Netanyahu to distract from October 7 heat
Yocheved responded to Bonzel's attack by accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of sending him to incite against her in order to distract from the brewing controversy surrounding intelligence warnings from the UAE and Egypt that Netanyahu is accused of having ignored ahead of the October 7 massacre.
"Netanyahu sent his appointee to incite against me so that people wouldn't talk about the intelligence warnings that reached him, and about the personal warning calls he received that could have prevented the failure."
She pressed the attack, saying that "Netanyahu’s lies and slander will not help him; the people of Israel understand full well that he is responsible for the failure. He abandoned me on October 7th, abandoned my husband Oded and 45 other hostages taken alive to die in captivity, and continues to jeopardize our security."
She concluded, saying "I have no fear - not of him, and not of the circle of agitators surrounding him," before sending an open invitation for the public to join a rally at Hostage Square to hold "all those responsible" to account.
Politicians weigh in on the controversy
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, responded to Bonzel's statement in a post on X/Twitter, saying, "Yocheved Lifshitz is a hero. Netanyahu needs to look her in the eye, ask for forgiveness, and explain how 1,200 Israelis were murdered and 251 kidnapped on his watch."
He accused the prime minister of failing in his responsibilities on October 7 and of running from accountability for the deadly massacre.
"He has recruited people to his party who wish Yocheved back to hell," he attacked.
"In these elections, we will replace the government of neglect and lawlessness with a government that sanctifies life, protects citizens, and demands accountability from those who fail. Yocheved, you have overcome the unthinkable and chosen to fight. You give us all strength and inspiration. We are with you."
MK Efrat Rayten, of the Democrats, also publicly responded on X, writing, "The shocking and despicable statements voiced against her by Netanyahu's handpicked candidate cross every moral red line. Wishing for her to return to Hamas captivity is a rock-bottom failure of values and a moral disgrace. Such a person is unfit to be a public representative."
She continued, saying, "Dear Yocheved, I love you, and it is my duty to continue standing by your side out of a sense of responsibility, and to be worthy of you and of everyone who was abandoned by the Netanyahu government on October 7.

Ukraine uses drones to deliver food to Russian-occupied Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28

23:18:23 KST

Ukraine uses drones to deliver food to Russian-occupied Oleshky
KYIV, Sept 28 - Ukraine's military has used drones to deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, the governor of Ukraine's Kherson region said, as officials warn about a worsening humanitarian crisis.
Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said on Sunday that, in the latest operation, heavy-lift drones delivered about four tons of food and medical supplies to 100 locations across the town simultaneously.
Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has been under Russian occupation since 2022.
Prokudin said that close to 2,000 people, including about 50 children, were being held "hostage", without food, electricity and water, and accused Moscow's forces of preventing them from escaping the town.
Ukrainian officials have warned of the situation in Oleshky becoming more dire.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has said that residents have endured months of food shortages and "extremely limited" access to basic necessities.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told Ukrainian media this month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate from Oleshky.
"People in the temporarily occupied Oleshky are being deprived of the basic means of survival. Russia bears full responsibility for this humanitarian catastrophe and its consequences," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday.
The Kremlin said last week that Oleshky had critical problems with food and medicine supplies, but that Russia's military was working to resolve them. REUTERS

Albares welcomes ambassadors of Associated Observer States and new Observers ahead of the Madrid Summit
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:18:21 CEST
23:18:21 KST

On Monday 28 September, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, welcomed the ambassadors of the twelve Associated Observer States and the three countries that are set to formalise their entry as new Observers, with the aim of strengthening their participation in the Ibero-American Community and promoting their involvement at the highest level. In the context of the Ibero-American Summit to be held in Madrid on 4 and 5 November, Spain is reinforcing its commitment to more active participation by Observer States in the Ibero-American Community.
This meeting provided an opportunity to outline the Summit’s programme, encourage ministerial participation from the Observer countries and exchange proposals on how to deepen their involvement in the activities and work of the Ibero-American Conference.
Angola, India and Turkey will join as new Associate Observers, and the Association of Caribbean States (ACS) as a Consultative Observer at the Ibero-American Summit, following the decision taken by the Ibero-American Foreign Ministers on 24 September in New York.
The Ibero-American Conference currently has 12 Associate Observer States: Germany, Belgium, France, Hungary, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, the Philippines, South Korea, Japan, Haiti and Morocco, and 20 international organisations as Consultative Observers. These new members expand the Ibero-American Community’s network of partners and offer new opportunities for dialogue and cooperation.
The meeting forms part of the Spanish Pro Tempore Secretariat’s commitment to strengthening and deepening relations between the Ibero-American Community and its Observers.
Minister Albares highlighted Spain’s commitment to ensuring that the Observers are active partners in building a more visible, influential and effective Ibero-American space.

The latest action from India's youth-led 'cockroach' movement is targeting the country's election chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

Why India's cockroach movement wants the election chief out
September 28, 2026
India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties have demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar after a newspaper investigation alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision.
According to the probe, published in The Indian Express newspaper, some key decisions linked to the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls that began last year were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.
The Indian Express said that fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data.
In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission of India (ECI) acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
The allegations presented "only one part of the picture," and "differing views" were a routine "part of decision-making," the ECI said in a statement cited by local media.
'Cockroach' movement founder calls for demonstrations
Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke called Kumar "the biggest threat to India's democracy" and demanded his resignation.
Dipke threatened to launch nationwide protests, beginning in Mumbai on October 2, the birthday of India's founding father Mahatma Gandhi, if Kumar did not quit by Saturday.
The Saturday deadline passed without Kumar stepping down.
After Mumbai police denied permission for the planned October 2 protest, Dipke posted on X calling on supporters to submit to mass arrests rather than comply with the ban.
Supporters staged protests on Friday and pledged to continue mobilizing despite the restrictions.
Opposition parties echoed the CJP's criticism of Kumar and the Election Commission.
Pawan Khera of the main opposition Congress party said that "Gyanesh Kumar has done nothing short of treason."
"If decisions relating to the SIR were taken without the knowledge or approval of two of the three election commissioners... then those decisions and the entire SIR exercise are legally invalid," Khera said on social media.
Congress and other opposition parties have accused the ECI of colluding with India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to manipulate voter lists and win state elections in recent years, charges both the commission and the BJP have denied.
What are the demands of India's CJP movement?
The 'Cockroach' movement, which has millions of followers on social media, forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July following widespread student-led street protests.
The group has laid out three demands: Kumar's resignation and criminal proceedings against him, a freeze on the SIR and the suspension of all upcoming elections, and the repeal of the 2023 law on the appointment of the election commissioners of India.
Civil rights activist Amrita Johri said the CJP's decision to target the poll panel reflects wider concerns over the lack of transparency surrounding the SIR.
"There is an absence of public consultation or a clear explanation for launching the exercise, as well as the findings of the newspaper that the two election commissioners had raised repeated objections to key decisions," Johri told DW.
"Restoring public confidence will require Kumar's removal, stopping the SIR and an independent review of the millions of names excluded from the draft rolls."
From education protests to electoral politics
Political activist Sudheendra Kulkarni sees the CJP's latest campaign as that of a pressure group rather than an emerging standalone political force.
"I do not see any separate political future for the CJP. It may remain as a pressure group for some time. But as the next parliamentary election approaches, it will have to align itself with the opposition alliance," Kulkarni told DW.
Others see greater weight in the CJP's shift.
Political analyst and commentator Radhika Ramaseshan said the CJP widening its focus will not weaken what it started.
"I don't think if the CJP enlarged the ambit of its concerns and built protests around [them], it would take away from the salience and power of the first issue it highlighted," Ramaseshan told DW. "Voter rights and enfranchisement is fundamental to a citizen's existence, to upholding the sanctity of the Indian constitution."
"These are not abstractions or procedural matters. They impinge on the lives of first-time voters who make up the bulk of the CJP," she added.
What happens now?
With Kumar refusing to resign, attention will now turn to the CJP's promise of street protests starting in Mumbai on October 2.
But a protest group alone cannot simply remove a CEC. Under India's constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a process requiring action by both houses of Parliament and a special majority, on grounds of proved misbehavior or incapacity.
"The CJP's significance would be in increasing pressure and forcing scrutiny of the ECI's functioning," former Chief Election Commissioner S Y Quraishi's told DW.
He argues that the reported unilateral decisions are the more serious issue and should be subjected to an independent legal and technical audit.
"The practical route is judicial scrutiny, not street removal. The decisions taken unilaterally by the CEC in a three-member commission could be challenged as invalid, with the Supreme Court potentially needed to intervene," he said.
"Where the commission will not act, the Supreme Court will have to step in," added Quraishi.
The CJP's latest campaign puts it directly into one of India's most contentious disputes over electoral administration.
Whether it can sustain that momentum against the Election Commission will be a very different test for a movement that is still trying to define its place in Indian politics.
Edited by: Keith Walker

Russia preparing document banning diesel exports for one month more

Irkutsk Aviation Plant to produce 36 MC-21s per year, expand capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

IRKUTSK, September 28. /TASS/. The Irkutsk Aviation Plant has the capacity to produce 36 MC-21 aircraft per year, Andrey Soinov, Director of the Irkutsk Aviation Plant, a branch of the Yakovlev Public Joint Stock Company of the United Aviation Corporation (UAC) of Rostec, said, adding the investment program implies that it will be further reequipped.
"We plan to continue implementing the investment program, which suggests the acquisition of additional machine tools and equipment for blanking and stamping operations. We will say that current capacities allow for the production of 36 [units], but there are bottlenecks that we need to remove," he told reporters.
The enterprise intends to expand capacity by the time the planned production rate of 36 aircraft per year is reached, Soinov added. "There were delays in funding the program, but all decisions have now been made at the government level. Consequently, the remaining parts of this investment program will be implemented between 2027 and 2029," he noted.
That said, it is not planned to increase MC-21 production beyond 36 aircraft per year in the near term, the plant’s chief stressed, adding that though ramping up capacity is technically feasible, the manufacturer considers ensuring a stable production workload to be critically important.

UN panel hosted by Türkiye calls for safer digital systems for children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:14:21 UTC
23:14:21 KST

Serife Cetin and Enes Canli
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Queen Mathilde of Belgium and the spouses of several world leaders called for stronger international standards to protect children from online risks during a UN panel organized by Türkiye's Ministry of Family and Social Services in New York.
The panel, The Invisible Architecture: Building Safe Digital Systems for Children - Advancing International Standards and Shared Responsibility, was held at the UN headquarters on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly's high-level week.
The event was organized under the auspices of Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, in cooperation with UNICEF and the Office of the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children. It was attended by Turkish Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas.
Opening the panel, Queen Mathilde warned that rapid advances in artificial intelligence were creating new risks for children.
"Children cannot be the subjects of a global technology experiment or guinea pigs for business models based on data collection and attention," she said.
She stressed that child safety must become a central objective of AI governance, going beyond parental controls, content moderation and data protection.
Preparing children for physical and digital worlds
Serbian first lady Tamara Vucic thanked Emine Erdogan for bringing participants together, emphasizing that children must be prepared for both the physical and digital worlds through education and responsible technology use.
Gambian first lady Fatoumatta Bah Barrow called on governments to enforce stronger laws and urged tech companies to introduce stricter safeguards, warning that online threats can easily cross national borders.
Kenyan first lady Rachel Ruto said children's personal data, locations, photographs and online activities must not be treated as commodities, urging countries to take collective action.
Sierra Leone's first lady Fatima Maada Bio praised Emine Erdogan's leadership and highlighted the need to ensure that technological progress is accompanied by stronger protections against online exploitation, cyberbullying and privacy violations.
Lebanon's teen suicide
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam's wife, Sahar Salam, called for greater oversight of AI systems, recalling the suicide of a 15-year-old child in her country who was found to have been chatting with an AI system.
She stressed the need to monitor how such systems respond when children turn to AI during difficult times.
"We cannot expect children to understand the commercial logic of algorithms or assess whether an AI response is psychologically appropriate," she said.
Other participants, including the spouses of leaders from Lithuania, Burundi, Guatemala, Senegal, Romania, Chile and Canada, emphasized the importance of international cooperation, enforceable regulations and greater accountability for technology companies.
UNICEF Child Protection Director Sheema Sen Gupta praised Türkiye's efforts to place children's online safety higher on the global agenda, stressing that protecting children in digital environments is not merely a national priority but a global responsibility.
UN Special Representative on Violence against Children Najat Maalla M'jid also called for stronger accountability, emphasizing that governments, technology companies and the wider digital ecosystem share responsibility for creating safer online environments.

🔴 Live: Pope Leo leads Mass at Metz Cathedral on final leg of visit to France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28

Live: Pope Leo leads Mass in France's Metz after speech on Europe's roots and future
Pope Leo XIV urged Europe to remember its Christian history and appealed for peace and unity in a speech delivered in France's northeastern city of Metz on Monday, the fourth and final day of his visit. After touring the city in his popemobile, the pontiff later led a Mass at Saint-Etienne Cathedral attended by French President Emmanuel Macron. Follow our liveblog for all the latest.
Pope leads Mass in Metz cathedral
In his final event in France, Leo is celebrating Mass in the cathedral of Saint-Etienne (St. Stephen) in Metz, a city with a long history of conflict that was part of Nazi Germany during the war.
The cathedral, finished in 1522, is one of the greatest examples of French Gothic style, with its soaring vaults and stained-glass windows, some of which were later designed by Marc Chagall, a 20th-century Jewish artist.
In his homily, Leo said that Metz and its surroundings experienced evil, but now “bear witness to the whole world that reconciliation is only possible when one has the courage to break the chains of resentment.”
The cathedral’s stained-glass windows, designed by a Jew, are “an extraordinary symbol of ecumenism and interreligious dialogue,” where God’s light unites “different histories and cultures into a single marvelous mosaic of peace.”
French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte attend the Mass in Metz. Credit: Christian Hartmann, Reuters
“As we contemplate these stained-glass windows, we learn that Europe’s future does not lie in uniformity, but in the harmony of differences, where the wounds of the past become openings through which light shines,” he said.
The colored glass has given the cathedral the nickname the “Lanterne du Bon Dieu,” or “The Good Lord’s Lantern.
Pope Leo blessed Rafale pilots after joining Air France cockpit crew
Pope Leo spent half an hour in the cockpit of a plane earlier todayy, chatting with the pilots and speaking by radio to the crews of the Rafale fighter jets escorting his aircraft, Air France said.
"The Holy Father came into the cockpit for the entire Lourdes-Metz cruise phase," said Eric Marguerite, the flight's co-pilot.
"We had informal conversations with him. He is passionate about aviation, cars and mechanics in general," he added, after landing in Metz.
The flight, commanded by Captain Clemence Coussonneau, was escorted by two Rafale jets flying about 50 metres (yards) from the pope's plane.
"We handed the microphone to the Holy Father, who spoke to the Rafale pilots," said Marguerite.
"He offered his blessing to them and to all military personnel working to protect people and promote peace around the world."
Macron invokes Europe’s Judeo-Christian foundation as Leo visits
In his speech alongside the pope a short while ago, Macron said Europe was built on a "Greco-Roman and Judeo-Christian foundation", invoking the continent's religious heritage.
The remarks were notable from the leader of a constitutionally secular state, in a country that regularly agonises over national identity, religion and the place of faith in public life, notes Reuters.
Macron, who attended Leo's last mass in Metz on Monday after skipping other religious services, said Europe's heritage had helped crystallise "the primacy of the person" and later "the free and rational individual".
"Our Europe ... is above all a civilisation," Macron said. "This Europe of our cities and villages, schools and universities, cafes and public squares, was built on a Greco-Roman and Judeo-Christian foundation."

Pope urges Europe to help battle 'lies and deceit' in international ties
Pope Leo warned that relations between nations were becoming "increasingly uncivilised" with people boasting of "lies and deceit", and urged Europe to help "break this cycle".
"Relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilised. The value of keeping one's word is dismissed. Instead, people boast of lies and deceit," he said. "Europe can help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learned to cultivate and preserve."
Pope Leo urges negotiations as Ukraine war drags on
Pope Leo said that negotiators seeking to end war in Europe must be willing to sacrifice some of their positions to achieve peace, as efforts to end the bloody, four-year conflict between Russia and Ukraine continue to fail.
The first US pope, speaking in Metz, a city central to the European Union founding, lamented that "war has returned, even to Europe: a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day".
Offering his clearest political vision yet for Europe, Leo also spoke in favour of European integration and multiculturalism at a time the far right is gaining strength across the region.
The pontiff called on Europe to integrate migrants "as if they were part of one's own family".
Pope urges Europe to remember Christian history, strengthen democratic ideals
Pope Leo urged Europe to remember its Christian history in a speech delivered in Metz, the hometown of Robert Schuman, a founding father of the European Union, during his four-day visit to France.
"One cannot speak of Europe without mentioning Christianity," he said.
The pontiff praised European integration and multiculturalism, adding that dialogue with others was a "social and political necessity" and urging EU leaders to give "real substance" to words such as freedom, democracy and unity.
"Europe has flourished and progressed when it has been able to draw on the best aspects of its past and reinvent them in new and creative ways through encounters with others," the pope said.
President of the Conference of Bishops of France Cardinal Jean-Marc Avelines speaks

France's President Emmanuel Macron said Europe should return to the "courage of its founders" to become a force for peace in the face of resurgent nationalism.
Europe "must rediscover the courage of its founders – yes, courage – in order to become the force for peace, independence, and democracy that it is meant to be," he said in the presence of Pope Leo XIV in the northeastern city of Metz near the German border.
"The courage not to give in to withdrawal, to hatred of others, to the return of nationalisms that divide," he said.

Pope Leo XIV stated that “religious discourse” must help “disarm hearts and words” during a meeting with representatives of various religions in Metz.
“Invoking the name of God to legitimize violence or oppression is a desecration of that name. Nothing that distorts human dignity can claim to be authentically inspired by God,” the pope said.
“Religious discourse must constantly call for the disarmament of hearts and words. This is the direct responsibility of each of us, as guardians of our respective traditions,” continued Léon XIV. He spoke after the reading of the “Metz Appeal,” a joint declaration by representatives of religious communities in France calling for interreligious dialogue and peace.
🎥 Leo building on Francis's legacy while reincorporating 'more traditional elements of papal activity'
FRANCE 24's Erin Ogunkeye speaks with Miles Pattenden, historian of the Catholic Church at the University of Oxford.
For Pattenden, Pope Leo XIV’s visit to France is part of a broader recalibration of the papacy. While Pope Francis placed particular emphasis on the Catholic Church’s peripheries and the needs of the Global South, Leo is subtly bringing the Church’s historic European heartlands back into focus.
France is especially significant in this regard, given its deep historical relationship with Catholicism and its evolving relationship with Christianity, European identity, secularism and contemporary geopolitical debates.

Possible ban on US diesel exports to be killer for Europe — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:13:56 UTC
23:13:56 KST

MOSCOW, September 28. /TASS/. If Washington goes through with banning the export of diesel to other countries, it will put Europe in a very bad spot while not really helping the US either, Oleg Nikolayev, expert at the Stolypin Institute for the Economy of Growth, a member of the General Council of Business Russia, told TASS.
US President Donald Trump said earlier that he was very seriously considering imposing a ban on the export of diesel fuel.
"The ban on diesel exports from the US will have a severely negative impact on Europe as the share of American diesel currently accounts for up to half of European consumption," the expert said.
Nikolyaev admits the importance of US supplies to the European market may be one of the reasons why Washington is currently only considering the possibility of imposing restrictions. "This is precisely why the ban has not been adopted but is under consideration. Trump views it as a bargaining chip in economic negotiations with a former geopolitical ally," he explained.
The expert does not expect the potential export restriction to bring significant benefit to the United States itself. "It offers no benefit to America, except perhaps to plug the gap in the domestic market, which would not have arisen under other circumstances," Nikolayev said.
According to the expert, a potential ban could further complicate Washington’s relations with other countries and become yet another "disruptive step for the global economy."

Congo politician beaten to death after urging Ebola prevention on radio, his party says
The outbreak has left at least 3,901 dead. Sunday’s attack on Marie-Celestin Karondwa is the latest in a series of attacks on response teams
A senior member of Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death after taking part in a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative said on Monday.
The incident happened on Sunday in Butembo, North Kivu province, which has recently become a hotspot in the ongoing Ebola outbreak.
Marie-Celestin Karondwa, acting president of the UDPS party’s federal executive committee in Butembo and a party spokesperson, was attacked by residents of his neighbourhood after appearing on a radio show during which he promoted Ebola prevention measures, the UDPS federation in Butembo said in a statement.
The party said the attackers beat him, looted his belongings and set his house on fire. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many were involved or what motivated it.
But the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease (...) and the threat it poses to the population”.

Stop the Russian Terrorist Killers and Arsonists!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:11:00 UTC
23:11:00 KST

Today the heart of Ukraine’s capital was hit again – in broad daylight a Russian assault slammed into one of the buildings of the historic National Academy of Sciences buildings in central Kyiv.
Black smoke billowed over the city center as flames ripped through upper floors. Researchers, archivists and staff climbed onto windowsills – clinging on for their lives as firefighters fought their way through the heat and smoke to reach them. One person was killed and several others were critically wounded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
There were no military targets here: no ammunition depots, no troops, no command posts. There was only a center of research and historical memory gutted because Moscow keeps using missiles and drones as a weapon of terror against civilians.
For more than four and a half years (over 1,600 days of full-scale war) Ukrainians have lived with this reality every day. What happened in Kyiv today is happening everywhere else – Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Odesa, Dnipro, and elsewhere. And in recent weeks, the Russians have ramped up the attacks even more.
Russia’s strategy has never been simply about the front line. It is a calculated effort to wreck normal life, break the country’s spirit and make Ukraine unlivable.
Yet keeping attention and political will over a long war is getting harder in Western capitals too. Pressure shows up in cautious diplomatic statements, protracted debates, disagreement over how to use seized Russian assets, and the need to balance urgent needs with domestic constraints.
Medical Center in Central Kyiv on Fire After Russian Jet-Powered Drone Attack
The magnitude of human and material damage Ukraine is suffering, and the broader threat, require faster coordination. Ukraine’s partners have provided vital support; now it is for them to make that support more predictable and effective.
The suffering and destruction we see in Kyiv and throughout Ukraine remind us that fatigue cannot weaken a coherent long-term strategy. If attacks on homes, hospitals, schools and research centers become routine news, then the rules of the global game Western countries claim to uphold begin to unravel.
If an aggressor with nuclear weapons can invade a neighbor without consequences, hit city centers and wait for the world’s attention span to run out, then no country’s borders are safe. Ukraine’s partners have already made major political, financial, and military commitments.
What we need now is to reduce delays, clarify how supplied weapons are used, and ramp up enforcement against sanctions evasion so collective support has maximum impact. Vladimir Putin’s gamble is that free societies will lose focus one day. Unity (with practical support) is the best answer. Diplomatic statements count, but they must be backed up by missile interceptors, civilian protection, and community recovery capability.
On top of that, support for Ukraine and its partners should have several practical priorities. Strengthen air defense. More Patriot, NASAMS, and IRIS-T batteries, along with a steady supply of interceptor missiles, would help partners build on existing assistance and protect Ukraine’s cities even better.
Enforce sanctions harder. Missiles hitting Kyiv still contain Western microelectronics bought from third-party supply chains. More coordination among governments and companies can disrupt those gray-market networks and reinforce existing sanctions.
Build a durable security architecture. Europe and Ukraine need a long-term framework based on credible defense commitments and deeper integration into European defense structures (less uncertainty in Eastern Europe would increase deterrence and help secure the continent’s eastern border over the long term).
The fire at the National Academy of Sciences tells us what is at stake. Ukraine is fighting for its existence but also defending a basic principle of globalism – force alone should not rewrite borders or erase nations; democratic Europe, the values of the free world, and the principles of the UN Charter are defended.
Ukrainians have endured more than four and a half years without friends and allies who’ve been indispensable. That partnership will be maintained only if air defense supplies are reliable and strategic clarity is assured.
The democratic world’s challenge is to stay focused and turn shared principles into consistent action. Cooperation, timely decisions, and long-term resolve will help Ukraine defend itself and strengthen Europe as a whole.
But at a minimum, after four and a half years of letting Russia off the hook, close the skies over Ukraine, or better still, open them to civilian flights by curbing unbridled Russian terrorism.

TotalEnergies will buy back $2.5 billion (€2.2bn) of its own shares in the fourth quarter, up from $1.5 billion (€1.3bn) authorised for the third, and raise its dividend by more than 5% a year through 2030, as high oil prices boost the French energy giant’s earnings.
TotalEnergies, the French oil and gas major, is returning more cash to investors.
Presenting its strategy in New York on Monday, TotalEnergies said its board had approved buybacks worth $2.5 billion (€2.2bn) for the last quarter of 2026 and between $2 billion (€1.7bn) and $2.5 billion (€2.2bn) for the first quarter of 2027.
That compares with $1.5 billion (€1.3bn) authorised for the third quarter of this year.
The board also adopted a policy on Sunday to increase the dividend by more than 5% a year for financial years 2026 to 2030, and confirmed it aims to return at least 40% of cash flow to shareholders.
The bigger buybacks come as TotalEnergies expects its gearing ratio, which measures how much of the company is financed by debt, to fall below 10% by the end of this year, from 13.1% at the end of June.
By Monday afternoon, TotalEnergies' shares were up roughly 2% from Friday's close following the announcement.
Riding high oil prices
The payouts come as elevated crude prices are boosting the earnings of oil majors.
Brent averaged $103.8 a barrel in the second quarter, when TotalEnergies posted adjusted net income of $6 billion (€5.2bn).
The company also confirmed it aims to grow energy production, spanning oil, gas and electricity, by 4% a year through 2030, with oil and gas output rising by more than 3% a year on average between 2025 and 2030.
TotalEnergies expects free cash flow in 2030 to be around $10 billion (€8.7bn) higher than in 2025, assuming the same energy prices. That would amount to an increase of more than $4 per share, the firm said.
TotalEnergies said its portfolio of projects in Namibia, Nigeria, Libya, Malaysia, Mozambique and Papua New Guinea, together with its existing reserves, would allow it to maintain oil and gas output at around 3 million barrels of oil equivalent a day through 2035.
It also set an ambition to grow oil and gas production by 2% to 3% a year over the 2030–2035 period, drawing on exploration and discovered resources.
Electricity generation is expected to grow by more than 20% a year to reach 100 to 120 terawatt-hours by 2030.
The Integrated Power division, which includes its renewables and electricity business, should break even on free cash flow this year and turn positive in 2027. Electricity is expected to make up a quarter of the company’s energy mix by 2035.
To support its growth plans, the company expects to make net investments of $14 billion (€12.3bn) to $17 billion (€14.9bn) a year from 2027 to 2032. It also reaffirmed its goal of halving direct and energy-related emissions from its oil and gas activities by 2030 compared with 2015.

Likud candidate who told captivity survivor, 'I wish there was a way to return you to Hamas,' offers apology
Candidate Itzik Bunzel lost his son during the war, while Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was kidnapped with her husband Oded; she was released after 17 days, but her husband was murdered in captivity
Likud Knesset candidate Itzik Bunzel is receiving significant backlash after writing a strongly worded post on Facebook on Monday to captivity survivor Yocheved Lifshitz. In the post Bunzel wrote, "I wish there was a way to turn the wheel back and return you to Hamas."
He was responding to comments Lifshitz made in a Channel 13 interview earlier this week. During the interview, Lifshitz, who was reacting to the Likud campaign's boast about returning the abductees from Gaza, "They didn't return a single abductee, and that's one big lie," she said. "The truth is that Miriam Adelson bought us with a hundred million dollars that she gave to Trump and told him you would return all the captives, and that's what happened."
Lifshitz added that if Netanyahu wins the upcoming elections, it will be "a disaster for this country."
Bunzel responded, stating that "the one who rescued you from the darkness of the tunnels of Gaza was not Miriam Adelson, but hundreds of heroes who went out into the inferno to bring you back alive, and some never returned." He continued: "Our sons paid with their lives and the blood of the heart of every home in Israel so that you could sit safely in your home. How pathetic, outrageous, and disconnected are your words."
Suggested articles
Bunzel ended his explosive message saying, "hatred for Netanyahu has driven you crazy" and that "silence in the face of such abjectness is an unforgivable sin."

He abandoned me on October 7th; he abandoned Oded, my husband, and 45 other hostages who were taken alive only to die in captivity; and he continues to undermine our security."
The former hostage ended her statement claiming, "I have no fear, neither of Netanyahu nor of the group of instigators surrounding him. I invite the public to come this evening to the 'Catastrophe Sukkah' at Hostages Square. We will not let anyone remove this failure from the public agenda until we hold everyone responsible to account."
Despite the initial statement, Bunzel has offered an apology, releasing one on Monday. In the statement the Likud candidate wrote, "As a bereaved father who lost his son in the war to bring back the hostages, I was pained to see the harsh things said that disparaged our fighters; however, in a storm of emotion, I wrote a sentence regarding Yocheved Lifshitz in the context of Hamas that I did not mean, and I wish to apologize for it."
Lifshitz, a resident of Kibbutz Nir Oz, was released after 17 days in captivity. Her husband's body was brought to Israel in February 2025.
Bunzel was in the news last week for a different reason. The bereaved father of Staff Sgt. Amit Bunzel, who fell in combat in the Gaza Strip, sang "Am Yisrael Chai" on Thursday evening in the UN General Assembly hall in New York as Netanyahu entered to deliver his address. "When Netanyahu entered the hall at the UN, I stood up and shouted loudly for all the nations of the world to hear: 'Am Yisrael Chai,'" he wrote. This is in contrast to the dozens of country representatives who left the chamber as the speech began.

Russian strikes on data centers: will the occupiers leave Ukraine without the internet?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:09:03 EEST
23:09:03 KST

Russian strikes on data centers: will the occupiers leave Ukraine without the internet?
Kyiv • UNN
Russian attacks damaged data centers and temporarily affected hundreds of thousands of subscribers. An expert explained why the decentralized internet will withstand them.
Russia’s latest systematic strikes on data centers in Ukraine are causing temporary problems for hundreds of thousands of subscribers, forcing the authorities to take additional security measures. At the same time, experts emphasize that because of providers’ autonomy and the decentralized architecture, the aggressor country will not be able to completely shut down communications in the country, UNN reports.
Details
Starting last week, Russia began systematically striking data centers in Kyiv, claiming that they "provide communications services and computing power for the Armed Forces of Ukraine."
For example, on September 23, Russia struck the "Parkovyi" ICC, resulting in internet problems for approximately 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region.
On September 26, the COSMONOVA data center, which the Russians struck twice in one day, announced that it would no longer operate due to extensive damage. The company is containing the consequences, relocating and restoring services.
Following a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced strengthened protection for data centers and other facilities in the communications sector.
"Additional decisions were also made to protect and guarantee the uninterrupted operation of our data center infrastructure and other facilities that are critically important in the communications sector. These decisions must be fully implemented at all levels, and this is the personal responsibility of government officials and the heads of the special services," the President said.
In a comment to UNN, digital technology expert Oleksandr Hlushchenko explained that a data center is a facility where racks with hard drives are located, where data and databases are stored, and from which services are distributed. He emphasizes that a data center is a separate type of activity; an internet provider/telecom operator represents other types of activity, each with its own infrastructure and network architecture, and they should not be confused with one another.
Hlushchenko said that Russia is primarily trying to destroy the economic component—businesses that create jobs and pay taxes, through which the Armed Forces of Ukraine are financed by taxpayers.
"At the same time, they are waging a cognitive war against Ukrainians: when ‘everything is bad, everything is lost, Zelenskyy, Poroshenko, Taras Hryhorovych Shevchenko are to blame—anyone but Russia and the Russians.’ And kinetic strikes on data centers and sites with operators’ equipment will lead to the fact that for some time, until repairs or the restoration of operations take place, communications may degrade for those operators whose backbone network or equipment has been damaged. There may also be some degradation in access to data that was in a given data center, whether it was destroyed or damaged," Hlushchenko said.
At the same time, the expert notes that, as a rule, a data center must have several power connections, generators, and redundant internet connectivity (access to the network). Data is generally stored in the cloud, with copies kept at other data centers, and not always in Ukraine.
"Therefore, in the event of the physical destruction of the infrastructure, time is simply needed for restoration. For example, last week, after a kinetic strike, my personal website… one of the data centers was not operating for two days. The hosting provider simply deployed the backups at another site, and it resumed operation," the expert said.
Hlushchenko reassures people that a complete shutdown of the internet in Ukraine is not possible.
"Look, don’t listen to charlatans. There cannot be communication disruptions in Ukraine. It is physically impossible to destroy the internet in Ukraine. It is simply physically impossible for one straightforward reason: Ukraine has never had a Ministry of the Internet; a thousand enterprises have always operated in Ukraine providing communications services. As a rule, these are their own channels, their own server sites with equipment, their own connections to backbone operators, data centers, internet exchange points, and peering connections with other operators. Therefore, it is physically impossible to destroy the internet in Ukraine," the expert emphasizes.
He adds that there may be disruptions in a certain part of the network of the operator that was affected by a kinetic strike, and until it is restored, there may be some degradation in access to the data located in the data center.
"It is possible. But for the connection to actually deteriorate... one would have to ask what ‘connection’ means. For some people, ‘Ukr.net’ is the entire internet, while for others, Facebook is the entire internet, and they go no further. But that is not the internet. The internet is a large decentralized network with a host of participants connected to one another by communication cables, exchanging data among themselves like a web," the expert notes.
Hlushchenko noted that if problems with access to the internet arise in the future, and if someone needs network access, they should have at least two SIM cards.
"If one (operator — ed.) has connection problems, or a base station goes down or is destroyed, then at least there is a second one. If we are talking about a household, there is an opportunity… because there is high competition in Ukraine, and at a minimum, a subscriber has the option of connecting... at least several other service providers operate in their area — these are internet operators. Connect a second fiber-optic provider; rely on fiber optics. If we are talking about Starlink, this is a subscriber-side solution. Those who say that we will now install Starlink at an OSBB [condominium association] and provide everyone with internet simply do not understand that, in fact, they are trying to build a provider. At a minimum, Starlink should be the entry point for the internet — this is called an uplink — and a distribution network, which physically does not exist, must be built in the building. Therefore, Starlink is an individual means of accessing the internet. If someone does not want to bother, has the money and the technical possibility, they can purchase Starlink for themselves. But there is one small ‘but’: if, say, a data center hosting a particular website is damaged by a kinetic strike and the website is currently not working, then whether it is Starlink, fiber optics, or mobile internet, there will still be no access to it, because the source itself is offline," the expert concluded.
