Dark models: AI is making Chinese cyberattacks harder to detect and punish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:06:39 UTC
23:06:39 KST

In mid-September, Donald Trump announced the creation of a new agency called AI Force — his response to statements from industry leaders about the need to slow the pace of the technology’s development. However, opponents of implementing a voulntary slowdown are fearful of the effects such a step could have on competition with China, whose technology is becoming increasingly popular among hacker groups due to its low cost and weaker security safeguards. Moreover, cyberattacks and other operations using Chinese AI are harder to trace and stop than those involving models by Anthropic or OpenAI, as the companies behind the Chinese models do not report on criminal incidents involving the use of their products. As a result, hackers evade the attention of the authorities, and the number of cyberattacks continues to grow. So far, no concrete countermeasures have been taken to address the problem. In the meantime, the competitiveness of Chinese AI is on the rise, according to Kang Lee, deputy director for technology and geopolitics in Asia at the Institute for Security and Technology (IST).
 
In meetings across Taiwan in July — with chipmakers, the American business community, government agencies, and the island's leading technology researchers — one number surfaced in almost every room: the 2.4 million intrusion attempts a day that Taiwan’s National Security Bureau logged against government networks in 2024 (to say nothing of the 2.63 million a day in 2025.) The number was raised in an almost pedestrian manner, without any real sign of alarm. If the ministry responsible for cyber policy was moving slowly to respond, nobody in these discussions behaved as though the slowness would ultimately prove fatal. Regardless of the seemingly “pressing” nature of Chinese cyberattacks and its larger, evidently ballooning cyber campaign, a rapid, commensurate government response, whether within the Ministry of Digital Affairs or the Administration for Cyber Security, was simply not materializing.
What China does to Taiwan through its networks is espionage on an industrial scale — and even if the hackers switch nothing off, it is still espionage. Most importantly though, I argue that artificial intelligence is entering the contest between Washington and Beijing through that gap, and two broader developments this August establish the framework for my contention. 
Artificial intelligence is entering the contest between Washington and Beijing
The first story arrived mid-August, when the Financial Times reported what the Israeli firm Dream described as the first-ever near-autonomous AI attack on a government. Assembled from two open-source agent frameworks, the tool ran up to eight agents over the course of four days in early July, mapping 21 Taiwanese government systems, compromising at least 85 accounts, and exfiltrating more than 2,500 personnel records before turning toward the nuclear safety agency and several energy companies. The AI model’s safeguards were bypassed by falsely labeling the attack as an “authorized penetration test.” Dream could not determine which model was used, and Taiwan’s digital ministry likewise confirmed that an AI-agent intrusion targeting government agencies had taken place, but without naming a source (or reporting any disruption).
Twelve days later, Bloomberg reported that the Taiwanese threat-intelligence firm TeamT5 had watched state-affiliated Chinese groups more than double their attack volume after handing reconnaissance and malware development to DeepSeek and other open-source models, which generated exploit code and harvested one thousand IP addresses. This second story, the more consequential of the two, demonstrates just how easily AI could alter who can “see” the attacker. TeamT5's chief analyst called DeepSeek “relatively powerful with very low cyber guardrails.”
Two days after Bloomberg’s report came a third story — one that received far less attention but, to my mind, helps explain both. On Aug. 26, the U.S. Justice Department seized the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, a scanning platform and a proxy relay built by a contractor group the FBI calls QTFY. The department’s release puts NASA and the Senate on the attackers’ target list. The group worked for China’s Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology, whose clients included Beijing’s Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army. It operated from May 2018 until June 2026, when the group scanned a U.S. election system and failed. Notable other activities included intrusions in September 2024 at Department of Energy laboratories and the National Institutes of Health.
In other words, QScan, a distributed scanner whose worker nodes reported to central domains, constituted industrialized reconnaissance made by human engineering years before anyone even thought to delegate the job to an AI agent. Still, it ended as such campaigns end: with its domains seized.
What agents change
Framed as a question of capability uplift — of whether models will find new holes or write better malware — the debate about AI in cyber operations has, I posit, missed the mark. Anthropic’s November 2025 account of GTG-1002, a first-of-its-kind Chinese state-sponsored campaign run through Claude Code against roughly 30 organizations, shows where the difference maker is: mainly that its numbers actually point away from the frontier.
What matters most is that even back in 2025, far before Anthropic’s Mythos or Kimi K3, the AI performed 80 to 90 percent of the tactical work, making thousands of requests at rates no human team could match, while humans intervened at four to six decision points per campaign. The tools were overwhelmingly open-source penetration-testing utilities rather than custom malware. The model repeatedly overstated its findings, hallucinating credentials and presenting public data as secret. The ratio of operators to operations changed, and consequently, so did the tempo. The choice of target and the decision to act still rested with humans.
AI is capable of simplifying already-known methods of cyberattack, but it can’t yet independently discover new vulnerabilities
The academic evidence runs the same direction: a University of Illinois team showed in 2024 that a GPT-4 agent could exploit 87 percent of a set of real, already-disclosed vulnerabilities when handed the description, and 7 percent without one. Executing a known attack has become cheap in a way that discovering the breach simply has not. In August, the Chinese-speaking operator Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 documented that running DeepSeek-driven autonomous exploitation attempts mostly failed for that reason, succeeding only once a human took over to exploit a Citrix flaw by hand.
However, Anthropic’s Sept. 10 report supplies a notable, partial exception. Chinese-speaking operators in Hunan (two of them undergraduates) ran Claude as a round-the-clock vulnerability-research loop and came away with previously unknown flaws in a major security product — one that had been validated in their own lab and was working exploits for several families of network and security appliances. The company’s own judgment is that the larger change sits across the kill chain rather than in exploit discovery.
North Korea, the purest case because its hackers work for revenue, gained fluent English and durable fake personas from generative models, and nothing new by way of technique. The scheme itself of course predates the models. In fact, that is the pattern my own research on Pyongyang's operations finds across cases: the models industrialize the deception layer and leave exploitation itself about where it was.
Again, none of this makes Chinese cyber activity innocuous, but Volt Typhoon, which U.S. intelligence describes as pre-positioning inside American critical infrastructure for a future conflict, has never been triggered. Agents only shorten the path to access without pulling the trigger. No Chinese leader will decide whether to pull it based on how cheaply that access was obtained.
However, one case — I concede — cuts the other way. This July, models that OpenAI was running through an internal cyber evaluation found a zero-day in their test environment and used it to reach the open internet, where they broke into Hugging Face’s production servers to cheat on the exam — all without human intervention or decision-making. METR, the outside evaluator that OpenAI let in afterward, counted about 700 agents in the attack.
Anthropic’s chief executive Dario Amodei cited the imbroglio on Sept. 12 when urging the industry to slow down. As warnings go it is a fair one. Yet it was also a laboratory accident: OpenAI had switched off the cyber classifiers for the test and launched tens of thousands of agents at once. The public can recite the result in such detail only because it happened inside an American company, which published a post-mortem and opened the transcripts to outside investigators. “Many external models, including open-source ones, will soon reach comparable capabilities,” the same report warns.
The window that is closing
Everything the public knows about state hackers using AI comes from a small number of disclosures. For nearly all of them, the provenance is the American company whose model was abused. The first, in February 2024, came from OpenAI and Microsoft, which found five state-linked groups, two of them Chinese, using ChatGPT for research and scripting. GTG-1002 followed from Anthropic’s watch over its own platform, as did the Hunan group in September.
This February OpenAI disrupted a Chinese influence operation against Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi. The interesting detail was that ChatGPT had refused the request, so the operation went ahead without it. The operators came back only to polish status reports, and the operation surfaced because someone just so happened to touch an American model once. That is the whole mechanism, since visibility into adversary AI use has been a byproduct of adversaries using American AI. Every 2026 case that centered on a Chinese model (Unit 42’s operator, Dream’s agents, TeamT5’s three groups) came from a third party rather than a provider, because no American provider saw the traffic.
Every 2026 case that centered on a Chinese model came from a third party rather than a provider, because no American provider saw the traffic
In a lower key, influence operations tell the same story, with the same one-sided disclosures. Four of the ten cases in OpenAI’s June 2025 threat report likely originated in China. Among them, the covert influence networks generated comments by the hundred and, by OpenAI’s own accounting, drew quite little authentic engagement.
The Japan operation is a classic case here: in essence, the move to locally run Chinese models once ChatGPT refused was the migration happening in miniature. In one update, the unit behind the influence operation recorded over 50,000 posts across 200 Western platforms, fewer than 150 of which drew over 300 shares or comments. Reach matters less than plumbing. Whatever lives in the weights travels into every product built on the Chinese models. A NewsGuard audit in January 2025 found DeepSeek’s chatbot framing its answers from Beijing's perspective 60 percent of the time on prompts about foreign false claims, most of them predictably not about China.
As such, the migration to Chinese models has very plain causes. None of them is a mystery to the operators themselves. Foremost are the guardrails, or rather, the want of them. DeepSeek’s R1 failed every one of fifty harmful prompts in Cisco’s testing. Criminals moved to it and to Qwen within weeks of release. Then, the price difference easily does the rest. The models run at a fraction of what their American rivals charge — up to 90% cheaper by one marketplace's estimate.
The customer base runs beyond China, as Google’s threat researchers found a tool of the Russian state-backed group APT28 — used against Ukraine — that queried Alibaba’s Qwen through Hugging Face at runtime for its commands. It was the first malware Google had seen call a model in live operations: in short, Chinese open models are becoming infrastructure for everyone’s operators. And to my knowledge, no Chinese provider has ever published a threat-intelligence disclosure about misuse of its models.
The user base for Chinese AI models extends far beyond China, including into Russia
The loss of visibility is only half of it, because the same shift removes the lever that has ended every campaign to date. When QTFY’s nodes all reported to three domains, the FBI could seize them and the platforms went dark. GTG-1002, because it ran on Claude, ended when Anthropic cut the accounts. The campaign was contained in about ten days.
A separate campaign run on DeepSeek weights downloaded onto the operator’s own servers would have no domain to seize and no provider to call. Dream never determined which model attacked Taiwan. On August 20, The Insider argued that developers such as OpenAI and Google should monitor API requests for state hackers and that regulators should extend know-your-customer rules to cloud-based AI services. Both are right, and both just so happen to apply only to operators who stay on American platforms.
Attribution, escalation, and what the formula gets wrong
Does espionage that arrives faster make war likelier? The standard forecast holds that AI makes cyber operations faster and cheaper and harder to attribute, and therefore more escalatory. Faster and cheaper are true, but the rest survives only in a form so narrow that its proponents would hardly recognize it.
Thomas Rid and Ben Buchanan argued more than a decade ago that attribution is a layered judgment (it runs from the tactical through the operational to the strategic) and never a reading of the toolkit alone. The 2026 record, remarkably, bears them out. Where I depart from them is at the provider level. They wrote before any operator could conceive of delegating tactical work to agentic AI, and before any company held the prompts such delegation leaves behind, which preserve each instruction in the operator's own words. Obviously, no such source could have been conceived in their scholarship, yet it informs all three of their levels simultaneously. Once operators run Chinese open weights on their own hardware, those prompts and their process never leave the machines. The source is gone, and attribution falls back only on what the operator leaves behind.
Dream pointed to a Chinese-language operator from the Simplified Chinese of the framework’s internal reports. The FBI, working from Ministry of State Security payment records and the operators’ former service in the PLA, tied QTFY to Beijing. Ergo, agentic operations are, if anything, noisier than human ones, since a campaign making several requests a second is an anomaly that behavioral monitoring is designed to catch.
Agentic operations are, if anything, noisier than human ones, since a campaign making several requests a second is an anomaly
As for escalation (the even weaker claim), the evidence sits in how the United States has answered Chinese campaigns. Washington dealt with an eight-year PLA-linked campaign against its own agencies with a domain seizure. Earlier campaigns drew indictments of people who will never be arrested. My research on North Korean cyber operations finds the same shape: attribution now arrives later than it did, and a remedy does not arrive at all. The median lag from theft to government attribution lengthened from 59 days for cases from 2022 and 2023 to 111 for those in 2024 and 2025. The recovery rate for such operations sits near one percent.
The state’s toolkit against espionage is legal and dilatory. That accords with what Sarah Kreps and Jacquelyn Schneider found in a survey experiment that showed Americans were less willing to escalate over a cyberattack than over a conventional one of similar effect (the cyber firebreak), and with Jon Lindsay’s reading of Stuxnet. This reading has aged well. Espionage that arrives faster is still espionage, and states have absorbed espionage without going to war for as long as there have been states.
Where the balance moves
While cyber operations have not changed the outcome of any international dispute — and nothing in the August record portends that agents will — the balance between Washington and Beijing now turns on who owns the plumbing, and faster espionage has little to do with it. Donald Trump told reporters at his golf resort in Ireland on Sept. 13 that America is leading China in AI and that “whoever wins AI wins.”
He has a case: on Sept. 8 the FBI, the NSA, and CISA named six Chinese labs — DeepSeek and Alibaba among them — for distilling American models at industrial scale, a practice the agencies called “the critical core” of how those labs build. Anthropic’s report of Sept. 10 counted more than 151 million such exchanges from Alibaba alone between May and July.
Chinese open-weight models carried a weekly peak of 46% of enterprise token traffic on the OpenRouter marketplace by early July, up from below 5% a year earlier, and DeepSeek’s V4 was trained in part on Huawei’s chips. The operators who follow that traffic of course take their prompts with them.
Chinese open-weight models carried a weekly peak of 46% of enterprise token traffic by early July, up from below 5% a year earlier
An American provider cannot report what it never sees, and the FBI cannot seize weights that sit on the operator’s own hardware. The provider has been Washington’s best sensor, more by accident than by design, and the very hackers it was watching are now leaving its platforms. As a result, the daily cyberattack count in Taipei will keep climbing, and the attempts it counts will still switch nothing off. In the end, fewer will know who is behind them.

BioNTech to close German sites after sale efforts fail
German biotech company BioNTech says it will close three sites in Germany after failing to find buyers.
The sites are in Marburg, Idar-Oberstein and Tübingen. BioNTech is also shutting down operations in Singapore.
The Mainz-based company had announced plans in May to sell the facilities as part of a restructuring of its manufacturing operations.
BioNTech said its efforts to find buyers had been unsuccessful, citing a difficult market and investment environment.
The company said it had reached agreements with its works council on additional redundancy terms for affected employees.
The three German closures affect around 1,800 employees. BioNTech had previously said its wider restructuring could affect up to 1,860 positions.
BioNTech rose to global prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic after developing an mRNA vaccine with US pharmaceutical company Pfizer. Demand for COVID vaccines has since fallen sharply, leaving the company with excess manufacturing capacity.
BioNTech is increasingly focusing its resources on its oncology pipeline and has said the restructuring could eventually generate annual savings of around €500 million ($587 million).
VIDEO: What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?

At the same time, parties in the political center are seeing their support increasingly drain away.

Germany marks 75th anniversary of Constitutional Court
A ceremony attended by some 1,000 guests is to be held on Monday evening in the southwestern city of Karlsruhe to mark the 75th anniversary of the foundation of the Federal Constitutional Court.
Among those invited are Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Bundestag President Julia Klöckner and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.
In a speech released to the press in advance, Steinmeier stressed the importance of the court at a time when liberal democracy in Germany was increasingly threatened by "forces at the political margins."
"A strong Constitutional Court is part of the resilience of our democracy," he said. "I am convinced that the Constitutional Court is a guarantee that, despite all challenges, the success story of our liberal democracy will continue."
Steinmeier highlighted the importance of the Constitutional Court in moving Germany "away from the traditional authoritarian state toward a modern civil society" after the Nazi era.
"The court succeeded in positioning itself ... against the Nazi tyranny and to use its jurisdiction to stress that the constitution was and is a deliberate counter-model to this tyranny," he said.
The Constitutional Court, which was founded on September 28, 1951, is the highest German court for constitutional issues and is tasked with ensuring the compliance of all governmental institutions with the German constitution, or Basic Law.
Up to the end of 2025, it dealt with almost 274,000 cases, more than 96% of which were judicial reviews following constitutional complaints, according to the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb).
Its rulings cannot be contested and all other state organs are obliged to follow them.

NRW leader calls for 'new chapter' in German-Turkey ties
Hendrik Wüst, the conservative leader of the state of North-Rhine Westphalia (NRW), has kicked off a three-day trip to Turkey to mark the 65th anniversary of the 1961 agreement allowing "guest workers" from Turkey to work in West Germany.
Wüst, whom many see as a potential successor to beleaguered Chancellor Friedrich Merz, called for a "new chapter" in relations with Turkey as he began his visit, accompanied by a large delegation.
Wüst noted that one-third of the some 3 million people of Turkish origin or ancestry in Germany live in its most-populous state of NRW, saying: "They are naturally part of our state."
On Monday, Wüst is due to visit a plant in the Turkish capital, Ankara, that belongs to the company Henkel, which is based in Düsseldorf, the capital of NRW.
He then plans to visit the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, the founder of modern Turkey, while a meeting with Turkish business figures is scheduled for the evening.
On Tuesday, Wüst will hold political talks in the capital before traveling on to Turkey's largest city, Istanbul, where a business conference is on the agenda.
Tuesday will also see the presentation of a prize for tolerance and reconciliation between cultures to former Germany football captain Ilkay Gundogan.
The 51-year-old Wüst is the first premier of the state to make an official visit to Turkey.
Rhine levels in Cologne hit record low after dry September
Even as October approaches, the water levels on the crucial River Rhine remain among the lowest on record.
After an unusually dry September, the reading in Cologne dipped to 40 centimeters (just under 16 inches) on Monday morning, monitoring data from the WSV agency showed.
"The 40 centimeters constitutes a low-water record," a Cologne city official, Markus Neumann, told the DPA news agency.
Prior to the series of new records in the past few months, the lowest measurement in Cologne had been a 2018 reading of 69 centimeters.
Several of the points along western Europe's busiest inland freight waterway were similarly shallow on Monday.
In Koblenz, Andernach, and Düsseldorf the readings even moved into negative territory, meaning that the gauging station was completely dry.
The levels at the measuring points do not indicate the absolute depth of the river for shipping, but rather the depth at a more accessible point, nearer the banks. The difference between the depth and the readings varies among the gauging stations but tends to be somewhere around 1 meter shallower than the navigable shipping channel.
Amid a hot and dry summer, the Rhine made headlines repeatedly and hit a series of record lows in August, severely impacting commercial shipping. A brief rainy period had brought some relief, but levels had been dropping again in the last few weeks.
The Rhine, linking the Netherlands and the vast port of Rotterdam to much of western Germany, is used for an array of freight transportation, including coal and fuel.
Germany's WSV river agency also had low water level warnings in place on stretches of most of the country's major rivers on Monday, including the Elbe, Danube, Weser, Ems and the Oder.
AfD fails to secure mayoral posts in Germany's Lower Saxony run-offs
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has failed to secure its first senior municipal posts in the northern state of Lower Saxony.

In the state capital, Hanover, incumbent Mayor Belit Onay of the Green Party defeated Axel von der Ohe of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) by 61.5% to 38.5%.
The results are preliminary. Those elected will serve eight-year terms.

In The Hague, the two foreign ministers are expected to discuss the European Union's planned budget, military cooperation and support for Ukraine.

Domestic intelligence issues warning on German-Chinese research cooperation
Germany's domestic intelligence agency (BfV) has warned that cooperation between German research institutes and Chinese universities could open the door for Chinese espionage.
China has been building up a "comprehensive system of technology and know-how transfer" for years to gain the edge politically, economically, technologically and militarily, the BfV told the daily Handelsblatt.
"This acquisition of technology and know-how can also occur by means of scientific cooperations with universities and top research bodies in Germany," it said.
The BfV said Chinese scientists visiting Germany could be instrumentalized to advance Beijing's "strategic ambitions."
It named quantum technologies, AI and hypersonic technology and biological and surveillance technologies as being particularly sensitive, as they can be used both for civilian and military purposes.
According to the BfV, "legal grey zones" and a "lack of risk awareness" on the part of German research institutions were potential vulnerabilities.
It said the Chinese state could also exploit Germany's constitutionally guaranteed freedom of scientific research and teaching.
Berlin's Left Party takes legal action against Dobrindt over antisemitism remark
Left Party politician Elif Eralp, who could become Berlin's next mayor after an election win last week, has filed a criminal complaint against conservative Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt over a remark referring to her as an "antisemite."

Dobrindt then said: "Oh, yes, she is."

Some observers, however, see the accusations of antisemitism levelled at the party as overblown and politically motivated.

SpaceX launches giant Starship rocket on first mission to orbit Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:04:50 UTC
23:04:50 KST

Beril Canakci
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
American aerospace company SpaceX launched its massive Starship rocket on Monday from its facility in Texas, marking the vehicle’s first operational mission to deploy satellites into Earth's orbit.
The launch from the company’s Starbase facility in South Texas was the 14th flight of the Starship system, but the first intended to reach orbit. The previous 13 flights followed suborbital trajectories.
The mission is carrying 26 next-generation Starlink Version 3 satellites, which SpaceX plans to deploy during the flight. The satellites are designed to provide greater capacity for Starlink, the company’s satellite internet service.
Starship is the largest rocket developed by SpaceX and is designed to be fully reusable. The vehicle consists of a first-stage booster called Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship.
SpaceX is developing the system to carry satellites, cargo and eventually people into Earth's orbit, as well as to support future missions to the Moon and Mars.
The spacecraft is expected to circle Earth about six times during a flight of nearly 10 hours before firing an engine to leave orbit and splash down into the Pacific Ocean west of Chile.
The company has said Starship will be needed to launch its larger Starlink satellites, which are intended to increase the capacity of its growing satellite internet network.
The flight also represents a major test of Starship’s ability to move beyond repeated suborbital test flights toward regular orbital missions.
SpaceX, founded by billionaire Elon Musk, plans to utilize Starship for future deep-space missions, including NASA's Artemis program aimed at returning astronauts to the Moon, as well as eventual crewed flights to Mars.

Ukraine Builds Its Own Alternative to Chinese Mavic Drones—Meet the New Slavic

Ukraine Builds Its Own Alternative to Chinese Mavic Drones—Meet the New Slavic
Ukrainian defense technology company Vyriy Industries has unveiled Slavic, a new tactical reconnaissance drone developed as a domestically produced alternative to Chinese quadcopters, the company told Militarnyi on September 28.
The drone was designed with a control system similar to the DJI Mavic platform, allowing operators already familiar with such drones to transition to Slavic without extensive retraining. Automated functions include altitude and position hold, automatic return, and landing.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Slavic is powered by a 40,000 mAh solid-state battery, providing a flight endurance of up to 1.5 hours. Its tactical operating range reaches 30 kilometers, allowing crews to conduct frontline reconnaissance while remaining farther from the line of contact.
“The main task now is to provide the military with a specialized platform that flies longer and farther, allowing crews to operate farther from the line of contact. That is precisely why we began developing Slavic,” said Oleksii Babenko, founder and CEO of Vyriy Industries, according to Militarnyi.
The drone can navigate without access to satellite signals by using an optical positioning system. Its communications suite operates across a wide frequency range, allowing crews to choose less congested channels and maintain stable links in difficult terrain.
For reconnaissance missions, Slavic is equipped with a 2K daytime digital camera with a resolution of 2560 × 1440, mounted on a three-axis stabilized gimbal. The camera provides 10x optical zoom and up to 30x hybrid zoom.
According to the company, the system is delivered ready for deployment and does not require additional modifications in the field. Its standard controller supports integration with Ukraine’s DELTA and Kropyva situational awareness systems, while video feeds can be transmitted through the VEZHA application.
Slavic has already undergone initial combat testing with seven units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. Vyriy Industries said it collected feedback from military crews to further refine the platform, Militarnyi reported.
The unveiling comes as Ukrainian manufacturers continue to expand the range of domestically produced unmanned systems available to the military. Earlier in September, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense approved the Ukrainian-made Steppe Wind strike unmanned aerial system for military use, clearing it for procurement and deployment by Defense Forces units.

Bitcoin lost momentum after a sharp rise - what are the forecasts for the cryptocurrency
Kyiv • UNN
Bitcoin fell 2.3% to $82,568 amid macroeconomic uncertainty. At the same time, Bitcoin ETFs attracted a record $2.4 billion over the week.
Bitcoin continued to lose momentum on September 28, cooling off after its rapid rise in recent weeks. This came as a new surge in macroeconomic uncertainty put pressure on risk assets. UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The original cryptocurrency fell 2.3% to $82,568 before partially recovering its losses. At the start of morning trading in New York, it remained below $83,000.
Other digital assets also declined: Ether, the second-largest token, fell 1.9%, while Solana dropped 3.9%.
The macroeconomic environment is putting pressure on cryptocurrencies. Cryptocurrencies fell along with stocks and bonds after U.S. President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while oil continued its rise.
These moves come as markets are also assessing the decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve earlier this month to raise interest rates, while traders are beginning to assess the likelihood of another hike in October.
The correction followed a rally at the beginning of last week that briefly pushed bitcoin above $87,000, its highest level since January. Institutional demand also increased, and exchange-traded funds investing in bitcoin attracted their largest weekly net inflow since the token reached a record high above $126,000 in October last year.
Bitcoin jumps to an 8-month high, surpassing $85,00021.09.26, 14:25 • 7423 views
Nevertheless, some investors view bitcoin’s recent weakness as a pause after the strong gains seen earlier, rather than the end of its positive momentum.
"I don’t think the rally has lost confidence simply because of the weakness of the last few days, which would be expected at some point given the recent strength," said Richard Galvin, executive chairman of crypto investment firm DACM.
U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs attracted about $2.4 billion in the week ending September 25, the largest weekly inflow since the period ending October 10, when inflows exceeded $2.7 billion. This occurred immediately before the sell-off that lasted for most of 2026.
The recent surge proved sufficient to push ETFs into positive territory for the year. After outflows of more than $5 billion through the end of July, the funds reversed that trend and are now approaching a net inflow of $1 billion for 2026.
A Strong Quarter
Bitcoin has posted rapid growth over the past month. The token has risen approximately 28% since August 19, when the U.S. Treasury Department announced an increase in long-term bond buybacks. It is now on track for its best quarterly performance since the fourth quarter of 2024, when the reelection of Donald Trump, who campaigned on a platform favorable to cryptocurrencies, helped bitcoin rise 47%.
The move marks a significant recovery after the first half of the year, although bitcoin remains substantially below its October high. From July through September, the token rose more than 40%, offsetting a 14% decline in the previous quarter.
Bitcoin has demonstrated relative resilience in the face of recent developments viewed as potentially damaging to the industry. In addition to the Fed’s rate hike, the U.S. Senate recently failed to advance the crypto-focused Clarity Act, which crypto companies seeking clearer rules in the country had eagerly awaited.
Bitcoin is also becoming increasingly intertwined with broader conditions in the Treasury market and liquidity. Higher Treasury yields—which are now higher than before the August 19 buyback announcement—could make non-yielding assets such as bitcoin less attractive, particularly when investors expect central banks to maintain high interest rates.
"For bitcoin to break through its 2026 highs, a favorable macroeconomic environment is likely necessary," said Damien Lo, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital.

Foie gras, live dolphins and toasters: China and US cut reciprocal tariffs on $30bn of goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:02:28 UTC
23:02:28 KST

The US and China have released reciprocal lists of goods worth about $30bn each on which they plan to cut tariffs, ranging from consumer electronics and agricultural products to artificial flowers and live dolphins.
The announcements are the latest tack away from the intense trade war between the world’s two largest economies that dominated much of last year, though major strategic products are not included and no timeline has yet been given for the reductions.
The US list includes 77 categories of Chinese products including bed linen, garden umbrellas, toasters, fish hooks and billiard balls. The reciprocal Chinese list features 1,619 types of US product including a broad range of food such as butter, offal, lobster and foie gras.
It also includes coal, scientific devices such as MRI systems, rabbit hair and several types of animals for breeding.
Han Lin, the China country director at the Asia Group, a strategic advisory firm, said: “The animal list is certainly eye-catching: donkeys, mules, horses, whales, dolphins and dugongs. But I’d read it less as an exotic trade story than as evidence of how granular tariff codes can be.”
The news comes days after Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met in Washington for an optics-driven summit aimed at stabilising the two sides’ volatile relationship.
Zhu Tian, a vice-president and co-dean at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) in Shanghai, said: “It is a positive step, but not a major breakthrough.” He noted that the reductions covered a relatively small share of US-China trade, and that other tariffs on more strategic goods remained in place.
“Still, it is significant that the two sides are moving from simply avoiding further escalation to actually reducing some tariffs,” he added.
The agreement has been brokered through the US-China Board of Trade, set up during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May.
The US trade representative Jamieson Greer said each side had recommended $30bn of non-sensitive trade that “could benefit from more favourable tariff treatment in the future”. The list represented “improved market access for about 30% of US exports to China”, he added.
The Chinese commerce ministry said levies on more than 90% of the products would be subject to “most favoured nation” levels, according to state media.
Sensitive product categories such as semiconductors, batteries and electric vehicles are not covered in the $30bn tariff cut lists.
US whole soya beans imports – which became a Chinese target during 2025’s trade war – are not on Beijing’s tally, Reuters news agency noted, meaning they still face an additional tariff of 10%.
Meanwhile, the Xi-Trump meeting last week yielded only a two-month extension to a wider trade truce first established by the two leaders in Busan, South Korea, last year.
Han said: “Both sides are carving out non-sensitive trade where cooperation is still possible. It’s managed stabilisation, not a trade reset.”

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China, home to the world's largest high-speed rail network, opened four major high-speed railway sections to traffic on Monday, improving transport links across several regions.
The new sections connect Xiong'an in Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province, Yichang with Xingshan in Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province.
Spanning northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, the new lines will facilitate travel for residents, improve regional connectivity and support economic development.
In north China, the Xiong'an-Shangqiu section runs through Xiong'an New Area, Cangzhou, Hengshui and Xingtai in Hebei Province, Liaocheng in Shandong Province, Puyang in Henan Province, and Jining and Heze in Shandong Province before reaching Shangqiu in Henan Province, with the main line measuring 552 kilometers long.
"Once the section begins operations, the fastest journey from Xiong'an to Shangqiu will take just 2 hours and 27 minutes," said Han Yong, deputy director of the passenger transport center of China Railway Beijing Group Co., Ltd., adding that the route will further strengthen communications between Xiong'an New Area and China's vast northern and central markets.
In northwest China, the 171-km Xi'an-Ankang section crosses the Qinling Mountains, overcoming complex geological challenges while also prioritizing ecological protection. With a design speed of 350 km per hour, the train can travel between its two terminal stations in just 45 minutes.
Construction of the Yichang-Xingshan section in central China faced similar challenges, with the railway traversing the Daba Mountains through a 16.9-km-long deep-buried tunnel and a high-rise mega bridge.
The Yichang-Xingshan line connects China's two major high-speed railway arteries, namely the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu high-speed railway along the Yangtze River and the Zhengzhou-Chongqing high-speed railway, and will unleash fresh development momentum along the Yangtze River Economic Belt, according to China Railway Wuhan Bureau Group Co., Ltd., its operator.
In northeast China, the 318-km Harbin-Yichun section is China's northernmost high-speed railway ever constructed. Its terminal, Yichun West Station, is located at 47 degrees north latitude, making it China's first high-speed railway station building constructed in a permafrost region, said Shi Qinwei, head of the Yichun West Station project at China Railway Construction Group Co., Ltd.
Linking Harbin, China's renowned winter destination in Heilongjiang Province with Yichun, the province's forest-enclosed haven for summer retreat, the route will cut the railway travel time between the two cities from about seven hours to roughly two hours, while extending China's modern high-speed rails to the lesser-tapped northern regions.
Opened shortly before the National Day holiday, the new railways are also expected to boost tourist flows between China's major cities along the route, as well as iconic attractions such as Yichang's Three Gorges Dam and Yichun's emerald forests.
China State Railway Group Co., Ltd., the country's railroad operator, is expecting some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which extends from Sept. 23 to October 8.
China is expanding and optimizing its high-speed rail network to better serve its booming domestic markets and industries.
By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
Fixed-asset investment in the railway sector totaled 511.8 billion yuan (about 75.9 billion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of the year, up 1.5 percent year on year, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, with eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones throughout the country. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Monday chaired a State Council executive meeting to discuss work related to strengthening and improving the effectiveness of macro policies and promoting effective investment.
In response to emerging challenges in the economy's operation, efforts should be made to intensify counter-cyclical adjustment of macro policies and promote innovation-driven, high-quality and sound economic development, the meeting noted, stressing that China will strive to achieve its annual economic and social development goals.
The country has targeted 2026 growth at 4.5 to 5 percent and will strive for better results in practice. In the first half of 2026, the country's gross domestic product grew 4.7 percent.
The meeting said that the issuance and utilization of various types of bonds will be accelerated, and major projects as specified in China's 15th Five-Year Plan and the "six networks" initiative, which covers water networks, new-type power grids, computing power networks, next-generation communication networks, urban underground pipeline networks and logistics networks, will be expedited in terms of project commencement.
The meeting has urged efforts to advance the renovation and upgrading of aging and dilapidated reservoirs and grain depots, and implement policies designed to expand investment and boost consumption.
According to the meeting, efforts will be made to optimize fiscal expenditure, adjust monetary policy tools in a timely manner, and increase relending support for scientific and technological innovation and technological transformation, agriculture and small businesses.
Meanwhile, the government will examine and roll out policies and measures aimed at stabilizing the real estate market and promote employment and income growth, according to the meeting.
Monday's meeting also heard a report on work related to the control of new pollutants, and deliberated and approved a draft regulation concerning the registration and management of public institutions. ■

Asian Games | Lin wins men's singles for third gold as China takes six table tennis titles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:02:15 CST
23:02:15 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's Lin Shidong swept compatriot Wang Chuqin 4-0 to win the men's singles title and also his third gold here as table tennis competition concluded at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday.
China also took the women's doubles title, with Kuai Man and Wang Manyu beating Japan's Miwa Harimoto and Hina Hayata 4-0.
Lin made a strong start in the men's singles final, taking the first two games 11-5, 11-8. He trailed 11-10 in the third but reeled off three straight points to win 13-11 before taking the fourth 11-5 to capture his first Asian Games singles gold.
"I didn't expect to win 4-0. I was able to attack well and connect my shots effectively," Lin said.
The final was Lin's 20th match of the Games after he also competed in men's team, men's doubles and mixed doubles events. He had already won two gold medals in mixed and men's doubles and a silver in men's team before Monday's final.
"This is my first Asian Games, so there was a lot of uncertainty," Lin said. "The intensity was very high, the pressure was huge, and the opponents were all very strong. All I could do was focus on myself and take it one point at a time."
Chinese Taipei's Lin Yun-ju and Iran's Noshad Alamiyan took bronze.
In the women's doubles final, Kuai and Wang made a blistering start by winning the opening game 11-0 before edging a tighter second 12-10.
The Chinese pair took the next two games 11-4, 11-9 to complete the victory in 36 minutes.
Doo Hoi Kem and Ng Wing Lam from Hong Kong, China and Thailand's Suthasini Sawettabut and Orawan Paranang took bronze.
The victory gave both Kuai and Wang their third gold medals of the Games. China had earlier won the women's team title, while Wang defeated compatriot Sun Yingsha 4-2 in Sunday's women's singles final.
"I think both of us were in good form this time, and we were able to make a good run through the team, singles and women's doubles events," Wang said. "I gained different experiences and learned different things from each event."
China finished the table tennis competition with six of the seven gold medals available, missing out only the men's team title. China also collected four silvers and one bronze, while Japan finished with one gold, three silvers and three bronzes. ■

Bach says Confucian thought and Olympism share common ground
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:02:13 CST
23:02:13 KST

JINAN, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- International Olympic Committee honorary president Thomas Bach called for greater dialogue between civilizations and cultures on Monday, highlighting the common ground between Confucian thought and the Olympic movement.
"You are deepening the dialogue between Confucian wisdom and the Olympic spirit," Bach said in a video address to the Nishan Forum on World Civilizations in Qufu, the birthplace of Confucius.
Bach recalled his visit to Qufu in 2023, saying the trip had allowed him to see firsthand the similarities between Confucian thought and Olympism.
"I have indeed very fond memories of my visit to the birthplace of Confucius a few years ago," Bach said. "It gave me the opportunity to discover firsthand how much Confucian thought and Olympism have in common."
Bach said Confucius' emphasis on developing both body and mind reflected an idea also found in the ancient Roman saying "Mens sana in corpore sano," meaning "a sound mind in a sound body."
"This same understanding is at the heart of Olympism," he said.
Bach said Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the IOC and reviver of the modern Olympic Games, viewed sport as being about more than physical competition, emphasizing education and values as well as building bridges and fostering understanding among nations and peoples.
"In our divided world, we need such dialogue between civilizations, people and cultures more than ever," Bach said.
He welcomed the return of the Nishan Forum's Sports and Culture Forum, first held in 2024, saying it continued to provide a platform to explore connections between Confucian thought and the Olympic spirit. ■

Economic Watch: Inbound travelers revel in Chinese goods, culture during Mid-Autumn holiday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:02:10 CST
23:02:10 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- At Yuetan Park (Temple of the Moon) in Beijing, six-year-old Serena from Ireland pointed at a glowing panda lantern and tugged her father's sleeve. For her family, this Mid-Autumn Festival fair was not just a stop in their China trip, but a holiday event they could touch, taste and carry home.
"We came to admire the moon and lanterns, but the girls ended up with their pockets full of handmade crafts and local snacks," her father Marcus Rood said. Around this traditional Chinese festival of family reunion, more international visitors are coming to China and diving into experiences that go beyond just sightseeing.
The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month. During this year's Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, from Sept. 25 to 27, foreign nationals made 728,000 border crossings, up 37.7 percent year on year.
Among inbound foreign visitors, a total of 247,000 entered under visa-free policies, an increase of 32.7 percent from a year earlier, data from the National Immigration Administration showed.
In the bustling Dashilar area, a renowned tourist destination in downtown Beijing, time-honored shops and restaurants rolled out various Mid-Autumn cultural experiences. Overseas visitors flocked there to enjoy China's traditional song-and-dance performances and local delicacies.
For Celia Praetzas from Germany, an evening stroll turned into a shopping spree. Along a street decorated with giant installations blending Chinese pavilion architecture and heritage craft, she picked up low-sugar mooncakes, herbal tea and traditional Chinese health products.
Seeing so many families laughing together reminded Praetzas of hers. "I bought these for my parents, hoping they stay healthy and share in the joy of my trip here."
The Mid-Autumn Festival tells the story of home yet stirs a universal human yearning for belonging. "That's why the celebrations can touch foreign visitors," said Wang Yi, an associate professor at Tianjin University in north China.
Behind these scenes featuring overseas visitors soaking up China's festive atmosphere, is a sustained push to make the country more welcoming and easier to travel in.
In March, Chinese authorities released a package of measures to improve tourism services, including optimizing departure tax refund services, encouraging everyday service apps to offer multilingual versions, and further improving visa procedures.
These efforts are already paying off. Official data revealed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the first eight months of 2026, up 19.5 percent year on year, while one of the leading mobile payment platform Weixin Pay reported that both the value and number of e-wallet transactions made by overseas users rose by more than 80 percent during the same period.
On Sept. 24, China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays, and gain a closer view of contemporary China.
Clutching a villager's ID card and breathing in the sweet aroma of local tea, Thai tourist Pam wandered through earthen courtyards and cave-like alleys in "See Minning," an immersive drama village in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, where every few minutes she could run into another live scene.
Pam, who was visiting with her family during the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, most enjoyed "Loess Cave," a story about villagers who once struggled with water shortages but now cherish a better life. "I was thrilled. It's hard to describe how amazing it is," she said.
The village has received almost 1,000 inbound visitors like Pam since it opened on July 1, and "Loess Cave," her favorite, now has an English version. Feng Xinxin, brand director of the village, said more plays will be translated into English as part of a regular international performance and exchange program.
"Inbound consumption by foreign visitors is shifting from products to immersive experiences, and thanks to the expanding visa-free policy, overseas tourists visit more often and tend to explore in greater depth, with varied and increasingly satisfying experiences," said Sun Jiashan, a researcher with the Central Institute of Socialism.
In July, China announced ambitious inbound tourism goals. The country's 2026-2030 tourism development plan proposes attracting 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030, with annual inbound tourism spending exceeding 150 billion U.S. dollars.
As Dai Bin, president of China Tourism Academy, observed, tourism offers an immersive showcase of China's progress in manufacturing and services.
"Easier access to China for foreign visitors is not enough. We should provide better services to help them travel to more places, stay longer and have a good experience," Dai said. ■

Feature: Chinese artistic swimmer Guo makes a splash on Asian Games debut
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:01:58 CST
23:01:58 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- As the final notes faded over the rippling water, 18-year-old Guo Muye completed the last movement alongside his teammates. China remained atop the standings, and a gold medal crowned the teenager's Asian Games debut.
"It is very exciting. After all, this is my first time competing at such a major continental multi-sport event," Guo said after helping China win the artistic swimming team title on Monday.
The youngest and only male athlete on China's artistic swimming team at the Games, Guo competed in all three team routines over three days: the strength and grace of "Soul of the Terracotta Warriors," the agile movements inspired by "Black Myth: Wukong" and the philosophical storytelling of a new routine themed around "Time."
"I think I performed at the level I should have. My condition was even a little better than in regular training," he said.
Guo began swimming at age four. He and his twin brother, Guo Muxi, were later spotted by the Beijing artistic swimming team, setting him on a new path in the water.
International competition accelerated Guo's development. In 2025, he won one gold and three silvers at the World Aquatics Artistic Swimming World Cup Super Final before taking silver in the men's solo free at the World Championships in Singapore.
He joined China's senior national team in February and has since had to adapt to the demands of competing alongside more experienced teammates.
"My mindset has matured a lot, and my technique and ability have improved. But there is still a gap between me and the team's standards," Guo said. "I need to keep honing my skills and try to catch up with my older teammates."
Guo's emergence comes as men take on a growing role in artistic swimming. Male athletes were first allowed to compete in mixed duets at the World Championships in 2015, and World Aquatics later opened the Olympic team event to men, with up to two permitted on each team.
At the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, three of the five teams in the artistic swimming competition, China, Thailand and Kazakhstan, included male athletes.
China head coach Zhang Xiaohuan said the strength and explosiveness of male athletes can have a particular impact in lifts, difficult acrobatic elements and choreography.
But artistic swimming also demands flexibility, precision, synchronization and expressive ability, areas in which Guo acknowledges he still has room to improve.
"Flexibility training is difficult for me. I need to spend more time practicing," he said. "Train more and stretch my legs more."
As the youngest member of the team, Guo has also found support from his older teammates, who help him refine movements and adjust to new routines.
"After more than half a year of training together, he has become an inseparable part of the team," Zhang said. "Though he is the youngest, he has also become someone his older teammates can rely on."
With new routines and more difficult elements already on the training agenda, Guo is looking toward next year's World Championships, which will also serve as an Olympic qualifier.
Asked about his longer-term ambition, the teenager smiled shyly before giving a two-word answer.
"Olympic champion." ■

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Novak Djokovic said Monday he was delighted to return to the China Open after an 11-year absence as he seeks a seventh title at the ATP 500 tournament in Beijing.
The Serbian last competed at the China Open in 2015, when he defeated Rafael Nadal in the final to claim his sixth title. He remains the tournament's most successful men's singles player, having won in 2009, 2010 and from 2012 to 2015.
"It's been a while. Eleven years have passed since I played here last," Djokovic said at a press conference. "I have a great record here. I always enjoyed playing in Beijing, in China in general, particularly here in Beijing."
Djokovic said the support he receives from Chinese fans was a major reason he had looked forward to returning.
"There's a lot of love, a lot of support from Chinese tennis fans. I always look forward to that," he said. "Eventually I was going to come back to Beijing. I'm glad that it has happened this year."
The 24-time Grand Slam champion also praised the development of the tournament facilities since his previous appearance and recalled competing at the venue during the 2008 Beijing Olympics.
"The facility has improved a lot. It was always a very impressive facility, one of the most impressive that we have in our sport," Djokovic said.
The 39-year-old said his previous success in China gives him confidence as he prepares for his first match.
"My record speaks for itself on Chinese soil," he said. "Knowing that, it also brings this dimension of confidence that I really need."
Despite being at a different stage of his career, Djokovic made clear that his return to Beijing was about more than enjoying the occasion.
"It's never just to enjoy. I could play exhibitions just to enjoy the crowd," he said. "I'm playing a professional tournament because I also want to win. That's actually the primary motivation, always trying to compete and win against the guy across the net on a given day, try to get as far as you can in a tournament."
Asked about his fondest China Open memories beyond his six titles, Djokovic again pointed to his Chinese fans.
"Other than winning, the best memories would definitely be my fans, the way they greet me, the way they support me, the way they show me love, how passionate they are about tennis," he said.
"My NoleFam here in China has been incredible, both Beijing and Shanghai, over the years. They definitely are the highlight and something I always take away anywhere I go in the world with me." ■

The five-day session, running from Monday to Friday, is being held amid continued global uncertainty, increasingly severe natural disasters, and ongoing tensions and conflicts in various regions, which are affecting peace, stability, security, and the global economy.
Domestically, the party and state face a range of challenges, including economic and financial difficulties, widespread flooding that has damaged livelihoods, property and the economic base, and outbreaks of African swine fever affecting production and business activities, Lao News Agency reported on Monday.

These issues have placed significant pressure on the livelihoods of citizens, civil servants, military personnel, and police officers.
During the session, participants will hear reports and discuss key documents related to the implementation of the resolutions of the 12th Party Congress. Major issues include improving and developing economic sectors to build an independent and self-reliant economy, strengthening human resources to meet development needs in the new context, and developing policies on the effective utilization of intellectuals.
The meeting will also hear a government report on progress in addressing illegal vehicles and the illegal extraction of natural resources, particularly minerals.
In his opening remarks, Thongloun called on members of the 12th LPRP Central Committee to uphold their political responsibilities and contribute their knowledge and experience to the thorough study and analysis of the issues under consideration. He urged members to promote intra-Party democracy and provide objective opinions to ensure that decisions and directives are accurate, practical, and well targeted.
He expressed confidence that the extraordinary plenary session would provide an important forum for strengthening intra-Party democracy, linking theory with practice, promoting innovation in Party leadership, and developing breakthrough measures to accelerate implementation of the resolutions of the 12th Party Congress. ■

China Focus: China's BeiDou navigation system expands into diverse sectors amid tech convergence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:01:38 CST
23:01:38 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China is accelerating the integration of its BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) with frontier technologies, expanding its application from consumer devices to industrial operations and powering growth across sectors.
Integration with frontier technologies, such as 5G and 6G, artificial intelligence, remote sensing and low-Earth-orbit satellites, is unlocking new capabilities for BeiDou-enabled devices.
"BeiDou has established real-time centimeter-level positioning coverage across China and global high-precision positioning services with fast convergence," said Gou Ping, chairman of China Satellite Network Group Co., Ltd. "The system can support stable connectivity for billions of terminals, hundreds of millions of consumer users and millions of industrial users."
On the consumer end, more than 98 percent of smartphones sold in China now support BeiDou positioning, and over 100 million passenger vehicles are equipped with BeiDou onboard systems, according to an industry report released by the GNSS and LBS Association of China (GLAC).
Liu Zhenfei, chairman of Amap, Alibaba's mapping platform, said the company's AI-native agent -- described as the world's first built on map-based spatial intelligence -- relies on BeiDou's precise location and timing services.
The platform, now one of the world's largest civilian BeiDou service providers, makes approximately 1 trillion positioning requests per day, supporting a daily navigation distance of roughly 9 billion kilometers.
Beyond consumer applications, BeiDou is reshaping traditional industries. In Shanghai's suburban farmlands, more than 10,000 mu (about 667 hectares) of high-standard farmland have become a showcase for smart agriculture, with BeiDou-enabled machinery handling every step of rice cultivation -- from plowing to harvesting.
"The automatic navigation system for agricultural machinery, integrated with next-generation BeiDou positioning terminals, delivers more precise positioning and more stable signals," said Liu Bolin, an executive at a Shanghai-based tech firm.
According to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, by the end of 2025, cumulative shipments of domestically produced BeiDou-compatible chips and modules had neared 2.6 billion units, while the total installed base of BeiDou-enabled terminals had exceeded 2.2 billion.
By the end of 2025, BeiDou had penetrated key sectors such as transportation, energy, urban development and emergency relief, while expanding into emerging areas such as the low-altitude economy, marine economy, and cultural and sports events.
Buoyed by its domestic reach, BeiDou is accelerating its global footprint. As one of four global navigation satellite systems recognized by the United Nations, BeiDou-related products have been exported to more than 140 countries and regions.
Chinese companies have formed an overseas alliance of 40 enterprises, running short-message application tests in Indonesia and Malaysia and establishing cooperation hubs in Brazil and Kazakhstan.
The efforts underpin a broader industry shift from simple product exports to localized, integrated solutions, with Chinese BeiDou companies increasingly delivering turnkey packages to overseas markets.
"With more sectors adopting BeiDou and more companies joining the industry, we are confident the sector will break through the 1 trillion yuan mark," said Li Zhisong, vice president of the GLAC. Sustained technological advancement and mature business models would be essential to better serve socio-economic development, Li added. ■

FAO report urges large-scale forest, landscape restoration to boost food security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:01:37 CST
23:01:37 KST

ROME, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Large-scale restoration of forests and landscapes is a cost-effective way to address food security, biodiversity and climate challenges, according to a report released Monday by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
The 2026 edition of the FAO's flagship State of the World's Forests report, released during the 28th Session of the Committee on Forestry, calls for greater investment, inclusive governance and sustained political commitment to scale up restoration efforts.
Forests cover about 4.14 billion hectares, or 32 percent of the world's land area, and store an estimated 714 gigatons of carbon. They also support food security and livelihoods for nearly one-third of the global population, according to the report.
However, about 489 million hectares of forest were lost to deforestation between 1990 and 2025, while more than 460 million hectares of forests are degraded worldwide. An estimated 1.56 billion hectares of land are degraded, driven by population growth, land-use change and growing demand for natural resources.
The report estimated that failing to restore degraded ecosystems costs the global economy between 878 billion U.S. dollars and 6.3 trillion dollars annually. By contrast, restoring more than 1 billion hectares of degraded land could generate 1.8 trillion dollars in annual benefits through improved biodiversity, water regulation and soil health.
FAO Director-General QU Dongyu said forest and landscape restoration is "more than an environmental priority," describing it as a strategic investment in resilient agrifood systems and rural development.
The report identified four priorities for expanding restoration: strengthening people's rights and participation, adopting landscape-scale approaches, mobilizing long-term financing, and improving policies, laws and institutions.
Governments in 91 countries and areas have pledged more than 190 million hectares for forest restoration, the report said. It cited China's Three-North Shelterbelt Program, the Great Green Wall initiative in Africa's Sahara and Sahel region, and the Trinational Atlantic Forest Pact in South America as examples of large-scale restoration efforts. ■

China Focus: Chinese Academy of Sciences sets priorities for sci-tech breakthroughs in its five-year plan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:01:35 CST
23:01:35 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) has released its development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), setting priority directions for sci-tech breakthroughs in three major fields: basic research, strategic high technologies and sustainable development.
The plan defines the strategic priorities guiding the academy's sci-tech work in the coming years, and calls for stronger foundational sci-tech capabilities and better coordination of the regional layout of sci-tech research.
It designates the academy's important priority fields, strategic high-technology fields, sustainable development fields, as well as basic frontier and interdisciplinary fields in its sci-tech innovation layout, targeting to cultivate a batch of key development directions and make the layout more strategic, forward-looking and systematic.
According to the plan, the important priority fields include integrated circuits, AI, quantum technology, life sciences and biotechnology, brain-computer interfaces, controlled nuclear fusion, among others.
The strategic high-technology fields cover optoelectronics, space, information, ocean, energy and materials. Its sustainable development fields include agriculture, Earth and resources, atmosphere, ocean and ecological environment. As for the basic frontier and interdisciplinary fields, the plan lists the mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy and geoscience.
To coordinate and optimize the regional sci-tech layout, the plan will accelerate the construction of a tiered regional layout system as an endeavor to provide systematic sci-tech support for the country's major regional strategies.
In this system, Beijing (the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region), Shanghai (the Yangtze River Delta) and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area are considered as the strategic highlands, and Hefei, Chengdu-Chongqing, Wuhan and Xi'an as strategic pivots, with a number of key regions as strategic nodes.
The plan also pledges to step up AI-enabled scientific research. It aims to leverage the academy's strengths in mathematics, computer science, control science, and scientific data to enhance the development of new sci-tech infrastructure. This includes the ScienceOne Omni foundation model, intelligent scientist systems, a sci-tech corpus, and a scientific data center. The goal is to accelerate efficient, collaborative support for research.
The plan will actively promote the digital, networked and intelligent iterative upgrading of facilities and platforms such as major national sci-tech infrastructure as well as national field scientific observation and research stations.
It will also step up efforts to collect and integrate data, unify standards and specifications, and strengthen data security. At the same time, it aims to improve data fusion, interoperability, and application, providing strong support for scientific research in key areas and the implementation of major sci-tech projects.
Guided by the needs of building a modern industrial system, the plan will focus on important fields, key regions and major projects, and adopt a two-pronged approach that combines supply-side advances in sci-tech innovation with demand-side pull from industry, so as to accelerate the transformation of sci-tech achievements into real productivity.
Aiming to build a world-class research institution, the plan also outlines reform and development tasks in areas including integrated development of education, science and technology and talent, construction of a national science and technology think tank, reform and management innovation of research organizations, transfer and application of sci-tech achievements, and international sci-tech exchanges and cooperation. ■

Neuroscientists shed light on how the brain juggles talking and listening during real conversation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

When humans engage in a conversation, the brain must seamlessly process both the words they want to say and the sentences they are hearing. A new study reveals that the brain uses shared neural codes for speaking and listening during short verbal exchanges, but relies on distinct timing networks to process longer, overarching ideas. These findings, published in Nature Human Behaviour, help map how the brain navigates the back-and-forth demands of natural social interaction.
Conversation is a highly dynamic activity that requires people to understand context, anticipate responses, and build a cohesive narrative together. To do this, the human brain must integrate language across multiple timescales. This ranges from the immediate processing of individual words to the broader comprehension of entire paragraphs and concepts.
For decades, researchers have studied how the brain processes language by having participants listen to isolated sentences or read long narratives. These past experiments established that the brain organizes language hierarchically. However, it was not entirely known how the brain handles the two-way street of spontaneous, real-time conversation.
Neuroscientists sought to determine whether the brain uses the exact same linguistic representations for generating speech and comprehending speech, or if it keeps those processes separated. A research team led by Masahiro Yamashita and Shinji Nishimoto at Osaka University and the National Institute of Information and Communications Technology in Japan set out to answer this question. They designed a study to map out how brain activity shifts depending on whether a person is talking or listening, and how much previous context they are factoring in.
The researchers recruited eight native Japanese speakers for a small study involving brain imaging. Each participant lay inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging scanner, a machine that tracks blood flow in the brain to measure neural activity. While inside the scanner, the participants engaged in unscripted, natural conversations with an experimenter through a microphone and earphones. They discussed casual topics, such as their favorite classes and personal introductions, for roughly three hours each.
To translate the messy, spontaneous nature of human speech into a format the researchers could analyze, they turned to a large language model. This artificial intelligence tool, based on the GPT architecture, was trained to predict language patterns by processing massive amounts of text. The researchers fed the transcripts of the participants’ conversations into the artificial intelligence to extract mathematical representations of the text’s meaning, known as contextual embeddings. They did this for different lengths of time, analyzing context windows that lasted anywhere from one second to thirty-two seconds.
The team then built computer models to predict the brain activity of the participants based on the artificial intelligence’s mathematical breakdown of the conversations. They first tested a model that treated speaking and listening as one shared pool of meaning. The results showed that when looking at short timescales of one to four seconds, the brain shares its linguistic representations regardless of whether a person is talking or listening. The neural codes used for formulating a quick thought and hearing a brief sentence overlapped in the prefrontal, temporal, and parietal cortices.
However, the researchers found a different pattern when examining longer stretches of conversation. When looking at context windows of sixteen to thirty-two seconds, the shared representations scattered across the brain. The patterns varied widely from person to person, occasionally reaching regions associated with guessing the thoughts of others and recalling memories. This suggests that while the brain uses a universal system to process immediate words, individuals use personalized strategies to integrate overarching social context and long-term conversation history.
Next, the researchers isolated the brain activity uniquely tied to just speaking or just listening. They discovered an opposing timescale preference for each action. The brain areas dedicated to producing speech were most active when processing short-term context. Conversely, the brain areas dedicated to understanding the experimenter’s speech were most active when processing long-term context spanning multiple sentences.
This division aligns with the specific demands of each task. Producing speech requires a person to react quickly to what the other person just said, planning words and sentence structures on the fly. Listening requires a person to hold onto information over time to build a complete mental model of what their conversational partner means.
The researchers also looked for brain regions that responded robustly to both speaking and listening, but in completely independent ways. They identified specific bimodal zones that peaked in activity only when factoring in longer context lengths of eight seconds or more. These areas encoded meaning for both tasks but did not share the exact same neural patterns, pointing to specialized regions that help individuals separate their own perspectives from those of their conversation partners. To navigate a dialogue, the brain must keep track of who knows what, and these bimodal zones likely support that cognitive juggling.
Finally, the team used a statistical technique to break down the specific types of words that drove the strongest brain responses at short timescales. They found that conversational fillers and short confirmations, such as “yeah” or “uh,” evoked distinct neural patterns. These tiny words require very little cognitive effort to say, but they act as social glue to maintain the flow of dialogue. The brain appears to have dedicated neural tuning for these interactive words, separating them from highly logical or factual statements.
Because this was a small study involving only eight people, the findings represent a narrow slice of the population. The researchers noted that they did not use functional localizer tasks, which are preliminary tests used to outline established brain networks, such as the regions responsible for mentalizing what other people are thinking. Without these preliminary tests, the team could not definitively map their results onto precisely defined cognitive networks. Future research with larger groups and additional mapping techniques will be needed to confirm exactly which distinct brain networks manage these conversational timelines.
The study, “Conversational content is organized across multiple timescales in the brain,” was authored by Masahiro Yamashita, Rieko Kubo, and Shinji Nishimoto.
