Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

The 81-year-old singer said the time has come to end his career on the road.
“After more than six decades, ‘The Final Encore’ will without doubt be my last tour,” Stewart said.
“I have sung the music I love since I was 19 years old, and I have had the privilege of taking it around the entire world to all of you. It has given me a life that is far more fantastic than I could ever have imagined,” he said.
Stewart had to interrupt his “One Last Time” tour in August this year after having a stent inserted into a coronary artery, according to a statement from his representative reported by CNN.
A stent is used to keep a narrowed coronary artery open, including in cases where the artery has been affected by atherosclerosis.
Stewart began making music as a teenager. His career took off in the late 1960s, when he became a member of several rock bands, including The Jeff Beck Group and The Faces.

His major breakthrough as a solo artist came in 1971 with “Every Picture Tells a Story,” which included the song “Maggie May.”

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.
Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, says companies need to pay attention to their security.
This applies both to physical security and cybersecurity, according to Rasmus Anderskouv, DI’s deputy director for societal security and emergency preparedness.
“Hybrid attacks against Denmark and Danish companies are unfortunately a new normal that we have to relate to,” he said in a press release.
DI describes the situation as serious and calls for closer cooperation between public authorities and the business sector.
Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.
The United States will pay for any new American military bases established in Greenland under a new security and defense agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen says.
“To the extent that the Americans are to build American bases in Greenland, that is of course something that the Americans finance,” Løkke told Ritzau.
At the same time, Løkke said the agreement contains “no financing elements”.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that an agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland was being reached without costs for the United States.
“There will be no cost to the US,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, with the words “no cost” written in capital letters.
Asked how that could be the case if the US will finance new bases, Løkke said:
“You’ll have to ask him about that.”
“But it is not as though they have to pay ground rent,” he added.
Løkke said the “further terms” for the two new US military bases in Greenland still need to be agreed upon.
The bases must also take the environment and Greenlandic lifestyle and culture into account, he said.
“These are important things that strengthen Greenland in relation to the 1951 agreement,” Løkke said.
He also emphasized that the US pays for improvements at Pituffik Space Base, the only US military base currently in Greenland.
“That is, after all, completely obvious,” he said.
Pituffik Space Base was previously known as Thule Air Base and has around 150 US military personnel stationed there.
Under the new security and defense agreement, the US has been granted permission to establish new bases in the settlement of Narsarsuaq and in Mestersvig.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a written response that the new agreement between the three countries “does not concern financing”.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The announcement comes as the global education fund faces financial pressure, with several donors expected to reduce their contributions.
Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.
“When more children in the world’s poorest countries go to school and learn to read and do math, it creates fertile ground for economic growth and new markets for Danish business,” he said.
The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.
Stena Line has ordered two new hybrid ferries for the route between Frederikshavn and Gothenburg, with the vessels expected to enter service in 2030.
The company announced the order in a press release Wednesday.
The ferries will be built at a shipyard in China. They will be E-Flexer vessels with room for 1,500 passengers.
The hybrid ferries will run on both electricity and conventional fuel. They are expected to continue doing so until charging options allow them to operate fully on electricity.
“It is a historic investment for Stena Line, which gives us the opportunity to take another step in the sustainable modernization of our fleet,” Niclas Mårtensson, CEO of Stena Line, said.
“They support our goal of reducing CO₂ emissions and preparing the fleet for future environmental requirements,” he said.
Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.

Uzbekistan bets on tax breaks and new rules to become Central Asia’s tech gateway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:54:01 UTC
22:54:01 KST

A new business framework is intended to let foreign companies test innovative products, recruit international specialists and expand across regional markets. Investors see opportunities, while authorities finalise the rules ahead of a planned launch in early 2027.
Uzbekistan plans to offer international technology companies tax exemptions on qualifying investment returns and special rules for testing new products, as it seeks to turn Tashkent into a base for expansion across Central Asia.
The country adopted legislation in August establishing Enterprise Uzbekistan, a special business regime for technology companies and investors. It is expected to become operational in early 2027.
Tax breaks, global talent and product testing
Under the new regime, investors will be exempt from tax on dividends and other income earned from investment activity carried out under the special regime.
Companies will also pay no corporate tax on profits from priority activities under Enterprise Uzbekistan’s special regime, while sales within the centre and exports by its participants will be subject to zero-rated VAT.
“It means a lot, but most importantly, it means 100% foreign ownership,” Sultonmurod Rasulov, Head of Strategic Partnerships at Enterprise Uzbekistan, told participants at the Enterprise Uzbekistan Summit during ICT Week in Tashkent.
“You can use investment instruments that your foreign international investors already know. You can hire globally on international employment standards.”
Full foreign ownership is already permitted in Uzbekistan. Enterprise Uzbekistan will also accommodate foreign companies, branches and representative offices.
Foreign specialists who meet the criteria for highly qualified employees will also be exempt from personal income tax on eligible salaries and dividends.
Foreign employees of participating companies will also be able to obtain visas lasting up to three years without requiring separate work permits.
Another significant addition is the regulatory sandbox. Companies will be able to test new technologies, normally for up to 12 months, under specially adapted rules that may include temporary exemptions from certain requirements and simplified licensing procedures.
“And if you are building something that the rules were not designed for, the regulatory sandbox will allow you to test it first,” Rasulov explained.
For developers of artificial intelligence applications or new financial services, that could provide an alternative to navigating regulations written before their products existed.
Attracting international investment
International venture capital funds already operate in Uzbekistan, financing local startups and seeking opportunities in the country's expanding technology sector.
Golden Gate Ventures opened an office in Tashkent in June, in partnership with the Uzbek-Oman Investment Company. The firm plans to develop its investment activities in Uzbekistan while helping technology companies expand between Central Asia and the Middle East.
Michael Lints, Founding Partner MENA at Golden Gate Ventures, believes the new regime could encourage other international investors to establish operations in the country.
“I think it helps getting foreign investors to launch their funds in Uzbekistan,” he told Euronews. “It's gonna help with cross-border deal flow as well.”
“So we'll get more investors, more founders to come and launch here,” he said.
From Uzbekistan to the wider region
Bahodir Ayupov, Vice President of Global Business Development at Enterprise Uzbekistan, said international technology companies may be deterred by their unfamiliarity with Uzbekistan’s legal system.
For Ayupov, a sign of success would be companies seeing Enterprise Uzbekistan “as an integral part of their expansion plans”, rather than simply as a way to enter the Uzbek market.
His longer-term ambition is to see “big tech companies coming to this region through Uzbekistan”, using the centre as a base to expand into other Central Asian markets.
The first test comes in 2027
Although the legal framework has been adopted, many of the detailed regulations governing Enterprise Uzbekistan are still being developed.
Officials are inviting technology companies and investors to help shape those rules before the new regime begins operating.
Farhod Ibragimov, CEO of Enterprise Uzbekistan, identified regulatory stability as one of the principal concerns international investors raise when considering a new market.
“The first question is: how long will these incentives remain in place? Will they still be available over the next ten years?”
The new regime is designed to remain in force until 2100, providing a long-term framework for investment decisions.
Mark Beer, Chairman of the Metis Institute, said attracting companies at launch would be only the beginning. The longer-term challenge will be to maintain investor confidence and remain competitive with other international business centres.
“The real test of any environment is about 10 years from now, because trust takes 10 years to build,” he said.
Beer argued that the centre should review its performance against competing jurisdictions and adjust its rules if growth stalls. “Tweak the regime and monitor again.”

Who is Nasrin Sotoudeh, the winner of Vaclav Havel prize?
September 28, 2026
Human rights lawyer Nasrin Sotoudeh is one of Iran's best-known human rights activists. On September 28, she was awarded the Council of Europe's Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize.
In 2026, Sotoudeh was one of three finalists for prize. The other nominees were the Iranian-American journalist and women's rights activist Masih Alinejad and the Hungarian human rights lawyer Marta Pardavi.
The Council of Europe is honoring Sotoudeh's longstanding commitment to human rights and her work, which she has carried out at considerable personal risk.
The council said Sotoudeh campaigned against compulsory hijab laws and the death penalty, "despite repeated arrests, lengthy imprisonment and great personal risk."
Who is Nasrin Sotoudeh?
Human rights lawyer Sotoudeh is committed to women's rights, the rights of political prisoners, and the abolition of the death penalty. She has represented numerous activists, journalists, members of religious minorities, and people sentenced to death.
"In moments like this, we remember past struggles, we recall our shared ideals and we think of the individuals across the globe who stand with us," Sotoudeh in a video statement from Tehran.
As early as 2012, she was awarded the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize, along with film director Jafar Panahi. At the time, she was in prison and was unable to accept the award in person.
In 2019, she had been sentenced to 33 years in prison and 148 lashes. One reason for the sentence was her work as a lawyer for women who had protested against Iran's headscarf mandate.
Even while in prison, she continued her advocacy for human rights. In 2020, Sotoudeh went on a hunger strike at Evin Prison to protest the conditions of detention and the situation of political prisoners. That same year, she was among the recipients of the Alternative Nobel Prize (Right Livelihood Award) and learned of the award while in prison.
Voice for women's rights in Iran
During Iran's nationwide "Woman, Life, Freedom" protest movement in 2022, Sotoudeh once again became a leading voice for the rights of Iranian women.
Her decades-long commitment symbolizes the enduring resistance against state restrictions and repression. She has been arrested repeatedly and sentenced to long prison terms, including in April 2026. In May, she was released on bail.
The Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize recognizes "outstanding civil society action in defense of human rights" in Europe and elsewhere. The prize is worth €60,000 and is awarded by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) in cooperation with the Charter 77 Foundation.

Heat pump sales soar across Europe after states cut electricity taxes, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:53:52 UTC
22:53:52 KST

Sales of residential heat pumps jumped across Europe in the first six months of the year as the Iran war sent oil and gas prices rocketing and some countries lowered electricity taxes.
Homeowners bought 1.16m heat pumps across 12 European countries, up from 1.05m in the first half of 2025, according to the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA).
Iran’s de facto closure of the strait of Hormuz, an important shipping passage, severely disrupted the flow of oil and gas shipments and sent the price of crude oil as high as $126 a barrel in late April.
Soon after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February that started the war, the European Commission published plans to encourage EU governments to lower electricity taxes and speed up the shift from fossil fuels oil and gas to renewable sources of energy.
Soaring energy prices and electricity tax changes have fuelled the growth in heat pump sales so far this year, said the EHPA, which has long argued that the popularity of the heating systems depends heavily on the price of electricity.
Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, the pumps transfer heat energy from one place to another and can be used for warming and cooling a home.
In its electrification action plan, the commission said tax on electricity should be no higher than that on gas. Brussels hopes to amend the network charges that consumers pay on their utility bills to reward flexible options such as heat pumps.
Heat pump sales have risen in European countries where electricity taxes have been cut, the EHPA said. In Germany, a subsidy scheme has led to heat pumps being the No 1 heating tech being installed, it added.
The 12 countries covered in the data are Austria, Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal and Sweden.
Paul Kenny, the EHPA director general, said: “Europe is ending its addiction to a toxic, costly drug from dodgy suppliers: gas. The sooner electricity becomes the most affordable solution, the quicker we’ll get clean.
“The fix? Dropping taxes on electricity and shifting them over to fossil fuels. The European Commission has made this clear – but now all EU governments must enact it, following in the footsteps of the Netherlands and Belgium.”
The industry body found that taxes on electricity were often higher than on gas, which drives up the cost sharply. In the UK, electricity costs more than four times as much as gas, similar to Belgium. The only country where the ratio is higher is Romania, where electricity prices are five times as high as those for gas.
The EHPA said countries that taxed electricity more than gas saw slower adoption of heat pumps and were more dependent on fossil fuels. It pointed to Belgium, where heat pump uptake remains low, although the government announced tax changes for 2026 that will cut electricity costs by 3% and raise gas costs by 3%.
Separately, a two-year study by the London-based Centre for Net Zero found that installing solar panels and a battery in a UK home saves £681 a year on average. Families’ annual bills fell by almost two-thirds (62%) after they received free solar panels and a battery, based on smart meter data used to calculate their electricity bills, in news first reported by the Times.
Great Britain recorded more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, according to government figures published in July.

Iraq looks for oil export alternatives to the troubled Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:53:28 UTC
22:53:28 KST

Iraq looks for oil export alternatives to the troubled Strait of Hormuz
The continued blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has forced Iraq to look for alternatives to export its oil.
In his speech at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Friday, Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi spoke about the challenges his country has faced amid the ongoing war between the United States and Iran.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has cut off Iraq’s sea-based trade, including oil exports – a lifeline for the country.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Detained Tunisian flotilla activists: Worsening health amid family anguish
- list 2 of 4‘My hands are empty’: Displaced Palestinians struggle to survive
- list 3 of 4‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines?
- list 4 of 4Mapping Israel’s 300 checkpoints: Where they are and how they work
Iraq has been unable to export about 90 percent of its oil via the Gulf and has lost $60bn in oil revenues since the war began.
“We are watching with concern the fallout over shipping and maritime freedom in the Strait of Hormuz, which has triggered a crisis of rising global oil price,” al-Zaidi told the assembly.
It is evident that the financial crisis caused by lost oil receipts has presented the Iraqi government with a mountain of challenges.
Oil revenues make up about 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget and the decline in exports has impacted the government’s ability to pay salaries and prompted protests in Baghdad.
The Iraqi government is looking at a range of austerity measures to deal with the deficit, but they are unpopular with the population.
Al-Zaidi suggested that boosting oil production in the coming years and diversifying export routes could increase government revenues. That could be achieved by developing existing export channels, such as the Iraq–Turkiye Pipeline (ITP), or establishing new ones with Jordan and Syria.
But none of the proposals provide a quick solution to Iraq’s economic woes, with the Strait of Hormuz – for long the main gateway for Iraqi oil to the rest of the world – remaining effectively closed for the foreseeable future.
Iraqi political and security analyst Sarmad Al-Bayati told Al Jazeera that the lack of quick solutions for Iraq’s oil export conundrum is a major problem for the country.
“At present, the only option is to export through the Strait of Hormuz, which depends primarily on the situation in the strait,” Al-Bayati told Al Jazeera.
“Other alternatives, such as oil exporting routes through Syria or Turkiye, or even future plans to extend a pipeline through Jordan, are unrealistic and impractical at the moment, offering no real solutions to Iraq’s current crisis if the situation remains as it is in the strait.”
Strait of Hormuz
Iraq has relied on inefficient ship-to-ship transfers to get some oil out via Basra and other Gulf ports, with small boats carrying cargo through the Strait of Hormuz under US military protection.
Ali Nazar, the head of Iraqi Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO), told a recent session in the Iraqi parliament that Iraq’s oil export capacity was 4.2 million barrels in September, but actual average exports were much lower at 2.5 million barrels. Before the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq was exporting 3.5 million barrels per day.
SOMO is offering discounts of $26.5 for each barrel for medium oil and about $28 for heavy oil, he added. Despite that, the company is struggling to find buyers due to continued attacks on vessels transiting the strait.
“It isn’t an easy task. It is extremely difficult. It requires high-level coordination with shipping companies,” Nazar said. “The competition is very intense. Kuwait and Qatar have offered larger discounts, reaching up to $35 per barrel.”
Iraqi oil ministry spokesman Salim al-Rikabi said that 70 million barrels of oil were exported from Iraq in August, with revenues of around $4.5bn.
An oil ministry source told Al Jazeera that this was only oil exported from Iraq’s southern oil fields that went through Hormuz.
Iraq continues to export crude through Turkiye using the Iraq–Turkiye Pipeline (ITP). Basra Oil Company manager Bassem Abdul Karim recently said that 250,000 barrels of oil were being transported daily by road from Iraq’s southern oil fields to a storage facility in Kirkuk in northern Iraq.
With sea routes still largely blocked, there are plans to raise volumes to 750,000 barrels.
Last month, Iraq and Turkiye signed a one-year extendable agreement to export at least 750,000 barrels per day through the ITP to the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, marking a significant step in diversifying Iraq’s export routes.
But industry experts say the Strait of Hormuz remains the only viable long-term solution for Iraq to overcome its financial burden.
“Honestly, Iraq has lagged far behind in finding export alternatives before the crisis in Hormuz began and failed to account for the possibility that it might one day lose its ability to export through the Strait of Hormuz,” Hassan Hafidh, a former OPEC spokesman and specialist in oil and gas affairs, told Al Jazeera.
“All the other alternatives the Iraqis are discussing will not solve their export crisis and the Strait of Hormuz remains at the current time the only way for Iraq to ship the quantities that secure the revenue that Iraq needs.”
Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair told parliament last week that the situation in the Strait of Hormuz remains highly unstable and tense.
Iraq could face a sudden blow to its ability to export limited amounts of crude at any time with Iran and the US no closer to reaching a deal to end the war and reopen the strait.
“Even if we can export three million barrels a day right now, there are no guarantees we can sustain this level due to the unpredictable future of the Strait of Hormuz,” Khudhair said.
“If the war drags on, exports will drop. The entire import and export operations hinge on one vital factor, safety in the strait.”

Bulgaria takes part in two of five new EU defence projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Monday 28 September 2026 16:00
Monday, 28 September 2026, 16:00
PHOTO EPA / BGNES
Font size
Bulgaria is taking part in two of the first five European defence projects of common interest approved by the Council of the EU, BNR's Brussels correspondent Angelina Piskova reported.
The country is among 28 participants in DECODER (DronE and Counter Drone European Resolve), alongside 26 other EU countries, Norway and Ukraine. It is also among 17 participants in IMSD (Integrated Maritime and Seabed Defence), again alongside Norway and Ukraine.
DECODER is valued at between €3.5 billion and €5 billion through 2033 and includes joint procurement of drone and counter-drone systems and the creation of a European network of drone technology centres.
Investment in IMSD is estimated at €43–72 billion. The project includes a common information-sharing system and joint procurement of naval platforms, underwater and unmanned systems, intelligence and surveillance equipment, and underwater warfare capabilities.

The Chess Federation calls on the SBU to open a treason case against Podolyak over his appointment to FIDE&apos;s leadership

The Chess Federation calls on the SBU to open a treason case against Podolyak over his appointment to FIDE's leadership
Kyiv • UNN
The Chess Federation of Ukraine asks the SBU to assess Mykhailo Podolyak's actions and open a case over his appointment to FIDE's leadership. The organization does not recognize him as Ukraine's representative.
The Ukrainian Chess Federation (UCF) has appealed to the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) to open criminal proceedings against Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to the President of Ukraine, because of his joining the leadership of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), headed by sanctioned businessman Timur Turlov, reports UNN.
On September 26, 2026, a new president of the organization was elected at the FIDE General Assembly. He was Timur Turlov, who has been under sanctions imposed by a decision of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine and enacted by a decree of the President of Ukraine since October 2022. In addition, according to available information, other effective sanctions against Turlov are being prepared. At the General Assembly meeting, Timur Turlov announced that Ukrainian citizen Mykhailo Podolyak and Russian Federation citizen Pavel Kolobkov had been appointed to the positions of FIDE vice presidents
The UCF emphasized that it had not authorized Podolyak to represent the Federation at FIDE, noting that he has no connection to the Ukrainian Chess Federation or chess life in Ukraine.
Russian Federation citizen Pavel Kolobkov, a former sports minister of the Russian Federation, cannot hold positions at FIDE, since the membership of the Chess Federation of the Russian Federation in FIDE is currently suspended. The UCF demands that Mykhailo Podolyak and Pavel Kolobkov not be appointed to the positions of FIDE vice presidents
The UCF believes that Podolyak's actions, committed during the full-scale armed aggression of the Russian Federation, undermine sovereignty and have a negative impact on Ukraine's image.
The UCF asks the Security Service of Ukraine to assess Mykhailo Podolyak's actions and open criminal proceedings concerning treason against Ukraine's national interests. The UCF also calls on the Ukrainian public and mass media to properly assess Mykhailo Podolyak's actions. When you hear an air-raid alert, the sounds of Shahed drones, missiles, and explosions, know that at that time Mykhailo Podolyak is cooperating with the Russians as a FIDE vice president
Context
As previously reported, on Saturday, September 26, Timur Turlov, president of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, was elected president of the International Chess Federation. Turlov won in the second round, receiving 110 votes. At the age of 38, he became the second-youngest FIDE president ever elected.
Delegates representing 196 national chess federations took part in the election, with three candidates competing. In the first round, Turlov received 96 votes, Vadim Rosenstein (Germany) received 76 votes, and Jan Henrik Büttner (Germany) received 20 votes. A total of 192 votes were cast.
In the second round, Turlov won with 110 votes against 85 (196 votes in total), becoming FIDE's eighth president. He replaced Arkady Dvorkovich, who had served two terms as president, from 2018 to 2026.
On September 21, Turlov wrote on the social network X: "Ukraine is one of the world's most prominent chess nations. Its remarkable tradition has produced generations of outstanding players and coaches. Even during an exceptionally difficult time for the country, Ukrainian chess has remained strong and enjoyed international respect."
He added that FIDE is a global organization and cannot function in isolation from what is happening in the world. Ukraine should have its voice in the room when decisions are discussed and adopted, as well as the opportunity to directly raise issues important to its chess community.
"I would like to invite Ukraine to join our team and nominate its representative for the position of FIDE vice president if we are elected. Mykhailo Podolyak, continuing our recent conversation, I would personally like to ask you to consider this proposal and help bring Ukrainian representation in the FIDE leadership to life," Turlov added.
Podolyak responded as follows: "I am very interested in international federations leaving intrigue and politics behind. I want them to focus on returning to their fundamental goals: promoting humanism and determination, as well as achieving leadership through fair and open competition."
"Of course, I am also very interested in FIDE restoring its historic glory as the \"capital\" of intellectual sport. Moreover, I am deeply convinced that Ukraine should play a much more significant role in world sport — so that its voice is heard regularly, reasonably, and loudly. I support your reformist vision and am ready to personally join the new FIDE team," Podolyak wrote.
Several days later, the Ukrainian Chess Federation issued a statement, which said that the Federation:
-  does not support Timur Turlov's candidacy in the FIDE presidential election, as he has been under sanctions since October 2022, imposed by a decision of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine and enacted by a decree of the President of Ukraine; 
-  has not received an offer from Timur Turlov to delegate a representative of Ukraine to his team; 
-  did not authorize Mykhailo Podolyak to represent the Ukrainian Chess Federation on Timur Turlov's team.  
Mykhailo Podolyak has no connection whatsoever with the Ukrainian Chess Federation or Ukraine's chess community; he has never helped or assisted the UCF in any way, nor has he had any connection with FIDE. In order to include a country's representative in the FIDE leadership, under the FIDE Statutes, a nomination from the national chess federation of the country the representative represents is required. Hungary lifts PM Peter Magyar’s immunity over phone he allegedly grabbed and threw into Danube
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:47:22 UTC
22:47:22 KST

Hungary’s parliament voted Monday to lift the parliamentary immunity of three lawmakers, including new Prime Minister Peter Magyar, allowing criminal investigations against them to proceed. 
Magyar, who is leading a political, media and judicial overhaul aimed at reversing measures introduced during former prime minister Viktor Orban’s 15 years of illiberal rule, is suspected of theft over a June 2024 incident in which he allegedly grabbed a man’s phone during an altercation at a nightclub and threw it into the Danube River. 
The incident at the center of prosecutors’ request to investigate Magyar occurred on the night of June 20-21, 2024, nearly two years before he won the general election and came to power. Magyar, who was already leading the opposition Tisza party and emerging as Orban’s main rival, went dancing with friends at an upscale Budapest nightclub.
There, he grabbed the phone of a man who, according to Magyar, had been continuously filming him, his friends and other young people and refused to stop despite repeated requests. Magyar later went outside and threw the phone into the river.
Magyar said at the time that the man filming him was not simply a bystander but a “paid provocateur from Fidesz,” Orban’s party, and claimed he had followed Magyar and his friends on previous nights as well.
The future prime minister said the man deliberately filmed them and other young people at close range and shouted insults at them in an attempt to provoke them and cause a disturbance.
Magyar’s opponents, meanwhile, circulated allegations that he had become drunk at the club, behaved wildly, harassed women and was “escorted out by security guards,” claims Magyar rejected as complete lies.
Divers later recovered the phone from the bottom of the river for the investigation.
Magyar rejected the claim that his actions amounted to theft and accused investigators of pursuing a case opened during Orban’s rule, involving damage that he said barely exceeds $300, as politically motivated “theater.”
In recent days, the new prime minister also criticized prosecutors for seeking to lift his immunity at the same time as those of two former ministers from the Orban era, who, unlike Magyar, are suspected of offenses involving the alleged misuse of tens of millions of dollars in public funds and the receipt of millions more in bribes.
Despite his criticism, Magyar asked members of his party ahead of Monday’s vote to support lifting his immunity.
“I did not commit a crime, and I take responsibility for all my actions. Someone who has nothing to hide stands openly before the law,” he told lawmakers.
He stressed that everyone is equal before the law, from a factory worker to the prime minister.
Parliamentary immunity, as in Israel and other European democracies, is intended to protect lawmakers from politically motivated prosecution and allow them to perform their duties and express their views without fear of arrest or legal action.
Hungary’s previous government under Orban had sought to strip Magyar of his immunity when he was a member of the European Parliament, but the European Parliament repeatedly refused to do so.
In Monday’s vote, lawmakers also approved lifting the immunity of two former ministers in Orban’s government who are suspected in separate cases. A total of 139 of parliament’s 199 members voted in favor of lifting the immunities, with no votes against or abstentions. 
One case involves former culture minister Balazs Hanko, who is suspected of misusing $53.6 million from Hungary’s National Cultural Fund. Prosecutors allege that Hankó personally intervened in the allocation of money from the fund, which is intended to support cultural projects, based on political considerations and used the funds to cover costs related to Fidesz’s campaign ahead of elections held in April.
The second case involves Orban’s former development minister Miklos Sesztak. He is suspected of receiving $37.2 million in bribes and improper commissions. The case is linked to vehicle procurement at Hungary’s state-owned bus company and government construction projects.
The two investigations come as Magyar’s government conducts a broad effort to uncover what it describes as years of massive fraud and theft of public funds under Orban.
Magyar claims corruption and misuse of public money cost Hungary between 8% and 10% of its gross domestic product in recent years under Orban’s rule.
Lawmakers from Orban’s Fidesz party and its former coalition partner, the Christian Democratic People’s Party, boycotted Monday’s vote, arguing that the allegations against their representatives amounted to “political tyranny” by Magyar’s government. iLoveSzeged.com

'We can solve this problem': Renewed hope of replacing dirty cooking fuels that kill millions every year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:46:48 UTC
22:46:48 KST

“I believe if your neighbour’s house is burning, you help them. Africa is our neighbour,” said IEA executive director Dr Fatih Birol.
Dirty cooking fuels are back on the global agenda, after the first ever high-level event was held during the UN General Assembly (22 September).
Leaders gathered to tackle one of the world’s biggest silent killers: dirty cooking fuels.
Clean cooking is defined as fuels and equipment that significantly limit or avoid the release of pollutants harmful to human health.
In Africa, where four in five people cook over open fires and basic stoves, it is the second leading cause of premature deaths among women and children. Globally, there are an estimated 2.5 million premature deaths each year from household air pollution.
The International Energy Agency (IEA), along with the governments of Norway and Kenya, convened the event.
"Nearly four in five households in Sub-Saharan Africa still lack access to clean cooking. Women bear the greatest burden, risking their health to provide a cooked meal for their family. Access to clean cooking has become a national development priority, and several countries in Africa are reporting rapid progress. Let us seize on this momentum to support investments at scale," said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Despite the scale of the problem, IEA chief Fatih Birol says that Europe can help solve it with relatively little money. As he wrote in a landmark report in 2023, “The barriers to delivering on the promise of clean cooking for all are not technical.
“What is encouraging and disturbing, in equal measure, is that this huge environmental, economic and human challenge could be solved with relatively modest investment.”
How could clean cooking help mitigate climate change?
Lack of access to clean cooking is a cross-cutting issue: entrenching people in poverty, stealing women’s time, inflicting respiratory and cardiovascular disease, and increasing planet-heating emissions.
Cooking with ‘dirty’ fuels like charcoal, firewood, coal, kerosene and agricultural waste generates high levels of pollution. In the case of wood from forests, it also eats into valuable carbon sinks.
“There is a real climate benefit here,” Dr Birol said in 2024, of the transition to clean cooking. “I think this could play a very important role to keep the lungs of the world in Africa.”
The IEA’s report situated the problem within different national contexts. Switching to ‘clean’ cooking fuels like liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and electric hot plates will increase emissions by a certain amount in the short-term, depending on a country’s power system.
However, taking into account the reduction in methane and other greenhouse gas emissions from the incomplete combustion of fuelwood and charcoal in basic stoves - plus forests saved - the IEA foresees a net reduction of 1.5 gigatons of CO2 equivalent by 2030. That’s an enormous amount: roughly the same as the amount of CO2 emitted by planes and ships in a year.
How much money is being invested in tackling dirty cooking fuels?
The 2024 Summit on Clean Cooking in Africa hosted in Paris by the IEA and partners was attended by 60 countries and mobilised more than $2.2 billion (€1.9 billion) in new financial commitments.
Since then, the IEA has tracked the delivery against those commitments and more than a third of the pledged funding has been deployed to projects across 28 African countries, while more than 120 new clean cooking policies have been introduced.
According to the IEA, the pace of people gaining access to clean cooking in Africa is now 30 per cent higher than the average over the past five years, despite headwinds from the disruptions to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Why Europe should take the lead on encouraging clean cooking
“In addition to it being ethical, there are some other co-benefits for Europe,” Dr Birol said in 2024.
If Europe does not offer support, he suggests there are “other countries around the world who said they would do it with… maybe some other agendas.”
Steps to increase the social and economic prosperity of Africa will help to address immigration too, he suggests, and save money in the long run dealing with the instability that energy poverty creates.
“I believe Europe has all the means to do it,” he told Euronews.
The IEA estimates that only $4 billion (€3.7 bn) of annual investment is needed to ensure all African households have access to clean cooking technologies by 2030.
“We can solve this problem in Africa,” Dr Birol concludes.
Cleaning up the clean cooking carbon credits market
One important source of funding comes from the cookstove carbon credits market.
Credits are bought by companies and governments in industrialised countries wanting to offset their own emissions by financing clean cooking projects in non-industrialised countries.
But, as with the wider carbon market, investigations have found serious issues with some of these schemes. One recent study found that cookstove projects that generate carbon offsets are overstating their climate benefits by 1,000 per cent on average.
“We don’t want these very important credits that are essential to help solve this issue go the same way as large hydro credits in the past,” Dan Wetzel, head of tracking sustainable transitions unit at the IEA, told a press briefing before the event.
The Clean Cooking Alliance has been leading efforts to tighten up the market, with new methodologies set to be endorsed at the summit.
“Carbon credits are part of this solution, but it is not the main part,” Dr Birol says. “We are going to announce that we are only allowing the good quality of carbon credit schemes to be considered here because we know that there are some misuse of carbon credit schemes around the world.”

Germany on Monday pledged strong support for the International Criminal Court (ICC) amid recent attacks by US President Donald Trump against the UN court.

Ukraine admits failure to plug $27 bn defense gap
Ukraine and its Western backers still have not found a way to cover the unexpected $27 billion hole in this year’s defense budget, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky said. Despite the funding gap, Koretsky urged Ukrainians to “gain optimism” – while announcing plans to raise VAT next year.
The scope of the defense gap became clear in late August after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day PR pressure campaign on Russia, which involved long-range strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure. The escalation triggered a response from Russia, including attacks on military-related logistics, most notably the key port of Odessa.
Zelensky’s request to Kiev’s European backers to plug the gap reportedly caught them off guard, with EU officials privately questioning whether Ukraine is spending efficiently or overstating its needs. Publicly, Brussels has still not endorsed the figure of $27 billion. EU Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said there are “open questions,” while insisting on a “detailed assessment.”
Speaking to TSN on Sunday, Koretsky said the $27 billion gap is part of the $155 billion total military-related budget this year. He acknowledged that there has not been substantial progress in talks with European nations on the issue. “The question is that through our joint efforts, we have not yet found coverage for these expenses.”
He noted, however, that Ukraine managed to find $7 billion for military needs by cutting current expenses and reallocating resources.
Though the $27 billion shortfall should formally be covered by the end of the year, Zelensky warned that much of the money is needed sooner, saying drone orders for early 2027 must be paid for in October and November.
The prime minister also acknowledged that the conflict with Russia has “shaken” everyone and called on Ukrainians to “stock up on patience” and “gain optimism.” He also confirmed that the draft 2027 budget includes a 1% VAT increase, and acknowledged that this is an unpopular decision. “Unfortunately, there are no other sources,” he said.
Ukraine has already raised several taxes and excise duties this year, including doubling the profit-tax rate on banks to 50%.
As Kiev struggles to fill the defense gap this year, total military-related needs are expected to rise from $155 billion this year to $175 billion in 2027, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry. On Monday, First Deputy Finance Minister Roman Yermolychev stated that around $70 billion would have to be met through partner funding.
The EU has tied much of the funding to Ukraine’s progress in adopting reforms, including governance and tackling corruption, as several measures remain stalled in the parliament. Brussels also signaled this week that around €20 billion in budget support is available for Kiev this year, but warned that “timely implementation [of the reforms] is key to enabling the [EU] Commission to proceed with the corresponding disbursements as planned.”

Study: Going to the theater a chance to develop self-empathy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:44:00 UTC
22:44:00 KST

Study: Going to the theater a chance to develop self-empathy
University of Tartu doctoral student Merilin Jürjo studied what happens in our minds during a theater performance and why some productions resonate with us while others do not.
Jürjo was prompted to study the subject by the realization that previous theater research often treats audience members as a single group, overlooking the individual. As a theater scholar who also works as a psychologist, she wanted to look more closely. "To see what happens to an individual, I needed to do the work that seemed to be missing," Jürjo said.
Several interconnected mechanisms shape how an audience member responds psychologically to a performance, from attention and memory to emotion. The model Jürjo developed looks at the process over a broader period: It begins before the performance, as expectations take shape, and culminates in the theater with cognitive and emotional processing and the creation of meaning.
Jürjo emphasizes that a theater experience is always deeply personal because no one enters the auditorium as a blank slate. "Experiences, attitudes and beliefs — these are the lens through which we view the world and the performance," she explained.
That personal outlook gives rise to what is known as a "horizon of expectations," or a prediction about what will happen onstage. If what the audience member sees does not match those expectations, cognitive dissonance may arise. Jürjo sees this as a valuable opportunity to learn: "If I feel mental discomfort, which is what cognitive dissonance is, I have to either change what I already think and believe or decide that my view is more accurate than what is being presented. A great deal of mental work related to what is happening onstage actually begins at that point."
Compared with other art forms, theater has a distinctive quality rooted in the audience and performers sharing the same time and space. "Theater happens here and now and it involves human bodies. Our brains respond differently to bodies," Jürjo said, describing the effect of the shared space between audience members and actors.
She cited Vanemuine Theater's production of "The Beauty Queen of Leenane," in which hot oil is poured onto an actor's hand onstage. Although viewers can rationally understand that it is a theatrical trick, mirror neurons in the brain begin to work, triggering emotional empathy. The viewer's body responds to the action onstage as though they themselves were feeling pain, setting the theater experience apart from, for example, watching something on a screen.
Theater as a mirror of the self and a safe space
Although theater can create opportunities to engage with difficult personal issues, it is not therapy. "We shouldn't give the false impression that we can all go to the theater and all our mental health problems will disappear," the psychologist stressed. "But theater does offer a good, safe space to encounter certain issues and understand the difficulties people face."
Jürjo pointed to the Estonian Drama Theater's production of "Prima Facie," which deals with a rape case and the legal proceedings that follow. "When we talk about trauma patients, the memory of the trauma often remains stuck at the moment it happened. The memory is so fragmented that the brain cannot put together a narrative — there is only that one image. But theater moves forward, offering a chance to see that the story does not end with the trauma," Jürjo explained.
Watching characters from a distance can also help people develop empathy for themselves. While people often find it difficult to show themselves compassion, a production can offer a new perspective. "A useful question in therapy is: What would you say to your best friend? Here, we can turn that into: What would you say to this character? Would you blame them? Most likely not," the psychologist added.
Jürjo believes the model of how audiences respond to performances could also have practical value for directors and playwrights, helping them better understand the feelings of people in the audience. "When dealing with more difficult subjects, you can pause to think about your audience: Who might be the most vulnerable person in the room and what message will they take away? It's a good way to shift perspective for a moment and consider whether the person in the audience can truly receive the message I want to convey from the stage," she said.
Merilin Jürjo's doctoral dissertation, "A Psychological Model of Theater Performance Reception," was supervised by University of Tartu professor of theater studies Anneli Saro and lecturer in school psychology Astra Schults. Stockholm University professor emeritus Willmar Sauter served as the opponent. The full dissertation is available in the University of Tartu's digital repository.
