Punjab's election drug debate has old players in new roles: BJP, Congress attack as AAP defends its record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:31:57 UTC
22:31:57 KST

NEW DELHI: "The sarpanch is also responsible for my death. I had questioned Cheema about drugs. My son takes drugs. My house was sold. I don't have anything and finally now I have consumed poison. The problem of drugs has not been solved anywhere in Punjab."Those were among the last recorded words of Gulzar Singh, a 47-year-old Dalit man from Dirba in Sangrur district, before his death. His family alleged that he had been pushed to the edge after questioning Punjab finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema about the easy availability of drugs in the area.Gulzar died, but his words reverberated across poll-bound Punjab. The BJP, Congress and Shiromani Akali Dal trained their guns on the Bhagwant Mann government, accusing it of failing to control the drug menace. AAP hit back, questioning their own records in power.Drugs have shadowed election after election in the state. Captain Amarinder Singh went into the 2017 polls promising to break the backbone of the drug trade within four weeks. Five years later, AAP sought votes with its own promise of eliminating the menace within months.
Now, with Punjab headed for another assembly election in 2027, drugs are again moving to the centre of the conversation.Only the roles have changed.AAP, which once attacked Congress and the SAD-BJP government from the outside, now has nearly five years in office to defend. Congress wants to use AAP's old promises against it. And the BJP, still trying to expand its footprint in Punjab, has launched perhaps its biggest statewide campaign yet around the issue.
BJP takes the drug battle on the road
Leading the opposition charge is the BJP, which has the weakest presence in the state as of now, but is making the strongest pitch for power.The Punjab BJP, on September 18, launched its 13-day 'Nasha Mukt Yatra' to turn its anti-drug campaign into a statewide political roadshow ahead of the 2027 assembly elections. The party divided its campaign into four yatras covering nearly 4,000 km and all 117 assembly constituencies.The campaign will end on September 30, with Union home minister Amit Shah likely to address the concluding rally. All the top BJP leaders including Union ministers and party chief ministers from other states have joined the campaign against drugs in Punjab.
BJP leader Anurag Thakur said the state has to be made 'Aam Aadmi Party Mukt' for turning it into 'Nasha Mukt'
Yet the BJP has a political history to answer for too. For 10 years, from 2007 to 2017, it shared power with the Shiromani Akali Dal, the period AAP repeatedly points to whenever its record on drugs is questioned.
From four weeks to three months: Punjab's many deadlines
Ahead of the 2017 election, Amarinder Singh's four-week promise became one of the defining messages of the Congress campaign. He later clarified that his pledge was about breaking the backbone of the drug supply chain rather than completely eliminating every trace of drugs within a month.By 2022, the roles had changed. AAP was the challenger and Arvind Kejriwal and other party leaders promised quick action, speaking of tackling the menace within three to four months of forming the government.The BJP has done its homework well. It knows that the drug menace in Punjab is deep-rooted and hence has sought a timeframe of two years to eradicate it. However, Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan has claimed that the BJP will destroy and eliminate the entire drug network within six months if voted to power in the state.Therein lies Punjab's problem: Congress cannot remind AAP about its three-month promise without being reminded of its own four-week vow. BJP cannot attack AAP without being taken back to its decade in government with SAD.Almost every party pointing fingers today has a past of its own to explain.
Congress, SAD join the attack
The Congress narrative on the drug menace seems to have been lost in the face of BJP’s high-decibel anti-drug campaign. The party, which for a long time was struggling to set its own house in order amid infighting, has done little till now to capitalise on the alleged failures of the AAP government to tackle the drug menace.The first big Congress show on the ground was only after Sachin Pilot took charge as state incharge and managed to get the rival state unit factions on one stage to protest against Punjab minister Cheema over the suicide of Gulzar.
Punjab finance minister blamed BJP-SAD for the drug menace in the state,
Pilot said: “If someone raises their voice against drugs, they face such attacks. I believe the government can go to any extent to suppress and conceal these voices. There are two sets of laws in the country, one for ministers and another for the common man. This cannot go on. I feel the government is completely on the back foot regarding the issue of drugs.”He then turned to AAP's pre-2022 promise: “The Aam Aadmi Party had promised in Punjab that they would eliminate the drug menace within three months of forming the government. They stand completely exposed. I sense a stir for change in Punjab, and change will happen.”Leader of opposition Partap Singh Bajwa has blamed both the AAP-led state government and the BJP-led Union government for turning the state's drug crisis into a political blame game instead of dismantling the drug supply chain.“Bhagwant Mann cannot wash his hands of responsibility by talking about cross-border, the BSF and Mundra Port. At the same time, the BJP cannot absolve itself by blaming Punjab while the international border, ports and the national drug-trafficking network fall within areas where the Union government has a critical responsibility. Punjab's youth need action, not a Mann-Modi blame-game,” Bajwa said.
Channi hits out at AAP govt
The Congress challenge is daunting. While on the one hand it has to target the AAP government’s failures, on the other, it also has to prevent the BJP from running away with the anti-drug fight initiative.SAD faces much the same problem. Bikram Singh Majithia recently took a jibe at the Punjab government when he said: “Under AAP's regime, delivery of drugs is faster than that of food.”Bathinda MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal has also appealed to women in Punjab to unite and launch an ‘andolan’ to free the state from the drug menace, including through ‘thikri pehra’, a community policing practice in which people guard their localities during emergencies.
Bathinda MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal has appealed to women in Punjab to unite and launch an 'andolan'
AAP hits back: What about the years before 2022?
AAP's response is to ask its rivals to look backwards before judging the Mann government.Punjab minister Cheema, who is at the centre of the row over Gulzar’s suicide, shifted the blame to the BJP and the SAD.“The BJP should look at its own record. The drug menace intensified during the 10 years of the SAD-BJP government from 2007 to 2017. It was during that period that terms such as 'chitta' and 'smack' became widely associated with Punjab, with countless young lives being destroyed by addiction,” Cheema said.Countering the BJP offensive, AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal has alleged that the majority of narcotics entering the country originate from Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled states and major maritime entry points controlled by the Centre.Kejriwal alleged: “Today, 80% of the drugs are coming from BJP-ruled states - Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, UP, Delhi. Has the BJP failed to stop the drug trade in its own states, or does it not want to stop it? Their government has been in power in Gujarat for thirty years, and the highest drug trade is there. Drugs enter India through Mundra Port, and stopping that is the responsibility of the central BJP government.”Bhagwant Mann, meanwhile, has launched the ‘Soorma’ campaign to honour drug-rehabilitated people with specially crafted ‘Soorma’ rings and T-shirts. The chief minister said the initiative aimed to transform recovered drug victims into “Ambassadors of Hope”, who will lead the fight against addiction at the grassroots.
Beyond the blame game, what do the numbers say?
The Mann government has numbers with which to defend itself.Punjab Police says its ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ campaign has resulted in tens of thousands of cases and arrests. More recent state figures put the tally since March 2025 at 61,824 FIRs, 81,433 arrests and 3,918 kg of heroin seized.AAP presents the numbers as evidence that the state machinery is finally going hard after the networks. Its opponents turn the argument around: if such large quantities are still being seized and so many people are still being arrested, how deeply rooted does the trade remain?High seizures can show a crackdown is working but they can also show the scale of the problem being confronted.The government says its strategy now goes beyond policing. It has expanded treatment and rehabilitation under ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’, with 547 OOAT centres, 219 de-addiction centres and 91 rehabilitation centres, besides programmes involving schools and local communities.
For AAP, this forms the other half of its defence: the battle against drugs cannot be measured only through FIRs and seizures but also through treatment and rehabilitation.
Punjab has seen this cycle before.
In 2017, anger over drugs was directed largely at the SAD-BJP government and Congress promised quick action. By 2022, Congress was on the defensive and AAP used the same issue to argue that Punjab's traditional parties had failed. In 2027, AAP is the incumbent being asked many of the questions it once asked others.The slogans have changed and the roles have reversed, but the question has survived different governments and different deadlines: after so many promises to make Punjab drug-free, why is the state heading into yet another election talking about the same problem?
Priyanka Mukherjee is an Assistant News Editor at The Times of India, where deadlines rarely slow down. Often juggling breaking news, long-form explainers and the everyday chaos of the newsroom, she is usually managing stress, chasing clarity and trying to log off on time (rarely successful). She also cares deeply about stories around women’s rights and social change, while two very opinionated dogs make sure she never truly switches off.

Israel lashes out as Dutch customs check for settler goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:30:43 UTC
22:30:43 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel lashes out as Dutch customs check for settler goods
Dutch authorities have reportedly searched the luggage of passengers arriving in Amsterdam from Tel Aviv for products originating in illegal Israeli settlements, days after a ban on the import, purchase and sale of settlement goods took effect.
Passengers travelling on an El Al flight from Tel Aviv to Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport said they were subjected to thorough customs checks after landing, according to Israeli and Dutch media reports.
The searches came days after the Netherlands began enforcing restrictions on goods produced wholly or partly in Israeli settlements in territories occupied by Israel.
Dutch Customs has separately confirmed that officers are authorised to inspect passengers' luggage to enforce the measure, which took effect on 22 September and applies to commercial imports as well as souvenirs, gifts and products carried for personal use.
However, Dutch authorities have not publicly confirmed whether the reported checks on the El Al passengers were specifically ordered as part of enforcing the settlement goods ban.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported on Sunday that passengers arriving from Tel Aviv had their luggage searched for products originating in settlements in the occupied West Bank and Golan Heights.
The broadcaster described the checks as unusual but did not report whether prohibited goods were found or whether action was taken against any passengers.
The conservative Dutch publication Nieuwsrecht also reported that travellers arriving at Schiphol from Tel Aviv were passing through the "Nothing to declare" lane when a customs officer called passengers arriving from Israel over for additional checks.
According to accounts subsequently reported by Israeli newspaper Ynet, passengers were required to put their luggage through an X-ray machine.
Passengers cited by Israeli media claimed officials appeared to be looking specifically for wine, dates, olives and other goods potentially originating in illegal Israeli settlements in occupied East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Golan Heights.
Dutch media also reported that a unit of the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee had been assigned to conduct additional checks on passengers arriving on flights from Israel.
Netherlands bans settlement goods
The Netherlands began enforcing its ban on settlement goods on 22 September, targeting products linked to Israeli settlements established on occupied territory.
Official Dutch Customs guidance states that "all goods that were wholly or partly obtained or made in an unlawful Israeli settlement" are prohibited from entering the country.
The Dutch government says the measure is intended to prevent economic activity in the Netherlands from contributing to an unlawful situation in territories occupied by Israel.
The prohibition applies not only to commercial importers but also to individual travellers carrying settlement products as souvenirs, gifts or for personal use.
Even affected goods purchased before the restrictions came into force cannot be brought into the Netherlands after 22 September.
Customs officers may question travellers about where products originated and inspect their luggage. If the origin cannot be established, Customs may seize the goods and draw up an official report, after which Dutch prosecutors determine whether further action should be taken.
The restrictions do not apply to products originating within Israel's internationally recognised pre-1967 borders.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are illegal under international law. Israel disputes the international legal position on their status.
Israeli anger over Dutch crackdown
The reported airport searches triggered criticism from supporters of Israel's settlement movement, including US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.
Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel who has repeatedly defended Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, called the Dutch measure "insane" in a post on X.
"There were some people from Netherlands in our church this morning who are flying back tomorrow & have to check their souvenirs to make sure they aren't from Judea/Samaria — possible 6 yr prison term," Huckabee wrote.
"A Nativity set from Bethlehem could put you in prison! Insane!"
Huckabee's intervention comes despite the ambassador himself having recently described violent Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians in the occupied West Bank as terrorists.
In August, Huckabee called settlers besieging Palestinian homes in Qusra, including a home belonging to a Palestinian-American, "Israeli terrorists", describing their actions as "thuggish behaviour".
He later stood by the terminology, arguing that deliberately frightening people into changing how they live constitutes terrorism.
His criticism of the Dutch restrictions also relied on an example that does not accurately reflect the scope of the ban, as Bethlehem is a historic Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank, not an Israeli settlement.
A Palestinian-made Nativity set originating in Bethlehem would therefore not fall under the Dutch prohibition simply because it was produced in the occupied West Bank.
The measure specifically targets goods originating in Israeli settlements deemed unlawful by the Netherlands, rather than imposing a blanket ban on Palestinian products from the occupied territories.
Israel retaliates against Dutch diplomats
Israel has meanwhile retaliated against the Netherlands over its measures targeting illegal settlements, revoking the Israeli-issued diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats working at the Netherlands' Representative Office in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.
Israel's foreign ministry informed the Dutch embassy on Sunday that diplomats operating in Ramallah must return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the Dutch government's actions and said that if the Netherlands wished to continue representing its interests with the Palestinians, it could do so "from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the State of Israel".
Saar also warned that countries taking alleged "hostile and unilateral" measures against Israel would "lose influence and relevance in the region".
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen criticised Israel's decision as "unnecessary" and stressed that the Dutch measures target illegal Israeli settlements rather than Israel itself.
"Our temporary sanctions are not targeted against Israel, but stem from our obligation to not contribute to the unlawful situation of the illegal settlements," he said.
The Netherlands has framed its restrictions as part of its obligations under international law not to contribute economically to Israeli settlements established on occupied Palestinian territory.
The dispute comes amid growing European pressure over Israel's continued settlement expansion and settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Israel has taken similar diplomatic measures against the United Kingdom, France and Canada as Western governments have increased measures targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.

Russia hammers Ukraine's capital with major daytime drone strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:26:02 UTC
22:26:02 KST

Russian strikes on Ukraine kill at least 7, including woman at Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences
Kyiv, Ukraine — Russia's round-the-clock bombardment of targets in Ukraine killed at least seven people and wounded more than 50 others, officials said Monday.
Moscow's forces pounded apartment buildings, offices, data centers and a building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in downtown Kyiv in a brazen daytime attack.
CBS News' Aidan Stretch was forced to take shelter again due to more incoming Russian weapons not long after he arrived Monday at the scene of the strike on the science academy.
The attacks followed a week of diplomatic efforts at the United Nations to get traction for negotiations on ending Moscow's full-scale invasion that began 4½ years ago.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov indicated Monday that the chances of making speedy headway on forging a peace settlement were bleak after recent Ukrainian attacks, including during recent parliamentary elections in Russia.
"Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months," Peskov told reporters. "That is happening right now."
On Saturday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in a fiery speech to the U.N. General Assembly that "Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the Trump administration is interested," seeking, as Moscow has done throughout the war, to portray a rift within the NATO alliance.
Russian drone attacks across eastern Ukraine
Russian drone attacks on the Kyiv region killed four people and wounded eight, officials said.
A woman was killed in a Russian strike on Kyiv's Shevchenkivskyi district on Monday afternoon, the Kyiv city military administration said. The strike hit the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the latest cultural landmark in the capital to be damaged. Russian forces also hit a pharmaceutical company and gas stations in Kyiv.
One drone struck an office center in central Dnipro during working hours Monday, killing three people and wounding at least 12, local authorities said.
A Russian strike on a nine-story apartment building in the northeast city of Kharkiv wounded 43 people, including 11 children, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said.
Four people, including two teenage girls, were hurt when a Russian drone struck a residential area in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv region on Sunday evening, said Viacheslav Chaus, head of the regional military administration.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces struck two data centers in Kyiv, as well as gas stations in the Ukrainian capital. A distribution hub belonging to the Nova Poshta postal service was struck in the southern city of Odesa, it said.
The Russian military also hit a cargo ship in the Black Sea and another one in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk, the ministry said. The strikes aim to curb Ukraine's grain exports, though they may also create food shortages in countries that rely on Ukrainian imports.
The Russian aerial attacks regularly hit civilian areas. Moscow claims it targets only military-related sites.
Ukraine claims small gains along entrenched front lines
Battlefield positions have changed little since last year, in part because swarms of drones severely restrict troop movements, but Kyiv's forces launched a recent offensive, code-named Operation Vivaldi, on part of the 800-mile front line.
Ukraine's Third Army Corps said Monday it had recaptured another 20 square miles from the Russians, bringing the total to 68 square miles since the offensive began several months ago.
The corps said that in order to break through Russian defenses, it converted Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carriers into kamikaze vehicles that blew up the strongest Russian fortifications. The operation has also used ground robots to attack Russian positions.
The claimed breakthroughs came in the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine, which the bigger Russian army has been trying in vain to conquer.
Russian officials made no immediate comment on the Ukrainian claim.
Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said Russian troops captured the villages of Novovodiane in the Donetsk region and Ulanove in the northern Sumy region.
It was not possible to independently verify the claims.
Zelenskyy said long-range strikes on Russian soil hit two defense plants in the Tula and Voronezh regions and oil facilities in the Krasnodar region, all in southern and western Russia.
Ukraine's long-range drones have repeatedly targeted Russian fuel depots and industrial plants that are a mainstay of Moscow's economy and war effort.
Ukrainian drone attacks overnight started fires at three infrastructure facilities in Russia's Krasnodar region, local emergency officials said Monday, without identifying the locations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 254 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Tehran gallery traces capital’s past, explores future of smart tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:21:27 UTC
22:21:27 KST

Tehran gallery traces capital’s past, explores future of smart tourism
TEHRAN – A new gallery in Tehran is taking visitors on a journey through the capital’s political, social, cultural and artistic history while using digital technology and artificial intelligence to offer a glimpse of how tourism in the city could evolve in the future.
The “Stories of Tehran” gallery opened at the Kushk-e Bagh-e Honar cultural complex in the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone on Sunday, coinciding with World Tourism Day and Tehran Week. The exhibition runs from September 27 to October 8 under this year’s World Tourism Day theme, “Digital Agenda and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Redesign Tourism.”
The gallery brings together historical maps, illustrated timelines, infographics, photographs and interactive features, to name a few, to present different chapters of Tehran’s history, from its early development and eventual selection as Iran’s capital to its political and social transformations in the modern era.
Among the subjects presented are some of the city’s earliest known developments, its old plane trees, food culture, historic buildings and major political and cultural events. A section also documents damage inflicted on historic buildings and cultural spaces during the recent war with the US and the Israeli regime.
Seyyed Mohammad-Hossein Hejazi, managing director of the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, said the event was designed to introduce Tehran’s tourism attractions and present the city through its past and future.
“Unfortunately, Tehran has mostly been viewed as a transit city in recent years rather than a final destination for tourists,” he told reporters.
Hejazi said the exhibition was part of broader efforts to introduce the capital’s attractions from different perspectives and strengthen its position as a tourism destination.
Digitalization is also being incorporated into plans for tourism services in the Abbasabad zone. Hejazi said Tehran Municipality’s “Shahrzad” application had been linked to a planned tourism card for the Abbasabad area.
The card, which has not yet been launched, is modeled partly on systems such as the Istanbulkart and Dubai Pass, he said. It is expected to eventually provide access to a range of services, including public transportation, museums, recreational facilities and tourism and leisure attractions.
Hejazi said the Abbasabad area had been selected as a pilot site for the initiative and that a trial could potentially begin in the coming months.
The “Stories of Tehran” concept itself dates back to the COVID-19 pandemic, when international tourism came to a halt. According to Alireza Moghaddam-Nia, director of tourism at the Abbasabad zone, the area at the time sought to provide virtual journeys through Tehran by drawing on the knowledge and experiences of tour guides, tourism businesses and other industry stakeholders.
The exhibition’s central timeline stretches across the gallery walls and traces major events in Tehran from the Safavid and Qajar periods to contemporary history. Historical maps of the old city are also eye-catching.
Visitors can hear stories about the city and interact with replicas and toys associated with old Tehran. The exhibition also incorporates elements of the city’s natural heritage, including its long-lived trees, rather than focusing solely on monuments and historical events.
One of the main features is the use of artificial intelligence and digital technology to create interactive tourism experiences. Visitors can take virtual tours of countless locations across Tehran and use a QR-code-based service to create photographs of themselves against images of the city from different periods.
The organizers say the idea is to combine digital tools with physical and immersive experiences rather than allow technology to replace direct engagement with destinations.
“The technology can facilitate tourism services and the travel experience, but it should not replace the tourist’s real experience,” Sara Mirzaei, deputy head of tourism and recreation at the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, said.
She cited emerging tools such as smart glasses capable of translation and content generation as examples of technologies that could make travel easier.
The exhibition also looks at the history of the 560-hectare Abbasabad area, which today contains a number of Tehran’s major cultural, tourism and recreational facilities, including the Tabiat Bridge, Ab-o-Atash Park, Mina Dome, Bagh-e Honar, Book Garden and the Museum of the Islamic Revolution and Sacred Defense.
According to Mirzaei, the transformation of the area into a cultural and tourism zone followed years of planning and efforts to determine an appropriate future for the site. The exhibition traces that history and highlights how the area eventually developed into one of Tehran’s major cultural and recreational destinations.
The organizers say the gallery is partly intended to challenge the perception of Tehran as merely a transit point for tourists.
The exhibition also contains a distinctive element looking far beyond the present: a mailbox for letters addressed to Tehran’s mayor in the year 1450 in the Iranian calendar, equivalent to 2071–72.
Visitors are invited to write down their hopes, expectations and ideas for the future of Tehran and place them in the mailbox. The box will be sealed after the exhibition and preserved for opening in 1450.
Mirzaei described the idea as a paradox of the digital age. At a time when physical correspondence has largely given way to email and messaging applications, visitors are being invited to put their thoughts on paper and entrust them to the future.
The juxtaposition is deliberate: an exhibition centered on artificial intelligence and digital tourism has created space for one of the oldest forms of communication, a handwritten letter.
The broader program accompanying the exhibition includes educational panels, specialist workshops and film screenings focusing on smart tourism, tourism platforms, historical urban landscapes, safe travel and new technologies. Other programs comprise a screening of a documentary about the Omidvar brothers, the famed Iranian globetrotters, a workshop on rediscovering Iran and sessions on the role of emerging tourism technologies in developing smart urban economies.
The Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, described by its organizers as a major green and recreational hub in the capital, is also seeking to strengthen its international tourism profile.

EU extends EUMAM training mission for Ukrainian troops by two years
The European Union has extended the mandate of the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM), which provides training for Ukrainian military personnel, for another two years as part of an update to the mission.
Source: Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, at a press conference following a meeting of the Foreign Affairs Council (Defence), as reported by European Pravda
Details: The EU will continue the EUMAM mission for another two years.
"On training, member states agreed on the first step of strategic review of EUMAM, extending our mission for Ukraine for another two years," Kallas said.
She added that the EU will "move ahead with establishing a coordination cell in Kyiv, focusing on battlefield lessons and also strengthening military education".
For reference: The main task of EUMAM is to train Ukrainian military personnel, including individual training, unit cohesion exercises and specialised training. The mission also coordinates EU member states' training efforts for Ukraine and is funded, among other sources, through the European Peace Facility.
Background:
- Kallas previously said that €900 million from the €6.6 billion unlocked from the European Peace Facility had been earmarked for EUMAM.
- On 28 September, it also became known that the Netherlands will allocate €10 million for the operation of training centres for military personnel in Ukraine.

He made the remarks at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, a day after a suspected terror plot targeting RAF Fairford, a UK military airbase in Gloucestershire, in southwestern England.
A major incident was declared Sunday in a village near the base that hosts US Air Force operations, with 85 households evacuated after police arrested five men in connection with an investigation involving suspected offenses under the Explosives Act.
“There is a live police investigation and I can’t provide much further detail than that which is reported,” Streeting told the conference.
“But I do want to say that our friendship with America is the closest alliance of any two nations on earth, and we will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm.”
He praised British security services, armed forces and police for their response to the incident.
$8B submarine infrastructure contract
Streeting also announced a £6 billion ($8 billion) contract to build docks for Britain’s nuclear submarines, describing it as “one of the biggest defense procurement decisions in a generation.”
“There is neither an economic nor a moral justification for Britain’s defense sector hiring thousands of workers from abroad when we have one million young people out of work here at home,” he said.
“But solving that problem needs more than words; it demands bold action, and that’s why today the chancellor and I are taking one of the biggest defense procurement decisions in a generation: the contract to build the docks for our nuclear subs, our ultimate deterrent, £6 billion worth of work,” he noted.
“Today, we commit to that contract staying in this country, supporting thousands of British jobs for years,” he said.
'Spending on defense comes with choices and trade-offs'
Streeting warned that higher defense spending would involve difficult choices, amid debate over the impact of increased military expenditure on the UK economy and public services.
“I know that more spending on defense comes with choices and trade-offs,” he said.
“But our critics on the right need to understand that you don’t make your country stronger by making our people poorer.”
Addressing critics on the left, he added: “And I also have to say directly to some of our critics on the left: you are not defending our public services by attacking investment in our national defenses.”

Estonian actors protest onslaught of artificial intelligence in new EU rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

Estonian actors protest onslaught of artificial intelligence in new EU rules
The Estonian Actors' Union is concerned that proposed EU changes to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) would make it easier for AI to use actors' voices and likenesses.
Reimo Sagor, head of the Estonian Actors' Union, said the proposed changes would significantly weaken personal data protections and open the door to unchecked AI training on actors' performances.
"Our main concern with the digital omnibus package is that it would loosen the requirements governing the processing of personal data, the need for such processing and the obligations of those who process it. These requirements would be weakened and the ambiguities introduced would give AI developers an opportunity — because they need to develop AI technology — to use people's personal data, including actors' faces, voices, likenesses and movements," Sagor said.
According to Sagor, they could do so without seeking separate permission, providing sufficient transparency or paying the actors. "This is a problem even now, but in the future it would be fully permitted by law. That is completely unacceptable to us," he said.
Sagor said another serious concern is that the definition of personal data would become less clear, particularly when it comes to actors' movement patterns.
"We would also face a situation in which the meaning of personal data, or what counts as someone's personal data, becomes less clear. For example, if AI learns how an actor moves, that data — how the movement is produced — actually contains the actor's personal data: their original movement pattern. If, under the new wording, that pattern on its own is supposedly not considered personal data because it cannot at that point be linked to a specific actor, it could then be used in an AI system. Studios using AI could reproduce the original actor from those movements," Sagor explained.
Sagor: The Estonian state does not offer creators enough protection from AI
The Actors' Union wants the Estonian government to take more decisive action, both domestically and at the European Union level.
"Together with our umbrella organizations — the International Federation of Actors and other partners — we expect the personal data provisions in the digital omnibus package not to be weakened so much and the wording not to be made so vague and open to interpretation," Sagor said.
Sagor said actors also expect the existing wording of the GDPR to be respected and its protections strengthened.
"We expect the Estonian government to say this publicly and clearly, both here and in Europe. The Estonian Actors' Union believes our small country has not done enough to protect the rights of actors and performers more broadly, including musicians and singers, in the field of AI. Now is the time to do so," Sagor stressed.
He added that the union has imposed its own restriction on the use of AI.
"The Actors' Union has opted out of having its members' performances used to train AI. In other words, we do not permit AI to be trained on our members' performances. This information is also on our website and we very much hope it will be respected. If anyone wants to use our actors' performances — their voices or anything else — to train AI or produce videos, they must ask for separate permission," Sagor said.
Minister: Small states can protect rights of creative professionals in cooperation
Minister of Culture Heidy Purga (Reform Party) confirmed that the ministry had received the Actors' Union's letter and shared its concerns.
"We have received the letter from the Actors' Union, we agree with it and we will certainly do our best to stand up for their rights," Purga said. The minister said the issue would be addressed soon.
"Copyright protections will be discussed at a meeting of culture ministers in the NB8 format in Tallinn in early October. We have serious discussions planned there about the future development of AI as a whole, particularly copyright issues — how small countries might reach agreements and support one another," Purga said.
Purga stressed that cooperation between countries is crucial to regulating AI.
"Above all, this requires agreements. Small countries cannot achieve as much or gain the same support on their own — a single voice may be a little too weak. But by reaching agreement together, we can present a stronger position," the minister said.
Kristi Värk, head of the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs' data protection law division, also said the ministry was aware of the actors' concerns and understood their worries about the use of their voices and likenesses. She said it was too early to comment in detail on what the final legislation would say.
"Discussions are still underway in the Council of the European Union, which is one of the co-legislators. The provision that concerns actors is currently being discussed in great depth, but it is still very difficult for me to say exactly where those discussions will lead," Värk said.
Värk added that Estonia's current position is that all applicable legal bases must be ensured when developing AI.
"Consent is one of those legal bases. Estonia's position also calls for additional safeguards and we need to consider what those might be and how we can provide them to different people. We are looking for the best solutions together with all the other member states," Värk said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Mari Peegel

Hong Kong checkpoints to handle 7.44 million passenger trips for National Day break
Immigration Department says figure includes inbound and outbound trips by Hongkongers and visitors using sea, land and air control points
Hong Kong’s checkpoints are expected to handle about 7.44 million passenger trips over mainland China’s National Day “golden week” break, while people movements are anticipated to peak this weekend.
The Immigration Department said on Monday that the figure would include inbound and outbound trips by Hongkongers and visitors travelling via the city’s sea, land and air control points between October 1 and 7.
The department also said it anticipated that the most popular control points would be those at Lo Wu, the Lok Ma Chau Spur line and Shenzhen Bay, but added that none of the city’s checkpoints would have their service hours extended.
Authorities earlier said they expected the city would welcome 1.29 million mainland visitors over the break. Last year’s figure reached 1.4 million thanks to a longer holiday period of eight days that included the Mid-Autumn Festival.

Hong Kong wages rise 3.4% in June, with government expecting further gains
Adjusting for inflation, overall real wages grew by 1.6 per cent in June year on year, keeping basic pay growth ahead of rising living costs
Hong Kong wages rose by 3.4 per cent year on year in June, with the government forecasting further pay rises ahead on the back of sustained economic expansion and labour demand.
Figures released on Monday by the Census and Statistics Department showed that the 3.4 per cent nominal wage rise was broad based across all surveyed industries.
After adjusting for inflation using the consumer price index (A), overall real wages grew by 1.6 per cent in June year on year, keeping basic pay growth ahead of rising living costs.
A government spokesman said that wages and labour earnings had continued to increase solidly in the second quarter of the year.

Ukrainian Drones Strike Edelweiss-95 Oil Depot in Russia’s Krasnodar Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:16:25 UTC
22:16:25 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Drones Strike Edelweiss-95 Oil Depot in Russia’s Krasnodar Region
Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Krasnodar region, sparking a significant fire at a fuel storage facility operated by wholesale trader Edelweiss-95, an independent Russian news channel ASTRA reported on September 28.
Residents in the village of Novotitarovskaya reported hearing the sound of incoming drones followed by multiple heavy explosions near the local railway lines.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The attack in Krasnodar is part of a wide Ukrainian drone campaign that has severely disrupted Moscow’s war economy. By systematically targeting critical refineries and storage depots, these strikes, launched in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, have cut Russian gasoline production to just 65% of seasonal demand while inflicting over $12 billion in overall damages on the Russian oil industry.
Following an OSINT analysis of eyewitness video footage from the scene, researchers at ASTRA confirmed that the Edelweiss-95 oil depot had been struck and was actively burning.
The targeted facility is a critical logistics hub for the regional fuel trade. According to company information highlighted by ASTRA, the depot has a storage capacity of 4,500 cubic meters and a private railway siding dedicated to receiving and dispatching petroleum shipments.
Edelweiss-95 has operated in the Russian market for 30 years, specializing in the wholesale distribution of Euro-5 diesel and high-octane gasoline (AI-92, AI-95, and AI-100). The independent outlet ASTRA noted that the company sources its petroleum products directly from Russia’s largest oil refineries.
Before the strike, the company said its private depot enabled rapid logistics, allowing fuel shipments to be processed and dispatched within a single working day. While the massive fire was confirmed by ASTRA, the exact extent of the damage to the facility’s storage tanks and rail infrastructure remains unclear.
Ukrainian drones have also recently struck Russia’s Ilsky oil refinery in the same region overnight on September 26, sparking fires at the 6.6-million-ton capacity facility that supplies the Russian Armed Forces.
While local authorities only acknowledged blazes at unnamed enterprises, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the operation, and independent OSINT analysts verified footage of the burning refinery, which was previously targeted on August 8 to degrade Moscow’s military supply chain.

Russia Calls It “Iva”—But Its Mystery Air Defense Missile Looks Iranian or Chinese
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:15:55 UTC
22:15:55 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Russia Calls It “Iva”—But Its Mystery Air Defense Missile Looks Iranian or Chinese
Russian mobile air defense teams may have begun using Chinese-made QW-18 or QW-19 or Iranian copies of shoulder-fired surface-to-air missiles, according to footage aired on Russian television and analyzed by OSINT researcher TheDeadDistrict on September 28.
The unidentified weapon appeared during training with a mobile fire group from Russia’s 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian personnel referred to the system as “Iva,” but its appearance does not match any known man-portable air defense system currently fielded by Russia.
Instead, the launcher closely resembles either Iran’s Misagh-3 or China’s QW-18A/QW-19 family, Militarnyi notes.
MANPADS are compact shoulder-fired surface-to-air missile systems designed primarily to engage low-flying aircraft, helicopters and other aerial threats. Russian mobile fire groups increasingly use such weapons as part of layered defenses against Ukrainian drones.
One particularly notable detail in the footage is the apparent absence of identifying markings on the launchers, potentially obscuring the systems’ origin.
A closer examination of the weapon’s nose section appears to strengthen the case for a Chinese system. An additional component visible on the Russian launcher is consistent with features seen on Chinese QW-series weapons but does not appear on available imagery of Iran’s Misagh-3.
It remains difficult to determine whether the system is specifically a QW-18 or QW-19. An Iranian connection cannot be ruled out either.
Iran manufactures its own Misagh family of MANPADS based on Chinese designs and has also continued purchasing Chinese air defense weaponry.
In July 2026, reports emerged of an Iranian deal with China covering as many as 400 MANPADS, including QW-12 and FN-16 systems, with the package valued at approximately $60 million to $70 million.
That raises the possibility that any Chinese-origin systems reaching Russia could potentially move through an intermediary rather than arrive through a publicly acknowledged direct transfer.
The appearance of an apparently foreign MANPADS with a Russian air defense formation would also raise questions about Moscow’s ability to produce enough short-range air defense weapons domestically to meet growing wartime demand.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has pulled apart Russia’s RM-48U ballistic missile, revealing a weapon assembled from repurposed S-300 and S-400 missile components and packed with foreign electronics, including dozens of parts from US-based manufacturers.

‘We’ve never been in this situation’: Ex-diplomat warns of unprecedented sanctions on Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:15:40 UTC
22:15:40 KST

Avi Pazner, a former Israeli ambassador to Italy and France, warned Monday that Israel could face unprecedented diplomatic isolation and sanctions resembling those imposed on South Africa in the final years of apartheid if the government or its policies do not change. Pazner, who also served as communications adviser to former prime minister Yitzhak Shamir and later chaired Keren Hayesod, made the warning in a message to an internal group of former Foreign Ministry officials, details of which were obtained by ynet.
“Most of us witnessed the process South Africa went through when economic and diplomatic sanctions were imposed on it in the mid-1980s, leading to the collapse of the apartheid regime in the early 1990s,” Pazner wrote.
“At the moment, apart from isolated cases such as in the Netherlands, the sanctions are not being applied, and for now they are directed only at the West Bank,” he continued. “But if the current coalition wins the election, I have no doubt that Israel will enter a situation we have never experienced before in terms of sanctions and boycotts, which will expand from the territories to the entire country.”
His message came amid controversy over customs inspections of passengers arriving in the Netherlands on flights from Israel.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry issued a warning overnight to Israelis planning to travel to the Netherlands following reports of unusually lengthy baggage inspections. The ministry said travelers could face “lengthy and intrusive baggage checks” after a Dutch order banning goods originating in Israeli settlements in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights took effect.
According to the Foreign Ministry, violating the order is a criminal offense that could result in fines or imprisonment.
Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea wrote Monday that several Western European countries that were once considered among Israel’s closest friends were preparing potentially severe sanctions.
“It is no coincidence that these measures have not been completed,” Barnea wrote. “They will keep the weapon loaded and the safety on until October 27, and then, if Netanyahu forms a government, they will begin to act.”
Separately, former Supervisor of Banks Yair Avidan told ynet Monday that there was significant uncertainty over how far sanctions could go and how widely they might spread.
“In an extreme scenario, which could become a working scenario, the sanctions could include leading European banks ending banking activity with Israeli banks,” Avidan said.
His comments came as several countries, mainly in Europe, discuss sanctions targeting Israeli companies and potentially Israel’s banking and financial system over violence in the West Bank and the continuing stalemate in the Gaza Strip.

Euronews explains: Does the EU have enough gas for winter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:13:54 UTC
22:13:54 KST

With winter approaching and gas storage at record-low levels, EU governments are bracing for soaring costs as they compete with Asian buyers to secure supplies and avert power outages.
The European Union is heading into winter with a thin gas cushion, prompting Brussels to warn that the bloc’s energy price crisis could become a supply problem.
In a recent letter to EU capitals seen by Euronews, Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said gas storage levels remain “exceptionally low” after a summer in which hot and dry weather forced countries to burn more gas for electricity, reducing the amount available to refill underground reserves.
Meanwhile, the global market remains deeply affected by the US and Israeli war against Iran, which has cut liquefied natural gas (LNG) flows through the vital Strait of Hormuz to just 15% to 25% of pre-war levels.
On Monday, gas-rich Qatar said it was extending force majeure on LNG shipments to Asian and European customers by another month, with deliveries to the latter set to resume in December.
The result: EU countries keep scrambling to fill their storage levels ahead of winter without incurring astronomical bills.
What is gas storage?
Under EU law, member states need to store natural gas underground — usually in large underground facilities, such as depleted gas fields or salt caverns — when there is plenty of gas available and prices are relatively favourable.
When demand rises, especially in winter, gas can be taken back out and sent into the gas network to heat homes, supply businesses and generate electricity.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, EU countries are obliged to refill their storage levels to 90% by 1 November in a typical year. Given how natural gas prices skyrocketed due to the Middle East disruption, the European Commission gave capitals flexibility in March, allowing them to refill as little as 75% to 80% to avoid panic buying.
"With winter soon approaching, we must continue our preparatory work. Making use of the flexibility provided by the Gas Storage Regulation and reducing the filling target to 80% can help alleviate immediate pressure on prices and refilling costs," reads Jørgensen's letter.
Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Ireland, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta and Slovenia do not have gas storage facilities. However, under the EU's gas storage law, they must make solidarity arrangements with other member states to secure their gas reserves.
Are we running out of gas?
Jørgensen said there are currently no immediate risks to security of supply and stressed that the current energy crisis is "very different" from that in 2022, when the EU abruptly cut Russian gas following the war in Ukraine. Back then, European countries did not experience actual gas shortages or mandatory rationing that left homes without gas.
However, EU storage levels are now lower than they were in 2022, averaging around 70%. Latvia (47.1%), the Netherlands (52.1%) and Germany (55.6%) are registering some of the lowest fill levels based on industry data from 13 September. In contrast, by November 2022, EU gas storage levels averaged 94.9% and ended the year at 83.4%, according to the Commission.
Despite German gas storage levels trailing well behind the EU average and the previous year's figures, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy said on 21 August that it anticipates no winter shortages.
Energy analyst Emil Constantinescu, Founder of EnergyRiskIQ, noted that "the physical buffer is improving, but the market is still attaching a substantial premium to future gas availability and external supply risk".
Nonetheless, the real verdict will come on 8 October, when the EU's association of Europe's transmission system operators, ENTSO-G, is due to unveil its gas supply outlook for the winter.
Why is gas price linked to supply?
With supply tight and demand high, gas is getting more expensive. The smaller the storage buffer, the harder and more expensive it becomes to replenish reserves before winter.
Before the Middle East conflict escalated, Europe's main gas price benchmark, the Dutch TTF, was trading at around €30–31 per megawatt-hour (MWh). It is now around €72–74/MWh — more than twice as high — after briefly jumping above €80–89/MWh earlier in September.
Even if the EU's top energy leader said that the bloc is better prepared than it was before the 2022 energy shock, its low gas stocks leave it less room to absorb another global supply disruption without paying a heavy price.
Dutch Climate Minister Stientje van Veldhoven said that the Netherlands wants the EU to end its mandatory natural gas storage filling targets when the current rules expire in 2027, arguing that forcing countries to fill their gas reserves to set levels puts an unfair burden on them.
Gasunie, the Dutch natural gas infrastructure and transportation company operating in the Netherlands, voiced similar concerns, citing the country's increasing dependence on international gas flows.
"We recommend preparing for a crisis that could last several months. Ultimately, it is for policymakers to determine what level of risk the Netherlands is prepared to accept," Gasunie recently stated.
What is the worst-case scenario?
Energy analysts argue that if the EU experiences a severely cold winter combined with continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz, global LNG prices could nearly double current prices, forcing Europe to aggressively outbid Asian markets for US gas.
Ultimately, a gas shortage could turn into an electricity crisis because of the way power grids and energy markets are designed. Since many power plants rely on natural gas to make electricity, a drop in the gas supply quickly drives up power bills and strains the grid.
Ronald Pinto, principal insight analyst at the market intelligence firm Kpler, said that gas shortages aren't foreseen at the moment. However, in such an event, the power sector would likely feel the impact.
"Gas often ends up as the marginal producer, particularly in winter; a gas shortage could propel a TTF rally, which could in turn lead to high power prices across Europe. The situation could be exacerbated if it coincides with cold temperatures and low wind generation," Pinto told Euronews.
Europe's energy crisis comes at the worst possible time for EU countries, which have already introduced tax cut measures, subsidies, and other market-based tools to cushion soaring prices — while struggling with domestic finances.
A deteriorating scenario could prompt the Commission to coordinate joint gas purchasing to ensure lower prices and better distribution, as it did in 2022. French President Emmanuel Macron recently urged Brussels to revisit the measure.

Can birdwatching help stroke recovery? Researchers say it could aid communication skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:13:40 UTC
22:13:40 KST

Watching birds has become a meaningful part of stroke recovery at the University of Montana, offering a natural, low-pressure way to practise communication, researchers say.
In Montana, in the United States, a surprising animal has become part of stroke patients’ recovery journey.
Cooper's hawks, a bird native to North America, may offer stroke survivors a chance to connect, talk, and build community around birdwatching, helping them regain communication skills often lost after a stroke.
One of the most common consequences of a stroke is impaired ability to speak, understand speech, read, and write, known as aphasia. It affects approximately one-third of stroke survivors — an estimated 11,000 people acquire it every day.
“Aphasia is an identity theft,” said Catherine Off, a researcher at the University of Montana. “People with aphasia do not have intellectual challenges. They are themselves inside their own head. The challenge is that their language function has changed.”
She co-directs the Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Program (ICAP) at the University of Montana, aiming to counter these effects.
Participants usually attend four days a week for four weeks, providing roughly 80 hours of rehabilitation. Each stroke survivor is paired with a trained communication partner, typically a graduate student in speech-language pathology, who supports communication during the activities while avian ecologists lead on content.
“Communication function doesn’t improve until you want to communicate about something,” Off said. “We’re out of the therapy room now. We’re saying: Enjoy being with people, enjoy being outside and let the communication come.”
For stroke survivors living with aphasia, maintaining typical conversations can be difficult and that’s where birdwatching comes in, moving interactions from the purely linguistic towards broader communication, such as pointing, drawing or looking through photographs.
This allows survivors to remain socially engaged even when verbal output is limited, researchers say in a new paper published in the journal Frontiers in Bird Science.
While early results are encouraging, the researchers note that the program is still in its conceptual stage, and they are currently working to gather the formal clinical evidence needed to prove its long-term effectiveness.
Need to improve stroke survivors' quality of life
The incidence and prevalence of stroke are expected to continue rising over the next 25 years. It is currently the third leading cause of adult death and disability worldwide, and the lifetime risk of having a stroke has risen by more than 50% over the past 17 years.
At the same time, the number of people who survive a stroke is increasing, highlighting the need to maintain their quality of life as they age.
The Montana researchers warned that unequal access to high-quality prevention, acute care and rehabilitation services further complicates recovery. Birdwatching, they argue, could also improve accessibility.
“Birds are one of those rare things where your entry point can be anywhere – from sitting and staring out a window to mapping out a trail to see a unique species,” said Victoria Dreitz, an avian ecologist in the university’s Wildlife Biology Program.
“You can start where you’re at. What do you have in your backyard? That’s what it's about,” Dreitz said.

====================================================================================================

'They traded us away': Students suing Columbia describe years of hostility over Palestine advocacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:10:07 UTC
22:10:07 KST

In October 2023, shortly after Israel's war on Gaza began, a truck began circling Columbia University's campus.
It displayed the names and photographs of pro-Palestinian students and branded them the university's "leading anti-Semites."
For Bhavana Bellamkonda, one of the students featured on the truck, it marked a moment when hostility toward pro-Palestinian advocacy became personal – and frightening.
"The conditions on campus were becoming more and more hostile, and students were fearing for their safety," Bellamkonda, who has since graduated from Columbia, told Anadolu.
Now, Bellamkonda is among a group of current and former students who, along with Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil and Columbia's Palestine Working Group (PWG), are suing the university over allegations of years of anti-Palestinian discrimination, indifference to harassment and retaliation.
The lawsuit, filed in Manhattan federal court this month, accuses Columbia of violating federal civil rights law by failing to protect students from threats, doxxing and other harassment over their Arab or Muslim ancestry or advocacy for Palestinian rights.
The case also brings renewed attention to Khalil, who was detained by US immigration authorities in March 2025 and held for 104 days in Louisiana, about 1,300 miles (2,092 kilometers) from his family.
He missed the birth of his first child while in detention.
Khalil, a US lawful permanent resident, was released in June 2025 but remains locked in a legal battle with the Trump administration over efforts to deport him.
According to the plaintiffs, however, the hostility they experienced at Columbia began long before Khalil's detention.
Bellamkonda described incidents of bullying and harassment, including Muslim students having their hijabs pulled off and being called "terrorists."
"I myself was called a terrorist in one of my classes by an Israeli student who's actually the research assistant for the Dean of SIPA," she said, referring to Columbia's School of International and Public Affairs.
She argues that Columbia's failure to address such incidents helped create an environment in which pro-Palestinian students became increasingly vulnerable, and says the university's handling of the "coordinated harassment" helped pave the way for Khalil to be targeted by immigration authorities.
The lawsuit alleges that Columbia knew pro-Palestinian students were facing persistent threats, doxxing and harassment but failed to adequately protect them.
"Columbia laid the groundwork for my targeting by the Trump administration through its deliberate indifference and discrimination against Palestinian students," Khalil said in a statement related to the lawsuit.
"For over two years, we pleaded with Columbia, and Columbia did not care," he said. "They traded us away. We are suing because no one should go through the hell Columbia put us through."
Bellamkonda said some of the information displayed on the truck naming students and calling them anti-Semites had been pulled from CampusGroups, a university platform requiring a login.
After a similar truck appeared at Harvard earlier that month, she said students asked School of International and Public Affairs Dean Keren Yarhi-Milo for protection and for information that could facilitate doxxing to be removed from university systems.
"Ultimately, we didn't receive support from Columbia. Instead, it felt like the dean … got frustrated with us for asking for this support," she said. “Advocacy for Palestinian rights or any human rights shouldn't make someone disposable.”
A Columbia spokesperson declined to comment on the pending litigation but told Anadolu the university is committed to a campus where all students feel "welcome, supported, and safe" and are protected from discrimination and harassment.
The spokesperson also defended Yarhi-Milo, saying she had supported students of all backgrounds, including Palestinian, Arab and Muslim students, and was committed to maintaining a campus "free of discrimination and harassment."
Mohammad Ibrahim Zubairi, a Pakistani graduate of Columbia’s School of International and Public Affairs, told Anadolu that his advocacy for pro-Palestinian students and the backlash he faced affected his academic and professional plans.
He said tensions escalated after he encouraged US citizen students to exercise their right to protest on behalf of noncitizens, including Khalil, who was in ICE detention at the time.
"I was asking others to protest in this incident. I was asking US citizens to use their voice," he said. "Then someone started accusing me of being aggressive and inciting violence."
"Instead of just saying, ‘this is your own constitutional right,’ they told me that I wasn't a resident of the country and that I should have checked my violence at the door," he added.
Zubairi, who received a full scholarship for his master's degree, said the turmoil also disrupted his professional plans, with much of the time he would have spent looking for work instead devoted to advocating for his detained friend.
"I was not really expecting the experience to be as hostile as it was," he said.
He said Columbia was the first place where he experienced what he viewed as institutional pressure over his identity and political advocacy.
Zubairi said speaking out against what he called "all this unjustifiable violence" was treated as incompatible with being "a good Muslim man."
"As if you're going to be a Muslim on campus, you just can't be criticizing the West," he said.
Coming from Pakistan, Zubairi said he was surprised by the censorship and pressure he encountered in the US, where "they talk about freedom of speech, civil liberties," and where "the civil rights struggle was born."
He eventually returned to Pakistan.
"I was just kind of disillusioned with the US in general," he said.
He said he was uncertain whether, after publicly associating himself with pro-Palestinian activism, he would be allowed to return to the US under the current administration.
Brittany Finley, an attorney representing Khalil and the other plaintiffs, said the university not only failed to protect pro-Palestinian students but also subjected them to disciplinary action.
Finley began representing students in those proceedings after Columbia established its Office of Institutional Equity (OIE) in August 2024 as a centralized office to handle reports of discrimination and discriminatory harassment.
She alleges that the office began targeting pro-Palestinian students, including Khalil, almost immediately.
Even before Khalil’s detention, she said, "I was witnessing the fear that these students had."
"Columbia itself, as an institution, went after students through the OIE proceedings," Finley said.
"From its inception, this organization existed to target Palestinian students," she alleged, saying the proceedings were "intended to intimidate these students and try to stifle their advocacy efforts."
Finley said Khalil was repeatedly subjected to OIE proceedings that she viewed as baseless.
"They targeted him multiple times, all in meritless ways of trying to frame him as a person who he is not," she said.
She said the pressure on pro-Palestinian students intensified after Oct. 7, 2023, and eventually extended to the Palestine Working Group, which remains indefinitely suspended.
Finley said Khalil repeatedly warned Columbia that he was being harassed and "horribly doxxed by Columbia affiliates" in the days leading up to his ICE detention.
In early March 2025, he filed a report with the Office of Institutional Equity and emailed Columbia’s president
"I haven't been able to sleep, fearing that ICE or a dangerous individual might come to my home," Khalil wrote. "I urgently need legal support, and I urge you to intervene."
In the email and report, Khalil said Columbia affiliates had publicly accused him of being a "national security threat," questioned his immigration status, tagged Secretary of State Marco Rubio in an accusatory post and exposed him to threats "both online and within Columbia-affiliated spaces."
He was detained the following day.
The plaintiffs are seeking damages, the reinstatement of the Palestine Working Group and restored campus access for Khalil, according to the lawsuit.
Khalil remains barred from Columbia's main campus despite graduating while in detention, while the Trump administration continues its efforts to deport him.
"His cases haven't been resolved and Columbia hasn't offered any sort of support," Finley said. "They've only reached out to him to ask him to move off of campus property after he was released from detention."
