How the Iran war has rewritten the Gulf's security calculus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:10:01 UTC
22:10:01 KST

Breadcrumb
How the Iran war has rewritten the Gulf's security calculus
The US-Israeli war on Iran and its chaotic spillover effects across the Middle East and beyond have forced the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) members to come to terms with new realities.
Calculations about the Gulf’s security architecture are being reassessed, and Gulf states have been seriously questioning longstanding assumptions about the United States’ commitment to their security in the face of regional threats, chiefly from Iran, which retaliated against US and Israeli attacks by firing missiles and drones at the GCC states since the outset of this conflict on 28 February.
Looking ahead, what will emerge from this conflict is unclear. There will not be imminent reconciliation between Gulf Arab monarchies and Iran. Nor will the Gulf Arab monarchies make a straightforward move away from Washington.
What appears likely is a complicated transition whereby the GCC members reduce their dependence on the United States, bolster their own military capabilities, further diversify defence partnerships with alternative powers, and explore ways to manage tensions with the Islamic Republic diplomatically.
What could emerge is a more fragmented Gulf order whereby GCC states seek greater autonomy from Washington while still counting on the United States to remain an indispensable military force in the sub-region.
Dr Mehran Kamrava, a professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, does not envision Washington reducing its commitment to GCC members.
“There has been talk that some of the US military bases that dot the region are damaged beyond repair and that the US may not rebuild them after the war is over. Still, it seems doubtful that at least in the short to medium run, the United States would reduce its security commitment to the Persian Gulf states in any significant way,” he told The New Arab.
Any new Gulf security order must include Iran
The Gulf Arab monarchies clearly recognise that Iran is their permanent neighbour, and it is impossible to simply exclude Tehran from the Gulf’s future security architecture, as demonstrated by recent statements from high-ranking officials.
In his address to the United Nations General Assembly this month, the Emir of Qatar Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani called for a “regional system of collective security” and said that “we remain convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, through reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, in order to avert war”.
Similarly, Anwar Gargash, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed’s Diplomatic Adviser, recently argued that there needs to be direct dialogue between Arab states and Tehran about the region’s future and a “new mindset” in how Arab states approach Iran.
Efforts to pressure Iran have produced limited results, explained Dr Kamrava. Pointing to a “realisation that the effort to marginalise and isolate Iran, not just economically but also in military and security matters, has yielded little success,” he told The New Arab that “the GCC impetus to assume a confrontational posture in relation to Iran, as was the case in the 2010s, has clearly backfired”.
Dr Kamrava stressed that the Islamic Republic has posed much less of a threat to its GCC neighbours when these Arab states engaged Tehran diplomatically compared to the times when they sought Tehran’s isolation.
“Moreover, Iran has long called for the articulation of a regional security arrangement that takes into account all regional actors instead of only a select group of them. If Iran does indeed become part of a broader security arrangement with its GCC neighbours, there is far greater likelihood of stability and reduced tensions than has been the case so far,” he added.
Dr Ghoncheh Tazmini, author of ‘Power Couple: Russian-Iranian Alignment in the Middle East’, explained that statements such as those made by the Emir of Qatar and Gargash do not suggest that a “reset” in GCC-Iran relations is coming soon.
Such statements appear to be acknowledging the basic geopolitical reality that whatever GCC members’ differences are with Tehran, Iran is a major regional actor whose interests and capabilities cannot be wished away.
“What these statements suggest is a recognition that Iran cannot be excluded from any durable security order in the Persian Gulf. Qatar’s emphasis on collective security and Gargash’s call for direct Arab-Iranian dialogue point to greater regional agency: the states of the Persian Gulf cannot leave the terms of their security entirely to negotiations between Tehran and Washington,” she told The New Arab.
More than seven months after the United States and Israel began this war on Iran, GCC states are making different assessments about what can be done to realistically achieve stability, economic diversification, and secure trade routes. Each of these is extremely difficult to achieve without engaging the Iranians diplomatically and relying excessively on external powers.
This does not mean that GCC members are anywhere close to trusting Iran or overcoming their grave concerns about Tehran’s regional foreign policy. This is especially so for the Gulf Arab states which have suffered the most from Iranian missile and drone strikes since late February.
This change in GCC states’ assessments about how to deal with Tehran “brings them closer to an idea Iran has promoted for years, namely that the region's security should be managed by regional actors,” said Dr Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, in an interview with The New Arab.
“Gulf Arab states resisted that proposition in the past because they feared it would legitimise Iranian influence. Increasingly, however, there is a recognition that any durable regional order will have to include Iran and that dialogue may offer a more realistic path to stability than continued reliance on an uncertain external security architecture,” he added.
Pushing for regional mechanisms to prevent the next war
Calls for a “regional system of collective security” and advocacy of direct Arab-Iranian dialogue are understood within the context of GCC states increasingly seeking ways to manage regional security beyond traditional deterrence.
The absence of an inclusive framework in which rivals can address disputes before they escalate has become increasingly problematic.
“The GCC, for all its limitations, managed this well among its members between 1981 and 2017 when various combinations of members defused bilateral tensions and potential clashes through GCC channels,” Dr Rory Miller, a professor of international politics at Georgetown University in Qatar, told The New Arab.
“Of course, such calls for these conflict resolution and management mechanisms are going to be more common now than ever because when you have a security vacuum you have two options: fill it through offensive actions, such as the militarisation of differences, and defensive engagement, such as conflict management through negotiation,” he added.
“In these terms, these calls by [the Emir of Qatar and Gargash] strongly signal that the defensive route is what Gulf countries are considering now.”
Diversifying defence partnerships without replacing Washington
As Gulf Arab states call for more regional diplomacy, there is also a growing recognition of their need for more robust drone and missile capabilities, along with greater interest in domestic defence industries and diversified weapons procurement.
Gulf governments will seek to reduce their exposure to changes in Washington’s foreign policy by enhancing regional defence cooperation, strengthening indigenous military capabilities, and developing relationships with a wider range of international partners to gain greater autonomy from the United States, albeit without attempting to replace Washington.
While this trend is not new and was set in motion by past episodes, including the 2019 Aramco attacks and Israel’s attack on Doha last year, the ongoing regional crisis has served to accelerate it, with events of this year highlighting how exposed the GCC states are to insecurity while so dependent on the United States as a security guarantor.
Lessons learned
As a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Gulf Arab governments have been forced to learn important albeit painful lessons about both Iran and the United States.
For starters, as Dr Kamrava explained, GCC states can no longer shrug off Tehran’s threats to attack US military installations in the Gulf.
“Iranian warnings of attacking American assets in the Persian Gulf, of which there were plenty before the war, should not be ignored. This is something that Iranian visitors to the Arab states would often repeat, and they were repeatedly ignored. That can no longer be the case,” he told The New Arab.
Dr Quilliam pointed out the extent of Tehran’s means to hit GCC states hard, particularly in their vulnerable areas.
“Iran has shown that it retains the capacity to inflict considerable economic and security costs on the region despite years of sanctions and attempts to constrain its behaviour,” he said in an interview with The New Arab.
“At the same time, Gulf leaders have been reminded that Washington’s priorities are not always aligned with their own. The US can enter or escalate a conflict and then leave regional states to deal with many of the consequences,” added Quilliam, who sees these dynamics encouraging GCC members to coordinate more closely with each other.
Economic ambitions depend on a more secure region
The Gulf Arab monarchies can no longer treat economic security and national security as separate concerns. Disruptions to maritime trade, energy exports, investment flows, and critical infrastructure can quickly undermine the ambitious and grandiose economic diversification agendas such as Saudi Vision 2030, which have become central to the Gulf’s future.
“For governments focused on economic transformation, the protection of supply chains, maritime routes, critical infrastructure and investor confidence is now as important as conventional defence,” Dr Quilliam told The New Arab.
The Strait of Hormuz clearly highlights this vulnerability, bringing us to the fact that geography itself can become a strategic instrument.
Although the GCC states possess vast financial resources and increasingly advanced military capabilities, these countries lack the means to eliminate the strategic importance of a narrow maritime passage through which a substantial share of global energy trade transits. This comes with significant implications.
The future Gulf security architecture will have to protect the infrastructure, trade routes and economic relationships on which the region’s prosperity depends.
“The overriding lesson is vulnerability. The war has demonstrated how quickly the states of the Persian Gulf, their infrastructure and their economies can become exposed to a conflict involving Iran and external powers. It has also demonstrated the continuing importance of Hormuz: geography itself can become a strategic instrument, and military superiority cannot entirely remove that reality,” Dr Tazmini told The New Arab.
“Hormuz has for centuries been a space in which Iran, the Arab states of the Persian Gulf and external maritime powers have encountered one another. What has changed strikingly is Iran’s position within that geography: a Strait that once exposed the limits of Iranian maritime power has today become an important instrument of Iranian strategic influence. That historical reversal will form part of the context in which any post-war regional order takes shape,” she added.
Between Washington, Tehran, and greater autonomy
Looking at the bigger picture, what seems to be emerging is a Gulf that has lost its willingness to remain so dependent on the United States for security.
Nonetheless, throughout the foreseeable future, Washington is set to continue serving as the dominant external military actor in the Gulf even as GCC states pursue their efforts to diversify their defence relationships beyond the United States by turning to states such as China, France, Pakistan, Turkey, and Russia.
Not lost in the equation is the fact that the experience of being attacked by Iran has likely strengthened the case for GCC states to directly engage Tehran and seek to establish regional mechanisms capable of preventing disputes from escalating into wider conflicts.
“I think the dilemma for these Gulf states is on the one hand there is a desire for dialogue, for reaching some sort of an accommodation with Iran to explore possibly a new security architecture with Iran that includes Iran’s concerns in terms of security for the entire Middle East,” Dr Nader Hashemi, the director of the Prince Alwaleed Center for Christian-Muslim Understanding at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, told The New Arab.
“But, on the other hand, all of these countries are still deeply dependent in terms of their military relationship, their intelligence cooperation, their political relationship with the United States,” he explained.
“So, it’s not easy for these Gulf states to move in the direction of a new relationship with Iran when they will be pressed by the United States to maintain the status quo.”
Ultimately, the order that emerges following the current US-Iran crisis will probably not be a return to the pre-28 February model, nor a total break from it.
In all likelihood, a new balance will be struck whereby Washington’s power remains important, but the Gulf Arab states are increasingly serious about greater self-reliance, diversification of defence partnerships, and diplomacy with Iran.
A key question for the post-war Gulf will be whether the GCC members can successfully establish durable institutions that permit them to mitigate, manage, and contain their tensions with Iran while maintaining their close partnerships with the United States.
“My own view is that nothing is going to change as long as Donald Trump is in the White House. The next president might create more space and room for these Gulf states to renegotiate a new relationship with Iran in terms of the region’s security architecture while at the same time maintaining a close alliance with the United States,” said Dr Hashemi.
“One thing is clear is that long-standing assumptions within these Gulf states regarding their national security strategy have completely unravelled and come undone. We’re in the process of transformation and it’s unclear what’s going to happen next.”
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics

EU seeks hybrid threat playbook without duplicating NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:09:16 UTC
22:09:16 KST

EU foreign and defence ministers backed further work on a new protocol for responding to hybrid threats, while stressing that it must complement rather than duplicate NATO.
The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said European foreign affairs and defence ministers urged her and the EU executive to not to duplicate North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) protocol when developing a playbook to deal with hybrid threats.
“Many stress that it has to be absolutely complementarity with NATO,” she said at a press conference following a foreign affairs council meeting in Brussels on Monday. “We don't create anything additional, but this has to work hand in hand.”
Kallas could not say how many of the 27 member states supported the anti-hybrid warfare mechanism, as not all ministers took to the floor to give their views.
“Today was a very initial discussion, which means that we take this forward,” she said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first unveiled her proposal for a so-called “emergency security protocol” in mid-September during her State of the European Union address.
The protocol aims to help member states coordinate their responses quickly when a hybrid threat is identified. It would sit under the umbrella of the new Security Strategy, spearheaded by Kallas and von der Leyen, expected for publication by the year's end.
Von der Leyen said in her State of the European Union address that this would be “Europe’s own Article 4”.
When triggered at NATO level, Article 4 requires member countries to consult whenever an ally feels its territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.
It is the precursor to Article 5, the collective defence principle stating that an attack on one is an attack on all.
Asked by Euronews how the EU’s emergency protocol would not mimic NATO’s efforts, Kallas said NATO’s Article 4 does not necessitate action. “It's not any kind of action plan,” she said.
“The emergency protocol is rather which tools can be used at the moment for aggression that is not armed aggression that is under the threshold of Article 5."
‘No new pledges today’ on supplying Ukraine Patriot interceptor missiles
Ukraine’s Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara briefed EU ministers via video link on the country's frontline situation, with Kallas stating he made it “very clear” that air defence support remains the country’s top priority.
Kallas entered the meeting highlighting that member states and allies could use the opportunity to provide Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine from their own stockpiles to shoot down Russian airborne threats.
Ukraine desperately needs more US-made Patriot air defense systems as a shield against Russian ballistic missiles. But Patriots are in short supply after the war in Iran began, further depleting American stocks.
Experts have estimated it could take around three years for the US to restore stocks of advanced missiles and defensive interceptors to pre-war levels.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously said Ukraine needs hundreds more of the interceptors to survive the upcoming winter, with the country receiving only 1% of the missiles it needs from Washington.
“On the interceptors, unfortunately, there were no new pledges made today,” Kallas clarified.
Spain and Greece have previously been lobbied by Brussels to hand over interceptors from their respective arsenals, however, have so far refused to provide any to Kyiv, citing security concerns.

Medical nurse sentenced to 18 months in prison for accidentally killing patient  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:08:02 UTC
22:08:02 KST

RIGA - The Riga City Court on Monday handed down a prison sentence of 18 months to a medical nurse from the Children’s Clinical University Hospital (BKUS) who, last November, accidentally killed a patient by mixing up medications.
As an additional penalty, the nurse was barred from practicing medicine for four years.
However, the court ruled not to award EUR 500,000 in moral damages claimed by the victim’s family.
Judge Imants Dzenis explained that, after reviewing the case law cited by the defense, the court concluded that awarding compensation for moral damages in this case would be premature. The victim's family therefore should be given the opportunity to seek compensation through civil proceedings.
The defendant’s legal representative noted that the defense would consider appealing the judgment and requested that a full written judgment be prepared. She emphasized that legal considerations suggest that actual imprisonment might not be applicable as a punishment for the defendant.
During the trial, the judge imposed on the defendant the base sentence and additional penalty requested by the prosecution, so the prosecutor currently sees no grounds for appealing the verdict, LETA learned from the prosecutor’s office.
The parties to the case may request that the court prepare a full judgment, and, once received, the judgment may be appealed within ten weekdays.
Information in the court calendar indicates that the defendant is Jelena Ugurenko. The nurse has admitted her guilt and expressed remorse, the defendant’s defense lawyer Aldis Liepins previously told reporters.
He noted that the medication mix-up had been a "fatal coincidence of circumstances" and a great misfortune. He also said that no one becomes a medical nurse with the intention of causing such a tragedy.
As reported, the nurse was charged with negligent performance of her professional duties, which, due to her carelessness, resulted in the death of a minor, the Prosecutor’s Office informed LETA.
The prosecutor’s office notes that the defendant, as a healthcare professional, prepared a sodium bicarbonate solution prescribed by a doctor during her shift in late November of last year for administration to the patient the following day. According to the indictment, by negligently performing her professional duties, the nurse failed to verify that the medication had been prepared correctly, as, while preparing the infusion bag, instead of a sodium bicarbonate solution, she prepared a potassium chloride solution but labeled it "Sodium Bicarbonate."
The next morning, the patient began receiving the incorrectly prepared solution. Shortly thereafter, she began complaining of dizziness and difficulty breathing.
Despite resuscitation efforts, the patient’s life could not be saved. Due to the administration of the potassium-containing solution, the child suffered irreversible cardiac arrest, resulting in her death.
Currently, the defendant is subject to a non-custodial security measure, as well as a prohibition on practicing her profession as an additional security measure.

Logistics company Venipak has increased the number of compartments at its most popular parcel lockers in Latvia by around 15% this year. The expansion of parcel locker capacity in Latvia forms part of more than €2.5 million in investments in infrastructure development and modernisation across the Baltics. The company’s total investment this year is its highest in several years. At the same time, logistics terminals in Lithuania and Estonia are being expanded and modernised, while process automation is also being increased.
This year, Venipak is placing particular focus on increasing parcel locker capacity in the most heavily used locations. The number of compartments at the company’s most popular parcel lockers in Latvia has increased by around 15%. Parcel locker capacity is also being expanded in Lithuania and Estonia.
“In Latvia, we are currently focusing on increasing capacity in locations where parcel lockers are used most intensively. This allows us to handle larger parcel volumes, particularly during the busiest periods of the year. Our goal is to ensure that, even as parcel volumes continue to grow, deliveries remain convenient and timely for our customers,” says Sanita Bērziņa, CEO of Venipak Latvia.
Increasing automation and terminal capacity across the Baltics
Alongside the expansion of its parcel locker network, Venipak is investing in the development and automation of its logistics terminals. Rapidly growing parcel volumes and labour market conditions are prompting the company to place increasing emphasis on technological solutions and reducing reliance on manual processes.
Most of this year’s investments are being directed towards infrastructure development projects in Lithuania. From September, the company is moving into a new terminal in Klaipėda that is approximately 60% larger than its previous facility and covers 3,900 square metres. The upgraded infrastructure will enable Venipak to handle twice as many parcels as before.
This autumn, a new automated parcel sorting conveyor will also be installed at Venipak’s largest logistics terminal in Kaunas, increasing sorting capacity from 3,000 to 7,000 parcels per hour.
“Kaunas is our main logistics hub in Lithuania, connecting parcel flows across the Baltics and Poland with the rest of Europe. The new sorting line will enable us to process parcels faster and more accurately, while also increasing the overall efficiency of the network,” says Andrius Ladauskas, CEO of Venipak.
In the first half of 2027, Venipak also plans to relocate to a new 13 500-square-metre logistics terminal in Vilnius. The project represents a total investment of €16 million.
Expansion is also planned in Ukmergė and Šiauliai in Lithuania, as well as at the Tartu terminal in Estonia. The company is also considering opening an additional terminal in Estonia and modernising other sorting centres.
Venipak currently operates around 800 parcel lockers and 25 logistics terminals across the Baltics. The company employs approximately 1000 people and works with around 350 independent couriers.
Venipak Group generated revenue of €85.6 million in 2025, with EBITDA reaching €12.4 million.

RIGA - European Union member countries should use the current period of fiscal flexibility to gradually restructure their budgets, taking into account that defense spending will be higher in the foreseeable future, European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis (New Unity) told LETA.
Increasing defense spending is particularly relevant for Latvia, which shares a border with Russia, but this puts pressure on other budget items and the budget deficit, said Dombrovskis.
From 2025 to 2028, EU member countries will have additional flexibility under EU fiscal rules regarding defense spending, which may amount to up to 1.5 percent of gross domestic product annually.
According to Dombrovskis, during this period countries can increase defense spending without immediately adjusting other budget expenditure items or revenues. A return to the usual EU fiscal rules is to begin in 2029.
Dombrovskis noted that countries must also address budget sustainability issues. In Latvia, these issues may not be as pronounced as in other countries with high debt levels. Interest rates on government borrowing currently remain relatively high, and all countries must work to put their budget deficits and debts on a downward trajectory, he said.
When asked about support for eastern border regions provided for in the next EU multiannual budget, Dombrovskis explained that a member country's status as an eastern border region is one of the criteria used in calculating the national allocation. In the European Commission's proposal for 2028-2034, Latvia would be allocated EUR 9.3 billion, and Latvia's status as a border region has already been taken into account in this calculation.

Families welcome guilty verdict over Mali crash that killed 116

The French court on Monday fined the airline €225,000 ($256,000; £193,000), the maximum penalty, over the crash that killed all 116 people on board flight AH5017 from the Burkina Faso capital, Ouagadougou, to Algeria's main airport in Algiers.
Swiftair's defence rejected the French investigation, describing the case as "a botched job".
Spanish prosecutors had previously closed their own investigation without bringing any charges.
The airline has 10 days to appeal.
The court said "negligence" in Swiftair's training had "certainly contributed to the accident".
The McDonnell Douglas MD-83, owned by Swiftair and leased to Air Algérie with its crew, crashed in northern Mali on 24 July 2014.
Those killed included 54 French citizens, 23 Burkinabè nationals, as well as Lebanese and Algerian passengers and six Spanish crew members.
The crash happened as the aircraft flew through a storm in the semi-arid Sahel region, south of the Sahara Desert.
Investigators found that the anti-icing system had not been activated, causing ice crystals to form on pressure sensors. This led to an automatic reduction in engine power and the subsequent crash.
The trial opened in Paris in March, more than 12 years after the disaster.
Nathalie Police, who lost her 65-year-old father Didier and her 18-year-old half-brother Nicolas, attended the entire four-week trial.
Outside the court on Monday, she stood alongside Tricot. Both welcomed the ruling.
"The amount of money was never the end goal. We are relieved that justice has finally been delivered," Tricot told the BBC.
"No amount of money could bring back our loved ones."
Tricot heads the French national federation for victims of terrorist attacks and collective accidents, which joined the case as a civil party.
She said it had been difficult to coordinate with families in Algeria and Burkina Faso who also lost relatives, but hoped the ruling would bring them some peace.
"The conviction is an important step towards recognising criminal responsibility for the disaster."
Sébastien Busy, a lawyer representing most of the victims, described the conviction as a relief. He said Swiftair would also have to cover legal costs, which could exceed the €225,000 fine.

====================================================================================================

For years Ukraine could jam or switch off Russia’s battlefield comms. Rassvet may be the first it can’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:06:30 UTC
22:06:30 KST

Russia's low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation Rassvet went from a few minutes of connectivity over Ukraine to two stable windows lasting more than an hour each in just five months. The system was built by the Russian private company Bureau 1440 as Moscow's answer to Starlink.
As of now, it is nowhere near matching SpaceX's 10,000-satellite network—but the gap between what Russia has now and what it needs is closing, and the tools that could slow it down mostly sit unused. When Ukraine and SpaceX bricked Russian-obtained Starlink terminals earlier this year, Russian assaults froze across the front—proof that cutting satellite command-and-control links matters more than disrupting guidance. Russia is now building its own links. The most consequential tool that could slow that down is Western sanctions against Bureau 1440 itself.
Four years of Western sanctions have failed to cut Russia off from the foreign components its missile and drone factories rely on: parts manufactured after sanctions were imposed still reach Russian assembly lines within months. Rassvet is a new version of the same problem. The system is still being built and relies on imported components whose exact origin is disputed—some experts point to American and European parts reaching Russia through sanctions-evasion networks, others say the core hardware is built from off-the-shelf Chinese components. Its manufacturer remains unsanctioned by any Western government, while some of the infrastructure needed to expand production has already been struck by Ukraine.
Six minutes in March, two hours by August
In March 2026, Bureau 1440 launched its first operational batch of 16 Rassvet satellites from Plesetsk Cosmodrome. Each pass over Ukraine created a window of six to 10 minutes, Serhii Beskrestnov, callsign Flash, a Ukrainian presidential adviser on defense technology, estimated at the time.
By late August, the picture had changed. Tracking data from N2YO showed four passes a day and two stable communication windows lasting more than an hour each. Satellite communications expert Volodymyr Stepanets said that 12 of the 16 satellites from the first batch had reached their operational altitude of 550 km, three were still ascending, and one had burned up—likely due to a manufacturing defect. A second batch of 16 went into orbit in July, though those satellites struggled to reach their target altitude and some may reenter the atmosphere.
The second batch may be climbing faster than the first did at the same stage. Still, Russia is far from the 200–250 satellites Beskrestnov considers necessary for stable, round-the-clock coverage, and the altitude of roughly 550 km is still short of the roughly 800 km the constellation is designed to reach.
What Rassvet would change on the battlefield
Russia is unlikely to have any civilian use in mind for these communication windows. The satellites transmit in the Ka and Ku bands—high-frequency signals that are difficult to jam and difficult to detect.
Right now, Ukraine's electronic warfare can push Russian drones offline: a Shahed flying low through a jammed zone loses its link and drifts off course. A satellite relay overhead would change that. The drone holds its course, receives updated coordinates mid-flight, stays below radar, and strikes. The constellation could do this for long-range strike and naval drones alike—letting them operate through electronic warfare at very low altitudes, where Ukraine's air defenses struggle to see them.
Bureau 1440 has also developed user terminals small enough to fit on Geran-type attack drones and cruise missiles. Gerans have struck Ukrainian territory, including Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, almost continuously over the past month. A terminal on a Geran would turn a one-way munition into a weapon that can be redirected after launch. Unlike the Starlink terminals Ukraine relies on, which are geographically restricted, Russian terminals are expected to face no such limits—the same terminal that connects a Geran over Kyiv Oblast would work over Berlin or Paris.
The sanctions lever—and the gap in it
Rassvet's parent company, IKS Holding, is one of Russia's largest hardware and software developers. The US sanctioned the holding, its then-owner Anton Cherepennikov, and the subsidiaries Kryptonit and KNS Group on 24 February 2023. Cherepennikov died under unexplained circumstances, but the company keeps operating.
Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) says the holding serves as a personnel reserve for the Federal Security Service (FSB). The first deputy CEO of IKS Holding is Boris Korolyov, son of FSB First Deputy Director Sergei Korolyov, according to the SZRU. He took the post at 27 in 2023, after Cherepennikov's death.
More importantly, though, is the company that actually builds the satellites—Bureau 1440—and its leadership. Ukraine has placed the company on its own sanctions list, but Kyiv's unilateral designations carry limited trade enforcement power, because these people and this company are absent from Western lists. At Euromaidan Press's request, the US-based research organization C4ADS confirmed that Bureau 1440 and its leadership sit outside every Western sanctions regime, and called designating the manufacturer the single most visible and effective step available.
Ukrainian brigades detail Starlink crackdown: Russian terminals “became just bricks,” assaults disrupted
From the Ukrainian side, Viktoriia Vyshnivska, a senior analyst at the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO), told Euromaidan Press that sanctions on Bureau 1440 are not a magic button—but they are not pointless, either. Because Bureau 1440 uses Western equipment, designating the company would directly affect trade in those boards and components, she said. Any Western manufacturer that kept doing business with the company would also risk investigation and legal consequences.
Given the reach of Russia's sanctions-evasion networks and its close ties with China in joint production and technology sharing.
"We shouldn't expect a magical effect," Vyshnivska said.
But sanctions would make direct trade impossible and raise the cost and difficulty of sourcing Western components.
Even if the useful window is short, making supplies more expensive and harder to find is the point.
Many of the goods Bureau 1440 uses are already banned from sale to Russia under EU export controls, Vyshnivska noted. Yet Bureau 1440 itself is still absent from the sanctions lists. Her recommendation: Bureau 1440, its current owners, its parent company, the key related entities and individuals, and its main suppliers should all be designated.
Diplomacy: Ukraine goes to the ITU
Beyond that, Ukraine is trying to act on its own on several fronts.
The first is diplomacy. On 28 August, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine had sent a formal note to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates radio frequencies, demanding that Ukrainian territory be excluded from Rassvet's service areas across all frequency bands. The system's use over Ukraine "has nothing to do with civilian purposes," he wrote on X.
Days later, at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland, Sybiha handed partners a list of nine legal entities linked to the project and urged them to impose sanctions.
The EU had already moved once: its 21st sanctions package, adopted on 23 July, targeted the Rassvet network. But the main gap is not closed, and that round stopped short of the manufacturer, leaving Bureau 1440 and its chief executive off the lists.
Hitting the supply chain with weapons
Another lever is direct strikes. In mid-August, Ukrainian-made Flamingo cruise missiles struck an industrial zone in Samara that houses the Progress Rocket Space Center—the only plant in Russia that serially assembles the Soyuz-2.1b rockets used to launch Rassvet into orbit. Satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ showed a collapsed roof section 85 meters long and 35 meters wide over Building 106A, the hall where crews wire the rockets' control systems and cabling. The channel reported two missile hits on that hall.
If the hall was destroyed, production could stop entirely, and switching to other Russian launch vehicles would take significantly longer and add complexity. Drones also attempted to strike Plesetsk Cosmodrome, from which both 2026 batches were launched.
Both targets—the factory that builds the rockets and the site that launches them—are needed if Russia is to expand Rassvet production.
The timeline: 5.5 to eight years, if nothing changes
Russia plans to expand the constellation to 292 satellites by the end of 2027, Deputy Chief of Ukraine's Defense Intelligence (HUR) Vadym Skibitskyi said. Moscow's longer-term goal is 924 satellites by 2035.
After SpaceX cuts off Starlink access, Russia launches first 16 satellites of its own “Rassvet” alternative
With 32 satellites already launched in two batches, 260 more are needed. At 16 satellites per launch, that requires roughly 17 launches. At a four-month interval between launches, deploying them would take roughly 5.5 years even if every launch succeeded and every satellite reached its target orbit. That most likely won't fully work out: one satellite from the first batch is already lost, two from the second batch may be lost as well, and none of them has yet reached the required altitude.
Russia also depends on the scarce Soyuz-2.1b rocket. The rocket has averaged only six to eight launches per year since 2022—most committed to GLONASS navigation satellites, ISS resupply, and military payloads—limiting Russia to a theoretical maximum of roughly two Rassvet-dedicated launches per year, or 128 Rassvet satellites over four years at that rate.
There is still time to shut this project down or slow it. Vyshnivska put the useful window to slow Rassvet at about a year. Russia, by Ukrainian calculations, needs five to eight years to see it through.

SpaceX’s Starship lifts off in make-or-break orbital test flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:06:27 UTC
22:06:27 KST

SpaceX’s Starship is on a mission to prove itself. The largest rocket ever built lifted off from the company’s Starbase facility in South Texas on Monday at 8:49 A.M. EDT, soaring toward space atop its giant Super Heavy booster. This test flight—the 14th fully integrated launch—is more than just another Starship shakedown: it is the first time the enormous spacecraft has propelled itself into orbit around Earth.
If today’s test succeeds, Starship will surpass its biggest hurdle yet in SpaceX’s race to make the vehicle its new workhorse for space launches, replacing the wildly successful Falcon 9. If it fails, it will be yet another reminder of just how audacious SpaceX’s hopes for Starship really are—and how far the company must go to build a robust, reliable orbital transportation system.
Flight 14’s vehicle is the third-generation version of Starship, standing about 124 meters (407 feet) tall when stacked with its Super Heavy booster. That first stage, Booster 21, powered the vehicle upward using 33 Raptor 3 engines. After stage separation, Booster 21 performed a controlled return and splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Meanwhile, Starship accelerated toward orbit. About 25 minutes after liftoff, it reignited one of its three sea-level Raptor engines to raise and circularize its trajectory. (The ship also carries three vacuum-rated Raptor engines for in-space maneuvers.) Incredibly, SpaceX seemed unsure as to whether to push ahead to orbit, calling off that part of the test for a brief moment before deciding to go for orbit minutes later.
At that point, Starship became an orbital spacecraft. The vehicle reached an altitude of roughly 275 kilometers and is expected to make about six orbits of Earth during its nearly 10-hour mission. Along the way, it deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites—the first operational payloads to be carried to orbit by Starship. Three of those satellites will also beam back imagery of Starship’s heat shield, which must remain intact to ensure the spacecraft doesn’t break apart and burn up during reentry. If all goes well, at mission’s end Starship will perform a deorbit burn and attempt a controlled splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Chile.
A test of SpaceX’s grand vision
Starship occupies an unusual place in the history of rocketry. Unlike all previous launch systems, it’s designed to be fully reusable: both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft would be recovered and flown repeatedly in normal operations.
Intended to carry both crew and cargo, Starship is the linchpin of SpaceX’s grand vision of launching a million data center satellites into orbit and separately sending astronauts to the moon and, eventually, to Mars.
That radical vision has depended on a chain of technological achievements: entering orbit, deploying payloads, surviving reentry, making pinpoint landings and achieving smooth recoveries—and then repeating the sequence flawlessly, again and again, to reach the frequency of flights necessary to make Starship’s economics work.
Today’s flight does not prove all of those things. Neither the Starship or booster will attempt a tower catch (that may happen during the next test flight, according to SpaceX), and Flight 14 won’t demonstrate any of the daunting orbital propellant transfers required for missions to the moon or Mars.
For more than three years, Starship’s development has been defined by a series of spectacular successes and failures, accruing incremental progress in between. The fourth flight, in 2024, demonstrated controlled splashdowns of both stages. Flight 5 saw the first-ever tower catch—a dramatic recovery of a Super Heavy booster using the launch tower’s mechanical arms. Later launches introduced major vehicle upgrades, including the current third-generation Starship. Flights 12 and 13 successfully tested this new generation, although the booster on Flight 13 was lost during landing.
A major failure during Flight 14 wouldn’t doom SpaceX’s plans for Starship—but it would complicate them. The company uses a “test to failure” philosophy, pushing its systems to their limits to identify problems. But if Flight 14 doesn’t deliver on all its aims, the result will be more costly delays, more hardware redesigns and more hurdles.
To the moon and beyond
Of all Starship’s promises, the most notable may be the vehicle’s role in NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the moon. The space agency has selected a version of Starship as one of two potential Human Landing Systems (HLS) for Artemis. Under the current plan, SpaceX is developing Starship HLS for Artemis III—a low-Earth orbit test mission in 2027—and for a crewed lunar landing, the Artemis IV mission, in 2028.
That version of Starship must be refueled in Earth orbit via a succession of tanker flights by other Starships before heading to the moon. The Starship would then depart Earth orbit, travel to lunar orbit and rendezvous with astronauts there for a down-and-back foray to the moon’s surface. NASA’s inspector general has said this will require more than 10 tanker flights, with the first refueling beginning more than 200 days before the crewed mission.
That is a wildly ambitious plan. And it means today’s orbital test, if successful, would not merely be good news for SpaceX. It would begin reducing one of the fundamental uncertainties hanging over NASA’s lunar plans, adding credibility to the space agency’s controversial Artemis architecture.
But the reverse is also true: a serious failure today would come at an awkward moment for NASA.
NASA’s inspector general also concluded earlier this year that Starship HLS is behind schedule for future Artemis missions, warning that further technical problems could spiral into greater delays for the entire program. This no doubt contributed to NASA’s decision to shift an actual crewed landing from Artemis III to Artemis IV, and it reinforces the space agency’s choice to also pursue Blue Origin’s Blue Moon vehicle as another Human Landing System, creating some redundancy in the lunar architecture.
But after Blue Moon’s ride to space, Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, suffered a catastrophic explosion on the launch pad during preflight testing in late May of this year, the status of this second option for Artemis lunar missions is also in question.
This makes it hard to understate NASA’s reliance on Starship—and hence on a successful Flight 14—for keeping Artemis on schedule.

Mediators reportedly continue work with Iran, US toward likely deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:05:00 UTC
22:05:00 KST

Mediators are still working with Iran and the United States on a deal to end fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with indirect talks expected to resume Monday, three officials told The Associated Press.
The details were revealed as the war enters its eighth month after causing widespread economic suffering. Multiple efforts to allow safe shipping on one of the world's most crucial waterways have failed.
There was uncertainty over the weekend after President Donald Trump told journalists he had rejected Tehran’s latest proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, releases frozen Iranian assets and waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Iran’s foreign minister, however, remained in New York and said he awaited word from mediators. Qatar has been mediating.
Two of the officials speaking to the AP Monday confirmed that mediators are working with both sides on a proposal that would include reopening the strait and lifting the U.S. blockade and then removing sanctions.
According to the draft text being discussed, the strait would reopen in accordance with a separate deal that Iran has been discussing with Oman, on the other side of the strait, and it would include no tolls – something Tehran has pursued.
That deal seeks to temporarily manage shipping traffic on what was seen as an international waterway before the war.
The two officials also said that despite Trump’s public comments, the U.S. has not officially rejected the current proposal, indicating that his remarks may have been a negotiating tactic.
The third official said the U.S is seeking Iranian concessions on its nuclear program, including allowing inspectors to enter the country. Under the Memorandum of Understanding the two sides signed in June that collapsed within days, Iran's nuclear program was meant to be discussed over a 60-day period.
All three officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss behind-the-scenes diplomatic negotiations.
One official reported positive signals coming from both sides. A second reported "slight progress" over the weekend. The third said mediators are still trying "to soften" the positions of both sides.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
While Iran’s latest proposal echoes the June deal, a key difference is speed.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a closed-door meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly last week that Tehran had pitched the deal as benefiting Trump in the midterm elections.
Araghchi later told journalists that "the seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan."
Both the U.S. and Iran have been hurting economically – the U.S. from high oil prices as Iran attacks ships on the strait, and Tehran from the naval blockade and a growing number of U.S. sanctions that bottle up its oil sales. Brent crude, the international standard, is above $108.
For months, the two sides have been trying to outlast the other, while regional countries put up with missile and drone attacks as Tehran claims to target U.S. military assets in the region.
Reflecting Iran's impatience, a rare statement Monday attributed to the theocracy's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei noted the "painful blows" that enemy forces have received near the strait. "Before long, the Arabian Sea, too, will be rid of them," the statement added.
The latest proposed deal again seeks to end the fighting on all fronts, including in Lebanon. But a new front has emerged in recent weeks as Iran-backed rebels in Yemen are now perched on another crucial waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. That has further pressured global markets.
Iran argues that the Houthis have their own demands and that their conflict with neighboring Saudi Arabia is separate from the U.S.-Iran war, but Iranian officials said they are willing to help in finding a settlement between the Houthis and the Saudis, one of the officials said.

In run for Brazil's presidency, Flavio Bolsonaro tests staying power of his father's legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:02:36 UTC
22:02:36 KST

In run for Brazil's presidency, Flavio Bolsonaro tests staying power of his father's legacy
SAO PAULO, Sept 28 - From the bare-walled, 12-square-meter cell where he was serving a 27-year sentence for a failed coup plot, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro passed his most prized asset to his eldest son: his blessing to follow in his political footsteps in 2026.
"Let's go, it's you," Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the main right-wing candidate in the October 4 presidential election, remembers his father telling him in late 2025, over the rattle of the cell's air-conditioning unit.
The younger Bolsonaro immediately accepted the mission: "He was humiliated and convicted because the system did not want him in public life," he told Reuters last December, soon after announcing his candidacy for the presidency.
The two men now have a chance to exact revenge on the politicians, judges and special interests they blame for driving Jair Bolsonaro from public life and ending his far-right, populist makeover of Latin America's largest economy.
The 45-year-old senator is polling neck and neck with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has long been one of the region's most powerful figures and is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term.
The strength of Bolsonaro's bid, and the loyalty of the right-wing electorate to the former president, have turned Brazil into a test case for a belief embraced by many on the left around the world: that prosecuting and imprisoning a populist leader can contain the movement he or she built.
Carlos Melo, a professor of politics at Sao Paulo's Insper institution, said that former President Bolsonaro may be the most vocal figurehead of a movement that has long existed in Brazil and worldwide.
"The far-right goes beyond Bolsonaro," he added.
'IT HAD TO BE A BOLSONARO'
The competitiveness of the younger Bolsonaro's bid for power came as a surprise to many.
Unlike his brothers, he had faced corruption allegations, including leading an alleged kickback scheme that prosecutors said benefited relatives of Adriano da Nobrega, a former police officer accused of heading a gang of hired killers.
Of the former president's three eldest sons, the senator was also the least combative, softening the edge that was central to his father's rise and presenting himself as a "more centered Bolsonaro."
The announcement of his candidacy rattled markets, with bankers alternating between high-level meetings and cautious distance for much of the campaign.
Other conservative parties were skeptical, too, with some right-wing candidates announcing their own bids for the presidency.
For months, Flavio Bolsonaro tried and failed to convince others to join his ticket, ultimately settling on a little-known lawmaker from his own Liberal Party as his running mate.
"There was an initial lack of communication, owing perhaps to Flavio's first presidential run," said conservative Senator Tereza Cristina, a prominent agribusiness leader who was prevented from accepting the role of Bolsonaro's running mate by her party's leadership.
Still, Liberal Party loyalists seemed confident of their choice.
"It had to be a Bolsonaro," Valdemar Costa Neto, the head of the Liberal Party, told Reuters.
GLOBAL CONSERVATIVE EMBRACE
Despite the initial sour welcome at home, Senator Bolsonaro's bid was quickly embraced by the global conservative movement, which is eager to see Brazil join the regional right-wing wave that has brought Argentina's Javier Milei, El Salvador's Nayib Bukele and Ecuador's Daniel Noboa to power.
Senator Bolsonaro has followed the same playbook as many of those Latin American right-wing populists, uniting conservative factions around Christian traditionalism, free-market economics, and a fierce hostility to the left.
He is pledging to cut taxes and embark on an aggressive fiscal adjustment to lower long-term borrowing costs in Brazil. The platform has pleased the business community and investors, though economists say the proposals are short on specifics.
"Flavio sees a broader global realignment at stake and wants to be part of it," said Paulo Kramer, a political scientist and former campaign adviser to Jair Bolsonaro.
With the help of his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who was removed from his position as a member of the Brazilian Congress after he moved to the US, Flavio Bolsonaro managed at the end of May to get a meeting with US President Donald Trump, who described him as "a smart young man who loves his country, Brazil, very much!"
During his first term in the White House, Trump established a close political and personal friendship with Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio Bolsonaro's attempt to rekindle that alliance, however, has left many Brazilians cold.
His meeting with Trump was preceded by Washington's announcement of steep tariffs on Brazilian imports, giving Lula an opportunity to brand Flavio and Eduardo Bolsonaro as "traitors."
Polls showed Brazilians blamed the Bolsonaros more than Lula for the tariffs, which were imposed in July.
"I don't think President Trump has helped Flavio at all," said Thomas Shannon, who served as a U.S. ambassador to Brazil during the Obama administration. "I think that was more harmful to Flavio."
DARK HORSE
Having overcome the initial skepticism over his candidacy, Senator Bolsonaro's campaign faced its biggest blow in May, after an investigation revealed he had asked a disgraced banker, who was accused of leading a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme, for money to fund a Hollywood biopic of Jair Bolsonaro.
Production contracts outlined $12 million in transfers from a fund connected to the banker, Daniel Vorcaro, to a U.S. fund managed by an attorney representing Eduardo Bolsonaro.
After first denying involvement, Flavio Bolsonaro admitted that the banker had funded the movie, but maintained there was no wrongdoing, merely "a private sponsorship, with no strings attached."
The revelation, however, triggered swift backlash. The senator saw his support drop in polls and some of his allies turned openly critical. Romeu Zema, a businessman who is also running for the presidency, called it "a slap in the face."
Newly unsealed court records revealed that the Federal Police in July had opened an investigation into Flavio Bolsonaro for corruption, money laundering, and illicit capital flight linked to the movie project.
He dismissed the probe as a "political hit job" and has since recovered in the polls with less than two weeks to go before the first round of voting. A second round will be held on October 25 if no candidate wins a simple majority. If Bolsonaro wins, he would be sworn in some four years after thousands of supporters of his father rampaged through Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential offices, smashing windows, furniture and artwork in the worst attack on state institutions since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s.
The prospect of a Bolsonaro returning to the Planalto Palace in Brasilia where presidents carry out their duties is raising the possibility of fresh institutional clashes.
If elected, Flavio Bolsonaro would likely move quickly to undo two legal blows to his family: his father's house arrest in Brasilia and Eduardo Bolsonaro's conviction for coercion related to a U.S. lobbying campaign that prosecutors said sought to pressure Brazilian Supreme Court justices not to convict the former president.
Freeing his father is Flavio Bolsonaro's main goal, something the presidential candidate alluded to during an Independence Day rally earlier this month.
"I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest," he said. REUTERS

Estonia's women finish 42nd, men 66th at Chess Olympiad
Estonia's women's team finished 42nd and the men's team 66th as the 46th Chess Olympiad concluded in Samarkand, Uzbekistan on Sunday.

Estonia finished 66th among 206 teams competing with 12 match points. Individually, Siroš was Estonia's most successful player, scoring 5.5 points from eight games.

Latvia is committed to fibre optics: it exports more than 90% of its production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:59 UTC
22:00:59 KST

Latvia is focusing on a technological niche: fibre optics. It exports more than 90% of its production. This versatile technology, made from synthetic quartz, is flexible and capable of transmitting ultraviolet and infrared rays.
Dr Ints Ūdris, a vascular surgeon and phlebologist, uses fibre-optics every day in his operations. They are flexible and can transmit light, ultraviolet and infrared rays. Since 2016, Ūdris has been working with one of Latvia’s leading companies in the sector, Lightguide, to develop catheters. They are very thin and flexible; the heat isn’t concentrated in a single point, the procedure is less invasive and the recovery is quicker, he says, holding up a fibre-optic catheter., he says, holding up a fibre-optic catheter.
The region of Latgalia, which borders Lithuania, Russia and Belarus, is the centre of the Latvian fibre-optic industry. A range of specialist companies has sprung up in the town of Līvāni, thanks to the European project: Optical Fiber Valley, the fibre-optic valley. At Lightguide, for example, they produce around 20 million metres of optical fibre a year, tailor their products to each customer’s requirements and export to more than fifty countries. According to Santa Vucina, the quality manager, the products they manufacture have a wide range of applications.“In the case of simple medical devices, consisting of a single fibre and a basic connector, we manufacture around one million units a year,” she says. “Fibre optics transmit light from point A to point B with virtually no loss, which makes it possible to carry high-energy or highly precise signals. Some of our optical fibres are as thin as a strand of hair," she says. “Here we work with fibres whose core has a diameter of approximately 50 micrometres, perhaps a little less; but we do not work with tiny fibres such as those used, for example, in telecommunications. We currently have no information to suggest that our products have been used in military technology, but it is a possibility," she explains.
The total budget for Optical Fiber Valley exceeds €5.4 million, of which 40.4% comes from the European Cohesion Policy and 59.6% from companies and organisations associated with this project.
It is expected that by 2036 the fibre-optic sector will account for 10% of Latvia’s GDP
Demand for optical fibre in the medical sector and other areas is booming in Europe. The Latvian Investment and Development Agency (LIAA) promotes this business activity, notes Vita Balode Andrews, head of the Export and Innovation Services Department.
In medicine, this type of fibre-optic instrument is used “in proctology, plastic surgery, liposuction, urology, ophthalmology and cardiology,” explains Dr Ints Ūdris, adding that not only do they improve patients’ quality of life, but these medical devices also consume “approximately four times less energy than twenty-five years ago”.

How adults feel about their ADHD depends heavily on their specific symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

A new study published in the Journal of Attention Disorders suggests that how adults feel about their attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder depends on their specific symptoms. Researchers found that individuals with higher levels of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms tend to view their condition more positively, while those with primarily inattentive symptoms are less likely to see their diagnosis as an advantage. These findings highlight the diverse ways people experience and interpret their neurodevelopmental differences.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a condition that begins in childhood and often continues into adulthood. The diagnosis is based on two main categories of symptoms. The first is inattention, which involves difficulty focusing, sustaining attention, or staying organized. The second category is hyperactivity and impulsivity, characterized by excessive physical movement, restlessness, or acting without thinking. For many years, medical and psychological research focused heavily on the negative impacts of these symptoms, such as difficulties in school, struggles with emotional regulation, and challenges in relationships.
Recently, the rise of the neurodiversity movement has encouraged scientists to look at the other side of the coin. Earlier qualitative studies gathered personal stories showing that people with ADHD often identify real strengths and silver linings in their condition. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that adults diagnosed with ADHD reported experiencing notable personal strengths, identifying positive themes like high energy, unconventional thinking, and a drive for novelty. Similarly, a 2018 interview-based study revealed that many adults with ADHD identify distinct personal strengths and resilience linked directly to their diagnosis.
This qualitative foundation sparked recent efforts to study these positives numerically. A 2024 study took early steps to measure these strengths, finding that people with more ADHD traits in the general population also scored higher on traits like cognitive flexibility and sensory processing sensitivity. The new research, led by Gili Katabi of Tel-Aviv University, builds on this momentum by creating a formal scale to measure positive attitudes toward ADHD. The authors wanted to test whether these positive feelings depend on whether someone’s symptoms are mostly hyperactive or mostly inattentive.
To explore this, the researchers developed the Positive Attitudes Toward ADHD Scale. This questionnaire was designed to capture how individuals perceive the positive aspects of their own condition, based on themes from previous interviews like creativity, dynamic energy, and resilience. Participants rated their agreement with various statements on a five-point scale. The team then recruited three distinct groups of adults with ADHD to test the scale and see how scores related to symptom types.
The first sample included 84 young adults in Israel with formal ADHD diagnoses who completed the questionnaires in a laboratory setting. This initial group helped the researchers confirm that the new scale was reliable and captured a wide range of attitudes. The second sample involved 125 adults in Israel who also participated in the lab. For this group, the researchers conducted structured clinical interviews by phone to verify that the participants still met the criteria for ADHD at the time of testing, while excluding those with heavy alcohol or cannabis use.
The third sample was an online group of 126 English-speaking adults residing in 24 different countries. These participants provided detailed written information about their diagnosis and treatment history to confirm their status. Across all three groups, participants filled out the new attitude scale alongside a widely used checklist that measures the frequency of their inattentive and hyperactive/impulsive symptoms over the past six months.
When analyzing the results, the researchers found that more frequent ADHD symptoms overall were associated with more favorable attitudes toward the condition. However, breaking the symptoms down into the two main categories painted a more detailed picture. Across all three samples, a higher frequency of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms strongly predicted more positive attitudes toward having ADHD.
In contrast, inattention symptoms showed a very different pattern. Higher levels of inattention tended to associate with less positive attitudes toward the condition, though this negative association was not statistically significant across every sample. The researchers also ran a follow-up test with 35 participants from the second sample to measure their general life satisfaction. They found that the link between hyperactive symptoms and positive attitudes remained distinct, indicating that the new scale was capturing specific feelings about ADHD rather than just a generally happy outlook on life.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that young adult hyperactivity and impulsivity predicted higher relationship and job satisfaction later in life. Together, this body of research suggests that the physical and mental energy associated with hyperactivity might foster traits like curiosity and enthusiasm that people learn to appreciate over time.
There are a few things to keep in mind about these findings. The new scale relies entirely on self-reporting, meaning it captures how people feel about their own condition, not objective measurements of their abilities. Endorsing statements about creativity or flexibility does not necessarily mean a person would score higher on a behavioral test of divergent thinking. The study focuses on subjective opinions, which are important for understanding self-esteem and coping, but are separate from observable advantages.
Another detail to consider is the potential for reporting biases based on how society views different symptoms. Hyperactive and impulsive traits might be easier to reframe in a positive light, such as viewing restlessness as boundless energy. Inattentive traits, like spacing out or forgetting things, might feel less socially acceptable and harder to spin positively. Additionally, the researchers noted that their scale did not include questions about hyperfocus, a common experience where people with ADHD become intensely absorbed in tasks they find interesting, which might have skewed the results away from the inattentive dimension.
Future studies could incorporate reports from friends or family members to provide a more rounded view of how these traits manifest in daily life. Scientists might also test whether these contrasting attitudes exist in children and adolescents, or if they are unique to adults who have had more time to adapt to their neurodevelopmental differences.
The study, “ADHD Individuals’ Positivity About Their Condition Varies by Their Levels of Hyperactivity/Impulsivity Versus Inattention Symptoms,” was authored by Gili Katabi, Merav Huss, Steve Lukito, Tycho J. Dekkers, Edmund Sonuga-Barke, and Nitzan Shahar.

Chinese commercial reactor achieves nuclear fusion with clean hydrogen-boron fuel
Feat hailed as ‘significant and valuable contribution’ to global research on magnetic confinement hydrogen-boron reactions
2-MIN READ2-MIN
1
 Listen
Dannie Pengin Beijing
In a first, a Chinese company has achieved high-parameter hydrogen-boron plasma control, marking a “significant and valuable” advance in research into neutron-free magnetic confinement fusion.
ENN Group, based in Langfang, Hebei province, announced on Monday that its EXL-50U spherical device – a compact tokamak that uses a magnetic field to confine charged gas, or plasma, for nuclear fusion research – had successfully achieved hydrogen-boron fusion reactions.
“This marks the first time a commercial fusion company has achieved a hydrogen-boron fusion reaction on its own device,” the company stated.
Currently, mainstream-controlled nuclear fusion research, represented by the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) in France, predominantly uses deuterium-tritium (D-T) as fuel.

These are the best-value winter sun destinations to head to in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

The new report looked at the cost of common holiday purchases like meals, drinks and sunscreen to discover where you’ll get the most bang for your buck.
Summer is officially over, and while the weather is still pretty fantastic right now, we can practically feel the dark, windy, cold nights creeping up on us already.
To beat the inevitable seasonal depression, an escape somewhere sunny is a must – but we don’t want to pay a premium for it.
Luckily for us, Post Office Travel Money has just unveiled its Winter Sun Report 2026 which compares the costs of common holiday purchases such as meals, drinks, sunscreen and insect repellent across 24 destinations to see where your money goes furthest.
This year, Cape Town in South Africa came out on top, closely followed by Mombasa in Kenya.
While I’m not sure I’d agree it’s a winter sun destination (although the winters are relatively mild in comparison to some European ones), Tokyo is in third place, followed by Colombo in Sri Lanka and Phuket in Thailand.
The highest entry from Europe is the Algarve, which came in sixth, followed by Spain’s Costa del Sole and Tenerife in the Canary Islands.
Further afield, Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic came ninth, with Malaysia’s Penang rounding out the top 10.
On the flip side, the most expensive winter sun destinations include Scarborough in Trinidad and Tobago, St. George's in Grenada, and Funchal in Madeira.
The best-value winter sun destinations for 2026
- Cape Town, South Africa
- Mombasa, Kenya
- Tokyo, Japan
- Colombo, Sri Lanka
- Phuket, Thailand
- Algarve, Portugal
- Costa del Sol, Spain
- Tenerife, Canary Islands
- Punta Cana, Dominican Republic
- Penang, Malaysia

Peru’s penguins are on the brink. A super El Niño could make it worse.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Peru’s penguins are on the brink. A super El Niño could make it worse.
Scientists running a ‘living laboratory’ are preparing for the birds’ eventual return
The first time I was in Punta San Juan, the desert was flooded with birds. It was 2012, and I was making a short documentary film about the cormorants, pelicans and penguins that made this arid peninsula in southern Peru one of the largest gatherings of seabirds on Earth.
At the time, this 133-acre reserve — a patch of rock and sand jutting into the frigid waters of the Pacific Ocean — was home to more than a quarter million seabirds, including 300,000 Guanay cormorants (Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum) and some 3,000 Humboldt penguins (Spheniscus humboldti).
One of the few species of desert penguin, the Humboldt live along the arid coast of Peru and Chile, where they nest in burrows dug into guano deposits or small cliff caves. Punta San Juan was home to the largest colony in Peru.
By 2025, there were fewer than 500 penguins left. Avian flu had spread through the reserve in 2022 and 2023, crashing seabird populations and spreading to marine mammals such as sea lions and seals. El Niño struck next. The climate pattern is characterized by months of warmer than usual sea surface temperatures in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Those warm waters pushed anchovy — the penguins’ main food source — deeper and farther out to sea. Industrial fishing operations put even more pressure on the surviving animals.
Ecologist Susana Cárdenas-Alayza, who has run the Punta San Juan Program in partnership with Cayetano Heredia University, the Peruvian government and American zoos for more than 20 years, is increasingly alarmed. As a scientist, Cárdenas-Alayza says, she is used to dealing with numbers and controlled variables, “but diseases and climate events escape my control.”
Now, the reserve is facing a new threat: a potential “super” El Niño. Soaring sea surface temperatures are disrupting the cold, fish-rich waters of the Humboldt Current, which flows past the peninsula. When I returned in July, much had changed from my first trip, when streams of penguins lined the cliffs of the reserve. This time I saw only five penguins — and several abandoned nests with cold eggs. When food is scarce, penguins either stop reproducing or leave their nests altogether to search for a more favorable habitat, Cárdenas-Alayza says. They often starve along the way.
The destruction has also been hard on the reserve’s volunteers, who protect the penguins in what Cárdenas-Alayza calls a “living laboratory.” For decades, volunteers from around Peru and the rest of the world have counted birds, recorded their diets and built artificial nests to keep penguin chicks safe. In the summer of 2025, they even launched a “penguin patrol” to safeguard the Humboldts from workers harvesting guano, nitrogen-rich bird droppings essential for agriculture. Wanting to pitch in, the workers built a temporary, half-kilometer-long wall out of sacks of guano to shield the penguins on their daily walk to the sea.
Keeping research going — and morale high — in the emptying ecosystem has been one of the biggest challenges of Cárdenas-Alayza’s career. No one knows how long the current El Niño will last — or when the fish will return.
Nevertheless, Cárdenas-Alayza says she still has hope. Many species in Punta San Juan are philopatric, or loyal to their territory. That means that even when they leave in search of food or other resources, they eventually come back.
Biologist Patricia Majluf, who founded the Punta San Juan Program in 1979, shares one example of resilience: The El Niño event of 1997–98 decimated the reserve’s sea lions and seals. Penguin numbers dropped into the low hundreds. But the animals eventually mounted a remarkable recovery, helped by a major reduction in anchovy fishing quotas in 2006.
Scientists are busy preparing Punta San Juan for the animals’ return. Cárdenas-Alayza briefed incoming members of Peru’s Congress on the situation in July, and she and her fellow researchers are lobbying hard for stricter fishing quotas. They are also championing a new ecosystem restoration strategy, a collaborative framework that engages fishing communities, companies, students and even local chefs to help the reserve’s animals recover.
Back in Punta San Juan, Cárdenas-Alayza’s team is pressuring the government to reinforce a protective concrete wall around the reserve. In the meantime, they are trapping invasive species that prey on young birds, such as foxes and rats. They are also developing AI tools to speed data analysis from remote cameras monitoring breeding among the surviving Humboldt penguins.
As I prepared to leave, Cárdenas-Alayza, Majluf and I shared a meal of chifa, a Peruvian-Chinese cuisine that is a traditional Sunday dinner for Peruvian families. The three of us talked about our experiences teaching and people we had known at the reserve — and Cárdenas-Alayza teased Majluf, saying she was her “conservation mom.” It was at that moment that I realized what kept drawing me back to the reserve. I had come to document the region’s desert penguins, but I had learned so much more: Conservation isn’t just about science; it’s about relationships. At the end of the meal, we all opened our fortune cookies. Cárdenas-Alayza laughed when she saw hers: “Mountains are meant to be climbed.”
Anna Elisa Sotelo’s work on this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.
