Bose Launches New Wired Earbuds After More Than a Decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Bose used to make lots of wired headphones. But it’s been a minute. Specifically, it’s been 11 years. Since then, wired headphones entered 2026 having a serious moment, with sales up for the first time in five years—10 percent in the back half of 2025 and 20 percent at the start of 2026. Young people are driving the trend, including celebrities sporting wired earbuds and literally writing songs about them.
Bose president of consumer audio Raza Haider (among others at the company) noticed. He dropped off his teen at college last year and saw wired earbuds left and right. A return to wired earbuds seems to be a national trend—it’s certainly popular among the Gen Z and Gen A of New York City, and the teenage kids of WIRED staffers too.
The new Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds come to the market just in time to capitalize on this trend. Launching them, from idea to final product, took the company around eight or nine months, said Haider. This is much faster than most audio releases I’m familiar with. Haider explained that Bose has been working toward enabling faster, more efficient production to accelerate new product launches, revisions, and collaborations.
Testing the Bose Wired Earbuds: Are They Any Good?
I was one of a few reviewers to get these earbuds ahead of launch. I’ve had them for only four days, and they’re technically a late-stage prototype, not the final product, so this is more of an impression than a full review. But so far, so good.
As with any wired headphones, the simplicity is a big part of the appeal. There’s no battery to charge, no app to download, no Bluetooth to fiddle with, and no latency to ruin your TV show or video game.
Already, the Bose earbuds leapfrog cheaper wired pairs (like Apple EarPods) in sound quality and active noise canceling (ANC). They have clear detail across lows, mids, and highs, especially for something at this price point. More importantly, the noise canceling is a godsend. I can listen to music at more comfortable levels, even during a commute or café stop.
What I don’t love: The central control panel is a little heavy. It has a volume up and volume down, as well as a play/pause/noise-canceling mode switch button, but it weighs down the cable. It’s pretty flush against my torso, which is nice, but it also weighs down the earbuds in my ears. The cable tension it adds is annoying, especially compared to the tension-free experience of using wireless earbuds. The cable is thick and premium-feeling, but it inevitably ends up tangled inside of the included soft pouch.
The earbuds have (removable) silicone wing-tip stabilizers, and the box comes with extra ear tip and stabilizer sizes to find your best fit. The buds come in black, white, and a limited-edition mint color, and they start shipping October 15. You can preorder starting today at Bose and Best Buy.
While Bose's return to wired headphones feels significant, wired earbuds never truly went away. Here are some of WIRED's favorites that are currently available to buy.

Red Bull challenges in India the ban on calling its beverages "energy drinks" and does not rule out financial losses
Kyiv • UNN
Red Bull filed a lawsuit with the Delhi High Court over the ban on using the name «energy drink» without a warning. The company said there were risks to its investments.
The Austrian beverage producer Red Bull has filed a lawsuit against India’s food regulator over a ban on using the term "energy drink" without prior notice; according to court documents, the decision is negatively affecting the company’s current and planned investments in India, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
In June, India ordered producers of beverages with high caffeine content that are sold as "energy drinks" to stop using this term. Authorities rejected attempts to block the regulatory intervention in a rapidly growing market that is projected to reach a value of $1.6 billion by 2028.
The move sparked a conflict, as companies such as Pepsi, Red Bull, Monster Beverage and Reliance (owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani) feared that abandoning the category could harm brands whose image is built on the promise of an instant energy boost, as well as negatively affect sales, Reuters reports.
In the first lawsuit challenging the decision, Red Bull approached the Delhi High Court on September 25. The petition (which is not public but was reviewed by Reuters) claims that established procedures were violated because the company was not given prior notice.
Red Bull’s Indian subsidiary said that the "sudden ban" on using the term—in the absence of changes to the product standards themselves—"creates significant regulatory uncertainty and negatively affects" the company’s current and planned commercial investments.
In addition
Energy drinks raise concerns among health regulators in many countries around the world because of their high content of caffeine, sugar and taurine (an amino acid). In particular, in England, their sale to people under the age of 16 will be banned from April next year.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political party review: The Progressives – attractive promises, an expensive programme and experience in power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:57:10 UTC
21:57:10 KST

Author: Ilona Bērziņa
The Progressives (PRO) define themselves as a social democratic and green political force, advocating broader public services, more progressive taxation, environmental protection and equal rights. At the same time, the party’s values agenda – marriage equality, the Istanbul Convention with all the controversy surrounding “social gender” and “gender ideology”, as well as calls to recognise the State of Palestine (one may recall the “Free, free Palestine!” chants by the PRO-linked youth organisation Protests in Brussels shortly after the Hamas attack on Israel) – clearly alienates conservative voters.
The Progressives have been known as a political party since 2017, although the association Progresīvie had already emerged in 2011. Its original aim was to bring ideas of social equality, progressive taxation and a Nordic-style welfare state into Latvian politics.
The party’s first chairman was Māris Indulis Graudiņš. A year later, Roberts Putnis took over the position. Under his leadership, the party won 2.6% of the vote in the 2018 Saeima election and 2.9% in the 2019 European Parliament election.
Following the disappointing European Parliament result, Putnis announced that he was stepping down as chairman. After publicly criticising the party’s work and internal processes, he was expelled by the Progressives’ board in June 2021. This triggered a sharp public dispute and raised a particularly uncomfortable question for the party: how much criticism was it actually prepared to tolerate? (Incidentally, Riga taxi drivers say that this aversion to listening to any criticism and the tendency to recognise only one truth – their own – remains fashionable among the party leadership to this day.)
When the party entered the 14th Saeima and Andris Šuvajevs was elected co-chairman, the political force began a kind of “coming of age”. Its task was no longer merely to defend its ideology, but also to prove that it was capable of shaping national policy, reaching compromises with coalition partners and taking responsibility for what it had accomplished. How well or poorly it succeeded is for everyone to judge for themselves.
What do the ratings tell us?
In the latest SKDS poll, conducted from the 4th to the 16th of September, 6.2% of Latvian citizens surveyed said they would vote for the Progressives. In August, the figure was 8.8%.
The decline of 2.6 percentage points is the largest among the parties in this poll and the Progressives’ lowest SKDS result since March. The party has fallen from third to fourth place.
Meanwhile, in the September poll conducted by Latvijas Fakti and Faktu logs, the Progressives’ rating increased by 1.2 percentage points. Support among all respondents stood at 8.3% in September, while among respondents who had already made their choice it reached 12.4%.
It should be remembered that the two polls use different methodologies, which is why their results differ. In any case,
PRO is currently among the political forces whose entry into the Saeima appears practically assured.
PRO is no longer a new political force whose mistakes can simply be overlooked. The party has been in government, and voters can assess what it has contributed while holding the levers of power.
The controversies surrounding former Defence Minister Andris Sprūds and drones, as well as disputes over former Transport Minister Kaspars Briškens’ responsibility for the transport sector – including the rising costs and delays of the Rail Baltica project – are therefore unlikely to work in PRO’s favour.
What does the programme promise?
The Progressives offer three broad priorities: economic development through renewable energy and the defence industry, reducing the cost of living, and protecting democracy.
More specifically, they promise to reduce the tax burden on low and middle incomes, increase family benefits, develop affordable rental housing, introduce an annual cap on co-payments for reimbursable medicines, and establish a single monthly public transport ticket.
The programme’s emphasis on housing affordability, public transport, opportunities for young people, human rights and climate policy suggests that the party’s core electorate consists of younger, educated and socially liberal voters, particularly in urban areas.
At the same time,
promises concerning pensions, medicine costs, family benefits and services in the regions are equally visible.
All of these objectives are worthwhile and necessary, but it should not be forgotten that Latvia’s general government debt had already exceeded 20 billion euros by the end of 2025, with interest costs amounting to approximately 312 euros per Latvian resident per year. Meanwhile, the consolidated 2026 state budget envisages approximately 16.1 billion euros in revenue and 17.96 billion euros in expenditure.
The point is that a party seeking to present itself as a pragmatic political force must also be able to explain where it intends to find the money to finance all these attractive castles in the air.
Tax relief, higher benefits, increased healthcare investment and at least 5% of GDP for defence simultaneously require clear choices about state budget priorities. Voters have grounds to ask which promises the Progressives would implement first – and how they would pay for them.
The programme also includes support for marriage equality and the Istanbul Convention,
the independence of public media, protection of old-growth and biologically valuable forests, and climate policy.
At the same time, the party promises defence spending of at least 5% of GDP and closer cooperation with NATO and European partners. Its “left-wing” orientation therefore relates primarily to taxation, social protection and public services; in security policy, its programme is clearly Western-oriented.
The programme is broad enough to conclude that some voters are attracted by the party’s emphasis on social justice and accessible healthcare, while others are drawn by environmental issues, human rights or its clear pro-European position. Still others vote for the Progressives because they want to see a different political generation.
What will Riga voters do?
This is indeed an interesting question, because judging by the results of the 14th Saeima election, the Progressives are to a large extent a “Riga party”.
In 2022, the party won five of its ten seats in the capital, two in Vidzeme and one each in the Zemgale, Kurzeme and Latgale constituencies.
But that was before the Progressives came to power in Riga.
From today’s perspective, it can be said that the decisions made by PRO councillors concerning Riga’s streets are far more tangible to residents than the wording of the party’s Saeima election programme. Someone who has to take a child to school or kindergarten every day, deliver goods or find a parking space also judges politics by whether they can still get home conveniently.
The restrictions on through traffic on Vārnu Street have become a symbol of this PRO policy.
They vividly demonstrate an approach in which restrictions are introduced first and their consequences are considered only after protests begin.
Moreover, this example also demonstrates what critics see as an arrogant style of governance – one need only recall the heated meeting concerning the same Vārnu Street restrictions. Residents who had collected more than 3,000 signatures and expected concrete concessions instead had to settle for yet another evasive response.
It is a classic example of poor communication and of how those in power, in trying to please one group, can make life considerably more difficult for many others.
It cannot be ruled out that the perceived arrogance of the Progressives’ leadership in Riga is one of the factors behind the party’s decline in the SKDS poll.
Leaders and responsibility
The party’s candidate for prime minister and number one candidate on its Riga list is Andris Šuvajevs. He shapes the Progressives’ economic and social policy platform and is seeking to present the party as a credible force capable of forming a government.
Agnese Lāce, the party’s co-chair and leader of its Kurzeme list, is one of its most recognisable figures following her time as Culture Minister. Andris Sprūds, leader of the Vidzeme list and former Defence Minister, represents the party’s security policy wing.
In Zemgale, the list is headed by former Transport Minister Atis Švinka, while in Latgale it is led by Saeima MP Leila Rasima. MP Antoņina Ņenaševa and former Transport Minister Kaspars Briškens are also running in Riga.
Experience in government is both the party’s greatest advantage and a risk.
Voters can ask what Progressives ministers actually achieved while overseeing two particularly challenging sectors – defence and transport.
Rail Baltica represents an especially uncomfortable test. Serious questions remain over the project’s deadlines, financing and communication. Admittedly, the project’s problems did not begin with the Progressives, but heading the Ministry of Transport is about more than offering clever explanations in front of television cameras – it also means taking responsibility for how the party dealt with those problems.
When it comes to PRO’s political “red lines”, the firmest boundary has been drawn against Latvia First. The dispute concerns both political style and differing views of democracy and human rights.
With the National Alliance, the sharpest disagreements concern family rights, the Istanbul Convention and migration, although the two political forces may find common ground on security policy.
The Progressives, meanwhile, compete with New Unity for pro-European voters who trust state institutions,
while offering a more pronounced social and green policy agenda.
Overall, for some voters the Progressives symbolise progress and European development, while for others they represent unwanted social experimentation – including what is described as the imposition of so-called “gender ideology” – and left-wing economic policies.
Right-wing and economically liberal politicians and businesspeople often describe the party’s programme as populist or excessively left-wing. Critics argue that the party’s proposed social spending could increase the tax burden on businesses and slow economic growth.
This makes PRO one of the most widely debated and polarising political forces in Latvian politics.

AI at heart of Roche's future strategy

AI at heart of Roche’s future strategy
Swiss pharmaceutical giant Roche outlined its ambitious future plans, which include greater use of artificial intelligence to speed up research and development discovery, at its pharma investor day on Monday.
Teresa Graham, head of the pharmaceuticals division, said the Basel-based company had many promising potential blockbusters in its pipeline. While Roche was hit by research setbacks and revenue losses due to expiring patents in 2022, the group has got itself back on track thanks to an ambitious programme, she told attendees at Roche’s “Pharma Day” on Monday.
“Our track record since last year’s “Pharma Day” underscores our progress. Since then, we have achieved our targets in ten regulatory-relevant trials and advanced six programmes to the regulatory phase, with a further three entering Phase II,” she said.
Roche has up to 20 new active substances that could reach the market by 2030. Some, such as the breast cancer drug giredestrant, have the potential to generate peak sales of more than CHF30 billion ($36 billion).
What’s the state of the pipeline?
Roche introduced “The Bar” at the end of 2023 as a new evaluation framework for its research pipeline. Since then, drug candidates have had to meet certain criteria in order to proceed to further development.
More
How a clash with Roche exposed cracks in Swiss drug pricing system
Roche’s chief medical officer, Levi Garraway, stressed: “‘The Bar’ has become the guiding principle for our research and development.”
The selection process for potential candidates has become significantly more rigorous. “We have reduced the number of projects whilst significantly increasing the overall value of our remaining portfolio,” he said. The result is that the success rate for projects reaching the crucial Phase III of clinical development stood at 65% in 2025 and has so far been more than 80% in 2026. At the same time, development times have been shortened and costs reduced.
Roche and AI
Artificial intelligence is playing an increasingly important role for the pharma group. Roche does not simply want to use AI for individual analyses, but to integrate it as early as possible and throughout the entire drug discovery process, from understanding a disease, through the search for new drug targets, to the selection and optimisation of drug candidates.
More
Science podcast: the AI revolution in drug development
Aviv Regev, Head of Genentech’s Research and Early Development (gRED) department, presented “Lab-in-the-Loop”. AI models analyse large volumes of biological and chemical data, make predictions based on this, and these are then verified in the laboratory. The new experimental results are in turn fed back into the models.
“It is important that our confidence in the reliability of these models grows over time, but AI cannot replace clinical trials in humans,” he said.

Russia hits a Kharkiv high-rise overnight, injuring 43 people, then kills four in daylight strikes on central Kyiv and Dnipro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:54:25 UTC
21:54:25 KST

A Russian strike on an apartment building in Kharkiv injured dozens of people, many of them children, early on 28 September, regional prosecutors reported. Through the rest of the day, Russian drones hit Kyiv, Dnipro, and other cities, killing civilians in several of them.
Russia has moved much of its aerial campaign to jet-powered drones that fly too fast for the cheap interceptors Ukraine built against older models. Every switch to a faster weapon reopens gaps in city defenses that Ukraine had only just begun to close.
Two floors partly destroyed in a Kharkiv apartment block
Russia hit a nine-story building in Kharkiv's Saltivskyi district around 04:00. By early afternoon, the count had risen to 43 injured, including 11 children, prosecutors said.
A man of 43 and a girl of 14 remain in hospital with blast wounds, and the others have moderate or light injuries, Kharkiv Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. Three children lived in the apartment that took the hit. Their father carried them out himself, and none of them was seriously hurt.
The strike hit the second floor and destroyed the ceiling between the third and fourth floors. Rescuers brought 32 people out of the building. Across the district, the attack damaged 18 apartment buildings and blew out more than 1,500 windows. More than 100 volunteers are helping city services seal them, Syniehubov added.
A resident who fled Kramatorsk a year and a half ago said her family never heard the blast itself.
"We didn't hear any explosion. Glass came pouring down, and a column of smoke stood there," Yuliia Baldzhy told Suspilne Kharkiv. "The children were sleeping in another room, and my husband and I barely squeezed through, grabbed them, and got out."
Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said the city had not taken a hit "of this level" in some time. Officials are still establishing the weapon. Syniehubov named guided aerial bombs (KABs) and counted six of them over the oblast in the past day. Prosecutors named a UMPB-5, a Russian munition, as the preliminary version. Terekhov said the city was checking whether it was a KAB or a Banderol, a small cruise missile.
Russia has hit Kharkiv high-rises with guided bombs before. In November 2024, one such strike injured 25 people, including an infant.
Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them?
Kyiv hit through the night and into the day
In the middle of the working day, a Russian jet drone struck the main building of the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv's historic center. The attack killed a woman and injured five people, the Kyiv City Military Administration said. Three of them were hospitalized, Klitschko said. People climbed out of windows to escape the fire.
"Russia will definitely get a response to this," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Overnight and into the morning, Russian drones hit a gas station in Obolon, a café by a gas station, office buildings, and a 16-story residential building in Podil. The attacks injured three teenagers in Podil, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. A 17-year-old boy was hospitalized.
Nationwide, Russia launched 165 drones overnight, 79 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 112, and hits were recorded at 14 locations.
The capital is now under attack daily. On 27 September, Russian strikes injured nine people in Kyiv, and Russia hit a Kyiv data center twice. That evening, a Russian drone struck the Stolychnyi market in Sofiivska Borshchahivka, just outside the city, and killed two people. Zelenskyy wrote that one of the two killed in Kyiv Oblast was a citizen of Azerbaijan.
Deaths in Dnipro and Synelnykove
Around 11:15, a Russian drone hit a business center in central Dnipro, killing three people. The number of injured rose to 15, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said. Rescuers led 47 people out of the burning building, regional council head Mykola Lukashuk said.
"Nearby are residential buildings, a park, a library, offices, shops. The center of Dnipro. In the middle of the working day, hundreds of people are here," Hanzha wrote.
In Synelnykove, a Russian strike on a logistics company's branch killed one person. It injured three others, including a 15-year-old boy now in hospital in serious condition.
Overnight, Russian drones also hit infrastructure in the Vasylkivka community and a market in Nikopol.
Strikes across other regions
In Kharkiv Oblast on 27 September, a Russian FPV drone killed a 67-year-old driver in Shestakove, prosecutors said. A drone on fiber-optic control also killed a 41-year-old woman in a car in Velykyi Burluk and injured a 46-year-old man.
Explosions sounded in Poltava overnight. In Rivne Oblast, a Russian attack damaged a detached house without injuring anyone. In Odesa Oblast, Russia struck a warehouse, and an evening attack injured a man of 62 and a woman of 63. Zelenskyy also listed a Palau-flagged ship hit in Odesa Oblast and an ice cream plant damaged in Zhytomyr Oblast, in the same post.

Lithuania to showcase culture, arts in 52 countries during EU presidency

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

Lithuania will showcase its culture and arts in 52 countries across six continents during its presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of next year, the Foreign Ministry said on Monday.
The cultural programme will include concerts, exhibitions, cinema, performing arts and literary presentations, alongside joint projects with international creators. It will span more than 100 cities worldwide and cover over a dozen artistic fields, ranging from music and visual arts to dance, theatre, architecture and culinary heritage.
"Europe exists not only in treaties or institutions. It lives through people wanting to know each other, sharing experiences and creating a future together. Culture opens a special opportunity for dialogue, from which trust and sustainable partnerships are born," Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said.
The ministry noted that while the programme builds on long-standing international work by Lithuanian cultural institutions and artists, it will also provide opportunities to reach new audiences.
Events will target diverse groups, from teenagers and policymakers to diplomats and regular festival-goers at concert halls and museums worldwide.
More than 70 cultural events will be held in Brussels alone. The programme will be launched on January 22–23 in the Belgian capital and Antwerp by opera soloists Asmik Grigorian and Edgaras Montvidas, performing with the Lithuanian National Symphony Orchestra.
The Year of Lithuania in Germany will also begin on January 28 at Hamburg's Elbphilharmonie, featuring Grigorian, Montvidas and the National Symphony Orchestra.
Presentations of contemporary music, jazz, literature and dance are scheduled across Germany.
Lithuanian cultural events are also slated for Japan, the UK, Poland, Italy, France, the United States, Scandinavia, Ukraine, Moldova and Latvia. Featured projects include a performance by Happyendless in Ukraine, a concert by pianist Onutė Gražinytė in Latvia and a folk art exhibition in Tokyo.
The programme is funded with 2.1 million euros from the EU presidency budget, plus an additional 300,000 euros from the Culture Ministry. The full international and national schedule will be released in December.

Thames Water apologised for the lack of water. A spokesperson said: “Our specialist team is now on site and working to stop the water flooding from the broken pipe.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hires Wall Street economist David Zervos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:53:03 UTC
21:53:03 KST

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has hired veteran Wall Street economist David Zervos, the longtime chief market strategist at Jefferies, as a counselor in the Treasury Department. Zervos was a CNBC contributor.
Bessent announced the hire Monday in a statement obtained first by CNBC. Zervos will serve in a broad advisory capacity and is expected to begin immediately.
He has backed Bessent's recent decision to increase buybacks of some long-term Treasury debt and has called for lower interest rates from the Federal Reserve.
Zervos in a brief interview called himself a "Wall Street geek" and said he was excited for his third stint in government. Bessent "has done an incredible job in this administration at guiding the economy through a lot of tumultuous periods," Zervos said.
"Whether it's trade, whether it's war, he's stepped up," he said of Bessent.
Zervos will add intellectual firepower to the Treasury after a series of staff departures that have drawn some attention. Seven of the department's 16 Senate-confirmed appointees had left the department as of mid-August, the Washington Sun reported. Bessent is on his third chief of staff since becoming Treasury secretary in January 2025.
Fellow Wall Street economist Joseph Lavorgna of SMBC Nikko served in a similar role as counselor to Bessent before leaving in March. The position doesn't require Senate confirmation.
Bessent handles an especially broad portfolio for a Treasury secretary. He has been effectively President Donald Trump's top negotiator on China and has been closely involved in policy debates about artificial intelligence, although Trump on Friday said Bessent would not add a role as the administration's top AI advisor.
Zervos was considered by Trump to run the Federal Reserve, though the president ultimately chose Kevin Warsh for the job in January.
Zervos has worked at Jefferies, a New York-based investment bank, since 2010.
Zervos has a doctorate in economics and has worked twice for the Fed. The first time was at the start of his career, in the early 1990s, when he did technical economics and interest rate research. He left for the private sector and returned to the Fed in 2009 as a visiting advisor in the wake of the financial crisis. Warsh was a governor at the Fed then, though it isn't clear if he and Zervos worked together directly at the time.
Zervos will serve as a special government employee, he said in an email to his clients. That status allows him to avoid some often-onerous divestiture requirements that come with other federal appointments, but it restricts how long he can hold the position. Zervos said he expects his term to end in April 2027.
Zervos said last year he believed interest rates should be "much lower." Since Warsh took the job, Zervos has said he thinks Warsh can make room for lower interest rates by cutting the Fed's balance sheet. Those reductions are one of Warsh's top priorities.
The Fed raised interest rates earlier this month for the first time since 2023. That decision prompted frustration from some economists in the Trump administration, but Bessent has been more circumspect. He said Sunday in an appearance on Fox News that the Fed "should have an open mind" about how to manage the economy.
Bessent has intervened in Treasury markets as interest rates have continued to rise. The 10-year Treasury hit 5.2% on Friday, a level last seen in 2007, powered by a strong economy, competition for capital from the artificial intelligence build-out and concerns about inflation as the Iran war continues.
Zervos, in a CNBC appearance last month, backed Bessent's decision to increase buybacks of some long-term Treasury debt, a move that may have eased pressure on some Treasury yields. Some on Wall Street had criticized the buybacks, but Zervos said he supported them.
"I don't see how you could fight this when the firepower and the cards are all sitting in the Treasury Department," Zervos said.

US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry make travel less predictable as countries cancel flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:53:00 UTC
21:53:00 KST

Can US sanctions ground Iran's aviation industry?
September 28, 2026
US sanctions are pushing Iran's weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo.
Earlier in September as part of "operation economic outcast," the US Treasury Department targeted Iran's aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and potentially lose access to the US financial system.
The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies.
For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington's broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.
Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.
For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.
The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.
For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.
Major Middle East routes canceled
Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously for safety reasons that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia have been seriously disrupted.
On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.
Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.
A passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.
As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the "J-1" general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.
Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.
The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.
More travelers use land crossings
With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.
One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.
"The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close," he told DW anonymously.
For families, older people, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.
Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.
That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.
Iran's shaky aviation industry
Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions.
Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.
An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.
When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.
Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran's GDP.
"Iran's aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time," Salavati told DW.
"The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money," Salavati added.
Iran isolated by air and sea
Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.
Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.
If those first connections disappear, Iran's international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.
The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult.
If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states.

U.S. Embassy Issues Security Alert to Citizens in U.K. Amid Suspected Terror Plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:50:40 UTC
21:50:40 KST

The U.S. embassy in London has issued a security alert for American citizens in the U.K. following a suspected terror plot near an RAF airbase used by the U.S. military, which led to five arrests on Sunday.
“U.S. citizens are encouraged to exercise caution and be mindful of personal security,” read the notice responding to the incident near RAF Fairford. “U.S.-associated facilities, gatherings, and organizations may be at heightened risk. U.S. citizens are advised to follow instructions of local authorities for their personal safety and security.”
The alert reminded Americans that the U.K. in April raised its national terrorism threat level to “severe” from “substantial,” a decision made after an antisemitic attack in London was declared a terrorist incident by police. The “severe” level, according to the Metropolitan Police, means “an attack is highly likely.”
The warning came hours after British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after they were detained near RAF Fairford in southwest England, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran, in the early hours of Sunday. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base, which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) previously said could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military.
The U.K.’s Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) confirmed in a statement to TIME Monday that the five arrestees were British nationals in their 20s who live in London.
“Specially trained CTP investigators have been examining the scene overnight and have been carrying out a range of activity, which have led to multiple new lines of enquiry,” read the statement.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme early Monday that it is too soon to speculate over the motives during a live investigation. Questioned about a potential Iran link, he said: "We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies."
Similarly, CTP’s deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans said she was “very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised,” but stressed more time is needed to work through the case.
The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. "The Circulation of such fabricated speculations... will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the U.K.," it said Monday.
What we know about the arrests at RAF Fairford
Gloucestershire Police, the local authority responsible for the area that includes the airbase, received a call from a concerned resident at 12:45 a.m. local time on Sunday, regarding three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the airbase.
The local resident, a farmer, told police they had found the road blocked by three white vans. “I saw a large group of hooded and masked men. When they saw me, they ran ahead of me… I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place,” she later told the BBC.
Armed officers responded to the call and five men were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act, as well as section 5 of the Terrorism Act.
Gloucestershire Police evacuated residents from around 85 nearby households and put a cordon in place while the British Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team examined the vehicles. The incident is now being handled by CTP.
While the farmer who alerted police has been hailed for their actions, Streeting has indicated they only had a “partial picture” of the matter and appeared to suggest U.K. security forces had been aware of a suspected plot involving RAF Fairford.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday claimed the suspects had been “under view for a long time.”
"Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great… and we got them,” Trump told reporters.
When asked if Trump had been correct, Streeting did not reject the assertion.
“Our security services and our police, they don’t ask for praise, but I think it was a proud moment yesterday to see the President of the United States recognize the extraordinary work that our police and our security and intelligence services do every day throughout the year and throughout the world to keep us safe,” he said. “That’s all I want to say this morning on that.”
TIME has asked the Ministry of Defense and Downing Street whether the British authorities were already investigating a potential plot.
Speaking at the Labour Party conference later Monday morning, Streeting celebrated the U.K. and U.S. alliance as “the closest of any two nations on Earth” and vowed the two countries “will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm.”

21:50:26 KST

In a speech from Metz, Pope Leo XIV invoked Europe’s Christian roots and urged leaders to defend the international rules-based order.
Pope Leo XIV has praised multilateralism as “the best defence against the desire for dominance” in a speech in the French city of Metz, the birthplace of Robert Schuman, one of the founding fathers of European integration.
The pontiff lamented a world marked by conflict, from war and hunger to deteriorating personal relations, describing an “increasingly uncivilised” climate. He also criticised the “lies and deception” he said were fuelling growing distrust between citizens and governments.
Speaking in Schuman’s hometown, a city closely associated with European reconciliation, Leo said Europe could break this vicious cycle by reaffirming its commitment to the rule of law and dialogue.
"Europe can break this cycle by upholding the principle of respect for others, which it has successfully cultivated and maintained, having demonstrably shown over the past eighty years that it is possible to express divergent opinions, demands, and interests through dialogue rather than confrontation," he said.
The Pope delivered his address in French in the presence of French President Emmanuel Macron, who is due to attend a Mass with Leo later on Tuesday.
Although the Pope did not explicitly mention Russia's war against Ukraine, he condemned what he qualified as a new “pointless massacre" on European soil.
"It is necessary to engage in patient dialogue, to show courage in negotiations, and to be willing to compromise on certain positions for the greater good of peace."
Leo XIV also urged Europeans to remember the continent’s Christian roots, describing Europe as more than a geographical entity and instead a “cultural and historical reality”.
“We cannot speak of Europe, then, without mentioning Christianity,” he said, arguing that its traditions could coexist with efforts to shape the continent’s future.
Europe, he added, “has flourished and progressed when it was able to draw on the best aspects of its past and reinvent them in new and creative ways through encounter with others.”
Metz, a city steeped in European history
The choice of Metz as the venue for the Pope’s address was rich in European symbolism.
Located in France’s northeastern Lorraine region, close to the German border, the city is the birthplace of Robert Schuman, one of the founding figures of European integration.
But Metz’s history also reflects the conflicts that shaped modern Europe. The city changed hands several times between France and Germany and was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1940, following France’s defeat and occupation.
The Élysée Palace said Monday’s programme was designed to highlight the “European and cross-border dimension” of Lorraine, a region at the crossroads of several countries with a shared and often painful history of war.
EU leaders and the heads of European institutions were invited to attend the event, although only a handful joined French President Emmanuel Macron, including representatives from Monaco, Andorra and Luxembourg.
The gathering also brought together representatives of different faiths, including France’s chief rabbi, Haïm Korsia, and Chems-Eddine Hafiz, rector of the Grand Mosque of Paris.

Blood tests reveal why astronauts get constipated in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:49:59 UTC
21:49:59 KST

Blood tests reveal why astronauts get constipated in space
Astronauts’ gut bacteria shift within weeks of entering space, potentially revealing why constipation is so common in microgravity.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of Copenhagen
- Summary:
- Spaceflight may dramatically change the gut within weeks, causing bacteria to break down more protein as food moves more slowly through the intestines. The shift could help explain astronaut constipation and may have wider effects on health, making it an important concern for future missions to Mars.
- Share:
Constipation is a familiar problem for astronauts, but scientists have not fully understood why spending time in space can disrupt normal digestion.
New research from the University of Copenhagen, conducted in collaboration with NASA, offers a possible explanation. Scientists analyzed blood samples from 52 astronauts who spent months aboard the International Space Station and found signs that the digestive system begins changing relatively soon after astronauts leave Earth.
"We see changes in astronauts' blood samples that indicate that the gut bacteria begin to ferment protein to a greater extent than usual within weeks after the astronauts arrive in space, and this change continues until they are back on Earth," says joint first author and associate professor at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports, Giorgia La Barbera.
Gut Bacteria Shift Toward Protein
Protein fermentation occurs when bacteria in the intestines begin breaking down protein rather than fiber because available dietary fiber has already been used. The process is not unique to astronauts and can also occur in people on Earth.
The researchers suspect that microgravity may slow the movement of food through the digestive tract. If food remains in the intestines longer, bacteria have more time to turn to protein fermentation.
"The lack of gravity in space probably causes food to move more slowly through the intestine, and this fits with the fact that we are seeing signs of increased protein fermentation. This may also help explain constipation in astronauts," says co-author of the article Henrik Roager, who is also an associate professor at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports.
Gut Changes Could Affect the Brain
The findings came from an investigation of metabolites in astronauts' blood. Metabolites are small molecules circulating through the bloodstream that can provide clues about how the body is functioning.
By analyzing these molecules, researchers can learn about processes ranging from diet and metabolism to what is happening inside the intestines.
The results could matter beyond digestion because changes in the gut can influence other parts of the body, including the brain.
"We know that products of protein fermentation [are] often associated with negative health consequences, such as kidney damage, potential effects on mood or reduced ability to focus, among others," says Lars Ove Dragsted, senior author of the study and professor at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports.
Why This Matters for Missions to Mars
The findings could become especially important as space agencies prepare for longer missions to the Moon and eventually Mars. Astronauts on those journeys may spend far more time away from Earth's gravity than crews currently stationed aboard the International Space Station.
"When we plan for longer journeys in space - for example to Mars countermeasures may be needed to mitigate negative effects of space travel on the intestines," says Giorgia La Barbera.
Researchers say several approaches might help reduce these digestive changes.
"Our findings can inform potential interventions - either directly through increasing dietary fiber, supplementation with prebiotics or other types of treatments that promote peristalsis and decrease gut transit time. This would help reduce protein fermentation and thus provide a healthy gut environment and avoid negative health consequences," adds Henrik Roager.
Peristalsis refers to the coordinated muscle contractions that move food and waste through the digestive system. Supporting that movement could shorten the amount of time material remains in the intestines and reduce the opportunity for excessive protein fermentation.
The Findings Could Also Help Patients on Earth
The work may also have implications far beyond spaceflight.
People who spend extended periods confined to bed often experience constipation as well. Researchers suggest that slowed intestinal movement in these patients could potentially produce similar changes in gut fermentation.
"You can use this knowledge to help bedridden patients. They also experience constipation and likely also have increased protein fermentation that may aggravate health conditions," concludes Lars Ove Dragsted, senior author of the paper.
What Is Protein Fermentation?
Protein fermentation happens when bacteria in the gut begin breaking down protein after they no longer have enough fiber available.
The process is more likely when food remains in the intestines for an extended period, even if a person does not feel noticeably constipated.
As bacteria digest protein, they produce various metabolites. These molecules can enter the bloodstream and travel throughout the body.
Some can also influence the brain through the gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking the digestive tract and the brain.
Previous research has associated metabolites produced during protein fermentation with effects on the brain, including anxiety and reduced ability to concentrate.
Why the Results Were Unusually Clear
Research on blood metabolites can be difficult to interpret because metabolism differs considerably from person to person.
The unusual nature of the astronaut data helped researchers overcome some of that variability and strengthened confidence in the pattern they observed.
"The samples we have analyzed come from a total of 52 different astronauts, on different missions and across many years. This is very different from how you normally do a study. So, it is quite impressive that our method has been able to show so clearly that there is consistently more protein fermentation," says joint first author and assistant professor Jan Stanstrup.
How the Study Was Conducted
The researchers examined how human metabolism changes during spaceflight by measuring metabolites in astronauts' blood.
Their analysis indicated that protein fermentation in the intestines increases when astronauts leave Earth and enter microgravity. The blood samples also revealed smaller changes associated with fish and caffeine consumption.
Rather than searching only for predetermined substances, the researchers used a so-called non-targeted approach. This allowed them to analyze the broad range of metabolites in the blood and identify which ones changed during spaceflight.
The samples came from three studies conducted aboard the International Space Station. Even though only small quantities of blood were available, researchers were able to perform additional analyses and extract more scientific information from the existing studies.
The collaboration between researchers at the University of Copenhagen and NASA also highlights the international scientific cooperation made possible by the ISS.
NASA researchers Sara R. Zwart and Scott M. Smith contributed to the study. University of Copenhagen researchers Giorgia La Barbera, Jan Stanstrup, Henrik M. Roager and Lars Ove Dragsted also contributed.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Giorgia La Barbera, Jan Stanstrup, Sara R. Zwart, Scott M. Smith, Henrik M. Roager, Lars Ove Dragsted. Longitudinal metabolomics profiles reveal increased gut microbial protein fermentation during Spaceflight. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74979-w

US response to UN pandemic talks ‘severely weakens’ global planning, says leading health expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:49:30 UTC
21:49:30 KST

The United States government’s decision to block a major global declaration on pandemic preparedness “severely weakens” the effort, and signals intent to disrupt international cooperation, says Prof Lawrence Gostin, a leading expert on global health law from Georgetown University.
The United Nations general assembly had been due to adopt a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response on 25 September after a high-level meeting on the subject.
The document would have seen countries agree to work together in solidarity to tackle global health threats and express concerns that the world remains unready to deal with future pandemics.
However, the US delegate said it was “not in a position” to support the text, blocking its adoption by consensus – the UN process whereby negotiated documents are assumed to be agreed unless there is an objection.
Italy also rejected the document, while the EU delegate said that although it was “fully and unreservedly committed to the important overarching objective”, there were “red lines” around some references to intellectual property, such as whether the transfer of technology between countries should be voluntary or mandated – a key sticking point in the ongoing World Health Organization treaty negotiations.
Dr Erica Schwartz, the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said critical issues remained unresolved, referring to “the inclusion of divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus” and references within the document to ongoing, WHO-led negotiations over the fair sharing of vaccines and drugs between countries in any future pandemic.
It is understood that the Trump administration was unhappy with mentions of equity and universal access to sexual and reproductive healthcare services. Earlier this year, President Trump signed executive orders expanding a “global gag” rule that bans US aid recipients from work related to abortion to also include bans on diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and what it called “gender ideology”.
A separate WHO-led agreement governing how the world should respond to future pandemics is on hold while countries try to find agreement on the issue of pathogen access and benefit sharing – or what countries should be guaranteed in terms of vaccines and treatments in return for sharing data on any emerging diseases on their territory. The US withdrew from the WHO shortly after Trump took office.
UN documents of this kind do not impose legally binding requirements on countries but instead serve as a sign of commitment and intent.
Gostin said: “Since this is a political declaration, its value is only as strong as the political will to adopt and implement its provisions. The US decision to dissent severely weakens the document.
“For many decades, it was American financing and scientific innovations that were the bedrock of outbreak detection and response. This signals a clear US intention not to cooperate globally to health threats common to all nations. There is no rational reason to reject a political commitment to preventing and responding to dangerous outbreaks. The only thing gained by the Trump administration is to put a stick in the wheels of international cooperation.”
The US has been accused of exploitation in its pursuit of individual agreements with poorer countries in return for aid.
The political declaration is still likely to be adopted when it is considered again at a later UN general assembly meeting where a majority rather than consensus vote is needed.
Helen Clark, a former prime minister of New Zealand and a co-chair of the Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response, said: “It is disappointing that the high level meeting was not asked to endorse the political declaration which had been negotiated by member states. Agreeing to collaborate to prevent, prepare for and respond to pandemics should not be controversial.”
Eloise Todd, the executive director and founder of Resilience Action Network International, said: “It is unacceptable that member states were unable to advance a political declaration at the close of the high level meeting on Friday, and an unfortunate reminder of the continued challenges to drive consensus for the global good in the current geopolitical environment.”

BRICS mechanisms promote better mutual understanding than EU — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:47:08 UTC
21:47:08 KST

ISTRA, Moscow Region, September 28. /TASS/. BRICS’ more flexible approach to integration allows member states to develop greater mutual understanding than EU countries, Gustavo de Carvalho, head of the African Governance and Diplomacy Program at the South African Institute of International Affairs, said.
"I would like to look at how BRICS has operated since its creation. I think it is a good example of how mutual recognition of diversity and mutual understanding can work. The European integration process is based primarily on a highly maximalist approach, aiming to bring everyone around one common idea, regardless of whether you agree with it or not. BRICS, in my view, functions rather in the opposite way. And perhaps that is precisely why this format works," he said at the annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club.
De Carvalho added that for BRICS members, differences "do not become something painful." The expert said the bloc’s members can view disagreements differently and identify a minimum common denominator to at least outline a direction for further work or create space for reaching a consensus in the future.
"That is how rivals such as China and India are able to interact within BRICS. Because ultimately, there may be deep disagreements between us, including completely different understandings of certain situations, but this does not make the grouping any less relevant or significant for its members," he continued. "And I think this is particularly important at a time when multipolarity can be viewed as a kind of desirable vision of the world."
About the meeting
The 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, titled "Responsibility for the Future: Limits of Possibility or Possibilities Without Limits?", is being held in the Moscow Region from September 28 to October 1. The club’s flagship conference brings together 120 participants from 40 countries.

€14 million cut from road funding for 2027, delaying project completion

€14 million cut from road funding for 2027, delaying project completion
The completion of some road maintenance projects due for 2027 will be delayed, Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) said.
A total of €288 million had been planned for road maintenance next year, but the new plan announced as part of the 2027 state budget will see €14 million less spent in this area, Leis went on.
Besides Rail Baltica, are there any other investments that are being postponed?
Yes, as on the one hand defense spending has increased and on the other hand there is the budget deficit and the target of minus 4 percent had to be met, so practically everyone has to make savings somewhere, and all the ministries did so as well.
Including, of course, the Ministry of Climate, as our volume of investment is the largest after the Ministry of Defense, and our road investments are the largest. Under the current plan, if we had budgeted €288 million for all road maintenance next year, then under the current plan it will be €274 million, meaning roughly €14 million less.
However, that is a very small difference compared with how much has been invested in roads over the past two years and will also be invested in the coming years – Estonia has never invested this much before. If you look at the big picture and the situation as a whole, things are normal.
Could you please also give some kind of figure for how many of those investments are being postponed?
Not yet, because we have only just finalized the state budget on the government side. It will now also go to the Riigikogu, so at the moment we do not yet have any kind of list or precise plan of what to postpone. All of these projects are such that they will not be canceled in the future, but postponed. Whether by a few months or a year, they will not be canceled. In the big picture, this is not a problem.
The construction of some roads is being postponed and you do not yet have a specific plan, but perhaps you can name some other projects whose construction is being postponed?
I cannot name any at the moment, but we are reviewing all the areas within the Ministry of Climate to see what needs to be brought forward or, conversely, what can be postponed. To a large extent, this also depends on the availability of external funding. It is often the case that some funding can be obtained earlier and some later.
Road construction is a good example, where last year 45 kilometers of two-plus-two road construction got under way on the Pärnu highway largely because, for the first time in several years, we were able to use such a large amount of external funding. In the coming years, how we are able to use European funding will certainly also be a determining factor.
A bigger change will come from 2028, when the new EU budgetary period starts. Then, across Europe as a whole, there will be twice as much funding for infrastructure projects as in the current period. From Estonia's perspective, the future looks bright specifically in terms of funding these major projects.
One thing I would highlight is that there had been questions for a while about continuing the reconstruction of apartment buildings. We announced the last round last year – I think it was at the end of the year – so there was a gap of almost a year. It is now set out in the state budget that there will be €80 million for apartment building reconstruction in each of the next two years. This is a very necessary support measure both for the sector and for the public.
If some larger projects are now being postponed, when can they be expected? Of course, at the moment it is difficult for me to understand which projects these are if nothing more specific can be named.
I would put it in black and white: The Transport Administration will start putting together the road maintenance plan once the Riigikogu has approved the budget, and then it will also become clearer which roads will be postponed or brought forward. For example, a supplementary budget is currently being considered by the Riigikogu, and we received an additional €11 million for roads for this year.
The situation changes more quickly than over the course of a year – indeed, we received an additional €11 million for this year, which is an extra bonus. That could be directed towards the reconstruction of projects that had already been designed and could be carried out quickly.
I am saying this because, overall, road funding is still significantly higher by the amount of the motor vehicle tax than it was in 2024 and 2025. In terms of the sector as a whole, the situation is good.
Could you nevertheless name at least one road or project whose completion is being postponed, so the reader can understand what to expect?
Urban roads are not normally covered by the state budget.
These are intercity roads, then.
Yes. I would not venture name one off the top of my head at the moment, as those 2+2 [lane] road construction projects are the biggest and they are ongoing; they will already be completed in 2027, and some in 2028. No, I will not name any off the top of my head at the moment, as the cut is not significant enough right now that I should immediately say anything on that, or rather, we are only now beginning to analyse what the most sensible solutions are – what goes ahead or what gets postponed.

Cantor brings Jewish music lost in Kristallnacht back to Germany - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:44:36 UTC
21:44:36 KST

Nearly 90 years after Nazi pogromists burned synagogues, Torah scrolls, musical instruments and scores across Germany during Kristallnacht, an Israeli-born cantor is working to bring the country’s lost Jewish musical heritage back to life.
Assaf Levitin, a Germany-based cantor and deputy chairman of the German Jewish Cantor Association, has launched Hashivenu, a collaboration with the renowned music publisher Edition Peters to recover and republish Jewish cantorial works that disappeared after the destruction of Germany’s Jewish communities. His co-author is Cantor Amnon Seelig, the association's chairman. The first volume, released on Friday evening ahead of Sukkot, contains 18 works for cantor, mixed choir and organ dating from 1838 to 1938.
The story behind the creation of Hashivenu is historically significant.
The opus brings back into existence the German Jewish cantorial works that were destroyed or disappeared in the Kristallnacht pogroms of November 9-10 1938, under the instruction of the National Socialist Party.
Of the 1,400 synagogues and Jewish institutions destroyed during Kristallnacht, multiple organs, pianos, and other instruments were also burned, as were Torah scrolls, musical works, and other musical items which had been central to the community for 100 years.
Germany: The birthplace of Reform Judaism
Levitin's meticulous archival renewal creates a full circle: Germany is the birthplace of Reform Judaism, and Levitin is allowing canonical music of this tradition to reenter Reform spaces once more.
The collection itself spans the spectrum of religious practice - not just Reform Judaism. It includes the works of Yisrael Meyer Japheth of Frankfurt, who wrote for a male acapella choir with male altos and sopranos, and the work of Jackob Dymont, who wrote a cantor male solo and male choir acapella score for Kabbalat Shabbat.
But what Levitin said makes the collection so interesting is the music written for organ and a mixed choir. Of course, this kind was meant to be played in a reform setting, as female voices and instruments were not allowed in Orthodox synagogues on the Sabbath.
"The common denominator of this period is that it was the time of the Haskalah, and this was the first time when Jews went to study in universities. Musicians went to study in music academies at the height of the Romantic era, [which influenced their composition]."
As an example, Levitin spoke of Salomon Sulzer in Vienna, who had earned enough money to commission composers to write pieces for him. Sulzer asked his friend, the famous early Romantic composer Franz Schubert, to write music for Psalm 92. This became the only piece of music Schubert composed for a synagogue in Hebrew.
"Some of these pieces were written by very, very good and well-known composers of their time who were not even Jewish, and they had many organ players who were not Jewish composing music for the synagogue," Levitin said, nevertheless stressing that non-Jewish composers were the exception.
The process of sifting through the archives was lengthy.
There are 400 titles in the Freimann collection in Frankfurt, which is where the pieces were sourced from. The whole collection is around 20,000 pages. Some scores are just two pages, but some are thick books.
"For example, the cataloged title 'Schir Zion' by Salomon Sulzer shows just the year and the city where it was published, but then you open it and see that Schir Zion is the volume for Shabbat and has 400 pages with 700 titles in it. Even if you throw out some works, you may still be left with 150 pieces to look into."
"I had to explore the liturgical context and if it's good enough," Levitin continued, adding that not everything the composers wrote was "necessarily amazing."
"Sometimes, they wrote one or two amazing pieces, and the rest is okay. But some of some things are really excellent music. And I just wanted to represent as many composers as possible."
He did, however, say to himself that there was no need to preserve works if they are "not good enough."
"My take as a musician is I have to save it if I cannot leave it in oblivion. The things where it's just a crying shame that nobody knows it."
Kristallnacht: 'The night where music died'
Kristallnacht, he said, was "the night where music died."
"Where could you do a service with an organ after Kristallnacht? All the organs were burned down, never to be rebuilt. After the Shoah, they didn't have the cantors anymore: either they fled, or they were murdered. And the congregations, the people who came back to Germany, they didn't have the synagogues with organs. They quickly built small synagogues; nobody thought of building the organ again."
Levitin spoke of how important it is to present this collection as a body of German music - part of the German canon - rather than purely Jewish music intended for synagogue.
He recalled a conversation with a friend who is a German conductor, who told him: "This is German music. It was written in German by German composers in Hebrew for the synagogue, but this is a whole genre of German music."
"I was very moved that he said that," mused Levitin. "Because the part that Jews took in the cultural life in Germany until the Nazis came was huge. It was important for me to talk about not only how terrible it is that everything disappeared, but to take a look at the work and say 'this is sublime music, this is excellent music.'"
While the current collection focuses on Shabbat, Levitin plans the next collections to focus on Yom Kippur, Rosh Hashanah, Hanukkah, and life cycle, among others.
He and his team are halfway through the second collection, but he hopes the whole anthology will be completed in about 4-5 years.
He told The Jerusalem Post that his work is intended to be comprehensive. "I do not want to only bring one or two pieces back in the repertoire and say 'never again.'"
"I don't want 'never again.' I want it back."

Sudan, Egypt reject Ethiopia claim of backing Tigray opposition
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Sudan, Egypt reject Ethiopia's accusation of backing Tigray opposition groups
Sudan and Egypt have rejected Ethiopian accusations that they are backing opposition groups fighting federal troops in Tigray. The exchange follows a return to large-scale conflict in Ethiopia’s northernmost region, raising fears that the fighting could spread beyond its borders.
In a statement on Sunday evening, Sudan’s army described the accusations as "baseless", said it would "not allow any infringement of its sovereignty" and called on Addis Ababa to "exercise accuracy and responsibility and resort to dialogue".
The response came after Ethiopia’s chief of general staff, Field Marshal Jula, accused "foreign powers" of supporting an opposition alliance led by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) in its offensive against government troops.
"The Tigray front and the alliance cannot achieve anything on their own unless they are pushed, supported and supplied by Sudan, Egypt and other forces," a statement issued on Friday read. The army chief also accused Eritrea of backing armed groups and fighting federal troops.
The TPLF, which largely governs the semi-autonomous region, formed an alliance with Fano, a rebel group from neighbouring Amhara, and five other groups. The alliance launched an offensive on Wednesday, seizing airports and clashing with federal troops in northern Ethiopia. Fighting that began in 2020 killed thousands and displaced tens of thousands more before the parties signed a cessation of hostilities agreement in November 2022.
Sudan’s army, in turn, accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed of "supporting and backing" the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudanese government forces since civil war broke out in April 2023.
Khartoum alleged that Ethiopia was providing "training and supplies and the use of Ethiopian territory in military activities including strategic drones and suicide drones" in support of the paramilitary group. Addis Ababa has denied similar accusations in the past.
Relations between the two countries worsened in May when Sudan accused Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates of involvement in a series of large-scale drone attacks targeting Khartoum Airport. Sudan alleged that the drones had taken off from Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar Airport.
Tensions with Egypt
Egyptian sources have also denied any involvement in the renewed fighting in Tigray and Amhara.
Speaking to Asharq Al-Awsat newspaper, an Egyptian source described the allegations as "not meriting a response". The source said Cairo has "nothing to do with such polemics” and maintains “a consistent and strict policy of non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries".
The exchange follows renewed tensions between Cairo and Addis Ababa over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Egypt and Sudan want a legally binding agreement on how the dam is operated. Egypt relies on the Nile for more than 90% of its freshwater, while Ethiopia says the Blue Nile dam is vital to its electricity supply.
Last week, Egyptian Water Resources Minister Hani Sewilam said Ethiopia needed to understand that building a dam on a river shared by many states was "not like laying a carpet in their homes". He rejected Ethiopia’s position that decisions about the water source rest with Addis Ababa alone.
Ethiopia responded days later, accusing Cairo of a "crude colonial mentality".

Syrian presidency orders spending cuts, tighter fiscal discipline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:44:04 UTC
21:44:04 KST

Abdulsalam Fayez and Mohammad Sio
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
The Syrian presidency on Monday instructed government bodies to rationalize public spending, cut unnecessary expenditures and strengthen fiscal discipline “under the current circumstances.”
The presidency’s General Secretariat directed government institutions to “rationalize public spending, reduce unnecessary expenditures and reorder the priorities of investment projects according to their necessity and feasibility, while ensuring that the core functions of public bodies are not affected,” the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) said.
Salaries and wages, as well as spending needed to maintain health, education, water, energy, security and public safety services, will be exempt from the cuts, according to the agency.
Necessary operational and preventive maintenance will also be excluded from the measures, in line with efforts to strengthen fiscal discipline and improve the efficiency of public resource use.
The presidency also ordered a reassessment of approved investment projects according to their level of necessity, with priority given to projects linked to the continuity of essential services, public safety and the protection of assets and critical infrastructure.
The General Secretariat said the measures are aimed at “maintaining the balance of the state budget, strengthening fiscal discipline, improving spending efficiency and directing available allocations toward priorities and essential services.”
It also stressed the need to review areas of expenditure that can be reduced in a way that generates savings in public funds without affecting the continuity of government institutions.
The directive comes as Syrian authorities seek to stabilize the country’s economic and public-service sectors after 14 years of revolution against the Bashar al-Assad regime.
Key sectors, including health, education, water and electricity, continue to face major challenges because of extensive infrastructure damage and the destruction of thousands of service facilities during the war waged by the Assad regime, while the government is seeking to improve conditions across the country.
