Ethiopia accuses foreign powers of backing anti-govt rebels
Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan are backing armed militias seeking to overthrow Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, the country’s military chief has claimed.
Field Marshal Birhanu Jula made the accusation on Saturday amid renewed fighting involving the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an armed political group that controls much of Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.
“Neither Shaebia [Eritrea] nor the TPLF can achieve anything alone, even if they are allied, unless they are backed, supported and supplied by Sudan, Egypt and other external powers,” Jula said in an interview with the military’s media outlet.
On Sunday, Sudan dismissed the accusation as “baseless.” Army spokesman Asim Awad Abdelwahab countered that Ethiopia was allowing support for Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to pass through its territory. Egypt and Eritrea had not publicly responded to Jula’s claims as of Sunday.
Ethiopia has increasingly strained relations with the three countries. Addis Ababa and Cairo have long been at odds over Ethiopia’s giant dam on the Blue Nile, while Ethiopia and Sudan have an unresolved border dispute. Relations with Eritrea have also sharply deteriorated despite Asmara having fought alongside Ethiopian government forces during the previous Tigray war.
The accusations come days after seven armed groups formed an alliance aimed at ousting Abiy’s government. The coalition brings together former enemies, including the TPLF and the Amhara Fano National Movement, which fought on opposing sides during the 2020-2022 war, as well as the Oromo Liberation Army.
Fighting has since intensified. TPLF-aligned forces seized airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire last week and detained federal personnel, according to the African Union, forcing Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the region. Clashes have also spread into neighboring Amhara and Afar.
The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) claimed on Thursday that it had killed 272 TPLF fighters and captured another 260 during a counteroffensive. The battlefield figures could not be independently verified.
Jula said the military was responding with “wisdom and restraint,” warning that another major war would have devastating consequences for civilians.
The African Union has urged the sides to immediately de-escalate and return to direct talks, saying the airport seizures violated commitments under the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. It has also urged Ethiopia’s neighbors not to take actions that could further fuel the conflict.
The Pretoria deal ended a two-year war between federal forces and the TPLF that resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths. Eritrea backed Addis Ababa during that conflict, while Fano forces also fought alongside the federal government before later turning against it.

Diesel prices record high in the United Kingdom

LONDON, September 28. /TASS/. The average cost of diesel fuel in the United Kingdom has reached a historic high of 1.9918 pounds ($2.65) per liter, according to the automotive services company RAC.
The previous record was set in June 2022 and totaled 1.9909 pounds per liter. As a result, filling up a typical family car with a 55-liter tank will now cost 110 pounds ($146), which is 31 pounds ($41) more than before the war in Iran began.
The record-high diesel price "will mean extra costs not just for motorists at the pumps, but for anyone buying goods or services whose delivery or provision depends on diesel trucks and vans," said Simon Williams, the RAC’s head of policy. The costs resulting from the increased price of diesel "will be passed on to consumers," he added.
Gasoline prices have also hit a new high since late February, reaching 1.74 pounds ($2.31) per liter, with the average cost of a full tank now at 95.8 pounds ($127). This is 22.8 pounds ($30.3) more than before the US and Israel began launching strikes against Iran.

A Muslim preacher from Melbourne, known as Abu Ahmad and associated with the Al Bayyinah Islamic Center in Springvale, urged his followers to take up arms against Christians and Jews, according to local reports.
Speaking during a sermon in July, Ahmad instructed adherents not to take Jews and Christians for friends and declared that devotion to Allah carries an obligation to oppose and fight enemies.
"For the sake of Allah, it includes the obligation to declare enmity for his sake, opposition for the sake of Allah," Ahmad said in a clip posted to the center's social media feed. "It is to declare opposition: indeed, to take up arms against his enemies, to shun them and to stay far from them both in word and deed."
According to local reports, Ahmad's extremist rhetoric has drawn national attention due to documented ties linking his Melbourne institution to controversial Sydney networks. The Al Bayyinah Islamic Center, established in Springvale in 2024, has received ongoing support from Sydney-based preacher Wissam Haddad, who was previously linked to the Al Madina Dawah Center in Bankstown, a prayer hall also reportedly attended by alleged Bondi gunman Naveed Akram.
Local reports noted that Ahmad visited Haddad's Sydney center in early 2025 to deliver a sermon criticizing "infidel" Western powers, and an ABC Four Corners investigation previously uncovered institutional links between Haddad and the Melbourne prayer center.
One Nation leader calls for government to act against Islamic extremism
One Nation leader Senator Pauline Hanson issued a media release on Monday criticizing federal authorities and calling for immediate, targeted federal powers to confront fundamentalist Islamic extremism.
"Fifteen people were murdered in a terrorist act at Bondi," Senator Hanson said. "Now Australians are reading reports of an Islamic preacher urging followers to take up arms against Australian Christians and Jews. How much more do Albanese and Burke need to hear?"
Hanson argued that broad laws covering the entire community are insufficient and urged the government to directly target preachers encouraging terrorist violence, recruiters, and support networks. "We need stronger federal powers to shut down the extremist and fundamentalist mosques and Islamic prayer centers," Hanson stated. "Give ASIO and the AFP the resources and targeted powers to dismantle these networks. If current laws are inadequate, change them."
Robert Gregory, President of the Australian Jewish Association, told The Jerusalem Post that the episode demonstrates deep-seated failures in national security and social cohesion.
"It is hard to believe that this long after the Bondi terrorist attack, Australia has still not seen a major crackdown on radical Islamic preachers and extremist religious centers," Gregory said.
"Australians are rightly alarmed by reports of a preacher speaking about an obligation to ‘take up arms’ against enemies and telling followers not to take Jews and Christians as friends. If this sort of hatred is being preached in Australian religious centers, Australia has serious problems with extremism and social cohesion."
Gregory added that the incident raises broader questions about unmonitored extremist messaging. "The obvious question is - how many other Islamic preachers are spreading similar messages that have simply not attracted media attention? Australian Jews have been warning for years about rising antisemitism, radicalization and failures in Australia’s immigration and national security settings. Antisemitism has surged in Australia, and after the Bondi attack, these warnings can no longer be dismissed."
Australia security expert not surprised by increased antisemitism
Australian security expert Daniel Lewkovitz told the Post that the latest developments reflect decades of political inaction. "This is no surprise to anyone who has been paying attention for the last 20 years," Lewkovitz stated.
"In 2005, at a Government-funded Islamic school in Melbourne, a visiting imam was overheard telling students that Jews were putting poison in bananas. Newspapers covered it, and there was outrage. The school should have been closed down with deportations to follow. Instead, the Headmaster is still there, and the school is now Victoria's largest Islamic college whose main source of income is government grants."
Lewkovitz pointed to a continuing trajectory of unaddressed extremist indicators over the past decade. "In 2015, the same headmaster told students ISIS was a plot by Western countries (claiming Israel and America were behind it). Ten years later, ISIS inspired the murder of 15 Jews at Bondi Beach. Again, nothing much happened. So with the latest incident in Victoria being quite similar in terms of hatred, I'd be surprised if anything happens this time either. Politicians just need to wait until the news cycle moves on and can then return to funding these institutions and trying to secure their vote."
Lewkovitz cautioned that short-term political calculations continue to compromise national safety. "Regrettably, there is a consistent pattern, particularly in Western Sydney, of politicians willing to sacrifice national security in exchange for votes in marginal seats. Europe has shown exactly where this ends and what's taken 30 years in Europe has taken 10 in Australia."

Eight Jewish educators named winners of global Jewish teachers award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:43:38 UTC
21:43:38 KST

Eight Jewish educators from around the world have been named winners of the Global Jewish Teachers Award, a joint initiative of Israel’s Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, The Jerusalem Post and UnitEd, in partnership with Herzog College and the World Zionist Organization’s Department of Education.
The award recognizes educators who strengthen Jewish identity, foster connections to Israel and contribute to Jewish communities worldwide.
More than 200 nominations were submitted following a global campaign inviting Jewish schools and parents to nominate teachers. Candidates were assessed by a professional committee of education experts from Herzog College, with finalists then reviewed by an international judging panel chaired by Minister for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Amichai Chikli.
The winners, in alphabetical order, are:
- Meir Bunytow, Beit Hayladim School, Mexico
- Marina Grushevskaya, Lauder Etz Chaim School, Russia
- Raquel Hakim, Yeshurun Torá, Buenos Aires, Argentina
- Rahel Israeloevitch, Yabne Henri Schilli, Paris, France
- Dina Jacobson, Yavneh College, London, United Kingdom
- Anat Kampf, Margolin Hebrew Academy, Memphis, USA
- Tal Kattan, King David Primary School Linksfield, Sydney, Australia
- Tzvi Lew, Yeshiva University High School for Girls, New York, USA
The educators will be recognized at the upcoming Global Jewish Educators Conference, scheduled to take place in Jerusalem in October. Each recipient will also receive a $2,500 cash prize from the Mayberg Foundation’s Jewish Educator Impact Fund.
Jerusalem Post Group CEO Inbar Ashkenazi said, “Behind every confident Jewish child and every engaged Jewish community stands a teacher who made a lasting difference. Through the Jewish Teachers Award, we are proud to recognize the educators whose passion and leadership ensure that our shared heritage continues to flourish."
Avi Cohen-Scali, Director General of the Ministry of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, said, "The future of the Jewish people is built every day in classrooms around the world. Jewish educators are the ones instilling Jewish identity and a deep connection to Israel in the next generation. This bond to Israel and Jewish heritage is critical. That is why the Ministry is deeply committed to empowering educators with educational tools and building a global network across Jewish communities worldwide."
Rachel Fink, Director of Education at UnitEd, said the award provides an opportunity to recognize the work of Jewish educators. “UnitEd works today with over 850 Jewish schools, spanning more than 50 countries. Every day, I see the depth and dedication behind the work of teaching, and I have the privilege of meeting devoted teachers for whom educating the next generation is their life's mission. This competition is an opportunity for us, as a global community, to pause for a moment and thank Jewish educators,” she said.
“We recognize the invaluable role of Jewish educators in developing the Jewish identity of their students,” said Manette Mayberg, President and Trustee of the Mayberg Foundation. “Our gift is an opportunity to additionally honor these special role models whose careers in Jewish education have strengthened the Jewish future."
Rabbi Professor Avishalom Westreich, President of Herzog Academic College, said honoring Jewish educators for their accomplishments is essential. “For decades, Herzog Academic College has viewed strengthening Jewish education around the world as part of its core mission. Celebrating exceptional Jewish educators sends a powerful message: education is our strongest response to uncertainty, and our greatest investment in the future,” he said.
“Through our longstanding work with educators and Jewish schools across the globe, we are privileged to help ensure that this award reflects excellence, diversity, and a shared commitment to the future of the Jewish people."
Gael Grunwald, Deputy Chairman of the World Zionist Organization and Head of its Education Department, said Jewish education plays a central role in passing Jewish values and traditions between generations. “Jewish education is one of the most impressive enterprises of the Jewish people. As Rabbi Sacks said, 'The Egyptians built pyramids, the Romans built theaters, and the Jews built schools.' Jews did not invest in columns and walls, but in passing on values and tradition to the next generation.
“During the competition, I was exposed to more than 100 incredible stories about educators who took their role several steps further and succeeded in passing Judaism on to the next generation. We still have a lot of work to do, but we can be proud of our generation and the resources it invests in this important mission."
Written in collaboration with Israel’s Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, UnitEd, Herzog College and the World Zionist Organization’s Department of Education.

Democrats to probe lucrative Trump family business deals if they win midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:43:33 UTC
21:43:33 KST

Corporate donors to US President Donald Trump's ballroom and participants in business deals brokered by Trump family members are expected to be among the first targets of investigations if Democrats take control of the House or Senate in November's midterm elections, multiple Capitol Hill staffers, lawmakers and attorneys told Reuters in recent days.
Control of either chamber would give Democrats subpoena power and funding to bolster investigative staff, enabling them to launch probes as early as February and potentially triggering lengthy legal battles that would place the Trump family business empire squarely in the spotlight.
The investigations could dominate the second half of Trump's term after two years of dealmaking in which the Trump family expanded into crypto, drones, artificial intelligence and prediction markets, while the president's personal wealth grew by an estimated $2.2 billion.
“I don't think the Democrats are going to have patience. They'll expect documents pretty quickly. You're not going to play the old run-out-the-clock game,” said Ashley Callen, a lawyer with law firm Jenner & Block who was previously general counsel to Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson.
US House of Representatives Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York told reporters on September 17: “We're going to hold the crooks accountable, beginning on day one.”
The Trump administration criticized the potential for investigations. "Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to obstruct and baselessly target President Trump’s commonsense agenda,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said in an emailed statement to Reuters.
Corporations are a ripe target for investigations because, unlike the White House, they cannot claim their activities are protected by executive privilege.
Of particular interest are Trump-linked crypto firms and Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, according to Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, although both cautioned there is no definitive list of targets yet.
Companies with ties to Trump and his family are conducting urgent preparations, including hiring lawyers for internal audits and crisis communications firms for public outreach, according to interviews with corporate counsels, crisis management specialists, congressional staff and lawmakers.
Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island unveiled a report on Thursday, saying oil and gas companies won tax breaks, subsidies and looser environmental regulations after Trump asked them for $1 billion in donations during his 2024 presidential campaign, adding yet another potential avenue for investigation.
Democrats to focus on Trump family
Adam Schiff, a Democratic senator from California, warned companies not to delete any records related to transactions with Trump and his administration.
“We can make life very difficult for the administration if you abuse legitimate oversight requests of Congress,” Schiff said in an interview, citing Congress’ power over funding for agencies.
Among transactions Schiff is focused on is the proposed sale of a portion of Yosemite National Park to a private developer with ties to Republican campaign committees. "In this administration everything is for sale, including our most precious gems like Yosemite," he said.
But the prime target for Democrats appears to be the Trump family - especially Donald Jr., who has entered into a flurry of business deals since his father won office in November 2024.
“The First Family has been making money hand over fist,” said Schiff.
Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner "is a corporate executive that we absolutely will need to talk to," said Raskin, who could become chair of the powerful Judiciary Committee if Democrats take control of the House.
He said Kushner has not responded to two letters inquiring about his private equity firm Affinity Partners' dealings with Middle East "oil monarchies and governments" while he also represents the United States in diplomatic negotiations.
Raskin pointed to deals Kushner secured with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates while serving as a presidential envoy. "That's an outrageous conflict of interest," he said.
Kushner is a US special envoy for peace but not a government employee. Federal employees are subject to rules prohibiting them from engaging in activities that could affect them financially.
Chad Mizelle, a lawyer for Kushner, said in a statement that allegations against him are false. "And to date, no one - not even Jared's critics - has identified a single applicable rule or regulation he has violated," Mizelle said.
Raskin also singled out a $620 million Pentagon loan to rare-earth startup Vulcan Elements announced some three months after an investment by Don Jr.'s 1789 venture fund.
"He seems to have a clairvoyant sensibility of exactly who is going to get government contracts and who is going to get favorable government regulatory treatment in the Trump administration," Raskin said.
In a statement to Reuters, a Vulcan spokesperson said the company "did not ask or solicit its investors to facilitate the Pentagon loan" and that it would continue to engage with Congress in "good faith."
1789 Capital hired top law firm Quinn Emanuel to handle congressional investigations and is already signaling its intention to rebuff Democratic inquiries.
“1789 Capital welcomes legitimate congressional oversight,” it said in a response to Congress dated September 9, “but it has no intention of being held hostage to political gamesmanship.”
In a statement to Reuters, a 1789 spokesperson said "Rep. Raskin has offered no proof of wrongdoing, only politically motivated accusations," adding that his letter demonstrated "a troubling lack of financial literacy."
Jeopardy for corporate executives
Republican Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota dismissed the need for such investigations and told Reuters that Democrats could face a backlash from voters by "fixating and obsessing on Donald Trump and his personal life and his dealings, rather than on the things that matter to the American people."
But some Republicans may join Democrats' efforts. Freshman Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah called for Don Jr. to be investigated for allowing a Russian oligarch to pay for his wedding parties in the Bahamas.
Firms will have to decide whether to quickly comply with investigations, which could incur Trump’s wrath, some of the lawyers said. Failure to cooperate with Congress could put executives in legal jeopardy and trigger consumer blowback.
"There is the reputational risk always with any congressional investigation," said Kevin Edgar, a BakerHostetler law partner and former congressional aide.
One lawyer, who requested anonymity to protect clients, said an ideal outcome could actually be being sued by the White House to stop them from producing information on the grounds of executive privilege. “It gives them the ability to say: Mom and dad tell me what to do,” the attorney said.
Some companies were already referring information requests to the White House.
In a previously unreported July 1 letter seen by Reuters, ballroom contractor Clark Construction responded to a request about “ballooning costs” from Blumenthal by saying the terms of the deal required all information to come from the White House.
Blumenthal, who is in line to chair an investigations panel, told Reuters: "We will use our subpoena power, absolutely," if Democrats win control of the Senate in November.

As the only carrier operating directly between the two countries, Air India's return will reopen possibilities for Israeli and Indian travelers, who have had to rely on layover flights during its absence.
Air India to join Delta, United in Ben-Gurion's list of foreign long-haul carriers
Once flights resume, the company will join Ben-Gurion Airport's list of foreign long-haul carriers, which currently includes US carriers Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.
Delta resumed its JFK-Tel Aviv route on September 7, while United resumed its similar Newark-Tel Aviv route two days later.
James Genn contributed to this report.

Trump ‘very seriously’ considering diesel export ban as global supply crunch worsens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:41:13 UTC
21:41:13 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has suggested the White House is still considering a diesel export ban as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle soaring fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump told a Fox News reporter on Sunday, while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Illinois.
"That can oftentimes lead to a little bit of an increase on gasoline for cars, so we're looking at it very seriously. We may do it," he added.
Trump has previously indicated support for an export ban as retail diesel prices have climbed to fresh record highs, saying earlier this month that a decision would be made quickly "one way or another" on whether to implement a ban.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said the White House is considering restrictions rather than an outright ban, while Politico reported last week that the Trump administration was preparing a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days.
The idea of the world's largest diesel exporter implementing an outright ban has prompted firm pushback from the U.S. energy industry, while analysts have warned that the move could backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis.
Diesel prices have soared amid hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, with the conflicts disrupting vital oil and fuel trade routes. Average U.S. diesel prices hovered around $6.50 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA, up sharply from a year ago but just below their record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22.
Commodity strategists at Morgan Stanley have said an export restriction from the U.S., which has become an important source of marginal diesel supply amid reduced flow from Russia and the Middle East, would likely lower U.S. diesel prices initially — "but with potentially adverse reactions downstream."
"Not only would diesel prices be higher globally, but there could be a feedback loop to US gasoline prices as refinery runs adjust," strategists at Morgan Stanley said in a research note published Thursday.
'The biggest problem for the global oil system'
Benedict George, head of European product pricing at Argus Media, said some form of U.S. restriction on diesel exports would likely send European diesel prices and premiums against crude "to a new unprecedented level," noting that the U.S. has supplied about half of Europe's diesel imports over the last couple of months.
"It's really important to be clear that there is no measure yet and it's very unclear whether there will be a measure at all and what the measure will be even if there is a vision," George told CNBC by telephone.
When talking to oil traders in Europe, it's clear that they mostly doubt the U.S. is going to restrict diesel exports, given how challenging a move would be for U.S. oil companies, George said.
In the U.S., soaring diesel prices have put additional financial strain on farmers and agricultural workers as well as drivers and households ahead of the November midterm elections.
The American Petroleum Institute, an oil lobby group, was among those to have quickly contested the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban when Trump initially appeared to back the idea last week.
In a statement, API CEO Mike Sommers said that "restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem—exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers."
He added, "The answer is more supply and more flexibility—not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse."
Trump has previously urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices.
Ukraine, which fears an extremely difficult winter period amid expectations of another Russian assault on its energy infrastructure, has previously characterized Russian oil refineries as legitimate military targets.
Argus' George said Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries have added a whole new layer to the global supply crunch, making diesel "the biggest problem for the global oil system, whereas before it was one of several very big problems."
What next for the global diesel supply crunch?
Asked for his outlook on how long the global diesel supply crunch could last, George said the uncertainty is so extreme that some traders have simply given up trying to forecast the market.
"One trader was saying to me recently that he doesn't bother trying to forecast now because it feels like a waste of effort. You have literally no idea what is going to happen," George said.
"We don't know if the U.S. will introduce any restrictions, but I think all anybody has talked about is a short-term measure, so two or three months at an absolute most … so there is a kind of time horizon on the U.S. restriction of exports, if it were to happen," he said.
"But on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, who knows? I mean, literally nobody knows. Nothing has worked so far to resolve that situation and similarly for the semi-closure of the Strait of Hormuz."
— CNBC's Spencer Kimball and Michael Bloom contributed to this report.

Estonia's R&D funding might not hit agreed-upon 1% of GDP next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:41:00 UTC
21:41:00 KST

Estonia's R&D funding might not hit agreed-upon 1% of GDP next year
Under an agreement reached years ago, the state is to spend at least 1 percent of GDP on research and development. However, funding may fall short of that target in the coming years.
In 2018, party leaders, scientists and business leaders signed a public agreement supporting an increase in research, development and innovation funding to 1 percent of GDP.
The draft 2027 state budget approved by the government on Monday does not provide funding for research at that level. According to the draft's explanatory memorandum, research and development funding will be maintained at the level agreed in the 2025–2028 state budget strategy: 0.97 percent of GDP next year. To do so, however, the government will reduce state budget funding for research and development by €2.5 million in 2027.
Education Minister Kristina Kallas said at a government press conference that research funding will total €455 million next year. The same amount is planned for research and development in both 2028 and 2029.
"It won't keep pace with the 1 percent target because, as a share of GDP, it will fall, even though the nominal amount won't," Kallas said.
According to Kallas, the final amount of research and development funding will become clear after Estonia reaches an agreement with the European Commission on its national plan. Negotiations with the EU over funding for the plan are still underway.
"Unfortunately, the agreement on the national plan will be left to the next government. This government has decided that funding cannot fall below €455 million, but any additional funding will depend on negotiations over external funds," the education minister added.
Kallas noted that external funding will run out in 2029, which would have led to a significant decline in research and development funding in the 2028–2029 state budget strategy. To maintain the €455 million allocation and avoid a cut in nominal terms, the government decided to add money from the state budget.
"So a substantial amount of state budget funding has been added, but it still won't reach 1 percent," Kallas said.

Zelensky faces backlash over appointment of judge accused of persecuting EuroMaidan protesters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:38:13 UTC
21:38:13 KST

Zelensky faces backlash over appointment of judge accused of persecuting EuroMaidan protesters
President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to appoint a controversial judge accused of issuing unlawful rulings has sparked a wave of criticism.
On Sept. 25, Zelensky appointed Viktor Kytsiuk as a judge of Kyiv’s Pechersk District Court for life. The Kyiv Independent has requested comments from Kytsiuk and the President's Office and will publish their responses once they are received.
Kytsiuk is one of the most high-profile judges accused of issuing unlawful rulings against protesters during the the 2013-2014 EuroMaidan Revolution, or Revolution of Dignity, which ousted pro-Russian President Viktor Yanukovych. Activists and legal experts see his appointment as a victory for Ukraine's corrupt judicial establishment and a blow to EuroMaidan ideals.
Kytsiuk's appointment followed decisions by Zelensky to appoint several other judges accused of unlawfully persecuting EuroMaidan protesters and violating ethics and integrity standards earlier in September.
These include Taras Zayets, Maryna Lozynska, Olena Izovitova-Vakim, Viktoria Parnenko, Hanna Lebedeva, and Anton Kotliar.
The president is supposed to appoint judges nominated by judicial bodies automatically under Ukrainian law but this norm conflicts with the principle that he can only appoint judges who meet integrity standards, Mykhailo Zhernakov, head of judicial watchdog Dejure, told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 28.
The recent judicial appointments have been postponed for years but now Zelensky decided to suddenly appoint a number of highly controversial and tainted judges, Zhernakov said.
"(Kytsiuk) is a highly significant figure," Roman Maselko, a former lawyer for EuroMaidan activists and ex-member of the High Council of Justice, wrote on Facebook on Sept. 26. "It would be no exaggeration to say that he and Judge Oksana Tsarevych are among the best-known judges associated with EuroMaidan cases. Their rulings during the (2013-2014) Revolution of Dignity became one of the catalysts for legislation requiring a review of all judges involved in EuroMaidan cases and for the launch of judicial reform."
Maselko argued that "holding them accountable — or, at the very least, removing them from office — was seen as one of the key tests of whether the reform was actually working and whether judges would face consequences for arbitrary and manifestly unlawful decisions."
Kytsiuk was appointed as a judge in 2009 for five years, and his term expired in 2014.
In 2015, Kytsiuk was charged with issuing unlawful rulings against protesters during the 2013-2014 EuroMaidan Revolution.
Specifically, Kytsiuk stripped protester Serhiy Poyarkov of a driver's license despite the fact that lawmaker Volodymyr Yavorivsky testified in court that he — not Poyarkov — had been driving the car.
Kytsiuk also stripped EuroMaidan activist Mykhailo Cherkasenko of a driver's license. He was at home at the time a traffic police officer claimed to have stopped him, according to three witnesses who testified in court.
According to the investigators, all cases involving EuroMaidan activists were manually assigned to Kytsiuk and Tsarevych by a court employee using the login credentials of Kytsiuk’s sister. The investigators interpreted this as unlawful interference in court cases.
The High Council of Justice decided in 2017 not to appoint Kytsiuk as a judge for life due to the criminal case against him.
However, in 2019 the Supreme Court canceled the High Council of Justice’s decision, opening the way for Kytsiuk’s potential re-appointment.
In 2020, a Ukrainian court acquitted Kytsiuk.
Maselko accused prosecutors of sabotaging the case despite solid evidence of wrongdoing and thus enabling his acquittal.
At the same time, a highly controversial Constitutional Court ruling annulled criminal liability for unlawful rulings in 2020. Legal experts and activists saw the decision as an effort by the corrupt establishment to block reforms.
"The unreformed Supreme Court has already reinstated dozens of judges widely regarded as lacking integrity after the High Qualification Commission of Judges and the High Council of Justice had previously moved to dismiss them," the judicial watchdog Dejure said on Sept. 21.
"As a result, the president was presented with judicial nominees who clearly failed to meet the constitutional requirement of integrity.... For seven years, Zelensky, as guarantor of the Constitution, refused to appoint members of the judicial establishment who had effectively rigged the selection procedures."
The watchdog added that "now the president has abandoned that approach and is appointing judges in batches with little scrutiny... and he will now bear political responsibility for the anti-Ukrainian rulings that may be handed down by judges associated with EuroMaidan cases."

2026-09-28

21:38:08 KST

The United Nations General Assembly may have ended over the weekend, but a photo taken during a meeting on its sidelines has continued to draw attention around the world.
The image shows senior U.N. official Tom Fletcher appearing to bow before Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The photo, which drew headlines in Iranian media, angered Israeli and Jewish figures. Hillel Neuer, executive director of UN Watch, wrote: “Shame. Former British diplomat Tom Fletcher, now head of the UN's relief agency, bows to Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi whose regime just massacred tens of thousands of protesters in January. Fletcher often echoed Iranian regime talking points against the US and Israel.”
Israel’s U.N. ambassador, Danny Danon, also criticized Fletcher, asking: “Did the regime’s 'humanitarian work' against its own protesters come up, Mr. Fletcher?”
24 meetings, including with major powers
The Iranian delegation sent to the General Assembly had an exceptionally busy diplomatic agenda. The Islamic Republic was represented at the gathering by President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Araghchi. According to a CNN review, Araghchi met with representatives of at least 24 countries during his visit to New York, including the foreign ministers of leading European powers.
Araghchi met, among others, with European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and his counterparts from Britain, France, Germany, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia and Ukraine. He also met with Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, shortly after Iran attacked U.S. targets inside the Hashemite kingdom. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and spoke with representatives of Western media.
But the highlight of Iran’s diplomatic activity during the General Assembly was Araghchi’s meeting with Steve Witkoff, an envoy for U.S. President Donald Trump. After the meeting, Araghchi told Western journalists that he had presented a new proposal in negotiations between Tehran and Washington. Reports overnight said Trump had rejected the proposal and was preparing for further military strikes, but from the Iranian perspective, the significance lay in the fact that the meeting took place at all.
Araghchi also heard tough messages directed at his country in other meetings. According to the BBC, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told his Iranian counterpart of “Britain’s unwavering determination” to confront threats on British soil from Iran-linked actors, including attacks targeting the British Jewish community.
Other foreign ministers urged Araghchi to reach understandings on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and stressed the need for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict with the United States.
The attempted attack in Britain and the possible Iran connection
Fletcher, who previously served as a British diplomat, was not the only figure in Britain to face criticism for meeting with Araghchi at the General Assembly. Miliband also met with the Iranian foreign minister on the sidelines of the annual gathering.
Tom Tugendhat, the opposition’s shadow foreign secretary, said: “The Iranian regime has done nothing to justify any senior British minister meeting their envoys. They are murdering protesters, threatening our allies and arming terror groups – including the Houthis – as well as threatening communities in the UK. Shaking hands gives them a credibility they have failed to achieve through violence.”
The meetings took on added significance after British police on Sunday declared a “major incident” in the village of Whelford, near Royal Air Force Fairford, a base used by the U.S. Air Force and from which warplanes have departed for bombing missions in Iran.
Hours later, authorities revealed that five men had been arrested there on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack. Three commercial vehicles loaded with explosives were found in their possession. Photos taken by a local resident showed the suspects shirtless on a sidewalk, their hands cuffed behind their backs, as British security forces searched them.
It later emerged that the suspects had been arrested only about 320 meters, or 350 yards, from the base. British media reported that security authorities were investigating whether Iran had sent them to carry out the attack. Iran had already threatened in July to strike bases such as Fairford if U.S. aircraft continued taking off from them to bomb targets on Iranian territory.
During the latest war, Britain initially prevented the United States from using British bases to carry out strikes on Iran. Then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer later allowed U.S. forces to launch “limited” strikes from those bases against the Islamic Republic, targeting missile sites in particular, including sites used to launch Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Weapons stolen from Ukraine front line handed to notorious neo-Nazi unit
Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) has announced the transfer of weapons worth about $100,000 confiscated from an alleged smuggling ring to the notorious Azov Corps.
The cache, including about 17,000 rounds of ammunition, grenades, single-shot anti-tank grenade launchers, land mines and other weapons, according to the Ukrainian agency, was handed over this week, having been seized in May.
A criminal group had used a humanitarian vehicle to transport the weapons stolen from the front line to Ivano-Frankivsk Region in Western Ukraine, the DBR has alleged.
The weapons were intended for sale on the black market, but will instead be used by Azov, the agency said, describing its members as “defenders of Ukraine.”
Azov originated as an ultranationalist Ukrainian volunteer militia amid the country’s bloody armed coup in 2014, before being incorporated into the country’s security forces. The unit has been widely accused of atrocities and war crimes by both Russia, which designated it a terrorist organization in 2022, and Western organizations, including the UN, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International.
Prior to the escalation of the conflict with Russia in 2022, US lawmakers had sought to restrict military assistance to the unit, citing its members’ far-right ideology. Western governments have since expanded their cooperation with the formation.
Moscow has for years warned that the Ukraine conflict would become a major source of illicit weapons for criminal groups and has alleged that elements within the Ukrainian state could be protecting trafficking networks.
Law enforcement agencies in several European countries have also warned about the risk that weapons from Ukraine could enter criminal markets.
Ukrainian organized crime tends to become joined at the hip with corrupt officials, as showcased earlier this month by the exposure of a protection racket operating in the prosecutor general’s office, which collected fees from scam-call centers.
The accusations by Western-backed anti-graft investigators forced the resignation of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko. The former key ally of Vladimir Zelensky has fled the country and reportedly resides in Vienna now.

Egypt-Israel trade sees dramatic June surge despite Gaza war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:37:03 UTC
21:37:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt-Israel trade sees dramatic surge in June despite Gaza war, regional tensions
Israel recorded an increase in economic ties with Egypt, with official data showing a doubling of exports and imports between the two sides during the final month of the financial year that ended in June 2025/2026.
This came after a relative slowdown in the growth rate of trade, which exceeded 24% between January and the end of May of the same year.
Official data showed a rise in trade between Egypt and Israel during June 2026, with Egyptian exports to Tel Aviv rising by about 148% and Egyptian imports from Israel increasing by about 127% year-on-year.
Trade statistics for June alone showed an increase in both directions.
Egyptian exports to Israel rose to $38.857 million in June, compared with $15.677 million in June 2025, an increase of $23.18 million, or 147.9%.
At the same time, Egyptian imports from Israel jumped to $266.376 million, compared with $117.294 million a year earlier, an increase of $149.082 million, or 127.1%.
However, during the first half of 2026, Egyptian imports from Israel fell to about $1.188 billion, compared with $1.234 billion in the same period of 2025, a decline of about $45.7 million, or 3.7%.
The total value of trade between the two sides during the first half of the year therefore fell slightly to about $1.362 billion, compared with about $1.374 billion during the same period last year, with a change in the composition of trade in favour of Egyptian exports.
The latest report by Egypt's Central Agency for Public Mobilisation and Statistics showed that Egyptian exports to Israel rose between January and June 2026 to about $174.1 million, compared with $140.1 million during the same period in 2025, an increase of $34.1 million, or 24.3%.
Uptick in trade
June figures show that the increase in Egyptian imports from Israel during a single month, at about $149.1 million, was more than three times the increase in Egyptian exports to Israel during the same month last year.
A comparison between cumulative and monthly data shows a clear difference in the trade trajectory.
During the first six months of the year, Egyptian exports to Israel rose by 24.3%, while imports from Israel fell by 3.7%. In June alone, however, both exports and imports surged.
The data was included in the June 2026 monthly foreign trade bulletin issued by the Central Agency for Public Mobilisation and Statistics.
It uses preliminary 2026 data against 2025 figures that were reviewed by the finance, foreign trade and industry ministries and the government statistics agency.
According to the latest available 2025 merchandise trade data from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Investment, Egyptian exports to Israel were led by salt, sulphur, stone, cement and lime products, worth about $88 million.
These were followed by inorganic chemicals at $28.2 million; electrical and electronic machinery and equipment at $27.1 million; plastics and articles thereof at $20.4 million; vegetable, fruit and nut products at $13.9 million; articles of stone and cement at $12 million; paper, cardboard and articles thereof at $10.5 million; and vegetables, roots, potatoes and edible tubers at $9.6 million, in addition to cement and building materials.
A source familiar with the matter at the Federation of Egyptian Chambers of Commerce told The New Arab that official statistics on exports and imports cover goods destined for Tel Aviv but exclude those allocated to the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.
The latter are recorded as part of trade between Egypt and Palestine under the trade classification of Arab countries.
In the same context, official statistics showed that natural gas and mineral products dominate Egyptian imports from Israel, according to 2025 data from the government statistics agency.
Egyptian imports of mineral fuels, oils, waxes and bitumen amounted to about $2.28 billion, compared with total imports from Israel of about $2.34 billion.
Foreign trade data show that Israel was among the most important Asian countries in Egypt's trade during the first half of 2026.
Total trade between the two countries, based on import and export data, stood at about $1.36 billion during the period, compared with about $1.37 billion in the first half of 2025, with a change in the composition of trade in favour of Egyptian exports.
Factories unable to meet needs
In this context, customs and logistics expert Nadia Al-Morshdy attributed the increase in imports to factories' need to purchase production supplies because manufacturers are unable to meet their needs from the domestic market.
She warned that the government does not appear interested in increasing reliance on manufacturing to reduce imports while encouraging investment in real estate and infrastructure sectors that consume most state investment.
Al-Morshdy told TNA that pressure on foreign trade during the first half of 2026 came from several simultaneous factors, including: higher energy import costs, increased intermediate goods, production inputs and supplies for factories and investment projects, ranging from heavy transport and technological equipment to growth in some categories of consumer and food goods, wheat, cars and durable goods.
Meanwhile, a report by the government statistics agency showed that the largest single increase in Egypt's overall imports of intermediate goods came from imports of raw forms of non-monetary gold.
The value of these imports rose to about $4.05 billion during the first half of the year, compared with only $240 million a year earlier, an increase of nearly $3.81 billion.
During the first half of the year, Egypt's total exports rose to $28.02 billion, compared with $26.12 billion, while non-oil exports reached about $24.07 billion, compared with $23.79 billion, according to the statistics agency.

Türkiye’s Roketsan launch systems to ensure independent access to space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:35:40 UTC
21:35:40 KST

Goksel Yildirim, Fuat Kabakci and Emir Yildirim
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Turkish defense firm Roketsan’s launch systems will help ensure independent access to space as Ankara expands investments in satellite systems to grab a larger share of the global space economy.
 
Roketsan CEO Murat Ikinci, speaking ahead of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) to be held in southwestern Türkiye, told Anadolu that efforts are underway to develop domestic platforms to deliver heavy payloads into orbit. The firm is focused on the Simsek 1 and Simsek 2 satellite launch systems, developed in coordination with the Defense Industries Agency (SSB).
“Countries that dominate the space field, especially those that have these technologies of their own, do not share any of the underlying technologies like navigation, propulsion, thermal, or materials with other countries, so by bringing these at our center of excellence established in 2020, through collaborations with universities and industry partners, we’re striving to establish us as a key player in space,” he said.
Ikinci stated that Roketsan has conducted a number of probe rocket tests since 2016 to validate its homegrown spaceflight solutions, as the trend among global aerospace leaders to withhold their proprietary technology prompted Türkiye to develop its own sovereign capabilities.
“We’ve largely completed the process of validating the solutions we developed for space and establishing a track record in space-related activities with the successful launch of Simsek 1 in the first phase and subsequently Simsek 2,” he added.
The Simsek 1 program aims to engineer a launch vehicle capable of placing a 400-kilogram (882-pound) payload into a 500-kilometer (310.6-mile) orbit. Building on the foundation of this project, a contract was signed last year for the Simsek 2 system to provide the capacity to deliver a 1.5-ton payload into an orbit of up to 700 kilometers (435 miles).
Roketsan plans to commercialize the Simsek 2 platform through global collaborations, positioning Türkiye as a global satellite launcher for its allies.
The firm has also established a defense and aerospace supply chain of nearly 2,500 active business partners to support its manufacturing goals. The majority of these partners currently assist with missile production, while the company is working to upgrade the capabilities of its qualified suppliers so they can participate in global space projects.
“Roketsan aims to create an ecosystem and build an entire supply chain so we do not face significant difficulties competing in the market,” Ikinci said.
He noted that the firm is collaborating with a wide range of partners, including universities, public institutions such as the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye’s (TUBITAK) space division, and the Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry.
Ikinci stated that Roketsan is also one of the key players in Türkiye’s National Space Program and its lunar objectives.
“We’ve assumed the responsibility to develop the platforms that will carry our payloads into space, one of the most critical components of this program,” he said.
He noted that the lunar program requires coordination among institutions and other allied countries, which he believes will further accelerate Türkiye’s progress in deep-space exploration.
He mentioned that Roketsan is a major sponsor of the IAC 2026 event to be held in Antalya, where the firm will foster new scientific collaborations.

Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:32:15 UTC
21:32:15 KST

Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.
"You can't have agents roam around and drift around the company, and so you have to find a way to container it," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
Huang said the new platform is essentially "a browser for agents," providing a containment system that only allows access to things an agent needs to do its job.
The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July. That's when OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached Hugging Face, which operates an open-source developer platform.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company. "From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers. But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
"You have to think about what you could have done, what's the solution for it," Huang said in a podcast with The New York Times' Ezra Klein released last week, referring to recent incidents. "In the future, improve your process so that you could avoid this from happening again."
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off an industry firestorm two weeks ago, urging AI model developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of the models spinning out of control, an argument that was supported by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk.
Nvidia's new offering is an engineering solution to the agent safety issue, Boitano said.
"Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can't govern what agents can access or do," Boitano said.
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities. Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
Nvidia named Cisco, Microsoft, Oracle, CoreWeave, Dell, HPE, Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners. Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.
"We can't have a successful AI industry if the world doesn't think it's built or confident that it's built and deployed safely," Huang told CNBC on Monday.

Are Germans Becoming Fascist Again?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:31:32 UTC
21:31:32 KST

The September 2026 regional election in Saxony-Anhalt appeared, in view of the small population of 2.12 million in this East German state, as a minor European event. Yet, the election represented a historic turn in the political development of the Federal Republic of Germany, Europe’s largest country and economy, since 1949 when the FRG was founded.
For the first time, a right-wing radical party, “Alternative for Germany,” known by its German abbreviation AfD and founded in 2013, has achieved, with a result of 43.8%, a victory of such proportion in a regional election.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The AfD has gained 39 of the 83 seats in Saxony-Anhalt’s regional parliament and thereby come close to an absolute majority of mandates. Coalition talks and parliamentary voting rounds during the next weeks will show whether the AfD will manage take over also the executive of Saxony-Anhalt. A regional state government dominated by the AfD – if it materializes – would represent an even more fateful new trend in German politics.
Moreover, Sachsen-Anhalt’s landmark election was not an outlier within formerly communist eastern Germany. Two weeks later, there were elections in the neighboring, northeast German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Here again, the AfD received a regional landmark result of 38.2%, on Sept. 20, 2026.
Being a nationalist, Eurosceptic and anti-immigration movement as well as a culturally monist, politically illiberal, yet economically libertarian party, the AfD stands at the right fringe of Germany’s otherwise liberal, pro-European party spectrum of Christian, social, free and green democrats.
Germany Warns Russia Against Escalation in Rare Wadephul-Lavrov Talks
Some of the AfD’s regional organizations, including that in Saxony-Anhalt, have been classified by the Federal Service for the Protection of the Constitution as “extremist,” i.e., as opposed to Germany’s constitutionally enshrined liberal-democratic order. Because of the AfD’s ambivalent stance to Germany’s fascist past, even many other European right-wing radical parties, such as France’s National Assembly, refuse to cooperate with the German nationalists, at the European level. On the contrary, Elon Musk and Donald Trump have both publicly greeted the electoral success of the AfD.
While the AfD contains a fascist faction, neither the rise of the organization as a whole nor its growing electorate during the last 10 years indicate an impending return to German Nazism. Instead, the AfD functions in many ways as a protest party which manages to channel social frustration, political disappointment, and cultural pessimism. That concerns especially East Germany, which had been part of the Soviet bloc in 1945-1990 and today comprises (without Berlin) 12.4 million of Germany’s 83.5 million inhabitations. On the territory of the formerly communist, so-called German Democratic Republic (GDR), the AfD is far more popular than on the territory of West Germany which has been a political democracy since the 1949.
Often East Germans’ dearth of democratic experience and the socio-economic turbulence of the 1990s transition are used to explain their different voting behavior. These traumas – as well as an outflow of young people and women, a low presence of Christian churches, and a rapidly ageing society – are standard explanations for the “Ossis” (Easterners) preference for both far left or far right anti-systemic parties. In East Germany itself, there is also a widespread belief that, allegedly, “Wessis” have been insufficiently respectful of “Ossis.”
What might be the strongest determinant of low support of liberal democracy in East Germany, is that, under Soviet occupation, it had missed out on West German society’s liberalization and pluralization in the aftermath of the 1968 student revolutions throughout the West. Since the 1970s, Western societies have become increasingly shaped by individualism, pluralism, feminism, ecologism, post-colonialism, cosmopolitanism, and similar anti-conservative ideas.
East Germans in the GDR, however, were shielded from these trends by the Iron Curtain until 1989. They thus preserved, more so than West Germans, remnants of the traditionally hierarchical, illiberal and ethnocentric German political culture that goes back to the immediate post-war and even pre-war periods.
The most important gap between the cultural developments of West and East Germany concerns the depth of thinking about the historical and political meaning of the 1933-45 fascist period for post-war Germans. In West Germany, the Nazi mass crimes and German responsibility for them, historical failure of German anti-fascism and their implications for today have become discussed, researched and problematized within an all-encompassing multi-decade deliberation. This national debate has become known under the label Vergangenheitsbewältigung which can be translated as “coming to terms with the past.”
To be sure, the educational policies, critical approaches and public discourse concerning the origins, nature and consequences of German crimes under Nazism were extended to the territory of the former GDR as a result of Germany’s reunification in 1990. Yet, East Germans’ only belated and partly imposed participation in Vergangenheitsbewältigung has led to far less skepticism towards right-wing extremism than in West German society. It also resulted in a higher degree of anti-Americanism in the East than in the West of Germany.
Today, this expresses itself through, among others, more support for the anti-Western regime of Vladimir Putin and tolerance for the Moscow connections of the AfD. While all centrist German parties have become supportive of Ukraine, Germany’s far right as well as far left have taken a more or less pro-Putinist position, and are opposed to both sanctions against Russia and military help for Kyiv.
So far, the proportional, parliamentary and multi-party political system of Germany is limiting the influence of the AfD as it remains a growing, yet isolated and stigmatized political force. Unless the German nationalists become more moderate – as, for example, the Swedish and Italian radical right have recently become – and thus a possible coalition partner, the AfD’s direct influence on Germany’s domestic and foreign policies will remain limited.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

China is no longer just the world’s factory. It’s the HQ
Manufacturing capacity is moving overseas but China, as a global hub for innovation and development, remains the ‘industrial brain’
The global electronics industry is entering a structural transition. For over two decades, China served as the dominant manufacturing centre, with an unmatched concentration of suppliers, skilled labour, infrastructure, logistics and engineering capabilities. That concentration is being diluted. But interpreting this as the decline of Chinese manufacturing would be a mistake.
According to the Boston Consulting Group (BCG), since 2017, the share of electronics manufacturers from China – Taiwan, Hong Kong and the mainland – with overseas production has risen to 56 per cent from 12 per cent. BCG based its analysis on 942 publicly traded companies with annual revenues above US$500 million, including 314 headquartered in China. This transformation is remarkable.

Ben-Gvir vows to kill Palestinian prisoner in campaign video
Unknown

2026-09-28

Breadcrumb
Ben-Gvir threatens to kill imprisoned senior Hamas figure ahead of Israel vote
Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has released footage of himself threatening to execute a Palestinian prisoner, as he campaigns for greater power over Israel's military and pushes for the mass displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The video, published on Sunday less than a month before Israel's 27 October election, shows Ben-Gvir confronting Hassan Salameh, a senior Hamas member imprisoned by Israel since 1996 over his alleged involvement in deadly bomb attacks in Jerusalem.
"These are the conditions I gave you. But it's not the end. I want to kill you. I want to put you to death," Ben-Gvir tells Salameh while flanked by armed, masked guards.
Telling Salameh he would go to hell in the afterlife, Ben-Gvir added: "But here I'm responsible for hell."
Ben-Gvir said the encounter represented "closure", recalling that as a teenager he had demonstrated following the 1996 Jerusalem bus bombings for which Salameh was convicted, before becoming national security minister decades later.
In a post accompanying the footage, Ben-Gvir made clear that the video was also tied to his political ambitions ahead of next month's election.
He said that if appointed defence minister in Israel's next government, he would work to execute Palestinian prisoners such as Salameh and advance the "voluntary migration" of Palestinians from both Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The Palestinian Prisoner's Society (PPS) said in a statement on Monday that the Salameh video was part of a wider pattern of using Palestinian detainees for "political and electoral one-upmanship", accusing Israeli politicians of competing to appear the most "hardline" and violent towards prisoners.
The group warned against dismissing such videos as mere election propaganda, arguing that repeated threats against Palestinian prisoners and their leaders posed a genuine danger to their lives.
Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party has said it will demand control of the defence and justice ministries as part of negotiations to join the next government.
His proposed "migration" policy envisages removing much of Gaza's Palestinian population and encouraging Palestinians in the occupied West Bank to leave, proposals Palestinians have rejected as forced displacement and critics have described as ethnic cleansing.
Earlier this month, Ben-Gvir unveiled a more detailed Gaza plan, dubbed "Disengagement 710", which included establishing a government ministry dedicated to facilitating Palestinian emigration.
The confrontation with Salameh is also the latest in a series of videos in which Ben-Gvir has used Palestinian prisoners and detainees to promote his policies.
In August 2025, he entered a prison to confront Marwan Barghouti, the imprisoned senior Fatah leader and former Palestinian legislator who remains one of the most prominent Palestinian political prisoners.
Footage showed a visibly gaunt Barghouti listening as Ben-Gvir told him that Israel would "wipe out" anyone who harmed Israelis.
More recently, Ben-Gvir filmed himself confronting Palestinian women held at Damon prison, mocking complaints about access to water and medical supplies and boasting about deteriorating conditions for Palestinian prisoners under his tenure.
He has repeatedly presented the worsening of prison conditions as one of his principal achievements as national security minister.
The videos have also brought Ben-Gvir into conflict with Israel's own election authorities.
In June, the Central Elections Committee ordered him to remove footage showing him taunting activists detained after attempting to reach Gaza by flotilla.
Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg ruled that the footage constituted election propaganda produced through the improper use of public resources.
The committee had previously found that videos of Ben-Gvir touring a prison and police boat similarly constituted illicit use of the security forces for campaigning.
The latest video comes after Ben-Gvir secured one of his longstanding political objectives in March, when the Knesset approved legislation allowing the death penalty in specified cases involving Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks. Nobody has yet been executed under the law.
Ben-Gvir's increasingly explicit election platform goes beyond prisons, as the Jewish Power leader has long advocated Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank and Palestinian displacement, and has made obtaining the defence portfolio a central demand ahead of the election.

Despite Kremlin’s Claims – European Arms Sales Grow, Russia’s Fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:29:27 UTC
21:29:27 KST

Figures published by the Russian Center for the Analysis of World Arms Trade (TSAMTO), claim Moscow has exported around $15 billion worth of arms and weapons, which it says is equivalent to 12.55 percent of the global volume.
The pro-Kremlin news site www1.ru published the figures, without questioning the data, on Sept. 24.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, the article does somewhat signal questions about the reliability of the figures. It says the Russian figure has “a special status in the ranking methodology,” as “open statistics for Russia after 2022” – the year of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – “are currently not available.” It states the $15 billion “represents an expert assessment by the center’s analysts.”
Russia’s figures contradict the assessment made by Sweden’s Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) figures for 2025, published in March 2026, which TSAMTO has dismissed as being “unverified.”
Ukraine’s Defense News on Monday cited Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) which explains the disparity between the figures claimed by TSAMTO and those of SIPRI.
SZRU says the Swedish figures are based on the actual records for the transfers of weapons systems while Russia’s are based on the Kremlin’s claims. SZRU categorizes this as a “familiar tactic” where unfavorable figures are simply replaced with those the Kremlin wants to promote.
Russia Wants Ukraine to 'Pay the Price'
Fact verses fiction
In its March survey of the global arms trade between 2016 and 2025, SIPRI said the volume of major arms transfers had increased by 9.2 percent.
According to SIPRI, the biggest increase, 9.7 percent of all arms transfers went to Ukraine – a direct result of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion – and similar increases among European states, some of which tripled their imports between 2021 and 2025. European suppliers also moved into the “top 10” of exporters with France, Germany and Italy leading the way.
The US, which is historically the world’s largest supplier of arms, also saw an increase of 27 percent, globally, but a staggering 217 percent increase in US arms exports to Europe. Meanwhile, it said arms imports to all other regions of the world had decreased.
According to SIPRI, Russia saw its arms exports fall by a colossal 64 percent during the period – with its share of global arms exports shrinking from 21 percent in 2016–20 to 6.8 percent in 2021–25 (almost half the figure Moscow claims), with the bulk of its sales going to India (48 percent), China (13 percent) and Belarus (13 percent).
These figures underlined the ZSRU assessment that, despite Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s best efforts, Russia’s share of the global arms market, and by implication its standing in then world, has fallen to its lowest level since arms sales statistics were first published – including during Soviet times.

Spanish government representative in Ceuta quits over border rush fallout
MADRID, Sept 28 - Spain's representative in its North African enclave of Ceuta resigned on Monday, citing personal reasons after weeks of intense scrutiny over the handling of a border rush involving the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco.
The crisis erupted in late July, when more than 72,000 migrants reached Ceuta, overwhelming reception facilities and intensifying debate over migration policy at one of the European Union's two land borders in Africa.
Most of those migrants subsequently left, though thousands of others remain in the self-governing enclave, and the minority leftist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez in Madrid has struggled to contain the political fallout.
Government Delegate Miguel Angel Perez Triano, who oversaw coordination between the Ceuta government and Spanish state agencies and security forces, defended his handling of the crisis but said the subsequent scrutiny, coupled with what he called a campaign of harassment against him and his family, had become unbearable.
"My family doesn't deserve that I should stay on any longer," he said, citing insults, threats and an instance when somebody left a funeral wreath outside his office.
He said the government delegation had no operational control over the border or security forces and that no information available beforehand indicated that so many migrants would enter the enclave.
The Madrid government has repeatedly said that although it received alerts of possible border crossings, nothing pointed to a rush on the scale ultimately seen in Ceuta.
Spain's High Court is conducting an investigation into the events and is due to hear testimony this week from Perez Triano's former chief of staff.
Speaking to Cope radio station on Monday, Spanish Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres estimated that up to 3,500 migrants remained in Ceuta outside the enclave's reception facilities. REUTERS

Pope Leo urges concessions to end war in Ukraine

Pope Leo XIV and Emmanuel Macron shake hands at the Robert Schuman Conference Centre in Metz, France, on Sept. 28, 2026. | Pool photo by Benoit Tessier via AFP/Getty Images
Pope Leo XIV encouraged compromise and urged warring parties to make concessions to secure peace in Ukraine during a closely watched speech about Europe in France.
“Sadly, war has returned, even to Europe,” the pope said in the eastern city of Metz. “We need to commit ourselves to patient dialogue, to show courage in negotiation and to be willing to give up some positions for the greater good of peace.”
The pope addressed European issues on his final day of an official visit to France, during which he held talks with President Emmanuel Macron, celebrated a large-scale mass in central Paris, and urged dialogue and compassion for migrants.
Advertisement
In a speech delivered to a packed room, the pope did not specify what concessions he thought Kyiv or Moscow might have to make to secure peace. Russian forces are persistently bombing Ukraine and attempting to push forward in the Donetsk region, but the Kremlin’s military has so far failed to subjugate Kyiv after more than four and a half years of all-out war.
The pontiff has taken an active role in recent months, pushing for an end to hostilities in Ukraine. In August, Leo sent Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the equivalent of his foreign minister, to Moscow to meet with officials including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Another Vatican envoy is set to visit Russia this week.
The visits highlight that Leo is adopting a more proactive role in trying to mediate over Ukraine, with Europe largely absent in diplomacy with Russia, though German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul did meet with Lavrov in New York at the weekend.
The pontiff has repeatedly called for the end of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, and expressed hope that negotiations would resume and lead to a diplomatic solution.
In his speech on Europe, the pope also praised Robert Schuman, one of the founding fathers of the European Union and a practicing Catholic. He also urged migrants to be welcomed “as if they were part of one’s own family,” at a moment when anti-immigration parties are on the rise across Europe, including in France where Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally is topping the polls.
“We must grasp the historical significance of what is taking place, namely an unprecedented encounter between peoples and cultures, which calls us to rediscover our roots in new and creative ways, while at the same time listening carefully to others,” he said.

Kallas noted the ministers had made no new decision on missile transfers. Member states and partners could supply missiles from their own stocks "in exchange for later replacement," she said.

Experts estimate that, even if fighting in the Middle East ended immediately, replenishing depleted stocks would take years at current production rates.

Ninth-century Arabic silver coins found near Viking trading centre in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:25:52 UTC
21:25:52 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Experts believe they may have belonged to merchants travelling to or from the Viking Age port of Truso, which was situated nearby.
The silver dirhams date back around 1,200 years, to the first half of the ninth century, before the founding of the Polish state. They may have remained in circulation until the turn of the 10th/11th century, the time of the settlement’s collapse.
The discovery of the “new treasure” was announced last week by the Archaeological and Historical Museum in Elbląg. It did not reveal who had unearthed them, but said that the find had taken place during a legal search in a forest near the town of Młynary, just east of Elbląg.
After conservation and processing work, the coins will be included in the collection of the museum, whose archaeologists will also visit the site hoping for further finds.
The museum’s Jakub Jagodziński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the find consists of “six early medieval Arabic dirhams and two fragments of these silver coins”. He said that they are provisionally dated to the first half of the 9th century, but a more precise estimate will be possible after they are processed.
The coins could have belonged to merchants travelling along the routes leading to or from Truso or to Prussian guards who later collected tolls on these routes, Jagodziński explained.
Truso was a Viking Age port of trade set up by the Scandinavians on the shores of lake Druzno near the Vistula river delta. Established by the late 7th century and active until the early 11th century, its location enabled trade extending towards Kyivan Rus, Byzantium and the Islamic world.
Historians knew of Truso’s existence because of the account of the Anglo-Saxon traveller Wulfstan of Hedeby. Centuries-long efforts to find the precise site proved fruitless until it was finally discovered in the early 1980s by the young archaeologist Marek Jagodziński, Jakub’s father.
Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website.
More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland.
In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP.
“Therefore, when hoards of Arab coins are discovered in Poland, they are divided into several pieces. Whole coins are also found, but much less frequently,” he explained.
