“Britain has it harder now. We had 13 years of flatlining tory growth in living standards when Cameron’s austerity gutted our public services, when Johnson’s Brexit hammered our exports and Truss’s mini budget crashed our economy,” he said.
He also accused Reform of taking a reckless approach to the public finances while prioritising the interests of “dodgy” billionaire donors, saying that Nigel Farage was “Liz Truss with a bitcoin account.”
Healey’s local apprenticeships announcement comes as ministers await recommendations from a highly anticipated report by Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness.
The chancellor also said he wanted to usher in a “new age of industrialisation,” announcing £6bn of contracts for our British shipyards
Using Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool to spell out his agenda for government, Burnham has pledged to “rip the plaster off” to fix Britain’s social care system and announced a new help-to-buy scheme to support young people to get on the housing ladder.

Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:25:21 UTC
21:25:21 KST

Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
A remarkably complete “Cretaceous rabbit” fossil from Mongolia has overturned a 40-year-old idea about early mammal evolution.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- American Museum of Natural History
- Summary:
- A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.
- Share:
A remarkably complete fossil discovered in Mongolia's Gobi Desert is changing how scientists view mammal evolution during the age of dinosaurs. The newly identified species, described in the journal Nature by researchers from the American Museum of Natural History, Stony Brook University, University of Arizona, and Arcadia University, provides new evidence about an extinct group of mammals called zhelestids.
For decades, many scientists thought zhelestids were closely related to modern placental mammals. The new fossil suggests otherwise. Instead, zhelestids appear to have belonged to a very different branch of early mammals, overturning an interpretation that was based largely on fossil teeth.
"This discovery illustrates why fieldwork remains indispensable to understanding life's history," said the study's lead author Andres Giallombardo, who found the specimen as a graduate student on a Museum-sponsored expedition in 2004. "It was the thrill of a career to find a new species so completely preserved that also solves a longstanding scientific problem, and a reminder that the Gobi Desert, which is well known for fossils, continues to change science."
Fossil Teeth Pointed Scientists in the Wrong Direction
Zhelestids have been known to paleontologists for nearly 40 years, but most discoveries consisted of isolated teeth or incomplete remains. Their teeth were unusually specialized for eating plants compared with the sharper teeth used for eating insects that are common among many Cretaceous mammals.
Those features led some paleontologists to propose that zhelestids represented an unknown group of hoofed mammals. Scientists also debated whether they might have been placental mammals living during the Cretaceous, part of the broad group that today includes humans and most living mammal species, or whether they were part of a separate lineage that independently evolved similar characteristics.
Molecular clock studies have supported the possibility that placental mammals originated well before the end of the Cretaceous. The newly described fossil, however, provides physical evidence pointing in another direction.
"Molecular models based on living animals can predict the past, but fossils provide the evidence needed to test those predictions," said study coauthor Paul Velazco, a comparative biologist at Arcadia University.
A Nearly Complete Skeleton Reveals the Animal's True Identity
The new species, Tamirkhan balcarceli, was discovered in the eastern Gobi Desert and is the most complete zhelestid specimen found so far. Because so much of the animal is preserved, scientists can now see what members of this mysterious group actually looked like.
Tamirkhan has the low, rounded teeth associated with zhelestids. But it also possesses long, continuously growing incisors and several distinctive skull features seen in zalambdalestoids, a group of small, shrew-like insectivore mammals.
Its limbs provide another important clue.
"Tamirkhan's hind legs are long and slender with distinctive ankles, traits that are unmistakably zalambdalestoid," said study author Shawn Zack, a paleontologist at the University of Arizona.
Taken together, those features led the researchers to conclude that zhelestids were neither placental mammals nor especially similar to placentals. Instead, they were part of the zalambdalestoid group.
The finding also suggests that Cretaceous mammals may not have been as anatomically varied as scientists might have inferred from their teeth alone. The rounded teeth associated with zhelestids, which resemble those found in many plant-eating mammals, were probably an example of convergent evolution. This occurs when unrelated animals independently develop similar traits as they adapt to comparable ways of life.
Why Teeth Cannot Always Reveal the Whole Animal
The discovery highlights the risks of reconstructing an extinct animal from only a small part of its skeleton.
"More than 200 years ago, French naturalist Georges Cuvier famously argued that a single tooth could allow scientists to predict the anatomy of an entire animal," said study coauthor Maureen O'Leary, a paleontologist at Stony Brook University and research associate at the Museum. "While teeth remain among the most informative fossils available, this work demonstrates that teeth cannot always tell us how the whole animal looked."
Measuring between 6-7 inches from head to tail, Tamirkhan had unusually elongated hind limbs that gave it an appearance somewhat like a rabbit. Paleontologists have sometimes informally called zhelestids "Cretaceous rabbits" because they resembled rabbits despite being only distantly related to modern ones.
The Gobi Desert Continues To Reshape Mammal Evolution
The specimen also demonstrates the exceptional scientific value of the Gobi Desert. Along with fossil sites in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan, the region is one of the few places where zhelestids have been preserved.
"The Gobi is one of the only places where we routinely recover such remarkably complete Cretaceous mammals," said coauthor Michael Novacek, a curator in the Museum's Division of Paleontology who has co-led annual expeditions to the Gobi since 1990 in partnership with the Mongolian Academy of Sciences. "These extraordinary fossils continue to transform our understanding of mammalian evolution."
The researchers were also able to place the new species within the mammal family tree using MorphoBank, a comprehensive research platform for studying mammalian evolutionary relationships. First published in 2013, the database has grown for more than a decade as scientists have added an increasing number of important fossil species. It now provides the most comprehensive framework yet assembled for analyzing relationships among early mammals.
Other authors on this study include Eva Hoffman from Yale University.
Fieldwork and laboratory research in the Gobi Desert were supported in part by the Margaret and Will Hearst Paleontological Research Fund and the Frick Laboratory Endowment at the Museum. The research also received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation, grant numbers MRI-R2 0959384, EAR 2506729, and EAR 2506727.

Journal Reference:
- Andres Giallombardo, Eva A. Hoffman, Maureen A. O’Leary, Paúl M. Velazco, Shawn P. Zack, Michael J. Novacek. Cretaceous zhelestid mammals are zalambdalestoids. Nature, 2026; 657 (8133): 973 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10861-5

Turkish comedian convicted over Erdogan ‘insult’ but freed pending appeal

- Goktas defended his satire as political critique, arguing Erdogan should accept humour, highlighting a tougher stance on freedom of expression in Turkey today.
- His arrest sparked protests and inspired younger comedians like Fatih Yilmaz to continue stand-up, despite fears of government crackdown on critics.
AI generated
Istanbul - An Istanbul court convicted a popular Turkish comedian on Sept 28 of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and another offence but ordered his interim release pending appeal, an AFP reporter in the courtroom said.
Following a lively opening session in which Deniz Goktas, 32, offered a quick-witted defence that had much of the courtroom in stitches, the judge convicted him on two charges, sentencing him to just over 19 months prison.
But until the sentence is finalised – which only happens after it is reviewed by an appeals court – the judge ordered his release.
It was not immediately clear how long the process would take.
Known for his dry wit and political satire, Goktas has spent nearly three months in Karatepe high-security prison since his arrest on July 3, a week after a YouTube video of his Dead Sea show went viral, reaching nine million views.
Goktas went on trial for insulting Erdogan, incitement to public hatred and praising crime and criminals.
The judge convicted Goktas on the first charge.
He then amended the second charge to “insulting religious values” and convicted him of that too, while acquitting him on charge three, the correspondent said.
When the hearing opened, Goktas took to the stand to weave a defence rich in political satire, making witty observations that frequently had the courtroom in fits of laughter.
‘Can’t take a joke’
In the indictment, prosecutors singled out a line in which he called Erdogan “a shy dictator” but Goktas insisted there was “no criminal element” there.
“Dictator is not an insult: it is a political characterisation,” he said.
“As the president and leader of the party that has ruled the country for 25 years, a political comedy show in which Erdogan’s name is never mentioned would be neither sincere nor have any connection to reality,” he reasoned.
“Erdogan should be open to the art of satire,” he added, denying the charges against him.
None of Turkey’s most famous comedians or political satirists had been prosecuted in the past, when “these kinds of criticisms were received much more positively... by society and those in power than they are today”, Goktas continued.
“The laws protecting freedom of expression have not changed since that time. But today, a comedian is sitting in a cell.
“The joke hasn’t changed. What has changed is the increasingly fragile leadership that can no longer tolerate the joke.”
Among the audience were several comedians from Istanbul’s TuzBiber comedy club – where Goktas reportedly began his career in 2019 – alongside observers from the Dutch and American embassies.
Humour, Goktas told the court, was a centuries-old part of Turkish culture but there should be “no place for censorship, bans or detention when it comes to artistes on the stage”.
‘Makes me feel proud’
He asked to be acquitted and released.
“Three months have been taken away from my life. I quit smoking, so I’ll add three months to the end of my life anyway,” he said, drawing laughter and loud applause as he left the stand.
Goktas’s arrest was the latest in a widening crackdown on anyone seen as critical of Turkey’s Islamo-conservative government or its values.
The crackdown has netted hundreds of people, including politicians, artistes, musicians, journalists and LGBTQ activists.
Outside in the pouring rain, around 50 protesters gathered, chanting: “Denis Goktas is not alone!”
Among them was a student from Alanya near the southern resort city of Antalya whose appearance is strikingly similar to Goktas and who recently started doing stand-up.
“I am not afraid to do stand-up after his arrest. I will keep doing it,” 22-year-old Fatih Yilmaz told AFP.
“His arrest made me feel proud. His strong stance and the way he keeps making jokes from his prison cell keep me going.”
Turkish media said the Ankara-born comedian began his career at TuzBiber in Istanbul and has gone on to perform at venues across Europe and the United States. AFP

The ship is now safely under tow towards Paradip. ICG units remain on active sentinel watch—ensuring safety & protecting our oceans 24/7."The specialist Damage Control Team boarded the tanker, deployed submersible pumps to remove water from its ballast tanks and sealed damaged sea-pipelines to stabilise the vessel.
An ICG Pollution Control Vessel and an Offshore Patrol Vessel were also diverted to the site to support pollution response and maintain surveillance. A Dornier aircraft confirmed that the minor palm-oil sheen observed in the area had completely dissipated, the Coast Guard said.The ICG said its units remained on watch as the ship was towed towards Paradip.
Recent Coast Guard rescue operations
Earlier, on September 11, the Coast Guard evacuated 21 crew members from merchant vessel MV KMAX EMPEROR after it collided with another ship, MV TRUE MARINER, near the outer anchorage of OTB Kandla in Gujarat.On August 21, the Coast Guard also carried out search and rescue operations after cargo vessel MV Ocean Winner sank in the Bay of Bengal, around 290 nautical miles off Paradip. The ship was carrying about 71,200 metric tonnes of iron ore fines from Odisha to China and had 24 crew members on board, including 20 Chinese nationals, one Bangladeshi and three Myanmar nationals.

EU allocates €325 million for five defence projects, four include Ukraine

EU allocates €325 million for five defence projects, four include Ukraine
The European Commission has allocated €325 million to support the establishment and implementation of five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI), with Ukraine taking part in four of them.
Source: European Pravda, citing the European Commission press service
Details: The industrial projects focus on five priority areas: drones and counter-drone systems, maritime and seabed defence, space, air and missile defence, and strengthening security along the EU's eastern flank.
"Member states, together with the support of the EU, are joining forces, pooling their expertise and investing together in the capabilities we need. From drones and air defence to space, maritime, and the security of our Eastern Flank and the European Union as a whole, the five projects focus on the areas where we need to move faster to build a stronger, more resilient European defence," said Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defence and Space.
EDPCIs are large-scale industrial projects which provide a framework for member states to work together on major defence initiatives that are too large or too complex for individual countries to develop on their own. The projects are designed to cover the full lifecycle of defence capability development, from creation to deployment and operation.
On average, 18 member states participate in each project, and Ukraine participates in four of the five projects. The commission is expected to take part in the EDPCIs, provide financial support and continue to help member states coordinate their implementation.
The funds have been allocated under the €1.5 billion European Defence Industry Programme.
Background:
- Earlier, Lithuania said the European Commission would consider a request from the Baltic states for an additional €500 million to bolster drone defences.
- On 28 September, EU defence ministers will discuss the possibility of transferring Patriot air defence interceptor missiles to Ukraine from EU member states' stockpiles in exchange for later deliveries from the manufacturer funded by Ukraine.

New bill to soften Starmer-era scrapping of jury trials, justice secretary confirms

LIVERPOOL, England — Justice Secretary Alex Norris confirmed that a new Courts Bill will seek to address criticism of the Keir Starmer-era plan to scrap up to half of all jury trials in England and Wales.
Norris, who replaced David Lammy as justice secretary in July, told an upcoming episode of the “Politics at Sam and Anne’s” podcast that the new bill — heading for the Commons in October — will include “major structural reforms” to speed up court hearings. But he said critics of culling jury trials “had been listened to” since new Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated in the summer that he would prefer an outcome which entailed “not reducing access to jury trial.”
Officials told POLITICO Sunday night that one solution may be a return to original recommendations by Justice Brian Leveson, who was asked by Norris’ predecessor Lammy to review the courts system in a bid to tackle a major backlog that is delaying cases.
Advertisement
Lammy went further than Leveson, pushing beyond his recommendation for judge-and-magistrate panels to replace juries in some cases and instead backing single-judge courts. The proposal raised concern among some lawmakers that a defining principle of the English justice system is under threat.
“We have heard the concerns about the balance between the speed [of the] justice system and people feel[ing] confident about the process,” Norris said Monday morning.
Early release
Norris has also been tasked with solving the hot-button issue of early release for prisoners, a Starmer-era bid to ease overcrowded jails. The justice secretary cited measures intended to reassure the public, including increased restriction zones for those released on bail for serious offences, and more sophisticated tagging of offenders.
But Norris also ruled out any changes to the early release of stalking and domestic violence perpetrators, with a major tranche of releases due to begin in October heavily criticized by victims’ and women’s rights groups.
“We would like to have gone further and kept more categories of offender in prison for longer, but we also have to have enough prison places in this country,” he said.
The bailing of sex offender Zafer Dogan back to the London address where his offences — which included making thousands of AI-generated paedophile images — took place unleashed fierce criticism last week from Mark Rowley, the London Met police chief. Rowley blasted a system in which “victims are left fearful” and criticized the “unfathomable decisions” of the justice system.
Norris said he has had “conversations” about the criticism with the London police chief.

Harles Tammeleht: Business tourism could help Tallinn hotels survive the winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

Harles Tammeleht: Business tourism could help Tallinn hotels survive the winter
A conference center at Tallinn's Linnahall could bring visitors during the low season and help hotels and restaurants operate year-round, writes Harles Tammeleht.
According to the Estonian Convention Bureau (EKB), organizers of dozens of international professional conferences have considered Tallinn in recent years but ultimately chose other destinations. Most of these conferences draw between 1,000 and 3,500 participants, while the largest attract more than 7,000. Together, they represent nearly 60,000 delegates and an estimated €65.5 million.
Nearly all of these conferences have more than 1,000 participants and none of Tallinn's existing venues was suitable for them.
According to consulting firm Gaining Edge, the leading criterion in choosing a destination for an international conference is whether its venues have the capacity and facilities the event requires. The availability of hotels also matters.
Tallinn is ruled out because it lacks the necessary venues. Organizers generally need more than one large room: they also need smaller rooms nearby for working groups, as well as space for exhibitions, networking and catering. These requirements are why the planned large arena would not remove the need for a conference center. Estonia needs both.
Tallinn is the only capital in the Nordic and Baltic region without a large, multifunctional conference and exhibition center that meets international standards. Tampere, for example, has a population of 245,000 and hosts nearly 900 events a year. Vilnius' LITEXPO hosts 1,300, while Riga has the ATTA Center.
A conference's significance for hotels
Take an event with 2,000 delegates, each staying an average of four nights. About 85 percent of delegates at international professional conferences arrive from abroad and need a hotel room, though some share with a colleague or companion.
That amounts to 5,900 room nights or about 1,480 rooms each night. In Tallinn's hotel market, which has more than 7,100 rooms, that would occupy 21 percent of the city's total room capacity at once.
Alongside the large conference hotels, midsize and smaller hotels would fill up too. During the low season, those hotels might otherwise be half empty or closed altogether. One such event would generate about €470,000 in room revenue during the low season. Delegates' direct spending in Estonia would total approximately €2.1 million, of which nearly €540,000 would go to taxes.
International professional conferences are planned three to five years in advance and generally avoid the summer months.
Consider what would happen if the Estonian Convention Bureau's forecast proves correct and the center brings Tallinn an additional 18,000 business visitors a year or roughly eight large international conferences. Hotel occupancy would rise by 2.5 percentage points.
Two and a half percentage points may not sound like much, but it means an additional 26,600 room nights in the months when occupancy is lowest. In the hotel business, a few percentage points of winter occupancy often determine whether the year ends in a loss or a profit.
More important still, conference demand enters the market differently from leisure travel demand. During the low season, a hotel usually fills its last rooms by lowering prices. A conference room block, however, comes at a contracted rate that is generally higher than what the hotel would otherwise charge for a room in January.
Conferences are also known about well in advance. A leisure traveler books two weeks ahead; a large international conference books two to five years ahead. A hotel that knows two large conferences are coming to the city in February the year after next can plan staffing, renovations and pricing very differently from one that faces each winter with uncertainty.
Labor and investment capacity
That brings us to two problems the accommodation sector has complained about for years, both directly fueled by seasonality.
The first is staffing. Estonia's long-term tourism strategy identifies staff turnover caused by seasonality as one of the main obstacles facing accommodation and food service businesses. It sets a goal of raising the sector's value added per employee from €21,839 to €48,000. More consistent demand throughout the year is essential to reaching that goal: it allows businesses to retain permanent staff, invest in training and pay competitive wages. A seasonal hotel cannot do that, however much it wants to.
The second is accommodation capacity itself. According to an analysis by Tallinn's Strategic Management Office, the city will need another 1,400 to 2,200 rooms by 2040 to accommodate the projected number of overnight stays. But a new hotel cannot be built on the strength of seasonal demand alone. The return on such an investment is calculated over years, not three months.
Catering and the rest of the city
Conference delegates differ from the average visitor chiefly in how long they stay. An international conference delegate is known to spend about €1,045 per trip in Estonia, compared with €316 for the average foreign tourist, according to the border survey. The difference in daily spending is smaller, but two-thirds of delegates stay for three to six nights and 25 to 40 percent extend their visit for a vacation. The average foreign tourist stays 2.6 nights.
According to the border survey, foreign tourists spend an average of €34 a day on food and drink. Coffee breaks, lunches, receptions and gala dinners paid for by conference organizers come on top of that. EIS (Estonian Business and Innovation Agency — ed.) estimates that local businesses earn more than 40 percent additional revenue while an event is taking place.
Unlike some other types of visitors, conference delegates stay in the city: they sleep in hotels, eat in restaurants, use transportation and shop at local stores. According to EIS, 60 percent of international conference delegates would like to return for a vacation.
Linnahall
The Estonian Convention Bureau considers Tallinn's Linnahall suitably located and believes it could accommodate a main hall with more than 3,000 seats, a modular conference area for more than 7,000 delegates and over 10,000 square meters of exhibition space. Such a venue would also make it possible to host trade fairs, cultural events and other international gatherings that bring guests to the city's hotels and restaurants.
For the center's business model to work, it would need an operator with international expertise that actively attracts events. Nor would a conference center alone solve the seasonality of Estonia's tourism industry. Tallinn is in a region through which approximately 2,750 international conferences and trade fairs with 500 to 4,000 delegates rotate each year, so the demand already exists.
Estonia's long-term tourism strategy for 2025–2035 lists the availability of a multifunctional conference center as a measure to track. Tallinn accounts for 69 percent of overnight stays by foreign visitors in Estonia, which means Tallinn's low season is also Estonia's low season.
For years, the accommodation and food service sector has been tasked with increasing value added, lengthening visits and reducing seasonality. But those three goals cannot be achieved together without the facilities to host multiday international conferences.

September 27 votes: Swiss Abroad less dismissive of food security initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

September 27 votes: Swiss Abroad less dismissive of food security initiative
The two proposals put to the vote on Sunday, which were overwhelmingly rejected by the Swiss electorate as a whole, did not fare any better among the diaspora. On the issue of neutrality, Swiss citizens living abroad voted in a remarkably similar way to the rest of the country. The food security initiative, however, received slightly more support.
Sunday’s votes resulted in both initiatives being rejected by more than 70% of the vote. The neutrality initiative, which sought to enshrine a strict interpretation of neutrality in the constitution, was rejected by 70.2% of voters and by all the cantons.
The vote by Swiss citizens living abroad on this issue was almost exactly the same. In the 12 cantons for which the Federal Statistical Office has detailed figuresExternal link, expatriates rejected the initiative by 70.4%.
Such a high degree of similarity is rare, notes Agnese Zucca, project manager at the gfs.bern institute. “This sends a clear message of unity regarding what the population wants in terms of neutrality, whether they live in Switzerland or abroad,” she explains.
Zucca is not surprised by the clear rejection by the Swiss Abroad, “which is consistent with the way Swiss citizens living abroad tend to vote on this type of issue relating to foreign and security policy”.
More
Six takeaways from the rejection of the neutrality initiative
For Zucca, what is most notable is rather that Swiss citizens living abroad – who are generally more urban and progressive, and who generally vote further to the left – did not reject the proposal even more decisively than the rest of the country.
Looking at how Swiss cities voted, she says there are varying levels of support, but these were much lower in certain cities such as Bern (11% in favour), Zurich (17%) and Basel (19%).
A ‘counterpoint on environmental issues’
The food initiative also suffered a real drubbing at the ballot box. Nationwide, 72.5% of voters said no. Here too, every canton rejected the proposal.
However, among the Swiss Abroad, the rejection was less resounding. Nearly 37% of expat voters supported the proposal – nine percentage points higher than the figure for the Swiss population as a whole.
This result was anticipated by the gfs.bern research institute. The latest Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) poll even predicted this 37% approval rate among Swiss citizens living abroad.
For Agnese Zucca, there were no surprises “not only because we know that Swiss citizens living abroad tend to vote more to the left, but also because we have seen the same kind of trend in recent years, for example with the CO₂ Act and the initiatives on pesticides or drinking water.”
“Swiss citizens living abroad are more sensitive to environmental issues and almost always provide a counterpoint to the domestic population,” she concludes.
Zucca adds that the core demands of the initiative were, on the whole, supported by the Swiss population. It was the specific issues – relating, for example, to the funding or feasibility of the measures – that ultimately tipped the balance in favour of a no vote.
“It is conceivable that Swiss citizens living abroad were less exposed to these arguments, but also that these arguments carry less weight for them than for Swiss citizens living in Switzerland,” she observes.
Average turnout
Nationwide, this vote saw a turnout of 47% of the electorate – a figure that is towards the lower end of the average (49% over the last five years) and lower than in other votes this year. Among Swiss citizens living abroad, turnout stood at 24%, which is also in line with the average.
This modest turnout comes as no surprise to Agnese Zucca. The neutrality initiative was the driving force behind this referendum, she said. However, “early polls were already suggesting that it was mobilising support mainly among the Swiss People’s Party electorate,” she points out. “Subsequently, it became quite clear that it was not likely to secure a majority, which probably explains why it did not mobilise voters to any great extent.”

Strengthening Latvia’s security requires both investment in defence and economic growth,the expansion of domestic production and close cooperation with allies. Latvia Shares its Public Administration Modernisation Experience with Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:16:56 UTC
21:16:56 KST

On 11 September, a delegation of Ukrainian state secretaries and representatives of civil society organisations visited the State Chancellery to gain insight into Latvia’s public administration practices. Discussions focused on the role of state secretaries and department heads in the public administration of Latvia, practical examples of modernisation and innovation, as well as approaches to human resource management, motivation and training.
The Ukrainian colleagues were introduced to the main areas and activities of public administration modernisation in Latvia. Representatives of the State Chancellery emphasised the important role of dialogue between the state and service users, as positive personal experience can help increase public trust – one of the indicators that both countries seek to improve. “Citizens expect more forms of direct communication and participation that enable the public administration to listen to what they really need,” said Ilona Anna Eklona, Head of the Public Administration Policy Department. She also highlighted the importance of data in decision-making that is a key focus of the work of the State Chancellery’s Analytical Service, and the introduction of ex-post evaluations, which help assess the actual impact of a legal act 3–5 years after its adoption.
The discussion was held at the State Chancellery’s Innovation Laboratory, where its head, Evija Taurene, introduced her Ukrainian colleagues to the laboratory’s operating principles and the results it has achieved. The laboratory serves as a methodological centre that helps the public sector to understand the needs of society and address specific challenges in policy development, service improvement and the reduction of administrative burdens. A team of innovation and service design experts also trains change leaders to promote a broader shift in service culture and mindset within public administration.
The guests were also presented with Latvia’s approach to developing human resources policy in public administration and examples from practice, with particular emphasis on a people-centred approach, close cooperation with institutions, and the significant role of heads of institutions in driving change and strengthening public administration capacity. “Our approach to developing human resources policy is based on partnership – on open dialogue, shared understanding and solutions that we develop together,” emphasised Ērika Todjēre, Head of the Human Resources Policy Department. The guests were particularly interested in Latvia’s experience in the selection and development of senior managers, as Ukraine, while continuing its public administration reforms, needs to strengthen its professional approach to selecting senior managers. Latvia’s approach to strengthening cooperation with the academic community by forging closer links between public administration, research and knowledge was also welcomed.
The public sector in both Latvia and Ukraine is facing generational change, rapid technological development and the need to acquire new skills and knowledge at a fast pace. Agita Kalviņa, Director of the School of Public Administration, heads a training centre that organises and delivers specialised training and courses tailored to the needs of the public sector. “The transformation of human resources is meaningful only when it is systematic and training is targeted at developing the competences required by the institution and for the specific post,” she emphasized in a discussion with Ukrainian representatives involved in public administration reforms.

On 13 July, the Prime Minister took part in a ceremony to unveil a commemorative plaque honouring the Baltic Way, the Baltic peoples’ non-violent resistance campaign, on Île aux Cygnes, an island in the River Seine near the Eiffel Tower. The unveiling ceremony was also attended by the Estonian Prime Minister, the Deputy Speaker of the Lithuanian Seimas, the Mayor of Paris and the French Minister for European Affairs.
The Prime Minister, accompanied by his spouse, travelled to France at the invitation of French President Emmanuel Macron and took part in the official celebrations marking the French Republic’s National Day, including an official dinner and the military parade marking Bastille Day. The soldiers of the Latvian Armed Forces also took part in the military parade.

Prime Minister and President of the European Council Discuss Latvia’s Priorities for the Next EU Multiannual Budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:16:08 UTC
21:16:08 KST

On Wednesday, 26 August, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs met with the President of the European Council, António Costa, to discuss the security situation on the EU’s Eastern Flank, the next EU multiannual budget, support for Ukraine and the instrumentalization of migration.
During the meeting, the Prime Minister emphasized that the European Council will have to take key decisions that will shape Europe’s future towards the end of this year.
From Latvia’s perspective, one of the most important issues is the security of the EU’s Eastern Flank and ensuring that this is adequately reflected in the EU’s budgetary priorities. Latvia has significantly increased its investment in national defence. This year, 4.91% of gross domestic product (GDP) has been allocated to defence, while from next year onwards at least 5% of GDP is earmarked for defence. Since 2022, Latvia has allocated nearly EUR 1 billion to strengthening its eastern border. The specific circumstances of the EU’s eastern border must be taken into account both in the allocation of national funding and in access to EU funds.
“Latvia lies on the external border of the EU and NATO, and we face threats from Russia and Belarus on a daily basis. This is not just Latvia’s border – it is the external border of the entire European Union and NATO. Therefore, due consideration must also be given to the specific situation in our region in the EU budget negotiations. Investment in Latvia and other Eastern Flank countries is also an investment in the security of Europe as a whole,” the Prime Minister pointed out.
The Prime Minister also pointed out that security risks affect Latvia’s economy and that the European Union must show solidarity, be secure and economically competitive. “A strong economy is a prerequisite for being able to invest sufficiently in both defence and the welfare of our citizens,” the Prime Minister stressed.
The talks also covered fair competition, including the need to ensure more equitable direct payments for Latvian farmers. Latvia’s position is that, in the next EU budget period, it is unacceptable for Latvian farmers to continue receiving one of the lowest levels of support in the EU.
A significant part of the talks was also devoted to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and European support for Ukraine. The Prime Minister shared the conclusions from his recent visit to Kyiv and spoke about what he had witnessed there, which confirmed how vital it is to continue supporting Ukraine in its fight for freedom and independence. In the Prime Minister’s view, discussions on the transfer of Russia’s frozen assets to Ukraine should be resumed.
The visit of the President of the European Council to Latvia forms part of his annual tour of EU Member State capitals, during which he meets with national leaders to discuss national priorities and jointly prepare for key EU decisions.

====================================================================================================

State Institutions Work Jointly to Strengthen Electoral Security Ahead of the Saeima Elections in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:16:07 UTC
21:16:07 KST

In order to ensure that every voter can make their choice freely and securely on 3 October and that the public can have confidence in the conduct of the elections and the voting results, state institutions have been preparing purposefully and systematically for the 15th Saeima elections since January this year. Technical solutions have been prepared and tested, potential security risks have been identified and mitigated, response scenarios for various situations have been refined, and public information campaigns have been coordinated.
On Tuesday, 8 September, the Cabinet of Ministers heard an informative report on the work of the inter-institutional group, including the communication strategy for the integrity of the 15th Saeima elections. The report summarises the work carried out by the responsible authorities, their planned actions, the most significant risks and measures to mitigate them, while the strategy sets out common principles for informing the public.
Election security begins with preparation and extends through every stage of the process
To ensure that the electoral process is as secure as possible, the relevant authorities take steps well in advance. Well before the day of the elections, state institutions prepared both for the conduct of the elections and for potential attempts to undermine public confidence in the electoral process. The authorities paid particular attention to foreign influence and information manipulation, including AI-generated content and deepfakes, cyber-attacks and technical disruptions, illegal campaigning, covert funding and vote-buying, as well as physical threats and risks to public order.
The authorities are also preparing for various alerts and threats that may arise during the elections. The law provides for the possibility of extending polling station opening hours should voting have to be temporarily suspended due to an airborne threat, while the Central Election Commission (CEC) has developed clear response procedures for polling stations to ensure that decisions can be taken swiftly should such a situation arise.
Security – practical and verifiable solutions
In the 15th Saeima elections, ballot papers will not be scanned during the vote count; polling station staff will count the votes manually. Although manual vote counting may take longer in some cases, it also helps to alleviate concerns raised this spring, following the corruption scandal involving IT companies, about the potential impact of automated solutions on the election outcome. Accuracy and transparency are paramount in vote counting, which is why the process is strictly regulated by law to ensure that it is secure and traceable. Election results will be received gradually from polling stations, and every voter will be able to follow the results on the website of the Central Election Commission (CEC). The stability and security of the information technology systems used in the organisation of the elections will be monitored by a special operational team, which will immediately inform the relevant authorities of any risks identified.
IT systems are also being thoroughly tested ahead of the elections, including through the involvement of the relevant national security and cyber security authorities, as well as through independent audits. Particular attention is paid to the systems’ resilience to potential cyber threats, so that potential risks can be identified and mitigated at an early stage. The Electronic Online Voter Register (ETVR) will be used in the 15th Saeima elections. It enables electronic verification of voters’ eligibility to vote and facilitates accurate and secure voter registration. Since 2021, the ETVR has also enabled voters to cast their votes conveniently at any polling station of their choice. In preparation for the 15th Saeima elections, practical training on the use of election IT systems has also been provided to municipal election commissions and polling station commissions.
Consistent, timely and clear communication
The communication strategy for the integrity of the 15th Saeima elections, developed by the State Chancellery and its partners, sets out three main objectives: to strengthen public trust in the electoral process, to encourage participation, and to build resilience against attempts to undermine the integrity of the elections. The authorities will use coordinated messages, promptly clarify incidents and refute false information, as well as openly report on the conduct of the elections, casting votes for deposit before election day, the counting process and security checks. The authorities will also keep the media informed about preparations for the elections, the security measures in place and current trends in the information environment.
The State Chancellery, together with its partners, regularly monitors the information environment and analyses the experience of other countries. The Consumer Rights Protection Centre has identified the responsibilities of the relevant authorities and established rapid communication channels with the largest online platforms, including Meta, Google, X and TikTok.
The main official source of information on the electoral process, voting procedures and results is the website of the Central Election Commission. Meanwhile, the State Chancellery’s ‘Black on White’ project brings together information on electoral integrity, the risks of disinformation, manipulation techniques and the role of the relevant authorities.
Voters’ actions matter
According to the results of a sociological survey carried out by ‘TNS Latvia’ on behalf of the State Chancellery, in July this year 73.3% of Latvian citizens stated that they planned to take part in the Saeima elections – 4.4 percentage points more than in March. At the same time, 36.2% of Latvia’s residents are concerned about possible interference in the elections by Russia or another country hostile to Latvia. These figures show that, alongside the secure organisation of the elections, the public needs regular and transparent information about the state’s preparedness and actions.
We urge members of the public to check election-related information against official sources, to view emotional or sensational statements with a critical eye – particularly in the run-up to the election – and not to rush into sharing unverified content. Particular caution is required when encountering images, audio or video that appear realistic but have been artificially created. It is not the role of state institutions to influence people’s political choices – their role is to safeguard a fair process, equal opportunities and every voter’s right to vote freely.
We would also like to remind you that any Latvian citizen aged 16 or over may observe the conduct of the elections at polling stations, provided they register in advance in accordance with the procedure laid down by the Central Election Commission. This is an opportunity to see the electoral process first-hand, observe how voting and vote counting take place, and verify for themselves that the process is secure, transparent and conducted in accordance with established procedures.

While Visiting Ukraine, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs Discusses How Latvia Can Draw on Ukraine’s Wartime Experience to Strengthen Its Resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:16:07 UTC
21:16:07 KST

On 23 -24 August, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs paid a working visit to Ukraine, where he met with the President and Prime Minister of Ukraine and took part in the events marking the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Ukraine’s independence, as well as in meetings of the leaders of the Nordic and Baltic countries (NB8) and the Coalition of the Willing.
“Ukraine’s security is linked to the security of Europe as a whole, including Latvia. During the visit, it became clear that Latvia and Ukraine can cooperate more closely in several areas and make practical use of Ukraine’s wartime experience. Ukraine’s experience in managing cyber threats and civil protection risks, as well as in developing drone and counter-drone solutions, is of particular significance. We want to turn this cooperation into practical action, strengthen the exchange of information and experience, and develop joint solutions. Ukraine’s experience also contributes directly to Latvia’s security. We must therefore draw on this experience to strengthen our capabilities and preparedness for various threats well in advance,” emphasises Andris Kulbergs.
Cooperation on Ukraine’s reconstruction was also discussed during the talks with Ukrainian leaders. Latvia can share its experience and provide solutions to the construction of modular buildings, as well as in cogeneration and the energy sector, thereby strengthening Ukraine’s resilience and contributing to its reconstruction. During this visit, the Prime Minister continued the discussions launched at the Ukraine Reconstruction Conference in Gdansk regarding the representation of Latvia’s economic and business interests across various sectors, while also paying particular attention to Ukraine’s economic recovery, critical infrastructure, energy security and investment attraction.
The Latvian Prime Minister also discussed the implementation of the Latvia–Ukraine drone agreement with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi, including co-production and technology transfer, with a view to strengthening cooperation between the two countries in the defence industry. Funding has also been secured for the transfer of obsolete TEC-2 equipment to Ukraine, including the costs of its transportation, and Latvia, Germany and Ukraine are continuing to work to resolve the necessary legal and administrative issues so that the equipment can be transferred to Ukraine.
At the meeting of the leaders of Ukraine and the Nordic and Baltic countries (NB8) in Kyiv, unwavering support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity was reaffirmed. The meeting emphasised that the NB8 countries will continue to provide Ukraine with political, military, financial, humanitarian and economic support for as long as necessary. The leaders agreed to strengthen Ukraine’s defence capabilities, expand cooperation in the defence industry and co-production, and support Ukraine’s path to the European Union and NATO. They also reaffirmed their commitment to continue working on Ukraine’s recovery and reconstruction and to step up pressure on Russia through further sanctions.
On 24 August, the Latvian Prime Minister also took part in the Coalition of the Willing meeting, where, together with representatives of other countries, discussed further support for Ukraine and the most pressing security issues. During the meeting, the Prime Minister emphasised the particular importance of strengthening Ukraine’s air defence by providing the necessary military assistance and supporting its ability to protect the population and critical infrastructure, particularly during the coming winter. The need to coordinate partners’ actions and to maintain long-term military and financial support for Ukraine was also emphasised.
During his working visit to Ukraine, the Prime Minister also met with Lieutenant General Oleg Ivashchenko, Head of the Ukrainian Defence Intelligence Service, and Oleksandr Polkad, Acting Head of the Ukrainian Security Service. The meetings focused on the current security situation, Latvia’s support for Ukraine in its fight against Russia’s aggression, and opportunities to deepen cooperation between Latvia and Ukraine in security and defence.
At the end of the visit, the Prime Minister visited the Latvian Embassy in Ukraine, where he met with the Ambassador and the embassy team. He heard about the embassy team’s day-to-day work in challenging wartime conditions, as well as other current issues concerning cooperation between Latvia and Ukraine. The Prime Minister thanked the embassy team for their work and for maintaining Latvia’s presence in Ukraine even under these circumstances.

Benjamin Satterley, pro wrestler known as "Pac," dies at 40

Benjamin Satterley, pro wrestler known as "Pac," dies at age 40
Benjamin Satterley, an English-born wrestler known for high-flying moves that delighted fans worldwide, has died. He was 40.
The death of Satterley, who was known as "Pac," was announced late Sunday on All Elite Wrestling's website. The website did not list a cause of death.
"Our condolences go out to Satterley's family, friends and fans," All Elite Wrestling wrote on social media.
Satterley, who was from Newcastle upon Tyne, began his wrestling career in 2004 and signed in 2019 with All Elite Wrestling, where he held multiple championships.
He competed and lost to Andrade El Ídolo on Saturday in Chicago in the AEW National Championship.
Satterley began his wrestling training when he was 18 after developing an interest for the sport through his aunt, who was a fan of the WWF, according to MN2S, his booking agency.
He quickly rose to prominence, earning nicknames like "The Super Superman" and "The Man That Gravity Forgot." He began his international journey in 2007 and wrestled under the name of Adrian Neville from 2012 to 2018.
After signing with AEW, he became the inaugural AEW International Champion and a two-time AEW World Trios Champion.
Tributes for Satterley have poured in.
"The greatest export from our country. Also the greatest human being," fellow wrestler Will Ospreay wrote on X. "Honored to have shared the ring with you so many times. You truly are such a hero to myself and many others."
"The best lad… We love you," wrote fellow wrestler Kevin Owens along with photos of him and Pac.
Wrestler Alexa Bliss wrote on social media: "I cannot believe this. RIP PAC 💔"

Century-old building renovated in China's Tianjin to boost tourism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:14:13 CST
21:14:13 KST

Tourists watch an immersive drama at the former site of L'indo Bank of China in Tianjin, north China, Sept. 27, 2026. Built in 1912, the former site of L'indo Bank of China is one of the landmarks in Tianjin's Jiefang North Road historical and cultural block, witnessing the development of the city's financial industry in modern times.
This building had undergone many historical changes and had been used successively as an art museum, an international auction house, and a museum of Western art. However, due to the scarcity of exhibitions, it had been idle for a long time until the latest renovation.
In 2025, Beijing Performance & Arts Group, together with Tianjin North Performing Arts Group, initiated the revitalization of the building, creating an immersive performance scene while preserving its original appearance.
This April, the newly renovated building was officially opened to the public, and visitors can view a live-action exhibition here during the day and watch an immersive drama at night.
Up to now, the renovated building has received approximately 30,000 visitors. (Xinhua/Zhao Zishuo)

Iran has no plans for talks with U.S. during delegation's New York visit: media
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:14:09 CST
21:14:09 KST

TEHRAN, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Iran has no plans to hold negotiations with the United States during its delegation's current visit to New York, Iran's official news agency IRNA reported Sunday night.
IRNA cited a source close to the Iranian delegation, which is in New York to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, as rejecting "contradictory" reports about talks between Tehran and Washington.
The source said Iran's considerations and positions were conveyed to the American side "explicitly and clearly" through the Qatari mediator on Sept. 22, and that Tehran is awaiting Washington's response.
According to the source, there is no plan for a new round of negotiations with the American side, and Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi will leave New York for Tehran on Tuesday.
On Sunday, Iran's Foreign Ministry quoted Araghchi as saying that the country had not yet received the U.S. "definitive" views through the mediators on its proposed seven-day plan to cease hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
He added that Iran had conveyed its plan and conditions to the American side through the mediating countries and had seen U.S. President Donald Trump's initial reaction to the plan, "but nothing has been conveyed to us yet by the mediators."
Araghchi noted, "Of course, the U.S. president has made many contradictory statements, something we unfortunately hear from him quite often. We are waiting for definitive views to be conveyed to us via the mediators, and we will make our decision based on that."
He had earlier said that under Iran's plan, the country would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States accepted its conditions.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
On June 18, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts, including Lebanon. Under the MoU, they were scheduled to hold negotiations within a period of 60 days, which ended on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement, but the talks' fate remains unclear following a series of recent escalations between the two countries. ■

Delhi gov't rolls out measures to tackle recurring winter air pollution
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:14:02 CST
21:14:02 KST

NEW DELHI, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The local government in Delhi, India's capital territory, on Monday announced a slew of measures to curb air pollution, which typically worsens in the winter from November to February.
The measures include higher parking charges, a ban on construction and demolition work, staggered office timings, and a 50-percent cut in on-site staffing at government and private offices, with essential services exempted.
The steps will be introduced in phases from Nov. 1, with some curbs continuing until February 2027.
The measures to control air pollution well in advance are aimed at limiting pollution sources and reducing vehicular movement in the national capital during the months when air quality typically deteriorates sharply.
Delhi, home to over 30 million people, is among the most polluted cities in the world.
Industrial emissions and vehicular traffic are major sources of air pollution, alongside rampant construction activity. Poor wind speed and stubble burning, or farm fires, in neighbouring states also contribute to the decline in air quality.
For years, Delhi's air quality turns hazardous as winter approaches. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Four world records fell in the men's 85kg and 95kg weightlifting divisions at the 2026 Asian Games on Monday, with lifters from the DPR Korea and Iran claiming one gold medal apiece.
Ro Kwang Ryol of the DPR Korea broke two world records to win the men's 85kg title, while Kazakhstan's Alexey Churkin also set a world record in the same category.
Ro lifted a world-record 214kg in the clean and jerk and posted a world-record total of 379kg to claim gold. Churkin set a world record of 173kg in the snatch on his way to silver with a total of 378kg, while China's Chen Shunnan took bronze with 374kg.
Standing atop the podium, Ro was overwhelmed with emotion.
"When the national flag went up, remembering all the drops of sweat shed until then, the sweat shed during training and thinking of the motherland, tears came out without me realizing. I couldn't stop them," Ro said.
After failing his first two snatch attempts, 21-year-old Chen lifted 163kg on his third. He then lifted 211kg in the clean and jerk, briefly setting a world record before Ro raised the mark to 214kg.
Chen said he felt rushed and tense during his first two snatch attempts as other competitors changed their weights.
"On my third attempt, I slapped myself twice to pull myself together," Chen said. "It was a close call, but I got the lift."
Churkin, who missed out on gold by a single kilogram in the total, was disappointed.
"I was thinking about winning the gold medal and maybe I got a bit over-excited about that, so I am disappointed about winning the silver," he said.
Later Monday, Iran's Ali Alipour set a world record total of 398kg to win the men's 95kg title.
Alipour snatched 180kg before lifting 218kg in the clean and jerk for a winning total of 398kg.
Kazakhstan's Nurgissa Adiletuly took silver with 394kg, while Tu Yi of China, gold medalist at the 2026 Asian Weightlifting Championships, took bronze with a total of 384kg.
Despite being unhappy with his performance, Tu said he enjoyed the atmosphere at the Asian Games and the opportunity to interact with athletes from different countries and regions.
"I swapped many pins with them," he said. "Some athletes come from nations facing tough conditions, and it is extremely hard for them to attend competitions. Others are from more developed countries and compete simply to enjoy the sport. It is truly a collision of diverse cultures."
The women's 86kg, men's 110kg, women's over-86kg and men's over-110kg divisions are scheduled for the final day of weightlifting competition on Tuesday. ■

Interview: AIIB to boost infrastructure connectivity via scaled-up financing -- president
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:13:59 CST
21:13:59 KST

by Xinhua writers Ren Jun and Zhou Qianxian
BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) plans to double its annual approved financing to about 20 billion U.S. dollars by 2030 to further meet members' development needs, AIIB President Zou Jiayi said in a recent interview with Xinhua in Beijing.
In Zou's view, the AIIB's plan to double lending requires a commitment to turning financing into real development outcomes, using more innovative financing tools, upstream project preparation and broader partnerships as well as upholding multilateralism and maintaining professionalism, prudence and high-standard governance.
The bank has always upheld the principle of multilateralism and supported members in achieving long-term and sustainable development, Zou noted.
Multilateralism is also a form of infrastructure, one that builds mutual trust and promotes cooperation, enabling countries to jointly address challenges and achieve development even when they have differences, she added.
"While expanding lending, we will continue to innovate business models and lending products, ensure projects are implemented effectively and deliver development impact," Zou said.
The AIIB has maintained steady growth momentum. This year, the bank approved its first project in South Africa to support urban governance and operations. Through a debt guarantee, it supported Pakistan in issuing its first panda bond in China, while the bank also launched the Energy, Food Security and Economic Resilience Facility, via which it has supported Bangladesh and Fiji in strengthening their fiscal, climate and disaster resilience.
The 11th annual meeting of its board of governors is scheduled to take place on Sept. 28 and 29 in Doha, Qatar. With the theme "Tomorrow's Infrastructure: Impact and Innovation," the meeting marks the AIIB's transition into its second decade, and highlights its continued focus on scaling up sustainable infrastructure investment across AIIB members.
The annual meeting aims to seek guidance from AIIB governors on the AIIB's development direction for the next growth phase, offer a platform for deepening international cooperation and partnerships, and catalyze greater public and private investment in infrastructure.
Since taking office in January this year, Zou has visited about 30 member countries in Asia, Africa and Europe, and exchanged views with representatives from their governments, development partners and the private sector.
The members hope the AIIB can provide more infrastructure financing to support their green and low-carbon transition and the development of transport corridors, digital infrastructure and other areas, Zou revealed.
"Although our members are at different stages of development, their need is highly consistent: infrastructure is a key underpinning for development," she said.
Since the AIIB began operations in 2016, its membership has grown to 111, with over 400 projects approved, benefiting 43 members within and beyond Asia.
"In a world fraught with risks and challenges, the AIIB will continue to uphold the principles of openness, inclusiveness and collaboration, promote regional cooperation, deepen connectivity between Asia and the world, and contribute greater certainty to global sustainable development and international cooperation," Zou said. ■

The leaders will be joined by representatives from all walks of life at the ceremony, which will be broadcast live by the China Media Group.
In 2014, China's top legislature adopted the decision to establish Martyrs' Day. Observed on Sept. 30, one day before National Day, the day commemorates those who gave their lives for national independence and prosperity.
Since the first Martyrs' Day, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, has maintained the tradition of paying homage to fallen heroes on the day.
This year marks the 77th founding anniversary of the People's Republic of China and the 105th founding anniversary of the CPC.
It also marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which lasted from 1934 to 1936. A themed exhibition is being held at the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution in Beijing to commemorate that epic military trek.
During the Long March, the CPC-led Red Army soldiers braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and treacherous grasslands, with some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers.
The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution. ■

HELSINKI, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Sweden's Social Democratic Party leader and former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson said on Monday that she would return her exploratory mandate to the speaker of parliament later in the day, giving up her current attempt to form a new government.
Andersson told a press conference that her decision came after the Left Party announced that it would support incumbent Speaker Andreas Norlen, a Moderate Party lawmaker, in Monday's election for speaker.
She said she had accepted the mandate on Sept. 18 and had since held talks with several parties over the possibility of forming a government.
She said Sweden has a long-standing tradition under which the speaker comes from the largest party in the governing camp. The Left Party's decision to back the Moderates' candidate meant that a new parliamentary constellation had emerged, she said, adding that "this new constellation should also be given the opportunity to try to form a government."
Taking into account the Left Party's decision and her talks with other parties, Andersson said she saw no possibility of forming a government at present. She added that it remained to be seen how the situation would develop in the coming weeks.
Left Party leader Nooshi Dadgostar rejected Andersson's suggestion that her party and the Moderates had formed a new political bloc. She said the party backed Norlen because of his extensive experience as speaker and in overseeing government formation talks, and that the decision should not be interpreted as a political alliance.
Sweden held its parliamentary election on Sept. 13. The final results gave the Social Democrats, Left Party, Green Party and Centre Party a combined 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, while the Moderate Party, Sweden Democrats, Christian Democrats and Liberals won a combined 173 seats.
The Social Democrats emerged as the largest party with 99 seats. Outgoing Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson subsequently submitted his resignation.
On Sept. 18, Norlen tasked Andersson with exploring the possibility of forming a government that could be accepted by parliament. ■

By sportswriter Shan Lei
GENEVA, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Leaders of international federations will gather in Lausanne next week for the 2026 SportAccord Forum, with the changing global events landscape, technology and the future of hosting among the key issues on the agenda, SportAccord Managing Director Kelly Fairweather said Monday.
The forum, to be held from October 5-7 at the Olympic Museum in Lausanne, Switzerland, will take place under the theme "When the Playbook Changes: Leading Sport in a New Reality."
"This year's theme, 'When the Playbook Changes: Leading Sport in a New Reality,' reflects the range of pressures federations are navigating at once," Fairweather said.
"The program looks at economic and geopolitical change, the international events market, how sports reach and retain participants, and decisions about technology and data. These issues affect federations in different ways, but all require leaders to make choices about where to focus their resources."
Topics listed by SportAccord include new ways to grow sport, technology decisions facing sports organizations, changes in the global events landscape and the future of hosting.
"We start with the decisions facing international federations and ask where a conversation with peers and specialists would be most useful," Fairweather said. "That keeps the program focused on practical questions rather than trends for their own sake."
International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry is scheduled to deliver the opening address.
"We are delighted that IOC President Kirsty Coventry will open this year's forum," Fairweather said. "Her address, alongside contributions from IOC leadership and future Olympic hosts, will be an important part of the conversation."
The forum aims to bring international federation leaders together to share experiences, discuss ideas and build relationships.
"Whether a federation is large or small, many of the decisions it faces are similar: how to grow participation, strengthen its finances, use technology well and develop the right events strategy," Fairweather said. "Hearing how others approach those choices can help leaders find a way forward."
This year's event will also feature a new SportAccord City Forum session, designed to bring city representatives and sports leaders together to discuss the opportunities and impact of hosting major events.
"No federation delivers its sport alone," Fairweather said. "It needs cities and regions to host events, commercial partners to help make them viable, and service providers with the expertise to deliver them. Those organizations, in turn, need to understand what federations are trying to achieve." ■

The Hungarian Parliament has lifted Magyar’s immunity in a case involving a stolen phone
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
15:12:39 EEST

The Hungarian Parliament has lifted Magyar’s immunity in a case involving a stolen phone
Kyiv • UNN
139 lawmakers supported lifting Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s immunity. The case is linked to a phone that he allegedly threw into the Danube.
On Monday, Hungary’s parliament voted to lift the parliamentary immunity of Péter Magyar, Hungary’s prime minister. This decision made him the first sitting head of government in Hungary’s history to have his legal immunity lifted while in office. Euractiv reports, UNN writes.
Details
Lifting his immunity allows prosecutors to continue examining a case dating back to June 2024—nearly two years before Magyar won the election and defeated Viktor Orbán. The incident occurred at the Ötkert nightclub in central Budapest, just a few weeks after that year’s European Parliament elections.
According to prosecutors, Magyar was relaxing at the club when he noticed a man filming him. At the time, eyewitness accounts and available video footage showed Magyar dancing in the company of young women, with some media outlets reporting that some of them were underage.
Prosecutors allege that after a verbal altercation, Magyar snatched the phone from the man’s hands and put it in his pocket. Despite the owner’s repeated requests, Magyar refused to return the device.
After security guards escorted him out of the nightclub, Magyar reportedly headed toward the Danube. The victim and several other witnesses followed him. Investigators allege that, upon reaching the riverbank, he "deliberately threw the phone into the Danube."
Additional information
Magyar previously had immunity as a Member of the European Parliament.
At the time, the European Parliament’s Legal Affairs Committee refused to lift his immunity. The committee said the case appeared to be a politically motivated attempt by Orbán’s administration at the time to remove its main opponent.
Following Monday’s vote, in which 139 lawmakers supported lifting his immunity, the Hungarian authorities can now question the prime minister and formally bring him into the proceedings. During the meeting, Magyar’s Tisza party representative on the Immunities Committee did not provide a detailed defense of the prime minister’s actions.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28

21:11:23 KST

Kyiv is turning to international partners to help cover its wartime spending needs, with Brussels set to bring together donor countries and financial institutions on Tuesday.
Ukraine has cut its $27 billion (€23.7 billion) funding shortfall to $20 billion (€17.6 billion) through austerity measures, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Sunday, although he warned that it “remains an open question” how to plug the remaining gap.
The spending cuts will affect areas including road repairs and cultural projects, while military salaries will be protected.
"We are looking for optimisation and redistributing available sources to set priorities. The armed forces are the top priority for all of us," Koretskyi said in an interview with the TSN news outlet, stressing that military salaries will be protected.
"The priority is whether it leads to survival or not. This is the only approach to making certain decisions," he said.
Kyiv is in talks with the European Commission, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other allies over how to plug the budget hole, which affects the Ministry of Defence and risks delaying much-needed weapons deliveries.
Russia’s recent escalation has added urgency to the search for funding.
“With joint efforts, we have not yet found a way to cover these expenses,” Koretskyi said.
The prime minister insisted the $27 billion was not a request for fresh money, as the figure was already part of the annual war costs, estimated at $155 billion (€136.3 billion), that Ukraine communicated to allies in February.
Ukraine sent the Commission a similar assessment as Brussels prepared its €90 billion support loan, he said. The loan has been split evenly, with €45 billion earmarked for 2026 and another €45 billion for 2027, and payments already underway.
Ukrainian officials have floated the idea of frontloading a share of the loan, but that would leave less money next year and could worsen the situation.
Commission officials are still trying to pin down the precise extent of the budget deficit and have urged Ukraine to speed up reforms to unlock roughly €20 billion in financial aid available this year.
Brussels will host a new meeting of the Ukraine Donor Platform on Tuesday with representatives from allied nations and financial institutions.
"We want to bring together international partners ready to discuss how we can bridge the budgetary gap," a Commission spokesperson said.
