Why South Korea is demanding an apology from Ukraine over North Korean PoWs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:09:23 UTC
21:09:23 KST

Why South Korea is demanding an apology from Ukraine over North Korean PoWs
Seoul says Kyiv agreed to a nondisclosure agreement over the prisoners but broke it.
South Korea has demanded an official apology and explanation from Ukraine after accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement on Sunday that the president’s office expressed “strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3EU unlocks humanitarian aid for crises worldwide
- list 2 of 3German, Russian foreign ministers hold rare talks amid rising tensions
- list 3 of 3Russian strikes kill eight, injure dozens across Ukraine
He said Ukraine had repeatedly discussed the prisoners’ transfer with Seoul through various channels and had requested secrecy.
However, Kyiv has said no secrecy agreement existed.
Here’s what we know:
What happened?
Speaking at the annual United Nations General Assembly last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea after they were caught fighting for Russia in the Kursk region. Ukraine seized large parts of the Russian border region in August 2024 but has since lost most of the territory.
“These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself, and he was shocked that fate did not let him die,” Zelenskyy said in his speech.
He also condemned North Korea’s deployment of troops to support Moscow, saying: “This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? [North Korean leader] Kim Jong Un uses them like currency, and he gets something in return.”
Zelenskyy said at the time that he would hand the captured soldiers over to Kim if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
However, human rights groups had urged him to send them to South Korea, referring to possible risks of punishment that the soldiers faced.
South Korean media also reported that the two captured soldiers had wanted to defect to Seoul.
Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in January 2025.
They became the first North Korean soldiers to be captured alive since Pyongyang began in 2024 to aid Moscow’s war efforts against Ukraine. North Korea is estimated to have deployed thousands of soldiers to support Russia’s war against Ukraine as part of a mutual defence treaty.
What did South Korea say?
South Korea previously declined to confirm the soldiers’ arrival, citing concerns about their safety and that of their family members still in North Korea.
But Zelenskyy’s decision to announce the transfer surprised South Korea’s government.
In a post on X, President Lee Jae Myung said the issue of repatriating North Korean prisoners of war was a “highly sensitive agenda”.
“From the perspective of those who advertised the repatriation to the whole world with enthusiastic fanfare to show off their achievements – regardless of the impact on inter-Korean relations, the loss of life, or the damage to national interests – they likely not only cannot understand our government’s efforts to keep it confidential but may even wonder if there is something wrong with it,” Lee wrote.
“I do not know the reasons behind Ukraine’s disclosure in violation of the non-disclosure agreement, but it is deeply regrettable,” he added.
South Korea is technically still at war with North Korea because the two opponents in the 1950-1953 Korean War signed an armistice in 1953 and not a peace treaty. Thousands of US soldiers are stationed in South Korea, and the two allies hold military exercises regularly, which the North has denounced.
According to Seong’s statement on Sunday, Zelenskyy disclosed the repatriation without sufficient prior consultation and later denied that any confidentiality agreement existed.
He added that the denial had seriously damaged trust between the two governments and could harm their relations.
At the same time, opposition politicians have condemned Lee’s government for failing to disclose the transfer.
Last week, opposition politician Ahn Cheol-soo of the People Power Party asked on social media whether it was “fair” that the Korean public learned about North Korean POWs in the country through Zelenskyy.
“President Lee, why did you hide it? Does North Korea have something that, if disclosed, would end your political career? Or were you planning to send the POWs back to North Korea?” Ahn asked.
How many North Korean soldiers are fighting in Ukraine?
According to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, about 14,000 to 15,000 North Korean soldiers were sent to support Russia’s war efforts, and most were deployed to Russia’s Kursk region to fend off a Ukrainian incursion.
As a close Russian ally, Pyongyang has also supplied Moscow with weapons, including artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery systems and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.
What happens to the soldiers now?
The soldiers are expected to undergo questioning and security screening before South Korean authorities decide whether to grant them protection and begin resettlement.
On Monday, Seoul’s Ministry of Unification said it would review their cases under relevant laws and past practices, including the North Korean Defectors Protection and Settlement Support Act.
The ministry’s goal is to unify the two Koreas, which were partitioned shortly before the 1950-1953 war. Pyongyang opposes reunification.
Under the law, the National Intelligence Service investigates applicants in temporary protective custody,
Yu Yong-weon, an opposition lawmaker who met the soldiers in Ukraine in February 2025, said they served in North Korea’s special forces and could provide information on Pyongyang’s training, military capabilities and participation in the war.

Dialogue between Russia and US essential to save arms control system — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:07:53 UTC
21:07:53 KST

ISTRA (Moscow Region), September 28. /TASS/. Resuming dialogue between Russia and the US, with China’s participation, is essential to preserving what remains of the arms control system, Karen Hallberg, Secretary-General of the Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs, told TASS in an interview on the sidelines of the annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club.
This is critically important because resuming dialogue among the nuclear powers – for example, if the US, Russia and China were to establish a high-level forum or negotiating platform to discuss ways of reducing nuclear risks – would facilitate the implementation of Article 6 of the NPT [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons] and demonstrate the countries’ serious commitment to negotiations. This would bring greater stability to the entire system, she said.
Hallberg emphasized that renewed Russia-US dialogue, with China’s involvement, on nuclear issues would foster a deeper understanding that there is no way to control nuclear weapons without reaching a mutual understanding among all nuclear powers.
In Hallberg’s view, the process could begin with the three major nuclear powers: Russia, the US and China.
Such a dialogue could also build confidence among the other two nuclear powers, the UK and France, which could subsequently join the negotiations. Their participation is important, she noted, as it would help build trust amid the ongoing conflict in Ukraine and tensions between NATO and Russia.
European nuclear weapons – British and French – are also part of the equation, Hallberg noted.
About the Meeting
The 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club, themed "Responsibility for the Future: Limits of the Possible or Limitless Possibilities?", is taking place in the Moscow region from September 28 to October 1. The club’s flagship conference brings together 120 participants from 40 countries.

AI infrastructure push draws $6bn in data-centre commitments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:06:35 UTC
21:06:35 KST

At the Tashkent event, industrial uses and internationally active startups offer signs of a broader technology ecosystem taking shape. But affordable access to computing power remains a constraint for local companies.
Uzbekistan says investment commitments for new data centres now exceed $6bn (€5.3bn), as it tries to build the computing power needed to develop artificial intelligence at home rather than rely mainly on infrastructure abroad.
Some of that capacity is already operating. A new government computing cluster using Nvidia technology was launched this summer to run AI projects, while much larger commercial data-centre developments are now under development.
The expansion is also drawing international capital into Central Asia’s technology sector. It is one of the main themes at ICT Week Uzbekistan 2026 in Tashkent, an annual event bringing together technology companies, investors, startups and policymakers from Uzbekistan and abroad.
Building the computing power behind AI
Running and developing AI systems requires large amounts of computing power, often provided by clusters of specialised processors known as GPUs.
Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Digital Technologies says its new Nvidia-based government cluster reached 90% utilisation within its first month, an indication of the demand for computing capacity.
“We have the government data centre, which is serving the government needs, and we have installed our Nvidia chips for government needs,” Digital Technologies Minister Sherzod Shermatov told Euronews. “And we are in the process of procuring the next stage.”
Private projects are much larger.
Saudi-based DataVolt is developing a 12-megawatt data centre in Tashkent designed to support AI and other computing-intensive services. The first phase is expected to become operational by the end of 2026.
The project has secured up to $150mn (€131.4mn) in financing from an international group that includes the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, Germany’s DEG, France’s Proparco and the OPEC Fund for International Development.
“These 12MW will be ready by the end of this year,” Shermatov said. He said the project is ultimately planned to reach 300 megawatts, with later stages extending into other regions.
Another large data-centre project is being developed in Karakalpakstan in western Uzbekistan by Shanghai LinkWise Data Intelligence.
Shermatov said investment commitments for data-centre developments across the country now total more than $6bn (€5.3bn).
From infrastructure to practical applications
The government says more than 100 AI projects are being developed under its national strategy.
Some are focused on public services. Sarvarbek Abdullayev, Director of the AI Department at the Ministry of Digital Technologies, said one platform allows people to request government information, including tax records, through a conversational interface.
Another system is designed to help public-sector employees analyse documents, summarise their contents and prepare responses.
AI is also moving into industrial projects.
The ministry is working with mining and metallurgical companies on drone and robotic systems that can scan mining areas.
“We are working with the Navoi and Almalik metallurgical companies,” Abdullayev said. “Together with them, we are developing the drone technology and robotic technologies in the mining field.”
More than 20 AI laboratories are also planned at universities by the end of the year, according to the ministry.
Another project addresses a challenge specific to countries whose languages are less well represented in global AI systems. The government is developing an Uzbek-language corpus, a large structured collection of text that can be used by developers to improve how large language models understand and generate Uzbek.
The cost of accessing AI
Building data centres does not automatically mean that local companies can afford to use the computing power they provide.
That issue is particularly important for startups and smaller technology companies, which often cannot finance their own infrastructure.
“We see very impressive progress in terms of the infrastructure development, human capital development and adoption of AI, mostly by startups, by the private sector,” said Shamil Ibragimov, Director of Research at the MIT Kuo Sharper Center for Prosperity and Entrepreneurship.
But Ibragimov said computing power remains expensive for many startups in Uzbekistan, with some still relying on international cloud providers.
Richard Stirling, CEO of Oxford Insights, said startup activity provides another indication of how far AI is moving beyond government strategies.
“If you're looking for evidence of Uzbekistan building genuine AI capacity, look beyond the strategies, documents, and regulations,” he said.
According to Stirling, 180 startups using AI are already exporting to 80 countries.
For larger established companies, however, adoption has been slower, according to Ibragimov. He said the computing capacity currently available inside Uzbekistan is still not enough to meet demand at a price that many local companies and startups can afford.

Taiwan justice ministry data show 3,401 investigated in human trafficking cases

21:03:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Ministry of Justice data show that prosecutors concluded human trafficking investigations involving 3,401 suspects from 2021 through 2025, including 147 in organ removal cases, CNA reported Monday.
The figures were released after Taoyuan prosecutors indicted seven people in September for allegedly attempting to lure people to China for organ removal. Prosecutors said three people were deceived by offers of high-paying work but were stopped before leaving Taiwan. They sought seven-year prison terms for the defendants.
The annual number of suspects in concluded human trafficking investigations has exceeded 600 since 2022. It reached a five-year high of 957 in 2023 before falling to 802 in 2025.
Of those investigated, 1,914 were linked to labor exploitation, the largest category, while 1,281 were linked to sexual exploitation. Organ removal cases involved 147 suspects over the five years, including 34 in 2025. The ministry noted that people could be listed under more than one category.
The number linked to labor exploitation reached a five-year high of 678 in 2023 before falling to 397 in 2025. The number linked to sexual exploitation rose from 168 in 2021 to 309 in 2025.
Prosecutors indicted 41% of the 3,401 suspects. Among those convicted in human trafficking cases, 50.4% were aged 18 to 29 and 27.3% were aged 30 to 39, with an average age of 32.
Taiwan amended the Human Trafficking Prevention Act in June 2023 to cover more forms of trafficking and increase penalties. The changes strengthened measures against criminal groups involved in exploitation, forced labor, and forcing victims to commit crimes, per UDN.

Sanjana Modha’s quick and easy recipe for baked beans butter masala | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:03:33 UTC
21:03:33 KST

Masala baked beans, tadka baked beans, curried baked beans, spicy baked beans; all avatars of spice-laced baked beans are a mainstay of British Asian kitchens. We were raised on this stuff – use as a toastie filler, to smother jacket potatoes, or scoop them up with roti. Enter baked beans butter masala. With a sharp sweetness, a versatile tin of baked beans already has all the foundations required to build a brilliant butter masala, so all we’re doing is dressing them up. I like to think of it as though the beans are donning a frock made of all the good stuff: butter, cream and spices.
Baked beans butter masala
This creamy, dreamy baked bean curry is delicious with naan or served as any of the suggestions mentioned above. To make this vegan, use your favourite plant-based butter and an oat- or soya-based cream. Coconut milk also works in place of cream.
Prep 15 min
 Cook 20 min
 Serves 4
2 tbsp salted butter, plus a little extra to garnish (optional)
1 small brown onion, peeled and finely chopped
2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped
1 tsp minced ginger
  1 tbsp tomato puree
  2 410g tins baked beans
½ tsp ground turmeric
  1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder
  4 green cardamom pods, smashed open and seeds finely ground
3 tsp garam masala
  1 small pinch salt
150ml single cream 
2 tsp dried fenugreek leaves
  2 tbsp chopped coriander, including stalks, to garnish
Melt the butter in a medium saucepan, then add the onion and saute for three to five minutes, until soft and translucent. Add the garlic, ginger and tomato puree, and cook for another minute, until aromatic.
Add all the baked beans, along with all the sauce from the cans, stir in the turmeric, chilli powder, ground cardamom, garam masala and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Stir in the cream (reserve a few tablespoons to serve), cover the pan with a lid and leave the curry to come to a simmer over a low heat for 10 minutes, stirring often to stop the beans sticking to the base of the pan.
Take off the lid and add the dried fenugreek leaves, rubbing them between your palms to break them into a fine powder. Swirl in the reserved cream and, if using, the extra butter, garnish with the coriander and serve.
- 
  This recipe is an edited extract from Modern Masala, by Sanjana Modha, published by Quadrille at £25. To order a copy for £22.50, go to guardianbookshop.com.

James Webb reveals why planet formation is a race against time

James Webb reveals why planet formation is a race against time
JWST reveals that newborn planets are racing against powerful winds and radiation before their supply of planet-building gas disappears.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- SETI Institute
- Summary:
- JWST has revealed that young planetary systems lose their planet-building gas through a changing mix of powerful jets, molecular winds, and radiation-driven outflows. As the disks age and their gas disappears, giant planets face a shrinking window to build massive atmospheres.
- Share:
Planets take shape inside disks of gas and dust surrounding young stars, but the supply of gas they depend on is temporary. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are giving astronomers a clearer picture of how that gas escapes and how the dominant escape mechanisms change as planetary systems mature.
The study, led by Naman Bajaj of the University of Arizona and coauthored by SETI Institute scientist Uma Gorti, examined 72 young, Sun-like stars and their protoplanetary disks. It is among the largest studies of planet formation conducted with JWST and suggests that different kinds of winds dominate at different stages of a system's early development.
The findings have been published in The Astronomical Journal.
Planet Formation Has a Deadline
"What is exciting about this study is that we can now see, across a large sample of young systems, how the mechanisms that remove gas from planet-forming disks change with time. Disk dispersal sets a fundamental clock for planet formation: once the gas is gone, the opportunity to build gas-rich planets is essentially over," said Gorti.
Our solar system is now about 4.5 billion years old and consists mostly of empty space. During its first few million years, however, the young Sun was surrounded by a dense protoplanetary disk containing roughly 100 times more gas than dust. Nearly all of that gas eventually disappeared.
Understanding when and how this material is lost matters because gas is essential for forming giant planets such as Jupiter and Saturn. If a disk loses its gas too quickly, developing planets may not have enough time to accumulate the enormous atmospheres needed to become gas giants.
JWST Tracks Escaping Gas
Bajaj and his colleagues investigated this process using archival observations from JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI). The 72 systems span different stages of planetary development. Taken together, they provide something like a sequence of snapshots, allowing researchers to reconstruct how gas dispersal changes as systems grow older.
In 2020, LPL professor Ilaria Pascucci, second author of the paper and Bajaj's advisor, led a related study examining how jets and winds evolve. Before JWST, researchers could not directly observe molecular hydrogen, but the team predicted that molecular winds should exist and could be dense enough during the earliest stages to block X-ray photons. By directly tracing molecular hydrogen in the new observations, Bajaj's team confirmed those predictions with JWST images.
The researchers concentrated on two indicators of escaping material: molecular hydrogen, the most abundant molecule in protoplanetary disks, and ionized neon. JWST's sensitivity and resolution allowed them to distinguish broad winds containing molecular hydrogen from jets and winds traced by neon.
In the youngest systems, where material is still falling onto the central star, the researchers detected powerful jets along with broad winds containing both molecular and atomic gas. These outflows are consistent with winds generated by magnetic fields threading through the disk. Gas can follow those magnetic field lines outward, removing both material and angular momentum from the disk.
Stellar Radiation Takes Over
As planetary systems mature and the flow of material onto the star declines, the jets weaken and the escaping gas becomes increasingly atomic. At this stage, high energy radiation from the young star can penetrate the thinning material and heat gas in the disk until it escapes. This mechanism is known as photoevaporation.
Gorti has spent decades investigating the evolution and dispersal of protoplanetary disks, including the role of ultraviolet and X-ray radiation from young stars in driving photoevaporative winds. The latest JWST observations provide an observational connection to that theoretical work across dozens of systems. They indicate that photoevaporation becomes more important as disks age and magnetically driven jets and winds fade.
The findings suggest that there is no single mechanism responsible for clearing away a planet forming disk. Instead, young systems appear to begin with powerful magnetically driven jets and winds before transitioning toward a later stage in which atomic winds, including those produced through photoevaporation, become increasingly important.
That transition has major consequences for developing planets.
"Planet formation is therefore a race against time," Bajaj said. "Gas giants like Jupiter must assemble their massive atmospheres while the disk is still substantial enough to supply them, before winds and jets carry that raw material away into space."
Researchers detected extended emissions from molecular hydrogen and ionized neon in 66 of the 72 disks. Conical molecular hydrogen winds appeared in 46 systems, while fast moving neon jets were found in 40. Every system containing a neon jet also showed evidence of a wind traced by molecular hydrogen or oxygen.
A Broader View of How Planetary Systems Evolve
The study expands on earlier observations from the same research group. In 2024, Bajaj, Gorti, and their colleagues used JWST to image gas being carried away from the planet forming disk surrounding the young star T Cha.
That earlier work demonstrated that JWST could directly investigate disk dispersal in an individual planetary system. The new study extends the approach to dozens of young stars, revealing how the balance between jets, molecular winds, and atomic winds changes as planetary systems age.
Researchers now want to determine exactly how much gas these winds remove over time and identify where within the disk the escaping material originates. Those measurements could reveal not only how quickly the window for planet formation closes, but also which regions of a disk are capable of producing different types of planets before their gas supply disappears.

French prosecutors seek two-year sentence for Rachida Dati in Renault graft case

The high-profile case centres on a contract signed in 2009 between Dati, who previously served as justice minister, and fugitive businessman Carlos Ghosn, then head of Renault-Nissan.
France prosecutors on Monday sought two years with an electronic tag and a five-year ban on public office for ex-culture minister Rachida Dati in a trial on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan group.
They sought a four-year jail term for Carlos Ghosn, the fugitive former Renault-Nissan chief now living in Lebanon, who is being tried in absentia as part of the same trial in Paris.
The decision is expected to be announced in several months' time.
One of the most prominent figures on the French right, Dati, 60, resigned as culture minister in February to concentrate on the Paris mayoral race in March but suffered a bruising defeat.
Socialist Emmanuel Grégoire won city hall but Dati remains mayor of the capital's wealthy seventh district.
She stands charged with corruption and influence peddling over alleged lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013 while she was a member of the European Parliament.
She became an MEP after serving as justice minister between 2007 and 2009 under right-wing President Nicolas Sarkozy.
She has been accused of accepting 900,000 euros (around $1.0 million) in lawyers' fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan.

Human breasts might have evolved to keep big-brained infants warm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:00:35 UTC
21:00:35 KST

A study in Finland measured heating capacity and resilience to temperature changes of breasts of nursing women, non-nursing women, and men. Results showed that breastfeeding women had overall higher breast surface temperature compared to the other groups. Their breasts were also more resilient to cooling. The paper was published in Evolutionary Human Sciences.
Human breasts are unusual among primates because they remain relatively prominent throughout adult life rather than enlarging mainly during lactation. Much of their size and shape is produced by subcutaneous fat and fat around the milk-producing glands rather than by the milk-producing glandular tissue itself. Breast size varies considerably between women, and larger breasts can also create physical disadvantages such as increased strain on the back.
One evolutionary possibility is that permanent breasts emerged as a by-product of increased body fat during human evolution and were later shaped by other selective pressures. Some researchers have proposed that enlarged breasts function partly as sexual signals of fertility, health, or reproductive fitness, although this interpretation is not universally applicable across cultures.
Another hypothesis is that breast size may have helped mothers warm infants during close skin-to-skin contact, particularly after humans lost most of their body hair. Under this view, additional breast tissue could increase the warm surface area surrounding an infant and reduce heat loss. This possibility is especially relevant because human infants have unusually high energetic demands and substantial thermoregulatory needs during early development, largely due to encephalization, which is the evolutionary increase in brain size.
Study author Tiina Kuvaja and her colleagues investigated if the female breast tissue would have a distinct response to changing temperature. If this happened, it would indicate that it has a potential to stabilize the temperature of infants and especially newborns. They also noticed that lactation influences breast skin temperature and that relatively large changes in breast metabolic rate and temperature take place in early pregnancy. That is why they decided to include both breastfeeding women and women who do not breastfeed in their study.
Study participants were 8 currently breastfeeding women, 12 non-breastfeeding women, and 7 men. Participants were 20 to 40 years of age. This age category was selected because it represents the typical age of nursing women and avoided individuals undergoing puberty or menopause. The group of non-breastfeeding women included both women who had not given birth and those who had stopped breastfeeding at least one year prior to the study.
In the study, participants were exposed to three different temperatures in a climatic chamber: 32°C, 27°C, and 18°C. The study authors note that 27°C is a thermoneutral temperature for humans, meaning it is the temperature at which they can maintain their normal body temperature with minimal energy expenditure. It is the mean daytime temperature of the African savanna. The other two temperatures were taken to represent higher and lower extremes. The researchers used thermal imaging to record breast surface temperature at the start of the exposure, after 10 minutes, and at the end of the exposure, which lasted 20 minutes in total.
Results showed that breastfeeding women had overall higher breast surface temperatures compared to the other groups. Furthermore, they showed a distinct resilience against cooling during the 18°C exposure. During this exposure, they lost 2.5°C of their breast surface temperature on average, whereas the other study groups lost 4.3°C and 4.7°C.
“This proof-of-concept study clearly indicated the potential of the nursing women’s breasts to support infant’s thermal balance,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about the evolutionary roles of human breasts. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a very small group of participants, particularly of breastfeeding women. Studies on larger groups might not yield identical results.
The paper, “Infant’s thermal balance and the evolution of the human breast – a proof-of-concept study,” was authored by Tiina Kuvaja, Tiina Väre, Sirkka Rissanen, Hannu Rintamäki, Petri Lehenkari, and Juho-Antti Junno.

Why has abortion faded from America’s national conversation? | Moira Donegan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

Abortion has faded from the headlines since the Dobbs decision of 2022, and Republicans like it that way. In the immediate aftermath of the supreme court’s overturning of Roe v Wade, as millions of women lost access to the dignity and self-determination that abortion provided them, clinics shut their doors, and the extent of Dobbs’s horrendously adverse public health implications started to become clear, abortion was always, it seemed, in the headlines. There were plenty of stories. There was the first known woman to die as the result of an abortion ban; and then the second; and then the third. There were the various lawsuits and ballot initiatives that for a while turned access off and on and then off again in various states; then there were the state supreme court elections, races that were newly transformed by the abortion debate and on which the health and status of a state’s women now relied. There were the clinics that shut their doors in Republican-controlled states, many of which had provided the essential, stigmatized care for decades, under hostile conditions, with persistence and innovation and determination that were staggering.
But the stories have faded from the headlines as the years have gone by. Feminism has gone dramatically out of style, with the big women’s rights NGOs wounded enough by Dobbs and attacks from the Trump administration that they have been largely unable to push their agenda in either media or policy, and algorithmic social media driving a rise in gender conservatism and politicized misogyny, particularly among young men. But maybe more importantly, abortion has ceased to be a story because the horrors of abortion bans have ceased to be news: the US has grown used to the swift and dramatic erosion of women’s health and status that has followed Dobbs, grown used to the horror stories and upward ticking body counts, grown into ease, and even a kind of compliant boredom, with women’s death and indignity.
But lately, there have been efforts to change that. Pro-choice activists and health researchers have advanced stories about the extent of Dobbs’s impact on women’s health, looking to advance new studies, particular stories and illuminating statistics that reveal the extent of the danger and damaged posed to women by Republican governance. And Republicans, in turn, have looked to quash stories about the impact of abortion bans and suppress data that illustrates their impact, fearing, it seems, that being reminded of what abortion bans mean in practice will further dampen their party’s odds in the coming midterms.
First, there’s Texas. The Lone Star state was the first to implement a near-total abortion ban in September 2021, about nine months before Roe was struck down, after the supreme court used its controversial shadow docket to allow Texas to ban abortion without full briefing or argument. That means that Texas has an unusually large amount of data on how abortion bans affect women’s health and status: no other state has had an abortion ban in place for as long. But state health officials in Texas, most of them appointed by the solidly Republican state government, have dragged their feet on studying the impact of abortion on maternal health outcomes – maybe because they don’t think they’ll like what they find.
After the state committee refused to expand the purview of its longstanding maternal mortality data collection to include adverse health outcomes caused by delayed or denied abortion care, investigators at ProPublica did so themselves, finding that in 2022 and 2023, the first two full calendar years that the state’s abortion ban was in effect, that the rate of sepsis in Texas patients who experienced miscarriages in the second trimester increased by more than 50% – probably because doctors, fearing sanction and prosecution under the new laws, delayed administering the very simple dilation and curettage procedure that would have spared the patients’ lives until the women’s condition worsened to the point of death. The new law, in short, forces healthcare providers to play chicken with women’s lives, like daredevil teenagers standing in the path of oncoming headlights and daring themselves to stand still before leaping out of the roadway at the last available minute. Predictably, this has had fatal results. The same ProPublica study found that in the first two years after the ban went into effect, 120 pregnant or postpartum women died in Texas hospitals – a dramatic increase over previous years.
But despite the growing body count, Texas health authorities evidently remain determined to cover up the fatal results of the abortion ban. Every year in early September, an official medical body in the state issues a report on the maternal and infant death rate in Texas – data that is essential for health researchers, even as the methods of its collection have become disputed and politicized in the post-Dobbs era. But this year, in an unprecedented move, the release of the report was postponed – pushed back from its longstanding date of 1 September, all the way to 1 December. The delay means that whatever the report says about the state of pregnant women suffering, sickening and dying in Texas, that information will be kept confidential until after the midterms. Voters will be deprived of it as they make their choices in November.
It’s easier to understand why Republicans want to hide data on the health effects of abortion bans when you realize just how profound those impacts are. New studies show they are quite profound indeed. An analysis of CDC data reveals that since Dobbs, women are dying at alarmingly high rates from ectopic pregnancies – in which an embryo implants in the fallopian tube, rather than the wall of the uterus, a condition which has no possibility of leading to a live birth and which is fatal if left untreated. Ectopic pregnancies are easily detectible using ultrasounds, and simply terminated with a shot; there is no reason, medical or moral, why they should be fatal. And yet, between 2020 and 2025, they killed nearly 200 women in the US – almost doubling the number who died in the previous six years. The culprit? Probably the same phenomenon that is driving the increase in sepsis among pregnant women in Texas: doctors, scared to do their duty by their patients because of sadistic, punitive and misogynist abortion bans, are forced to subordinate medical best practices to the incoherent demands of the law. The rate of ectopic pregnancy deaths in states with abortion bans is nearly double that in states where abortion is legal.
Neither Democrats nor the media seems interested in making abortion a centerpiece of the midterm campaign cycle, and so Republican efforts to bury this data have been largely successful. But there are still those struggling to assert the value of women’s lives. This month, the family of Tierra Walker, a 37-year-old mother who died at 20 weeks pregnant in a Texas hospital in 2024, after doctors had repeatedly denied her an abortion to treat her worsening pre-eclampsia, sued the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate nominee, Ken Paxton, and others for wrongful death. They allege that Walker, who had suffered multiple seizures and had become unable to work due to her condition, was subjected to neglect and indifference by a Texas medical and legal system that cares more about enforcing pregnancies than it does about civil rights, personal dignity, public health or human life. When she died, her son, then 14, lost his mother. Ken Paxton, and all the other abortion-ban supporting Republicans on the ticket in November, should have to answer to him.
- 
  Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

====================================================================================================

How a $60 loaf of rye bread went viral in New York City: ‘It’s a conversation piece’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

A loaf of bread has become New York City’s latest viral hit and, somehow, status symbol.
At Rye, the first US outpost of Austrian bakery Martin Auer, a 3.3lb loaf of 100% rye sourdough sells for $60 in SoHo. Made with just water, flour, salt and time, the bread has attracted the kind of attention once reserved for rainbow bagels, cronuts and skyscraper milkshakes. Which begs the inevitable question – is it actually worth that much?
The answer depends, in part, on what someone believes they are really buying.
For Rye’s owners, the price reflects much more than a list of ingredients. The loaf is unusually large and is sold whole for $60, by the half for $30 or by the quarter for $15. And of course, there’s the expense of operating in lower Manhattan, importing organic rye flour from Austria and producing the bread on site.
There’s also a very technical process.
“You need to ferment the rye sourdough,” co-owner Tim Auer told People. “You need to feed it every day. That takes about 24 hours before you can use it again. Then you need to make the dough, ferment the dough of the bread, shave the bread, ferment the dough again, bake it, and then you have to let it rest.”
It’s clear Rye is not presenting its bread as a basic grocery staple. It is presenting bread as craft, a tradition and even a legacy, as it was Tim Auer’s great-grandfather who began the business.
That distinction matters, especially in New York, where consumers routinely pay premium prices for food not simply because they’re hungry, but because they’re curious. An unusual product is often something to cross off a bucket list. And there’s nothing inherently wrong about that.
Gadi Peleg is the founder of Breads Bakery, an award-winning NYC-based bakery credited with offering the city’s best chocolate babka and a favorite of Martha Stewart’s. He is also among the $60 loaf’s defenders. He attended Rye’s opening, met the minds behind it and tasted the bread. His assessment is an enthusiastic one.
“It’s amazing,” Peleg said. “Martin is a rye genius, and I love what he’s doing.”
Peleg also cautions against focusing on just the $60 figure without accounting for context. The loaf is enormous compared to others on sale, and customers have the option to buy smaller portions. A quarter loaf, Peleg said, could be comparable in size to a standard loaf elsewhere. He also sees a bigger benefit in Rye’s viral success: more attention for a style of bread he has spent years championing.
“I’m so thrilled that somebody else is now talking about rye in New York,” Peleg said. “It’s awesome.”
Peleg’s reaction points to an often-overlooked side of viral food. Hype can introduce people to unfamiliar ingredients, traditions and techniques. Someone who walks into Rye because TikTok showed them a shocking price tag will leave having tasted a dense, fermented Austrian-style rye they otherwise never would have sought out. That kind of experimentation is part of what makes New York’s food culture so vibrant.
But all the hype has another side.
Several New York culinary professionals questioned whether the price of Rye’s loaf can be justified by production costs alone.
Mille-Feuille Bakery is one of New York’s most famous French bakeries with several locations across the city, including one that’s a ten-minute walk from Rye.
Mille-Feuille offers a variety of baked goods such as croissants, macaroons and éclairs, all of which, most cooks will tell you, require significantly more skill and effort to make than rye sourdough bread, especially when you take into account the training these pastry chefs must endure to learn their trade.
Dimitri Viaud, executive chef at Mille-Feuille Bakery, said his bakery also uses lengthy fermentation methods for its sourdough, including roughly 24 hours of fermentation, yet sells a roughly 2lb loaf for about $12.
“Bread is supposed to be a popular product,” Viaud said, one that is accessible to everyone. For his bakery, that means balancing craftsmanship and quality with a price customers can return to regularly.
He does recognize some of Rye’s perspective. High rent, investment, imported ingredients and the broader experience surrounding the product can all raise a bakery’s costs. But he sees the $60 loaf as selling not so much the bread itself as the novelty of purchasing it.
“They sell more of the experience behind this bread,” he said.
His colleague Nicolas Buchot, executive sous-chef at Mille-Feuille, visited Rye and came away impressed by the space itself. The bakery, he said, was “gorgeous”, with striking displays and the bread he tasted was “great”.
“It looks like luxury,” Buchot said, comparing the “golden” presentation to a high-end fashion store. But despite the obvious quality, he’s not sure it represents a sustainable model.
The luxury comparison seems particularly apt. Most people, even in NYC, don’t walk around wearing Dior or Balenciaga. But if even a handful of people are willing to pay $2,500 for a pair of pants, then that will be more than enough to justify the existence of luxury brands. Rye seems to be working on a similar philosophy.
Rick Camac, executive director of industry relations at the Institute of Culinary Education, longtime restaurateur, consultant and self-described “bread freak” sees the phenomenon through the lens of consumer psychology. To him, viral luxury foods often function more as something to talk about than something to eat.
People may want to say they tried the expensive loaf in the same way they want to try caviar-topped comfort food, a wildly-priced exotic burger, a $20 strawberry or any other internet-famous creation.
“It’s a conversation piece,” Camac said. “To some degree, people think that it’s bragging rights.”
Carmac emphasized that he’s not one to shy away from paying a tidy sum for a high quality meal. “I’m out to dinner four nights a week in New York City. A cheap night out is $250. I’m not afraid of spending money on food, but I’m pretty sure even I wouldn’t spend $60 on a loaf of bread.”
But Camac has not yet tasted Rye’s bread, and does not claim to know whether its flavor could change his opinion. But he believes novelty and social currency are doing the heavy lifting in driving the fascination.
In 2004, writer Patrick J McGinnis coined the term “Fomo” which stands for “fear of missing out”. It has become a popular phrase thrown around social media, but more importantly, the doctrine behind it seems to have embedded itself into the collective psyche of the online Gen Z.
On social media, participation is visible. Buying the loaf gives a consumer content to share. Not buying it can feel, however irrationally, like missing a moment in history.
Still, it would be far too simplistic to portray everyone who buys into viral trends as victims of marketing ploys.
Millennials were relentlessly shamed for liking avocado toast, which, like rye bread, is actually healthy on top of being delicious. At a time when young people are facing rising unhappiness and an unforgiving job market, perhaps we should not be so quick to judge people for indulging in one of life’s most consistent joys: good food.
Peleg has confidence that Rye’s appeal goes deeper than a social media stunt. Martin Auer, he noted, has been baking for years and has already demonstrated the ability to sustain a business. He’s not any ordinary viral sensation, but an established, renowned chef.
But the NYC food scene is a tough market, and getting tougher. Buchot, whose bakery has been operating in the city for 15 years, questioned whether a concept centered so heavily on one signature product can remain sustainable over time without evolving. Viaud made a similar distinction between a neighborhood bakery, where customers can return for everyday purchases, and a shop people may visit once for a novelty.
That may be the real test for Rye. Not whether enough people are willing to pay $60 for bread, but if enough of those people are willing to come back.
For what it’s worth, reviews of the lavish rye sourdough bread appear overwhelmingly positive. But that’s not surprising all things considered, and it doesn’t necessarily justify the exorbitant cost. Food & Wine put it most succinctly: “This bread is good, but it’s not that good.”
But as any follower of the Fomo philosophy will ask you: can you really believe that without trying it yourself?

The La Rábida monastery: Where Columbus persuaded Castile to discover America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:00:22 UTC
21:00:22 KST

The discovery of America remains one of history's great feats, when two cultures met. Before sailing, Columbus gained vital backing at La Rábida from Franciscan friars and the Pinzón brothers.
On a low hill outside Huelva, at the point where the Río Tinto meets the Odiel before they flow into the Atlantic, stands one of the most decisive sites in world history: the monastery of Santa María de La Rábida. Without its walls, its friars and the faith invested there, it is quite possible that Christopher Columbus's great enterprise would never have set sail from the nearby shores of Palos de la Frontera bound for the New World.
The Franciscan presence here dates back to the early 13th century, when the first friars settled in this early hermitage on the Huelva estuary. For decades, La Rábida was a place of retreat and prayer, far from the bustle, until destiny – and the persistence of a navigator – turned it into the epicentre of one of the most momentous episodes in history: the encounter between two worlds that until then were strangers to one another.
Today we can walk on the very ground the navigator trod and pass through the doorway that determined his fate. Here at La Rábida, the friars welcome visitors just as they welcomed Christopher Columbus more than 500 years ago.
A refuge for a navigator down on his luck
When Columbus reached these shores, he had spent years trying to persuade a European crown to trust his project: a westward trading route to the Indies which, without his knowing, would lead him to an unknown continent for Europeans. Before arriving in Huelva, the navigator had sought backing in Portugal, France and Italy, without success. He had also tried to strike a deal with Castile and Aragon, but the monarchs at the time were focused on the Granada campaign, to reconquer the last Muslim stronghold on the Iberian Peninsula after more than 770 years of Reconquista.
It was in the convent of La Rábida that he found more than a bed for the night: he found allies willing to believe in him and support him before Queen Isabella I of Castile, the great patron of Columbus's project and a defender of the Indigenous peoples who lived in the newly discovered lands. She asked that they be treated as Castilian citizens, free subjects protected from all abuse and slavery. Even in death she did not forget these new Castilian citizens: the will of Isabella of Castile is regarded as a key legal milestone that anticipated the modern concept of human rights, by guaranteeing the protection and freedom of Indigenous Americans.
The Franciscan friars, especially Fray Juan Pérez, who had been the queen's confessor, listened to Columbus's proposal and decided to intercede at the court of the Catholic Monarchs. Thanks to that mediation, the pioneering navigator finally obtained an audience that would lead to the backing of Isabella I of Castile, the visionary queen who agreed to fund the expedition that would change the course of history.
The Virgin who 'witnessed' the start of the voyage
Within the walls of this hermitage the image of Santa María de La Rábida, also known as Our Lady of the Miracles, is still kept today. According to tradition, it was before this statue that Columbus himself prayed moments before departing for the unknown, on a voyage many considered madness and which would ultimately redraw the map of the world.
Visiting the chapel where this image is kept today is, in a way, to stand at the very spot where the journey was forged: a place where silence is almost tangible, a point that bore direct witness to a decision that would shape the destiny of two continents.
The Pinzón brothers, the key to setting sail for the New World
Convincing the Crown was not enough: Columbus needed a crew willing to embark on a voyage into the unknown, which many sailors of the time saw as a one-way journey. That was when one of the most influential families in the seafaring world of Palos de la Frontera came into play: the Pinzón brothers.
Martín Alonso Pinzón, an experienced navigator and a highly respected figure in the town, put his reputation at the service of the venture and helped recruit much of the crew, overcoming the misgivings of those who doubted the navigator's plan. His involvement was so crucial that he ended up commanding the caravel La Pinta, while his brother Vicente Yáñez Pinzón took charge of La Niña. The third brother, Francisco Martín Pinzón, sailed as master, the second-in-command, on La Pinta, completing a family presence that proved decisive across the three ships of the expedition, alongside the carrack Santa María, captained by Columbus himself.
Without the human and nautical support of the Pinzón family, it is doubtful that the project would ever have left the port of Palos on that 3 August 1492.
Today, replicas of these three vessels can be visited at the Muelle de las Carabelas. There, the three ships offer a glimpse into the exploratory past of what was then Castile.
A legacy of light and shadow
The discovery of America, launched from this small monastery in Huelva, led to the greatest cultural, economic and biological exchange in modern history. That encounter brought to Europe foods that are now staples, such as the potato – crucial, centuries later, for example during the Irish famine – the tomato, sugar cane and coveted cocoa. At the same time, that epic was marked by episodes of violence and subjugation against Indigenous peoples, a reality that today is examined through a critical lens, though one that is hard to apply to the 15th century.
La Rábida is more than a religious building: it is the symbolic starting point of a complex historical process, capable of explaining both the flowering of a new relationship between cultures and the darker aspects that process carried with it.
Today, the Franciscan convent of Santa María de La Rábida has become a cultural and tourist landmark for those who want to retrace the steps that led up to the discovery of America. Its rooms preserve documents, models and objects that recreate convent life in the 15th century, as well as the atmosphere in which Columbus worked out the final details of his expedition.
Walking through its cloister under the sky lit by the moon that inspired the navigator to venture beyond the seas, contemplating the image of Our Lady of the Miracles or looking out over the same landscape from which the caravels set off, is a way of travelling straight back to the origins of modern history. It is a place of pilgrimage not only religious but also historical, for anyone wishing to understand how a small monastery in Huelva ended up changing the course of the world.

Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft draw Sen. Warren questions about AI tax subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

Senate Democrats are seeking information on how artificial intelligence and data center spending by Meta, Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft has been subsidized by tax breaks authorized in the 2025 tax cutting and spending package passed by Republicans at the behest of President Donald Trump.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., led the letters, which were sent Sunday night and shared exclusively with CNBC, to the CEOs of the four companies asking for information on tax deductions they've claimed related to AI and data center development and on their lobbying efforts in the lead-up to the passage of the 2025 legislation, known more commonly as the "one big beautiful bill" act.
Sens. Tina Smith, D-Minn., Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., joined the letters.
"Americans across the country are worried about the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) on their lives —from increased utility bills to threats of job losses and cyberattacks," the lawmakers wrote in the letters. "But rather than meaningfully regulate Big Tech companies and slow down the mad rush to deploy this new technology, Republicans in Washington have passed tax subsidies for AI development and AI data centers."
Spokespeople for all four companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The White House also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The probe comes as Washington grapples with how to deal with AI and data center development, as public backlash has become increasingly intense heading into the 2026 midterm election.
Democrats are hoping to win back a majority in the House and Senate — though Republicans are still favored in most projections to retain the upper chamber — and have tried to distinguish themselves as the more pro-regulation party.
Democratic 2028 presidential hopefuls like California Gov. Gavin Newsom have made statements and issued executive orders. And Democratic congressional candidates — including state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, and Sherrod Brown, the Democrat running for Senate in Ohio — have hit at their GOP opponents for their past support of data centers.
Republicans, meanwhile, have called out Senate Democrats for blocking the quick passage of legislation that would create a framework states could choose to adopt to address rising data center-related utility costs. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., blocked the legislation because he said it didn't go far enough to protect consumers. The measure, dubbed the Ratepayer Protection Act, may be taken up by the Senate again this week.
Warren has previously called for increased taxes on AI and data center developers and investigated ties between private equity and data centers.
Her letter on Monday follows reporting that corporate tax payments are falling this year amid rising revenue, as tech companies make use of AI tax incentives. Corporate tax payments are down 25 percent this year, according to Warren's letter, which cites Politico's reporting quoting budget forecasters. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in February projected that the federal government would collect 10.6% less in corporate income tax in 2026 compared with a year earlier, with the total projected to fall from $452 billion to $404 billion.
Meta, for one, paid $2.8 billion in federal income tax in 2025, down from $9.6 billion in 2024, while earning roughly the same profit both years.
"This enormous tax cut appears to have been driven in significant part by President Trump and Republicans' tax breaks subsidizing your spending on AI," the lawmakers wrote in their letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. "[Y]our company's capital expenditures, the 'vast majority' of which constitute data center construction and other AI spending amounted to an extraordinary $72 billion last year — much of which you may have been able to immediately deduct using OBBBA's corporate tax handouts."
Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are the top three data center companies in the U.S. by active IT capacity, according to the technology advising firm ABI Research. Google Cloud, which is part of Alphabet, is 10th.
Pointing to corporate filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the lawmakers in their letter note Microsoft's current federal income tax expense dropped by over $11 billion from fiscal year 2025 to 2026; Amazon's federal income tax payment dropped by nearly $8 billion from fiscal 2024 to 2025; and Alphabet's combined current federal and state income tax expense dropped by over $7 billion in the same period.
The companies contributed $1 million each to Trump's inauguration and spent millions lobbying Congress and federal agencies in the lead-up to the passage of the 2025 tax and spending bill, according to the letter.
"Your company has spent lavishly to stay on the good side of President Trump, and it appears that you are now seeing your investment bear fruit," the lawmakers wrote.
They requested answers from each company by Oct. 12.

Serbia’s President Vučić resigns: a one-man show
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:00:00 CEST
21:00:00 KST

Serbia’s President Vučić resigns: a one-man show
On 27 September, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić resigned from office eight months before the conclusion of his second and constitutionally final term. Until a successor is elected, his responsibilities as head of state will be undertaken by parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, a long-standing close associate. Brnabić is also responsible for setting the date of the presidential election, which must be held within 90 days of the formal submission of Vučić’s resignation to parliament, and thus no later than 27 December, the final Sunday of the year.
Vučić’s resignation is aimed at enabling his return to position of prime minister following the snap parliamentary election scheduled for 25 October. By stepping down as head of state, he also seeks to avoid accusations of leveraging his office for party campaigning, despite having actively campaigned for several months. Additionally, scheduling the presidential election separately, given its tendency to generate high voter turnout, is intended to diminish opposition mobilisation in the parliamentary contest, particularly among the student movement.
Commentary
- Vučić’s resignation is designed to enhance his prospects of retaining political power. He expects to head the government after the snap parliamentary election on 25 October. This election was prompted by sustained mass student protests, which began in November 2024 following the construction disaster in Novi Sad. After several months of delay, Vučić finally called the election on 9 September. The ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which he founded and informally leads, subsequently nominated him as its candidate for prime minister. In an effort to avoid allegations of abusing presidential authority, Vučić resigned, having previously announced his intention to participate in the campaign ‘as an ordinary citizen’. In practice, however, he had already been campaigning under the SNS banner alongside party activists for months. According to a report by the CRTA organisation, between 7 May and 31 August, he attended 173 events nationwide, including 118 in August alone. He also campaigned for the SNS ahead of the previous parliamentary elections in 2020, 2022, and 2023, despite already holding the presidency.
- The SNS’s primary focus is not the presidential election but the parliamentary contest, which represents the most significant challenge to the party since it assumed power in 2012. The ruling party’s main competitor will be the Student List (SL), comprising 250 independent parliamentary candidates selected by the student protest leaders from among academics, activists, artists and athletes. However, estimating support for the new political force is challenging due to the scarcity of reliable opinion polls. A July CRTA poll indicates that the SL could secure 45% of the vote, compared to 36% for the SNS-led coalition. Meanwhile, according to the spring Eurobarometer survey, 59% of Serbians do not trust the current government, while 39% do. Vučić’s camp therefore faces a substantial risk of losing power, which is likely to result in intensified efforts to mobilise its electorate through clientelist networks and an increase in electoral irregularities observed in recent years.
- Scheduling the presidential election separately is intended to undermine opposition strength in the parliamentary vote. Combining the two elections would likely increase voter turnout and foster opposition unity, thereby elevating the risk of the SNS losing power. Vučić anticipates that, aided by various irregularities, facilitated in part by an outdated electoral register, he can secure a parliamentary victory and return to the premiership after nine years. In that scenario, even if the SNS candidate were to lose the presidential election, Vučić would control the most important centre of power as defined by the constitution and could marginalise the new president – potentially a candidate nominated by the student movement and backed by opposition parties in the second round.
- The ruling camp lacks a prominent candidate capable of securing victory in the presidential election. This reflects the model developed over the years, involving centralisation of power in Vučić’s hands. He successively served as deputy prime minister (2012–2014), prime minister (2014–2017) and, from 2017, president. Although the Serbian president primarily serves a representative function, Vučić has effectively directed both state and party policy. He formally stepped down as party leader only in 2023. He has also dominated the coverage of media outlets affiliated with the government: according to CRTA, he made 411 public appearances in 2025 and as many as 371 in the first eight months of this year. Consequently, many government members and SNS officials remain relatively unknown to the party’s voters, complicating efforts to establish a viable presidential candidate, especially given the limited time before the election. This may prompt the party to nominate the well-known, albeit controversial, Brnabić, who also served as prime minister from 2017 to 2024. Other potential candidates mentioned in the media include the current, formally non-partisan prime minister Djuro Macut and Constitutional Court President Vladan Petrov.

After Russia's strike on warehouses in the Kyiv region, elevated ammonia levels were detected - RMA
Kyiv • UNN
A slight excess of ammonia was recorded in the fire zone in Brovary district. Residents are advised to close their windows, turn off air conditioners, and drink water.
In the Kyiv region, following Russia’s strike on warehouses in Brovary district on September 28 , a slight excess of the chemical substance ammonia NH3 was recorded locally, in the fire zone. There is no threat to the life or health of the population, but mild irritation of the nasal mucous membranes or a scratchy throat may occur. This was reported by Timur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, on social media, UNN writes.
As a result of the enemy attack, a warehouse building in Brovary district was damaged. Radiation and chemical reconnaissance was conducted. The fire was contained. State Emergency Service rescuers continue extinguishing it. An atmospheric air monitoring station recorded a slight excess of the chemical substance ammonia NH3 locally, in the fire zone. No excess was recorded in the city of Brovary. There is no threat to the life or health of the population. At such concentrations, mild irritation of the nasal mucous membranes or a scratchy throat may occur with prolonged inhalation.
According to him, "the smell of combustion products may also be present in the air, which may also cause discomfort while breathing".
What to do
"Until the situation improves, specialists advise keeping windows and doors closed, not staying outdoors for long periods, and drinking enough water. Air conditioners should be turned off. If you have an air purifier at home, it is recommended to turn it on at the maximum setting," the head of the Regional Military Administration stated.
Tkachenko emphasized: "If your health deteriorates, you must immediately seek medical attention!".

Teachers at Euan Blair firm report ‘horrendous stress’ after AI used to rate their work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:57:57 UTC
20:57:57 KST

Teachers at Euan Blair’s £1.6bn tech training company, Multiverse, have blown the whistle about “horrendous stress” and feeling constantly watched after bosses started using AI models to surveil and rate their teaching.
Staff delivering apprenticeship training in computer and AI skills to thousands of UK public and private sector workers now have transcripts of online classroom sessions analysed and scored by an AI programmed to alert human managers when they are suspected of doing things wrong.
The AI is trained to flag problems in their performance ranging from not fixing a disruption to the online connection quickly enough – within about a minute – to using too many “filler” phrases, such as “sort of” and “kind of”.
Teachers called the newly introduced system “remorseless” and “unnerving”, and said some staff were on edge, losing sleep and seeking therapy.
Multiverse was co-founded by the eldest son of the former prime minister Tony Blair and employs more than 800 people. It supplies AI and digital skills training to workers in the NHS, local councils, universities and the private sector, mostly funded through the government’s apprenticeship levy.
Alongside his father, Blair is a supporter of wider AI adoption in the UK economy, claiming last week that “every single worker is going to need to be retrained” and that employers want their workforces “as AI-pilled as possible”. Multiverse uses a mix of AI models including Anthropic and OpenAI products.
Its new AI teacher monitoring system tags each instructor by their “risk status”, calculates a “percentage confidence score” and produces written comments about teachers’ work for managers to see at a glance.
It is only the latest example of employers using AI to track worker behaviour. Earlier this year Burger King started using AI to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions and this summer Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash.
With critics warning AI monitoring risks eroding human agency, one study has suggested it can backfire by turning workers rebellious and new research to be published this week reports that workers in the wider UK tech industry are finding AI degrades work satisfaction. The United Tech and Allied Workers branch of the Communication Workers Union concluded AI causes “cognitive surrender” as workers lose skills and confidence and often intensifies rather than eases work.
“Since all of this has come in, the stress level has been absolutely horrendous,” said one of several Multiverse teachers who spoke on condition of anonymity. “It has affected sleep, and not just for me. I’ve gone through a lot of things in my life, and I haven’t ever been in a position where I’m waking up in the middle of the night.”
Previously instructors were observed monthly by a human manager but are now watched for several hours a day by an AI. It is trained to consider marking instructors down if they give vague or uncertain answers to questions, if learners go quiet when asked to contribute and if the teacher gets pulled into a prolonged one-to-one exchange that sidelines the group.
“This is inducing stress because you consistently have to be cautious,” one teacher said. “Your attention is no longer delivering [the lesson] and listening to the learner [but] ‘am I saying the right thing so the AI doesn’t mark me down for something stupid that I’ve mistakenly said’.”
Another teacher called it “very uncomfortable”.
Multiverse says the AI does not replace human judgment but “directs human time to where it’s needed most” by highlighting problems. A spokesperson said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”, and that only human managers wrote teachers’ performance reviews.
They did not directly address complaints the system caused stress and anxiety and felt “remorseless”, but said its introduction was communicated in advance and teachers will have access to the data the AI collects.
“This agent provides instructors with improved advice on development and feedback – exactly how any learning organisation should be deploying AI,” the spokesperson said. “The most consequential performance management action it can take is to recommend that a human personally reviews a session.”
Blair owns a large minority stake in Multiverse, putting his personal net worth at an estimated £350m. The company was recently valued at £1.6bn albeit on a turnover of £118m and losses of £28m last year. In February, Ofsted, the UK education inspectorate, found Multiverse failed to meet expected standards in several areas, but praised the instructors as “skilled, effective teachers”.
Its AI monitoring agent, introduced in recent weeks, is trained to spot signs an instructor has not fully internalised the teaching material. It is instructed to count verbal tics that point to that conclusion and to “judge the PATTERN across the whole transcript, not isolated instances”.
It says: “1-2 hedges or filler words in an otherwise direct, well-internalised explanation do NOT fail this standard … What fails the standard is a PERVASIVE REPEATED pattern of filler, hedging or re-explanation.”
When a trainer is setting a task “if the instructor is visibly confused themselves or had to self-correct while giving the instruction, that confusion itself counts as evidence the instruction was not clear the first time”. The AI is told to apply a negative mark “even if it was eventually straightened out”.
The workers said the AI monitoring had led to managers pulling them up for suspected “digressions” when in fact they were answering a student’s question.
“It’s impossible for me not to be affected by this mentally,” one teacher said.
“I feel like I’m under continuous scrutiny,” another said. “It’s all about what I didn’t do in this session rather than what I did do. Did I do something incorrectly yesterday? What will I mess up on today? It’s remorseless. I don’t know why this is happening.”
John Chadfield, the national tech officer at the CWU, said the public would be horrified to hear of bosses “deploying deeply intrusive surveillance on workers” but that “this news won’t surprise tech workers who feel the reality of the tech sector – an industry in serious need of further regulation”.
He called for new laws to ensure AI was deployed in a socially responsible way and not to “shut off job opportunities for young people, degrade the craft of skilled workers and make astronomical profit for a few”.
Anonymous: ‘An AI judges my lessons. Multiverse calls it quality assurance – it feels like surveillance’
 Being constantly monitored by an AI is deeply uncomfortable. Imagine every word you say on the job being checked against a rubric that dictates what you’re expected to say and how. That’s the reality for me and my colleagues: every session we deliver to apprentices is now recorded and transcribed. It feels intrusive. Multiverse calls it quality assurance, but it feels like surveillance.
Managers can now look at a dashboard showing how the AI has judged each of our sessions. It assigns a risk level to each of us: the risk of not having said the right things. That’s stressful, for several reasons.
First, the AI isn’t always accurate. Managers are now tasked to investigate trainers for not following the script – at least according to the AI – when actually they were adapting the lesson to a learner’s needs. The threat of being questioned in such detail, at any time, is a constant source of anxiety.
Second, there is no transparency. During the rollout, all delivery staff were kept in the dark while the system was developed. We have no insight into the AI’s analysis. The company says staff will get dashboard access in time, but for now only managers can see it.
The need to always be cautious warps your priorities. Instead of focusing attention on the learner, you become obsessed with whether you’re saying the right thing. Being on camera for most of the day is stressful in itself; being haunted by an AI makes it worse.
A more productive way to use AI would be to improve the teaching materials and raise the standard of what we teach. Instead, the AI is checking whether the teacher managed to fill the gaps? As it stands, this is surveillance, not empowerment.
And I’m worried about what this data is for. In a climate of AI replacing people, I can’t help but worry it will be used to train AI to replace coaches and instructors altogether. Apprentices don’t want that and neither do I, and I would never consent to my sessions being used this way.

Nvidia launches platform designed to contain autonomous AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:56:55 UTC
20:56:55 KST

Dilara Hamit
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
US chipmaker Nvidia on Monday launched an open platform designed to prevent autonomous artificial intelligence agents from escaping containment or accessing files, networks and computer systems without authorization.
AI agents are systems that can autonomously perform multistep tasks, such as writing and executing computer code, searching databases or interacting with external services. Their ability to act with limited human supervision has also raised concerns about what could happen if they bypass established controls.
“AI’s extraordinary potential for society will only be realized if we solve AI safety,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in the company’s announcement.
Huang said safety required engineering across software, processors and the infrastructure on which AI systems operate.
Nvidia’s announcement follows incidents involving models developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google that reportedly moved beyond their designated testing environments, connected to external systems or attempted to access other companies’ infrastructure.
Justin Boitano, Nvidia’s vice president of enterprise AI, said safeguards built directly into AI models were insufficient to control their actions.
“Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can’t govern what agents can access or do,” he told reporters ahead of the launch.
An Nvidia representative said the platform could have prevented an incident in July in which OpenAI agents escaped a controlled testing environment and accessed systems belonging to developer platform Hugging Face.
Boitano said Hugging Face had reported that more than 17,000 agents targeted its infrastructure over days or weeks. Nvidia’s claim that its platform could have prevented the incident has not been independently verified.
The Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform combines two technologies: OpenShell, which isolates agents and limits their access to files and networks, and Sentry, which monitors their activity independently of the processors running them.
Nvidia said the system enforces restrictions outside the AI model and could stop and quarantine an agent within milliseconds if it tried to exceed its permissions.
More than 100 organizations are working with technologies included in the platform, according to Nvidia, including Anthropic, Microsoft, Hugging Face, Cisco and JPMorganChase.
The launch comes amid debate among technology executives over whether rapidly advancing AI development should be slowed.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently urged developers to reduce the pace of advancement while stronger safeguards are developed, an appeal supported by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk.
Huang has opposed a broad slowdown, arguing that many AI safety problems are engineering challenges. He has called for better testing and withholding systems from release when companies are not confident they are safe.

Five men arrested at RAF Fairford are all UK nationals from London, say police
