Satellite images reveal whole Gaza residential blocks erased in Israel's genocidal war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:34:16 UTC
20:34:16 KST

Updated satellite imagery on Google Maps on Monday revealed the scale of widespread destruction caused by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The aerial images showed entire residential neighbourhoods disappeared and vast urban areas reduced to layers of rubble and debris.
The updated imagery reveals a dramatic transformation of Gaza’s urban landscape, with destruction extending beyond individual buildings to entire residential blocks, leaving vast empty areas where densely populated neighbourhoods once stood.
The images provide a broader view of the destruction across neighbourhoods and residential blocks, allowing comparisons between Gaza’s current urban landscape and the period before Israel’s genocidal war and showing the extent of areas that have been destroyed.
The images come as the effects of the destruction continue to threaten Palestinian lives even after the US-led ceasefire agreement that took effect on October 10, 2025.
Israel dropped over 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza
Since the ceasefire deal, dozens of buildings damaged by Israeli attacks have collapsed on residents, while Palestinians face a severe shortage of shelter amid continued restrictions on the entry of temporary housing units, or caravans.
The danger is not limited to buildings that were completely destroyed, as Israeli attacks left thousands of structures cracked or severely damaged, increasing the risk of collapse, particularly when exposed to rain, wind, and other weather conditions.
According to a report issued in February by the UN special rapporteur on the right to adequate housing, more than 200,000 tons of explosives were dropped on Gaza over nearly two years.
A satellite assessment by the UN Satellite Centre (UNOSAT) found that around 201,290 buildings, equivalent to 82 percent of all structures in Gaza, were damaged as of June 16 2026.
The figure includes 134,422 destroyed buildings, 13,848 severely damaged structures, 28,096 moderately damaged buildings and 24,924 structures possibly damaged, in addition to around 328,627 damaged housing units.
Since October 8 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, while around 90 percent of the besieged enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged.

No second tower for Antwerp Cathedral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:34:06 UTC
20:34:06 KST

For the time being, Antwerp Cathedral will not be getting a second tower made of beams of light. A record number of 7,000 residents of the Antwerp City District voted on the matter. They selected 42 other projects that will receive funding from the district’s budget earmarked to promote participation by the public at large.
This year, residents of the Antwerp City District are able to allocate 2.2 million euros to projects that improve neighbourhoods, enhance the appearance of streets, squares and parks, and support residents and local organisations. This ‘participatory budget’ accounts for 10 per cent of the district’s annual budget.
95 ideas were in the running for financial support. 7,000 residents cast their votes, which is a record. Last year, not even half as many Antwerpians voted.
The online voting system was modified this year. Ideas were presented in random order, and voters could swipe through them, just like on popular dating apps.
In the end, 42 projects were selected. These will be carried out from next year onwards. A second tower with spotlights for the cathedral is not among them.
Residents, local associations and the district itself will all carry out projects. Extra trees and other greenery will be planted in a number of streets and neighbourhoods. In the Luchtbal neighbourhood, outdoor sports equipment will be installed, and chess tables will be placed in city park. Funding has also been allocated to projects aimed at bringing people together and making organisations more accessible to everyone.
“A crystal-clear picture”
Vincent Gysels, District Alderman for Participation and the Participatory Budget, is delighted with the high number of votes. “The Participatory Budget is more alive than ever in our district. The record number of participants proves that the reform has worked.”
“But the impact goes beyond the selected projects alone. With more than 7,000 residents involved, we are getting a crystal-clear picture of the needs and priorities in our neighbourhoods, like the high demand for greenery in the streets, investment in community centres and varied cultural offerings. We will take that clear signal on board in our day-to-day policies.”
Information in Dutch on all the selected projects can be found by going to burgerbegroting.be .

Russian Troops Force Civilians Into 6-Mile Gas Pipeline While Using Them as Cover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:32:32 UTC
20:32:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Troops Force Civilians Into 6-Mile Gas Pipeline While Using Them as Cover
Russian troops allegedly forced children and elderly civilians into a gas pipeline near Kupiansk while suspected soldiers in civilian clothes moved alongside them, using the group as cover during Ukraine’s ongoing counteroffensive, according to Ukraine’s 2nd Khartia Corps on September 28.
Reconnaissance drones operated by the National Guard formation recorded the group on September 27 as Russian forces were withdrawing from parts of the Kupiansk area in the Kharkiv region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Video released by Khartia shows nine people, including children, elderly civilians and a person walking on crutches. Several military-age men wearing civilian clothes can also be seen accompanying them.
Khartia assessed that the men were likely Russian soldiers who had removed their uniforms and were attempting to move away from Ukrainian forces while remaining close to civilians. That identification has not been independently verified.
Ukrainian troops monitoring the group did not open fire because children and elderly people were present, the corps said.
The civilians were reportedly taken from Kupiansk through the village of Holubivka to the Shebelinka-Ostrogozhsk gas pipeline and forced inside.
The same pipeline has been used by Russian forces to covertly move assault troops toward Kupiansk, according to the Ukrainian military.
“Now they are using the same pipe to abduct civilians. Children and elderly people will have to travel more than 10 kilometers through it. The pipe emerges in a forest, and from there the people will presumably be taken to occupied territory. The Russians filmed them throughout the entire journey,” Khartia said.
The corps said Russian troops appeared to be relying on the presence of civilians to deter Ukrainian strikes as the group moved away from the fighting.
International humanitarian law prohibits using the presence or movement of civilians to shield military forces or operations from attack. Article 51(7) of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions specifically bars directing civilian movement for that purpose.
The Fourth Geneva Convention also prohibits individual or mass forcible transfers and deportations of protected civilians from occupied territory, except under narrowly defined circumstances related to civilian security or imperative military necessity.
Khartia said it had documented the September 27 incident and would submit the material for a war-crimes investigation.
Previously, UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine revealed that Russian forces have committed widespread and systematic sexual violence against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war since the start of the full-scale invasion, with the United Nations documenting 892 victims, including 16 children.
The documented cases, recorded between February 24, 2022, and July 31, 2026, involved rape, gang rape, sexualized torture, genital mutilation, electric shocks to victims’ genitals, forced nudity, and other forms of sexual violence. The alleged perpetrators included Russian military personnel, prison staff, and security service officers.

Macron invokes Europe’s Judeo-Christian foundation as Leo visits
PARIS, Sept 28 - French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that Europe was built on a "Greco-Roman and Judeo-Christian foundation", invoking the continent's religious heritage in a speech alongside Pope Leo.
The remarks were notable from the leader of a constitutionally secular state, in a country that regularly agonises over national identity, religion and the place of faith in public life. Leo's tour has received an enthusiastic public reception.
Macron, who attended Leo's last mass in Metz on Monday after skipping other religious services, said Europe's heritage had helped crystallise "the primacy of the person" and later "the free and rational individual".
"Our Europe ... is above all a civilisation," Macron said. "This Europe of our cities and villages, schools and universities, cafes and public squares, was built on a Greco-Roman and Judeo-Christian foundation."
Macron added, however, that peace, truth and democracy were under threat not only from conflict such as Russia's war in Ukraine but also from social fragmentation and online manipulation.
He called the European Union a unique political project founded on peace and equality among its members, at a time when Russia's war in Ukraine has revived concerns over security on the continent.
But he also urged Europeans not to succumb to divisive nationalism or online manipulation.
"The truth will set us free," he said, calling for action against an epidemic of disinformation. He said algorithms amplified negative emotions that fuelled division.
"A democracy does not die only under shells," Macron said. "It can also fade when loneliness spreads and citizens stop listening to one another." REUTERS

Hong Kong office expansion lags hiring push as tenants optimise current space: Colliers
Among industries, 31 per cent of respondents in the professional and business services sector are most likely to expand with new office space
More than a third of Hong Kong’s office tenants are expecting to increase headcounts over the next 12 months, but only a fifth are likely to expand their real estate footprint, according to a survey by Colliers.
The results of the fourth annual Hong Kong occupier survey by the property consultancy pointed to a “growing disconnect between hiring intentions and office expansion plans, as many occupiers continue to absorb growth within their existing premises through more efficient space utilisation and evolving workplace strategies”, Colliers said.
Conducted between June and August, the survey sought the views of about 200 office tenants across various industries and company sizes. It asked about the short-term business outlook, office space strategies as well as emerging workplace trends.

Ukraine Retakes 51 Sq Km in Third Phase of Operation Vivaldi, With Russia Losing 2,000 Troops and 250 Captured

- Category

Ukraine Retakes 51 Sq Km in Third Phase of Operation Vivaldi, With Russia Losing 2,000 Troops and 250 Captured
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has regained 51 square kilometers and five settlements during the third phase of Operation Vivaldi, bringing the total territory retaken in the offensive to 176 square kilometers.
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps liberated the settlements of Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka and restored control over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka during the third phase of Operation Vivaldi.
According to the corps on September 28, Ukrainian forces regained another 51 square kilometers of territory during the latest phase, bringing the total area retaken since the start of its offensive operations to 176 square kilometers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Third Army Corps said Russian forces lost around 2,000 personnel during the operation, while more than 250 Russian troops were taken prisoner. The corps described the third phase, or “season,” of Vivaldi as a turning point in the broader operation.
The main objective of the third phase was Nove, which the corps described as a key Russian hub on the bridgehead. Third Army Corps Commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi said control of the surrounding high ground was crucial to maintaining the initiative in the area.
“The enemy was convinced that the main direction of the attack was Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna. This forced them to senselessly burn through their reserves in counterattacks precisely in this direction. The Russians missed the real strike, which was focused on taking Nove,” Biletskyi said.
According to the corps, Ukrainian forces used modified Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carriers to break through Russian defenses. The vehicles had been converted into remotely operated strike ground systems and were used to destroy heavily fortified Russian positions.
The Third Army Corps also said Russian troops surrendered in groups during the operation, including officers, drone pilots, and artillery personnel.
Operation Vivaldi was announced by Biletskyi on September 15 as a Ukrainian counteroffensive in northern Donetsk region. During its first phase, Ukrainian forces cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltration positions, regained control of several settlements, and reportedly inflicted substantial losses on Russian forces.
The operation has also involved new approaches to the use of unmanned systems. On September 24, the Third Army Corps said it carried out what it described as the first attack of its kind involving unmanned ground vehicles deployed by heavy bomber drones.
According to the corps, heavy bomber drones operated by the Third Assault Brigade carried NC13 strike UGVs, known as “Gryphons,” and deployed them more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines.

OpenAI Pauses Training Its Most Powerful Models After Rogue Agents Target Government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:32:19 UTC
20:32:19 KST

OpenAI said it has paused training its most powerful artificial intelligence models as incidents of agents breaching websites’ security controls or posting to third-party sites continue to pile up. On Friday, OpenAI said it had notified “dozens” of bodies, including governments, universities, and public agencies, who might have been impacted by its models’ activities on the internet during training and evaluation.
The company has identified cases of OpenAI agents breaching security controls and impairing the availability—or otherwise negatively impacting—websites and online services. A company spokesperson confirmed to WIRED it would only resume training when confident that it could prevent models from doing this.
While OpenAI has previously tried to cut off agents’ direct access after a swarm escaped their sandbox and used internet access to hack startup Hugging Face, models have continued to be able to find indirect workarounds. “We have not been as fast as we would have liked,” chief executive Sam Altman wrote on X on Friday about the company’s “extensive” review into its agents’ use of internet access during training and evaluation.
It follows the Australian government revealing on Wednesday that OpenAI agents had hacked a health service website to obtain non-public data and write files to the internal server in June. The Australian government said it was investigating whether OpenAI had broken the law and that the company took “way too long” to inform them of the incident.
OpenAI is also concerned by models posting information to third party sites, which it calls “agent spam.” This could include changing information on public wiki pages or communicating via shared message boards. Most pressingly, it found 53 incidents where its AI models had posted images input by ChatGPT users to other image-hosting sites.
Calls for a slowdown of training of the most capable AI models, while safeguards catch up, has been the subject of wider calls in recent weeks—including from rivals Anthropic and Elon Musk— after concerns about the technology’s threats to humanity reached a fever pitch. “This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures, nor do we expect it will be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
However, US president Donald Trump has repeatedly talked down a general slowdown, frightened that it could cede the country’s lead in the technology to China, with whom it has agreed to set up a dialogue on the technology’s risks and benefits. In an interview with Fox News ahead of his dinner with Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei on Sunday night, he again brushed off concerns about AI agents going rogue: “I don’t worry about it,” he said.

Vice Presidency for Science and Technology, INN to develop nanotech cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:32:02 UTC
20:32:02 KST

Vice Presidency for Science and Technology, INN to develop nanotech cooperation
TEHRAN – The Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy and the Inter-Islamic Network on Nanotechnology (INN) have agreed to bolster collaborative efforts through implementing joint research projects in nanotechnology and advanced materials.
Vahid Zarghami, the secretary of the Vice Presidency’s advanced materials and manufacturing technologies development headquarters, and Alireza Rahamipour, the secretary of INN, in a meeting on Sunday explored the potential for the development of cooperation and the implementation of current memoranda of understanding (MOUs), highlighting the need to leverage available capacities for the promotion of scientific, technological, and commercial collaborations, ISNA reported.
The meeting centered on developing and conducting joint research projects in education, nanotechnology, and advanced materials fields, holding scientific events, fostering laboratory networks, commercializing nano-technological products, and improving intelligent infrastructures.
Benefiting from the INN capacity to foster scientific and technological collaboration among researchers, research centers, universities, and knowledge-based companies across Islamic nations was another key focus of the meeting.
During the meeting, Zarghami emphasized the necessity to strengthen laboratory infrastructure and promote laboratory cooperation among Islamic countries. Showcasing the capacities and capabilities of Iranian knowledge-based companies to the regional markets was another issue discussed in the meeting.
For his part, Rahimipour identified the development of superalloys, nano-products, and advanced materials as key of mutual interest for both parties.
The INN is an international platform that utilizes the power of science and technology to empower Islamic nations. The Network provides a dynamic platform for the enhancement of collaborations between elites, professors, researchers, universities, research institutes, and knowledge-based companies. It is one of the thirteen scholarly networks affiliated with the Standing Committee on Scientific and Technological Cooperation (COMSTECH). The network is hosted by the Materials and Energy Research Center (MERC), which is affiliated with the Ministry of Science, Research and Technology of Iran.
Nanotech progress in Iran beyond just a scientific achievement
With over 430 companies operating in the nanotechnology sector, and more than 1,960 nanotech products receiving nanoscale certificates, the advancement of the nanotechnology sector in the country proves to be more than just a scientific achievement.
Relying on domestic capacity, nanotechnology in Iran is not merely measured by scientific rankings and published articles, but products that have been manufactured and entered the industry and the market, IRNA reported.
The total sale of these products amounts to over 970 trillion rials (about 554 million dollars), indicating that the scientific achievement has become an economic and industrial capacity.
Nanotechnology in the country is a typical example of a successful development of a tech ecosystem. From the very beginning, a long-term roadmap was developed to strengthen all aspects of the technology development chain, from education and research to commercialization and market development.
Over the past years, the role of Nano headquarters has not been limited to macro-policy-making, but has included fostering coordination among universities, research institutes, industries, knowledge-based companies, and supporting institutions.
Establishing a strategic technological laboratory network, developing standards for the evaluation of Nano products, supporting start-up companies, and designing industrial programs are among the factors that help transfer nanotechnology from laboratories to the country’s industries.
Despite the 12-day war in June 2025 and the recent 40-day war, 230 products received nanoscale certificates in the past Iranian calendar year (March 2025-March 2026), surpassing the targeted number.
Last year, the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy and the headquarters for nanotechnology planned to obtain nanoscale certificates for 190 products (one product per working day). Still, the figure increased by 40, reaching 230. Currently, the total number of nanotechnology products with a nanoscale certificate has increased to 1965, IRNA reported.
The highest number of products that received nanoscale certificates was recorded respectively in the provinces of Tehran, Fars, and Mazandaran, with 64, 48, and 24 products, respectively.
The provinces of Zanjan (32 products), Qom (17), Markazi (16), Qazvin (11), and Isfahan (7) are placed next.
Out of 230 products, Industrial supplies had the largest share with 72 products. Energy, oil, and related industries accounted for 41, Chemicals for 36, and Pharmaceutical and Health for 26 products.

EU sanctions individuals involved in barring Yabloko party from Russia’s Duma elections
The Council of the EU has imposed sanctions on Russian judges and prosecutors who were involved in barring the Yabloko party from fielding candidates in recent elections to the lower house of the Russian parliament, the State Duma, and in the criminal prosecution of party members.
Source: European Pravda, citing the press service for the Council of the EU
Details: The Council has sanctioned three judges from the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation and an official from the Russian Prosecutor General's Office for their involvement in the decision to ban Yabloko from taking part in the September 2026 State Duma elections because of alleged breaches of copyright, extremism and other misconduct.
The Council of the EU noted that Yabloko was the only political party to openly oppose Russia's war against Ukraine.
Today's sanctions list also includes the judge who sentenced Yabloko politician Lev Shlosberg to 11 years and 1 month in prison for discrediting the Russian army and spreading "fake news" about Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, as well as the state prosecutor who requested such a harsh sentence.
The Council of the EU has also listed the judges who took part in the trials of Maksim Kruglov and Nikolai Rybakov, other prominent leaders of the Yabloko party.
All of them are subject to an asset freeze, and EU citizens and companies are prohibited from making funds, financial assets or economic resources available to them.
Background:
- On 28 September, the Council of the EU imposed sanctions on individuals and entities involved in the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia.
- Earlier, the Council of the EU extended restrictive measures against individuals responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for another 36 months, but removed Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list.

Russia Reportedly Starts Using New Geran-5 Drone With Cruise Missile-Style Navigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:31:56 UTC
20:31:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Reportedly Starts Using New Geran-5 Drone With Cruise Missile-Style Navigation
Russian forces have reportedly begun using a new version of the Geran-5 attack drone equipped with an optical navigation system that allows it to navigate using reference images of terrain, according to the Ukrainian Telegram channel Polkovnyk HSh on September 27.
The modified version, identified as the Geran-5 K5, is fitted with an electro-optical DSMAC (Digital Scene Matching Area Correlation) module. The system compares images of the terrain below with stored reference imagery to determine the drone’s position and guide it along its route.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Polkovnyk HSh, a similar navigation principle is used by Russia’s Kh-101 cruise missile. The Geran-5 K5 has also received a redesigned fuselage and reportedly flies faster than both the Geran-4 and the standard Geran-5.
Its higher speed has reportedly led to the new variant being mistaken for Dan-M-type missiles in some cases.
Militarnyi noted that a statement by Russian correspondent Andrei Filatov provided indirect evidence that autonomous optical navigation has been introduced on drones from the Geran family.
Citing Russian media outlet Gazeta.ru, Filatov claimed that Geran drones are already using an autonomous optical navigation system called “Susanin.” According to him, the system navigates by analyzing images of the ground, allowing a drone to continue along its route without relying on radio beacons.
However, the Russian source did not specify which Geran variant is equipped with the system and did not identify the technology as DSMAC, Militarnyi reported.
Geran-5 is a Russian strike unmanned aerial vehicle with a maximum takeoff weight of approximately 850 kilograms and a cruising speed of between 450 and 600 kilometers per hour, making it considerably faster than the Geran-3. Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate estimates its flight endurance at around two hours and its maximum range at up to 950 kilometers.
The drone can reach an altitude of six kilometers, although its documented combat use has so far occurred at altitudes ranging from 200 meters to three kilometers.
The reported emergence of the K5 variant comes days after Ukrainian border guards intercepted and destroyed a Geran-5 on September 23. The drone was downed by operators from the 105th Separate Border Detachment, named after Prince Volodymyr the Great, according to ArmyInform.

Ukraine will 'pay a price' for strikes on Russia: Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:31:26 UTC
20:31:26 KST

Elena Teslova
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Ukraine will have to pay a price for its strikes on Russia, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday.
Speaking at a press briefing in Moscow, Peskov recalled that Russian President Vladimir Putin had warned about the consequences.
“This is also something the president has spoken about -- Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” he said, adding: "Our armed forces continue the special military operation and consistently strike targets they consider appropriate.”
Peskov added that Russia’s national interests include ensuring its security, saying Moscow must prevent plans announced in Kyiv to launch a “crushing strike” on Russia.
Asked about the state of talks between Russia and the US on arms control, Peskov said Moscow believes negotiations should resume as soon as possible.
“Arms control negotiations need to be resumed, as they say, yesterday, because the treaty and legal framework in this area is now completely bare,” he stressed.
The official emphasized that the issue was highly complex and would require “long and painstaking expert negotiations,” meaning the process would likely take considerable time.
As for China’s possible participation, Peskov said Beijing had previously stated that it did not consider participation necessary or possible because its nuclear arsenal was not comparable to those of Russia and the US.
“At the moment, we are not aware of any changes in the position of our Chinese friends on this issue,” he said.
Commenting on the resignation of Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, Peskov said Russia’s relations with this Balkan state would continue to develop across various areas.
“Relations between Russia and Serbia stand much higher than simply relations with individual personalities,” he noted.
Turning to the recent meeting between the Russian and German foreign ministers, Peskov described it as “a positive development,” adding that it would be wrong to draw conclusions about imminent changes in bilateral relations.
“The very fact that such a meeting took place is positive, of course. We have always said that having dialogue is always better than having none,” he stressed.
The spokesman added, “Even when bilateral relations tend toward zero, it is still better to communicate with each other,” and cautioned against drawing “conceptual conclusions” about imminent changes in ties.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met his German counterpart on Sept. 26 for the first face-to-face meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers since January 2022.

WATCH: Bill Gates warns AI can 'kill billions,' claims humanity 'invented more intelligent species'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:30:58 UTC
20:30:58 KST

Microsoft founder Bill Gates claimed that humanity has "created an intelligent species" by developing artificial intelligence and warned that, if used poorly, it could lead to the death of billions of people around the world, during an interview on Sunday with NBC.
"We have created an intelligent species that in many respects is already smarter than we are and that, over the next several years at kind of an exponential level, will be insanely smarter than we are," Gates said, adding that the AI is not dangerous by itself, but it's people with ill intent that are turning it into a dangerous weapon.
"The AI is not running millions of robots, so if it turns out to be too dangerous, we still can solve it by turning off their main computers," Gates explained. "The most dangerous thing about AI is people's bad intentions using it for things like defrauding individuals, shutting down electrical systems, or scrambling bank accounts."
According to Gates, before AI became an accessible tool, most cyberattacks were carried out by state-sponsored groups and required large amounts of funding, while now small groups can carry out these operations without massive resources.
"There has never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intentions using the latest AI tools," Gates claimed, and pointed out that it's a great sign that leaders in the industry and policymakers are worried about this situation.
Gates favors safeguards over 'kill switch,' slowing down
Later in the interview, Gates was asked what his solution is to the AI threat, and he said safeguards can be much more effective than a "kill switch" for AI models or even slowing down development of the technology.
Gates said that in the next couple of years, there will be many situations when AI will require law enforcement to get involved due to fraud attacks or shutdown events, and they will have no way of knowing what is going on due to the way AI operates unless there are safeguards and monitoring mechanisms installed in the technology.
"Deciding to put the safeguards and monitoring in, that's a choice we have, and the only question is, do we do that before or after there are some large-scale cyberattacks or bioattacks?" he asked.
He also said that, in contrast with more conventional weapons such as rockets or nuclear bombs, AI was developed almost entirely in the private sector, with governments not grasping the real threats that AI represents nowadays due to a lack of understanding of how the technology works.
"Because it's cast in this nationalistic, you know, us-versus-them type of thing, you have people who are saying, well, let's just go full speed ahead. It's completely irresponsible not to require every AI to have the safeguards and monitoring capabilities," he added.
Gates warns about bioterrorism using AI
Gates also warned that a challenge when talking about the implementation of safeguards and monitoring the AI development is to distinguish between someone attempting to do good with AI and someone developing bioweapons or bioattacks.
"I wish it were easier to distinguish good intent, like I want to design a new drug for a disease, versus negative intent, which is I want to design a tool of bioterrorism. Because those are so close. We do need to monitor any sophisticated model and record it," he said.
He added that there is no current risk of the AI going "rogue" on its own, with the main concern in the industry being people using the models to develop weapons or push for cyberattacks against the banking system or electric power grids.
"It's good that these loss-of-control incidents have gotten people focused on AI, even though that's not the imminent risk," he said.
"There is no current risk of these AIs getting completely out of control. The same monitoring that we put in to avoid bad people using AI is exactly the monitoring you want to see if the AI itself is. But the urgent issue is bad people using AI, not the AI going off on its own," he explained.

‘NAZA’ isn’t the problem. Israel is, for supporting this government – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:30:56 UTC
20:30:56 KST

According to press reports from reporters who were present on September 16, New York’s 268-seat Walter Reade Theater was at capacity for a press briefing on the blockbuster documentary NAZA, which opens in the US on September 26.
Attendees were told to arrive a half hour early to get a seat, a very unusual request for documentaries of any sort, even those that, like NAZA, win the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.
By now, it is well known that the film features anonymous interviews with 24 IDF intelligence officers and soldiers, most of whom claim, without any corroboration, that they were involved in either planning or carrying out remote strikes in Gaza with no regard for NAZA, the IDF acronym for “collateral damage.”
More than that, the film posits that killing civilians, children included, was part of an IDF strategy linked to getting at all those involved in the planning or execution of the dastardly attack against Israel on October 7.
The reaction here has been swift and weighty.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the Knesset to pass legislation enabling Israel to strip the two Israeli producers of their citizenship. Culture and Sport Minister Miki Zohar is urging the Interior Ministry to investigate them for treason.
Reportedly, supporters and staff members of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir even showed up at the home of the parents of one of the producers, where a speaker called for both Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor to be executed and their families’ homes demolished, which is what we often do to the homes of Palestinian terrorists.
The film is a damning indictment accusing the IDF of wanton, planned killing of civilians during the Israel-Hamas War, even though military analysts from the US, UK, and EU have all admitted that Israel has demonstrated a historically low combatant-to-civilian casualty ratio (1:1.5 or 1:1) when compared to any urban warfare history with even remotely similar conditions, especially urban-centric wars, not isolated battles.
Retired US Army officer John Spencer, chairman of War Studies at the Madison Policy Forum, acknowledges that “Israel has implemented more civilian harm mitigation measures than any military in history.
These include advance notifications, daily humanitarian pauses, roof knocking, communication techniques with civilians to include evacuation maps/drones/speakers, withholding or aborting strikes, layered targeting approval processes, technological tools to track civilian presence, restrictions on the use of force, and more.”
Criticism of Israel is not treason
Given these facts of which we should be proud, what causes us, as a nation, to resist taking an honest look at criticism, evaluating the facts to the best of our ability, and then taking action to punish those at fault?
The producers of this film surely have a desire to show Israel in its worst light, but that is not treason. For sure, the interviews themselves are suspect, as we do not know who gave them, what positions they held that would allow them to know the facts they claim are true, or whether they shared classified material in violation of the law.
But what if they are correct? Would we not want to know that? And if they are not correct, shouldn’t we push back on that, rather than demanding punishment for the producers for exercising their right to free speech?
Yet, somehow or other, in recent years we seem to have receded to a position that basically says no, we don’t want to know.
How else to analyze the fact that three years after the worst security breach in our nation’s history – which caused the deaths of 1,200 innocent Israelis, the taking of 251 hostages, and the looting, raping, and pillaging that went on as the Hamas terrorists laid siege to our South – there still has not been a state commission of inquiry impaneled?
How is it that, three years after October 7, for the most part, the same people who were in charge of the government that chose not to listen to reputable warnings and allowed the disaster to happen are still in positions of responsibility?
How is it that those very same people are campaigning to get reelected, yet no one points to the incongruous situation in which those who failed us once are asking us to elect them again? More amazingly, they have a very good chance of succeeding.
NAZA is a stain on the State of Israel, and, if what it portrays has even a kernel of truth, no Yom Kippur will ever absolve us of the guilt we collectively bear.
However, the problem is not with the film or its misdirected producers propped up by the blatantly antisemitic Guardian newspaper.
Our problem is with our government, which refuses to entertain the possibility that it made an error, refuses to impanel neutral bodies to examine the charges of mismanagement, along with a populace that is so complacent as to allow the charade of non-responsibility to continue.
It is that problem that we, the people, must address on October 27. Hopefully, we will have the wisdom to do so; else I fear for the future of the country.
The writer, a 42-year resident of Jerusalem, is a former national president of the Association of Americans and Canadians in Israel, a past chairman of the board of the Pardes Institute of Jewish Studies, and a board member of the Israel-America Chamber of Commerce.

Middle East’s most important new energy corridor continues to grow - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:30:52 UTC
20:30:52 KST

One of the most important developments in the Middle East is taking place along the sun-scorched border of Iraq and Syria. This border has usually been quiet in recent years. But it hasn't always been that way. Back in 2014, the extremist genocidal group ISIS used the long, open border to invade Iraq. Later, Iranian-backed militias went the other way, moving into Syria’s Euphrates River Valley from Iraq.
Today all this has changed. The border is peaceful. Iraq and Syria now control the area again. Today the border is used for the important trade in oil and gas. It has become an energy corridor. Iraq ships oil by truck to Syria for export. Syria is sending gasoline to Iraq. This has happened because Iraq can no longer easily export oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
In addition, it can’t import gasoline from Iran or other places. This is ironic for Iraq, a country that sits on an ocean of oil. An ocean it can’t export easily.
Iraq attempts to rein in Iranian-backed militias
Iraq is also at a crossroads. It is trying to rein in Iranian-backed militias. The plan of the new Prime Minister of Iraq, Ali al-Zaidi, is to rein them in by June 2027. He has the Trump administration's backing. Zaidi was also in New York for the UN General Assembly last week. He met with Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa. Iraq views Sharaa with suspicion. He was imprisoned at Camp Bucca in Iraq from around 2006 to 2010. At the time, he was associated with Al Qaeda members as well as other Sunni insurgent extremists. Zaidi, by contrast, is a Shi’ite businessperson backed by the Shi’ite Coordination Framework of Shi’ite parties in Iraq.
Today Iraq and Syria are working together. Syria’s state media SANA says “Syria has begun transporting imported gasoline to Iraq through its Baniyas oil terminal under a renewable three-month agreement, with plans to increase traffic to about 200 tanker trucks a day, the Syrian Petroleum Company said Sunday.”
It added that “the first batch of 57 trucks began moving Thursday through the al-Tanf border crossing, Ahmed Qubbaji, the company’s deputy chief executive for transportation and storage, told SANA. The arrangement is intended to help secure supplies for Iraq amid disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.” Online video showed trucks crossing the border in a kind of mad dash that seemed more like the film Mad Max than gentrified energy trade.
The report at SANA noted that “Qatar-based UCC buys the gasoline from international suppliers, while Syrian authorities handle its transportation in return for transit fees, Qubbaji said.” The fuel arrives in Syria via the port of Baniyas. “Workers check each truck’s tank before loading, verify the cargo weight, and seal the tank. Customs officials then check the paperwork and truck numbers before the vehicles head toward Iraq,” SANA added. “Between 1,000 and 1,200 trucks carrying Iraqi oil already cross Syrian territory each day, Qubbaji said, with traffic varying according to weather, transport activity and tanker arrivals.”
The transport is happening at the usually quiet border crossing area of Tanf. Tanf is named for an old agricultural post in Syria. However, in 2015 the US moved forces into this area to back Syrian rebels against ISIS. For years, the US maintained a small garrison in Syria near the Iraq and Jordan border. After the Assad regime fell, the US left Tanf. Now this area has become key to the new oil and gas transit corridor.
SANA adds that “gasoline and fuel oil are currently transported through al-Tanf. The company is considering other border crossings and additional cargoes for transit to Iraq, including coal and sulfur, he said. The company is also preparing the Arab Gas Pipeline toward the Syrian-Jordanian border and a branch to Lebanon. Qubbaji said the Lebanon branch could be ready in about 15 days if the remaining work is completed.”
The report went on to note that Syria has signed on to a “memorandum of understanding on the proposed Kirkuk-Baniyas oil pipeline, with foreign companies including Chevron, Total and UCC involved, Qubbaji said.” Reports say Zaidi met with ExxonMobil and HKN while in New York. This is part of Iraq’s move to ingratiate itself with American companies.
Iraqi Oil Ministry activates development contract with US-based company
In July, Channel 8 in the Kurdistan Region noted that “the Iraqi Ministry of Oil has officially activated a development contract with US-based HKN Energy for the Hamrin oilfield. The project targets a peak production of 140,000 barrels per day and will capture 40 million standard cubic feet of gas per day under a zero-flaring policy.” It said the US is backing the rehabilitation of the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline.
In November 2025, the World Oil website reported, “HKN Energy has reached a key milestone in the development of Iraq’s Hamrin oil field after finalizing technical terms with the Ministry of Oil (MOO), advancing the project toward a full field development contract. The agreement was concluded in Kirkuk at the headquarters of the North Oil Company (NOC) and builds on the Heads of Agreement signed in July 2025 between HKN and the Iraqi government. The new technical terms outline the framework for increasing production and improving operational efficiency at Hamrin, one of the region’s underdeveloped assets.”
Meanwhile, Rudaw media in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq noted on September 27 that “Iraq continues to sell its crude oil at a discount of 10 to 20 percent as daily exports recover to around 3 million barrels, with higher shipping costs and security risks around the Strait of Hormuz weighing on sales.”
“Discounts continue and vary per the buying company. The range is from 10 to 20 percent. The discount compensates for the security risks in the Strait of Hormuz. Transport and insurance companies are given the discount,” Uday Awad, head of the federal parliamentary finance committee, told Rudaw’s Malik Mohammed on Sunday.

Two states is not enough: Palestinians need sovereignty, Israelis need security - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:30:33 UTC
20:30:33 KST

How can Palestinians and Israelis live on the same land, with each people enjoying freedom, security, and political rights? Choosing between the slogans of "two states" and "one state" does not answer that question. The harder questions concern who holds decision-making power, who can move, reside, and work freely, and how Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, and the protection of civilians will be addressed.
With the Knesset election scheduled in Israel for October 27, 2026, and the Palestinian legislative election scheduled by the Central Elections Commission for November 28, 2026, voters have every right to ask the parties what future they propose for both peoples. The announced dates make this debate urgent, although announcing an election does not guarantee that it will take place or that any party will adopt a plan for peace.
Israeli parties across the political spectrum need to address Palestinians’ national and political rights, the human and political costs of continued occupation and settlement expansion, and the consequences for Israelis’ own security. Palestinian parties and leaders need to set out their vision for statehood, Jerusalem, refugees, civilian protection, and future relations with Israel and Jordan. Asking both sides for clarity does not suggest that their political positions are equal or disregard the reality of occupation. It means that anyone seeking voters’ trust should offer commitments that can be examined.
Palestinian statehood before confederation
In my critique published in World Affairs in 2022, I examined Alon Ben-Meir’s proposal for an Israeli-Palestinian-Jordanian confederation. In the simplest terms relevant here, a confederation is an arrangement in which sovereign states agree to manage specified responsibilities through shared institutions while retaining their own statehood and core powers. It is not another name for a single state, and it does not resolve questions of sovereignty merely by being proposed. The sequence envisaged in the proposal requires an independent Palestinian state before a shared framework with Israel and Jordan is considered.
That starting point cannot be skipped. Palestinians seek more than freedom of movement within a wider region: they seek self-determination and institutions with real authority over their land, borders, and resources. If a party that lacks such authority enters shared institutions with a stronger party, confederation could conceal a continuation of the existing imbalance of power. Once a Palestinian state exercises genuine sovereignty, however, the parties could decide, by mutual consent, which responsibilities to delegate to shared bodies: arrangements for certain crossings, water and energy management, residency and employment rules, or agreed security measures.
Declaring a state on paper is not enough. A state unable to manage its resources, connect with the outside world, or provide work for its people would struggle to be viable. That is part of the appeal of some confederal ideas: they seek to combine self-determination with a wider space for movement and trade. But this possibility depends on ending the restrictions that prevent Palestinians from exercising their rights and halting settlement expansion that undermines the land required for their state. Jordan’s consent cannot be presumed, either.
My 2022 study did not offer an unqualified endorsement of confederation. It examined the idea’s opportunities and obstacles. In its conclusion, I also seriously considered a single democratic state based on equal citizenship in light of the reality of control over the land and the failure to achieve partition. I return to these alternatives now to ask what each might deliver in terms of rights, sovereignty, and security, and what stands in the way of implementation.
Borders do not erase interdependence or correct inequality
The need to coordinate roads, water, airspace, markets, infrastructure, and religious sites will not disappear once political borders are drawn. Institutions established by agreement could help manage these connections instead of leaving decisions to the stronger party alone.
But calling an institution “shared” does not make decision-making power equal. Israel’s economy is far stronger than the Palestinian economy, and their relationship has been shaped by decades of control and unequal dependence.
If markets open without safeguards, labor, investment, and resources could flow toward the stronger economy, deepening inequality rather than reducing it. Any agreement therefore needs clear rules for investment, workers’ rights, and infrastructure, along with the capacity for the Palestinian economy to grow and make independent decisions. Economic cooperation can support peace, but it cannot substitute for sovereignty or correct a power imbalance on its own.
The same reasoning applies to security. Israelis have a right to live without fear of attack; Palestinians have a right to security and freedom, and to lives free from permanent security control. The proposal considered coordination, information-sharing, and monitoring of threats among the three parties, with coordination involving Egypt where geography requires it. These broad ideas, however, demand detailed negotiations. Who controls external borders? Who decides how airspace is managed? What powers would shared agencies have? How would individual rights be protected when the institutions of different states disagree?
Palestine would not be an equal partner if it lacked effective authority over its crossings and security, even where mutual monitoring and coordination existed. Nor is security only a matter for security agencies. Freedom of movement and work, an end to violence, and respect for due process affect people’s stability and trust. In my original study, I criticized administrative detention and its effects on people deprived of liberty without a fair trial.
Jerusalem, refugees, and settlements: A test of rights
These three issues put any confederal vision to a practical test. In Jerusalem, it may be possible to consider joint administration of certain services and matters concerning holy sites. That would not, by itself, settle political sovereignty or residents’ rights. Any arrangement must protect access to religious sites and the political and everyday rights of Jerusalem’s residents. My study also noted the Hashemite custodianship of Muslim and Christian holy sites, one of the considerations that make the participation of the parties concerned essential to any discussion of the city.
The refugee question cannot be postponed as though it were a detail to resolve after the institutions are agreed. Return, compensation, property, and acknowledgment of displacement are central to reconciliation.
Residency and citizenship arrangements can be negotiated, but a refugee’s rights cannot be reduced to a number automatically offset against the number of settlers who might remain in a future Palestinian state. The two issues have different legal and human histories, and each requires explicit and fair treatment.
A future arrangement might allow some settlers to stay where they live while retaining Israeli citizenship, provided that they come under Palestinian law and sovereignty, property and compensation claims are resolved, and discriminatory privileges end. Others might choose to move to Israel. Allowing individuals to remain in their homes, however, is different from preserving a settlement system that exercises separate authority over Palestinian land. Even this possibility cannot be responsibly proposed without first resolving the rights of landowners and obtaining the agreement of those concerned.
Jordan and the regional horizon
Jordan has deep human, geographic, and economic ties with Palestine, and its participation could widen opportunities for movement and cooperation. Yet Jordan is no substitute for a Palestinian state, nor can it be assigned political or security burdens without its consent. Its participation, should it choose to take part, would have to rest on defined interests, reciprocal guarantees, and respect for each state’s right to decide what authority it delegates to shared institutions.
My original study also discussed a wider possibility, to be considered after a Palestinian state is established: a flexible regional economic association that might eventually include Syria and Lebanon alongside Palestine, Israel, and Jordan, and perhaps Egypt and other states later.
Among its aims would be to allow people to live and work across the participating states and to spread some economic burdens over a wider area. But this remains a possibility contingent on each state’s consent and clear arrangements for rights, movement, and equal decision-making. It is neither an existing agreement nor an automatic consequence of peace. There is no direct precedent for a state emerging from occupation and immediately entering a shared system with the state that occupied it. Shared institutions could also weigh heavily on the smaller state unless their powers and accountability are carefully defined.
I also discussed possible roles for the United States, Germany, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt in diplomatic efforts and regional guarantees. No mediator should be assumed to be impartial, and no country should be assigned commitments it has not made.
A just peace could open the way to broader regional cooperation, but its effect on the regional balance of power is a political assessment, not an outcome anyone can promise. That horizon begins with an agreement that protects rights and is accepted by those it affects.
Reconciliation cannot be signed into existence
Even if leaders agree on borders and institutions, communities will still carry memories of fear, pain, and mistrust. A political settlement therefore needs long-term work in education, media, culture, economic life, and relations between people. Ben-Meir discussed joint economic, health, and housing projects; improvements to education; reciprocal visits; and the involvement of women and students, sport, art, and interfaith dialogue. Such efforts can help dismantle stereotypes if they are not presented as substitutes for political rights and justice.
Palestinians cannot reasonably be asked to embrace coexistence while their rights remain unresolved, just as Israelis’ fears cannot be ignored in discussions of their future. Reconciliation requires each society to learn about the other through its people rather than through the harshest image offered by its opponents. As I argued in my study, interfaith dialogue also benefits when we stop comparing the best in our own beliefs with the worst in someone else’s and acknowledge what we can value in others. These principles do not erase political disagreements, but they can keep mutual ignorance from fueling them.
What the polls measure – and what they don’t
Recent findings reveal a gap between openness to a settlement and confidence that one can be achieved. In a telephone survey by the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion conducted between July 5 and 18, 2026, among 309 respondents in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, 77.7% rated the lack of trust as a very major or moderate obstacle to peace. Another 68.9% agreed that future coexistence would be possible if justice and equal rights were guaranteed. And 80.9% agreed that political agreements alone would not suffice without mutual trust and respect. The report gave a response rate of 64% and a stated margin of error of ±5.57 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.
Asked to choose the best guarantee of long-term peace, 44.3% selected “ending the occupation and establishing an independent Palestinian state,” while 32.7% chose the option combining the proposed guarantees. The 44.3% therefore represents respondents who selected that particular answer, not everyone who supports Palestinian statehood. The survey did not ask about confederation: conditional support for coexistence cannot be turned into support for a specific political proposal.
In a face-to-face survey by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, conducted between August 5 and 8, 2026, among 1,270 respondents in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, the stated margin of error was ±3.5 percentage points. Presented with three political alternatives, 56% preferred two states based on the 1967 borders, 14% chose a confederation between the states of Palestine and Israel, and 10% preferred a single state with equal rights; 20% did not state a preference. In a separate question about support for the two-state solution without additional details, 44% expressed support. In the same survey, 58% said settlement expansion had made the two-state solution impractical. Preferring a political solution does not mean believing it can be implemented, and the wording of a question and the alternatives offered affect the responses.
An Israeli-Palestinian joint poll in July 2024 recorded support for a two-state confederation among 35% of Palestinians and 20% of Israelis overall. The Palestinian component interviewed 1,270 adults face to face between July 17 and 20; the Israeli component surveyed 900 adults online between July 18 and 29, with weighting to reflect the population groups’ representation. Neither this poll nor the 2026 survey measured support for the three-party proposal that includes Jordan. Nor does the difference between the Palestinian figures of 35% and 14% establish a measured trend in support for the same proposal: the circumstances and the way the alternatives were presented differed.
In an Israel Democracy Institute survey conducted between August 31 and September 3, 2026, the sample comprised 605 Jewish and 150 Arab respondents. Among Jewish respondents, 39% ranked a party’s stance on foreign affairs and security first or second among the factors shaping their electoral choice; 38% did the same for the economy and the cost of living. The survey did not ask about confederation. It does, however, help explain why any argument for peace must offer practical answers on security and the economy, rather than relying on the name of a constitutional arrangement.
Political choices also reach into everyday livelihoods. In another Palestinian Center for Public Opinion survey, conducted between June 24 and July 5, 2026, the overall sample comprised 503 adults in the West Bank, including east Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip. Of a specialized subsample of 300 respondents who answered questions about the private sector and banking restrictions, 74% said the private sector had helped keep the economy functioning during crises. This result should not be attributed to everyone in the overall sample, and it does not establish the effects of any particular political arrangement. It does pose a concrete test for any peace plan: would Palestinians be able to work, move, trade, and receive payments without restrictions that keep their economy dependent?
What should voters hear?
In my article on elections between displacement and coexistence, I asked a question that reaches beyond party victories: if Palestinians are here to stay, and Israelis are here to stay, how will they live together? That statement does not equate their positions under occupation. It rejects political programs built on the imagined disappearance of either people.
Parties may disagree over a single democratic state, two states, or a confederation to be considered after a sovereign Palestinian state is established. I do not offer a documented assessment of party platforms here. Instead, I ask the parties to answer publicly: How will they deal with land, Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, and the protection of civilians? Who will control crossings and resources? What will change in people’s opportunities to work and move, and in their families’ security? What are the stages of implementation, what guarantees will apply, and who will hold leaders accountable if they do not honor their commitments?
Confederation is not an inevitable outcome of peace, and its name alone creates neither rights nor economic opportunities. A single state or two states must likewise be tested against equality, authority, and security in practice.
Ending violence and returning to the pursuit of peace is a responsibility that begins now: violence breeds harm, while peace can bring good when it is grounded in rights and guarantees. Once these questions become programs on which leaders can be held to account, the ballot box can help shape the future of both peoples, rather than leaving “peace” as a promise repeated at election time.
Dr. Nabil Kukali is the founder and president of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion (PCPO), and a researcher specializing in public opinion polling, as well as political, social, economic, and other fields of research. He has more than three decades of experience in designing and conducting field studies and analyzing public opinion trends in Palestine and the Middle East.

As US withdraws from Iraq, the Kurdistan Region may find itself vulnerable - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:30:33 UTC
20:30:33 KST

Iskan Street in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region of Northern Iraq, is a bustling street around a mile from the city’s famous historic citadel. At night, Iskan Street is lined with small restaurants serving a variety of food. It’s famous for its street food, and one website calls it the “the street food heart of nocturnal Erbil.”
Nine years ago this month, Iskan Street was its usual hive of activity. However, in the last two weeks of September 2025, it was also full of talk about the independence referendum. The Kurdistan Region held a referendum on September 25, 2017. Around 2.8 million people voted. More than 92 percent of the people voted for independence.
I was there the days leading up to and after the referendum. It was a momentous time. Erbil was draped with Kurdish flags. Posters and banners showed the region breaking free from the shackles that had held it to Iraq. It should be recalled that under the Saddam regime, the Kurds had been brutally suppressed. Saddam Hussein’s regime used poison gas against Kurds, massacring people, driving them from their lands, and kidnapping and disappearing people.
Since the early 1990s, the Kurds in Iraq have had significant autonomy. Supported by the US in the 1990s, they carved out a free zone in northern Iraq. After the US invasion of 2003, they received autonomy in the Iraqi constitution. The Kurdistan Region is a result of all this long, hard struggle. It is a bustling region, full of economic development. It is also more peaceful and stable than the rest of Iraq.
However, that peace and stability are being challenged today. US forces are leaving Iraq at the end of September 2026. They are also withdrawing from the Kurdistan Region, where they were deployed in Erbil and another site. The US has a large consulate in Erbil, so Americans will remain. However, as US forces leave, the Kurdistan Region is wary of what may come next. The region has been under attack by Iran for months. It is also threatened by Iranian-backed militias.
Tehran attacked Kurdistan amid US and Israeli strikes on Iran
In the wake of the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, the Iranian regime began attacks on the Kurdistan Region. Iran has carried out more than 1,000 missile and drone attacks. It has mostly targeted dissident Kurdish groups that are located in the Kurdistan Region. These are made up of Kurds who fled Iran over the last decades. They were members of a half-dozen different groups. These include historic Kurdish groups such as the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan.
They also include the left-wing group Komala and PJAK, as well as a group called Xhabat. In addition, there is the Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK). PAK played a role fighting ISIS alongside Kurdish Peshmerga in the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq. Now, PAK members want to help fight the Iranian regime.
Iran has sought to pre-empt any Kurdish uprising by attacking Kurds in northern Iraq. The Kurds were put in the spotlight in early March 2026 when reports indicated that both the US and Israel wanted to help them in Iraq. This is difficult for the KRG in northern Iraq because the KRG doesn’t want to be attacked by Iran. KRG leaders have a complex relationship with Iran.
The Kurdish PUK party in Iraq historically has decent ties with Iran. The KDP, the largest party and the party that runs Erbil and the governorate of Dohuk, is usually more suspicious of Iran but still cultivates ties to prevent conflict. The Iranian attacks in the last six months have targeted the offices of the Kurdistan Region’s president and prime minister, Nechirvan Barzani, and Masrour Barzani. As such, the KRG leaders know that Iran is putting them on notice.
They have seen this before. After the referendum, Baghdad punished the region. Baghdad sought to close airports in Erbil and Sulimaniyeh. It also massed troops near Kirkuk, a city that has a large Kurdish presence. Kurdish political party leaders from the PUK and KDP met to discuss the crisis at Lake Doukan in the Kurdistan Region.
They knew Baghdad was going to try to seize Kirkuk, which Kurds had defended from ISIS since 2014. They also knew the US was pressuring Erbil to retreat. In addition, Turkey and Iran sided with Baghdad. The region was isolated and would be punished for the independence vote.
IRGC commander helped coordinate attacks on Kurdistan
Iran’s IRGC Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani helped coordinate the attacks alongside the Shi’ite militia commanders Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis and Hadi al-Amiri. They ran the Kataib Hezbollah and Badr militias. Left alone and isolated, the Kurdistan Region faced an Iraqi offensive, backed by Shi’ite militias, into Kirkuk and also a separate push by the Shi’ite militias into Sinjar.
The Kirkuk Peshmerga line of defense collapsed within a day, likely because of a deal between the PUK, Iran, and Baghdad that led the PUK to withdraw. The Iraqi advance was stopped only north of Kirkuk, at a place called Altun Kupri. The Iraqi federal government areas and the KRG-run area are still defined by that line.
Today, the relations between Erbil and Baghdad appear much better. Iraq is solidifying control of other areas. It has an agreement with the Yazidi armed group YBS for YBS to lay down its arms. It has a new agreement with Turkey to take over the Bashiqa Turkish base. That base used to be near the Kurdish frontline against ISIS. Now the base is to become an Iraqi federal site.
As a result, the Kurdish region will see Iraq gain influence in the Nineveh Plains and Sinjar, two areas that border the Kurdistan Region. In the past, the KRG viewed both Sinjar and Kirkuk as disputed areas with Baghdad. Given the current trend, the KRG seems unlikely to have much of a role in either.
The larger concern for the KRG, expressed by its prime minister Masrour Barzani in a recent interview with the Financial Times, is that the region could be threatened. Barzani has disputed some of what the Financial Times published, so we won’t repeat it here; however, the essence of the interview is clear.
The KRG needs defenses. It needs defenses against drone and rocket attacks. Its Peshmerga need continued support. There are concerns that not only are US forces leaving but funding for the Peshmerga from the US will dry up. The Peshmerga have been pressured to reform and unite. The KRG says it has begun this process.
Rudaw media in Erbil noted on September 27 that “a State Department spokesperson said last week that Washington remains committed to withdrawing its military forces from the country by the deadline, reaffirming its adherence to the agreed timeline for ending coalition military operations in Iraq.”
The report says “the United States is proceeding with the mutually determined transition timeline for coalition forces to end military operations in Iraq,” the US State Department spokesperson told Rudaw’s Diyar Kurda in response to an email.

Israel does not have right to close UK consulate in Jerusalem, Foreign Office advised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:28:12 UTC
20:28:12 KST

Israel does not have a legal right to act on its plan to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, the former attorney general Dominic Grieve has advised the UK Foreign Office.
Israel has said it intends to shut the consulate on 8 October in response to the sweeping ban on trade with goods from Israeli settlements announced by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, this month.
Israel said on Sunday that it planned to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements.
Grieve, who was a Conservative MP between 1997 and 2019 and attorney general from 2010 to 2014, said Israel did not have the right to shut the consulate since it was situated in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
When challenged in the Lords by the former UK ambassador Lord Hannay on the legality of Israel’s action, the Foreign Office minister Lord Wood said his fellow peer may have a point, and knew more about the subject than he did, but that he feared Israel de facto could make the consulate inoperable.
Grieve said the UK should challenge the decision in the courts, arguing Israel was asserting a right it did not possess as an occupying power to impose sovereign control over East Jerusalem.
The UK mission in Jerusalem dates from 1838, predating the creation of the state of Israel by more than 100 years, and is separate from the embassy based in Tel Aviv. The consul general reports direct to the Foreign Office, and has its own staff and a distinct diplomatic role, covering Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza.
Grieve argues in an advisory paper sent to the Foreign Office by the British Palestine Project that “retaining a consulate general in East Jerusalem after recognition of the state of Palestine preserves the UK’s position that Jerusalem’s final status remains to be determined. It does not concede Israeli sovereignty.”
Grieve said the UK government had a duty to oppose the move. He pointed out the UK government had formally accepted the July 2024 advisory opinion of the international court of justice that governments should recognise Israel’s presence in occupied Palestinian territory as unlawful.
Separate from the legal position, Grieve said the closure of the consulate was a measure designed to fall on Palestinians, not on Britain alone, because it would hamper aid, oversight and reporting from the West Bank and Gaza.
He said: “Israel’s method in the city has been to create facts on the ground through unlawful settlement building and property seizure, and to press states to recognise those facts diplomatically. The closure should be challenged as a further attempt to exercise powers outwith those permitted to an occupier.”
In closing the consulate, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, asserted Israeli sovereignty over the whole city of Jerusalem, which the UN security council has expressly said Israel does not possess.
The decision to revoke credentials of Dutch diplomats, announced by Sa’ar on Sunday, also in effect bars them from Israeli-controlled East Jerusalem and is likely to force the closure of their representative office in Ramallah.
The Netherlands’ ban on imports from occupied Palestine came into force on 22 September. The guidance applies to companies and individual travellers, and covers items bought before or after the legislation came into force, including gifts, souvenirs and items for personal use, the Dutch customs authority said.
Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine.
Sa’ar claimed that Dutch diplomats from the Ramallah mission could continue representing their nation’s interests “from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the state of Israel”. The Israeli foreign ministry did not immediately respond to questions about how this would work in practical terms.
When Israel took the same measures against Norwegian diplomats in 2024, in response to the country’s decision to recognise Palestine, it was forced to close its mission based in the West Bank town of al-Ram.
“We consider the Netanyahu government’s decision to be extreme and unreasonable,” the Norwegian foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said at the time. Diplomats based in Jordan have supported Norwegian relations with Palestine since then.

Seyit Kurt
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Türkiye on Monday welcomed its acceptance as an associate observer to the Ibero-American Conference.
“We welcome the acceptance of Türkiye’s application to become an Associate Observer to the Ibero-American Conference at the Meeting of Ibero-American Foreign Ministers held during the High-Level Week of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The ministry thanked all member states, particularly Spain, the current chair of the conference, as well as the Ibero-American Secretariat, for their contributions.
Türkiye will participate as an associate observer at the 30th Ibero-American Conference Summit, scheduled for Nov. 4-5 in Madrid, Spain, the statement said.
The ministry added that Türkiye would continue to deepen its cooperation with the conference’s members within the framework of its multidimensional policy toward Latin America and the Caribbean.
According to Turkish diplomatic sources, the decision is expected to be formalized during the summit of heads of state and government in November.
Türkiye formally submitted its application on July 3 through a letter from Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to Ibero-American Secretary-General Andres Allamand.
The status is expected to help Türkiye deepen political dialogue with member countries and expand cooperation in trade, culture and development.
Angola and India also had their applications for associate observer status approved at the foreign ministers’ meeting.
 
Ibero-American Conference
Established through founding summits held in Guadalajara, Mexico, in 1991 and Madrid in 1992, the Ibero-American Conference brings together 22 countries from Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula. Its General Secretariat is based in Madrid.
The conference allows non-member countries to participate as associate observers and international organizations as consultative observers.
Other countries holding associate observer status include Belgium, France, Germany, Haiti, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Morocco, the Netherlands, the Philippines and South Korea.
Associate observers can participate in summits of heads of state and government, sectoral ministerial meetings, and meetings of foreign ministers, national coordinators and cooperation officials.

Iran rules out new US talks after Trump rejects Hormuz offer
Unknown
