Breadcrumb
Iran rules out new US talks after Trump rejects Hormuz offer
Iran has denied plans to take part in new negotiations with the US this week after President Donald Trump said he had expected further talks.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," state-run news agency IRNA said on Monday, citing an unnamed source on the Iranian negotiating team.
Trump told US news outlet Axios on Sunday that he expected new talks this week, a day after rejecting an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and return to peace talks.
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the US side … via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that Iran's negotiating team would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
The two sides held their first discussions in three months on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last week. The indirect talks saw Qatari officials mediate between an Iranian negotiating team led by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
"I expect more talks with Iran [this week]," Trump told Axios's Barak Ravid. "They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand."
Two regional sources also told the outlet that indirect talks could resume as soon as Monday.
Iran has proposed reopening the disputed waterway and restarting nuclear talks within seven days if the US agrees to meet a list of conditions.
They include an end to the US naval blockade, the lifting of oil sanctions, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and a permanent end to the war across the region.
The framework is similar to the memorandum of understanding agreed in June, which produced a short-lived ceasefire.
Trump rejected the proposal on Saturday.
"They made a proposal but I rejected it," he said. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly."
Since the collapse of the MoU, the US has ramped up economic pressure on Tehran, reimposing the blockade on Iranian ports and pressuring countries to cut ties with Iranian airlines.
Iran has seen its control of the strait challenged in recent weeks, as a US military effort to escort vessels through the waterway has helped oil and gas shipments reach their highest levels since the war began on 28 February.
Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guard has continued to attack ships in the strait. Iranian media reported that almost 20 ships came under attack on Friday and Saturday.
In a statement issued Monday, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said that Iran is "the first power in the world according to divine calculations".
Despite the immense damage inflicted on the country, Khamenei said Iran had emerged "stronger and more resilient" as a result of the regional wars.
Eight US Marines injured in Iran missile attack
Eight US Marines were injured in an Iranian missile attack in the strait earlier this month, NBC News reported on Monday, citing three US officials.
The Marines were not seriously injured but suffered smoke inhalation and possible traumatic brain injuries, according to the officials.
The attack took place on 14 September and had not previously been reported. All the personnel returned to duty shortly afterwards.
The Defence Department has come under increasing scrutiny over its disclosure of casualty figures during the seven-month war, with multiple US news reports raising questions over whether the publicly released figures capture the full toll of the conflict.
The Washington Post reported last week that at least 22 US service members had been killed in the conflict, citing six US officials. That is four more than the Pentagon has publicly announced.
At least 861 others have been wounded, according to the Pentagon's public database.
Qatar extends force majeure on gas shipments
QatarEnergy has extended force majeure on gas shipments to Asia and Europe by another month amid continued disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Bloomberg.
The state-owned company has notified Bangladesh and Pakistan that affected shipments would remain suspended through November, while Italy's Edison said deliveries had been cancelled until early December. At least one Indian buyer was also told that force majeure would remain in effect.
Qatar has been able to increase shipments in recent weeks as more vessels have navigated the strait, but flows remain well below pre-war levels.
The disruption has piled pressure on Qatari state finances and pushed gas prices in Asia and Europe to around their highest levels since late 2022.

Of the 267 passengers and crew aboard the vessel, 239 were rescued after it sank, while 15 passengers were confirmed dead. The wreck was located at a depth of 554 meters (1,818 feet) off Girne.
TRNC Prime Minister Unal Ustel announced on Sept. 19 that the body of another person who had been listed as missing had been recovered, bringing the confirmed death toll at the time to 15 and reducing the number of missing passengers to 13.

====================================================================================================

Physical decline may precede major cardiovascular events by a decade: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:24:44 CST
20:24:44 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Physical decline in older adults could be an early warning sign of a major cardiovascular event years before it occurs, an Australian-led study has found.
The study, led by Australia's Monash University, tracked more than 12,000 adults aged 65 and older using 14 years of data from the Monash-led ASPREE (ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly) trial, according to a university statement released Monday.
Participants who later experienced a cardiovascular event showed a noticeable decline in their ability to carry out everyday activities, such as walking, climbing stairs and carrying groceries, with the decline accelerating sharply in the five years before the event, said the study published in JAMA Cardiology.
For some outcomes, including heart failure and coronary heart disease death, differences in physical function were apparent at least a decade beforehand, while they emerged later for heart attack and stroke, the study showed.
Researchers assessed four measures of functional health annually, covering frailty, overall physical and mental abilities, and the impact of physical health on everyday functioning.
The study found that a simple questionnaire that could be completed in a few minutes could help track changes in physical function over time among older people, complement established cardiovascular risk assessments, and help guide earlier intervention. ■

China Focus: China's northernmost high-speed railway starts service
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:24:30 CST
20:24:30 KST

HARBIN, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's northernmost high-speed railway, running through a region of discontinuous permafrost in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, officially entered service on Monday.
The first train departed from the forest city of Yichun at 10:26 a.m. and arrived in Harbin, the provincial capital, at 12:05 p.m., according to China Railway Harbin Group Co., Ltd.
Harbin is a major ice-and-snow tourism destination, while Yichun is a popular summer retreat and forest tourism spot.
The 318-kilometer line has a designed top speed of 250 kilometers per hour and features nine stations, cutting railway travel time between Harbin and Yichun from about seven hours to roughly two hours.
"The Harbin-Yichun high-speed railway can substantially cut travel time between the two cities, while extending Harbin's economic reach northward," said Wu Xingping, a Harbin businessman who frequently travels to Yichun.
This railway extends China's high-speed rail network farther north into the Lesser Khingan Mountains. It underlines the country's efforts to direct more transport infrastructure investment toward border areas, forest regions and less-developed regions, while helping boost development and prosperity in northeast China's border regions, said China Railway Harbin Group Co., Ltd.
China has built the world's largest high-speed railway network. By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 kilometers, including more than 50,000 kilometers of high-speed rail.
The Harbin-Yichun high-speed railway is expected to help turn the ecological, agricultural, cultural and tourism resources of the Songnen Plain and the Lesser Khingan Mountains into industrial strengths, boosting both county economies and forest region transformation in northern Heilongjiang.
Yichun has long regarded forest-based ecotourism as a pillar industry, but its development has been constrained by transportation.
Wang Wei, director of the Yichun Municipal Bureau of Culture, Radio, Television and Tourism, said the new railway will bring Yichun into Harbin's "two-hour economic circle," creating opportunities for winter tourism, forest study tours and forest wellness tourism.
Apart from delivering more travelers, millions of residents in cities such as Yichun and Suihua are expected to benefit from improved connectivity, which will also facilitate business travel and closer industrial cooperation.
The line is expected to improve the flow of talent, technology and capital into northern counties and forest areas, supporting local industrial restructuring and transformation, said Sun Haojin, head of the Institute of Economics, Heilongjiang Academy of Social Sciences.
Building high-speed railways in high-latitude permafrost regions poses major engineering challenges. The new line crosses 14 sections of discontinuous permafrost belts with a combined length of 5.8 kilometers.
"The railway features the highest latitude and the widest annual temperature range among China's high-speed railways, and it is also the first to run through a region of discontinuous permafrost," said Liu Libin, chief engineer overseeing construction of a section of the railway with China Railway 22nd Bureau Group Co., Ltd.
The region has an annual temperature range of more than 70 degrees Celsius, with winter temperatures falling as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius.
Permafrost thaws in warmer periods and undergoes frost heave in freezing weather. Repeated deformation can cause subgrade settlement and track distortion, posing challenges to the safe operation of high-speed trains in such areas.
To address the problem, railway builders used a double-wall casing technique, filling the space between the casings with thermal insulation materials to reduce the effects of temperature changes on concrete pile casting as well as the surrounding permafrost, Liu explained.
Experts said the project provides valuable experience for the building of high-speed railways in other cold, permafrost regions. ■

Feature: Surging Chinese orders sweeten livelihoods for Cambodian mango factory workers, farmers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:24:28 CST
20:24:28 KST

Employees work at Zhong Bao (Cambodia) Food Science & Technology Co., Ltd. in Kampong Speu province, Cambodia, Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Van Pov/Xinhua)
KAMPONG SPEU, Cambodia, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Mean Samnang, a quality control supervisor at a Chinese-invested mango processing factory in western Cambodia, beams with pride as she watches the production line buzz with activity.
For Samnang and her co-workers, a recent surge in purchase orders from China has brought immense joy, translating into abundant work, higher take-home pay, and significantly improved livelihoods.
Having worked at Zhong Bao (Cambodia) Food Science & Technology Co., Ltd. for several years, Samnang has witnessed a steady, year-on-year increase in Chinese demand. She attributes this robust growth to two key factors: the factory's unwavering commitment to strict product quality and hygiene standards, and the naturally exceptional flavor of Cambodian mangoes.
"I am really happy to see clients placing orders, as our factory produces high-quality products and maintains strict hygiene standards," Samnang told Xinhua. "Every new order from our clients provides significant benefits, creating more jobs and increasing the income of our workers."
For local residents, the factory has become a vital anchor of economic stability. Beyond providing reliable employment, Samnang emphasizes that the company fosters a fair and respectful workplace culture, treating all employees equally without exploitation or discrimination.
"The company offers a decent monthly wage ranging from 400 to 450 U.S. dollars, and up to 500 dollars," she said.
Employment at the facility remains remarkably stable, with personnel working year-round. Driven by a steady influx of new buyers from China, the factory is bucking broader economic trends by actively recruiting even more local workers to keep pace with demand.
Bun Ranith, a mango packer at the company, shared a similar sentiment, expressing her delight with the factory's fair compensation and safe working conditions.
Ranith highlighted that China's growing appetite for Cambodian agricultural goods goes far beyond the factory walls. By importing products like mangoes, Chinese buyers are actively driving Cambodia's economic growth while directly uplifting the livelihoods of both rural farmers and factory workers.
Reth Songheng, chief administrative officer at Zhong Bao, said that the company specializes exclusively in dried mangoes. While China remains its primary export destination, the factory already has its sights set on expanding into the European market.
"The premium quality of our dried mangoes comes down to meticulous selection and slicing to exact standards," Songheng told Xinhua. "The final product is naturally delicious, which has made it highly competitive."
To sustain production, the factory sources more than 90,000 tons of fresh mangoes annually from a network of farmers and brokers across Cambodia, he said.
This massive operation translates directly into local jobs. The factory currently employs roughly 2,600 workers, drawing talent both from the immediate vicinity and neighboring provinces.
"In 2025, we exported 12,000 tons of dried mangoes to the Chinese market," Songheng said. "Backed by a fresh wave of purchase orders from China for 2026, we are actively scaling up production well past last year's benchmarks."
Songheng said that this rising demand creates a ripple effect throughout the local economy. Increased orders mean the factory can hire more staff and purchase more raw fruit, creating a win-win scenario where both factory workers and rural farmers enjoy higher incomes. ■

Thai Constitutional Court upholds Feb. election result, rules ballot QR codes, barcodes constitutional
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:24:25 CST
20:24:25 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Constitutional Court ruled on Monday that barcodes and QR codes printed on ballots in the February general election did not violate the charter's guarantee of voting secrecy, letting the election result stand.
According to a court statement, the nine-judge panel voted unanimously that the use of QR codes on ballots was constitutional and voted 8-1 that the barcodes on party-list ballots were also constitutional.
The court said the codes were used to control and verify ballots and did not directly reveal how anyone voted, as tracing a vote would require linking the ballot, its counterfoil, and the voter list.
After inspecting ballot storage sites, the court found that the Election Commission held these documents under sufficiently strict security.
The court also found no evidence that any person or agency had linked the documents to discover how a voter had cast a ballot.
It said the barcodes served legitimate purposes, including preventing counterfeit ballots, controlling ballot numbers, stopping ballots from being used in the wrong constituency, and managing printing within the time frame the constitution sets for holding elections.
However, the court said the matter had affected public trust in the Election Commission's handling of the election. It recommended the commission design future ballots without markings that could link voters to their votes and apply especially strict security to the ballots at issue in the case.
The country's Ombudsman petitioned the court after receiving 22 complaints over the Election Commission's ballot design in the Feb. 8 general election.
The complainants argued that the codes printed on ballot papers made it possible to trace voters and their choices, breaching several constitutional provisions.
About 37.8 million Thais voted in the election, which incumbent Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul's Bhumjaithai Party won decisively before leading the formation of a coalition government. ■

The EU has imposed sanctions on those involved in the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia
Kyiv • UNN
The Council of the EU has added 10 individuals and 17 organizations to its sanctions list for the deportation and assimilation of Ukrainian children. Their assets will be frozen and they will be banned from entering.
On September 28, the Council of the EU adopted a decision to impose restrictive measures on another 10 individuals and 17 entities responsible for actions that undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine. This was reported by the press service of the Council of the EU, UNN writes.
The decision concerns individuals and entities responsible for the systematic illegal deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to the russian federation and within temporarily occupied territories, as well as their forced assimilation, in particular through indoctrination and militarized education
Among the entities added to the list today are the Moscow City Tourism Committee and two Russian companies operating in the fields of children's recreation, tourism and entertainment and organizing events dedicated to Russian history, commemorative dates related to wars, as well as military-patriotic education.
The list also includes children's camps and sports centers in russia and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine because of their role in cultural reorientation, propaganda-based education and military-patriotic activities aimed at integrating children into Russian identity frameworks.
The sanctions package also covers the International Children's Camp "Sondovon" — a state institution in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. The camp participates in organized programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, coordinated with the russian federation and aimed at disseminating pro-Russian narratives.
The list also includes the president of the Republic of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, for facilitating the illegal deportation of Ukrainian children to camps located in his region; the minister and deputy ministers of education and science of certain occupied territories; the minister of sports and tourism of the self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic; as well as the heads of children's camps and schools for facilitating ideological indoctrination.
The individuals and entities added to the list are subject to an asset freeze. EU citizens and companies are prohibited from providing them with funds, financial assets or economic resources. Individuals are also subject to a travel ban, which entails a ban on entering EU countries or transiting through their territory

Hundreds camp in Madrid square to demand housing reform after 87-year-old’s eviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:23:44 UTC
20:23:44 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Around 600 people continued camping in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square on Monday, demanding action against evictions and soaring housing costs after an elderly woman was forced from her longtime home.
“It’s tough, but this is growing. With every minute, every hour that passes, there are more tents, more people, more determination, more hope, more expectations and more strength to achieve everything we set out to do,” Gonzalo Alvarez, a spokesman for the Madrid tenants’ union organizing the protest, told Spanish news agency EFE Monday.
EFE estimates that around 350 tents have been set up.
The protest was sparked by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen, who had lived in her home for 71 years.
With a monthly pension of €1,400 ($1,590), she had never stopped paying her longstanding rent and bills, which totaled around €500 a month, according to Spanish daily El Pais.
A property company bought her home in 2018 and later sought to raise the rent to €2,650, reducing its demand to €1,650 during negotiations -- still more than her pension.
Police forcibly removed her on Wednesday as hundreds of protesters tried to prevent the eviction. She has reportedly been staying in a hospital since then.
Demonstrations continued in the days that followed, with protesters setting up camp in Puerta del Sol on Saturday to press for immediate government action.
“We demand that the government move toward a new housing model in which housing is a right and not a business for a few,” Fernando de los Santos, a spokesman for the Madrid tenants’ union, told broadcaster Cadena SER on Monday.
The union is calling for indefinite rental contracts, regulation of room rentals, an end to excessive rent increases and stronger protections against evictions. It also wants action against practices such as landlords withholding deposits or failing to carry out repairs.
The government has said it is working “against the clock” to approve a housing decree on Tuesday, reviving measures from legislation that failed to pass parliament in July.
Negotiations include support for young homebuyers, protections for public housing and restrictions on investment funds buying residential properties. Tax measures affecting landlords, tenants, tourist rentals and the construction of permanently protected affordable housing are also under discussion.
However, Monica Garcia, a politician from the governing coalition’s Sumar alliance, said the sides remained far from an agreement that would meet people’s needs.
“Half measures and stopgap fixes are no longer enough. You are either with speculation or with families,” she wrote.
The protests came amid a prolonged surge in housing prices. Prices nationwide have more than doubled since early 2014, while those in the Madrid region have risen to around 2.3 times their level since then, according to national statistics institute figures reported by El Pais in August.

Segre urges antisemitism bill OK tweaked to exempt some criticism of Israel
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:22:51 CEST
20:22:51 KST

Holocaust survivor and Life Senator
Liliana Segre on Monday called for the unanimous approval of a
bill against anti-semitism if it is amended so that not all
criticism of Israel is automatically deemed anti-semitic.
                                    
                                       
				The 96-year-old survivor of Auschwitz said this would enable the
opposition, centre-left Democratic Party to reverse its
opposition to the bill.
                                    
                                       
				"It is essential to pass the antisemitism bill unanimously," she
said in a statement to ANSA, explaining that if necessary, "it
would be appropriate to be open" to a "non-essential amendment"
to the text.
                                    
                                       
				This amendment would clarify that criticism of the State of
Israel—like that of any other country—is permissible and should
not automatically be deemed antisemitic.
                                    
                                       
				 "I am making a renewed, heartfelt appeal to all parties," the
senator-for-life stressed, "to make a further effort of
generosity and responsibility, setting aside political
maneuvering and focusing on the higher interest of the country.
                                    
                                       
				"They must recognize that a rift over such a sensitive issue
would damage Italy's image and contribute to fuelling a climate
of intolerance and the spread of hatred."
Antisemitic hate crimes are on the rise in Italy.
                                    
                                       
				The president of the Left for Italy group and former PD MP
Emanuele Fiano, a critic of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin
Netanyahu, said in a newspaper editorial Monday that he was
ready to leave the PD unless it reverses its stance on the bill.
                                    
                                       
				"Do not accuse me of playing the victim, for you are barking up
the wrong tree. At stake is the spirit of a collective political
choice and, for me, the future of a modern Left—one capable of
countering the advance of backward-looking nationalisms with
something other than a Left that merely echoes the rhetoric of
decades past," wrote Fiano in his op-ed for Il Foglio.
                                    
                                       
				"The Democratic Party," he adds, "has decided to vote against
the bill on antisemitism, which was passed by the Senate and is
now under review by the Chamber of Deputies.
                                    
                                       
				"If that decision stands, it will represent an impassable
boundary for me.
                                    
                                       
				"I have asked my party—at both local and national levels—to
promote initiatives, meetings, and studies regarding what was
unfolding. Silence.
                                    
                                       
				"The news," Fiano continued, "reaches me at Birkenau. I am here
for the assembly of the International Auschwitz Committee—on
whose executive board I serve—and, together with a
representative of the German Roma community, I am looking at the
site where the 'Zigeunerlager' once stood—the sector where Roma
and Sinti people were imprisoned.
                                    
                                       
				"I tell him about my father, who remembered the night of August
2-3, 1944, when thousands of Sinti and Roma were gassed and then
incinerated, and that sector of the camp was completely and
permanently emptied.
                                    
                                       
				"I do not accept," the former Democratic Party MP adds, "that
the fight against antisemitism is portrayed as an obstacle to
criticizing the Netanyahu government, the Israeli army, or
settler violence. Such criticism is legitimate and necessary.
                                    
                                       
				 "In 2017," he continued, "(PD leader) Elly Schlein signed a
draft resolution against antisemitism submitted on behalf of the
Socialists and Democrats group (in the European Parliament), of
which the PD was a member.
                                    
                                       
				"One can certainly change one's mind, but in politics, one ought
to explain *why* one is changing one's position if the
circumstances haven't changed; otherwise, there is a risk of
losing one's identity.
                                    
                                       
				"I would like an Italian magistrate," he adds, "to tell me
exactly what would happen once the law is passed. Does the law
define specific offenses? Does it prescribe penalties? My
concern is that the Left should not leave the task of responding
to antisemitism to the Right," Fiano concluded.

MHA scraps 34 CISF posts after security withdrawal from Patanjali food and herbal park in Haridwar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:21:28 UTC
20:21:28 KST

CISF had been providing security to the Patanjali Food and Herbal Park since June 2015
NEW DELHI: The home ministry on Monday directed the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) to abolish all 34 sanctioned posts of its security wing at Swami Ramdev's Patanjali Food and Herbal Park Pvt Ltd in Haridwar, ending the sanctioned manpower structure of the deployed wing.The force had withdrawn its security from the premises on May 4. However, the ministry has now formally ordered the abolition of the posts that constituted the sanctioned strength of the deployed security wing.Earlier this month, the ministry delivered a letter to the CISF and conveyed the decision for the "abolition of the undermentioned 34 posts consequent upon withdrawal of CISF Security Wing from Patanjali Food & Herbal Park, Private Limited, Haridwar (Uttarakhand) on May 4, 2026".CISF had been providing security to the Patanjali Food and Herbal Park since June 2015, after a person was killed during a clash between the establishment's security guards and local truck union supporters. Following the incident, 10 persons, including Ramdev's brother Rambharat, were arrested in connection with the case.As per the order, the sanctioned strength of 34 personnel comprised one assistant commandant, four sub-inspectors, two assistant sub-inspectors, 11 head constables and 16 Constables.
The MHA also directed the CISF to ensure that "all pending and outstanding dues, if any, are reimbursed by the concerned management."The CISF's security services were funded by the food park's administration, with the establishment paying the Centre for the deployment of the paramilitary force.
Established under the 50th Act of Parliament in 1968, the CISF is a multi-faceted Central Armed Police Force under the MHA. Starting with a strength of 3,129 personnel, the force has since expanded to 2.20 lakh personnel, with deployments across almost all states in the country.According to ANI, the CISF currently provides security cover to 361 critical national installations, including 70 airports. The force also maintains 12 Reserve Battalions to respond to security exigencies and operates eight state-of-the-art training institutions across the country to train and strengthen its personnel.

Poland offers to host facility producing Patriot missiles for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:20:44 UTC
20:20:44 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the factory could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security.
The news was revealed by deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who also confirmed that Poland would seek to establish a Patriot servicing and production facility even if it does not host Ukraine’s.
Poland wants to host Patriot production
Poland has proposed that the US and Ukraine launch joint production of Patriot missiles. Warsaw is citing security concerns and is proposing to host the facility in Poland instead of Ukraine:
“If such a factory is planned to be built in… pic.twitter.com/syCkNt0o0V
— Belsat in English (@Belsat_Eng) September 27, 2026
Patriot missile systems have been a key part of Ukraine’s defence against Russian aerial attacks. However, Kyiv has suffered from a shortage of missiles used in the system, prompting President Volodymyr Zelensky to appeal to allies to transfer their interceptors as well as to allow Ukraine to produce them itself.
US President Donald Trump initially told Zelensky at a meeting in July that “we are gonna give you a licence to make Patriots”. However, he then backtracked on that offer later the same month.
But, following weeks of uncertainty, on Friday last week Zelensky claimed that Trump had personally told him he had made a “final decision” to approve a licence for Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles. Washington has not confirmed that development.
Asked about the issue on Saturday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told broadcaster TVN, “let’s see if it happens”. However, she added that, “we proposed that, if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in the so-called safe territory”.
Poland is already the primary hub for military equipment, goods and people being transported in and out of its eastern neighbour.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that, regardless of where the plant serving Ukraine is located, Poland would also still seek to establish a facility for servicing and, eventually, production of Patriots.
“What my interlocutors in Washington confirmed is that, even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, it does not change our efforts and does not rule out consent for Poland,” she said. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka was in Washington last week for talks with US officials.
In May this year, another deputy defence minister, Cezary Tomczyk, told TVN that Poland had “received preliminary approval from the US State Department to produce missiles for Patriot systems”.
The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism
It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026
In 2018, as part of its Wisła air defence programme, Poland signed a $4.75bn contract to purchase Patriot launchers and missiles from the US.
In October 2023, the first Patriot systems procured from the US were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport. In December 2025, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries.
Poland also has an agreement to domestically produce launchers for Patriot systems through cooperation between Polish state-owned defence contractor Huta Stalowa Wola SA and US defence giant Raytheon.
Poland has announced a $1.2bn deal that will see a Polish state-owned defence firm manufacture 48 launchers for Patriot missile systems domestically in cooperation with US defence giant Raytheon https://t.co/PQOjKvhqYM
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2024
The issue of Ukraine’s need for more Patriot missiles caused domestic political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition reacted angrily to reports that the government had handed over some interceptors to Ukraine.
In July, the government confirmed that it had done so. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that only five missiles had been transferred to Ukraine.
In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported that the Iran war had depleted America’s stockpile of Patriot missiles to 800 interceptors from roughly 2,300 before the war began.
Last week, Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, confirmed that his country has also proposed that it could manufacture interceptors and perhaps even entire Patriot systems.

Ethiopian pro-government forces claim capture of strategic Tigray town
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:17:24 UTC
20:17:24 KST

Ethiopian pro-government forces claim capture of strategic Tigray town
Sept 28 - Ethiopia's military and allied militiamen captured the strategic town of Alamata south of Tigray's capital, a pro-government militia said on Monday, turning the tables after an opposition offensive launched from the region last week.
Video posted by the pro-government Tigrai Peace Force on its Facebook page showed soldiers marching through the streets, waving Ethiopian flags. Reuters could not immediately verify the video.
Two diplomatic sources also said the town had fallen, while a third said the pro-government forces had entered but it was not yet clear whether they were fully in control.
Spokespeople for the Ethiopian military and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which is leading the armed resistance to the federal government, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The capture of Alamata would be a major boon to federal forces as they press towards the regional capital Mekelle, about 120 km (75 miles) to the north. An important supply hub for troops, food and fuel near Tigray's southern border with the neighbouring Amhara region, Alamata exchanged hands several times during a 2020-2022 civil war.
ETHIOPIAN MILITARY ACCUSES NEIGHBORS OF BACKING OPPOSITION
The fighting since last Wednesday in Tigray and the neighboring regions of Amhara and Afar has shattered a four-year-old peace deal, the Pretoria Agreement, that ended fighting that killed hundreds of thousands of people.
The 2020-2022 civil war stemmed from a breakdown in relations between the TPLF, a guerrilla movement turned political party that dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades, and Abiy, whose appointment as prime minister in 2018 ended the TPLF’s dominance.
In recent months, the TPLF and federal government have traded accusations of violating the November 2022 agreement. Three days before launching its offensive, the TPLF announced a new alliance with six other armed groups across Ethiopia aimed at overthrowing Abiy's government.
The renewed conflict adds to instability in the Horn of Africa, already unsettled by Sudan's civil war, frictions over Red Sea access and spillover from Middle East conflicts.
In comments broadcast on state media on Sunday, the top Ethiopian military commander, Berhanu Jula, reiterated previous accusations that Ethiopia's neighbour and historical rival Eritrea was supporting the opposition forces, alongside Sudan's armed forces and Egypt.
Eritrea and Sudan's army have denied the allegations. Egypt did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
TELECOMMUNICATIONS NETWORKS REMAIN DOWN IN TIGRAY
The conflict has raised fears of a return to the humanitarian crisis experienced during the 2020-2022 war when the federal government severed communications with Tigray and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted.
In Tigray, internet and phone networks remained disrupted for a fourth day. Four sources told Reuters on Friday that the TPLF had ordered the networks shut down. The TPLF has not responded to requests for comment about this.
Tigray is yet to recover from the devastating humanitarian toll of the 2020-2022 war, which pushed hundreds of thousands into famine conditions. Around 750,000 Tigrayans were still internally displaced as of February, according to the UN refugee agency, and the region is facing drought linked to El Nino. REUTERS

Why Netanyahu pushed for a UAE meeting before Israel's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:14:08 UTC
20:14:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Netanyahu was desperate for a UAE meeting before Israel's election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly made an unannounced visit to the United Arab Emirates on Sunday, meeting President Mohammed bin Zayed in Abu Dhabi after weeks of alleged Israeli pressure to secure the talks.
Days earlier, however, another planned visit had been cancelled at the last minute.
Israeli newspaper Maariv reported on Monday that the earlier visit had been fully arranged, with the Israeli side reportedly told shortly before Netanyahu was due to depart that Mohammed bin Zayed was not in the country.
According to the newspaper, however, subsequent checks indicated that the Emirati president was in Abu Dhabi at the time.
The revelations have raised questions over whether Mohammed bin Zayed had initially sought to avoid meeting Netanyahu, and why the Israeli leader was reportedly so determined to secure a visit weeks before Israel's 27 October election.
Why was Netanyahu desperate for a meeting?
Netanyahu reportedly placed considerable pressure on the UAE to arrange a visit before Israel's parliamentary election next month.
Emirati sources cited by Maariv described the pressure as "very heavy", reportedly involving telephone calls, approaches through associates and international intermediaries, and even references to future security cooperation.
The newspaper linked Netanyahu's efforts partly to a growing political controversy over reports that Mohammed bin Zayed had warned him about the possibility of a major Hamas operation shortly before the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israeli military bases and civilian settlements within and around the Gaza envelope.
Haaretz reported earlier this month that Mohammed bin Zayed spoke to Netanyahu roughly a week and a half before the attack and warned him that then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning significant action that could cause bloodshed and destabilise the region.
Netanyahu's office rejected the report, saying no such warning was given to the prime minister.
The UAE later said security matters with other countries are handled through the relevant agencies and that details of this kind are not discussed at the level of national leaders, a response The National characterised as rejecting the claim of a direct warning from Mohammed bin Zayed.
The alleged warning has become a contentious issue during Israel's election campaign, renewing scrutiny over what information reached Netanyahu and Israel's political leadership before 7 October, and why action was not taken to avert the attack.
Did Mohammed bin Zayed try to avoid the meeting?
There has been no official confirmation that Mohammed bin Zayed personally refused to meet Netanyahu, but Maariv's account suggests the UAE pulled out of an earlier planned visit at the last minute.
According to the newspaper, preparations had been completed for Netanyahu to travel to the Emirates several days before Sunday's eventual meeting. The visit was supposed to remain secret and only be disclosed after it had concluded.
"Everything was ready, the delegation was organised, and the cancellation message arrived shortly before departure," an unnamed informed source told Maariv.
The newspaper said the Emirati side then claimed Mohammed bin Zayed was "not in the country".
A subsequent check, however, indicated that the UAE president was in Abu Dhabi at the time, according to the report. The claim has not been publicly confirmed by Emirati officials.
A source speaking to Maariv at the time of the earlier cancellation said Mohammed bin Zayed did not want to become part of Netanyahu's election campaign and described relations between the two as having been troubled for some time.
The same source suggested that an unofficial and indirect denial published in the UAE ahead of a Jewish holiday may have been intended to compensate Netanyahu for the cancellation.
Despite the setback, Israeli efforts to secure a meeting continued and Netanyahu eventually travelled to Abu Dhabi on Sunday. A senior Israeli official confirmed to Reuters that Netanyahu met Mohammed bin Zayed during the visit.
Israel Hayom reported on Monday that Netanyahu was accompanied by senior Israeli security officials, including Mossad chief Roman Gofman, National Security Adviser Shmuel Ben Ezra and a senior official from the Shin Bet's VIP protection unit, as well as senior officials from the prime minister's office.
The newspaper said the delegation spent around six hours in the UAE, with Netanyahu meeting Mohammed bin Zayed for several hours.
In May, Netanyahu's office said he had secretly visited the Emirates during the war with Iran and met Mohammed bin Zayed. The UAE publicly denied that the visit had taken place, calling reports of unannounced visits or undisclosed arrangements unfounded unless officially announced by Emirati authorities.
What did Netanyahu reportedly ask MBZ to do?
Haaretz, citing Emirati sources, reported that Sunday's eventual meeting took place at the airport and that Netanyahu asked Mohammed bin Zayed to deny reports concerning their alleged pre-7 October phone call.
According to the report, Netanyahu also asked the Emirati president to deny other details relating to October 7 that could cause him political embarrassment and sought what was described as "moral support".
Those claims have not been publicly confirmed by Netanyahu's office or the UAE.
The visit itself was not announced in advance, and neither Netanyahu's office nor the UAE Foreign Ministry immediately commented on it.
No official Emirati statement has since been issued about the visit, while major UAE media outlets have not reported on it, raising questions over whether its disclosure was coordinated with Abu Dhabi or whether details emerged from the Israeli side without Emirati approval.

WHO representative highlights role of medical universities in evidence-based health policy

WHO representative highlights role of medical universities in evidence-based health policy
TEHRAN – Dr. Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran, has underscored the vital role of medical universities in strengthening national capacity for evidence-based policymaking, advancing research and innovation, and supporting resilient health systems in the face of emerging challenges.
On Wednesday, September 23, Jabbour, accompanied by a delegation, visited Isfahan University of Medical Sciences and Health Services (IUMS). The visit was organized by the Isfahan provincial governor’s office and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Jabbour met with Dr. Shahin Shirani, Chancellor of Isfahan University of Medical Sciences, along with senior health officials, including the director general for international affairs and representatives from the Ministry of Health and Medical Education and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Serving a province with a population of more than five million, Isfahan University of Medical Sciences is one of Iran’s leading medical universities, integrating healthcare delivery, medical education, and research through an extensive network of schools, healthcare and treatment centers, and research institutions.
Discussions during the visit focused on the vital role of medical universities in strengthening national capacity for evidence-based policymaking, advancing research and innovation, and supporting resilient health systems in responding to emerging challenges.
“Universities such as Isfahan University of Medical Sciences are not only centers of education and research. They are strategic partners in generating evidence, shaping policies, and strengthening health systems for future generations,” Jabbour said.
“WHO stands ready to support rapid assessments of health infrastructure and services in collaboration with national and provincial authorities to ensure continuity of essential health services and identify priority needs,” he added.
The visit also highlighted opportunities to strengthen cooperation with research institutions, including potential collaborating centers interested in becoming WHO collaborating centers and aligned with national health priorities. Isfahan University of Medical Sciences currently hosts a WHO Collaborating Centre for Research and Training in Cardiovascular Disease Control, Prevention and Rehabilitation, which has made significant contributions to research, training and policy development since 2003.
The visit concluded with participation in expert panels on “Health, Environment and Resilience of Essential Services” and “Innovation and Technology for Development,” reinforcing WHO’s commitment to advancing innovation, resilience and evidence-based health development.

Bryansk is the main launchpad for Russia's drone and ballistic strikes on Kyiv and on the Chernihiv and Sumy oblasts, and its lines likely carry supplies that feed those attacks. For nearly a month, Russian jet-powered drones have been striking Kyiv from the region.
Kovalchuk reports damage in three districts but adds that no one was hurt in those drone attacks.
The launchpad's railways take hits
On the Dyatkovo–Lyudinovo line, a drone attack brought down part of a bridge and derailed 10 cars, Kovalchuk says. In the Unecha district, 18 empty gondola cars derailed. In the Navlia district, a strike damaged the track without stopping trains.
Repairs will begin, he notes, once the National Guard has inspected the sites.
Russia's campaign dwarfs it
Ukraine's strikes on Bryansk are modest beside what Russia is doing to Ukraine's railways. In the first eight months of 2026, Ukraine's state operator logged more than 1,600 attacks on its rolling stock and infrastructure, Oleh Holovashchenko of Ukrzaliznytsia tells DW.
Russia has damaged more than 500 locomotives since the invasion, over half of them this year, and has increasingly hunted moving trains to sever the corridors that carry Ukraine's exports and supplies.
A drone finds a train near Poland
The campaign even reaches Ukraine's western edge. On 13 September, a Russian jet Geran struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn crossing in Volyn, two kilometers from the Polish border.
A dispatcher spotted the drone in time to evacuate the passengers, among them former CIA director David Petraeus, and a diplomatic train carrying former British prime minister Boris Johnson had left early.

EU expands sanctions for deportation and Russification of Ukrainian children, adding 10 individuals and 17 entities
The Council of the EU has sanctioned another 10 individuals and 17 entities for their involvement in the illegal transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia and within Russian-occupied territories, as well as their Russification, including militarised education.
Source: European Pravda, citing the press service for the Council of the EU
Details: The decision targets individuals responsible for the systematic illegal deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children to the Russian Federation and within temporarily occupied territories, as well as their forced assimilation, including ideological indoctrination and militarised education.
The entities added to the sanctions list include the Moscow City Tourism Committee and two Russian companies that provide recreation, tourism and entertainment services for children and organise events focused on Russian history, war commemorations and military-patriotic education.
Children's camps and sports centres in Russia and temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine have also been listed for their role in propaganda-based education and military-patriotic and cultural activities aimed at integrating children into a Russian identity framework.
The sanctions package also includes the Songdowon International Children's Camp, a state-run institution in North Korea which participates in organised programmes involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine in coordination with the Russian Federation and with the aim of promoting pro-Russian narratives.
The Council of the EU has also added Rustam Minnikhanov, President of the Republic of Tatarstan, to the list for facilitating the illegal deportation of Ukrainian children to camps in his region. The list also includes ministers and deputy ministers of education and science in certain occupied territories, the sport and tourism minister of the so-called " Donetsk People's Republic The "Donetsk People's Republic", or "DPR", is a self-proclaimed unrecognised quasi-state formation backed by Russia in Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast ", and heads of local children's camps and schools.
Those added to the list are subject to an asset freeze, and EU citizens and companies are prohibited from making funds, financial assets or economic resources available to them. Individuals are also subject to a ban on entering or transiting through EU territory.
Background: On 22 September, the Council of the EU decided to extend restrictive measures against individuals responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for another 36 months, but removed Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list.

First group of migratory pelicans spotted in northwestern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:11:37 UTC
20:11:37 KST

First group of migratory pelicans spotted in northwestern Iran
TEHRAN – The first group of migratory pelicans has been spotted at Solduz Wetland in Naqadeh County, northwestern Iran.
Akbar Qaemi, head of the Naqadeh Department of Environment, said a group of 35 pelicans had arrived at the wetland as part of their seasonal migration from northern areas toward warmer southern regions, IRNA reported.
He noted that the number of migratory pelicans at the wetland is expected to increase in the coming days, adding that most of the birds observed so far are juveniles that were born in Lake Urmia National Park and its surrounding areas and have begun their seasonal migration as temperatures fall.
In addition to migratory pelicans, various species of resident and migratory birds, including sandpipers, stilts, gulls, garganeys, coots, herons, and different species of ducks, are currently being observed at Solduz Wetland.
Naqadeh County is home to seven seasonal and permanent wetlands, which annually provide habitat for more than 10,000 migratory and resident birds.
Iran is the most important country in West Asia in terms of housing migratory birds in winter, as around two million birds fly each year to spend winter in the country’s wetlands, according to an official with the Department of Environment.
Encompassing numerous wetlands, reservoirs, and diverse water bodies, Iran welcomes millions of migratory birds every year. The country has also emerged as the most important stopover for migratory birds in their flight route from Siberia to the Nile, as sixteen percent of them select to spend the winter in the country, ISNA quoted Hassan Akbari as saying.
A diverse array of migratory birds fly to the country, with more than 160 species of aquatic and waterside birds identified in Iran, which is a significant number.
Despite limited water resources in the domestic habitats of the country, the study of the migratory bird population trend shows that the abundance and diversity of the birds that enter the country have not decreased. The majority of them have flown to the coastal areas of the Caspian and the Persian Gulf, though.
Iran hosts more than five percent of the world’s migratory birds in 450 sites in winter, Akbari said.
“Every year, some 30 to 40 million birds are counted all over the world, and the related statistics are recorded in the International Waterfowl Census (IWC) database,” he added.

Dmytro Lytvyn, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, replied to a critic on Facebook that "there was no agreement to remain silent" and that hiding the prisoners' destination "would also be wrong," the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
How the dispute unfolded
Zelenskyy announced the transfer on 23 September during a speech at the UN General Assembly. He said Ukraine had recently sent two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. He also described one soldier's attempt to kill himself after realizing he would be captured and accused North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of using his soldiers "like currency," pointing to Pyongyang's improved ballistic missiles and drone capabilities as what it gets in return.
The next day, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said the transfer should not have been disclosed and that the two sides had agreed to keep it private. A South Korean presidential official said Ukraine had told Seoul in advance that Zelenskyy might mention the transfer and Seoul had asked that the soldiers' destination not be disclosed, though it was unclear how he would phrase it, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
Who the two soldiers are
The two soldiers—Ri, 26, a reconnaissance sniper, and Baek, 21, a rifleman—were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025, according to their interview with South Korea's Chosun Ilbo. Both had served in North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau and later asked to go to South Korea in media interviews and handwritten letters to defector groups.
The two countries' foreign ministers discussed the prisoners' status in March and June, reaching a shared understanding that the case should be resolved under international law and humanitarian principles, according to South Korea's Foreign Ministry. On 8 July, at the NATO summit in Ankara, Lee and Zelenskyy agreed to handle the case on humanitarian grounds while respecting the soldiers' wishes.
The two soldiers arrived in South Korea the weekend before Zelenskyy announced their transfer at the UN General Assembly, opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon said.
North Korea's role in Russia's war
North Korea began sending troops to support Russia's war in late 2024, with initial estimates putting the deployment at more than 10,000 soldiers. Many were sent to Russia's Kursk Oblast. The two countries signed a strategic partnership pact with a mutual defense clause in Pyongyang in June 2024.

Florida pastor accused of role in Haitian president's assassination goes on trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:07:33 UTC
20:07:33 KST

Florida pastor accused of role in Haitian president's assassination goes on trial
Sept 28 - A Haitian American pastor accused by US prosecutors of helping orchestrate the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise so he could take over the Caribbean nation's leadership is due to stand trial in Miami on Monday.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon, 67, has pleaded not guilty to charges including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moise and could face life in prison if convicted.
Sanon has been detained since Haitian authorities arrested him days after the assassination. Police found boxes of ammunition, 19 passports and other items in a search of his home. He was transferred to the US in early 2023.
The trial in US District Court in Miami is the latest chapter in a sprawling international investigation into the July 7, 2021, killing of Moise, who was shot dead in his bedroom after armed men stormed his home near Port-au-Prince.
Among the witnesses expected to testify is Moise's widow, Martine Moise, who survived the attack.
Sanon is among dozens of people, including former Colombian soldiers, accused of carrying out and orchestrating the assassination, five of whom have already received life sentences. Prosecutors say the plot was largely organized and financed in South Florida, where Sanon lived intermittently starting in the 2000s.
Born in southern Haiti, Sanon studied medicine in the Dominican Republic before moving to Florida, according to local media outlets. He later appeared in online videos promoting himself as a potential leader who could bring change to Haiti.
Prosecutors allege Sanon helped recruit participants in the plot and hoped to become Haiti's president after Moise was removed from power. His lawyers acknowledge he had presidential ambitions but deny he was aware of the plan to kill Moise.
Several convicted defendants have pointed to Sanon as one of the ringleaders. His lawyers are expected to argue that his co-conspirators increasingly sidelined him as they turned their attention to other candidates to succeed Moise.
Authorities have said the conspiracy was driven by multiple political and financial motives, including a bid to install a new government and secure lucrative state contracts. Investigators and media reports have also linked the assassination to tensions between Moise and powerful figures allegedly connected to drug and arms trafficking.
Haiti has not had an elected president since Moise. The assassination plunged Haiti deeper into political turmoil and accelerated a security crisis that has allowed armed gangs to expand their control across much of the country.
US prosecutors initially charged Sanon with offenses related to the alleged smuggling of bulletproof vests to Haiti and later expanded the charges.
Sanon was originally expected to be the last defendant in the Miami case. But in August, US authorities charged 30 more suspects and brought 18 defendants from Haitian custody to the US.
Haiti is preparing for its first presidential election in a decade in December, but rampant gang violence and chronic corruption more than five years after Moise's assassination have cast doubts on the prospects of a credible vote. REUTERS

Adam Mubarak, Tunisian student in jail for Gaza flotilla support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:07:23 UTC
20:07:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Adam Mubarak, Tunisian student in jail for supporting Gaza Sumud Flotilla
Adam Mubarak's friends gathered outside the "Palace of Justice" awaiting the court's decision on their friend.
On 25 September, a judicial chamber at the Tunis Court of First Instance ordered 17-year-old Adam to be remanded in custody after he was detained while taking part in a solidarity march for detainees from the Gaza Sumud Flotilla on 19 September.
His case was referred to a specialised judge because he is a minor, while a hearing has been set for 6 October to consider the case again.
Tunisian activists became acquainted with Adam Mubarak through protests and civic activities, but tens of thousands of Tunisians learned about him after social media was flooded with news of his detention and imprisonment in what has become known as the case involving solidarity with detainees from the Sumud Flotilla, who have been held in prison for about seven months.
Before becoming a prisoner himself, Adam Mubarak was a third-year student at Raoued Secondary School in the suburbs of Ariana, northeast of Tunis.
He is also a prominent member of Mowfma, a youth group that has been active in cultural, artistic and field activities since its establishment in 2019, alongside its activities supporting the Palestinian cause.
Mubarak's colleagues at Mowfma said his involvement in civic activities was neither an isolated incident nor linked to the latest solidarity march with the Sumud Flotilla. They said he did not miss any of the youth group's activities and takes part in many environmental campaigns and field activities defending marginalised cities, and also supports causes that he considers part of the country's collective identity.
Mubarak's detention began after he took part in a march in the capital, Tunis, in solidarity with detained activists from the Sumud Flotilla that was trying to break the illegal Israeli blockade on Gaza.
Following the march, a campaign of arrests targeted several participants, including Mubarak.
According to a statement by Mowfma, Mubarak was detained after security forces raided his family home in the Café Amira area of Raoued. He was taken to the Aouina barracks before being held and then brought before the public prosecutor. His case was later referred to a judge for minors because he is 17, before a decision was issued to remand him in custody.
Within days, he went from being a student at a secondary school to being held in a prison for minors.
At Raoued Secondary School, news of Mubarak's detention prompted a response, with students organising a solidarity protest inside the school and holding banners calling for his release.
They chose direct slogans stressing that the school was Mubarak's natural place and that he should not be behind prison walls.
During the school protest, the banners carried by the students spotlighted Mubarak's activism, with photos of him present at many events, supporting residents of his neighbourhood in advocating for their right to live safely and protecting the area from pollution caused by sewage being discharged into the sea. Mubarak also regularly took part in community clean-up campaigns, as well as awareness campaigns about the dangers of drug addiction, which is widespread in working-class neighbourhoods.
Alongside his civic activity on environmental issues and his support for the Palestinian cause, he is also graffiti artist who expressing concerns affecting his neighbourhood and the country more broadly.
Weeks before his detention, he joined Mowfma activists in organising the "Twyza" amateur arts festival for marginalised areas.
Through the festival, the group sought to provide a platform for young, unknown talents in rap, poetry and theatre, while also organising discussions on environmental, social and economic issues affecting Raoued in particular and Tunisia more broadly.
His friends described him as a student, a friend and a young activist, labelling him as "weld el houma", a Tunisian dialect expression meaning the son of the working-class neighbourhood who cares about its problems.
For this reason, they chose to make their campaign humanitarian in its language before being political, raising the slogan that Mubarak should be returned to his home and school.
Mowfma said it was continuing to use peaceful civic means to demand Mubarak's release, while the organisation's president, Osama al-Taheri, said its members were pressing for his return to his family and school because he is a minor.
Adam Mubarak's case also reached parliament, where MP Mohamed Ali called for the immediate release of those supporting Sumud Flotilla activists and for all proceedings against them to be halted, and also called for an end to what he described as "dangerous" security practices.
The Tunisian MP wrote in a post on Facebook that "Adam Mubarak is a minor cub who should have been sitting in a classroom, not behind prison walls for legitimate and honourable actions calling for the freedom of prisoners detained in solidarity with Palestine.
"Imprisoning a minor cub is a practice that must be condemned and denounced, not only because it affects specific individuals, but because it reveals a dangerous slide towards turning expression, protest and solidarity into doors wide open to imprisonment," Ali added.

PROFILE – Who is Hassan Salameh, Palestinian prisoner threatened with execution by Israeli minister?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:06:39 UTC
20:06:39 KST

- Salameh was arrested in 1996 and Israel refused to include him in any prisoner release deals
After nearly three decades behind bars, Palestinian prisoner Hassan Salameh has returned to the spotlight after Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir published a video showing himself inside Salameh’s cell and directly threatening to kill and execute him.
Salameh appeared in the video handcuffed as Ben-Gvir told him: “I want to kill you. I want to execute you.”
The extremist Israeli minister later said that if he becomes defense minister, he would work to implement death sentences against Palestinian prisoners.
Ben-Gvir said the encounter took place around two weeks ago, while he published the video on Sunday.
The footage of Ben-Gvir inside Salameh’s cell and his death threat drew widespread Palestinian condemnation. Hamas said the Israeli minister’s death threat signaled “new killings” against prisoners.
 
Hamas affiliation
Salameh was born on Aug. 9, 1971, in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip and became involved with Hamas during the First Palestinian Intifada, which began in 1987.
He was placed in Israeli administrative detention five times during those years, according to the Palestinian Commission of Detainees’ Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society.
As the Palestinian-Israeli confrontation intensified during the intifada, Salameh became involved in Hamas’ military activities and later became one of the commanders of the Qassam Brigades, the group’s armed wing.
Palestinian sources say Salameh was close to former Qassam Brigades commander Mohammed Deif, who was killed by Israel in 2024.
His activities later extended beyond the Gaza Strip to the West Bank before Israel arrested him in Hebron in 1996 following an armed clash in which he was shot and wounded.
According to the Commission of Detainees’ Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society, Salameh underwent around four months of interrogation, during which the two organizations said he was subjected to torture.
He was sentenced in 1997 to 48 life terms, the third-highest number of life sentences imposed on a Palestinian prisoner after Abdullah Barghouti and Ibrahim Hamed.
Israel blamed Salameh for a series of attacks in 1996 following the assassination of senior Hamas commander Yahya Ayyash.
 
30 years behind bars
Salameh has spent nearly 30 years in Israeli prisons, including around 14 years in solitary confinement over two separate periods, according to the Commission of Detainees’ Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society.
His isolation ended following a hunger strike by Palestinian prisoners in 2012.
During his years in prison, Salameh’s family was able to visit him only twice, according to the same sources.
His mother, Khadija, died in March 2024 after years in which she had been denied visits with him.
In 2010, Salameh married released Palestinian prisoner Ghufran Zamel, but his family and Palestinian prisoner organizations say Israeli authorities have not allowed her to visit him since then.
Salameh’s activity in prison was not limited to organizational work, as he also turned to writing and documenting his experience in detention and solitary confinement.
Among his best-known works is “Five Thousand Days in the World of Barzakh,” which recounts his prolonged experience in isolation and has been documented by Palestinian prisoner organizations as part of Palestinian prison literature.
He also memorized the Muslim holy book, the Quran, during his imprisonment, according to Palestinian sources.
Salameh was elected several times to Hamas prisoners’ senior leadership body, which manages the movement’s organizational affairs inside Israeli prisons, according to the Prisoners’ Media Office.
 
Harsh detention conditions
In May 2025, the Prisoners’ Media Office said Salameh had been physically assaulted six times within two months and that his weight had fallen to 62 kilograms (137 pounds) because of “deliberate starvation” imposed by the prison administration under Ben-Gvir’s directives.
The Palestinian Prisoner Society documented another assault in August 2025 while Salameh was being transferred from Megiddo Prison in northern Israel to Ganot Prison in central Israel.
It said he was beaten while his hands and feet were shackled, with blows concentrated on his head.
Reports in July 2026 cited a leaked letter from Salameh from Ganot Prison in which he described food shortages, limited outdoor exercise space and deteriorating health.
He said he had been suffering from persistent diarrhea for a year and was awaiting medical examinations.
Salameh’s name has repeatedly surfaced in prisoner exchange negotiations between Hamas and Israel over the years.
During the 2011 prisoner exchange that resulted in the release of Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit in return for 1,027 Palestinian prisoners, Hamas sought to include Salameh among those released. Israel refused, and he remained among the prisoners it has consistently declined to free.
His name continued to feature in later negotiations as one of the prisoners serving lengthy sentences whose release became a sensitive issue in prisoner exchange talks.
Ben-Gvir’s threat against Salameh comes amid an escalation in Israeli measures against Palestinian prisoners and years of his advocacy for applying the death penalty against them.
Last March, the Israeli Knesset passed a law allowing the death penalty to be imposed on Palestinian prisoners by a vote of 62-48, amid support from Israeli right-wing parties.
Under the law, executions are carried out by hanging by guards appointed by the Israeli Prison Service, with their identities kept confidential and legal immunity granted to those carrying out the sentence.
The law also allows a death sentence to be issued without a request from the prosecution and does not require a unanimous decision.
The legislation drew widespread criticism and protests in several Arab and regional countries, amid calls for its repeal and for Israel to be held accountable over violations against Palestinian prisoners.

Medication mix-up led to child’s death – Latvian nurse sentenced to two and a half years in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:05:16 UTC
20:05:16 KST

Riga City Court on Monday sentenced a nurse at the Children’s Clinical University Hospital (BKUS) to two and a half years in prison after she accidentally mixed up medication intended for a patient last November, resulting in the patient’s death.
As an additional penalty, the nurse was banned from practising medicine for four years.
The court, however, decided not to award the 500,000 euros in compensation for non-pecuniary damages requested by the victims.
Judge Imants Dzenis explained that, after reviewing the case law cited by the defence, the court concluded that determining compensation for damages in these criminal proceedings could be premature. The victims will therefore retain the right to seek compensation through civil proceedings.
A representative of the defendant said the defence would consider appealing the ruling and would request the full written judgment. She stressed that legal considerations suggest that
an actual custodial sentence may not be appropriate in the defendant’s case.
The court imposed the same principal and additional penalties requested by the prosecutor during closing arguments. The prosecutor therefore currently sees no grounds to appeal the ruling, LETA was told by the Prosecutor’s Office.
The parties to the proceedings may ask the court to prepare the full judgment. Once it has been received, the ruling can be appealed within ten working days.
Information in the court calendar shows that the defendant is Jeļena Ugurenko. The nurse admits her guilt and regrets what happened, her defence lawyer Aldis Liepiņš previously told journalists.
He described the incident as a “fatal combination of circumstances” and a great tragedy. He also said that no one becomes a nurse intending for such a tragedy to occur.
According to the lawyer,
his client lives with what happened every day, has apologised to the victims, admits her guilt and regrets her actions.
Liepiņš also said that compensation for the harm caused has begun to be paid, although he did not disclose the amount.
The lawyer noted that the case also raises questions about work organisation and the storage of medicines. In his view, consideration should be given to whether dangerous medicines should be stored separately from other preparations in order to reduce the risk of similar errors in the future.
At the beginning of the first court hearing, the parties requested that subsequent proceedings be held behind closed doors. After hearing their views, the court granted the request, ruling that the case would continue to be heard in closed sessions, while the judgment would be announced at a public court hearing.
As previously reported, the nurse was charged with negligent performance of her professional duties, which resulted in the death of a minor patient due to her negligence, the Prosecutor’s Office told LETA.
According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the defendant, while working as a healthcare professional during her shift at the end of November last year, prepared a sodium bicarbonate solution prescribed by a doctor for administration to the patient the following day.
According to the indictment, while negligently performing her professional duties,
the nurse failed to ensure that the correct medication had been prepared.
When preparing the infusion bag, she used potassium chloride solution instead of sodium bicarbonate solution, but labelled the bag “Sodium bicarbonate”.
The following morning, administration of the incorrectly prepared solution to the patient began. Shortly afterwards, she began experiencing dizziness and breathing difficulties.
Despite resuscitation efforts, the patient’s life could not be saved. The administration of the potassium-containing solution caused irreversible cardiac arrest, resulting in the child’s death.
The defendant is currently subject to a preventive measure that does not involve deprivation of liberty, as well as an additional restriction prohibiting her from practising her profession.
As previously reported, following the child’s death at BKUS as a result of the medication mix-up, Health Minister Hosams Abu Meri (New Unity) ordered several investigations and inspections both at the hospital and at other medical institutions.
