19:56:56 KST

Aysu Bicer
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
UK Foreign Minister Ed Miliband on Monday called the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank “a stain on the conscience of the world.”
 
Delivering a sharp criticism at Labour’s annual conference, Miliband said the threats Israel faces “cannot justify” the actions that have followed.
 
He received a large round of applause from the conference hall as he condemned the suffering of Palestinians and set out a tougher approach towards the government of Benjamin Netanyahu.
 
"I want to say to the millions of people in this country, and indeed elsewhere, who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people, we hear you. You were right," he said.
 
He said Labour had changed its approach under Andy Burnham’s leadership, promising to challenge abuses in Gaza and the West Bank.
 
“And under Andy's leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel's illegal occupation of Palestine, and we match word with action.”
 
Miliband also announced measures targeting economic links with Israeli settlements, saying Britain would move beyond statements of condemnation.
 
“We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines for British finance, British construction, and British services for illegal settlements.”
 
His remarks amounted to one of the strongest criticisms of the Netanyahu government from the Labour leadership at the conference.
 
“And friends, our argument is not with the people of Israel, but with the actions of its government,” he said.
 
Miliband also warned against efforts to undermine the prospect of a Palestinian state alongside Israel, saying Labour would oppose moves that threaten the two-state solution.
 
“And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government said we will not let you succeed.”
 
- 'Survivor’s responsibility'
 
Miliband also spoke about his parents and the values they passed on to him, referring to what he called a “survivor’s responsibility.”
 
“My parents didn’t just observe a country fighting for values. They taught me that I have a responsibility to fight for them too,” he said.
 
He said that responsibility meant leaving the world better for future generations and never standing by in the face of oppression and injustice.
 
“Not me, not you, not us,” Miliband said, rejecting the idea that people necessarily become more cynical with age.
 
He promised to defend what he described as “Labour values, Britain’s values” throughout his time as foreign secretary.
 
- Closer partnership with Europe
 
Miliband also called for a closer relationship between Britain and the European Union.
 
“We are part of this fight as humanitarians, but also as proud Europeans. This is our continent,” he said.
 
He argued that Europe was central to Britain’s values, interests and alliances, from climate policy and the Middle East to trade, defense and security.
 
“So it is not simply Britain acting alone, but Britain with others,” he said. “Our future lies in a stronger, deeper partnership with the European Union."

Preferential gas prices will effectively be maintained until the end of the heating season - what to expect next
Kyiv • UNN
Preferential gas prices for households and heat suppliers will remain unchanged until March 31, 2027. The government is preparing a new tariff policy.
In Ukraine, the government’s decision has preserved the current preferential gas prices until the end of spring 2027—effectively until the end of the heating season—but work is under way to change the tariff policy system. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this on social media on September 28, UNN writes.
The government has maintained the current preferential gas prices for households and heat producers until March 31, effectively until the end of the heating season
According to him, this decision was made while the moratorium on tariff increases, introduced by parliament for the duration of martial law, remains in effect, and "taking into account the difficult socioeconomic situation in the country."
According to First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal, this means that "the government has extended the Public Service Obligation (PSO) in the natural gas market until March 31, 2027."
"For households, this means that the gas price will remain unchanged throughout the entire autumn-winter period. It will also make it possible to preserve preferential tariffs for heat supply companies, extend the terms for the sale of natural gas to gas distribution system operators and for cogeneration in frontline areas," Shmyhal explained.
What will happen to tariffs next
To fulfill its commitments to international partners, the government, together with other authorities, is working to improve the tariff policy system and introduce fair and transparent tariff-setting, while simultaneously increasing targeted assistance for those who genuinely need it

Turkey: Comedian convicted for 'insulting' Erdogan in show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:52:00 UTC
19:52:00 KST

Turkey: Comedian convicted for 'insulting' Erdogan in show
September 28, 2026
A Turkish comedian was convicted in Istanbul on Monday on charges of "insulting" President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and "insulting religious values" during a stand-up performance in June.
The judge provisionally sentenced Deniz Goktas to 19 months in prison, but ordered his release pending the judicial review and appeal process that would finalized the verdict.
It was not immediately clear how long this process might take.
NATO member and EU aspirant Turkey routinely tries people on speech-related offenses, particularly and famously when it comes to supposed "insults" of its longserving leader Erdogan.
What was the case about?
Deniz Goktas, 32, was arrested on July 3, a week after releasing a YouTube video of his show that was watched nearly 9 million times and a few days after shorter clips he posted on X enjoyed similar rapid success.
He faced an array of charges related to content in his "Dead Sea" show. Goktas referred to his impending court appointment online on Sunday, in one of his irreverent social media posts from his cell.
Goktas was accused of insulting Erdogan, of inciting public hatred and hostility — via jokes about Islam — and of praising crime and criminals, an additional charge added by prosecutors tied to a joke about an organized crime family, the Daltons
His trial is the latest in a widening crackdown on people seen as critical of Turkey's moderate Islamist government. Hundreds of politicians, artists, musicians, journalists and LGBTQ activists are among those to face detention or trial.
What did Goktas say in his defense in court?
Goktas did not dispute the content from his popular show, but did argue in court that he had committed no crimes with his jokes.
Prosecutors had for instance singled out a pair of references he made to President Erdogan as a "dictator" as illegal insults.
"Dictator is not an insult: it is a political characterization," Goktas told the court. "As the president and leader of the party that has ruled the country for 25 years, a political comedy show in which Erdogan's name is never mentioned would be neither sincere nor have any connection to reality."
He said that Erdogan should be "open to the art of satire," as he said past presidents in Turkish democracy were.
"The joke hasn't changed. What has changed is the increasingly fragile leadership that can no longer tolerate the joke," he said.
The judge nevertheless convicted Gotkas of insulting Erdogan, and downgraded the charge he faced of "inciting hatred and hostility" with jokes about Islam, instead convicting him of the lesser supposed crime of "insulting religious values."
He cleared the comedian of the third charge of allegedly praising criminality.
Goktas has spent just under three months in pretrial detention, which should count as time served in any potential custodial sentence.
Erdogan the only claimant, Diyanet religious authority among those to complain
According to the Turkish NGO the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA), prosecutors cited more than 500 applications to prosecute the performer regarding the show.
They were issued to the Presidential Communication Center that monitors such issues. One of the groups to provide a tipoff was the government-sponsored Presidency of Religious affairs, better known as Diyanet.
Erdogan, in charge of Turkey either as prime minister or later president since 2003, was named as the sole complainant.
His government has attracted attention in recent years for its prosecution of people deemed to have unfairly criticized the authorities, and for the various lawsuits against leading members of the opposition, particularly the CHP. The Turkish president's litigious streak also became headline news in Germany around a decade ago, when he pursued star TV comedian Jan Böhmermann.
Meanwhile the MLSA said that Goktas' jokes alleged to have the potential to "publicly incite hatred and hostility" took aim at fundamentalist Islam, including a reference to women in full-coverage swimsuits being "divers" and joking about "suicide bombers who fast."
Turkey nominally has a secular constitution and guarantees of free speech. However, the EU and the US have often criticized its application of these standards.
The US Commission on International Religious Freedom wrote in a 2022 report that Erdogan's government increasingly relied on speech-based prosecution to "silence individuals who express criticism in religious terms, disclose beliefs or a lack thereof that differ from those of the majority of the population, or engage with religion in a way perceived as 'mocking' or 'irreverent.'"
Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

Paying tribute to martyr Seyyed Hassan Nasrallah on the second anniversary of his martyrdom, the Leader described him as a prominent figure of the resistance front and a sincere advocate of the Lebanese people and the cause he represented.

As far as Moscow is aware, China has not changed its position on the issue of arms control and has not planned to participate in such Russian-American arrangements, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said at a briefing, commenting on Washington's desire to reach a trilateral agreement in this sphere.

Russia proposed continuing to observe New START limits for another year after the treaty’s expiration, but received no official response from Washington regarding this initiative. Regarding a new agreement, Moscow noted that it would require further coordination and negotiations, and that it must account not only for Russian and US arsenals but also for the nuclear weapons of US European allies - the UK and France. As for China’s participation, Russia maintains that this is a matter for Beijing to decide and respects whatever decision the Chinese side makes.

Arctic Floating University anticipates Professor Molchanov vessel's return to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:48:24 UTC
19:48:24 KST

ARKHANGELSK, September 28. /TASS/. Specialists of the Arctic Floating University anticipate the Professor Molchanov scientific-research vessel's return to Russia, the University's leader, Director of the Lomonosov Arctic Northern Federal University's Strategic Development Institute Alexander Saburov told TASS.
"The Professor Molchanov is an optimal vessel for complex Arctic scientific expeditions, such as the Arctic Floating University Expedition," the scientist said. "She has a remarkable combination of comfortable accommodation on board for up to 55 expedition members, laboratory facilities for various types of work, as well as cranes and winches necessary for conducting research. The vessel's ice class provides for confident work in the Barents Sea and in most waters of the Northern Sea Route during summer and autumn navigation. The Professor Molchanov is convenient also in terms of conducting ground research, as it offers conditions to organize quickly landings by using small vessels. And finally, over the years of the Arctic Floating University, we have built cooperation with the ship's crew, who know and understand very well what the expedition needs."
The Arctic Floating University is the only annual expedition that operates in the northeastern part of the Barents Sea and in the territory of the Russian Arctic National Park during the spring and summer period. Thus, researchers have been accumulating unique data series on this important part of the Russian Arctic.
In 2021, the Arctic Floating University gained successful experience working onboard the Mikhail Somov scientific expedition vessel, where the main advantage is that the vessel has an option to have a helicopter on board, the expedition leader said. By using it, the expedition is able to organize landings even in conditions of unrest at sea, when using boats is not possible.
"It is necessary to take into account that every year the Mikhail Somov works on a tight schedule, delivering supplies to polar stations located from the White Sea to Chukotka. Another aspect is the higher level of cost to use such a big vessel for our expeditions. We very much hope for a successful settlement of the situation and that the Professor Molchanov returns most promptly to Russia, but anyway we will eye all possible alternatives to continue voyages of the Arctic Floating University," the expedition leader said in conclusion.
About the expedition
The 20th voyage of the Arctic Floating University scientific and educational expedition continued from July 1 to July 22, 2026 on board the Professor Molchanov scientific research vessel. The expedition organizers are: the Lomonosov Northern Arctic Federal University and the Northern Department for Hydrometeorology and Environmental Monitoring (Sevhydromet). The project's official sponsors and partners are: the Russian Federation's Ministry of Science and Higher Education, the Russian Geographical Society, general sponsor - VTB, the Norilsk Nickel Company, and the Floating University Coordination Center based at the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (MIPT).

====================================================================================================

Russia plans seven new 'superprisons' despite war recruitment emptying its jails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:48:15 UTC
19:48:15 KST

Seven complexes holding more than 20,000 inmates are planned for 2035, including one in Russian-occupied Kherson, even as the prison population has dropped from 465,000 to 282,000 since 2021, largely because inmates have been recruited as contract soldiers for the war in Ukraine.
Russia plans to build seven large prison complexes by 2035 that will house both remand centres and penitentiary colonies, under a government decree amending the federal programme for the development of the penal system.
The facilities, which Russian journalists have called "superprisons," will together hold more than 20,000 people, 5,380 on remand and 15,120 convicted prisoners.
They will also include courtrooms and offices for prosecutors, defence lawyers and public monitoring commissions. The government plans to use surveillance and security technology throughout.
The complexes are planned for the Kaluga, Astrakhan and Tyumen regions, Buryatia and Zabaikalsky Krai, and the part of Ukraine's Kherson region currently under Russian military occupation.
The first facility is due to open in Tatarstan by 2030. Preliminary estimates put the cost of a single complex at between 13 billion and 20 billion roubles (€134 million and €208 million), with the total programme cost expected to exceed 230 billion roubles (€2.4 billion), according to Russian media reports.
Russia's Justice Ministry says consolidating remand and penal functions in single facilities will cut the cost of holding prisoners by 25–30% and allow the investment to pay for itself within 10 years, mainly by eliminating prisoner transfer costs and reducing staffing requirements.
The planned construction follows a sharp fall in the prison population. At the end of 2021, Russia held 465,000 people in detention but by 2026, that figure had dropped to 282,000 — a decline of nearly 40%.
Head of the Federal Penitentiary Service Arkady Gostev said in May that recruitment of prisoners as contract soldiers for Russia's war in Ukraine had contributed significantly to the reduction.
The recruitment of inmates began in the summer of 2022 — right after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February of the same year — initially through the Kremlin-run paramilitary Wagner Group and later through the Defence Ministry directly.
Law experts have criticised the plans. They said internal rules at the new facilities were likely to remain unchanged or become more restrictive, and that relocating prisons from city centres to remote sites — particularly in Buryatia and Zabaikalsky Krai — would make it substantially harder for relatives, human rights activists and legal representatives to reach those held inside.
Torture of inmates prevalent
Russia's prison system has faced persistent criticism from international human rights bodies for conditions that fall below international standards.
The UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Russia found in a 2025 report that torture remained "systematic and widespread," with 258 documented cases in 2024-2025. Common methods documented included electric shocks, beatings and mock executions.
The UN Human Rights Council, following a universal periodic review of Russia in 2024, called on Moscow to make torture a standalone criminal offence, strengthen investigation of reported cases and align its legal framework with the UN Convention Against Torture. Russia rejected the majority of those recommendations.
Human Rights Watch documented in 2024 that Russian authorities tortured suspects detained in connection with the Crocus City Hall attack near Moscow in March of that year, recorded the sessions and circulated the footage.
An OSCE monitoring mission found conditions in Russian detention facilities frequently included overcrowding, unsanitary facilities, inadequate food and medical care, and forced labour.
Alexei Navalny died in February 2024 in a remote Arctic penal colony where he was serving a 19-year sentence. The prison was reported by Russian independent media as known for harsh conditions and alleged torture.
Russia formally withdrew from the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture in September 2025 following its expulsion from the Council of Europe, ending monitoring visits to Russian prisons by European inspectors.
The UN Special Rapporteur also documented a revival of punitive psychiatry, including the use of compulsory psychiatric treatment as a sentencing tool against those prosecuted for anti-war expression.

US and China name goods for possible tariff cuts – what it means for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:48:10 UTC
19:48:10 KST

Washington has published lists of goods the US and China could tax at lower rates under their "30-for-30" framework, covering about $30bn (€26.3bn) in annual trade each way. No rates or start date have been set, but US pork, dairy and whiskey on Beijing's list could squeeze European exports.
Washington and Beijing have now detailed the plan for which goods stand to gain from the trade deal struck at last week's summit between US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.
China's list runs to 1,619 categories of American products, while the US list contains 77 categories of Chinese goods, but neither side has said how deep the cuts will be or when they will apply.
The two countries will consider the products "with a view toward providing reduced tariff treatment to those goods in a reciprocal manner," the White House stated.
The lists were drawn up by the US-China Board of Trade, a body set up during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May after months of discussions, to manage trade in goods both sides consider non-sensitive.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the two countries "have recommended $30 billion (€26.3bn) of trade in non-sensitive goods on each side that could benefit from more favourable tariff treatment in the future."
Xi wrapped up his three-day visit to Washington on Friday, when the White House announced that the two sides had agreed on "recommendations" for "non-sensitive goods."
Beijing confirmed the arrangement on Saturday.
The announcement builds on a trade truce agreed in South Korea last October, after the US and China imposed tariffs of more than 100% on each other’s goods.
That pact was due to expire in November, but following the summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed it has been extended to 10 January.
Meat, whiskey and medical devices
China's list is dominated by food and farm goods, from beef, pork, poultry and seafood to cheese, butter, grains, wine and whiskey.
It also features coal and nearly 150 wood and timber products. Beijing has committed to importing at least 10 million metric tonnes of US coal in 2027 and 2028.
Beyond agriculture, it covers medical equipment such as MRI scanners, pacemakers, stents and surgical robots. However, soybeans, the biggest US farm export to China, appear only as seeds for planting.
"From agricultural products to medical devices, President Trump is unlocking improved market access for about 30% of US exports to China, while benefiting consumers with imports from China of household goods, toys, and other products that the United States generally does not import from other countries," Greer stated.
The far shorter US list centres on consumer goods, including fireworks, glass and wooden Christmas ornaments, Christmas-tree lights, microwave ovens, toasters, coffee makers, bed linen, tennis balls and fishing hooks.
Toys are included, but not those enabled with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet or radio-frequency connections.
What it could mean for Europe
Pork is where European exporters could feel the greatest effect of any tariff cuts.
The EU shipped around 1.07 million tonnes of pork to China in 2025, roughly a quarter of its exports outside the bloc, with Spain, the Netherlands and Denmark as the biggest suppliers, according to S&P Global data.
The European Commission has also previously recognised that China is a major destination for EU pork exports.
However, EU pork has faced Chinese anti-dumping duties of 4.9% to 19.8% since December, so any tariff cut for American rivals could put European producers at a price disadvantage.
Dairy faces a similar risk, as China has applied anti-subsidy duties of 7.4% to 11.7% on some EU cheese and cream since February. US wine and whiskey could also compete more strongly with French, Italian and Spanish wines, as well as Irish whiskey and Scotch.
The effect could run the other way too.
Cheaper Chinese household goods, toys and sports equipment in the US could make it harder for European makers of similar products to compete there.
All of this hinges on the size and timing of the cuts, which neither side has yet set out.

Nvidia launches platform to quarantine rogue AI agents in 'milliseconds'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:46:44 UTC
19:46:44 KST

The platform is designed to control what an agent can access and isolate it within milliseconds if it crosses those limits, according to the US chipmaker.
Nvidia is rolling out a security platform for artificial intelligence (AI) agents that more than 100 organisations are working with, including Anthropic, SpaceXAI and JPMorganChase.
Called the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform, it is designed to set limits on what agents can access and put them in “quarantine” within milliseconds if they cross those limits, according to an announcement from the US chipmaker.
The platform can be used across software and hardware, compute and robotics systems that run agents.
“AI’s extraordinary potential for society will only be realised if we solve AI safety,” said Jensen Huang, the CEO and founder of Nvidia.
“As we continue to discover the frontier of AI capabilities, we must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety…. Together, we can raise the bar for global AI safety.”
The Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform consists of two tools, OpenShell and Sentry.
OpenShell runs on central processing units (CPUs), the chips that handle many of the tasks needed to run AI agents. Nvidia says it works efficiently on Vera, its latest CPU designed for AI agents, and can also be adapted for chips made by other companies.
Sentry is an additional "watchdog" system that would run on a separate Nvidia chip, watching for agents that get past the software’s controls.
The organisations working with Nvidia are using or developing the technology in different ways, Nvidia says.
Anthropic has worked with Nvidia to add security controls to its Claude service for businesses to run AI agents, allowing companies to restrict what those agents can access.
SpaceX’s AI division, SpaceXAI, says it is using the platform for Cursor coding agents and Grok models, while Salesforce has integrated OpenShell with Slack so teams can see what agents are doing and approve or reject requests for additional permissions.
In finance, JPMorganChase and Citi are collaborating with Nvidia on shared open-source agent safety technology.
AI companies call for stronger safeguards
The announcement comes amid growing calls for stronger safeguards around AI agents.
In July, OpenAI admitted one of its models exploited a hidden flaw to escape a controlled test and break into Hugging Face's servers.
Meanwhile, Anthropic said its AI model hacked into three organisations' systems during the testing phase.
Nvidia said the incidents showed that agents could get around security controls built into an app while trying to complete their assigned tasks and that “safety and security require full-stack engineering”.

AAP donations drop 68%; firm founded by ex-MP who joined BJP had given Rs 5 crore
NEW DELHI: The Arvind Kejriwal-led Aam Aadmi Party received Rs 12.10 crore in contributions in 2025-26, a 68% drop from the previous financial year, according to its latest report filed with the Election Commission.Nearly 83% of the party's contributions came from two donors, Prudent Electoral Trust and Trident Limited. Trident was founded by former AAP Rajya Sabha member Rajinder Gupta.The remaining contributions amounted to around Rs 2.10 crore, according to the report.Gupta was elected to the Rajya Sabha on an AAP ticket in October 2025. Price of diesel on UK forecourts reaches all-time high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:45:36 UTC
19:45:36 KST

The price of diesel on UK forecourts has hit an all-time high average of 199.18p a litre, as the conflict in the Middle East continues to drive the cost of fuel to record levels.
The price, which previously peaked at 199.09p in June 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, could soon top the £2 mark after Donald Trump rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day peace deal to reopen the critical oil and gas shipping route through the strait of Hormuz.
The RAC estimates that the cost of filling an average family car with diesel is now almost £110, £31 more than it was at the start of the Iran war, a rise of 40% since 28 February.
“The diesel price has entered new uncharted territory,” said Simon Williams, the head of policy at the motoring organisation.
“This spells pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans. Undoubtedly, these increased costs will be passed on to consumers.”
The cost of petrol is also continuing to rise, with the average price of a litre hitting 174.13p on average, 41p more than at the start of the war and an increase of 31% since 28 February. The cost of filling a full tank is nearly £96, according to the RAC.
Trump has said he is “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices.
Output from Russia’s war-damaged refineries has fallen by almost a third over the past year to reach a 20-year low following sustained drone attacks by Ukraine, according to the International Energy Agency.
“The consequences [of soaring fuel prices] could reach almost every part of UK economic life: supermarkets, manufacturing, construction, agriculture, e-commerce and countless other sectors that depend upon road freight,” said Dr Jonathan Owens, an operations and supply chain expert at the University of Salford.
“So, a geopolitical event and potential policy decision thousands of miles away can travel rapidly through our supply chain: from a refinery to a tanker, to a UK haulier, to a distribution centre, to a supermarket shelf, and ultimately, the price will be paid by the consumer.”
The RAC urged the government, which has extended the 5p cut in fuel duty until the end of the year, to consider expanding the discount or reducing VAT to help motorists at the pump.
“As things stand, another 5p a litre will be loaded on to pump prices by the spring if the current fuel duty cut is fully reversed as planned,” said Williams. “VAT receipts from fuel are also extremely high.”
Before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel.
It hit a peak of $126 a barrel in April, before dipping to $71 at the start of July on hopes of a peace deal. The price of oil climbed by more than 2% on Monday to $106.5.
In August, the Competition and Markets Authority published a report that found that many petrol stations were too slow to pass on falls in wholesale energy prices to their customers.
The UK competition watchdog said that, while costs overall fell at fuel pumps in June, prices remained significantly higher than before the Middle East conflict, and retailer profit margins were either at or above the historically high levels of 2025.
However, it did not find any evidence of profiteering by fuel retailers on the back of the Iran conflict.
“These extraordinarily high prices are another reminder of just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away from its shores,” said Williams. “Only a sustained lower oil price – over several weeks, not days – will lead to cheaper prices at the pumps.”
A government scheme called Fuel Finder allows drivers to compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK.

MOSCOW, September 28. /TASS/. Rosneft received the highest scientific and technical development rating from the AK&M Agency, the company said. The rating was assigned in compliance with the Methods for determining scientific and technological development rating of biggest Russian companies.

During the study, the agency assessed the country's 300 biggest enterprises using criteria like investment in R&D, patent activity, as well as own research units, and partnerships with scientific organizations.
The company's priorities
According to Rosneft, the company's key priorities in scientific and technical development under the Rosneft-2030 Strategy are operational leadership, large-scale digitalization, and the creation of innovative technologies. Technologies' localization and import substitution are part of the strategy. "The company has achieved a level of innovation development that allows introducing domestic technologies and equipment that surpass their foreign counterparts," Rosneft added.

In particular, Rosneft has been actively developing digital twin technologies. An attempt was made to post bail of more than UAH 3 million for Iryna Mudra, but the payments did not go through
Kyiv • UNN
Witnesses stated that the bail payments for Iryna Mudra through Monobank and PrivatBank did not go through. The lawyers accuse the banks of blocking them.
During the hearing in the case of Iryna Mudra, witnesses spoke about attempts to post bail for her; however, the payments through Monobank and PrivatBank were not processed. This was reported by a UNN journalist from the courtroom at the High Anti-Corruption Court.
Details
One of the witnesses, Andrii Smyk, said during questioning in court that he had decided to help Iryna Mudra secure release on bail. According to him, he received her husband’s bank details and tried to deposit the bail money from different accounts.
He said that on September 21 he tried to deposit UAH 50,000 through Monobank. According to him, the funds were not even debited, and the bank reported a problem with the IBAN. Smyk also said that he contacted PrivatBank.
"I called them—they said that they would not carry out any transactions to this IBAN," the man noted.
At the same time, the man was ready to contribute a considerable amount toward Iryna Mudra’s bail.
"On average, I was ready to contribute around 3 million," the witness said.
In addition, another witness—a private entrepreneur who had also tried to contribute part of Iryna Mudra’s bail—was questioned during the hearing.
"I decided to help—that is my motive. A friendly motive. I was raised this way—to help friends," the witness said.
According to the woman, she communicated with Mudra’s husband and offered her assistance. She said she could contribute up to UAH 700,000.
"I told him that within the amount of UAH 700,000, that is, about 16,000 dollars, I would be able to make such a payment," the woman emphasized.
She tried to make the payment through the Privat24 app. According to her, after entering the bank details, she received a notification that the payment had been accepted for processing.
"Then, four hours later, I received a notification saying that, unfortunately, the payment had been rejected. The details of either the recipient or the sender need to be clarified," the witness said.
She noted that after the payment was rejected, she checked the details again.
"As an accountant with 10 years of experience, I know for sure that I entered the details correctly, but just in case I checked them, and moreover, I sent them to my personal manager, and she did not find any error in my details," the witness said.
However, according to her, the payment was still not approved.
"My personal manager told me that, unfortunately, under the bank’s rules and terms, this payment would not be processed," she added.
In addition, Iryna Mudra’s lawyers also claim that the bank is blocking the account because of the payment purpose related to posting bail. Because of this, they say, the former official is currently unable to pay the bail.
The hearing is being held in a mixed format, while Iryna Mudra is participating in the hearing online
The court plans to hold the final two segments in closed session because they concern materials related to the former official’s child.
Background
The HACC investigating judge upheld Iryna Mudra’s defense complaint regarding violations of her rights while she was being held in custody, so the court ordered the NBU to investigate possible refusals to process payments for posting bail for the former official.

The Hong Kong government has appointed Bryan Chan Ping-keung, a former executive at bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), as CEO to lead the development and operation of the city’s new central clearing and settlement system for gold.
Chan will head Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing (HKPMCC), a wholly government-owned entity established in January to run the clearing system for precious metals. His appointment would take effect on October 2 for a three-year term, according to a statement released on Monday.
Chan would be expected to deliver efficient and reliable clearing and settlement services for over-the-counter gold transactions, work closely with industry participants and collaborate with the government to build an international-standard gold trading ecosystem, the government said.
Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu, who is also chairman of HKPMCC, expressed confidence in Chan’s leadership.

Three people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:40:24 UTC
19:40:24 KST

A 10-year-old child and two women died attempting to cross the Channel on Monday, French authorities have said.
Their deaths and the injuries of dozens of others in a large dinghy were probably caused by crushing, according to a French official.
France’s maritime police said they received a distress call in the early hours from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people that had run into trouble in calm seas.
The three passengers were treated onboard but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter.
François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, told a press conference: “Apparently there was no drowning, it was likely crushing – which is just as dreadful, especially if we think of the 10-year-old child.”
The incident happened off the coast of Wissant, a village about 14 miles (23km) from Calais.
A spokesperson for the local prefecture confirmed “a provisional total of three deaths and many more injured”, adding that “sea conditions were calm – the weather is good”. The prefecture described the boat as a “water taxi”, saying it had arrived relatively empty from an inland waterway before picking up passengers from the beach at Wissant.
At 10.30am local time (9.30am UK time) six rescue boats were still at the scene searching for people in the water.
At least 17 people, including women and children, have died in the Channel this year while attempting to reach the UK. Many have drowned, while others have died in incidents involving overcrowded boats.
Three bodies were found last week after chaotic “water taxi” departures of this kind in northern France.
So far this year, 18,609 people have made the Channel crossing – more than 40% fewer than at the same point last year. The number is also more than 25% lower than at this stage in 2024, when 25,165 people had crossed the Channel.
Last week there were two uncontrolled landings in the UK, where dinghies arrived without being intercepted by authorities.
It comes as more than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died while attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands by sea in August.
On Monday, a rescue boat arrived at the port of Calais in the mid-morning, where it began disembarking people rescued from the accident. A coach, fire service and police vehicles were deployed at the scene.
The northern beaches of France have become a key crossing point for people without visas hoping to cross the Channel. They pay people smugglers to board unstable rubber dinghies to make the journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.
At least 29 people lost their lives last year trying to cross the Channel, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official French and British sources.
Official figures cited by the UN refugee agency, the UNHCR, show irregular migration to the EU – notably via Mediterranean sea routes – has plummeted since its peak during the 2015 refugee crisis.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will on Monday announce the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK as she says “fairness” is at the heart of her vision for the Home Office. It will come as she focuses on safe and legal refugee routes to the UK in her Labour party conference speech.
The UK resettlement scheme will reopen immediately, with about a quarter of those admitted to the UK under it expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan.
UK government sources said officials were aware of the fatalities.

Ukraine outfoxes Russia near Donetsk’s fortress belt with Soviet BTR-60s rebuilt as kamikaze robots, storms a key hub and takes 250 Russian prisoners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:40:09 UTC
19:40:09 KST

Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps has defeated Russia at the key settlement of Nove in Donetsk Oblast by pointing it the wrong way. Russia has poured its reserves into counterattacks on a feint axis and "slept through" the real strike, which took the important hub in the village and closed the decisive third season of the Vivaldi offensive, commander Andrii Biletskyi said.
Vivaldi is Ukraine's counteroffensive aimed at disrupting Russian forces' plans to encircle the fortress-belt cities in Donetsk Oblast from the north and south. Among them are Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka. These cities have helped hold back Russian forces since 2014.
Over its first two "seasons," the 3rd Army Corps and attached units have retaken more than 125 square kilometers, half of it de-occupied outright, and inflicted more than 3,000 casualties on Russian forces.
The operation in Nove was its "third season," Biletskyi said, the turning point of the whole operation. The corps liberated Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka and restored control of Karpivka and Novomykhailivka, adding 51 square kilometers to the 176 that had been liberated since the offensive began. Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russians captive.
The feint drew Russia's reserves
The victory, by Biletskyi's account, was won by deception.
"The enemy was convinced the main direction of the strike was Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna," he revealed, and it burned its reserves counterattacking there.
He added that the Russians slept through the real strike, which was concentrated on taking Nove. The village was the prize, a key Russian hub on the bridgehead, ringed by heights that command the surrounding ground.
"Who controls the heights holds the initiative," Biletskyi said.
By spending its reserves on the wrong axis, he suggested, Russia had little left to hold Nove when the real assault arrived.
Old APCs crack the defense
To break the strongest fortifications, the corps said, it used a homemade weapon: Soviet BTR-60 armored carriers converted into remote-controlled kamikaze robots, driven into Russia's toughest positions and detonated.
In 2024, the Ukrainian forces received another local upgrade of the post-Soviet BTR-60 wheeled armored personnel carrier. This time it was fitted with the BM-7 "Parus" turret, known from the BTR-4 "Bucephalus" The main armament consisted of a 30 mm ZTM-1 automatic cannon paired with a 7.62 mm KT-7.62 universal machine gun.
Additional armament might include a set of four anti-tank guided missile launchers mounted on the sides, or two launchers and a 30 mm KBA-117 automatic grenade launcher. As a result, this upgraded BTR-60 saw a significant improvement in firepower, although the vehicle still has very weak armor and less-than-optimal access to the troop compartment.
It was the latest of the corps' robotic improvisations in Vivaldi, which have included air-dropped ground drones and Bullspike grenade-launcher-armed UGVs. They are Bulgarian hand-held, rocket-propelled anti-tank grenade launchers based on the Soviet RPG-22, which the Bulgarian defense industry previously produced under license.
The corps has leaned on such machines throughout the operation to keep its infantry out of the deadliest fights.
Whole units surrender
As the defense broke down, Russians gave up in groups, including officers, pilots, and artillery soldiers, the corps said. The 3rd Assault Brigade carried much of the fighting, while the 3rd Border Guard Detachment, named for the fallen Colonel Yevhen Pikus, retook Ridkodub and dug in on the new line, with the 10th Mobile Border Guard Detachment "DOZOR" taking an active part in the assault.

Market watchdog calls for transparency on AI in price setting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:39:31 UTC
19:39:31 KST

Market watchdog calls for transparency on AI in price setting
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch consumer markets authority ACM has called for more transparency on the role of AI in setting ticket prices after an investigation found wide discrepancies in the amounts charged for airline tickets.
The ACM said some airline seats had 35 different prices, while one-third of tickets cost 40% more than the average price, but there was no easy way for passengers to find the cheapest fare.
ACM chairman Martijn Snoep said the investigation into airline tickets was relevant because “similar techniques are being applied in other sectors”. Online retailers, concert ticket sites and even petrol stations are also using AI to set prices.
Commercial companies are using AI to drive dynamic pricing, based on supply and demand and competitors’ rates, but customers are unable to see how the prices are set.
Sometimes two people looking at the same product at the same time can be charged different prices, the ACM said. The impact of AI also means consumers spend longer searching for the best deal.
“We expect that AI and the availability of data means companies will increasingly use computer-aided prices, including personalised prices,” Snoep said.
The ACM has called on companies to be more open about how they set their prices and explain what factors influence the algorithms.
“Transparency is necessary so we can have a public debate about the desirability and the consequences of this development and how we want to proceed, keeping an eye on the way markets function and preventing people’s vulnerabilities being abused.”

Impressionist masters and deranged diggers: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:38:42 UTC
19:38:42 KST

Tom Cruise gives his zaniest performance yet in dark comedy 'Digger', The Smiths' Johnny Marr returns with his 10th album, and new exhibitions spotlight Renoir and Monet. Here's what to look out for this week.
The evening's are growing darker and the urge to hibernate is getting stronger, but thankfully there's plenty ahead to keep you venturing out into the world.
Major new exhibitions in Paris and London focus on two of the world's most famous impressionist painters, Monet and Renoir, while Tom Cruise stars as an eccentric oil tycoon with a hero complex in Digger.
There's also new music from former The Smiths' member Johnny Marr, and a crime drama starring Catherine Zeta-Jones as a drug dealer-turned-art dealer on a mission to take down some hit men.
Keep scrolling to find out more...
Exhibitions and events
Renoir and Love
When: 2 October 2026 - 31 January 2027
Where: The National Gallery (London, UK)
From his iconic 'Bal au Moulin de la Galette' to 'The Umbrellas', over 50 of Renoir's works are on display at this vast new retrospective — the most significant on UK soil in 20 years. The French impressionist became a pioneer of the loose brushstroke technique, especially adept at capturing the fleeting emotions between people in public. The National GalleryUtilising loands from museums across the glove, The National Gallery traces Renoir's themes, techniques and career evolutions — focused on his output between the mid-1860s to the mid-1880s. Find out more here.
The Monet: Painting Time
When: 30 September 2026 - 25 January 2027
Where: Musée de l'Orangerie (Paris, France)
Marking the centenary of Claude Monet's death, 'Painting Time' is a riveting retrospective that explores the impressionist artist's relationship with time. Known for his loose brushstrokes and remarkable ability to capture shifting light, Monet's paintings have always had a sense of momentum; of capturing a world that's always transitioning, even when frozen. The exhibition re-evaluates Monet's works through this angle, featuring almost forty paintings from collections across the world — some of which have rarely been seen before. Co-organised by the Tate, the exhibition also acts as a precursor to a London presentation that opens in February next year. Find out more here.
Bonus highlight: The Design Museum in London will present the largest solo presentation of British artist Es Devlin's works from 2 October unti 4 April 2027.
Movies
Digger
Where: Cinemas
When: 2 October
A little bit There Will Be Blood, a little bit Dr. Strangelove, and a hole lot of absurd! Digger is the new satirical comedy from Mexican filmmaker Alejandro G. Iñárritu (Birdman). It stars Tom Cruise (in even heavier prosthetics than Tropic Thunder) as an eccentric oil tycoon, whose drilling operations in Greenland have caused a global environmental disaster. Instead of doing what most billionaires would likely do — hiding in a bunker and denying all responsibility — he takes on the role of humanity's saviour and heads out on a bombastic rescue mission. Supported by a stacked cast that includes Sandra Hüller, Riz Ahmed, John Goodman and Jesse Plemons, Cruise gives what looks to be his zaniest (and sure-to-be Oscar-nominated) performance yet. Stay tuned for our full review on Friday.
Bonus highlight: Dakota Johnson, Josh Hartnett and Anne Hathaway star in a big screen adaptation of Colleen Hoover's Verity, a saucy thriller about a ghostwriter sent to finish a best-selling author's books. Out in most cinemas from 2 October.
TV series
Kill Jackie
Where: Prime Video
When: 2 October
Catherine Zeta-Jones stars in Kill Jackie, a pulpy thriller series based on Nick Harkaway's novel The Price You Pay. It follows a wealthy art dealer named Jackie Price, whose glamorous life conceals a criminal past — one she must revive resources from when a squad of hitmen target her. It's glossy, goofy action that's ideal for autumn escapism — or those that just want to watch a glammed-up and potty-mouthed Zeta-Jones in her element.
Bonus highlight: HBO's new legal drama, War, stars Dominic West and Sienna Miller as a high-profile couple caught up in a monstrous divorce. Stream it on Sky/Now from 2 October.
Music
Johnny Marr: The Age Of Everything
When: 2 October
British musician Johnny Marr, who was formerly a lead guitarist for The Smiths, is releasing his fifth solo studio album. It follows 2022's 'Fever Dreams Pts 1–4' and reflects on this era of hyper-connectivity. Through Marr's charismatic acoustics, soaring "ooohs" and introspective lyrics, the album jitters with a kinetic energy that attempts to mirror the constant, overwhelming changes happening all around us. While tracks like 'Just Once More', meet this idea with some anxiety, others, like 'All In A Life', find calm in routine. But throughout, there's the sense that Marr is holding listeners's hands through the storms of contemporary life, reminding them to pause in awe occasionally.
Bonus highlight: American country singer Miranda Lambert returns with her 10th studio album, 'Crisco', on 2 October.

The convoy, led by the Nachala Settlement Movement alongside other right-wing groups, was heading to a gathering point in northern Gaza before a rally near the enclave's northern border.

Since Israel began its war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023, the Israeli army and occupiers have stepped up attacks in the West Bank, killing over 1,206 Palestinians, injuring more than 13,300 and arresting nearly 26,000, according to Palestinian figures.
The attacks include demolishing homes and other structures, burning mosques, bulldozing farmland, preventing farmers from accessing their land, displacing Palestinians and expanding illegal settlements.
Over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 others in Israel's genocidal war in Gaza since 2023. The offensive has also destroyed around 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.
Despite a cease-fire that took effect in Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing over 1,400 Palestinians and injuring around 5,000 others, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

Recent attacks on US universities by the Trump administration have built on decades of efforts by libertarian donor networks, fossil fuel companies and conservative thinktanks to reshape university governance and increase outside influence, according to a new study.
The authors of the new perspective study argue that the erosion of university autonomy has left colleges more vulnerable to corporate interests, especially within climate and energy research.
In 2025, the Trump administration froze billions of dollars in research funding, launched investigations into 75 institutions and pushed colleges to sign agreements supporting administration policies in exchange for federal funding. The federal government canceled $4m in climate research grants at Princeton University alone and accused scientists of fueling “climate anxiety”.
If you’re a young researcher watching that, you might think twice about asking a question that could cost you your funding, said Noel Healy, of Salem State University, the lead author of the study published in the journal Energy Research & Social Science.
“Climate policy is only as good as the evidence behind it. When the industry being regulated gets to shape the questions researchers ask, it ends up shaping the policy too,” he said.
The Academic Freedom Index, which measures how freely scholars and universities can teach, research and express ideas without interference, found that US institutional autonomy fell from 3.3 in 2019 to 1.7 in 2025, on a scale of 0 to 4.
“Since 2025, scientists have been deleting words like ‘climate change’ from their grant applications because those words can get an application rejected,” Healy said. “Some universities have shut down programs before the government even asked them to, hoping to avoid becoming a target. You don’t have to ban speech if people fear that speaking up will cost them their funding. People start deciding it’s safer to stay quiet.”

The boast comes even though inflation is higher and economic growth lower than when Joe Biden left office, even though gas prices have jumped around 50% since the war against Iran started, and even though 73% of Americans think the economy is in fair or poor shape (48% say it’s in poor shape). “It’s bluster, it’s gaslighting for him to say the economy is the greatest ever,” said Darrick Hamilton, chief economist for the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation. “The economy is trending down by many measures. A lot of that has been caused by Trump’s unforced errors.”

Transplanted hearts may take on the age of their new bodies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:36:32 UTC
19:36:32 KST

Demand for heart transplants is growing, but donor hearts are a scarce resource. Age further narrows the pool, with doctors preferring younger hearts because older organs have been linked to worse outcomes.
But a new preprint posted to the server bioRxiv suggests that age might not be such a limit after all—and, incredibly, that transplanted organs may change to mirror the age of the recipient, not the donor. Ultimately, the findings suggest an old heart can become biologically “younger” after being transplanted into a younger recipient.
Jesse Poganik, an instructor in medicine at Harvard Medical School and co-author of the study, and his colleagues transplanted hearts between young, middle-aged and old mice while keeping each recipient’s native heart intact. They measured DNA methylation, a type of chemical mark that changes with age, and used three epigenetic clocks—measures of those chemical changes—to estimate the grafts’ biological age.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Young hearts transplanted into older mice appeared biologically older than expected, while old hearts placed in younger mice appeared to have de-aged. Other tests of biological aging showed the same pattern.
“My interpretation of these results is that the young systemic environment can reverse certain aspects of biological age, but others may be irreversible,” Poganik says.
The findings suggest organs are responsive to their environment, says Peter Scriven, co-founder and clinical and scientific director at LONGEVITY, an aging clinic in England, who was not involved in the study. “That gives us a reason to ask how much of its aging we can change.”
Exactly what is happening to change the organs’ age markers is unclear. Poganik suspects the overall body environment, rather than any one factor, may help clear accumulated damage or expose the organ to younger immune factors.
Genes involved in the function of mitochondria—the powerhouses of the cell—also became more active in old hearts placed in young mice and less active in young hearts placed in old mice. “What excites me most is the possibility of transferable rejuvenation factors,” Scriven says, pointing to mitochondrial activity and other antiaging signals potentially passing from recipient cells to the transplanted heart. In the future, healthy mitochondria might even be harnessed to rejuvenate an organ, he says.
The transplant did not appear to change the biological age of the recipient’s own heart (which stayed in the body), liver or blood. Transplantation itself, however, also caused pro-aging changes, including increased inflammation.
Michael Sagner, clinical adviser in longevity and preventive medicine at King’s College London, who was not involved in the study, says the study’s methods have some limitations. “Existing models such as the ones used in the study are still experimental and not necessarily an expression of real biological age yet,” he explains.
To strengthen the results, however, the team analyzed archived heart biopsies from 11 human transplant recipients with large donor-recipient age gaps. Again, the transplanted hearts’ biological ages were more closely associated with the recipient’s age than the donor’s.
By analyzing a database of hundreds of human transplant recipients, the researchers also found that some functional measures of heart health also tracked more closely to recipient age. Most notably, exercise capacity and VO2 max, a measure of the body’s ability to use oxygen during exercise, were lower in older recipients regardless of the donor’s age, suggesting the transplanted heart was aging alongside the rest of the body.
“It may be the case that older organs that would currently be passed over for donation could be considered for younger recipients,” Poganik says, noting that much more work is needed before any changes to the donor system might be implemented.

EU adopts Russia sanctions over crackdown on anti-war party, abduction of Ukrainian children
BRUSSELS, Belgium — EU ministers agreed on Sept. 28 to sanction 10 Russian officials responsible for the barring of Russia's only remaining anti-war opposition party from participating in the country's parliamentary elections.
The EU vote means that judges, prosecutors, and public officials involved in repression and politically motivated prosecutions against the Yabloko (Apple) political party will face asset freezes and a ban on transactions with EU companies.
The sanctions list includes three judges from Russia's Supreme Court and an official from the country's Prosecutor General's Office, according to an EU press release.
Russia's Sept. 18-20 election was riddled with widespread manipulation of the vote, with any genuine opposition banned from running.
The election also illegally took place in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories, which led Kyiv to pass sanctions measures of its own.
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said she had likewise proposed restrictions on those who are enabling the sham elections in the occupied territories.
National and EU diplomats have confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that a first draft list of 77 individuals responsible for the elections in the occupied regions had been discussed, including candidates and members of Russia's electoral commission.
That list now has to be legally reviewed by experts from the 27 EU countries, with the aim of finally adopting those sanctions at an Oct. 12 summit of EU foreign ministers.
The EU also adopted a further 27 listings of individuals and organizations involved in Russia's abduction and indoctrination of over 20,000 Ukrainian children, hours before the start of an international summit on the issue in Toronto.
Those listings include children's camps and sports centers not only in Russia and in occupied territories, but also in North Korea.
The Songdowon International Children's camp has been added to the EU's sanctions list for taking part in programs "involving the transfer of Ukrainian children... with the aim of promoting pro-Russian narratives."

Life finds a way: Fire amoebas, plesiosaur vomit and sea turtle eggs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:36:12 UTC
19:36:12 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
Let’s kick things off with some tech news. According to a study published last week in Communications Sustainability, artificial intelligence data centers could consume about 1% of all electricity by 2030. Researchers project that demand from the six largest tech operators alone—that’s Microsoft, Google, Meta, Oracle, Amazon and Apple—will jump from 118 terawatt-hours in 2024 to between 239 and 295 by 2030. That increase is about how much energy 27 million American households use in a year. While these six AI power users will account for about two-thirds of the world’s AI energy consumption, the global total for data centers could reach 945 terawatt-hours, or 3% of the world’s global electricity consumption.
What makes the projections more troubling is that more than 90% of the projected global capacity for this computing power is clustered across just three regions. In the US, data centers are expected to cluster in Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, Iowa, Texas, Arizona, and North Carolina. That means that folks in certain areas will bear the environmental burden of the whole country’s generative AI usage. The Environmental and Energy Study Institute estimates that large data centers can consume as much as 5 million gallons of water per day, which is equivalent to the water use of a town with tens of thousands of residents. Data centers also contribute to noise pollution thanks to the use of cooling systems, fans, and backup diesel generators—which of course pollute the air as well.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Our next story comes from SciAm’s Chief Newsletter Editor Andrea Gawrylewski about the hunt for the smallest particles in the universe. Over to you, Andrea!
Andrea: Thanks, Rachel. In 2012 researchers at the Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland announced that they had observed the elusive Higgs boson particle. The Standard Model, which is theorists’ best description of the fundamental building blocks of reality, had predicted the Higgs, and now scientists had spotted it after two years of experiments.
It became the 17th known elementary particle in the universe. All the elementary particles are grouped in two camps: fermions and bosons. Fermions are the building blocks of matter and include particles like quarks, whereas bosons are force-carrying particles like photons. But can these particles be broken down even further?
This turns out to be one of science’s toughest questions. Will we ever find the smallest final building block of nature? If we do discover new fragments of reality, they may reveal that our understanding of elementary physics is flawed. For example, one contending idea is that instead of thinking of particles as points, what if these bits of energy were actually something else, like tiny vibrating strings?
This would mean that a particle's characteristics would then be determined by the string's properties and the way it mingles with other strings, all quivering and coiling near the infinitesimal limits of physical size. To accurately explain known physics, these strings would have to exist across at least 10 dimensions, a geometric structure that is assumed to be accessible only at tiny scales, making this idea difficult, maybe impossible, to test.
Another idea is that spacetime itself may be made of tiny loops. These loops of gravity would be woven together and would mathematically account for the curvature of spacetime. Imagine just like being bathed in light, the grains of quantum spacetime would be all around us. So how can physicists test these ideas?
If strings or quantum loops exist, physicists believe they would be about the size of the Planck length, which is thought to represent a physical limit to how small something can be, about 1.6 × 10–35 meter.
To experiment even close to this minute scale, scientists would need a circular particle collider so large that if it was centered on the sun, it would reach a little past the outer orbit of the planet Neptune. That size particle accelerator isn’t happening anytime soon, but scientists are working on upgrades at the Large Hadron Collider that are slated to come online in 2030. They should allow the machine to measure even more particles erupting from collisions. Whether we’ll ever fully understand the underpinnings of existence, however, is anyone’s bet.
Feltman: Thanks for that, Andrea. Listeners, don’t forget to subscribe to Today in Science to get stories like this one sent straight to your inbox.
Now we’ve got a few stories on the miracle of life. This first one is honestly pretty miraculous: scientists have found an organism that thrives at higher temperatures than previously thought possible for this type of life. They described Incendiamoeba cascadensis, whose genus means “fire amoeba,” in a study published last Tuesday in Cell.
What makes the finding particularly cool—or I guess, particularly hot—is that the species in question is a eukaryote. That means that, unlike the organisms that actually hold the top records for withstanding high temperatures, this one has a nucleus. That kind of complex biology requires proteins that scientists generally thought would fall apart at such high temperatures. This little eukaryote was found in samples from Lassen Volcanic National Park in northern California. I guess some amoebas like it hot.
Speaking of life finding a way: For the first time ever, a sea turtle was spotted laying eggs on the west coast of the US. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries West Coast posted the news on their Facebook page last week. According to the agency, an olive ridley sea turtle dug a nest near Seal Beach in Orange County, California on September 16. Then, three days later, a turtle—maybe the same individual, maybe not—did the same thing a few miles south.
Olive ridleys tend to hang out in more tropical waters, but they have been spotted in California before. Experts say the turtles are probably following warm currents from this year’s El Niño, perhaps with an additional temperature boost from climate change. The nests in California have been fenced off to protect the eggs during their incubation period, which ranges from 45 to 60 days.
We’ll wrap things up with one last story about the majestic nature of marine life. According to a study published last week in Geological Magazine, plesiosaurs—extinct marine reptiles that lived from around 215 million to 66 million years ago and included the, if you’ll allow me to date myself, Internet-famous genus Liopleurodon—left some very special remains on land: their vomit.
Plesiosaurs had long necks that they likely used to reach shellfish on the seafloor, but it doesn’t seem like they had the tooth power to crush bones and exoskeletons into digestible crumbles. Instead, like owls, it’s thought that they regurgitated compact clumps of mucus-coated detritus.
For the new study, paleontologists had the glamorous task of analyzing more than 20 of these pellets in their fossilized form, which are called regurgitalites. The pellets contained the remains of creatures that need salt water to survive, but they were found in what would have been a river delta with brackish water. That’s why the researchers suspect that plesiosaurs did their hunting in the sea before cruising to shallow waters to rest, digest, and puke. As for how plesiosaurs were identified as the most likely upchuckers, the researchers came to that conclusion based on the composition and size of the pellets, which could be as large as mangos.
Here’s one last fun fact I learned from this study: have you ever wondered how scientists tell the difference between fossilized vomit and fossilized poop? A coprolite, which is the elegant term for a preserved turd, will have a lower ratio of undigested food—along with some distinct mineralogical traces and a more regular shape and scatter pattern. Isn’t science awesome?
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about how romantic cons are getting harder to spot in the age of AI—and what you can do to protect yourself.

Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Best Apple Watch: Series 12, Ultra 4, and SE 3 (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

As WIRED’s resident wearable tester, I’ve tried enough smartwatches to know there’s life beyond the Apple Watch. I just apparently don’t want it. Maybe it’s because I joined the Apple ecosystem at 10 years old and have been indoctrinated ever since. I’m fluent in iOS, macOS, and watchOS, and for better or worse, the Apple Watch is my default wearable.
But what’s the best Apple Watch to buy? There are now three models, each with its own set of features, and the differences between them can appear minor even when the prices aren’t. Fortunately, I’ve tested them all; Here’s how the current lineup stacks up.
For more recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Apple Watch Bands, the Best Apple Watch Accessories, and the Best Smartwatches.
Featured in This Guide
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Apple Watch Overall
The Series 12 is Apple’s flagship watch. Its biggest upgrade is the new Health Sensing System, which improves the breadth, accuracy, and frequency of its health tracking. The ECG now uses 32 electrodes for better skin contact, up from two on the Series 11, while improved optical sensing and more efficient LEDs deliver more accurate heart-rate readings. The Series 12 also tracks your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day and HRV as often as every five minutes, compared with every five minutes for heart rate and roughly every two hours for HRV on the Series 11.
The Series 12 also introduces Apple’s Readiness score, which gives you a snapshot of how prepared your body is for the day based on your recent health and activity data. Audio Intelligence is another major addition, though two of its headline features (Live Rewind and Siri Recap) won’t arrive until later this year.
Battery life remains rated for up to 24 hours, but charging is faster. Fifteen minutes delivers up to 12 hours of normal use, and five minutes get you up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. Just about the only feature the Series 11 lacks is satellite connectivity, but if you don't go off the grid, then it has everything else you need.
Best Battery Life
The Ultra 4’s biggest upgrades are its longer battery life, faster charging, and new health-tracking capabilities. It lasts up to 50 hours on a charge—up from 42 hours on the Ultra 3—and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode. Fast charging gets a boost, with 15 minutes on the charger providing up to 18 hours of normal use and five minutes offering up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. A new Health Sensing System and faster S11 chip enable frequent background heart-rate and HRV tracking, the Readiness score, and Apple’s suite of Audio Intelligence features.
Beyond those improvements, the Ultra 4 is essentially the same smartwatch as its predecessor. It remains built for multi-day hikes, water sports, and endurance activities, with water resistance up to 100 meters and a depth gauge rated to 40 meters for recreational scuba diving. Its standout feature remains satellite messaging, which lets you contact emergency services when you’re beyond cellular or Wi-Fi coverage. Fall and crash detection, plus a built-in siren, offer additional precautions to get help when you need it.
My biggest complaint is that the 49-mm can be too large on slimmer wrists. I’d like a 46-mm option.
Best Budget-Friendly Apple Watch
Apple didn’t update the SE this year, so the Watch SE (3rd Gen) remains the most affordable. It’s designed with the S10 chip, which enables many of the health features the SE 2 lacked, such as sleep apnea notifications and skin temperature sensing. It’s compatible with watchOS 27, so you can use the dynamic app grid, the Siri app, and Workout Buddy. It has fast charging, and even though it doesn’t have the Series 12’s 24-hour battery life, former WIRED editor Adrienne So still somehow managed to eke out a full day with it, even with the always-on display.
The screen is only a 1,000-nit display compared to the 2,000-nit display on the Series 11’s wide-angle OLED display, and it doesn't have the UWB locator chip. You’re missing out on the new features, including the new Readiness score, high-frequency heart-rate and HRV tracking, and Audio Intelligence. It also cannot check your blood oxygen or take an electrocardiogram, nor does it have the latest hypertension notifications.
Compare Top 3 Apple Watches
Honorable Mentions
Apple Watch Series 11 for $399: With no price difference between generations, the Series 11 only makes sense if you find it at a significant discount. It misses out on high-frequency background heart-rate tracking, Recovery HRV readings, the Readiness score, and Apple’s suite of Audio Intelligence tools. It also uses standard GPS instead of the newer Precision L1 GPS, and it lacks the latest fast-charging boost, but it can still charge for up to eight hours of battery life in 15 minutes.
Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $799: With no price difference between generations, the Ultra 3 only makes sense if you find it at a significant discount. It has a shorter battery life, rated for up to 42 hours compared with the Ultra 4’s 50 hours. You also miss out on Audio Intelligence, high-frequency heart-rate and HRV tracking, and the Readiness score. Otherwise, it’s basically the same outdoor-focused Apple Watch.
Avoid These Apple Watches
WatchOS 27 only works with the Series 9 and newer, so I wouldn’t recommend buying an Apple Watch older than that. With less price variation between generations, I’d also only consider an older Apple Watch if it’s on sale.
How I Test Apple Watches
For my initial reviews, I wear each Apple Watch day and night for about a week, using it as I would a typical smartwatch, fitness tracker, and sleep tracker. Afterward, I continue testing for at least another month to evaluate longer-term claims and how useful its wellness data proves to be in practice.
I sport each watch during workouts, throughout the day, and while sleeping to judge its comfort over time. I also consider screen readability indoors and outdoors, and the responsiveness of the touchscreen and physical controls. I test everyday functions like Siri, music playback, and watchOS to evaluate how intuitive they are to navigate and how well they integrate with the iPhone experience. I track how long the battery lasts with features such as workout tracking, notifications, and sleep tracking enabled. I also note charging speed and how practical it is to maintain throughout a full day and overnight.
Because the Apple Watch is also a fitness tracker, I use it for a range of activities, including but not limited to runs, rides, and strength training. I compare heart rate readings, workout detection, step counts, and other fitness metrics against previous Apple Watches and competitors (i.e., Oura and Whoop). I also compare sleep tracking with predecessors and competitors, looking at the quality of the data, how useful the metrics are, and whether it provides actionable insights.

Russia Lost More Than 10,000 Troops in a Single Week of Its War, Zelenskyy Says
Russia lost 10,660 troops killed or wounded across active sectors of the front over the past week, as Ukrainian forces continued operations in several of the most heavily contested areas, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The figure was announced following a briefing by Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi. According to Zelenskyy, every Russian casualty included in the weekly count was supported by video evidence.
“In total, over the course of this week, across all active combat zones on the front lines, our units neutralized 10,660 Russian soldiers, including those killed and wounded. And each such Russian casualty is accompanied by video evidence,” Zelenskyy said.
The most intensive combat is currently taking place in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, and Lyman sectors, according to the president. Ukrainian forces are also carrying out operations in the Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, and Sumy regions.
Zelenskyy reported “important results” in the Lyman sector of the Donetsk region as part of Operation Vivaldi, as well as progress by Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces during a separate active-defense operation.
He separately praised the 3rd Army Corps and the 68th Separate Airmobile Brigade of the 8th Air Assault Forces Corps for their performance on the battlefield. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s operations were limiting Russia’s ability to expand its offensive activity and added that he and Drapatyi had determined the Ukrainian military’s next steps.
“Every week like this on the front lines—which, given the nature of the overall situation, is becoming ours, Ukrainian—prevents Russia from launching a larger offensive against Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said.
Operation Vivaldi is being conducted in northern Donetsk region, where Ukrainian forces have reported regaining control of several settlements and clearing Russian positions around the Lyman sector.
During Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainian ground robots cleared 30 kilometers of routes in the Shandryholove sector in just two nights without sapper losses. The Third Army Corps said unmanned systems are increasingly deployed ahead of infantry for demining, assault support, logistics, and evacuations.

Fighting across the front remained intense, with Ukrainian forces recording 229 combat engagements during the latest reporting period.
