Ukraine Strikes Plant Tied to Kh-101 and Oreshnik Production—Satellite Images Show the Damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:35:06 UTC
19:35:06 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Plant Tied to Kh-101 and Oreshnik Production—Satellite Images Show the Damage
Satellite imagery has confirmed extensive damage at Russia’s Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant, a defense-industry facility linked to producing components for Kh-101, Kh-35U, Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, and the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile, Militarnyi said, citing the imagery on September 27.
Imagery published by the OSINT community Absolutely Reliable shows strikes across six buildings that house at least five production shops at the plant.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among the most heavily affected areas was Workshop 022, the foundry complex spread across two buildings. Satellite images show evidence of a fire and significant structural damage.
Workshop 024, responsible for mechanical processing, was also seriously damaged, with part of its roof collapsing following the strike.
Other affected facilities included Workshop 008, used for optics production, Workshop 009 for assembly work and Workshop 010, which handles electroplating processes.
The attack was carried out overnight into September 26 by the Ukrainian Navy together with the Security Service of Ukraine’s Alpha Special Operations Center.
Ukrainian forces reportedly used Neptune cruise missiles alongside Ruta, Palianytsia and BARS jet-powered drones in the operation.
The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation and serves as one of the group’s important optoelectronic manufacturing sites.
Its production includes radar and infrared seekers for guided missiles, thermal-imaging equipment and electronic systems used in precision artillery. The plant also supplies components for anti-tank weapons, weapon-stabilization systems for armored vehicles, aviation and UAV navigation equipment, laser systems and electronic warfare technology.
Leaked internal documents examined by researchers have linked the facility to at least several major Russian missile programs.
Those include the Kh-31P anti-radiation missile, R-74 short-range and R-37M long-range air-to-air missiles, Kh-101, Kh-35U and Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, as well as the Oreshnik ballistic missile program.
Open-source information also links the plant to components for KAB-250, KAB-500 and KAB-1500 guided bombs and the Kh-38ML short-range air-to-surface missile.
Previously, a missile attack struck the Russian city of Taganrog, with reports indicating that the Beriev aviation complex, a key facility involved in repairing and modernizing Russia’s Tu-95 strategic bombers, may have been among the targets.

Saudi Arabia nearly doubles oil exports in September — Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:35:02 UTC
19:35:02 KST

LONDON, September 28. /TASS/. Saudi Arabia exported about 5.4 mln barrels of oil per day this month, which is almost two times higher than in August when the country shipped around 2.4 mln barrels per day, Reuters reported, citing data from analytics company Kpler.
Crude oil exports from key Middle East producers rebounded in September to 12.8 mln barrels per day, the highest since the US-Israeli military operation against Iran started in late February. Prior to the beginning of the operation, exports in the region exceeded 18.8 mln barrels per day.
The rebound came following a recovery in exports via the Strait of Hormuz, the agency said. In September, exports were set to hit about 7.4 mln barrels per day, the preliminary data showed.

Diesel prices are surging. Ukraine is only part of the story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:35:00 UTC
19:35:00 KST

Why diesel prices are soaring and what it means for Europe
September 28, 2026
Even if you don't fill your own vehicle with diesel, its price has a big impact on your life.
While gasoline is mainly a consumer fuel for cars, diesel powers much of the wider economy, from freight transport and farming equipment to construction and industry.
That is why diesel shortages or price shocks can have a bigger economic impact than higher gasoline prices by raising the cost of moving goods and operating heavy machinery.
As businesses become strained, these higher energy costs will be passed on to consumers and add to a growing cost-of-living crisis and inflation. So what's driving global diesel prices higher?
The US blames Ukraine for diesel shortages
The United States and China are among the world's largest diesel producers. China keeps much of it for domestic use, leaving the US as the world's biggest diesel exporter.
Still, the weekly average price of a gallon of diesel is now $6.52 (€5.73) in the country, according to the US Energy Information Administration, a big increase from a year ago when it averaged $3.74 per gallon or two years ago when it averaged $3.53 a gallon.
President Donald Trump recently called on Ukraine's president to stop targeting oil refineries in Russia "because he's causing a shortage of diesel."
Russia is one of the world's other biggest diesel suppliers. But since 2022, some of its oilrefineries have been attacked as many as 15 times, according to the International Energy Agency.
The agency estimates that diesel production in Russia is down by nearly 30% from 2025 levels. Moscow has now restricted diesel exports to protect domestic supplies.
As Russian production declined, the US went into high gear to help make up the difference, but even this was not enough. And on September 22, Trump announced that his administration was also considering a diesel export ban.
Such a move is likely an attempt to bring down domestic prices ahead of the November midterm elections since energy prices and affordability have become important campaign issues.
Leading energy lobby groups have come out against such a plan, and many industry experts think a ban would be slow to bring down prices or could backfire by pushing US refiners to reduce production, push up prices, or both.
Europe is especially vulnerable to diesel shocks
For Europe, more expensive diesel could have dramatic consequences.
"Decades of policy incentives, such as tax advantages, left Europe's vehicle fleet far more diesel-heavy than regions like the US," said Georg Zachmann, a senior fellow at Brussels-based Bruegel think tank.
"As a result, the EU is structurally long on gasoline, which it exports, and short on diesel, which it must import," added Zachmann, who specializes in energy and climate policies.
In the EU, just over 38% of passenger cars are diesel and road transport, including freight, makes up 77% of total diesel and gas oil consumption, according to a briefing published by Transport & Environment, a Brussels-based advocacy group.
This reliance on diesel-powered transport "leaves drivers and businesses particularly exposed to oil and fuel price shocks," wrote Juliette Egal, the briefing's lead author.
The NGO calculated that EU drivers are paying €30 more for a 50-liter tank of diesel on average since the start of the war in Iran. An average German long-haul truck driver is paying an extra €236 a week.
Increased fuel costs for EU road transport add up to €270 million a day — of that, €203 million is for diesel, according to the briefing. Overall, the EU economy has seen additional costs of €40 billion from road diesel since the beginning of the war.
Why are diesel prices climbing faster than oil?
In the near term, Russia's crude oil processing volumes are the single fastest-moving lever, said Skip York, a nonresident fellow at Rice University's Center for Energy Studies in Houston, Texas.
"Each new wave of Ukrainian strikes shows up in diesel prices within days, unlike Hormuz, which has been running at a depressed but relatively stable flow rate for months," he added.
York points out that, perhaps surprisingly, crude oil production, the raw material needed to make diesel and gasoline, isn't the biggest constraint. That is why oil prices have moved modestly while diesel has soared.
"The oil bottleneck has shifted from 'not enough crude' in March/April to 'not enough refining capacity' since August," the expert told DW.
Now refinery disruptions matter most, he said, because "both the Ukraine drone campaign and the Hormuz conflict are knocking out working refining capacity faster than anyone can replace it."
Still, the Strait of Hormuz "is the bigger structural risk" for diesel prices in the long term.
Globally, refinery capacity has "dropped substantially, and diesel is particularly affected," agreed Zachmann.
Where will diesel prices go from here?
Prolonged fighting in the Middle East or Russia could add to the problems for Europe and other diesel users. US export restrictions could make this situation even worse.
US diesel exports to Europe are up around 37% since last year and now account for about 8% of European demand, says York. This makes the country an important alternative to diesel from Russia and the Persian Gulf.
If the US blocks exports, it would be a big shock and mean even higher diesel prices, said Zachmann. The question is whether the EU would retaliate and export less gasoline to the US "making both sides worse off" by pushing up both US gasoline prices and EU diesel prices.
Additionally, winter is just around the corner for the Northern Hemisphere. Refineries may struggle to meet demand for both heating oil and diesel, further tightening supplies.
A wave of refinery closures in Europe and the US since 2019 has made the diesel market vulnerable, said York, and this has hit the buffer of spare refining capacity that used to absorb shocks.
"Essentially, the market has fewer 'extra barrels' standing by," he underscored. "So, the loss of any barrel hits supply much more directly than it used to."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

WATCH: Ukraine Says Russian Troops Led Children Into Gas Pipeline to Cover Retreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:34:36 UTC
19:34:36 KST

Drone footage released by Ukraine’s Khartiia Corps shows a group that includes children, older people, and a person on crutches being led toward a pipeline. The corps says Russian troops used them to shield their withdrawal.
Russian forces forced civilians from the Kupiansk area in the Kharkiv Region into a gas pipeline while retreating from a Ukrainian counteroffensive, according to the National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The corps said its reconnaissance drones recorded the group on Sunday, Sept. 27. Nine people, including children, older residents, and one person using crutches can be seen in the footage. Men of fighting age wearing civilian clothes walk alongside them. The corps believes the men are Russian soldiers who removed their uniforms, but their identities cannot be established from the footage alone.
Труба для диверсантів у Куп’янську стала трубою для викрадення людей: окупанти женуть через газогін дітей і літніх людей, прикриваючи відхід власних сил.

Khartiia said the group was taken from Kupiansk through the village of Holubivka to the Shebelinka-Ostrogozhsk pipeline and led inside. Russian forces have previously used the pipeline to move troops toward the city, the corps said.
Ukrainian troops say the children and older people would have to travel more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) through the pipeline. It emerges in a forest, from where the group would likely be taken to Russian-occupied territory. According to troops, Russian forces filmed them throughout the journey.
Ukrainian troops spotted the group but did not fire because civilians were among them.
Lavrov Says Turkey Must Guarantee S-400 Systems Won’t Reach Ukraine
The corps allege that Russian soldiers relied on their presence to avoid attack as they withdrew. It said it had documented the incident and would submit the material for a war crimes investigation.
The incident could involve several violations of international humanitarian law. The Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits the forcible transfer or deportation of civilians from occupied territory. The Fourth Geneva Convention and Additional Protocol I prohibit using civilians’ presence or movement to shield military forces from attack. Combatants are required to distinguish themselves from civilians during military operations.
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children in a separate case.
The corps also suspects that the men accompanying the civilians were Russian soldiers who had removed their uniforms. Their identities cannot be confirmed from the footage alone.
Khartiia warned that Russian media may portray the footage as an evacuation or rescue, however, the civilians were instead forced into the pipeline while Russian troops withdrew alongside them, using their presence as cover.

Venipak invests over €2.5 million in Baltic infrastructure; increases parcel locker capacity in Latvia by 15%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:33:25 UTC
19:33:25 KST

Logistics company Venipak has increased the number of compartments at its most popular parcel lockers in Latvia by around 15% this year. The expansion of parcel locker capacity in Latvia forms part of more than €2.5 million in investments in infrastructure development and modernisation across the Baltics. The company’s total investment this year is its highest in several years. At the same time, logistics terminals in Lithuania and Estonia are being expanded and modernised, while process automation is also being increased.
This year, Venipak is placing particular focus on increasing parcel locker capacity in the most heavily used locations. The number of compartments at the company’s most popular parcel lockers in Latvia has increased by around 15%. Parcel locker capacity is also being expanded in Lithuania and Estonia.
“In Latvia, we are currently focusing on increasing capacity in locations where parcel lockers are used most intensively. This allows us to handle larger parcel volumes, particularly during the busiest periods of the year. Our goal is to ensure that, even as parcel volumes continue to grow, deliveries remain convenient and timely for our customers,” says Sanita Bērziņa, CEO of Venipak Latvia.
Increasing automation and terminal capacity across the Baltics
Alongside the expansion of its parcel locker network, Venipak is investing in the development and automation of its logistics terminals. Rapidly growing parcel volumes and labour market conditions are prompting the company to place increasing emphasis on technological solutions and reducing reliance on manual processes.
Most of this year’s investments are being directed towards infrastructure development projects in Lithuania. From September, the company is moving into a new terminal in Klaipėda that is approximately 60% larger than its previous facility and covers 3,900 square metres. The upgraded infrastructure will enable Venipak to handle twice as many parcels as before.
This autumn, a new automated parcel sorting conveyor will also be installed at Venipak’s largest logistics terminal in Kaunas, increasing sorting capacity from 3,000 to 7,000 parcels per hour.
“Kaunas is our main logistics hub in Lithuania, connecting parcel flows across the Baltics and Poland with the rest of Europe. The new sorting line will enable us to process parcels faster and more accurately, while also increasing the overall efficiency of the network,” says Andrius Ladauskas, CEO of Venipak.
In the first half of 2027, Venipak also plans to relocate to a new 13 500-square-metre logistics terminal in Vilnius. The project represents a total investment of €16 million.
Expansion is also planned in Ukmergė and Šiauliai in Lithuania, as well as at the Tartu terminal in Estonia. The company is also considering opening an additional terminal in Estonia and modernising other sorting centres.
Venipak currently operates around 800 parcel lockers and 25 logistics terminals across the Baltics. The company employs approximately 1000 people and works with around 350 independent couriers.
Venipak Group generated revenue of €85.6 million in 2025, with EBITDA reaching €12.4 million.

From 'Chud' to 'Bop': Most searched Gen Alpha slang terms of 2026 (so far) revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

10:33:14 UTC
19:33:14 KST

These are the most-searched-for Gen Alpha slang words for 2026 so far - and what they mean.
Let’s face facts: unless you’re part of Gen Alpha – the generation born between 2010 and 2024 – chances are you’re frequently overhearing or confronted with words, terms and vernacular that sound completely alien to you, leaving you feeling out of the loop or labelled as “unc”.
Fortunately, a study from Unscramblerer has helpfully analyzed Google Search trends data from January to the end of August to reveal the most-searched-for Gen Alpha slang terms of 2026.
Some you’ll have heard. Others will leave you thinking the retirement home beckons. All will give insight into the cultural conversations of the younger generations, revealing their preoccupations, habits and in some cases, insecurities.
Sticking to the Top 10 most-searched-for Gen Alpha slang terms, here’s what these ubiquitous expressions mean. (Incidentally, “unc” is short for “uncle” and is essentially a way for the new generation to call someone old. It didn’t make the Top 10.)
6-7
Yep, this one... And it’s still on top. It all started last year, and continues to completely ruin the joke “Why was 6 afraid of 7?” The utterly meaningless term has been traced to the Skrilla song ‘Doot Doot (6 7)’ and went viral thanks to an excitable scamp at a basketball game. It became so pervasive that it was crowned Dictionary.com’s 2025 Word of the Year. Usually accompanied by exaggerated up-and-down hand movements, what was supposed to be a flash-in-the-pan fad has gone from a trolling inside joke to a ubiquitous rallying cry for the brain damaged. At first, there was every reason to celebrate youngsters welcoming a level of absurd randomness into a world that routinely feels like it’s sinking into godless oblivion; its continued pervasiveness now leads to a Darwin-disproving form of despair.
Chud
For a cinematically literate generation, “chud” used to mean ‘Cannibalistic Humanoid Underground Dwellers” - a reference to the 1984 horror film C.H.U.D. Now, surly teens liberally dish out this insult to refer a stupid, ugly or downright repulsive person - to be used interchangeably with “loser”, “jerk” or “arsewipe”. Somewhat fascinatingly, the term “chud” has been embraced by people with left-wing political views when mocking right-wing trolls, fascists, ultranationalists and anarcho-capitalists.
Rizz
A shortened form of the word “charisma”, “rizz” was popularised by YouTuber Kai Cenat and describes a natural sense of charisma or flirting prowess. The term is innocent enough when used casually, but when overused by near-sociopathic and misogynistic pick-up artists, it frequently becomes a byword to excuse the worst tendencies peddled by the manosphere - the toxic internet subculture rooted in sexism and misogyny which is populated by noxious men with the IQ of a steak and ale pie.
Cap, No Cap
Cap = A lie / exaggeration / falsehood. No Cap = No lie / the equivalent of “for real”. Both terms are usually used at the beginning or the end of a sentence for emphasis and clarification. Alternatively, it could be used literally to describe someone with or without stylish headwear. Cap.
Mog / Mogging
A popular internet slang term meaning to outshine, dominate or outclass someone else. This can be in terms of various metrics, but usually in appearance, fashion and fitness. “His outfit mogs mine” / “I totally got jawmogged by that chud’s jawline” - that sort of thing.
Bop
What used to be a term for a catchy song has evolved into a derogatory insult – and a misogynistic one at that. It implies that a person (usually a woman) is promiscuous and Gen Alpha uses it as a way to bully, shame and degrade people online. As for the reason behind the use of the three-letter word, it refers to the motion during fellatio. Charming.
Larping / Larper
The term “larper” originally refers to a person who takes part in live-action role-playing (LARP) games. More recently, it has become an online put-down describing someone who is fake or pretending to be someone they’re not. It can be equated to a poser or someone who tries too hard. The term is usually found in the comment sections of content creators who pretend to be richer than they actually are or who try to sell people a lifestyle they don’t themselves possess.
Aura, aura points, aura farming
A not-so-distant cousin to “rizz”, “aura” describes a cool attitude and the charisma a person can exude. By extension, “aura points” are a fictional measure of coolness. As for “aura farming”, it’s the more pejorative descriptive – meaning trying to boost one’s perceived “coolness” by “larping”. Those who “aura farm” intentionally cultivate their persona through specific actions to appear cool. This can be through attempting to hang out with the popular crowd in order to increase one’s social clout; seeking to assert dominance through try-hard actions to gain attention; or jumping on the latest craze and making a public spectacle of oneself to mask one’s crippling sense of insecurity through the fleeting disillusionment that they’re “in”.
Sigma
It should just be the 18th letter of the Greek alphabet. But because we can’t have nice things, here goes... Positively, “sigma” refers to an independent and self-reliant person who knows what they’re about and couldn’t care less about arbitrary social hierarchies. However, the term “sigma” originates from the manosphere. They use the term as a step up from an “alpha male” and see “sigma” as the pinnacle of manhood – the lone wolf whose self-assured and dogged individualism sets him apart from “simps” (someone who shows “too much” attention for a "female”). If you feel the need to bathe in Clorox, get in line.
Crash out
This extremely popular term is pretty straightforward. It refers to having a breakdown, an emotional low point, or even a tantrum.
There we have it for the Top 10. As Randoh Sallihal, a spokesperson for Unscramblerer, states: “Using slang is a social signal. What people search for can tell us something about what they are trying to understand and participate in culturally.”
He adds: “Slang may look like a collection of throwaway jokes from the internet, but psychology suggests it is doing something much more interesting. Using slang helps people navigate identity and belong to a community.”
Anyone feeling reassured by these new social signals?

Legislative changes in Estonia to allow domestic mobile roaming during crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:32:43 UTC
19:32:43 KST

Starting the 1st of October, mobile network users will be able to connect to another operator’s cell tower during emergencies if their own operator’s service is interrupted, reports ERR News.
This new capability follows sweeping legislative changes regarding crisis situations adopted over the summer, which included a domestic roaming agreement among Estonia’s three major mobile network operators: Elisa, Tele2, and Telia. Domestic roaming will be available nationwide and will operate during severe emergencies affecting national security. It will not be available in instances such as power outages, which frequently occur during autumn storms.
From the 1st of October, if a customer’s mobile operator’s service becomes unavailable during an emergency, it will be possible to switch to the nearest operational tower of another operator. Mart Laas, a representative of the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, noted that the system would operate nationwide, as Estonia is small enough that implementing it at the level of individual regions would not be practical. Mobile phones will connect to the nearest operational communications tower if the user’s own network becomes unavailable. He added that
activating such a large-scale mechanism merely due to storms would be disproportionate.
It is intended for truly critical situations—such as war or other major incidents—where telecommunications networks have sustained severe damage, are non-functional, and would require a very long time to restore.
Tele2 operates approximately 1,500 telecommunications antennas in Estonia; some are mounted on tall towers, while others are located on building rooftops. Tanel Sarri, the company’s technology director, stated that a plan had to be prepared for various potential scenarios. This involved securing redundant external connections and preparing batteries and generators—measures the company has been working on for several years. According to Sarri, Tele2 is already prepared for crises, including power outages caused by storms. Key communication hubs are equipped with generators, while smaller sites utilize batteries, thereby ensuring mobile coverage—at least outdoors—even during power outages. The Crisis Situations and National Defence Act, adopted by the Estonian parliament in the summer and set to enter into force on the 1st of October, consolidates three existing laws into a unified framework. It mandates the delegation of specific crisis-time tasks to local governments and introduces a nationwide crisis plan.

Defence Secretary hails response to Fairford incident
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:31:04 BST
19:31:04 KST

Wes Streeting opened his speech to the Labour Party conference with remarks on the security operation around RAF Fairford, telling delegates that the work of the police, the armed forces and the intelligence agencies over the weekend was a small glimpse of what those organisations do unseen every day.
The Defence Secretary told delegates he was constrained by the live police investigation and could add little to what had already been reported. “Given events, you will understand that before getting into my speech today I want to say something about yesterday’s events around RAF Fairford,” he said. “You will understand there is a live police investigation and I can’t provide much further detail than that which is reported.”
He went on: “But I do want to say that our friendship with America is the closest alliance of any two nations on Earth, and we will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm.
“What we saw yesterday from our security services, our armed forces, and our police, was just a small glimpse of the extraordinary work they do every day, around the clock and around the world, behind the scenes and without recognition, to keep our country safe.
“To all of them, from all of us, thank you.”
Gloucestershire Constabulary declared a major incident on Sunday after arresting a number of men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, with properties evacuated in the village of Whelford next to the airfield and residents taken to a leisure centre nearby. In a statement the force said: “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident. It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the explosives act. A cordon is currently in place but we’d like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained.”
Explosive ordnance disposal teams examined several vehicles at the scene during the operation. ITV News has reported that counter-terrorism officers are investigating whether the plot has any connection to Iran.
Fairford, in Gloucestershire, is a United States Air Force forward operating location rather than an RAF flying station in the usual sense, and its long runway has made it the standing European base for American strategic bombers. B-1B Lancers are currently operating from the airfield, and the base moved to its highest force protection condition before the arrests were made, dispersing aircraft and reinforcing access points.
Bases used by American forces in Britain have drawn protest and intrusion for decades, and Fairford in particular was the subject of a well-known prosecution in the run-up to the Iraq war, when activists who broke into the site and damaged equipment were tried over several years. Those earlier cases turned on trespass and criminal damage, while the weekend’s arrests were made under the Explosives Act and are being handled by counter-terrorism officers.
Streeting used the rest of his speech to argue that the country is living through what he called a new age of insecurity, telling delegates that warfare has returned to Europe and that old alliances are being tested. The passage on Fairford was the only part of the address that touched on the weekend’s events, and he gave no further operational detail.
Anyone with information has been asked to contact Gloucestershire Constabulary, which continues to lead the investigation alongside counter-terrorism officers.

COMPASSO D’ORO INTERNATIONAL DESIGN AWARD OPENS SUBMISSIONS
Entries are open until January 20, 2027 for the Compasso d’Oro International Design Award 2027, organized by Association for Industrial Design (ADI) in collaboration with the Bureau International des Expositions (BIE). Centered on the theme ‘Design for Humanity at Play,’ the award invites designers, brands, and institutions participating in Expo 2027 Belgrade to submit projects developed between January 01, 2023 and December 31, 2026. Framing playas a vital mechanism for connection and speculative thinking, the competition challenges the creative community to explore how design can foster connection, participation, and resilience across nine distinct project categories.
Compasso d’Oro International Design Award 2027 | all images courtesy of ADI
DECADE OF GLOBAL EXPOS THROUGH THREE THEMATIC LENSES
For the 2027 edition, theADI’s award interprets play through three distinct lenses: ‘Power of Play’ centers on individual health, wellbeing, and sustainability; ‘Play for Progress’ shifts focus to scientific and creative discovery, leveraging trial and error to fuel innovation; and ‘Play Together’ views sport and music as universal connectors that rebuild community bonds. Across categories spanning living, lighting, food, communication, and social innovation, the call urges designers to anchor spatial and product solutions in shared human experience.
This initiative builds on a tradition of international Compasso d’Oro exhibitions connected with World Expos, including Milan 2015, Hangzhou 2017, and Osaka 2025. Solidified by a ten-year Memorandum of Understanding between ADI and the BIE to accompany major Expos through 2035, the platform offers participants extraordinary global exposure.
Compasso D’oro International invites global creators to explore participation, connection, and imagination through play
SOME DESIGNS WIN AWARDS, SOME BECOME HISTORY
Conceived by Gio Ponti in 1954 and managed by ADI since 1958, the Compasso d’Oro holds a singular place in design culture. On May 24, 2027, an international jury selects projects representing absolute excellence, conferring 20 Compasso d’Oro awards and up to 50 honourable mentions. The ceremony will also present up to three International Career Awards to non-Italian designers, companies, institutions, and schools that have advanced global design culture.
Selected finalists will be showcased in a dedicated Compasso d’Oro pavilion within the Best Practices area at Expo 2027 Belgrade through August 15, 2027, framed by six thematic weeks of public programming and interactive installations. Post-exposition, all awarded works permanently enter the ADI Compasso d’Oro Historical Collection at the ADI Design Museum in Milan, turning contemporary recognition into an enduring legacy.

I've Tested Over 100 Home Security Cameras. Here's Which to Buy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

A professional security system can be pricey, but installing a few of the best security cameras around your home is affordable and easy. Cover entrances, driveways, garages, sheds, and your main hallways, and you’ll be alerted to any unwelcome guests. Security cameras can even help deter would-be intruders and thieves.
Beyond the purchase price, expect ongoing running costs, and be prepared to sacrifice some privacy. It’s vital you trust the camera brand you invite into your home. It makes sense to pick one brand for easy app access and management. I’ve tested more than 100 different security cameras over the last decade, and five brands consistently dominate my recommendations. Whether you want cloud or local storage, serious AI smarts, or the cheapest cameras you can get without sacrificing quality, I’ve got you covered. And I’ve included more brands worth considering below, with a few that are best avoided.
Want more options? Check out the Best Outdoor Security Cameras, Best Subscription-Free Security Cameras, Best Floodlight Security Cameras, and Best Video Doorbells.
Best Subscription-Free Security Cameras: Eufy
For sheer feature-packed variety, Eufy security cameras are tough to beat. They’re easy to set up and use. They’re also reliable, and they don’t hide their best features behind a subscription. That means you can record locally on a hub, NVR, NAS device, or sometimes directly on the camera. My favorite Eufy cameras is the Indoor Cam S350, which is a good middle-ground in terms of price and features.
In fact, even this model will likely feel like overkill for most folks. It combines a regular camera with a 130-degree field of view that can go up to 4K with a 2K telephoto lens that provides 3X optical zoom. It also has 360-degree pan and 75-degree tilt controls, as well as AI tracking that works well. The camera also supports up to four preset positions it can patrol through, including the default position that it returns to after tracking a subject out of frame. There’s also privacy mode, two-way talk, and onboard AI to detect people, pets, and sounds. You can record locally with a microSD card up to 128 GB (not included), hook it up to a HomeBase S380 ($200), or subscribe for cloud storage from $4 per month. The Home Base S380 (previously called HomeBase 3) is a hub that connects to your router, ideally via Ethernet cable, and offers 16 GB of internal storage that can be expanded up to 16 TB with a hard drive.
The footage is crisp and detailed enough to zoom in on, though bright areas like sun streaming in a window can appear blown out. Because the frame rate is 15 fps, sometimes fast-moving subjects appear blurry. The motion detection is reliable, and you can set up privacy zones in the app. Notifications are swift and come with a thumbnail if you don’t mind uploading to the cloud (which is optional). I sometimes noticed a slight lag on the live feed, and the sound quality could be better. There is no HomeKit support, but you get Alexa and Google Assistant, though the camera was very slow and sometimes failed to load for me via Google.
This is my favorite pan-and-tilt camera right now, and it's a self-contained powerhouse with a fixed main lens that has a 130-degree field of view and records crisp, clear video at up to 4K, paired with dual 2K pan-and-tilt lenses that pan through 360 degrees and tilt through 70 degrees. The 8X hybrid zoom can blow up subjects up to 164 feet away. Tracking is very good, and you retain the fixed view, so there’s no risk of missing anything. The quick swap 10,000-mAh battery is rechargeable, but the included solar panel, which can go on top of the camera or nearby, was enough to keep mine topped off. The 32 GB of built-in storage is plenty for local recordings (expandable to 256 GB via microSD). But you can also get this in two or four cam kits with Eufy’s HomeBase S380.
If you like the S4 cameras, but you're able to go the wired route and run Ethernet cables, Eufy's S4 Max ($1,500) system employs Power over Ethernet (PoE) and comes with four S4 cameras and a network video recorder (NVR) with 2 TB of storage.
Here are a few more of the best Eufy cameras I've tested and recommend.
- A cheaper indoor pan-and-tilt camera: Eufy Wired Cam C31 for $60
- An excellent 4K package: EufyCam S3 Pro (2-Cam Kit) for $550
- A cheaper outdoor pan-and-tilt camera: Eufycam C37 for $90
- An affordable HD camera kit: Eufy C35 2-Cam Kit for $200
- A solar wall light camera: Eufy Wall Light Cam S4 for $250
Best Subscription Security Cameras: Arlo
Arlo is an excellent brand for security cameras that I've thoroughly enjoyed testing over the years, though unlike with Eufy, it'll require stomaching an expensive monthly subscription. Its hardware is relatively affordable for the quality it delivers. The cameras alert reliably, boast the best rich notifications, and the subscription provides generous cloud storage. Arlo also offers monitoring and emergency response as an optional extra. This is my favorite Arlo camera, the 2nd-gen Essential Indoor model.
With its compact design, clear video, and two-way audio, this Arlo camera matches performs reliably well. It can be placed on a shelf or wall-mounted, features a privacy shutter that lowers when the camera is not in use, and stores video in the cloud. The footage is detailed, and there’s no blurring on motion (the frame rate is 24 fps). Arlo’s second-generation Essential Indoor cameras are available in two varieties: a 1080p model and a pricier 2K model. I’m a fan of the app for its ease of use, loading speeds, and two-factor authentication, enabling you to log in to the live feed with your fingerprint or face scan (phone permitting). There’s also a built-in siren and smart home integration for Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant, and IFTTT, but not Apple HomeKit.
Unfortunately, cloud storage, accurate subject detection, and smart animated alerts require an expensive Arlo Secure subscription at $10 per month ($96/year) for a single camera. It’s a bit more palatable if you have multiple Arlo devices, as you opt for a $20 per month package ($216/year) for support for unlimited cameras. For folks with video doorbells or other cameras from Arlo, this camera is an obvious pick to keep things in a single app. But the lack of local storage might be a turnoff, and there are occasionally a few seconds of lag on the live feed.
The best security camera for outdoors is Arlo's Pro 6 as it records lovely crisp 2K resolution footage with HDR to prevent bright areas from becoming blown out or detail being lost in the shadows. This camera also boasts color night vision or a spotlight, clear two-way audio, and a built-in siren. Detection is rock solid and motion alerts are categorized by people, animals, vehicles, and packages. The notification system is swift and accurate, offering animated previews and screenshots with highlighted subjects that are easy to read even on a smartwatch screen. Arlo’s cameras are among the best at reducing false positives, and it’s easy to filter videos and tweak detection zones. 2K is sharp enough for most folks, but is you crave the best picture quality possible, the Arlo Ultra 3 (2-Cam Kit) ($350) steps up to 4K and offers everything you get from the Pro 6.
There are plenty of alternatives if you decide to go with an Arlo system. Here are the rest of the best Arlo cameras I've tested.
- An indoor pan-and-tilt camera: Arlo Essential Indoor Pan Tilt Zoom for $50
- A 4G LTE camera: Arlo Go 2 (Battery) for $200
- An outdoor pan-and-tilt camera: Arlo Essential Outdoor Pan Tilt Zoom for $60
Best Budget Security Cameras: TP-Link Tapo
Folks on a limited budget will struggle to find better quality security cameras at prices this low anywhere else. TP-Link’s Tapo line works well and is very affordable. The trade-off is that Tapo cameras lack proper end-to-end encryption, and the company’s router business has come under fire in the US. Here are my top Tapo picks:
Crisp video at a relatively low price makes the Tapo C120 very attractive. This camera is quick and easy to set up, with a handy magnetic base that can stick to the fridge, be wall-mounted, or sit on a shelf. It supports two-way audio (with a slight lag) and has a slot for up to 512 GB microSD cards to keep recordings local. Importantly, it offers smart detection (people, pets, and vehicles) without a subscription. I found the motion detection very reliable, and you can tweak the sensitivity and customize the notifications you receive, so you don’t get bothered by false positives. The color night vision is also above average.
You can set activity and privacy zones in the Tapo app, and there’s AI detection to recognize people, pets, vehicles, and the sound of a baby crying. This camera also supports the open Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP), making it easy to use with a network video recorder (NVR) or third-party software. This camera even has an IP66 rating, which means you can also use it outdoors (provided you can run the power cable). It works OK with Google Gemini or Amazon Alexa, though it was a little slow to load the stream on my Nest Hub.
On the downside, the frame rate maxes at 20 fps, so fast-moving subjects sometimes appear blurry, especially with low light. Rich notifications, including a snapshot of the subject, are bundled with the optional Tapo Care subscription, along with 30 days of cloud storage for clips, and it’s expensive at $3.50 per month for a single camera or $12 per month for up to 10 cameras. It also lacks Apple HomeKit or IFTTT support. Some folks may also have concerns about TP-Link, as its router business has been under investigation by the US government for alleged links to China.
If your budget is tight, the Tapo C110 ($28) is cheaper with only a few compromises (lower frame rate, no pet or vehicle detection, microSD limited to 256 GB).
This is a solid outdoor camera with a magnetic mount that makes it easy to angle and remove when it's time to recharge. It offers a 150-degree field of view, and sharp video at up to 2K and 30 frames per second, but you must change the default settings in the app to get the best from it. The lack of HDR might be a problem if it's in a spot with a lot of direct sunlight. The built-in spotlight enables color night vision, though it doesn’t penetrate far into the gloom, and I got better results with the black-and-white night vision. You will likely need to charge it every three months or so, unless you pair it with a solar panel. If you want sharper footage and don't mind spending a bit more, try the Tapo MagCam 4K Solar ($150). It comes with a solar panel and offers up to 4K footage, but the frame rate is limited to 15 fps.
TP-Link churns out many, many Tapo cameras. Here are the other best Tapo cameras I've tried.
- An indoor pan-and-tilt camera: TP-Link Tapo C210 for $30
- A hardwired outdoor camera: TP-Link Tapo C325WB for $70
- A 4K solar pan-and-tilt camera: TP-Link Tapo C660 for $170
- A 2K dual lens pan-and-tilt camera: TP-Link Tapo HybridCam Duo C246D for $70
- An affordable pan-and-tilt camera: TP-Link Tapo HybridCam 360 C216 for $40
- A 4K dual lens pan-and-tilt camera: TP-Link Tapo C675D for $230
Smartest Security Cameras: Google Nest
For the smartest AI detection, descriptions, and video filtering, Google’s Nest cameras are unbeatable right now. You need the relatively expensive subscription to unlock the top features, but if you’re already a Gemini fan and invested in Google’s ecosystem, it’s an easier sell. Camera choice is more limited, but here are my picks:
With an understated style, Google’s indoor Nest Cam comes in two subtle finishes to blend in with your decor, or a bright red “berry” paint job if you want it to stand out. It has HDR, footage is clear at 30 fps, with night vision that kicks on automatically when the lights are out, and the third generation ups the video quality from 1080p to 2K. There’s also two-way audio, enforced two-factor authentication, and accurate detection to alert you about people, animals, or vehicles. This latest model also features a wider field of view and animated previews that zoom in on the subject. You can install and use the Nest Cam through the Google Home app by scanning the QR code (it’s the fastest and easiest setup I’ve encountered), and it’s quick to load on Nest displays or a Chromecast with Google TV. (It's even accessible via a web interface.)
You only get six hours of history unless you sign up for a Google Home Premium (previously Nest Aware) subscription, which costs $10 per month ($100/year) for 30 days of event video history and familiar face alerts, but that covers all your Nest devices. (You can also use the camera in a Nest Hub Max as an indoor security camera.) Once you have tagged familiar faces, your notifications include their names, which is handy (and can be reassuring). It’s good to know when your kids get home versus when an unfamiliar face pops up. It’s not 100 percent accurate (it confuses my kids), but it’s closer than any other camera I have tested.
The overhauled Google Home app is much improved, quicker to load, and easier to navigate, and Gemini for Home provides more descriptive alerts, such as “cat walks around room” or “person walks out of gate." However, you have to subscribe to the costly Home Premium Advanced at $20 per month to get them. Advanced also enables you to pose questions like “Who opened the back door last night?” or “Did a package arrive today?” and provides a Home Brief summarizing the day's events. Sadly, there’s no local storage option, it lacks a privacy shutter, and the smart features that set it apart require expensive monthly fees.
Google's latest outdoor camera brings most of the same improvements as the indoor version, but it has an IP65 rating, making it suitable for all kinds of weather. It has a handy magnetic mount, but you must run the 18-foot cable to a power outlet. It also has a wider 152-degree field of view than its predecessor and 6X digital zoom capability, so it can zoom and crop on subjects for your animated notifications.
There are only a couple of other Google Nest cameras I've tested that I think are still worth considering for specific circumstances.
- A battery-powered outdoor camera: Google Nest Cam (Battery, Outdoor) for $200
- A hardwired floodlight camera: Google Nest Cam with Floodlight for $280
Best Security Cameras for Smart Homes and Apple HomeKit: Aqara
Some Aqara cameras can double up as smart home hubs, with Matter, Thread, and Zigbee support, which can be very handy if you have loads of smart home devices. There’s also wide smart home standard support, including Apple HomeKit Secure Video. If you go the Apple route, you can avoid using Aqara’s slightly confusing app.
Don’t be fooled by the cutesy look of the Camera Hub G350. The new model of Aqara’s indoor pan and tilt security camera is an impressively feature-packed device that’s perfect for smart home enthusiasts. This is a dual-lens camera with a 133-degree 4K lens and a 2.5K telephoto lens for zooming in on subjects (up to 9x hybrid zoom). The video is crisp, detailed, and vibrant, and the ability to zoom in is very handy. It also has onboard AI that works locally for automatic tracking of people, pets, and sound recognition. As a pan-and-tilt camera, you can spin through 360 degrees, tilt is limited (maybe 45 degrees), and you can fix preset positions to patrol and have it return to a fixed position after tracking a subject out of frame. You get a free trial of the cloud service Home Guardian, but you can also insert a microSD card for local recording. There’s also NAS support. The sleep mode, which you can schedule, has the camera lens roll up and shows a pair of closed eyes.
The G350 doubles as a smart home hub, with Matter, Thread, and Zigbee support, and compatibility with Apple HomeKit, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, Samsung SmartThings, and IFTTT. But there are caveats here. I had no issue adding it via the Matter code to my Google Gemini setup, but Google doesn’t yet support Matter security camera feeds for non-Nest devices, so it’s better to add it via the Aqara app for now. If you opt for HomeKit, Apple limits the camera features and resolution to 1080p. While it can also act as a Zigbee 3.0 hub to bring all kinds of sensors and accessories into your smart home fold, they must be Aqara Zigbee devices (third-party devices are not supported).
Sadly, recording at 20 fps means fast movement can cause blurring, particularly when it’s dark. I don’t like the way you are auto-enrolled into the cloud service (90-day event storage) free trial. While the app has a great range of options, it doesn’t have the best layout. Expect to spend some time rummaging around to configure the camera the way you want. Aqara has also paywalled a bunch of AI features, like filters and video summaries, and enhanced notifications.
This versatile outdoor camera doubles as a Matter controller and a Thread border router, which could be very handy if you have smart lighting in your garden. It's a 2K wired camera (Wi-Fi or PoE) with a 133-degree field of view, and the large sensor has an f/1.0 aperture that enables excellent color night vision. There's also a 100-decibel siren, two-way audio, and there's a spotlight. The onboard AI can identify people, vehicles, animals, and packages. Local recording is supported via internal storage, or you can subscribe for 90-day video history. An Aqara HomeGuardian subscription costs $5 a month or $50 a year for one camera and $10 a month or $100 a year for unlimited cameras. Sadly, some features like event filtering, SMS or email notifications, and video sharing require the subscription. If you have a HomeKit hub, such as a HomePod Mini or Apple TV, and an iCloud storage plan, you can opt for Apple's HomeKit Secure Video. It limits you to 1080p, but rich notifications let you play video clips right from your iPhone's lock screen.
If you opt for Aqara, there's only one other Aqara camera worth buying.
- A cheap 2K camera for indoors or outdoors: Aqara Camera G100 for $40
More Security Cameras Worth Considering
Reolink is a close competitor to Eufy and TP-Link Tapo cameras. It offers innovative security cameras that deliver decent quality footage at relatively low prices. They also support various local storage options. The Reolink Argus 4 Pro ($215) stitches two feeds together for a full 180-degree view, capable of covering the entire side of a building or multiple entry points. The Reolink Elite Wi-Fi ($160) is a hardwired version of the same camera. If you want a pan-and-tilt camera, the Reolink Altas PT Ultra ($220) is very good. You can link any of these with the Reolink Home Hub ($150) for 64 GB of secure storage indoors (expandable by up to 1 TB).
Wyze is another budget brand to consider. The Wyze Cam Pan V4 ($60) is one of the best panning cameras, and offers several improvements over its predecessor, including an upgrade to 4K footage and a built-in spotlight. The smart design allows it to spin 360 degrees and tilt 180 degrees to take in a whole room. I like the option to set waypoints in the app to have it cycle through, the privacy mode, the automatic motion tracking, and the ability to record locally on a microSD card (up to 512 GB). On the downside, you must subscribe for features like AI detection and rich notifications, starting from $3 a month ($20 a year) for a single camera, though that only gets you 14 days of video storage. The frame rate also drops to 15 (from 20) at night, and I found moving subjects, combined with the camera panning, resulted in blurry footage. I am testing Wyze cameras again after the firm beefed up its security policies, but the past security breaches may still give you pause if you’re considering its cameras for inside your home. I also tried the fixed Wyze Cam V4 ($36), which offers clear 2.5K video with WDR and better color night vision than previous versions with a spotlight. That one also has local recording via microSD card (sold separately).I've also tried out the Wyze Window Cam ($35), a 1080p camera that sticks directly to the inside of your window, the Wyze Cam Outdoor V2 ($100), and the Wyze Cam OG ($30).
Amazon's Blink budget brand is also very affordable. The latest Blink Mini 2K+ ($40) is a teeny camera that supports 2K video with 4x hybrid zoom and color night vision, though the field of view has shrunk slightly to 138 degrees. Motion detection is very reliable, but the catch is that you really need the subscription at $3 per month or $30 per year for a single camera, or $10 a month or $100 a year for unlimited cameras. You can technically record locally if you purchase a Sync Module 2 ($50) and insert a USB flash drive. But without a subscription, your live feed is limited to five minutes with no record option, videos are much slower to load, you don’t get people detection, and you can’t share clips. The original Blink Mini ($30) is even cheaper, but footage is only 1080p, bright areas can appear blown out, and the two-way audio often lags and distorts. You can also get the Blink Mini Pan-Tilt Camera for $40, which is a regular Blink Mini camera with a pan-and-tilt mount, so you can pan through 360 degrees and tilt through 135 degrees.
Philips Hue fans with Philips Hue smart lights may find the company’s security cameras intriguing. The Philips Hue Secure Wired Camera ($99) is a wired security camera with an optional weighted base. It feels solid and durable, and it has an IP65 rating. Video on the camera maxes out at 1080p but is crisp and deals with mixed lighting and moving subjects well. It offers a wide 140-degree field of view. Night vision is decent, there’s two-way audio, and it’s quick to send alerts or load the live feed in the Hue app. You get 24 hours of video history in the cloud for free, but if you want more than that, you need to subscribe for $4 per month ($40/year) for a single camera, which gives you 30 days of cloud storage and unlocks smart detection features. The person and animal detection works well, helping to filter out false positives. You can also set multiple activity and privacy zones. There’s vehicle and package detection, too, for outdoor use. There’s no local storage, but footage is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it. If you have a Hue bridge and lights, you can have the Philips Hue Secure trigger them.
Synology is better known for network attached storage. But if you have a Synology NAS, you might consider Synology cameras. They are National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) compliant, so they don’t use any components from certain banned (mostly Chinese) manufacturers and can be used by US federal agencies, and they're Trade Agreement Act (TAA) compliant, too. But they are kinda expensive for the feature-set and quality. You can read more about them in my Best Subscription-Free Cameras guide.
There are various other brands that I've tested that offer some decent cameras, such as Baseus, Swann, Annke, Lorex, Eve, Safemo, and Imilab, but I'd recommend going with something above over these.
Don’t Buy These Security Cameras
There are also several brands that I think you should avoid. I was disappointed after testing security cameras from Ulticam, Chamberlain, Nooie, Switchbot, Canary, Encalife, Winees, Noorio, Vosker, and Night Owl.
Security Camera F.A.Q.
Why Would You Want a Security Camera?
A security camera potentially provides peace of mind. You may want to ensure that no one enters your home when you’re not there, and collect video evidence of wrongdoing. They can be a deterrent for intruders if they are visible.
Many folks use indoor security cameras to check on children, pets, or elderly relatives from anywhere on their smartphone, and they can serve as baby monitors. Most security cameras enable two-way communication with people in and around the home. Some folks use cameras as smart home triggers to automate lighting.
How to Secure Your Security Camera
Security cameras are great tools, but you also need to protect your security from these cameras. You don't want to find out that a stranger has been watching you sit in your bathrobe bingeing trash TV for the third day in a row—or worse. If you follow these tips, you can be a vigilant and conscious consumer and still feel like your home is protected while you're away.
Avoid no-name cameras: If you type "security camera" into Amazon’s search bar, you’ll come up with hundreds of cheap options from brands you’ve never heard of. I don’t feel comfortable recommending them. You should always go with brands that clearly outline their privacy policies and make it easy to set up security protocols. That doesn't mean they can't be hacked—Wyze, Nest, Eufy, and Ring have all had breaches—but you probably won't be hung out to dry by a brand intent on protecting its reputation. Somewhat counterintuitively, it may be better to pick a brand that has had issues, because the increased scrutiny typically encourages them to improve their security practices. (This also depends on how they have responded to previous security breaches.)
Use a strong password and set up two-factor authentication: Setting a strong password you don't use for anything else is extremely important. Always change your password from the default, and also change the password for your Wi-Fi network, if you haven't already. Set up two-factor authentication (2FA) as soon as you create an account with the camera brand you've bought. It will make it harder for a hacker to gain access to your device, even if they do figure out your password.
Keep it updated: Make sure you're frequently checking for software updates (for your camera and router) that can patch any security issues that may have come up. Set your camera to auto-update if possible.
Turn it off: When you're home, or at least when you're doing something personal you wouldn't want someone to see, turn the camera off. Some cameras have a physical shutter that you can close or a sleep mode that obscures the lens. You could also turn the camera around for good measure.
What Features Should I Look for in a Security Camera?
Here are some of the main things to think about when you shop for a security camera.
Video quality: Going for the highest-resolution video isn't always the best idea. While 4K video definitely picks up more detail, it also requires more bandwidth to stream and more storage space to record than 1080p or 2K resolution. Folks with limited Wi-Fi bandwidth must be cautious. A wide field of view is good, so the camera takes in more, but can cause a curved fish-eye effect at the corners, which some cameras are better than others at correcting. If your camera is facing a mixed lighting location with some shadow and direct sunlight (or a streetlight), look for HDR (high dynamic range) or WDR (wide dynamic range) support, as it can prevent bright areas from blowing out or loss of detail in the shadows. Frame rate is also worth thinking about, as a low frame rate can cause artifacts and blurring with moving subjects, especially in low light. Drop below 20 frames per second (fps) and you can expect blurring and jerkiness.
Connectivity: Most security camera systems connect to your Wi-Fi router on the 2.4-GHz band. Depending on where you install, you may appreciate support for the faster 5-GHz band, but it is shorter range. Some systems come with a hub that can act as a Wi-Fi range extender. Bear in mind that you should never install a security camera in a location without a strong Wi-Fi signal.
Subscription model: Most security camera manufacturers offer a subscription service that provides cloud storage for video recording. It isn’t always as optional as it seems. Some manufacturers bundle in smart features such as person detection or activity zones, making a subscription essential to get the best from its cameras. Always factor in the subscription cost, and make sure you are clear on what is included before you buy.
Local or cloud storage: If you don't want a cloud subscription service, make sure your chosen camera offers local storage. Some security cameras have microSD card slots, while others record video to a hub device inside your home. You can also configure some cameras to work with network-attached storage (NAS) or a network video recorder (NVR). A few manufacturers offer limited cloud storage for free, but you can usually expect to pay somewhere around $3 to $10 per month for 30 days of storage for a single camera. For multiple cameras, a longer recording period, or continuous recording, you are looking at paying between $10 and $20 per month. There are usually discounts if you pay annually.
Placement is important: A visible security camera can be a powerful deterrent. You don't want to hide your cameras away. Also, make sure the view isn't peering into a neighbor's window or pointing into your bathroom. Most cameras offer customizable zones to filter out recording or motion detection for areas of the camera's frame.
False positives: Unless you want your phone to ping every time your cat wanders into the frame, consider a security camera that can detect people and filter alerts. Good cameras also enable you to set privacy or activity zones.
Night vision and spotlights: Security cameras generally have infrared night vision, but low-light performance varies wildly. You always lose some detail when light levels are low. Most night vision modes produce monochrome footage. Some manufacturers offer color night vision, though it is often colorized by software and can look odd. I prefer spotlights, as they allow the camera to capture better-quality footage, and the light acts as a further deterrent to any intruder. But they aren’t suitable for every situation.
Camera theft: Concerned about camera theft? Choose a camera that doesn’t have onboard storage. Some manufacturers have replacement policies for camera theft, especially if you have a subscription, but they usually require you to file a police report and have exclusions. Check the policy thoroughly before you buy.
Power: Plug-in security cameras need a power outlet nearby. Some can be hardwired or use Ethernet cables for power (PoE). If you want a device that you can place anywhere, choose a battery-powered camera.
Alternatives to Indoor Security Cameras
Do you really need a security camera inside your home? Most folks can guard against intruders and keep tabs on people coming and going with outdoor security cameras and a video doorbell, and presence sensors can be used to unobtrusively check no one is in your home when you’re not there. There are some good alternatives that don’t involve the risk of a live video and audio feed of you and your family in your private haven.
Can You Use a Phone as a Security Camera?
You don't need to spend money on a new security camera—an old smartphone will do as long as it can still connect to Wi-Fi. Just download a camera app (I like Alfred) to both your old phone and your new phone, then sign in with the same email address. Find a spot to mount your device and keep it charged, and you'll be able to view the camera feed through your current phone.
The field of view won't be as wide, the battery won't last as long, and the mount will probably be a lot less secure. Still, if you're going on a weekend vacation, it's a quick and easy way to set up something essentially for free. Alfred is available for iOS and Android. It offers motion detection and can set off an alarm when it sees someone.
How I Test Security Cameras
I test every security camera for at least two weeks, but often far longer. I run through the installation process and note any issues. I check that alerts come through correctly to my phone when I am home, connected to Wi-Fi, or away connected to a cellular network. I usually place two or more cameras in the same spot to compare picture quality, motion detection, and other features. I consider the image resolution, frame rate, and audio quality of videos and the live feed. I also check for lag with the live feed. I test the performance during the day, see how it copes with the sun facing the lens, and how it performs in the dark at night (testing both spotlight and night vision). I check how long the live feed and recorded videos take to load at different times of the day.
I play around with the settings in the app to try every mode and feature. I test any smart detection features to see if they can correctly identify people. I test the two-way audio for a short conversation and try the siren where applicable. I also test local storage and cloud storage options for recording videos. If there are any smart home integrations, I set them up and check how quickly the feed loads on a smart display. I always ensure the cameras I recommend support 2FA and test any additional security or privacy features.

Britain leads Europe in new defence factory investment
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:29:51 BST
19:29:51 KST

The United Kingdom has taken the largest single share of Europe’s defence manufacturing expansion since the start of 2024, attracting 34 of the 197 facility investments announced or opened across the continent in that period, according to research published by Cushman & Wakefield.
That share of 17 per cent puts Britain ahead of Germany, which accounted for 27 investments, France with 26 and Spain with 12. The property consultancy tracked announcements and openings between January 2024 and August 2026 covering drones, missiles, munitions, combat air systems and other advanced defence technologies, treating each as a driver of demand for industrial and logistics space.
The Defence Investment Plan committed an additional £15 billion between 2026-27 and 2029-30, taking planned defence investment to around £298 billion across the four-year period, and annual defence funding is expected to approach £80 billion by 2029. Governments across Europe are expected to spend more than €625 billion on defence equipment between 2026 and 2029.
The concentration of that money in Britain, France and Germany reflects their standing as the three largest defence producers in Europe, and Spain, Italy, Sweden, Turkey, Belgium and the Netherlands have also drawn significant new investment. Central and eastern Europe, led by Poland, accounts for a substantial share, weighted heavily towards artillery and munitions, which the researchers attribute both to proximity to the war in Ukraine and to those countries ramping up their own defensive capabilities while contributing to wider EU and NATO initiatives.
Artillery and munitions is the largest single category across the continent at 52 facility announcements, bolstered by the European Union’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production, and almost half of that activity is in central and eastern Europe. Aircraft and ships account for 43 commitments, driven in particular by Airbus, Safran and Leonardo, while investment in vehicles has come from BAE Systems, Patria, Rheinmetall, Iveco, Escribano and KNDS. Companies in systems and components have invested heavily as well, across radar and sensor systems, communications and navigation.
Ten of the 21 drone and autonomous vehicle production facility openings and investment announcements recorded since 2024 have been in the United Kingdom, the largest concentration anywhere in Europe. The research counts aerial, surface and ground systems together in that total, and describes their deployment in Ukraine and the Middle East as having driven substantial investment in development and production. Eight aircraft and naval manufacturing investments have also come to Britain, the second-largest share in that category.
Tim Crighton, head of logistics and industrial for the UK and EMEA at Cushman & Wakefield, said: “The UK is exceptionally well positioned to capture this next phase of defence-led industrial growth. Alongside established strengths in aerospace and naval manufacturing, we are seeing increasing investment in drones, autonomous systems and other advanced defence technologies. These sectors are creating demand across a broad range of industrial assets, from purpose-built production facilities to existing industrial buildings that can be adapted and brought into operation swiftly. Working across a range of these projects, we can see the significant investment going into these facilities which in turn is driving economic growth and new skilled employment opportunities.”
More than half of the investments across Europe, 54 per cent, involve newly created facilities, and 36 per cent are being delivered as new-build developments. The average unit size committed to is around 20,000 square metres, and the most frequently demanded buildings fall between 10,000 and 25,000 square metres. Converted buildings feature more heavily in the existing space taken, typically legacy industrial assets taken over wholesale for new production lines.
Many manufacturers can work from conventional industrial buildings adapted for production rather than purpose-built plants, though the research sets out where defence differs from an ordinary industrial letting. Some buildings require blast proofing, internal partitioning or segmentation, and depending on the machinery involved, reinforced floors or larger doors. Sites generally need enhanced security, including higher fences, advanced access systems and surveillance. Lease negotiations run longer because of security checks on the asset, the landlord and neighbouring occupiers, and because government approvals can form part of the conditions for contracting space. Tenants tend to seek greater rights to alter buildings from the outset rather than during a tenancy, and may ask for restrictions on access or enhanced security around a landlord’s inspections.
Industrial estates aimed squarely at the sector have begun to appear, among them Telford Defence and Business Park in the West Midlands, which received development permission in 2024 and has funding in place, marketing what it calls defence-ready opportunities within the established West Midlands cluster. Elsewhere, Estonia has developed the 204-hectare Ermistu Defence Industrial Park, which has secured four manufacturers and has room for more, and a 200-hectare scheme is proposed at North Kiviõli with an emphasis on energetic materials. Turkey’s Kırıkkale weapons industry zone, established in 2014 on land belonging to the state manufacturer MKE, has drawn private firms to build factories on the site.
Sally Bruer, head of EMEA logistics and industrial research at the firm, said: “What is particularly notable is how quickly defence manufacturers’ investment is translating into real estate requirements. More than half of the facility commitments we tracked involve new sites, reflecting manufacturers’ need to increase capacity and secure long-term production capability.
“As large procurement programmes move through the supply chain, we expect this to drive increasing demand for smaller and mid-sized industrial facilities across the broader supplier ecosystem as businesses expand production capacity to support the next phase of defence growth.”
Investment so far has been led by the prime contractors and their tier one suppliers, while Europe’s defence ecosystem takes in more than 2,500 specialist small and medium-sized firms. Expansion is harder for those businesses until orders are placed further up the chain and income starts to arrive, and survey work by GLOBCOM cited in the research found that fewer than half of tier two, three and four suppliers have seen the demand growth the primes and tier ones have enjoyed.

From answering questions to carrying out complex tasks: The next phase of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:29:49 UTC
19:29:49 KST

At the Google Cloud Summit in Doha, AI agents were a major focus as Qatar expands AI training and testing, raising questions over oversight and jobs.
Artificial intelligence is moving beyond generating text, images and answers. Now, developers are trying to get AI to carry out tasks on a user's behalf.
That shift to autonomous or "agentic AI" was a central theme at the Google Cloud Summit in Doha, where the company marked three years since opening its cloud infrastructure in Qatar.
Generative AI creates content in response to a prompt. AI agents go further, working through the steps needed to complete a task.
"Generative AI effectively is where you use AI through large language models to create net new content," Alex Rutter, Managing Director of Google Cloud's Artificial Intelligence business across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told Euronews.
"Agentic is much more focused... on the business process workflow," he added.
From answering questions to carrying out tasks
One area businesses are looking at is repetitive work that involves checking information across different systems.
Rutter gave the example of invoice reconciliation, where information on an invoice may need to be checked against payment and supplier records before a payment is approved.
"An agent is very well suited to that sort of highly repetitive database work, where it would drive a significant level of efficiency," he said.
The more AI is allowed to do on its own, though, the more important human oversight becomes.
Rutter said Google currently advocates keeping people involved in checking the results produced by AI agents.
"We still always advocate to having at this stage a human in the loop to verify for the business the results they're looking at, but the humans are looking at the exception rather than the entire data stack," he said.
The amount of oversight needed would depend on both the task and an organisation's tolerance for risk, according to Rutter. In areas such as medicine, he said AI should support rather than replace a clinician's decision-making.
Qatar expands AI training and testing
Google Cloud used the Doha summit to mark the third anniversary of its local cloud region and announced a new national skilling programme with Qatar Digital Academy.
The programme is expected to provide more than 50,000 learning opportunities in Qatar by 2030, with training aimed at different groups including workers, executives and developers, according to Google Cloud.
Ghassan Kosta, Regional General Manager for Google Cloud in Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and Iraq, said the company was also expanding its services to support more advanced AI systems.
"We are doubling down on our services to accommodate this agentic AI era," Kosta told Euronews.
"In our data centres, to cope with how the technology and how the AI is moving, you need also the right infrastructure in place."
Another initiative announced at the summit is an innovation lab developed by Qatar's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) in partnership with Google Cloud.
Amna Al-Kaabi, Head of Emerging Technologies at the ministry, told Euronews the lab would allow AI projects to be tested before being put into use.
"The core value of this partnership lies in linking technology experimentation within the lab to real sector needs," Al-Kaabi said, adding that the aim was to help projects move "from proof-of-concept stage to sustainable real-world implementations."
What happens to the workforce?
That ability to hand more work to AI also brings the conversation back to jobs.
Rutter cautioned that predicting those changes remains difficult, but said he expects managing AI agents to become part of some people's jobs.
"I think what is very real is we're going to have non-people managers, we'll then have agent managers, and then we'll have people that manage people and agents together," he said.
That could mean some workers eventually managing AI agents as part of their jobs.
But Rutter acknowledged it is difficult to predict how quickly that might happen. For now, companies are still figuring out where AI agents are useful and how much human oversight they need.
