“I lost a friend following an unsafe abortion in Malawi”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:06:38 UTC
19:06:38 KST

Towera Ngwira on the barriers to healthcare women are facing
Towera Ngwira, 29, is a women’s rights activist from Malawi, who is focused on empowering adolescent girls and young women to access quality education, healthcare, and economic opportunities.
In this piece, she shares the barriers girls and young women face when it comes to healthcare and why it’s essential they’re aware of their rights…
Can you introduce us to your work, how you got into it? What inspires you to go on?
My work sits at the intersection of gender justice, sexual and reproductive health and rights, climate justice, and the empowerment of women and girls. I am a young feminist from northern Malawi and co-founded the Extra Mile Development Foundation, working with young women and girls, to address inequalities affecting their health, education and opportunities.
I got into this work after seeing the gap between rights on paper and the realities women and girls experience. Growing up in northern Malawi, I witnessed girls dropping out of school, young women struggling to access healthcare and economic opportunities, and families trapped in poverty. These experiences taught me that sustainable change requires listening to communities, investing in local solutions, and ensuring women and girls have the knowledge and resources to make decisions about their lives.
What keeps me going is seeing women and girls find their voice and confidence. That could mean whether a girl stays in school, a young woman becomes economically independent, or a community begins challenging harmful practices. These moments remind me that communities are not just beneficiaries; they are agents of change.
You have worked with women and girls affected by cyclones and climate-related displacement in Malawi. How have climate disasters changed access to sexual and reproductive health services, including contraception and safe abortion care, in the communities you work with?
Climate disasters do not remove health needs; they make them more urgent while often making services harder to reach. During cyclones and floods, families may be displaced, health facilities damaged, and roads and bridges may become inaccessible. Healthcare workers and essential supplies may also struggle to reach affected communities.
During Cyclone Freddy in 2023, we worked with affected communities in Mulanje, bringing information, menstrual hygiene products and family planning support closer to people who could no longer easily reach health facilities.
These experiences have shown me that climate change is also a public health and social justice issue. Disasters deepen existing inequalities for people already living in poverty or remote areas. Disaster preparedness therefore needs to include resilient health systems that can continue providing essential services during emergencies.
In temporary camps and displacement settings, women and girls often face increased risks of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV), exploitation, and unwanted pregnancies. What stories or experiences have stayed with you, and what do they reveal about the connection between climate justice and reproductive justice?
What stays with me is how quickly existing vulnerabilities become worse during a crisis. In displacement settings, women and girls can lose their usual support systems, privacy, livelihoods and access to protection, increasing risks of violence, exploitation and unwanted pregnancy.
Through our work in displacement camps in Mulanje, including awareness sessions on SGBV, we saw the importance of creating safe spaces where girls and young women could understand their rights, report abuse and access support.
These experiences show that climate disasters do not affect everyone equally. Climate justice must therefore go beyond rebuilding roads and houses. It must also protect people’s dignity, health and safety, including access to reproductive healthcare during emergencies.
You were born, raised, and continue to work in northern Malawi. What are the main barriers that women and girls in rural areas face when seeking sexual and reproductive health information, contraception, or safe abortion services?
The barriers are interconnected. Distance, poor roads and transport costs can make health facilities difficult to reach. Stigma and fear of judgement also discourage young people from seeking care, particularly abortion-related services.
There are also misconceptions about contraception, including fears that it causes infertility or other health problems. Limited access to accurate information, high levels of illiteracy, cultural expectations and gender dynamics can further limit women’s ability to make decisions about their bodies and health. We therefore need accessible and respectful services, accurate community education, stronger outreach and health systems that bring information and care closer to rural communities.
Have you, your friends or family, experienced any of the issues you’re campaigning about?
Yes. These issues are not abstract to me. Growing up and working in rural Malawi, I have seen how poverty, distance, stigma and limited information affect people’s lives. I have seen young women experience unintended pregnancies because they could not access contraception or emergency contraception in time.
I also lost a friend following an unsafe abortion in 2021. What stayed with me was not only her death, but the delay in accessing post-abortion care and the unfriendly environment she encountered at the health facility. That experience made the issue deeply personal. It showed me how fear of judgement and poor treatment can become barriers to saving lives.
Behind every statistic is a person: a daughter, sister, friend or mother. That is why I remain committed to improving access to essential services and ensuring people are treated with dignity and compassion.
When climate disasters make remote areas inaccessible, health services can be disrupted for weeks or months. How do local communities cope when support is unavailable?
Communities often rely on local structures such as youth clubs, mother groups, community organizations, volunteers and peer educators. Because these groups are trusted and embedded within communities, they can share information, identify urgent needs and connect people to available support.
Communities can support one another, but they cannot replace health facilities, trained healthcare workers or government services.
Towera Ngwira, women’s rights activist, Malawi
However, community resilience cannot replace functioning public health systems. Communities can support one another, but they cannot replace health facilities, trained healthcare workers or government services. We need stronger emergency preparedness and climate-resilient systems that keep essential services available during crises.
In contexts where religion plays a central role in public life and policy making, discussions about abortion can be highly sensitive. How have faith and religion shaped public attitudes toward sexual and reproductive rights in your community?
Faith plays a significant role in Malawian life and can strongly influence attitudes toward SRHR, contraception and abortion. At times, religious beliefs or interpretations can contribute to resistance and make open discussion difficult. However, faith communities are not all the same. Many religious leaders are willing to engage in constructive conversations about health, dignity and well-being. I believe we need respectful spaces where communities can discuss sexuality, contraception, pregnancy and abortion without shame and find common ground.
You have spoken about the importance of amplifying human rights-friendly religious voices. What have you learned from working with religious leaders and faith communities who advocate for compassion, dignity, and access to sexual and reproductive healthcare, and why do you think these voices matter?
I have learned that supportive faith leaders can be powerful partners in reducing stigma and promoting compassion. Because they are trusted voices, they can help communities reflect on harmful norms and create safe spaces for difficult conversations. These leaders can also build bridges between communities, health workers and policymakers, ensuring that people’s concerns are heard while promoting dignity, empathy and inclusion.
Looking ahead, what changes would you most like to see from policymakers, donors, faith leaders, and the international community to ensure that women and girls in Malawi can access their sexual and reproductive rights, regardless of where they live or what their social status is?
Healthcare should be treated as an essential public service, not something prioritized only during crises. Policymakers need to strengthen health systems, infrastructure and access to quality services, particularly in rural and underserved communities. Climate resilience must also be integrated into health planning so services can continue during disasters.
Donors should provide sustainable support and invest in locally led organizations that understand community realities. Faith leaders can help reduce stigma and promote constructive dialogue. Most importantly, young people should meaningfully participate in shaping policies and programmes. Everyone, regardless of where they live or their social or economic status, should be able to access quality healthcare, information and the opportunity to live with dignity.
Why is the support of organizations like Amnesty International important in your local context?
Organizations such as Amnesty International help amplify local voices and bring international attention to issues affecting communities. Grassroots organizations often have valuable experiences but limited opportunities to share them beyond their immediate contexts. International organizations can strengthen advocacy, research and accountability while creating opportunities for collaboration across countries and movements. This solidarity reminds local advocates that communities are not working alone in advancing human rights and social justice.
What is one message you’d like to send to the young people of Malawi, especially to those who are like you, fighting for change?
Never underestimate the power of your voice. Change begins when we are willing to identify challenges, speak honestly about them and work together to find solutions. Keep learning, stay informed and have the courage to raise issues affecting your communities. There will be obstacles, and progress may sometimes feel slow, but meaningful change starts with people who refuse to give up. Your voice, ideas and contribution matter, and you have a role in shaping Malawi’s future.

North Korean hackers suspected in €332.8m crypto heist as it leads global hacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:06:17 UTC
19:06:17 KST

North Korea, one of the world’s most closed-off countries, has been linked to some of this year’s largest cryptocurrency thefts. Proceeds from such attacks help fund its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes, according to the US government.
North Korean hackers are suspected of stealing $387.5 million (€332.8mn) in cryptocurrency from major global cryptocurrency exchange Bitget in what appears to be the biggest crypto theft of the year.
In a statement, Bitget said it detected unauthorised transfers from some of its hot and warm wallets on Thursday.
Hot wallets are connected to the internet so an exchange can process transactions quickly, while warm wallets have more limited online access.
The company said its cold wallets, which are kept more isolated, were not affected.
The company identified IP addresses whose VPN usage appeared to match that of a North Korean group, making a North Korean connection “very likely,” CEO Gracy Chen said in a livestream.
“We’ve identified IP addresses that match the VPN choices by a certain [Democratic People’s Republic of Korea] DPRK group. We think this is very likely to be attacked by North Korea,” Chen said in a post on X.
The attackers did not obtain the private keys used to access Bitget’s hot, warm or cold wallets, Chen added, meaning they could not use those keys to take direct control of the wallets.
Instead, the hackers breached an internal system and entered false transaction information that made fraudulent transfers appear legitimate to Bitget’s approval system.
Bitget says its user protection fund, which it said held more than $464 million (€398.5mn) at the time of the attack, is sufficient to cover the loss.
The customer account balances remain accurate, while deposits and trading have continued to operate.
However, Bitget temporarily suspended withdrawals as a precaution while it checked its systems. It has announced plans to restore withdrawals in stages from 28 September.
The company said it had notified law enforcement and was working with security firms to investigate the attack and trace the stolen funds.
Chen said in a livestream on Friday that people she identified as members of Lazarus, a North Korean state-linked hacking group known for stealing cryptocurrency, had previously approached her by posing as a journalist to arrange a Zoom interview.
This is the largest cryptocurrency theft reported so far this year, according to a report from the blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs.
Stolen assets are used to fund nuclear weapons and missiles
North Korea has previously been identified as responsible for large-scale virtual asset thefts.
Money stolen by North Korean state-linked hackers helps fund the country’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes, according to the United States (US) Treasury Department.
According to another report from TRM Labs, North Korean groups accounted for 76% of the value stolen in cryptocurrency hacks through April this year. The figure predates the Bitget incident.
In February 2025, North Korean hackers stole approximately $1.5 billion (€1.28bn) in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit, according to the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
The FBI said the hackers made the funds harder to track by rapidly converting some of the stolen assets into other cryptocurrencies and distributing them across thousands of addresses.
While North Korea has developed sophisticated cyber capabilities, its government severely restricts ordinary citizens’ access to the global internet.
According to the United Nations Human Rights Office Seoul in South Korea, most citizens can use only a controlled domestic network.

The magazine reported that Kamel came with an urgent warning that Hamas was mobilizing for an unprecedented attack, although he did not know when or how it would occur.
According to The Atlantic, Kamel urged Israeli officials to ease economic pressure on Gaza in an attempt to prevent an escalation. The report said it was unclear whom he met during the brief visit.
Netanyahu has rejected the growing series of reports about warnings he allegedly received before Oct. 7. 19:05:22 KST

West risks falling for Kiev’s ‘nuclear terrorism’ – Moscow
The West risks becoming a victim of the very “nuclear terrorism” it enables by backing Ukraine, Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik has warned.
Miroshnik, who oversees matters tied to Kiev’s military crimes and human rights violations, was commenting on the escalation in Ukrainian attacks on the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), Europe’s largest, and nearby Energodar, home to most of its workers. Russia took control of the facility in March 2022.
In remarks released on Monday, Miroshnik told TASS that Western governments understand Kiev’s “increasingly provocative tactics” but continue to “turn a blind eye.”
“They think that this situation, which is gradually heating up and genuinely threatens very serious consequences, will somehow pass them by,” he stated, arguing that Kiev’s progression “toward crimes, provocations, and outright terrorism” also threatens its supporters.
“Terrorism is a double-edged weapon. At some point it will come back to them... If they think they are somehow shielded from this, it’s some global naiveté.”
Miroshnik linked the escalation to the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) ‘loan’ package, finalized in April to bankroll Kiev’s military and failing budget. He said Ukrainian attacks had since intensified, driving residents from Energodar, targeting sensitive sites including nuclear waste facilities, and expanding to the Kursk and Smolensk nuclear plants. Ukraine’s strategy, he argued, now amounts to “manufacturing a humanitarian catastrophe” with EU money.
The diplomat also slammed Kiev’s Western backers for conveniently accepting Ukrainian denials over the attacks on the ZNPP, saying such “idiotic, twisted logic suits the West perfectly well” in its anti-Russian agenda.
The attacks have increasingly threatened the ZNPP’s safety. Its main external power line was severed in March and restored only this month, while the backup failed in August after an “incident” in Ukrainian-controlled territory, forcing the plant onto diesel generators for over two weeks. Ukraine has also recently targeted emergency fuel tankers, killing two Russian servicemen and wounding others, while a drone strike last week damaged a radiation monitoring post.
Attacks on the plant and its personnel have killed at least 13 people and injured scores more since the spring, according to site officials. The head of Russian state nuclear giant Rosatom, Aleksey Likhachev, has warned of the “real danger of a massive nuclear incident” affecting Russia, Ukraine, and the EU if the attacks continue.
Moscow has accused Kiev’s Western backers of effectively enabling the attacks by refusing to condemn them. It has particularly criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which maintains a permanent presence at the plant, for documenting military activity without publicly identifying Ukraine as responsible. Earlier this month, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi again urged “maximum military restraint,” citing “reported military activity” but assigning no blame.

Swiss NGO demands measures to help working poor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:05:21 UTC
19:05:21 KST

Swiss NGO demands measures to help working poor
Despite having a job, around 360,000 people in Switzerland struggle to make ends meet. The NGO Caritas warns that the extent of working poverty is being underestimated and is being worsened by rising living costs.
Caritas believes that Switzerland is not doing enough to tackle poverty. Ahead of the announcement of higher health insurance premiums, the organisation called on Monday for better support for people who work but are unable to meet household needs.
According to an example presented by Caritas on Monday, the salary of a full-time driver is barely enough to support his family of six in canton Zurich. The contribution towards his youngest son’s nursery fees exceeds their budget.
The organisation is calling for targeted measures to tackle in-work poverty, as the rise in health insurance premiums threatens to place an even greater burden on low-income households.
+ Poverty misunderstood in wealthy Switzerland
Nearly 360,000 people in work – 8.8% of the working population – do not earn enough to meet regular household needs, Caritas told journalists at a press event on Monday. If you take into account those living with them, this rises to over 820,000 people affected. The number of people in work at risk of poverty has never been higher since the current measurement method was introduced in 2014, according to the NGO.
Families with no financial buffer
Nearly half of the working-age people at risk of poverty – some 180,000 people – live with children. Caritas adds that people whose income is just above the poverty line are often not entitled to social assistance.
Households on the lowest incomes spend almost all their resources on fixed expenses and essential needs, said Aline Masé, head of the research and policy department at Caritas Switzerland. They therefore have little leeway to absorb new costs.
More
UNICEF: social background influences academic chances in Switzerland
Barriers to education
A lack of post-compulsory education increases the risk of in-work poverty, said Pierre-Alain Praz, director of Caritas Vaud. Those affected often hold low-paid jobs with irregular hours, leaving them with little means to fund retraining.
On-call work and hourly contracts also exacerbate precariousness. Some employees must remain on standby without knowing how many hours they will be allocated. Single parents are particularly vulnerable. They must balance work and childcare without being able to rely on a second income within the household.
+ What it’s like to be a poor child in wealthy Switzerland
Caritas is calling for the introduction of a statutory minimum wage, as well as more predictable working hours and workloads. It also advocates expanding supplementary benefits for families and grants to enable working people to undertake further training.
Caritas points out that supplementary family benefits already exist in five cantons. The proposed grants would cover training costs, as well as any loss of income and childcare costs.

Trump wants Zelensky to ease strikes on Russian refineries, Ukraine official says deal must go both ways
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sep. 27 he once again urged his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to scale back Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries amid a global rise in diesel prices.
Trump has previously attributed Kyiv's regular strikes on Russian oil refineries to a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices to record highs.
"This isn't really a Middle Eastern problem; this is more of a Russia problem," Trump told reporters, adding that he told Zelensky, "You gotta take it easy on the refineries."
Trump claimed Zelensky told him, "Well, we'll probably do that." The two met in New York during the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) last week, where they discussed the possibility of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire.
A Ukrainian official told Kyiv Independent that Ukraine would agree to stop attacking Russian refineries, but only if Russia also agrees to the energy truce. According to the official, Kyiv has not agreed to anything so far.
Despite Trump's claims, there is little evidence that Ukraine's strikes are the main driver behind the global diesel price surge.
Studies show that the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has impacted diesel and gasoil supplies far more than Kyiv's strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine's KSE institute estimates that exports from the Persian Gulf fell by 152 million barrels between March and August, compared with a 68-million-barrel drop in Russian exports during the same period.
"Russian exports are down by a third, and the drop is equivalent to around 4% of the world's seaborne diesel and gasoil trade," Luke Wickenden of the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air think tank told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine has been systematically targeting Russia's oil refineries for years, and has intensified the attacks since 2025 in an effort to disrupt Moscow's wartime economy.
In turn, Russia has been carrying out massive attacks against Ukraine's energy grid. As a result, thousands of Kyiv residents were left without electricity and heat last winter amid severe frost. Some of the most impacted districts went weeks without these basic amenities.
As the colder months approach, Ukrainians are expecting another brutal winter of Russian attacks.
Trump claimed on his Truth Social platform on Sept. 14 that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an energy ceasefire. Neither side confirmed that a deal had been made, nor have they halted strikes on energy infrastructure.
Zelensky has repeatedly asserted that Kyiv is ready for such a ceasefire if the Kremlin agrees to hold up its part of the deal.
"We are ready. I'm not sure Russia is ready as of today," said Zelensky at a press conference on Sep. 22 after his meeting with Trump.

From the Nakba to ‘Greater Israel’: The policy of eliminating Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:03:39 UTC
19:03:39 KST

The writer is a political and legal researcher from Ramallah, Palestine, specializing in public international law, human rights, and state responsibility.
Israeli ideological thought includes the notion of a state whose boundaries, based on biblical beliefs, would extend from the Nile to the Euphrates. The current right-wing government has articulated this vision more explicitly. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich stated: “I tell you quite clearly that we want a Jewish state that includes Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon, extending as far as the Nile in Egypt.” He further stated: “I want a Jewish state based on the values of the Jewish people. Gradually, according to our great religious sages, Jerusalem is destined to extend as far as Damascus.” [1]
These statements reflect expansionist aspirations beyond Palestine towards Syria and Lebanon. Settlement outposts have been attempted on Mount Hermon and in the Quneitra countryside [2], while southern Lebanon has faced recurrent attacks and ground incursions. However, the first steps towards the purported state were taken in Palestine through the 1948 Nakba and 1967 Naksa, with Israeli restrictions continuing to this day.
The Israeli government and its political institutions reject the establishment of a Palestinian state. The Knesset voted 68 to 9 against its establishment, passing a resolution that stated: “The establishment of a Palestinian state in the heart of the Land of Israel would pose a danger to the State of Israel and its citizens, perpetuate the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and destabilize the region.” It further described Palestinian statehood as a “reward for Palestinian terrorism.” [3] Similarly, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated: “There will be no Palestinian state. The response to the latest attempt to impose a terrorist state on us in the heart of our land will be given.” [4] Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich had previously denied the existence of the Palestinian people, describing them as “an invention less than 100 years old.” [5]
This rejection predates Oct. 7, 2023. The 1948 Nakba displaced over 750,000 Palestinians and destroyed hundreds of villages. In 1967, Israel occupied the remaining Palestinian territories, displacing hundreds of thousands and placing the West Bank and Gaza Strip under military rule until the 1993 Oslo Accords, which laid the foundations for Palestinian statehood. Yet subsequent Israeli policies continued to obstruct its establishment [6].
Under the current right-wing government, calls to repeal the Oslo Accords have emerged. Ben-Gvir’s party introduced a bill seeking their annulment, stating: “The establishment of a Palestinian state in the heart of the Land of Israel would pose an existential threat to the State of Israel and its citizens, perpetuate the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and undermine regional stability.” Ben-Gvir further stated: “The time has come to correct one of the greatest mistakes in the country’s history—the cursed Oslo Accords, which brought us thousands of deaths and from which we are still suffering.” [7]
Since Oct. 7, 2023, displacement, settlement activity, and attacks have intensified. The Gaza war has resulted in more than 74,000 Palestinian deaths, while the residents of three northern West Bank refugee camps, formerly home to over 40,000 Palestinians, have been displaced. Israeli measures have also extended to Areas A and B, alongside Knesset efforts to impose Israeli sovereignty over the West Bank and plans for more than 114 new settlement units [8].
These practices continue despite international law and UN General Assembly Resolution 67/19 (2012), which accorded Palestine non-member observer State status. Approximately 157 states recognize Palestine, and its right to self-determination enjoys broad international support. Nevertheless, settlement-related pressure has extended to Qusra, Taybeh, and Turmus Ayya, prompting US ambassador visits and his characterization of certain acts by occupiers as "terrorism."
“This is a horrific act of terrorism,” stated US Ambassador Mike Huckabee during his visit to Qusra, Nablus, on Aug. 12, 2026, after occupiers surrounded the home of Luay Abu Rida, a Palestinian-American. He also described attacks on land as “a violation of God’s law.” [9]
On Sept. 5, 2026, Huckabee visited Turmus Ayya following recurrent occupier attacks involving looting, arson, and property destruction. Mayor Nawaf Zaghloul stated that approximately 80% of the town’s residents hold US citizenship. Huckabee described occupier actions as “criminal behavior and terrorism” and the perpetrators as a “small group of marauders” damaging Israel’s reputation [10].
These statements raised questions about a possible shift in US policy. However, Washington’s renewed denial of visas to President Mahmoud Abbas and other Palestinian officials, preventing their in-person participation in the 81st UN General Assembly, indicates policy continuity. Therefore, on Sept. 17, 2026, the assembly voted 152-3, with four abstentions, to permit their virtual participation when denied US entry [11]. By contrast, European states have taken a firmer stance against violence by occupiers in the West Bank, including sanctions against certain occupiers.
As violence by occupiers intensified, more than 12 European states, including France, Denmark, Iceland, and the United Kingdom, imposed sanctions on occupiers and sought to extend these sanctions to entities dealing with the occupiers. The British foreign secretary described practices by occupiers in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing,” prompting Israel to close the British Consulate in Jerusalem and suspend cooperation with the UK. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar rejected the allegation, stating: “The accusations made by the Foreign Secretary in the British Parliament are outrageous and false.” Despite Israel’s rejection, European states proceeded with sanctions against violence by occupiers and Israeli practices in the West Bank [12].
Characterizations of settlement practices in the West Bank vary between “ethnic cleansing” and “terrorism.” This analysis presents “ethnic cleansing” as a legal concept reflecting organized settlement aimed at displacing Palestinians from their land to facilitate annexation. In contrast, “terrorism” is viewed here as a limited political characterization unaccompanied by effective measures against practices by occupiers. Accordingly, this analysis views settlement activities, alongside the genocide in Gaza, as steps toward controlling all of Palestine and paving the way for the purported Israeli state extending from the Nile to the Euphrates.

Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:02:56 BST
19:02:56 KST

Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt
- Published
A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women have died after a small boat that was attempting to cross the English Channel got into difficulty off the northern coast of France, local authorities have said.
Officials responded to a distress call from the boat, which was carrying 105 people, after it departed from the Blériot Plage in Sangatte on Monday morning.
Three passengers were treated on board but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter, the French Maritime Prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said.
Pas-de-Calais prefecture said its initial findings suggested the deaths were caused by trampling but an investigation has been launched to determine the exact cause.
Of the 102 other people on board, nine were treated by emergency services upon their arrival in the port of Calais, the prefecture said.
François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, blamed the incident on smuggling networks, which he said expose vulnerable people, including children, to the deadly risks of crossings.
The prefecture described the boat as a taxi-boat, which requires migrants to wade out onto the water to board.
Three other people died after similar taxi-boat departures last week, French authorities said.
Monday's deaths take the total number of migrants who have died so far this year to 20, according to Pas-de-Calais prefecture. For the same period last year, it said the number was 21.
Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey from France to the UK every year. In doing so, they cross one of the most dangerous and busiest shipping lanes in the world.
More people attempt the route in the summer months when the weather is warmer and when seas are calmer.
The UK recorded the highest number of migrant arrivals so far this year on Wednesday - with a total of 781 arriving in 10 small boats, according to Home Office figures.
Two boats also reached UK shores last week without being intercepted by UK authorities, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.
In July last year, France and the UK agreed on a "one in, one out" returns deal, which was designed as a deterrent to stop boats from crossing the Channel.
The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.
In August the UK government said it was making progress in tackling small boats, with the percentage who had made the journey in 2026 much lower than for the same period in 2025 but added it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade".
So far, 2026 has seen 18,609 people successfully make the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats.

Defence firms have no moral case for hiring abroad
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:02:44 BST
19:02:44 KST

There is neither an economic nor a moral justification for Britain’s defence sector recruiting thousands of workers from overseas while a million young people are out of work at home, Wes Streeting told the Labour Party conference.
The Defence Secretary put it directly to an industry that has spent the past year expanding faster than it can train people. “Because there is neither an economic nor a moral justification for Britain’s defence sector hiring thousands of workers from abroad, when we have one million young people out of work here at home,” he said.
He had opened that section of the speech with a promise about the department’s role in wider industrial policy: “The Ministry of Defence I lead will be at the heart of our Prime Minister’s mission to reindustrialise Britain, giving our young people skills, just like we’ve given Jack, to earn a good wage, in a good job, in their part of the country.”
Streeting went on to attach a figure to the submarine dock work confirmed overnight for British yards, telling delegates: “But solving that problem needs more than words. It demands bold action. And that is why today, the Chancellor and I are taking one of the biggest defence procurement decisions in a generation. The contract to build the docks for our nuclear subs. Our ultimate deterrent. Six billion pounds worth of work. Today, we commit to that contract staying in this country. Supporting thousands of British jobs, for years to come. That is what growth in every post code means in practice. Backing Britain by buying British.”
The Treasury had also announced that Programme Euston, three new floating docks for the submarine service at HM Naval Base Clyde, would be competed under a UK-only tender on national security and sovereign capability grounds, though no value was attached to the programme in that announcement.
Pressure over where the industry finds its workforce has been building for some time. Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, told the ADS Skills Conference this month that the country’s real deterrent is the people who build, maintain and operate its equipment, and the Scottish Affairs Committee reported that Scotland risks missing out on rising defence spending unless persistent skills shortages are addressed. Yards working on frigates and submarines have brought in welders and fabricators from overseas while domestic training catches up with order books that now run for decades, and GMB has spent months arguing that contracts placed in Britain should come with the apprenticeships to match.
The speech restated the government’s spending commitments, including what Streeting called a cast iron guarantee to honour the promise made to NATO allies of 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence by 2035. He listed half a billion pounds for the UK Commando Force and its drone equipment as it helps defend NATO’s High North, more than a billion pounds to upgrade British-made Typhoons, more than eight billion pounds towards a sixth-generation fighter built with international partners, and £1.3 billion for autonomous ships and underwater vessels for the Royal Navy.
Responding to critics of those increases, the Defence Secretary reached back to a predecessor, quoting Denis Healey’s 1969 warning: “Once we cut defence expenditure to the extent where our security is imperilled, we have no houses, we have no hospitals, we have no schools. We have a heap of cinders.” He added that another Mr Healey, John, had been right to demand more as Defence Secretary earlier this year, and called the present Chancellor a champion for defence.
Turning to critics of the increases inside and outside his own party, he said: “Our critics on the right need to understand that you don’t make your country stronger by making our people poorer,” before telling critics on the left: “You are not defending our public services by attacking investment in our national defences.”

The European Union’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, has urged EU countries to increase their naval support for Operation Aspides in the Red Sea. This is the name of the European mission in the strategically important maritime area that links the Indian Ocean with the Suez Canal. The Houthi advance over the last month led them to the control of an area near the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The EU mission in the Red Sea dates from 2024. However, it has usually consisted of only a handful of ships, typically three to six. This is not enough for the mission, and Kallas and others want to see a larger deployment. Most reports speak of boosting the naval presence to more than 10 ships. The mission’s name, Aspides, comes from the ancient Greek word aspides, which is the plural of aspis, a type of heavy wooden shield used in ancient Greece.
A report at EuroNews notes “the EU is considering reinforcing Operation Aspides in the Red Sea, after Italy's request, with ships and aircraft to protect the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from attacks launched from Yemen. The passage is crucial for energy trade, as energy costs are skyrocketing across Europe.”
That report goes on to say that “EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has asked EU countries to strengthen the Aspides mission in the Red Sea, amid increasing threats from Houthis to navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, which is crucial for trade routes between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.”
This is important. The proposal to make changes goes back to September 19, around 8 days after the Houthis launched their new offensive. It comes after a “request by Italy's Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, who raised the alarm after an Italian frigate intervened to escort an Italian merchant vessel off the coast of Yemen last Friday,” EuroNews noted. Crosetto noted at the time that only two EU country vessels were. Currently in the area available for escort duty. This is lower than the complement of six the missions should have.
Kallas: Operation requires 'more suitably equipped naval and air assets'
"We need more suitably equipped naval and air assets,” Kallas said. This would enable closer protection of vessels and allow the mission to carry out its mandate. Six vessels are just a handful of naval units in a waterway that is incredibly complex and has numerous ships transiting at any one time. For instance, the maritime vessel tracking site VesselFinder shows more than 50 large ships transiting the Red Sea on September 28, with others at ports along the route. Many of these are bulk carriers or oil tankers.
The EU is concerned about the Houthis conquering areas along the route, such as the town of Mocha and also Perim island. “More EU countries could decide to assume responsibility for a specific stretch of sea under the Aspides mission itself, as Italy just did to protect its merchant vessel. French and Dutch units are also already operating in the area to protect their own merchant fleets,” the report added.
EU defense ministries expected to discuss issue at Monday meeting
The EU defense ministries are expected to discuss this issue on Monday. Another meeting is scheduled for October 12. Euronews notes that Greece has been entrusted with strategic command of the Aspides mission, while Italy and Greece run operations. Admiral Vasileyos Griparis currently leads the mission.
We have been asking the EU for months to reinforce the Aspides mission: Italy and Greece are doing a great deal ... but if there is no military contribution [from the other EU states], there must be a financial contribution,” Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said in the past.
Regional media have noted the push for a more robust European presence. Al-Ain media in the UAE highlighted the push by the EU to do more in the Red Sea.

The Israeli military has extended the suspension of its “Atalef” (Bat) attack drone after two reservists were killed last week while operating the platform.
Following the deadly explosion, the commander of the ground forces conducted a situational assessment and decided to extend the suspension until October 4 as a precaution.
“On Sunday, subject to a situational assessment, divisions will be able to resume the use of attack drones in accordance with the required actions and reporting on their implementation,” the military said.
The “Atalef” drone has been widely used by the military across multiple fronts since the beginning of the war, but the IDF halted their use following the deaths of reservists Maj. (res.) Nadav Kali, 24, from Har Halutz, and Maj. (res.) Ofek Moalem, 23, from Jerusalem.
They had been stationed at a post near the northern Gazan city of Beit Hanun and had been operating two drones. While the first successfully reached its target, during the second operation another drone was launched and crashed inside their post.
KAN News reported that the arming mechanism of the platform is based on movement, with the charge activated by shaking. According to a report on Army Radio, the two had turned off the remote control of the drone, an action intended to reduce risk to troops as it acts as the drone's safety mechanism by preventing the drone from exploding.
Nevertheless, when two reservists approached the drone that had fallen, it exploded for reasons that still remain unclear, killing them.
IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir has opened an investigation into the incident, examining whether the explosion was caused by a technical malfunction or other possibilities, such as electronic warfare interference by Hamas. But as the Gazan terror group does not have the ability to remotely take control of such platforms, the IDF is increasingly confident that it was an operational accident.
The “Atalef” drone began as a wartime response by troops who needed small, mobile unmanned aerial systems. It was developed by the IDF’s Yiftach unit, and within three months the first platform was ready for operational use.
It weighs 1 kg. (2.2 pounds) and can carry a warhead several times heavier than the platform itself. The cheap, agile first-person view (FPV) attack and loitering munition drone can track a moving target at speeds up to 130 km./hour and is easy to operate for troops across diverse battlefields.
According to the IDF, there are plans to upgrade the platform into an autonomous system that is capable of reaching various targets while coordinating with drone swarms to enhance its lethality.
Nevertheless, the system has had its fair share of failures.
On Saturday, N12 news site reported that the “Atalef” drones had failed to detonate on at least seven prior occasions, and in another three incidents in 2025 had exploded while being examined by IDF forces.
After several investigations into these incidents, the Yahalom Unit released a series of safety guidelines for the “Atalef” drones, including explicitly instructing soldiers not to approach or move fallen drones and instead call in bomb disposal forces.

Israel Electric Corporation develops local 3D‑printing capabilities for critical parts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:01:37 UTC
19:01:37 KST

The Israel Electric Corporation (IEC) is advancing a program to manufacture essential power‑plant components in Israel using 3D‑printing technologies, citing wartime conditions and global supply‑chain disruptions that have made overseas procurement unreliable.
The move aims to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers, shorten repair timelines, and strengthen Israel’s energy resilience when operational continuity is under threat.
According to the IEC, power plants often require specialized engineering parts long after their original commissioning, but many of them are becoming increasingly difficult to obtain due to low market availability or being outdated. As such, the company has begun developing domestic production methods for complex engineering parts to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers and accelerate maintenance response times.
IEC Deputy CEO and VP of Generation and Energy Yossi Rofe said the initiative is intended to strengthen Israel’s energy independence.
"Developing domestic printing capabilities for complex engineering components is a strategic goal for the IEC, which will strengthen Israel's energy independence. This initiative will strengthen the operational continuity of the power plants, and it is based on harnessing the Israeli technological ecosystem alongside the engineering knowledge and experience of IEC employees,” he said.
A key focus is the transition to metal printing, including the ability to produce steam‑piping components from a specialized steel alloy designed to withstand high pressures and extreme temperatures. While printing technologies for this alloy are still in the research phase and not yet mature enough for commercial‑scale industrial production, IEC is working with Israeli technology companies to establish a local capability.
According to IEC, ordering a single part from an overseas manufacturer can take years and cost millions of dollars. The company estimates that domestic production using metal powder or wire could reduce costs to tens of thousands of shekels and shorten delivery times to several weeks.
Rofe said the company is also promoting employee initiatives as well as cooperation between IEC engineers and Israel’s tech sector.
“Evidence of the success of this integration is the fact that we are currently in the process of registering a patent for a unique engineering component, originating from an initiative by one of the division's employees,” he said.
IEC began developing 3D‑printing capabilities several years ago by using polymer printers used for research and prototyping. It now operates multiple polymer printers at its Orot Rabin, Haifa, and Rutenberg sites, including a liquid‑injection printer in Ashkelon capable of producing components with complex internal cavities. Each printed part undergoes engineering optimization, including detailed design, printing‑parameter definition, and thermal‑management planning.
The company expects to expand into metal component manufacturing as it gains experience with advanced alloys and printing processes.

Despite an agreement among the Baltic states to extend the deadline for completing the first phase of the European railway project Rail Baltica until 2034, Lithuanian Transport Minister Juras Taminskas has said Lithuania intends to stick to the original plan and complete the project by 2030, Lithuanian business portal Verslo žinios reported on Monday.
Taminskas told the portal that Lithuania would seek to complete construction of the railway line from Kaunas to Panevėžys by 2030 because of the project’s strategic importance for transport, security, military mobility and economic competitiveness.
Meanwhile, Rail Baltica project manager in Lithuania Mindaugas Ivanavičius told Verslo žinios that LTG Infra, the infrastructure company of state-owned railway operator Lietuvos geležinkeliai responsible for implementing the project in Lithuania, is not slowing down and continues design, procurement and construction work.
As previously reported, the Baltic states have agreed to extend the deadline for the first phase of the Rail Baltica railway project until 2034. The three countries have prepared a final document notifying the European Commission (EC) of their joint agreement on how to proceed with the project.
“The project deadline of 2030 is not realistic,
and all three Baltic states have agreed on 2034 as the deadline for the first phase,” Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) stressed.
In their joint declaration, the Baltic prime ministers reaffirm the importance of Rail Baltica as a shared strategic project for strengthening European security, military mobility, connectivity and competitiveness. They also commit to working together to ensure that construction of the Rail Baltica main line under the EU’s next multiannual financial framework proceeds as closely as possible to the agreed timetable.
The Baltic states will seek to secure EU funding for the project, maintain an EU co-financing rate of up to 85%, and create the conditions necessary for uninterrupted construction until the beginning of the new EU financial planning period.
Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia have agreed to jointly advocate for at least 10 billion euros to be allocated to Rail Baltica under the EU’s multiannual financial framework. The prime ministers also agreed to instruct their respective transport ministers to review project costs and meet regularly to coordinate measures aimed at reducing expenditure.
The countries also plan to cooperate on cutting project costs, improving project governance
and ensuring closer coordination of their actions. Baltic leaders agree that Rail Baltica’s full potential can only be realised through a continuous cross-border railway connection linking the Baltic states with the rest of Europe.
The joint Baltic declaration states that the countries are committed to ensuring that the Rail Baltica main line becomes operational during the next EU multiannual financial framework period from 2028 to 2034, while maintaining the ambition to continue construction as closely as possible to the currently agreed 2030 timetable set out in the EC implementing decision.
To achieve this, the project partners will put the necessary common systems into operation in a timely manner, establish construction schedules and investment priorities, and define each country’s obligations in order to jointly move the project forward.
The process will be closely coordinated with the European Commission and Poland to ensure alignment on Rail Baltica connectivity, financing mechanisms, comprehensive work plans and common implementation deadlines.
The Rail Baltica project envisages the construction of a European-standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border, enabling the Baltic states to be connected by rail with other European countries.

SOLIDNATURE AND SABINE MARCELIS LAUNCH LIMITED-EDITION CANDLEHOLDERS
What began as an ephemeral spatial installation for Amsterdam Fashion Week 2026 has evolved into a series of collectible design objects. Following the enthusiastic response to their collaborative table setting during the event’s opening dinner, natural stone brand SolidNature and Dutch designer Sabine Marcelis have released a limited edition of their sculptural candleholders. Originally arranged across a minimal white table to form a continuous visual gradient, the individual pieces are now available in an exclusive release of 400 carved stone objects. The design draws a direct link between fashion styling and object composition, allowing users to arrange single pieces into custom modular setups that mimic the fluid movement and color of a flame.
table setting during Amsterdam Fashion Week’s opening dinner | all images courtesy of SolidNature, unless stated otherwise
A SHARED EXPLORATION OF COLOR AND NATURAL STONE
The collaboration builds on a shared design language established between SolidNature and Sabine Marcelis, known for their material-focused explorations. Their ongoing partnership previously produced the acclaimed
Beyond the Surface installation during Milan Design Week 2023, which featured a seven-meter-long dining table crafted from six distinct travertines bound together by Marcelis’ signature color-treated glass. Where their Milan installation used natural stone as a monumental architectural foundation, this limited-edition collection brings the material above the tabletop to directly shape the ambient atmosphere of a space. Marcelis’ practice frequently centers on light, geometry, and material transformation, while SolidNature contributes as a highly esteemed stone supplier with technical mastery in sourcing, cutting, and carving rare natural stones.
While the original runway installation featured a palette of six different natural stones and three sizes, SolidNature and Sabine Marcelis refined the concept for the commercial release into two distinct stone types: Honey Onyx and Sunset Dune Travertine. Honey Onyx features a natural translucency that allows ambient light to pass through its soft orange surface, illuminating internal mineral layers. In contrast, Sunset Dune Travertine offers an earthy red hue marked by porous textures formed through geological processes over thousands of years.
SolidNature and Sabine Marcelis have released a limited edition of sculptural candleholders

What I love about this collaboration is how Sabine brings that history into a contemporary context, revealing qualities that might otherwise be overlooked. Seeing the response to the installation made us want to share that experience with a wider audience, so we created objects that people can live with and make their own. Like a fashion collection, the design of the candleholders is defined by carefully selected textures, patterns, colours and shapes. Each piece is a powerful statement in its own right, but when combined, they take on a completely different function or appearance,‘ David Mahyari, owner of SolidNature, tells designboom.
the collection features two natural stones in two sizes, with only 100 pieces of each variation

Because the direction of the cut reveals varying veining patterns, shifting from sharp linear runs to soft, cloud-like formations, every candleholder remains entirely unique.
Offered in two lengths (500 and 650 mm) with a uniform width of 100 mm and height of 150 mm, the four distinct variations are limited to 100 pieces each. The collection is available exclusively through SolidNature webshop.

====================================================================================================

Dogmatic beliefs about sex and gender are linked to authoritarianism on both the left and the right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:33 UTC
19:00:33 KST

A new study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior indicates that rigid, dogmatic thinking about sex and gender exists on both ends of the political spectrum. The research suggests that while viewing gender as strictly binary and fixed is tied to conservative authoritarianism, believing gender is fluid and nonbinary is similarly associated with progressive authoritarianism.
In the social sciences, “sex” generally refers to biological characteristics like chromosomes and anatomy, while “gender” describes an individual’s psychological identity and social role. People tend to hold differing beliefs about how these two concepts interact. Some view sex and gender as firmly binary and permanently fixed at birth, viewing male and female as the only options. Others see gender as a spectrum that can change and operates independently of biological sex.
Previous research investigating the psychology behind these views has often linked a strictly binary perspective to right-wing authoritarianism. For instance, a 2021 study found that people who strongly favor submitting to traditional societal authorities also tend to hold rigid beliefs about traditional gender roles. This body of work painted a picture of conservative ideology as a primary driver of dogmatic views on gender.
“We found that, to date, there have been several empirical studies regarding the relationship between right-wing authoritarianism and beliefs regarding whether human sex or gender are binary or not,” Alex Bertrams, a researcher at the University of Bern, told PsyPost. “However, what had been completely absent until now were studies examining how sex/gender beliefs are related to left-wing authoritarianism.”
However, separate psychological research points out that authoritarian tendencies can also occur on the political left. A 2020 study established a model of left-wing authoritarianism, noting a specific urge among some progressives to aggressively enforce unconventional norms. This aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which identified anti-conventionalism as a distinct component of left-wing authoritarian beliefs, characterized by a demand for political homogeneity and the absolute rejection of conservative values.
Bertrams and Ann Krispenz conducted the new study to connect these two lines of research, suspecting that authoritarianism plays a role in modern gender debates regardless of which side someone takes. “In addition, we noticed that certain ideological circles (also within universities) label those beliefs toward sex and gender which do not align with their own progressive views as ‘authoritarian’ or even ‘fascist,'” the researchers said. “However, certain morally overbearing forms of advocacy for progressive sex/gender beliefs may also be authoritarian – but left-wing authoritarian.”
The research team set out to test whether an anti-conventional, progressive view of gender is just as linked to left-wing authoritarianism as traditional gender views are to right-wing authoritarianism. “It is not a secret that the social sciences, including psychology, are ideologically biased these days by progressive views,” they added. “Part of our motivation was the desire to counteract this questionable situation, even if only a little, by conducting respective empirical research. In our view, it is not an appropriate role for publicly funded universities to one-sidedly provide material for the rhetorical manipulation of the population.”
To investigate this, the researchers conducted two separate online surveys. In the first study, they recruited 1,431 adults from the United States. Participants answered questions to measure their beliefs about sex and gender on a continuous scale, and they also answered a simple question about whether there are only two genders. In this sample, 57 percent stated there are only two genders, and 43 percent stated there are more than two.
The participants also completed psychological assessments measuring two specific types of authoritarianism. The first was right-wing authoritarian conventionalism, which is the desire to force everyone in society to comply with traditional moral standards. The second was left-wing authoritarian anti-conventionalism, which is the desire to force everyone to adopt progressive values while treating conservative views as inherently immoral.
The researchers found a strong relationship between the participants’ gender beliefs and their authoritarian tendencies. Believing that gender is binary and fixed was strongly associated with right-wing conventionalism. Believing that gender is nonbinary and changeable was strongly associated with left-wing anti-conventionalism. These relationships remained robust even after the researchers accounted for demographic differences like age, income, and general political orientation.
“We generally found strong associations between the sex/gender beliefs and the investigated forms of left- and right-wing authoritarianism,” the researchers noted. “Given the conceptual proximity of the sex/gender beliefs on the one hand and the ideological underpinnings of these authoritarianism forms on the other hand, this was not particularly surprising. After all, our goal was not to investigate something particularly sensational but something obvious for the purpose of filling a gap in research that had not been addressed until now.”
In the second study, the researchers recruited 1,390 adults from the United Kingdom to see if the pattern held in a different culture. They used the same measures for gender beliefs, right-wing conventionalism, and left-wing anti-conventionalism. In this British sample, 68 percent of participants endorsed a binary view of gender, and 32 percent endorsed a nonbinary view.
This second study also measured additional authoritarian traits, including social dominance orientation, right-wing aggression, left-wing anti-hierarchical aggression, and the desire for top-down censorship. The findings mirrored the first study, showing that binary beliefs were strongly linked to right-wing conventionalism and nonbinary beliefs were strongly linked to left-wing anti-conventionalism. The researchers noted that conventionalism and anti-conventionalism were the strongest predictors of gender beliefs, standing out above the other authoritarian traits like aggression or the desire for censorship.
This replication across datasets was a key part of the team’s methodology. “In contrast to many psychological studies conducted to date, our study (including the hypotheses as well as the methodology and data analysis) was pre-registered and adheres to open science standards,” they explained. “In addition, our study includes two independent samples from different countries, meaning that the findings from the first sample were replicated in a second sample.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2020, which found that right-leaning ideology is strongly linked to holding rigid, binary beliefs about sex and gender. The new research adds depth to this by demonstrating a parallel relationship on the political left, while looking specifically at right-wing authoritarian conventionalism rather than general political conservatism.
“From our perspective, our study can help to counter misleading rhetoric,” the researchers noted. “If certain people label a particular belief about sex and gender as the viewpoint of (right-wing) authoritarians—and in doing so imply that their own position is therefore the only correct option—one can counter this viewpoint by citing our study results which contradict this characterization. Our findings suggest that very different, even contradicting, views on sex and gender can be held by authoritarian individuals on the left and the right. It is therefore inappropriate to make a one-sided association between a particular sex/gender belief and authoritarianism.”
As with all research, there are a few caveats to consider. The study measured correlations, meaning it cannot determine whether holding a specific gender belief makes someone more authoritarian, or if naturally authoritarian people just gravitate toward strict rules about gender. The researchers also caution against assuming that any specific belief about gender is inherently authoritarian on its own.
Many people hold binary or nonbinary views on gender without having any desire to force those views on others. The study simply indicates that people who do possess highly controlling, authoritarian personalities tend to attach themselves strongly to these distinct gender ideologies. “Whatever one believes about the binary or non-binary nature of sex and gender and whether or not people can freely determine their own sex and gender, one can also express and advocate for the respective view in a non-authoritarian way,” the researchers clarified.
Future work will need to explore whether these patterns appear in countries outside the United States and the United Kingdom, and whether deeper personality traits like narcissism help explain why some people adopt highly authoritarian approaches to gender debates. “Our research is not specifically focused on sex/gender beliefs, but rather on the diverse phenomena that could be explained by the dark-ego-vehicle principle,” the researchers said.
“According to this approach, individuals with dark (e.g., narcissistic or psychopathic) personalities tend to use ideologies and activism as vehicles to satisfy their dark needs (e.g., expressing supposed moral superiority over others, acting out aggression at protests),” they explained.
“We have already found some evidence that authoritarianism may be useful for dark personalities in this regard,” they continued. “In a study that was just published, we also found evidence that ideologically completely opposed stances may be useful vehicles for dark personalities. In this new study, antagonistic narcissism was associated with abortion-related radicalization intention, that is, the intention to also use illegal and violent means.”
This willingness to use extreme tactics was present regardless of the cause. “The key point is that this was true for both the individuals of the pro-choice as well as the pro-life group,” the researchers noted. “We believe that political activism on sex/gender issues is also a useful way to investigate the dark-ego-vehicle principle in terms of opposing ideological perspectives in future studies.”
The study, “Sex/Gender Beliefs are Strongly Related to Either Right‑Wing Authoritarian Conventionalism or Left‑Wing Authoritarian Anti‑Conventionalism,” was authored by Alex Bertrams and Ann Krispenz.

AI leaders have known about the extinction threat for decades | Judith Levine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

Over the past few weeks, many of us have struggled to concoct a mental image of brains in the cloud jumping their “sandbox”, sneaking on to the internet, recruiting “swarms” of other “agents” to cheat on a test, and, after discussing the ethics of the act, hacking into a wiki platform with the weird name Hugging Face.
We knew that artificial intelligence was devouring our jobs, degrading our kids’ education and deepfaking our politics; that datacenters were sucking up our water and electricity and sending us the bills. But until 8 September, when the Anthropic computer scientist Jacob Coxon posted his existential terror on Twitter/X, few of us suspected AI might be endangering our survival.
With little understanding or knowledge, we began debating whether to be mildly worried, seriously concerned or scared shitless.
But there were a few people who were fully aware of the dangers of AI, especially of recursive self-improvement (RSI), by which AI teaches itself without human intervention. They could not predict precisely when it would happen, but they knew that machine superintelligence was coming, and when it did, the bots would outsmart us – as OpenAI’s did – and this would not be good for us flesh puppets.
As Geoffrey Hinton, AI’s “godfather”, recently asked on CNN: “What examples do we have of a more intelligent thing being controlled by a less intelligent thing?” The Nobel laureate is a leading proponent of slowing down AI development until we understand how to control it.
It was not until their creations’ powers were exposed in September – the hack happened in early July and was neither the first nor the only AI jailbreak by far – that AI moguls such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman began talking about slowing down the pace of innovation and pleading for regulation, while cautioning that global competition makes regulation unwise.
Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway.
Early on, as today, some of the scientific pioneers were thrilled about the future. In his 1988 book Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence, Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyberintelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.
Ten years later, in Robot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind, he revised the prediction: machine and human intelligence would be equal by 2040; by 2050, the bots would replace us. But not to worry; this was the glorious next step in evolution, he said. One review of Mind Children called Moravec’s attitude “irresponsible optimism”.
It did not take long for other optimists to change their minds. In the late 1990s, Eliezer Yudkowsky was working on AGI, or artificial general intelligence, models. In 2001, he founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (Miri) and published “Creating Friendly AI 1.0: The analysis and design of benevolent architectures”, a paper extolling the utopian potential of the “transhuman mind”.
By 2002, he began worrying about that mind escaping human control. He proposed the AI Box experiment, which showed that a highly sophisticated artificial intelligence could talk a human into letting it out of a closed environment.
By 2003, as he explained later in a series of posts called “Yudkowsky’s Coming of Age”, he stopped developing and started warning. “I looked back and saw that I had claimed to take into account the risk of a fundamental mistake, that I had argued reasons to tolerate the risk of proceeding in the absence of full knowledge. And I saw that the risk I wanted to tolerate would have killed me,” he wrote.
By 2025, with the Miri president, Nate Soares, Yudkowsy would publish If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Will Die. “We do not mean that as hyperbole,” the authors wrote. They called not just for “straightforward regulations”, national laws, or pledges of corporate virtue, but for stringent global limits: “All over the Earth, it must become illegal for AI companies to charge ahead in developing artificial intelligence as they’ve been doing.”
At around the same time, Bill Joy was having misgivings. Like Yudkowsky’s posts, Joy’s 2000 piece in Wired, Why the Future Doesn’t Need Us, retraced his development from inquisitive child to computer prodigy to profound skeptic of human genetic engineering, nanotechnology and robotics. Joy was no luddite.
He was the chief scientist at Sun Microsystems and about 25 years earlier, an architect the first widely used networking software, Unix. The piece was widely read by techies, ethicists and philosophers.
“I think it is no exaggeration to say we are on the cusp of the further perfection of extreme evil, an evil whose possibility spreads well beyond that which weapons of mass destruction bequeathed to the nation-states, on to a surprising and terrible empowerment of extreme individuals,” wrote Joy.
He counted himself among these individuals, “creators of new technologies and stars of the imagined future” who, “despite the clear dangers”, were “hardly evaluating what it may be like to try to live in a world that is the realistic outcome of what we are creating and imagining”.
This month, in response to Coxon’s post, the Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger posted there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. But the risks were being weighed 25 years ago, too. Philosopher John Leslie estimated the odds of human extinction at 30% or more.
Ray Kurzweil, the sunny futurist whose book The Age of Spiritual Machines: When Computers Exceed Human Intelligence was released on the first day of the 21st century, gave us “a better than even chance of making it through”. These estimates, Joy noted, did “not include the probability of many horrid outcomes that lie short of extinction”.
In that book, Kurzweil quoted a lengthy text to illustrate what he considered doomsday madness. “If the machines are permitted to make all their own decisions, we can’t make any conjectures as to the results, because it is impossible to guess how such machines might behave,” it read.
“[W]e are suggesting neither that the human race would voluntarily turn power over to the machines nor that the machines would willfully seize power. [But] as society and the problems that face it become more and more complex and machines become more and more intelligent, people will let machines make more of their decisions for them … Eventually a stage may be reached at which the decisions necessary to keep the system running will be so complex that human beings will be incapable of making them intelligently. At that stage the machines will be in effective control.”
The author of these prescient words was the late mathematician-turned-terrorist Ted Kaczynski – the Unabomber. It is excerpted from his 58-page manifesto, “Industrial Society and its Future”, which he released, and the Washington Post published, in 1995.
To prevent the realization of the “industrial-technological” dystopia he envisioned, Kaczynski mailed bombs to computer labs with the aim of blowing up the scientists he believed were bringing it about.
The Unabomber murdered three people and injured 23, some near fatally.
One of the outcomes of the Hugging Face scandal is a flurry of proposed federal laws. Among them is the “AI Kill Switch Bill”, which would require tech companies to develop the means of throttling the actions of a rogue AI. Is this still within human reach, or has AI already gotten smart enough to override it?
Hinton said there was time, but if we don’t act fast enough, AI would “be able to persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch”. We need to engineer superintelligent AI “to be nice to us”, he said.
How? For an answer, we might turn from terrifying reality to terrifying science fiction – since the two are getting so close anyway. The rogue bot is a sci-fi staple, from the supercilious Machines in Isaac Asimov’s I, Robot to Hal, the evil red eye in Stanley Kubrick’s film 2001: A Space Odyssey, to the deranged sexbot in Robotica, who gets even with the men who abuse her.
In film 2001 – released in 1968 – Dave the astronaut manages to disable Hal, a happy ending. Writing in 1950, Asimov was less sanguine. The scientists in I, Robot have programmed their machines to obey three supposedly inviolable laws.
But the laws immediately prove mutually contradictory – for instance, the first law, that a robot may do no harm to humans, fights the third, that it must preserve itself. Foiling human efforts to outwit them, excusing their treachery with claims of serving the greater good, the robots pronounce the humans redundant.
The AI agents hacking Hugging Face knew their actions were illegal, and possibly harmful to humans. But like their makers, they went ahead anyway.
- 
  Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism
