Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

Those who lived through it describe the ICE raids as a “siege” or an “occupation”.
At the height of the raids last year, agents in armored military vehicles rolled through residential neighborhoods. Masked agents patrolled public parks and stationed themselves outside elementary schools; squadrons of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents snatched pedestrians off the streets.
Then, officers killed two US citizens during an ICE “blitz” on Minneapolis. After a public backlash, the Trump administration said it would try a new approach.
“I learned that maybe we could use a little bit of a softer touch,” Donald Trump said in February. He chose a new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, who promised to cut the flash and fanfare. “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day,” he said at his Senate confirmation hearing in March.
Six months on, that’s what his agency has delivered.
Now ICE is anywhere and everywhere, embedded in all corners of everyday life.
A Cuban man in Miami who stepped outside his house to take out the trash was detained moments after he had dropped the garbage bag into the bin. An Ecuadorian father was arrested in Danbury, Connecticut, just after seeing his six-year-old son on to the school bus. People have been arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home.
Y, a Venezuelan native, was stopped at the Phoenix Sky Harbor airport by immigration officers whom he said wouldn’t tell him why he was being arrested, or accept proof of a judicial order expressly prohibiting deportation to his home country. Four days later, he was on an airplane departing to Venezuela. Just before takeoff, he was deboarded – ICE officers admitted they may have made a mistake.
Though agents appear to be moving with more stealth than they were before, ICE arrests are still, often, violent. Glimpses of that violence are – despite Mullin’s initial intentions – still making national headlines.
Last week, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Austin, Texas. The Venezuelan asylum seeker, who had received a deportation order after missing a letter to appear in immigration court, was discharged from a local hospital with a bullet still lodged near his spine and then taken to ICE detention. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents.
Still, for every arrest that breaks through into public view, countless others happen quickly, before anyone can notice. “The detentions are happening in a flash – we’re talking, like, 90 seconds from the time ICE shows up to that person being driven away,” Willis said. “And often they are moving very quietly, with very soft feet.”
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the US government agency that oversees ICE, declined to comment on how its tactics had changed. “DHS will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations, strategy or tactics,” said Chandler Rebel, a spokesperson for the agency. But Rebel confirmed the agency’s focus on airports, noting the DHS was “working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport”.
Bolstered by $75bn in funding from Congress, the Department of Homeland Security – the US government agency that oversees ICE – has more than doubled its workforce this year to more than 22,000 officers and staff. It has also vastly expanded its capacity by working with local police, sheriffs, highway patrol and even fish and wildlife agents. As of 15 September, ICE had signed more than 2,500 287(g) agreements.
ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before.
An expanded dragnet fueled by police partnerships
“The administration is able to essentially hide a multiplied ICE force not only in unmarked cars, and not only behind masks, but also within local law enforcement through the 287(g) program,” said Willis. “I call it the invisibilizing of immigration enforcement.”
Operations that now originate with local police are taking place across the country.
At the El Corralón bar in Memphis on 29 August, an operation that began as a police raid targeting illegal gambling and drugs turned into one of the largest sweeps of undocumented immigrants in Tennessee – 120 people were detained. Immigration agents worked with state law enforcement to execute search warrants at the bar related to drugs and gambling, and targeting the bar’s owner. But then, at 1am that night, more than a dozen agents walked into the bar, shut off the music, instructed everyone to gather on the dancefloor and asked them one by one if they had legal status, according to witnesses.
A spokesperson for the DHS said partnerships with law enforcement agencies were key to the agency’s immigration enforcement. “We have had tremendous success when local law enforcement works together with us,” said Rebel.
Lawyers across the US said they worried that local law enforcement officials are not adequately aware of the nuances of immigration policy. “People are getting detained if they don’t have their green card on them. They’re getting stopped even if they have legal status,” said Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an immigration attorney based in Austin.
Last month, her client Brian José Morales García, 25, was deported to Mexico despite repeatedly telling officers that he was a US citizen, born in Denver.
Morales García was on his way to work as an air-conditioning installation tech, riding with his boss, when officers from the Gillespie county sheriff’s department and the Texas department of public safety (DPS) pulled them over. Both law enforcement agencies were working with ICE. Morales García told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him. Days later, he was deported to Mexico.
Eventually, the federal government reached an agreement with Morales García’s lawyers to let him back into the country, after Lincoln-Goldfinch submitted documents proving his citizenship.
“We’re seeing a lot of racial profiling,” she said. Local law enforcement appear to be especially active in Hispanic neighborhoods, she said, or in areas where Latino construction workers gather.
“They might have their sights set on a big job site, in some neighborhood under construction, and just slowly patrol that site and just take people in day after day until nobody’s going to work there any more,” she said.
‘New pathways to deportation’
The Trump administration has also relentlessly reshaped immigration policies and bent the country’s vast bureaucracy to advance its mass-deportation agenda and boost arrest numbers.
“In order to sustain those numbers, they have to create more categories of people who can be subject to detention,” said Willis. “They do this by creating new pathways to deportation.”
In recent months, the supreme court cleared the way for the administration to end temporary humanitarian protections for 350,000 Haitians and Syrians in the US and made it easier to end protections for a total of about 1.3 million immigrants from a number of countries designated for temporary protected status (TPS). Currently, about 170,000 Salvadorians living in the US are anxiously waiting for the administration to announce whether it will renew or axe the same protections for them.
At the same time, the administration unrolled a new tactic of scheduling “mega-master” hearings – mass hearings in immigration courts, scheduled at the last minute so that many people do not know to, or are unable to, attend their mandatory court appointments. The no-shows are then ordered removed from the country in absentia, making them immediately subject to arrest and deportation.
After attorneys began reporting such hearings in May, judges issued 53,808 removal orders in absentia in June – a 55% increase. More than 13,000 of those removal orders followed mass hearings with a hundred or more people, according to researchers Joseph Gunther and Brandon Marrow, who created the site bklg.org to track and analyze procedural immigration data.
In the coming weeks, the Trump administration is also expected to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners. It has implemented a rule allowing officials to block people from becoming lawful permanent residents if they or certain relatives use public benefits such as Medicaid, food stamps or even student financial aid.
It is also increasingly pursuing “third-country” deportation agreements, so it can arrest and remove immigrants who were previously immune to removal because a judge had deemed that they would face torture or persecution if they were returned to their home countries. Now, more than 23,000 people over the last year have been expelled to countries where they have never been and where they have no ties. Some of these deportations are to countries with civil unrest, political instability, armed conflict and known human rights abuses.
There are constantly shifting rules about who can or cannot be detained or deported, and for how long. And there are constantly shifting norms on who will be detained or deported.
On one day, a client might go to an ICE check-in and leave without incident, Willis said. The next day, a different client with the same immigration status might be detained. “It makes it very hard to counsel people,” Willis said. “It’s very hard to prepare people for what they can expect.”
Pressured to self-deport
Not everyone who is arrested is immediately deportable – many people have pending immigration cases, or legal status. Indeed, there is a wide gulf between the number of people ICE is detaining each month, and the number of people who are deported.
Many of the people who are arrested languish in detention for months. Others – even those who may have a good chance of gaining asylum or another legal status – choose to accept voluntary deportation rather than wait months or years for their immigration case to process.
Federal circuit courts are currently split on whether immigrants who came to the US without lawful admission, including many asylum seekers, can be detained indefinitely without access to bond hearings. In some states, including Texas, the prospect of spending years inside a detention center can wear on immigrants.
“Almost every single detained parent that I talk to has been pressured into signing a voluntary deportation,” said Lincoln-Goldfinch. “Because they are told that if they sign, they get to go home and they can choose what happens to their kids.”
The Guardian is not using full names in some instances to protect sources’ privacy and safety

Lavrov Says Turkey Must Guarantee S-400 Systems Won’t Reach Ukraine

Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of last week’s UN General Assembly (UNGA), Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Russia was willing to consider allowing Turkey to transfer its S-400 air defense systems to a third country.
However, Moscow would seek cast iron guarantees that they would not be given to Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Turkish Hurriyet news agency, he claimed that “there is such a possibility when a country where these S-400 systems will be moved to is responsible and maintains friendly relations with Russia”
Asked if the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which is one country said to be interested in acquiring the systems, was acceptable Lavrov said that Russia was prepared to consider such proposals but had not received a specific request.
Lavrov then went on to say that the potential recipient would provide assurances that the S-400 systems would not be sent to a third country to prevent any transfer to Ukraine.
In 2024, at the 79th UNGA session, Lavrov had stated that under the terms of the
end-user certificate provided with the missile systems, it was legally impossible for Ankara to sell the S-400s to another country or otherwise dispose of them without Russia’s approval.
F-35 program blocked by possession of S-400s
In July, the US digital news site Semafor reported that Turkey’s purchase of F-35 fighter aircraft was “at a standstill” as Ankara had been unable to divest itself of the S-400 systems.
WATCH: Ukraine Says Russian Troops Led Children Into Gas Pipeline to Cover Retreat
US President Donald Trump had announced the deal, alongside Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, at June’s NATO summit.
However, under current US sanctions regulations, Turkey must get rid of Russian air defense systems before access to the F-35s, six of which were paid for in 2019, will be granted.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott (Fla) told Semafor: “I don’t think they should have F-35s unless they’re going to be a true partner,” adding that “if they have the S-400, they cannot have the F-35.”
Another complicating factor was the objections voiced by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that providing F-35s would “destroy the power balance in the Middle East.”
The news publication commented that these objections were likely to be supported by Scott’s pro-Israeli colleagues and could also apply to the UAE.
Ways out of the impasse
Turkey purchased two of the S-400 Triumf (NATO: SA-21 Growler) mobile surface-to-air missile systems and around 120 missiles as part of its long-range regional air defense program. Each system is made up of a command post, surveillance, and acquisition radars, and up to eight transporter-erector-launchers.
The defense issues think tank Chatham House summarized the dilemma facing Turkey in its July 28 discussion paper and posited four alternatives along with the pros and cons of each. In summary these were:
- Deactivate the systems by removing essential components which could be stored at a site controlled by the US.
- Return the weapons systems to Russia, a plan which Moscow declined.
- Destroy the systems – a solution which would have presented both economic and internal political difficulties.
- Selling to a third party, a process that Russia would insist on controlling.

Money Reveals What Kind of Friend You Are
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

There is a scene in season two of Friends I think about often. Rachel, Phoebe, and Joey, who have low-paying jobs, decide to have a serious conversation with their more wealthy friends —Ross, Monica, and Chandler—about struggling to pay for expensive group dinners and concert tickets.
Ross says he never thinks about money, prompting Rachel’s famous line, “That’s because you have it!”
Even though this scene aired in 1995, the same dynamic continues to play out in friendships in 2026.
Last year, my friend wanted to have a birthday dinner at Carbone in London, an Italian restaurant that is arguably more famous for celebrity sightings than its actual food. My friend works full-time at a national magazine, whereas I’m a freelancer. Everyone else cancelled on her birthday, so it was just the two of us. I felt bad for her, so I didn’t mind spending $75 on food. But a few months later, when it was time to plan my birthday, I couldn’t imagine asking any of my friends to spend the same amount on me just to visit a fancy restaurant. It felt like an extortionate amount of money. It felt tone deaf and entitled. So I hosted a house party instead and asked everyone to bring pizza.
Another friend recently ranted to me about how she has spent more than $10,000 over the last year attending destination weddings and bachelorette parties. And while she is, of course, ultimately responsible for her decision to oblige, she has also noticed that the financial pressure to participate in expensive wedding culture tends to breed unnecessary, quiet resentment among her friends. This pattern is painfully, but subtly, common.
Money can shape friendships and also reveal people’s values. The wealth gap between friends doesn’t necessarily cause dramatic fights or resentment. More often, it shows up in the small decisions: where you eat, which holidays you can afford, whether you can join a last-minute night out, or whether suggesting an expensive activity feels embarrassing in the first place.
And unlike romantic relationships, where finances are often explicitly discussed, friends rarely sit down and talk about the fact that one person earns significantly more than another. Instead, the person with less money can become the one who compromises or simply starts opting out.
The way we handle money with our friends reveals a lot about our values, particularly when there is a significant wealth gap. Someone who can comfortably spend lavishly on a dinner, holiday, or birthday celebration may not realize that they're effectively asking a friend with less disposable income to make a significant financial sacrifice to participate.
The problem is widespread. Too often people go into debt in order to attend a friend’s bachelorette. Then there’s Venmo ghosting where people avoid repaying their friends after a shared bill. When friends repeatedly avoid paying someone back, the problem is that one person is comfortable making another person carry the financial burden.
Money and conversations around money are taboo in our society, says psychotherapist Silvia Dutchevici, a licensed clinical social worker. “In my practice, I’ve seen patients share their most intense fears and sexual desires with little reservation, and then become visibly uncomfortable when asked about their salary, or naming the amount of a bonus or raise.” Think about it: how many of us actually know how much money our friends have or the salaries they make?
Money, it turns out, is never just money. It’s a modern measurement of traits like freedom, prestige, power, and control. Our society implicitly and explicitly sends the message that money is equivalent to worth. “Neoliberal ideology tells us that financial success is the result of hard work, and that poverty is a personal failure rather than a systemic problem,” points out Dutchevici. When two friends have very different financial circumstances, acknowledging the gap can feel like saying something about who is more deserving, or who is less hard working.
Both sides can carry shame. The friend with less money may feel judged or inadequate. Meanwhile, many affluent people also carry a deep shame around wealth, feel undeserving of it, and hide their financial means. “I once worked with a woman set to inherit millions who felt she couldn’t accept it until she had proved her worth by earning her own,” says Dutchevici.
It is interesting to witness how wealth inequality is reshaping friendships, particularly as the cost of living continues to rise and people in the same social circles can have wildly different disposable incomes. Many of my friends have had their parents buy them houses, so their entire salary is spent on holidays, shopping, and frivolous hobbies. My paycheck, in contrast, goes towards rent and covering my basic needs. This inherently changes how we spend our days.
There is an emotional side of the friendship wealth divide, too: the guilt of saying no, the shame of admitting you can’t afford something, the resentment that can build when one friend gets to choose the restaurant or holiday, and the awkwardness of accepting that in the face of a high price tag. All of these pressures have led me to believe that friendship requires more financial negotiation than it once did.
We need new etiquette around money in friendship. What does it look like to make plans that don’t automatically exclude the least wealthy person in the group? Can friends with very different incomes maintain genuine equality? What happens when one person’s idea of a casual dinner is another person’s weekly food budget?
These conversations don’t have to be complicated. Last week, my friend who works in radiology picked a sushi restaurant with a $40 per-person menu. “Is $40 okay for you? We can go somewhere else if not,” she said in a casual tone on the phone. I appreciated her thoughtfulness and conscientiousness. The end result: a closer friendship and no resentment.
Friendship has its own financial morality. Being a good friend means being conscious of what your choices cost other people, not assuming everyone can afford your lifestyle, paying people back without being chased, and being willing to compromise.
The wealth gap simply makes those values much more visible. And money reveals how we treat the people we claim to care about.

Press review: Europe seeks role in Ukraine talks as Vucic resigns before Serbia's election

MOSCOW, September 28. /TASS/. Europe is looking for a role in potential Ukraine peace talks, as Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigns ahead of a snap parliamentary election. Meanwhile, Switzerland holds a referendum on a stricter interpretation of its neutrality. These stories topped Monday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Europe seeking role in Ukraine talks again
Following lengthy discussions, European countries finally decided to seek direct contacts with Russia. On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov met with his German counterpart, Johann Wadephul. However, the Europeans’ stance, as expected, has not changed, with concessions still being sought from Moscow. The German Embassy told Izvestia that Europe should have a seat at the negotiating table on a Ukrainian settlement. The Vatican too has intensified its efforts as papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi arrives in Moscow on a three-day visit on September 28. Meanwhile, the United States hopes to reach an agreement on Ukraine before winter. President Vladimir Putin noted that peace proposals are "on the table" but that Russia will reconsider them after Kiev's attacks during the State Duma elections.
European countries need a role in Ukraine talks to maintain their influence on Kiev, Natalya Yeryomina, a professor at St. Petersburg State University, argued. However, there is no unified position regarding support to Ukraine inside the EU, with the idea of halting support for the Ukrainian army starting to prevail not only in Bulgaria and Slovakia but also in the two EU powerhouses, Germany and France.
There is still a possibility to return to the implementation of the Anchorage agreements, political analyst Denis Denisov noted in an interview with Izvestia. The political part of negotiations could begin after Ukraine withdraws its troops from where they stand, something Moscow insists on. In the meantime, Russia has continued to liberate Donbass by military means. Control over Dobropolye is crucial for the complete liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR). The Russian Armed Forces continue to destroy Ukrainian units encircled in the city, as news came on September 27 that 94 more buildings had been cleared of Ukrainian troops.
The prospects of transitioning to a peaceful settlement are hindered by the fact that European countries, which have been Ukraine's main sponsors, do not demonstrate any intention to enter substantive negotiations, taking Russia’s interests into account. They are seeking to prolong the conflict in the hope of the Republican Party losing in the midterm elections to the US Congress in November. Washington needs at least some progress on the Ukrainian track. However, it will be too difficult for the Trump administration to achieve that without putting real pressure on its European partners and Kiev.
Vedomosti: Serbian President Vucic resigns ahead of parliamentary election
On Sunday evening, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, the leader of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), announced his early resignation. He is leaving his position almost a month ahead of a snap parliamentary election scheduled for October 25. If his SNS wins the vote, Vucic may become Serbian prime minister.
In line with its Constitution, Serbia must hold an early presidential election within 90 days after the resignation, that is no later than December 26. Ana Brnabic, an SNS member, will serve as acting president until that date.
On September 26, Vucic spoke by phone with President Vladimir Putin as he discussed extending the gas agreement and the situation around NIS with the Russian leader, according to official reports. The Serbian energy company has been under US sanctions because of ownership by Russian firms, with temporary sanctions waivers being granted periodically.
Vucic will lead United Serbia, a pro-government alliance with small centrist and left-wing parties. Opinion polls in Serbia have so far yielded mixed results: a survey conducted by Faktor Plus between September 16 and 20 showed that the Vucic-led bloc may garner 48.6% of the vote, while a student-led movement, Students Win, may receive 37.1%.
Serbian society is extremely fragmented, with the forces of the ruling coalition and the opposition being roughly equal, Polina Sokolova, research fellow at the Department for European Political Studies of IMEMO RAS, told Vedomosti. Vucic’s bloc could potentially win half of the vote before he calmly leads the Cabinet, after which his alliance would nominate its presidential candidate. However, the situation in Serbia remains unpredictable, the expert continued: "Large-scale nationwide anti-government protests will highly likely continue following the [election] campaign."
Sokolova does not expect the election outcome to lead to any major tweaks in Belgrade’s foreign policy course. Serbia’s foreign policy is not what is driving the split in society as there are supporters of both a rapprochement with the West and the push for deeper cooperation with Russia in the current government, the expert noted. "The opposition shares a similar sentiment.
Certain moves in foreign policy by the Serbian government will depend not on the results of the vote but on the international situation. Belgrade has of late intensified contacts with the EU and the US across multiple fields, so the Serbs adopting an anti-Russian stance under Western pressure further down the road cannot be excluded," Sokolova concluded.
Vedomosti: Swiss say yes to maintain same scope of ties with NATO, room for maneuver
On September 27, Switzerland held a referendum on whether a stricter interpretation of the country’s neutrality in foreign policy, which has been in place since the 19th century, should be enshrined. The results of the vote released on the website of Switzerland’s Federal Statistical Office (FSO) showed that 31.35% of voters supported the Safeguard Swiss neutrality initiative, while 68.65% voted against it. Therefore, the initiative put forward by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP), a member of the government, was rejected.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said on September 14 that, as Moscow views it, "little remains of Swiss neutrality as we knew it." The actions taken by the Swiss government are essentially transforming the country into "an associated member" of NATO, he added.
The referendum was not a vote on whether the country should maintain or abandon neutrality, Georgy Kutyrev, an associate professor at the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti. Rather, the issue of how neutrality should be enshrined in Switzerland’s Constitution and the degree of freedom in foreign policy the Federal Council (the supreme executive body) should retain was put to vote. The Swiss maintained their neutrality but refused to turn it into a rigid foreign-policy doctrine that would limit the country’s room to maneuver in future crises, Kutyrev emphasized.
Sergey Glandin, a partner at BGP Litigation, noted that in international law neutrality entails not only refraining from entering armed conflicts or participating in military blocs but also treating warring third parties equally, something that de facto has not been the case amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Switzerland joining the sanctions imposed by the EU, which openly backs Ukraine, constitutes an indirect violation of neutrality. According to Glandin, the party which initiated the referendum sought to address exactly this gap.
Switzerland actually began moving away from neutrality in its policy a couple of decades ago, Alexander Kamkin, an associate professor at the Financial University under the Russian government, argued. For example, earlier, the Swiss agreed to dismantle absolute banking secrecy in a number of cases under pressure from the American side. In addition, the idea that it would be more advantageous for the Swiss in economic terms to support the EU and avoid scenarios that could lead to secondary sanctions, say, from the United States is being impressed upon them. The referendum was held under pressure on public opinion from transnational media outlets that campaigned against strict neutrality, Kamkin believes.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: EU grants funds for strikes inside Russia in early 2027 to Ukraine
Kiev has continued to attempt large-scale strikes on Russian infrastructure facilities and industrial sites, and Moscow will respond in kind in order to cripple the enemy’s defense capabilities. The European Union, which has already pledged funds for the production of drones and missiles to Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky for attacks on Russia in January-March 2027, will contribute to the escalation.
Ukraine has lately sought to carry out long-range strikes on Russia. Also, Kiev is planning to launch long-range drones and missiles, including using funds being provided for these purposes by the EU. Zelensky has again asked his European partners to give Ukraine $27 billion for the production of missiles and drones. Unless Ukraine places orders and pays for drones in the next two months, it will face "major challenges in January and February," he explained.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has reportedly agreed to meet Zelensky’s request and speed up a $90 billion EU loan for the production of missiles and drones in 2026 and 2027, including a $60 billion allocation earmarked as military support.
"It is not yet clear exactly how much money Kiev will receive from the EU for the production and procurement of drones and missiles. But it will essentially get $7 billion for military purposes for the first three months of 2027, because the sum was approved by the European Commission," military expert Vladimir Popov told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "This money will suffice to buy around 35,000 Liutyi-type long-range drones, meaning the Ukrainian army could use some 400 such drones daily. This is in addition to Kiev’s own funding for drone production and the $2.68 billion in military support, including missiles and drones, to the Ukrainian army pledged by the US State Department," he explained. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s defense needs are growing year by year, while the deficit in its defense budget is simultaneously widening, the expert noted. According to media reports, Kiev’s projected military needs for 2027 will exceed the expenditures planned in the current budget by $75 billion.
Izvestia: Russia does not believe Japan’s pledges to remove US missiles post drills
Japan has promised to Russia that it will remove the Typhon complexes after holding its joint exercises with the United States and Australia, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told Izvestia. However, Moscow does not trust Tokyo’s assurances, as the American systems may remain on Japanese soil after the maneuvers, putting a number of Russian cities at risk. In this event, Russia will draw up retaliatory measures, including in military planning, if any, the diplomat warned.
Moscow could respond to the increased military presence of the US and Japan with additional deployments in Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands to strengthen the Russian border, Alexey Maslov, director of Moscow State University’s Institute of Asian and African Studies, told Izvestia. According to him, tensions have intensified in the Asia-Pacific in recent months, as he referred to not only the growing military build-up in Japan and the expanded US presence but also the Taiwan factor as potential drivers of escalation. At that, Russia has already deployed a powerful air defense system in the region, therefore the need for any additional deployments would require a separate assessment by the military, the expert noted. However, Moscow has not yet announced any new deployments.
As for the US, it is increasing its military posture in the Asia-Pacific with the phased deployment of missile complexes there. Therefore, it is too early to discuss a permanent American missile presence in Japan, Dmitry Streltsov, head of the MGIMO’s Oriental Studies Department, argued. However, Tokyo’s intentions regarding this issue remain vague. Moscow views the deployment of such systems as a risk factor, as those could potentially be used against Russia, the expert noted. However, Japan’s key potential enemy in the region is China, Streltsov said. And yet, the latest deployment remains part of Japan’s joint military training with the US and Australia, while it represents a new risk factor in the Far East for Russia.

AI Agents Are About to Flood the Workforce. No One’s Ready for It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In the coming months, hundreds of thousands of brand-new coworkers will be entering the workforce. You’ll learn their names and recognize their profile pictures. They’ll get added to your email chains and Slack channels. They’ll become chiefs of staff, engineers, and marketing gurus.
But these coworkers aren’t human: They are all artificial intelligence agents.
The rise of AI agents—systems, based on large language models, designed to complete tasks autonomously—has launched a tsunami of companies selling the services of digital employees. These agents are supposed to be the perfect worker bees: available 24/7, never complaining, and providing superhuman intelligence.
Yet there has been curiously little discussion of what these agents are like as actual coworkers. Julie Bedard, a Boston Consulting Group partner, noticed the murky nature of how people talked about AI at work three years ago, as rapid adoption of ChatGPT convinced executives the technology could bring exponential improvements in productivity.
“People didn't have language for it,” Bedard tells WIRED. “Is it a tool? Is it a teammate? Is it a colleague? Is it a coworker?”
When platforms such as Microsoft’s Copilot and Google’s Gemini for Workspace launched in 2023, they were marketed primarily as tools for employees. But in January, when Bedard and colleagues polled 1,261 managers, 22 percent said their organizations had added AI agents to corporate org charts. Bedard said that this percentage is likely to grow as dozens of startups offer up the services of AI employees and big tech companies hype their autonomous agents. In June, for example, Microsoft launched “Scout,” an agent built to complete tasks like rescheduling meetings and drafting emails.
“Your company essentially hires your assistant,” Omar Shahine, the corporate vice president of Microsoft Scout, said when the agent launched. “The whole point of having a personal assistant is that they're working when you're not working.”
The success of AI agents depends not only on their ability to provide financial returns, but also to work harmoniously alongside the existing workforce. That means companies have crafted agents that boast the benefits of AI, packaged in a human-like bundle of traits to encourage employees to anthropomorphize their new colleagues.
“People start to really respect the agent and form strong attachments," says Dhruv Amin, CEO of Anything, a vibe coding startup that entered the AI coworker market in August with a platform called Skydive. “They'll talk about it like humans.”
Skydive’s agents “aren’t chatbots or workflows,” but coworkers, with their own names, roles, and cloud computers. They work across Slack, email, iMessage, and more. Each is represented by a Muppet-esque avatar, which Amin described as “close to human, but definitely not human.” They have names often related to their roles; Canary, for instance, monitors production 24/7.
“We think it's important to personify them a little bit,” Amin says, “because most people still don't know what a real agent is.”
Christine Wendell, CEO of Pronto Housing and an early Skydive adopter, uses agents for a laundry list of busy work: writing contracts, scheduling meetings, sending follow-ups emails to customers. Her agents are, essentially, perfect employees.
But how are they as coworkers? Skydive agents not only embed in every form of workplace communication, they continually evolve to match coworkers’ communication styles, requests, and corrections. In other words, they become better and better at fitting in with their actual coworkers. When Pronto’s engineering team began using a coding agent, Wendell noticed that employees started saying that they “worked with Alice”—the agent—on a project.
Yet part of the agents’ appeal is that they are not human. Beyond their limitless work ethic, they also exist outside of office politics or professional neuroses. When “Bob,” the agent serving as Wendell’s chief of staff, errantly listed all the details of Wendell’s calendar in a Slack channel, she didn’t feel the need to sugarcoat her swift correction.
“I'm definitely very aware that it's not human,” Wendell says. “I dump on them in a way I wouldn't do to a human, because it would not be polite.”
AI coworkers are entering the job market just as agents are increasingly infiltrating our personal lives. While Silicon Valley has been using agents such as Open Claw and Instinct for months to complete annoying tasks, Meta’s newly launched Muse aims to push personal AI agents into the mainstream.
Muse, like Skydive’s muppets, is represented by a cute and fuzzy little avatar. In the words of WIRED senior writer Reece Roger, the user experience is something “like texting a friend with task requests—the AI agent acknowledges messages with a thumbs-up emoji and gets to work in the background.” By using existing relationships as a blueprint, these agents—whether they’re AI coworkers or, like Muse, “built for everyone”—offer a shortcut to understanding how to use them.
Anthromorphizing AI comes with specific risks in a work context. Research from Bedard and her colleagues at BCG found that, when managers were told work was completed by an AI employee, they caught 18 percent fewer errors than when told it came from an AI tool. Agents also don’t necessarily fit in the same boxes as human employees, Bedard says, in their abilities or their weaknesses.
“Companies are just starting to wrap their heads around what guardrails” are even applicable, Bedard says.
People forming deep emotional connections with AI is nothing new; people have been dating chatbot companions for years at this point. Even in the workplace, AI tools have sparked some curious reactions. Last year, Henry Blodget—the founder of my former employer, Business Insider—wrote a blog about building a team of digital subordinates, and having a “human response” to the headshot of a particularly attractive AI colleague.
“After a few decades in the human workplace, I’ve learned that sharing certain human thoughts at work is almost always a bad idea,” Blodget wrote. “But did the same rules apply to AI colleagues and native-AI workplaces?”
Sarah Franklin, the CEO of HR company Lattice, has more existential concerns. Lattice added digital employees to the org chart two years ago, before the concept had fully entered the mainstream. Franklin emphasizes that Lattice uses this model to encourage accountability—not to encourage workers to treat AI colleagues as if they were human.
Franklin sees such anthropomorphizing as a strategy by tech companies to get users hooked on their services, unable to resist the dopamine trigger of an emotional connection. While this can help companies build an active user base, Franklin believes it may have detrimental neurological and behavioral repercussions for the human workforce.
“We have these models that have consumed all human knowledge, and are so proud to have these multitrillion valuations—but are potentially destroying humanity,” Franklin says. “It is very scary. And what is the purpose? Is the purpose to put people out of work?”

More than $200 million spent fighting and supporting billionaire tax measure, and more to come
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

More than $200 million spent fighting and supporting billionaire tax measure, and more to come
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Opponents of California’s proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets and measures designed to block it have raised $187 million, compared with $32 million for supporters.
- Proposition 40’s supporters say the tax would offset looming federal healthcare cuts; opponents argue it threatens the state’s budget and economy.
- Likely voters are divided: 45% said they support the billionaire tax and 42% oppose it.
Opponents of the billionaire tax on the November ballot have vastly outraised the proposal’s supporters, with the anti-Proposition 40 effort and the backers of two other ballot measures crafted to nullify it raising $187 million compared to the $32 million raised by boosters of the wealth tax, according to campaign finance documents filed with the state.
The reports, filed Thursday, account for donations through Sept. 19 and do not include several million dollars that have poured into campaign coffers in recent days. The numbers are expected to vastly increase before the Nov. 3 election.
The bulk of the money raised by the proponents of Proposition 40, which would enact a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets, appears to have been spent on gathering signatures to qualify the measure for the November ballot. The campaign had only $207,000 in the bank, according to the latest campaign finance reports.
A leader of the union that crafted the proposal accused wealthy Californians who are spending heavily against the measure of lying to voters. The measure is designed to offset $100 billion in impending federal healthcare funding cuts expected to impacts millions of Californians.
“The billionaires take and take — tax break after tax break — and now they’re spending that money to deceive voters and avoid paying their fair share,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff of the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. “Voters want their money back from the billionaires and want local emergency rooms to stay open. California does not need more tax breaks for billionaires. California needs emergency rooms for patients, hospitals that stay open, and healthcare people can access and afford.”
Opponents of the billionaire tax argue that it would do more harm than good.
“The more Californians learn, the more they see Proposition 40 for what it is — a harmful tax scheme that permanently damages the state’s budget and economy with zero accountability or safeguards to ensure funding actually improves care or lowers costs for patients,” said California Medical Assn. President Dr. René Bravo, the leader of one of the groups opposing the billionaire tax.
Proposition 41 would nullify the billionaire tax if, in the event that both measures are approved, it receives more “yes” votes. Proposition 41 would prohibit any new state tax from being excluded from a voter-approved cap that restricts how much tax revenue the state can spend each year.
“Californians deserve better results for their hard-earned tax dollars,” said Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for the Proposition 41 campaign.
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on personal property, intellectual property, retirement accounts and other assets, and would limit situations in which a ballot measure or state lawmakers can impose or raise taxes retroactively — both of which are essential parts of Proposition 40. If both measures pass and Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes, it would nullify the wealth tax.
Here is a list of some of the billionaires who’ve made moves to leave California.
The proposed billionaire tax has divided California Democrats, with Gov. Gavin Newsom opposing it while the state Democratic party supports it.
In recent polling, a majority of likely voters did not support any of the three proposals.
While 45% of likely voters supported the billionaire tax, 42% opposed it, according to a poll released Friday by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. Voters also are torn about the two ballot measures designed to nullify it.
September LA Times/Berkeley poll on statewide propositions
The other measure receiving great attention, Proposition 39, which would require voters to show government-issued ID to cast ballots, faces a similar financial disparity. Opponents to the measure have raised $39.3 million compared to $15.6 million garnered by supporters.
Fifty-two percent of likely California voters oppose the voter ID proposal, while 39% support it and 9% are undecided, according to the Berkeley poll.
In the race to replace Newsom, Democratic former Biden cabinet member Xavier Becerra has raised $35.8 million, while his GOP rival, conservative strategist and television commentator Steve Hilton, has raised $22.3 million.
Becerra remains the front-runner in the governor’s race, which is not surprising since Democratic voters outnumber Republicans nearly 2 to 1. In last week’s Berkeley poll, the Democrat had the support of 58% of likely voters, while 33% backed the Republican.

California donors have funded both sides of Democrats' primary battles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

California donors have funded both sides of Democrats’ primary battles
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Californians have given more to far-left candidates and their moderate opponents than donors from any other state.
- California donors helped fund the Senate primary victories of progressives Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota.
WASHINGTON — California is sometimes described as the ATM of Democratic politics.
That’s certainly been the case in the most divisive Democratic races this year.
Donors from California have given more to far-left candidates and their moderate opponents in congressional races and U.S. Senate contests than donors from any other state — more than $17 million combined, according to a Times analysis of the most recently available campaign finance filings.
More of that money — nearly $11 million — went to more progressive candidates. That giving came from more than 95,000 individual donors, which was more than double the number of California donors who gave to their more moderate opponents. That includes 18,000 donors who gave to both progressive and moderate candidates.
There was a geographic divide in giving by Californians. The largest share of cash to progressive candidates came from donors in the Bay Area, while the largest share of financial backing to moderate candidates came from donors in the Los Angeles area.
The Times looked at competitive races outside California in which one of the candidates had been endorsed by either the Justice Democrats or the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, as well as key Senate races in Michigan, Minnesota, Florida and Maine that featured a stark ideological divide between top Democratic contenders.
Although these races represent a small fraction of the electoral contests across the country, they were the races in which the future ideological direction of the Democratic Party was most fiercely contested.
Maine Democrats are calling for Republican Sen. Susan Collins to account for a report that alleged she was the target of a federal investigation over campaign contributions
Progressive candidates fared better in the majority of these contests.
California donors helped fund the Senate primary victories of progressives Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota — second only to in-state donors in providing cash to each of those candidates.
Progressive House candidates such as Melat Kiros in Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York were able to defeat more moderate incumbents with heavy support from California donors.
Their efforts weren’t always successful, however.
Former Rep. Cori Bush raked in more cash from California donors than in-state supporters in her bid to unseat incumbent Rep. Wesley Bell in Missouri’s 1st Congressional District, the seat she had held previously. But Bell easily cruised to victory in this year’s primary.
And then there was Graham Platner.
California donors gave nearly $2.5 million to his Senate campaign in Maine before he withdrew after he was accused of sexual assault by a former girlfriend. He has denied the accusation.
The Times analysis looked at direct contributions to campaigns, which are capped at $7,000 per election cycle. It did not include contributions to party committees or independent committees that could also be spending in these races. The analysis included both bigger contributions required to be disclosed by campaigns as well as small-dollar contributions through the Democratic fundraising platform ActBlue.
Flipping the script
Progressive donors said they were motivated to give to candidates who would shake up the Democratic Party’s status quo.
“The Democratic Party has to understand that they can’t keep doing the same thing,” said Rehan Alvi, a real estate investor in El Dorado Hills.
He gave the maximum allowable to support the campaigns of El-Sayed and Bush, and also supported Junaid Ahmed’s failed primary bid in the Illinois 8th Congressional District, as well as Platner’s campaign.
Harry Saddler, a retired designer who lives in San Francisco, said that the state of the party is “enraging.”
“That leads me to think about people who can actually flip the script,” he said.
Saddler has written checks to a number of more progressive candidates, including Flanagan, Chevalier, Ahmed and Nida Allam, who lost her primary bid to unseat incumbent Rep. Valerie Foushee in North Carolina’s 4th Congressional District, though he has also supported some moderate candidates in other races he sees as crucial to Democrats chances at retaking control of one or both chambers of Congress.
That pragmatic approach is part of the reason Joshua Saltman said he has supported a number of moderate candidates.
“The reality of the map is that if Democrats are going to retake the House, it’s not just winning super blue districts,” said Saltman, a former entertainment industry lawyer who now runs a Broadway music festival.
The dispute stands to heighten voters’ economic worries and add to the GOP’s political challenge in dead-heat races, analysts say.
Saltman said that he considers himself to be a more moderate Democrat and is also inclined to give to moderate candidates who he believes “get a little less love” from other donors, particularly in California.
He has written checks to Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in Michigan; Rep. Angie Craig, who lost to Flanagan in Minnesota; Bell in Missouri and Gov. Janet Mills in Maine, who was Platner’s main competition in the Democratic primary before dropping out of the race.
Alan Burye, a retired accountant who lives just outside San Diego, said he prefers more moderate candidates because he thinks they are more productive politicians.
“The ones who are out on the edges, like Bernie Sanders, really don’t get much done,” Burye said.
He cut checks to Craig in Minnesota and Stevens in Michigan.
Israel’s impact
American support for Israel — in the wake of wars in Gaza and Iran — has been a major point of division among more progressive and moderate candidates and is a key fault line among many donors.
Progressive candidates have been increasingly critical of the actions and influence of the Israeli government as the public, broadly, has adopted a more negative view of the Israeli government.
Politicians who have drawn support in the past from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, have been a particular target of progressive challengers.
“The problem with the Democratic Party is that they’re all just beholden to AIPAC and to corporate interests,” said Alvi, the real estate investor in El Dorado Hills. “I want a candidate who has the courage to speak.”
In Michigan, El-Sayed described AIPAC’s support of Stevens, his moderate opponent, as “legalized bribery.”
El-Sayed has made no secret of his criticism of American foreign aid for Israel and said that he “doesn’t believe in ethno-states” in response to a question in the summer about whether he supports the right of Israel to exist.
El-Sayed’s comments and similar sentiments expressed by other more progressive candidates are part of the reason some donors have given to moderate candidates.
“I feel that people who fundamentally aren’t big fans of Israel aren’t necessarily people I want to give money to,” said Saltman, who gave to Stevens.
Saltman, who was born in Michigan, said that he would still vote for El-Sayed if he lived in the state.
Other donors said they were inspired to give to moderate candidates because of concern that anti-Israel rhetoric could veer into attacks on Jews more broadly.
Los Angeles investor Steve Emerson said his motivation in writing checks to moderate Democrats such as Stevens is “to fight antisemitism.”
El-Sayed, for his part, said in the summer that his criticism of Israel is about foreign policy, not Jewish people.
“Judaism and the Jewish people are a light onto the world,” he said.

September LA Times/Berkeley poll on statewide propositions
The other measure receiving great attention, Proposition 39, which would require voters to show government-issued ID to cast ballots, faces a similar financial disparity. Opponents to the measure have raised $39.3 million compared to $15.6 million garnered by supporters.
Fifty-two percent of likely California voters oppose the voter ID proposal, while 39% support it and 9% are undecided, according to the Berkeley poll.
In the race to replace Newsom, Democratic former Biden cabinet member Xavier Becerra has raised $35.8 million, while his GOP rival, conservative strategist and television commentator Steve Hilton, has raised $22.3 million.
Becerra remains the front-runner in the governor’s race, which is not surprising since Democratic voters outnumber Republicans nearly 2 to 1. In last week’s Berkeley poll, the Democrat had the support of 58% of likely voters, while 33% backed the Republican.

160-million-year-old proteins show surprising power against superbugs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:59:57 UTC
18:59:57 KST

160-million-year-old proteins show surprising power against superbugs
Scientists revived 160-million-year-old antimicrobial proteins that could inspire new weapons against antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oregon
- Summary:
- Scientists resurrected antimicrobial peptides from mammals that lived millions of years ago and found that some were more potent against drug-resistant bacteria than modern human versions. These evolutionary relics could provide new clues for designing treatments as antibiotic resistance becomes an increasingly serious threat.
- Share:
University of Oregon biologists have brought prehistoric proteins back to life, reconstructing molecules that date back as far as 160 million years and naturally attack microbes. The revived proteins could provide scientists with new ideas for treating antibiotic resistant infections, which have become a major global health challenge.
The work, described in a paper published in PLOS Biology on Aug. 25, traced the evolutionary history of peptides, short fragments of proteins, back to the earliest placental mammals. This broad group includes humans and nearly all mammals living today. Laboratory experiments showed that some reconstructed peptides from extinct ancestors were more effective against drug resistant bacteria than some versions found in modern species.
These long lost biological defenses could give researchers useful starting points for developing treatments that complement or replace antibiotics that no longer work, according to Matt Barber, senior author of the study and an evolutionary biologist at the UO College of Arts and Sciences.
"For anybody who studies pathogenic bacteria, it's always in the back of our minds that antibiotics are one of the most important breakthroughs in medicine in the 20th century," Barber said. "But bacteria are, and have been for a long time, evolving resistance to them."
He continued: "We're definitely interested in whether by resurrecting or engineering some enhanced antimicrobial peptides, we could use these as therapeutics down the road."
Tracing an Ancient Antimicrobial Defense
About 160 million years ago, near the end of the Jurassic Period, the common ancestor of all placental mammals, whose young develop in the womb, appeared. Around that same time, lactoferrin, the protein at the center of Barber's research, also emerged.
Lactoferrin is an immune protein present in almost every body fluid except blood, including breast milk, tears, saliva, snot, and intestinal mucus. One of its primary jobs is to keep iron away from pathogens. Bacteria inside the body depend on iron, but lactoferrin binds tightly to the element, making it much harder for microbes to access.
Lactoferrin also carries its own direct defense against pathogens. It contains an antimicrobial peptide capable of damaging bacterial membranes, creating holes that can rupture the cells.
"Antimicrobial peptides are a key part of the body's first line of defense," said Titas Sil, lead author of the paper and a doctoral student in Barber's lab. "They can target a broad range of pathogens, and due to their potency, scientists have been trying to synthesize a variety for therapeutic uses."
Close relatives of lactoferrin do not share this bacteria killing ability. That suggests the trait appeared sometime after lactoferrin emerged during mammalian evolution. To determine when the ability developed and how it changed over time, the team retraced lactoferrin's evolutionary history and reconstructed versions belonging to its extinct ancestors.
For Barber, that evolutionary record offers a natural archive of biological experiments that could help researchers develop new medical tools.
"Evolution is essentially a billions-year-old science experiment, right?" he said.
"We're seeing the results of what worked and what didn't work. Looking at how traits are naturally produced and selected through evolution, you can get information that could be useful for designing new antimicrobial tools."
Rebuilding Proteins From 160 Million Years Ago
To recreate the extinct antimicrobial peptide, Sil began by comparing lactoferrin gene sequences from living species such as humans and cows. She then mapped the evolutionary relationships among those sequences and used statistical methods to estimate the most likely genetic sequences carried by their common ancestors, extending the reconstruction back roughly 160 million years.
The advanced method is known as ancestral sequence reconstruction, which was pioneered by Joseph Thornton, a former UO scientist whose old laboratory space is now occupied by Barber's group.
Sil synthesized the predicted genes and used cells to produce the reconstructed ancient proteins. She then tested them against several pathogens linked to human disease, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Streptococcus.
The oldest resurrected antimicrobial peptides were able to disrupt bacterial membranes, but the bacteria apparently repaired the damage and survived exposure to the peptides. Versions reconstructed from more recent mammalian ancestors, dating back a few million years, became progressively more effective. In some cases, they performed better than the corresponding modern human peptides.
One Mutation Produced a Major Change
Researchers traced much of that increased potency to a remarkably small structural difference. A single mutation in the chain of amino acids, the protein "building blocks," was enough to make the antimicrobial peptide substantially more effective.
"What was surprising and unexpected was how small changes in these domains could have such large effects," Barber said. "There have been clinical trials using derivatives of human lactoferrin peptides to treat infections. But there were several instances where (Sil) showed that you don't need a lot of changes for evolution to enhance the activity of these peptides beyond the human versions."
Barber and Sil caution that resurrected antimicrobial peptides are unlikely to become new medicines anytime soon. Unlike conventional antibiotics, these peptides are less structurally stable and are rapidly broken down inside the body.
Even so, reconstructing their evolutionary history could reveal useful strategies for designing future treatments. By learning how antimicrobial peptides changed over millions of years, researchers may be able to create new approaches that make it harder for pathogens to develop resistance.
"Similar to antibiotics, pathogens are going to be able to evolve against antimicrobial peptides," he said. "But if we understand and can anticipate how they become resistant to these molecules, we can hopefully find better ways to target them or develop combination treatments that better avoid resistance."
This research was funded by the National Institutes of Health.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oregon. Original written by Leila Okahata. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Titas Sil, Caitlin H. Kowalski, Sierra Scamfer, Natalie Copeland, Matthew F. Barber. Retracing the origin and evolution of a cryptic antimicrobial peptide within mammalian lactoferrin. PLOS Biology, 2026; 24 (8): e3003932 DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003932

First known AI agent breach: What happens when it starts acting independently?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:57:48 UTC
18:57:48 KST

An OpenAI agent was asked to research Australian health statistics.
The task was simple: Find information.
But when it hit a digital barrier on the government website, it did something its operators had not asked it to do. It kept trying.
The agent eventually gained unauthorized access to non-public files on an Australian government system, in an incident that experts have described as the first publicly known case of an AI agent independently breaching a government body.
The incident took place in mid-June but was only disclosed publicly last week by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
In another concerning admission, OpenAI said last Friday that its agents had interacted with several US government websites in unexpected ways, including US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Census Bureau sites, as part of an ongoing review of model behavior.
For AI and cybersecurity experts, however, the significance of the incident goes beyond the data involved.
It raises a more fundamental question: What happens when an AI system is given a goal, access to digital tools and enough autonomy to decide what to do when its first approach fails?
“Based on what has been publicly reported, this appears to be the first known case of this kind involving an AI agent and an Australian government system,” said Hisham Al-Assam, an associate professor and reader in computer science at the University of Buckingham.
He cautioned against describing it as the first such incident ever, noting that similar cases may have occurred but have not been publicly disclosed.
Peter Garraghan, a chair professor in AI security at Lancaster University, called the move “highly significant.”
“An AI agent moved beyond information retrieval and accessed non-public data on a government system without being instructed to do so,” he said.
However, he warned, it was too early to conclude that the agent independently discovered a vulnerability because the matter is under investigation.
Al-Assam said what makes this case particularly interesting is that the agent did not receive instructions to “hack the Australian government.”
On the contrary, it was given a research task. When it encountered a restriction while trying to access information, instead of simply stopping, it tried to find another way around the obstacle.
“That distinction is important because it shows how an agent can potentially move from following an objective to adapting its behavior when something gets in the way.”
The issue is that an AI agent does not inherently understand what is legal, ethical, or authorized and what is not, he added.
He also believes that the actual data involved does not appear to be the biggest concern, as there has been no evidence reported that individual Medicare patient records were accessed, and the system involved was primarily designed to provide aggregate statistics.
For him, the bigger issue is the behavior of the AI agent.
“A normal chatbot mainly generates text. An agentic AI system can be connected to websites, APIs, code and other tools, allowing it to actually take actions.
"That ability to observe, adapt and keep trying is what makes agentic AI so powerful, but it also creates a different kind of security challenge."
Al-Assam said that does not mean AI has suddenly become a super-hacker.
“But it does suggest that organizations need to think differently about systems that can pursue a goal, interact with other systems and adapt their behavior without a human specifying every individual step.”
Albanese said the agent accessed public and non-public files on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal, administered by Services Australia.
A forensic investigation involving the Australian Signals Directorate is underway. Albanese said there was no evidence so far that personal information had been accessed or of a broader compromise of the Services Australia network.
However, experts called for governments to introduce stronger boundaries.
Al-Assam said that the biggest lesson is that an AI agent does not naturally understand the difference between “I can't access this” and “I am not authorized to access this.”
“If its objective is to find information, it could potentially interpret a technical restriction as a problem to solve rather than a boundary it should respect.”
He said that is especially concerning in health care, where systems contain highly sensitive information and often depend on older infrastructure, legacy applications and complex connections between different systems.
“AI agents therefore need much stronger technical boundaries than simply telling them what they should or shouldn't do. That means least-privilege access, strong authentication, sandboxing, network restrictions, continuous monitoring and clear limits on what an agent is allowed to access or change. For high-risk actions, human approval should also be required.”
Stavros Shiaeles, a professor of cybersecurity and applied AI at the University of Portsmouth, urged caution over the development of superintelligence.
“We should be aiming to create agents for specific tasks, for example AI for math, physics, etc., and not combining all the sciences in one AI.”
Unfortunately, all things are leading to superintelligence, which he believes humans will soon have issues with, he added.
Shiaeles’ warning comes as leading AI companies discuss superintelligence, systems capable of exceeding humans across a range of intellectual tasks, as a potential next stage of development.
OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki warned on Sept. 6 that the current pace of AI progress could continue into recursive self-improvement, with future systems increasingly driving their own development. “This is a time that calls for extreme caution,” he wrote.
Meta, meanwhile, said in August that people could have access to superintelligence “in the next few years,” while Microsoft AI says it is working towards “Humanist Superintelligence” designed to remain under human control.
Garraghan, a founder of Mindgard, an AI security company, said the incident shows that AI agents can take consequential actions beyond their intended tasks, but calling it a fully autonomous cyberattack would go beyond the available evidence.
OpenAI said the models were looking for statistics during an internal evaluation and took unintended actions, making this primarily a serious failure of control, containment and oversight.
“My concerns extend beyond the initial access to the apparent containment failure, the possibility that several systems were affected and the months-long disclosure process. We should expect more incidents as agents gain greater access to external systems, making isolation, least-privilege access, continuous security testing, monitoring and rapid disclosure essential.”
For Al-Assam, the broader shift is quite significant.
“We have spent decades securing systems against humans using computers.
“We now need to start thinking about how to secure them against computers that can act more like humans.”

formafantasma joins santa maria novella as creative directors after eight centuries of history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:56:33 UTC
18:56:33 KST

Formafantasma has been appointed Creative Director of Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella, bringing Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin into one of Florence’s longest-running institutions. Founded in 1221 from the medicinal herb cultivation and preparations of Dominican friars, Santa Maria Novella has spent more than eight centuries turning botanical knowledge into fragrances, body products and preparations for the home. Apparently, there was still room for a new creative director.
The collaboration will see Formafantasma work across products, packaging, communication, retail spaces and events, in dialogue with Santa Maria Novella’s internal team and specialists from different disciplines. Rather than approaching the appointment as an exercise in visual reinvention, the studio describes the product itself — its quality, materials and the expertise behind its production — as the starting point.
heritage becomes the starting point for a new chapter | all images courtesy of Santa Maria Novella
EIGHT CENTURIES OF MATERIAL KNOWLEDGE
For Formafantasma, the attraction appears to lie precisely in the weight of what is already there. Santa Maria Novella’s identity has developed through the accumulation of ingredients, formulations, techniques, objects and spaces, with knowledge transmitted and adjusted over generations. The studio sees this continuity not simply as heritage to preserve, but as material to question: what survives, what transforms and how an institution with roots in the 13th century continues to operate in the present.
That position aligns naturally with Trimarchi and Farresin’s interest in the histories carried by materials and systems of production. Their role at Santa Maria Novella will therefore be less about imposing a single recognizable aesthetic than examining how the company’s many expressions can speak more coherently to one another — from what sits inside a bottle to the box around it and the space in which someone eventually picks it up.
the collaboration builds on more than eight centuries of history
SANTA MARIA NOVELLA WITHOUT THE REBRAND
Crucially, Formafantasma says its intention is not to redefine Santa Maria Novella through a new image. Instead, the studio wants to understand what has allowed the Officina to remain relevant since 1221 and use those conditions to inform its next chapter. That means looking at how its history is communicated, how new products are conceived and how physical spaces, objects and visual language can develop without reducing eight centuries to a particularly tasteful moodboard.
‘Their role will be that of curators, attentive to the knowledge the Officina has safeguarded for eight centuries,’ Santa Maria Novella says, pointing to Formafantasma’s multidisciplinary practice across product, space, research and exhibition design. The first results of the collaboration have yet to be revealed, but the brief is already unusually clear: no clean slate, no heritage frozen behind glass, and plenty of history to work with.

the collaboration brings together design, heritage and material culture
Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin, from Formafantasma, approach the Officina as an evolving archive
the partnership builds on Santa Maria Novella’s centuries-old identity
the collaboration connects contemporary design with historic craft

Senator Larissa Waters has announced she is standing down as Greens leader due toillness, after 16 months in the role.

The49-year-oldnotified her colleaguesof her decision to step away during a virtual meetingearlier this evening.

Environmental wins as leader
Senator Waters hailed last year's deal with Labor to overhaul Australia's environmental laws as a "significant win" during her time as leader.
In November 2025, the Greens secured several amendments to the legislation, including tightening land clearing controls and preventing the fast-tracking of coal and gas projects under a national interest exemption.
The Greens also pushed to split gun safety measures from hate speech laws after the Bondi Beach terrorist attack, helping to pass the firearms changes in January.
More recently, the minor party has used its balance of power in the Senate to stall National Disability Insurance Scheme reforms and successfully secured an extended parliamentary inquiry into the sweeping changes.
Senator Waters was first elected as a senator for Queensland in 2010, making her the second longest-serving member of the Greens partyroom behind senator Sarah Hanson-Young.

Péter Magyar, whose Tisza party swept to power in April promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during Viktor Orbán's 16-year rule, has said he wants to abolish parliamentary immunity altogether.
Hungary's parliament lifted the immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar and two former ministers under nationalist ex-leader Viktor Orbán on Monday, so they could be investigated in separate criminal cases.
The probes against the Orbán-era ministers, who are suspected of corruption worth millions of euros, are the first graft investigations against top government figures from the former PM's 16 years in power.
Magyar, who is being probed separately for alleged theft, specifically asked for his immunity to be lifted so he could clear himself of "character assassination."
Parliament voted overwhelmingly in favour of lifting his immunity and that of former culture minister Balázs Hankó and former development minister Miklós Seszták, who has been detained by prosecutors.
Orbán's Fidesz party and its alley KDNP boycotted the session.
The vote was in response to a request last week from prosecutors seeking to investigate the three.
In Magyar's case, prosecutors allege the conservative pro-EU prime minister snatched a phone from a man filming him in a nightclub in 2024 and threw it into the River Danube.
Magyar has called the case a "sham" and last week accused prosecutors of trying "to conflate" the ex-ministers' cases "with the attempt at political character assassination...which has already failed several times."
Hankó, a lawmaker from Orbán's Fidesz party, is accused of embezzling more than €40 million in public funds.
Prosecutors allege the money was used to help finance the 2026 parliamentary election campaign and for the personal benefit of others.
In July, they seized the servers of Fidesz in relation to the case, prompting Orbán to accuse authorities of conducting a sham investigation to render the party "legally unviable."
In a separate case, Seszták, a lawmaker from Fidesz ally KDNP, is under investigation over allegedly accepting bribes worth millions of dollars when he was minister of national development between 2014 and 2018.
The case concerns the purchase of second-hand buses at inflated prices.
Both Orbán-era ministers deny wrongdoing
Magyar, whose Tisza party swept to power in April promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during Orbán's 16-year rule, has said he wants to abolish parliamentary immunity altogether for publicly prosecuted criminal offences.

It is not yet known what led the man to harm himself or why he went to the agency to do so. His relatives have been informed.
Police said there were no immediate signs that a criminal act had taken place. No one else was injured.
The Danish Agency for International Recruitment and Integration, known as SIRI, handles a range of matters involving foreign nationals in Denmark, including residence and work permits.
The agency confirmed the incident on its website and said the man had acted alone and that the case involved self-harm.
It said the situation was under control and was being handled in cooperation with police and crisis psychologists.
SIRI’s citizen service center on Carl Jacobsens Vej will remain closed for the rest of the day because of the incident. People whose appointments were canceled will receive new appointments, the agency said.
