Øresund Bridge to close to car traffic for emergency exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:55:30 UTC
18:55:30 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Ukraine&apos;s local budgets received a quarter more revenue from tourism than last year

Ukraine's local budgets received a quarter more revenue from tourism than last year
Kyiv • UNN
Local budgets received UAH 269.9 million in tourist tax revenue—23% more than last year. In four communities, revenues increased by 60%.
Ukrainian communities continue to increase tourism revenues. Over the first eight months of this year, UAH 269.9 million in tourist tax was paid into local budgets. This is 23% more than during the same period last year. At that time, revenues amounted to UAH 219.5 million. This was reported by the State Tax Service of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Details
The largest tourist tax revenues were recorded in regions with the most active tourist centers. In particular:
-  Kyiv – UAH 53.8 million;  
-  Lviv region – UAH 52.5 million;  
-  Ivano-Frankivsk region – UAH 38.2 million;  
-  Zakarpattia region – UAH 27.5 million.  
It is noted that the funds received are part of local budget revenues, while the dynamics of their inflows make it possible to assess the activity of the tourism sector and its contribution to the financial resources of the territories.
The positive revenue dynamics are also the result of joint efforts by the State Tax Service and territorial communities to improve the administration of the tourist tax.
A pilot project to improve the administration of the tourist tax in four communities in the Khmelnytskyi and Chernivtsi regions, launched by the State Tax Service in April this year, demonstrated its effectiveness. The declared tourist tax amounts in the participating communities increased by 60%.
The new tool makes it possible to obtain both an overall picture of tourist tax revenues across Ukraine and detailed information by regions, territorial communities, types of taxpayers, and types of economic activity
Recall
As UNN previously wrote, during the first four months of 2026, local budgets received UAH 112 million in tourist tax. Lviv region and Kyiv were the leaders in terms of revenue.

Eight Danish municipalities fail kindergarten staffing requirements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28

18:55:24 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.

“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Øresund Bridge to close for 3 hours Thursday evening
The Øresund Bridge will close to all car traffic in both directions Thursday evening as Danish and Swedish authorities carry out a major emergency response exercise, Copenhagen Police said.
The closure will last from 8 p.m. until 11:15 p.m. on October 1.
The exercise will include a scenario involving an accident in one of the tunnel tubes, Copenhagen Police told Ritzau in a written response.
Emergency vehicles will be visible on the bridge during the exercise.
Chief Police Inspector Peter Dahl of Copenhagen Police stressed that the operation is planned and that there is “no danger.”

Five men arrested Sunday morning near the RAF Fairford airbase are all British citizens from London and are in their early or mid-20s, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.

EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.
Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, says companies need to pay attention to their security.

Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.
The United States will pay for any new American military bases established in Greenland under a new security and defense agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen says.
“To the extent that the Americans are to build American bases in Greenland, that is of course something that the Americans finance,” Løkke told Ritzau.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.

Satellite images reveal vast destruction across Gaza following Israel’s genocide
Recent imagery shows entire residential neighborhoods erased, while damaged homes continue collapsing on residents
Jomaa Younis and Lina Altawell
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
ISTANBUL
Updated satellite imagery on Google Maps on Monday revealed the scale of widespread destruction caused by Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip.
The aerial images showed entire residential neighborhoods disappeared and vast urban areas reduced to layers of rubble and debris.
The updated imagery reveals a dramatic transformation of Gaza’s urban landscape, with destruction extending beyond individual buildings to entire residential blocks, leaving vast empty areas where densely populated neighborhoods once stood.
The images provide a broader view of the destruction across neighborhoods and residential blocks, allowing comparisons between Gaza’s current urban landscape and the period before the war and showing the extent of areas that have been destroyed.
The images come as the effects of the destruction continue to threaten Palestinian lives even after the ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
Since the ceasefire, dozens of buildings damaged by Israeli attacks have collapsed on residents, while Palestinians face a severe shortage of shelter amid continued restrictions on the entry of temporary housing units, or caravans.
The danger is not limited to buildings that were completely destroyed, as Israeli attacks left thousands of structures cracked or severely damaged, increasing the risk of collapse, particularly when exposed to rain, wind, and other weather conditions.
According to a report issued in February by the UN special rapporteur on the right to adequate housing, more than 200,000 tons of explosives were dropped on the Gaza Strip over nearly two years.
A satellite assessment by the UN Satellite Centre (UNOSAT) found that around 201,290 buildings, equivalent to 82% of all structures in the Gaza Strip, were damaged as of June 16, 2026.
The figure includes 134,422 destroyed buildings, 13,848 severely damaged structures, 28,096 moderately damaged buildings and 24,924 structures possibly damaged, in addition to around 328,627 damaged housing units.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged.

The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) have reclaimed 51 square kilometers (nearly 20 square miles) of territory and captured more than 250 Russian soldiers during the third stage of Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman direction of the Donetsk region, according to Andriy Biletsky, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps.
In a video address, Biletsky said Ukrainian forces had restored full control over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka and completely liberated Ridkodub and Katerynivka. He also said Ukrainian troops had captured Nove, a key settlement on the bridgehead.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This stage was a turning point for the entire operation,” Biletsky said.
“We have reclaimed another 51 square kilometers (19.7 square miles) of Ukrainian land, bringing the total reclaimed since the start of the offensive operations to 176 square kilometers (68 square miles),” he added.
According to the commander, control of the high ground around Nove was critical to maintaining the initiative in the area.
Ukrainian forces used converted Soviet BTR armored personnel carriers as ground-based kamikaze robotic systems to breach Russian strongpoints, he said.
Biletsky claimed that Russian personnel losses exceeded 2,000 troops during the third stage of the operation.
He also reported that more than 250 Russian soldiers had been taken prisoner, including officers, pilots and artillerymen. Biletsky said the prisoners could eventually be exchanged for Ukrainian soldiers held captive by Russia.

“The cinematic ‘Russians don’t surrender’ turned into the reality of entire units surrendering en masse,” he said.
Deception helped Ukrainian advance
Biletsky said Ukrainian forces relied heavily on deceptive maneuvers to conceal the direction of their main assault.
According to him, Russian forces were led to believe that Ukraine’s main offensive would target the Shandryholove-Zelena Dolyna area. This prompted Russian troops to commit reserves to repeated counterattacks there, allowing Ukrainian forces to concentrate their main effort elsewhere.
“The enemy was caught off guard by the main thrust aimed at capturing Nove,” Biletsky said.
He credited units of the 3rd Assault Brigade with playing a key role in the assault on the settlement, praising their offensive capabilities and professionalism.
Fighters from the 3rd Border Guard Detachment, meanwhile, regained full control of Ridkodub and quickly established defensive positions along the newly captured lines, according to Biletsky.
The commander described the third stage as a decisive phase of Operation Vivaldi, which he said had fundamentally changed the situation on the bridgehead.
“The Vivaldi music plays on,” Biletsky said at the conclusion of his address.
Vivaldi advances come as Lyman becomes a key battleground in Donetsk
The 3rd Army Corps publicly announced Operation Vivaldi on Sept. 15, after weeks of strict information silence.
Its stated aims include pushing back Russian forces, dismantling their infiltration tactics and disrupting their supply lines.
During the first phase, Ukrainian forces cleared Russian infiltration pockets around Novoselivka, Yarova, Koroviahyi Yar and Oleksandrivka and liberated the village of Serednie, which Biletsky described as a “shaping, preparatory phase.”
Biletsky had hinted that more was yet to come. “Vivaldi, as everyone knows, has four seasons. This is the first of them,” he said.
On Sept. 20, Ukrainian Defense Forces announced the results of the second phase, saying they had liberated Shandryholove and Derylove and established full control over Drobysheve. Across the first two phases, the corps said it had reclaimed 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory.
Russian forces reportedly lost around 800 soldiers during the second phase and more than 3,000 across the first two phases combined.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that Ukrainian forces had achieved significant battlefield results in the Lyman axis under this operation.
In a Telegram statement published on Sept. 27, Zelensky said he had received a report from AFU Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty. He also pointed to results achieved by the Air Assault Forces grouping in another active defense operation, without providing further details.
The Donetsk region battlefield remains particularly important as Russian President Vladimir Putin has sought to seize the remaining Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donbas, comprising the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. The Kremlin has long demanded full control of the regions as a condition for a potential settlement.
Ukraine rejects giving up its territory and sovereignty as a precondition for peace and has repeatedly called on Russia to agree to an unconditional ceasefire.
According to Zelensky’s latest statement, the most intense fighting is currently taking place along the Pokrovsk, Kostyantynivka and Lyman axes, while Ukrainian forces are also conducting combat operations in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv and Sumy regions.

Zuppi is scheduled to meet with Kremlin Aide Yury Ushako, among other senior Russian officials, which, the diplomat explained, demonstrates Russia’s appreciation of both the cardinal and his efforts and broader cooperation with the Holy See.
Earlier, the cardinal told TASS that he would arrive on a three-day visit to the Russian capital on September 28. As part of his mission, Zuppi will discuss the return home of children evacuated from the combat zone, POW swaps, problems facing civilians as a result of the Ukraine conflict and other humanitarian issues.

China said Monday that dialogue with the US is an “important pathway” for ensuring artificial intelligence benefits everyone, following an agreement to establish a formal framework for bilateral talks on the technology.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing was ready to maintain exchanges with Washington, responding to a question from an Anadolu correspondent at a news conference.
“This is an important pathway for global AI for good and for all,” he said.
Guo said China also advocates giving the UN a central role in establishing “a fairer and more equitable global AI governance system.”
Washington and Beijing agreed to establish the US-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s summit with US President Donald Trump at the White House last week, according to the US administration.
The first talks are scheduled for November.
“We are ready to maintain exchanges with the US through the artificial intelligence intergovernmental dialogue,” Guo said.
He described the engagement as part of building a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability” based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity.”
The framework aims to facilitate exchanges on AI’s risks and benefits and establish a bilateral communication channel for AI-related incidents.
According to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, future discussions could also address protocols for responding to critical threats, including uncontrollable autonomous AI agents and the spread of cyber and biological weapons capabilities to non-state actors.

2,100-year-old luxury tableware unearthed from ancient shipwreck off Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:44:56 UTC
18:44:56 KST

Yasemin Kalyoncuoglu
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Archaeologists have recovered thousands of ceramic artifacts, including 122 different forms and sizes of plates, bowls and trays, from a roughly 2,100-year-old shipwreck off Adrasan on Türkiye’s Mediterranean coast, the Culture and Tourism Ministry said Monday.
The underwater excavation, which began in 2025 off Adrasan in Antalya province, has uncovered the remains of a cargo ship carrying ceramic tableware from the ancient Mediterranean world.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said in a social media post that the artifacts offer a glimpse into the elaborate dining culture of the period.
“We are bringing 2,100-year-old tableware to light from the depths of the Mediterranean,” Ersoy said.
“The 122 different forms and sizes of plates, bowls and trays reveal the luxury dining culture of the period,” he said.
The main cargo consists of plates and bowls believed to have originated from the ancient settlement of Rhosus, in what is now Arsuz district in southern Türkiye’s Hatay province.
The finds include plates for nuts, soup bowls, fish plates and trays of various sizes.
The ministry said such products were particularly sought after in Rome and were among the luxury tableware traded across the Mediterranean.
Amphorae believed to have been produced on some Aegean islands were also found at the wreck, indicating that the ship carried goods from different production centers.
 
A connection to Cicero
The Rhosus ceramics are also mentioned in the correspondence of Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator.
In a letter to his friend Atticus in 50 B.C., Cicero wrote that he had ordered ceramic vessels from Rhosus for him, according to the ministry.
The reference indicates that tableware produced in the region was known in the Roman world.
Researchers say identifying ceramics associated with Rhosus at the Adrasan wreck could provide further insight into their role in ancient Mediterranean maritime trade.
 
How the ceramics survived
The condition of many of the plates and bowls is partly attributed to how the cargo was packed before the ship sank.
The ceramics were placed in wooden crates with clay between them.
The method helped protect the pieces from breaking during the sinking and contributed to their preservation for more than two millennia.
“These artifacts, which have survived in good condition to the present day because of the clay placed between them when they were packed into crates, preserve evidence of Anatolia’s production expertise and the Mediterranean’s trading history,” Ersoy said.
 
Trade route from Anatolia to Italy
Coins originating from Antioch and dating to the 1st century B.C. are also helping researchers date the wreck.
The findings indicate that the ship was operating within a trade network connecting Antioch, the Aegean, Greece and the Italian coast around the middle of the 1st century B.C.
Researchers believe the ship departed from Rhosus and was likely sailing toward Rome when it struck a shallow area during a storm and sank.
The wreck lies 42-55 meters (138-180 feet) below the surface. Underwater archaeologists continue excavations with the assistance of underwater robots.
Ersoy thanked the excavation team and others involved in uncovering the country’s underwater cultural heritage.
“I would like to thank our excavation team, which continues its work at a depth of 42-55 meters with the support of underwater robots, and all my colleagues who are bringing the cultural heritage of our ‘Blue Homeland’ to light,” he said.

Russia launches terrorism-related case against London councilor
The Russian authorities have announced a terrorism-related criminal case against a Russian-British woman who serves as a councilor in the London borough of Ealing.
Moscow has accused Ksenia Maximova of lobbying the British government to advance an anti-Russian government agenda, potentially in coordination with British Intelligence services and collaborating with a London law firm run by Ukrainian-British citizens allegedly on behalf of Kiev.
Maximova is associated with the Russian Anti-War Committee, backed by exiled oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky, and is an active participant in a network of groups based in the West that seeks to overthrow the Russian government and fracture the country by promoting Western military support for Ukraine, among other things.
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced on Monday that it opened a criminal case against her over alleged participation in an organization designated as ‘terrorist’ under Russian law.
As director of the Russian Democratic Society UK (RDS), which was designated as an ‘undesirable organization’ in Russia earlier this month, Maximova has overseen stunts by Russian emigres and artists protesting in support of Ukraine in front of the Russian Embassy in London.
She is also ‘consul’ for the Russian Anti-War Committee, which was declared a ‘terrorist organization’ by the Russian Supreme Court in March.
The RDS presents itself as “an alternative Russia,” and has lobbied for additional sanctions, including measures targeting Russia’s oil trade, the FSB said.
London has for decades harbored rich individuals who acquired their wealth abroad under shady circumstances, including Russian businessmen who amassed fortunes during the privatizations that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Former oligarchs, including Khodorkovsky, have used their resources and connections to support Russian opposition groups and undermine the Russian government.

EU mininsters plan response to hybrid attacks amid warnings of Russian sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:44:23 UTC
18:44:23 KST

EU foreign ministers are meeting on Monday to strengthen the bloc’s response to hybrid attacks, as EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warns that Russia is planning further sabotage across Europe.
The EU is drawing up a new mechanism to coordinate its response to Russian sabotage and other hybrid attacks, as European officials warn that Moscow is planning further operations across the continent.
European foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday have been tasked with developing the bloc’s so-called “emergency security protocol,” designed to help member states coordinate their responses quickly when a hybrid threat is identified.
“We need to be vigilant because we see in the intelligence that Russia is planning more sabotage acts,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said as she arrived for the talks.
Kallas said such attacks were aimed at European democracy, seeking to divide communities and intimidate them into withdrawing support for Ukraine.
“We have to keep this in mind while standing up to these threats,” she said.
The mechanism, spearheaded by Kallas and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, is intended to sit at the heart of the EU’s response to hybrid warfare.
Outlined by von der Leyen in her State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg in mid-September, it would form part of a new security structure and could be triggered by a member state when a hybrid threat is identified.
EU countries would then convene to coordinate their response.
Kallas said the mechanism would cover incidents that fall “under the threshold for armed aggression” but nevertheless require a response.
The urgency has been underscored by a series of recent incidents, including the breach of Finnish airspace by a Russian aircraft over the Gulf of Finland on Friday, prompting Finnish and Swedish authorities to scramble fighter jets.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said on his way into Monday’s meeting that Europe and NATO must take “bigger measures” and establish “stronger coordination” to counter such activities.
Asked about Friday’s airspace violation, Häkkänen said the incident should serve as a springboard for Europe to strengthen its air defences further. “We need money,” he said, adding: “We need joint procurements.”
Swedish Defence Minister Pål Jonson said Russia was seeking to “scare” and “intimidate” Ukraine’s allies through hybrid attacks, but argued that the strategy would fail as the EU continued to support Kyiv and impose further restrictions on Moscow.
“We welcome more measures when it comes to combatting the shadow fleet, when it comes to more sanctions, more visa restrictions, and of course with more support to Ukraine,” he said.
The incident came on the same day that the Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said the risk of Russian military action against NATO countries was growing, while describing an outright invasion as “highly unlikely” but not impossible.
Spanish daily newspaper El Mundo also reported last week that Russia could be preparing a drone operation targeting Spain, France and Italy.
Estonia’s newly appointed Defence Minister Martin Herem said on his way into the defence meeting that Tallinn's priority is to continue supporting Ukraine, whether through bilateral action or further discussions on the long-debated immobilised Russian assets.
“It’s all despite the fact that the Russian Foreign Minister (Sergey Lavrov) threatened us for that, and the Russian special forces are conducting sabotage acts,” he said.
Ministers are also expected to discuss the EU’s first Defence Readiness Report — described by Reuters as an assessment warning that the bloc is not rearming quickly enough to be ready to defend against Russia by 2030.
The year 2030 has been identified by various European intelligence agencies as a potential point by which the Kremlin could be ready to launch armed aggression against NATO allies.
To reduce that risk, EU member states must address gaps in air and missile defence, ground combat capabilities, naval forces, ammunition stockpiles and drones, according to Reuters.

Baghdad says no mission carried out by coalition forces inside Iraq since start of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:43:40 UTC
18:43:40 KST

Laith Al-Jnaidi and Mohammad Sio
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
International coalition forces have not carried out any missions inside Iraq since the beginning of 2026, Iraqi Air Force Commander Khalid al-Tamimi said Monday, stressing that his force is operating “independently.”
“No force from the coalition has carried out any duty inside Iraqi territory from the beginning of 2026 until now,” Tamimi said in an interview with the Iraqi News Agency, two days before the coalition’s mission in Iraq is scheduled to end on Sept. 30.
“All missions currently carried out by the Air Force are independent of coalition forces, and there is no direct support from them,” he added.
Tamimi said the Iraqi Air Force is working to build an integrated system of workshops, facilities and warehouses, noting that maintenance of Iraq’s F-16 fighter jets is being carried out “100% by Iraqi personnel.”
He said some levels of engine repair still require referral to Pratt & Whitney, a US-based aerospace manufacturer, while Iraqi crews handle part of the repair work locally.
Tamimi also said negotiations are advancing over the acquisition of Rafale fighter jets, adding that “the first batch under negotiation is for 14 aircraft,” without identifying the party involved in the talks.
On training cooperation, he said Rafale aircraft based in Jordan take part in monthly exercises with the Iraqi Air Force, while a drill scheduled to be held in France this year was postponed because of the war in the region.
Tamimi said Iraq’s air defenses provide radar coverage across the country, while fighter jets armed with air-to-air missiles and pilots remain on daily standby.
“We conduct a full daily aerial scan of all Iraq,” he said, adding that reports are submitted to the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces through the army chief of staff.
There are efforts to develop local manufacturing capabilities and a proposal to establish a separate command for drones, although work in this field remains at an early stage, the Iraqi commander added.
Turning to security threats, he said sleeper cells remain in remote and rugged areas but described the current threat as “very limited,” citing public vigilance and the capabilities available to Iraqi forces.
He said the Iraqi Air Force carried out 58,822 missions during the war against ISIS/Daesh terror group, including transport, reconnaissance and other operations, as well as supporting ground forces and striking the group’s positions.
Separately, Tamimi disclosed that an Antonov transport aircraft was taken out of service after being struck by a missile at a base in Baghdad, without specifying when the incident happened or who was responsible.
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 to end the military mission of the US-led international coalition in Iraq and transition toward bilateral security partnerships aimed at supporting Iraqi forces and maintaining pressure on ISIS to prevent its resurgence.
The US-led coalition was formed in September 2014 to fight ISIS and supported Iraqi forces during the campaign against the terrorist group. After its territorial defeat in Iraq in 2017, the coalition’s role shifted largely toward advising, assisting and strengthening Iraqi security capabilities.

“I ask you to pray for our tormentor,” he continued. “He needs this prayer most of all. Because no matter what happened, we must overcome the evil that occurred here in our abbey with goodness, love, and forgiveness.”
Mantykiewicz also appealed for people not to blame Ukrainians more broadly for the incident. There have been fears that the attack could prompt a backlash against Ukrainians, Poland’s largest immigrant group, who have already been experiencing a growing number of hate crimes this year.
“I also want to ask you not to blame the nation from which the perpetrator came,” said the priest. “The evil was committed by a specific person…responsible for their own actions. It was not done by other people. It was one person, one person alone.”

Disciples who help others with love, care, respect, help and kindness,” he continued. “It does not matter who they are, what nation they come from, what religion they are, or what colour their skin is; they are human beings…and we must not deprive anyone of their dignity.”
On Friday, the head of the Polish Catholic church’s council for migrants and refugees, Bishop Krzysztof Zadarko, gave a press conference at which he condemned the “outpouring of aggression and artificially stoked hatred towards Ukrainians that this event [in Jarosław] has fuelled”.
“The church can only appeal to the consciences, primarily of Catholics and Christians, but also of all people, that this is not the right response; it is downright reprehensible, and incompatible with the Gospel,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF.
“We are dealing with a tremendous tragedy, but shifting the blame of one person onto an entire society, ethnic group, or nationality is wrong,” he added.

EU approves major defense projects plan, with Ukraine featuring prominently
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:42:40 UTC
18:42:40 KST

The Council of the EU on Sept. 28 approved plans for five bloc-wide projects to bolster Europe's defense capabilities, with Ukraine participating in most of them.
The European Commission, the bloc's executive arm, proposed the projects in July to address shortfalls in key defense areas, namely air defense, maritime security, space, drone and counter-drone capabilities, and security along the EU's eastern flank.
EU defense ministers backed the plan on Sept. 28 after it was supported by member states' ambassadors on Sept. 16.
Ukraine is included in four of the five projects, with the space project being the lone exception.
"These projects further demonstrate the practical cooperation between EU member states to provide for our own security," said Irish Foreign and Defense Minister Helen McEntee, whose country holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU.
"Working closely with our partners Norway and Ukraine, together we are taking decisive steps to protect space, our skies, our seas, undersea cables, and our citizens who depend on them."
The first of the five proposed projects is dedicated entirely to drone and counter-drone technology, where Ukraine is expected to play an important role, and all EU countries are taking part except for neutral Malta.
DECODER, as it is known, is expected to cost between 3.5 billion euros and 5.5 billion euros ($4 billion to $6 billion), making it by far the cheapest of the five projects. That money will fund a network of drone technology hubs to facilitate testing and innovation, and improve interoperability.
Of likely more immediate interest to Ukraine is the air and missile defense project (EU-FIAMD), expected to cost 55-80 billion euros ($63-92 billion) by 2040.
While Ukraine is a world leader in drone warfare, the country's weakness lies in anti-ballistic missile defenses. Kyiv seeks to rapidly plug this gap as it braces for a new wave of Russian missile strikes this winter.
The scope of the newly proposed projects also ventures out into space, where Ukraine is not participating, and into the sea, where it is.
The "integrated maritime and seabed defense" project envisions bringing together military and civilian personnel, as well as drones, to monitor all types of sea-based infrastructure, such as fuel pipelines, wind turbines, and internet cables.
Western officials have raised alarm over suspected Moscow-backed efforts to sabotage and disrupt European undersea infrastructure, particularly in the Baltic Sea.
Rounding out the list of the five projects is its most expensive, the Eastern Flank Watch, estimated to cost between 60 and 100 billion euros ($69-115 billion) by 2036.
Unlike the other four projects, the Eastern Flank Watch cuts across combat domains and is instead geographically restricted, though the proposal argues that "it benefits all member states against concrete security threats and is open to extend its geographic area of interest."
Brussels announced the Eastern Flank Watch in October 2025, weeks after a Russian drone incursion into Polish airspace.

Chinese shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles appear in Russian service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:41:38 UTC
18:41:38 KST

- Russian state TV footage shows a Russian air defense unit with unmarked shoulder-fired missiles resembling China's QW-18A and QW-19, Militarnyi reported.
- The launchers were filmed with a mobile fire group of the 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region.
Russian air defense troops appear to be using Chinese-designed shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles, according to an analysis by Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi of footage aired on Russian state television.
The launchers were shown during an exercise by a mobile fire group of Russia’s 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region, in a segment broadcast by the state channel Rossiya 1 and shared on X by the account TheDeadDistrict. Mobile fire groups are small teams, often riding in pickup trucks, that Russia uses to hunt Ukrainian drones with machine guns and short-range missiles.
The soldiers in the report called the weapon “Iva.” But the launcher does not match any man-portable air defense system, or MANPADS, known to be in Russian service, Militarnyi reported Sept. 28. Russia’s own shoulder-fired missiles in current use include the Igla-S and the newer Verba.
Militarnyi said the launcher most closely resembles Iran’s Misagh-3 and China’s QW-18A and QW-19. Neither the launchers nor the missiles shown on camera carried any visible markings, which the outlet said could point to an effort to hide where they came from.
A closer look at the footage favors a Chinese origin, according to Militarnyi. The Russian launchers have an extra fitting on the front section that does not appear in available photos of the Iranian Misagh-3. The outlet did not rule out that it could be a newer Iranian version, but said no photos of Misagh launchers with that feature have been published. Militarnyi said it could not determine whether the system is a QW-18 or a QW-19. China’s state-owned CASIC showed the QW-19 at the DSA 2024 defense exhibition in Kuala Lumpur.
The weapons may have reached Russia through Iran, Militarnyi said. Tehran buys Chinese arms, including shoulder-fired missiles, and in July 2026 reports emerged that an Iranian deal with China covers up to 400 MANPADS, including the QW-12 and FN-16, at an estimated cost of $60 million to $70 million. Iran’s Misagh family is itself derived from China’s QW series, and Pakistan builds a similar missile under the name Anza-2.
Militarnyi said Russia’s use of foreign-made shoulder-fired missiles may indicate that its own industry cannot produce enough to meet the military’s needs. Mobile fire groups have become a main line of defense against the long-range drones Ukraine sends against Russian refineries, airfields and weapons plants, which increases demand for short-range missiles.
Ukraine has previously said it confirmed Chinese supplies of gunpowder and artillery systems to Russia, and Ukrainian intelligence services believe military cooperation between the two countries includes producing Chinese-designed weapons inside Russia. China has repeatedly said it does not supply lethal weapons to either side in the war.

Asian Games | Feature: 18-year-old Yan Ziyi throws her way into a new era
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:41:09 CST
18:41:09 KST

by sportswriters Cao Yibo, Yue Chenxing, Wang Qinou
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- With a roar, Yan Ziyi sent her javelin flying into the rainy night sky in Nagoya.
The crowd gasped as the big screen showed 70.46 meters, a result that secured the 18-year-old the women's javelin title at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday.
The throw, on Yan's Asian Games debut, broke the Games record by 4.37 meters. The previous mark of 66.09 meters was set by Chinese athlete Liu Shiying at the 2018 Jakarta Games.
It was also Yan's only throw of the final. She passed on her remaining five attempts, and nobody else came close. Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi of Japan took silver with 62.70 meters.
"I didn't expect to finish it with one throw. My plan was just to make my first two throws count," she said in the mixed zone, with tears still in her eyes.
The tears had a reason. Two weeks earlier, at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Yan threw 68.05 meters on her first attempt before withdrawing with a foot injury. Kitaguchi passed her with 68.92 meters to take the title.
Yan said she felt she had let people down. After claiming victory at the Asian Games, she said the weight was finally gone.
"I'm actually a pretty calm person. I don't show my feelings much," Yan said.
She has nothing but respect for Kitaguchi, a rival she has faced many times. Yan said she watches and learns from the Japanese star and feels more admiration than pressure.
"I can't say I'm stronger, because we are all chasing each other," Yan said. "Everyone is a target for me to chase."
Yan's journey began in a primary school PE class. After she once threw a softball farther than her classmates, a coach put her on the field team. At sports school, she started with the shot put before switching to the javelin.
People often call Yan a javelin prodigy, but she does not fully agree.
The road was not always smooth. "At the beginning it was really tiring, and I thought about giving up. But I stuck with it," Yan told Xinhua.
"Having talent isn't enough. I have to train so that my talent can show," she added.
Her body keeps changing, and so must her training. As she grows taller and heavier, she has to keep working on her run-up speed and adjusting her technique. Training, she noted, is not simply about repetition. "Learning new moves and new ways to train" is something she enjoys.
Age restrictions once kept Yan out of some senior international events. She said the wait gave her time to sharpen her technique and gain experience.
The results followed quickly. In 2024, Yan threw 64.28 meters at a national grand prix, setting a world U20 record. She won the U20 World Championships the same year.
In 2025, she threw 65.89 meters at the national championships despite carrying an injury. It was the fourth time she had broken the world U20 record.
In May this year, she threw 71.74 meters on her first attempt at the Diamond League meeting in Xiamen, breaking the Asian and world U20 records. It was also the second-best throw in women's javelin history, just 54 centimeters short of Barbora Spotakova's world record of 72.28 meters set in 2008.
Yan kept winning. Xiamen, Oslo, Paris and Monaco all went her way, with each winning throw exceeding 67 meters. In September, she came from behind in Brussels to win the Diamond League final and claim the season title.
Yan is now ranked No. 1 in the world. After her Monaco victory, the Diamond League posted a comment in all capital letters on social media: "ABSOLUTE DOMINATION."
Back in 2024, at 16 and too young for the Paris Olympics, Yan told Xinhua with a smile: "In the future, let's start a new era that belongs to me."
Two years later, that line sounds less like a wish and more like a plan.
"I can start a new era, because I'm still young. I have more time and more chances," she said.
Yan remains modest when the conversation turns to Chinese shot put great Gong Lijiao. "I don't think I can compare myself to her. She's a role model for me. I still have to keep learning from her and chasing what she's achieved," Yan said.
Yan's next targets are already clear: the world championships in Beijing, followed by the Olympics the year after.
"I plan to save the new record for the world championships in Beijing," Yan said after Sunday's competition. "So stay tuned for that." ■
