Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has been quoted as predicting that U.S. military forces will soon be driven out of the Arabian Sea.
In a message to mark Iran's Sacred Defense Week, the ayatollah — who has not been seen or heard from directly since the war began — said U.S. forces were unable to advance beyond the Arabian Sea, which leads to the Strait of Hormuz, "because of the painful blows they have received."
He added that soon, U.S. troops would be driven from the Arabian Sea, too.
U.S. forces have operated across the region since the war began, including to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in defiance of Iran's bid to control traffic through the vital waterway.
The wide-ranging message attributed by Iranian state media to Khamenei included praise for Iran's military forces, as well as for the former leader of the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon.
Khamenei was named Iran's new supreme leader soon after his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first round of U.S.-Israeli strikes, which sparked the war on Feb. 28.
The younger Khamenei has not been seen, even in video, since he was named the supreme leader, and senior U.S. officials have said he was likely seriously wounded in the same strike that killed his father.
Value of Iran's currency falls to all-time low against the dollar
The Iranian rial has fallen to a new historic low against the U.S. dollar, with the free-market selling rate surpassing 2.4 million rials per dollar on Monday.
Data from Pashizi, which tracks Iran's free-market exchange rates, put the dollar at around 2.4 million rials as Iran faces high inflation, sweeping sanctions and growing disruption to foreign trade.
Annual inflation has reached 61.4% in August, while food prices are reported to have risen 128% from a year earlier, according to data from Iran's Statistical Center.
Iran's U.N. delegation has no plans to negotiate directly with the U.S.
Iranian state media said Monday that Iran's delegation at the U.N. General Assembly in New York had no plans to hold direct talks with the U.S., after President Trump said he expected more negotiations to take place this week.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday he expected negotiations to continue this week, and added that the Iranian leaders were interested in reaching an agreement because they are "losing badly."
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side ... via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.

CBS/AFP
British police investigating possible Iranian links to suspected terrorist plot against U.K. air base used by U.S.

Iran says it is ready for either diplomacy, or a return to fighting as war reaches 7-month mark
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready for either diplomacy or a return to fighting in the war sparked seven months ago by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. He said it is now up to President Trump to choose which direction to go.
"We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi told NBC News' "Meet the Press."

President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to return to a ceasefire agreement that collapsed months ago as part of a seven-day plan that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.
Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.
Trump expects talks with Iran to resume this week

Egypt, Syria accelerate economic cooperation at Damascus talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:20:52 UTC
18:20:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt, Syria accelerate economic cooperation at Damascus talks
Government officials from Egypt and Syria have met to discuss means of advancing cooperation and increasing mutual investment and trade, amid what observers describe as a shared interest in the two countries for forging closer relations in the coming period.
The meeting, held in Damascus on 18 September, came under a government cooperation mechanism created by the two countries to enhance their economic ties.
It was the second to be held by officials from the two countries under the same mechanism, the first being held in Cairo in April this year.
Attending the latest meeting in Damascus was a host of officials from the two countries, who represented cooperation files designated as priority ones at this point.
Discussions between these officials during the meeting also focused on means of turning understandings reached in Cairo in April into action.
They also agreed to advance their two countries' cooperation in the same priority sectors, form technical working groups to enhance this cooperation and hold a joint business forum to explore trade and investment opportunities.
They also welcomed the formation of the Joint Egyptian-Syrian Business Council which convened for the first time on the sidelines of the Damascus meeting.
These measures, economists in Cairo said, reflect the presence of a mutual desire by Cairo and Damascus to advance cooperation and chart a new course in the two capitals' economic relations, in general.
Former dean of the College of Economics and Political Science at Cairo University Alia al-Mahdi said she believes economic cooperation chances between Egypt and Syria are huge.
"I think the newly-founded business council will play a big role in advancing their cooperation," professor al-Mahdi said.
Speaking to The New Arab, she added that council members would study the needs of the markets in the two countries and consequently trace the opportunities available in them in the coming period.
Egypt, she said, could offer a lot to Syria to push its post-Bashar al-Assad recovery and development efforts forward.
"Apart from political and diplomatic backing, Egypt can offer Syria its development expertise to help it bring its devastated infrastructure, including its electricity network, cities and roads, back into good shape," she added.
Accelerating pace
Egypt and Syria have been stepping up their economic cooperation since the downfall of al-Assad's regime in December 2024, with Cairo apparently eyeing the economic chances it can have in the new Syria, specialists said.
In 2025, trade exchange between the two countries rose by 29.2%, compared to 2023 (to $422.92 million from $327.43 million).
However, real trade exchange figures can be far higher, more than double this volume, economists said.
Banking SWIFT restrictions imposed on Syria before 2025 meant that most of its trade with other countries, including with Egypt, went to and from it through either Jordan or Turkey in a manner that did not reflect on official trade exchange figures.
The restrictions were removed in August 2026, as part of efforts to reintegrate the new Syria into the international community.
The removal of the same restrictions compounded Syria's removal by the US from the list of state sponsors of terrorism, and came almost three months after the European Union removed key Syrian government institutions from its sanctions list and restored the full application of the EU-Syria Cooperation Agreement.
These developments have made the new authorities in Syria more capable of making business with other countries, including Egypt, economists said.
The same developments have also allowed Egypt to pursue its goal of carving its share of the economic opportunities the post-Assad Syria offers, including in the fields of construction and investment.
Ahmed Ragheb Agha, deputy head of the Syrian side of the Egyptian-Syrian Business Council, said Syria has so many opportunities to offer other countries that want to cooperate with the Syrians.
"The current recovery phase in Syria opens up huge business opportunities for everybody," al-Agha told TNA.
Quoting United Nations figures, he estimated the cost of Syria's reconstruction at $200 billion.
Syria, Al-Agha said, is badly in need of investments in all construction sectors.
Roads, he said, need to be established, electricity plants need to be rebuilt, and water stations need to be constructed.
He also pointed to available investment opportunities in energy, renewable energy and telecommunications.
"The industrial and agricultural sectors are also open for investment, not to mention the tourism sector which needs to come back to life," al-Agha said.
Meanwhile, Syrian investments in Egypt amount to $1 billion, a figure that jumps to billions when unregistered or informal investments are taken into consideration.
These investments are present in the form of hundreds of companies and businesses launched by the Syrians who escaped to Egypt from the civil war raging on in their country between 2011 and 2024.
Egypt boasts a large Syrian community whose members have established their own successful economic models, benefiting from the Arab country's huge consumer market.
At the same time, Egyptian investors appear to look forward to seizing opportunities in specific sectors of the Syrian economy, including infrastructure, energy, real estate and building materials.
This comes as Egypt introduces itself as a reconstruction model for regional states, especially those seeking to recuperate from conflicts, economists said.
Political thaw
Efforts made by Cairo and Damascus to advance their economic, investment and trade cooperation come as the two capitals take measures to improve their political relations.
This happens at a time when Egypt appears to be partly overcoming the initial caution with which it received news of the downfall of the al-Assad regime and the emergence of the Ahmed al-Sharaa government in Syria.
In the past months, the two sides intensified their diplomatic and political contacts, even as they still have a long way to go to reach full political and diplomatic normalisation.
In June this year, Egypt approved Syria's candidate for chargé d’affaires at the Syrian embassy in Cairo, even as the two countries have yet to appoint mutual ambassadors.
The Syrian and Egyptian foreign ministers are also accelerating their contacts, having met last on 7 September to discuss cooperation, including in trade.
When asked about relations with Syria almost ten days later, Egyptian Minister of Information Diaa Rashwan ruled out the presence of differences.
"What appears on the surface doesn't reflect the presence of any differences between the two countries," Minister Rashwan said on the sidelines of the Arab Media Forum in Dubai.
He highlighted Syria strategic importance for Egypt and other Arab states, noting that Syria used to be Egypt's northern front yard when the two countries were in unity.
"Egypt cannot see Syria otherwise," the Egyptian minister said.

Melike Pala
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Sweden’s Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson on Monday abandoned her attempt to form a new government, saying she currently lacked the parliamentary support needed to proceed, according to public broadcaster SVT.
Andersson, who was tasked by parliament’s speaker 10 days ago with exploring the possibility of forming a government, said she decided to step aside after the Left Party announced it would support the Moderate Party’s candidate in the speaker election.
“I can state that there is currently no possibility for me to form a government,” Andersson said.
She said the development represented a “new constellation in parliament,” involving the Left Party and the Moderates.
Andersson pointed to the parliamentary tradition under which the largest party in a governing coalition holds the speaker post, saying it was therefore reasonable for the grouping that emerged around the speaker election to now try to reach an agreement on forming a government.
Asked whether she had abandoned her bid to become prime minister, Andersson said there were currently no conditions for her to move forward.
“How things develop in the coming weeks remains to be seen,” she added.
The decision leaves the next stage of Sweden’s government-formation process in the hands of parliament’s speaker.

Fact check: Did Denmark play 'Send in the Clowns' song before signing US-Greenland security deal?

Unknown Publisher

18:19:09 KST

Denmark's Ministry of Foreign Affairs denied any involvement in choosing the music played before the signing ceremony, but the claim continues to spread on social media.
Social media posts claim that Denmark deliberately played the song "Send in the Clowns" before US President Donald Trump joined Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen for a deal-signing ceremony at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The claim was shared on X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.
On X, for example, one post garnered more than 1.3 million views.
The clip shared shows a camera's close-up on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio while the song's lyrics include the line: "Where are the clowns? Send in the clowns. Don't bother, they're here."
While most posts claimed that Denmark chose the song, one Instagram post went further, stating: "Denmark just humiliated Marco Rubio at the United Nations!"
However, none of these claims is true.
There is no evidence that Danish officials or the media selected the music played before the event on 22 September.
The signing ceremony sealed a new security deal between the US, Denmark and Greenland, following months of tension over the US president's push to take control of the self-governing Danish territory.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, reached out to the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which said Denmark was not involved in the choice of music during the signing.
Yet, "Send in the Clowns" was nevertheless one of the tracks played before the event as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in the room.
The song, written by Stephen Sondheim for the 1973 musical "A Little Night Music", was performed by Judy Collins.
A replay on UN TV shows the song was played moments before Trump entered to sign the agreement with Frederiksen and Nielsen.
The US Mission to the United Nations did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US-Denmark-Greenland deal
The agreement closed after 10 months of negotiations and sought to end a diplomatic standoff triggered by Trump's repeated demands to take control of Greenland and refusal to rule out military force.
The US will be permitted to expand its military presence on Greenland through the modernisation and enlargement of its current Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of new defence areas, including at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
The agreement will also allow the US "free access to and movement between" defence areas in Greenland, "including the Territorial Waters, by land, air and sea", according to the terms of the deal, shared online by the Danish Foreign Ministry.
US aircraft may also fly over and land in any territory on the island.
The US reportedly operated 17 military facilities and more than 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War.
It currently operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base - the US Department of Defense's northernmost installation.
According to the US Space Force, Pituffik is used for missile warning, missile defence and space surveillance missions.
In a statement, Frederiksen said the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area", while Nielsen said it was "to the benefit of us all".
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte also welcomed the new deal.
On X, he wrote that the agreement enhances the collective security of NATO members and supports a safer and more stable future for them all.
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Located between the Arctic and North America, it is also regarded as strategically important to the US.

France faces pressure over disputed Indian Ocean island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:18:10 UTC
18:18:10 KST

French dispute with former colony over island intensifies
France must address a decades-old dispute with its former colony, the archipelago of Mauritius, over control of Tromelin Island, the island nation’s foreign minister has insisted. 
The Indian Ocean territory, which incorporates a huge oceanic economic zone, is part of Mauritius, Dhananjay Ramful told the UN General Assembly.
Mauritius maintains that Tromelin was among the dependencies ceded with Mauritius to Britain under an 1814 treaty. It formally asserted its claim in 1976, eight years after gaining independence. However, France continues to administer the largely uninhabited island and claims sovereignty over it.
“The island of Tromelin is an integral part of the territory of the Republic of Mauritius,” Ramful said in New York on Friday. He called on Paris to engage “in the spirit of friendship” to resolve the dispute. 
Tromelin covers about 1 sq km, but the surrounding exclusive economic zone exceeds 280,000 sq km and contains valuable fishing grounds. France has administered the island since 1954, when it established a meteorological station there.
The two countries signed an agreement in 2010 to jointly manage fishing, environmental protection, and research around Tromelin without deciding who owns it. France’s Senate approved the deal in 2012, but the government withdrew it from a scheduled National Assembly debate in 2017 amid opposition to joint management. The agreement remains unratified.
Tromelin is not France’s only territorial dispute with a former African colony. Madagascar claims four French-administered islands in the Mozambique Channel, while the Comoros claims Mayotte, which France governs as an overseas department.
Mauritius also has a territorial dispute with Britain over the Chagos Archipelago. London separated the islands from British-ruled Mauritius in 1965. In his UN address, Ramful called Mauritian sovereignty over Chagos “non-negotiable” and pointed to a treaty signed with Britain in May 2025 as a path toward settling the dispute.
Britain signed a treaty last year to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius while retaining the joint UK-US base on Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease. The deal followed a 2019 International Court of Justice opinion that Britain’s separation of the islands from Mauritius before independence was unlawful. The treaty has yet to take effect. US President Donald Trump has called it a “terrible deal” and opposed the transfer of the strategically important islands. Britain has put the agreement on hold, with Defense Secretary Wes Streeting saying last week that it “can’t go ahead without American support.”

Forgery of medical documents: why did Odrex clinic fail to provide the Odesa Regional Military Administration’s Department of Health with the medical records of the deceased patient?
Kyiv • UNN
The Department of Health of the Odesa Regional Military Administration refused to conduct a clinical expert assessment of Ihor Melai’s treatment at Odrex. This was due to the clinic’s lack of the original medical records, which had been seized by law enforcement officers. At the same time, experts emphasize that when originals are seized, certified copies of the documents must remain at the medical facility.
The Health Department of the Odesa Regional State Administration refused to conduct a clinical expert assessment of the treatment provided to deceased patient Ihor Melai at the private Odrex clinic. Odesa officials explained their failure to comply with the Ministry of Health’s instruction by the absence of the original medical documents, which had been seized by investigators. At the same time, record-keeping rules require the clinic to retain certified copies. Moreover, Odrex representatives publicly stated that such copies exist, UNN reports.
If the original documents are seized, copies of those documents, certified in accordance with the Rules, and an inventory of the seized documents must remain at the institution
Moreover, as Ihor Melai’s widow, Olha Melai, told UNN, Odrex representatives publicly confirmed that the clinic has such copies. In one comment, a clinic representative wrote:
"The clinic has its own copies of the documents, the treatment history, and the prescriptions. We are ready to sit down and compare them with you, point by point"
This statement directly contradicts the argument Odrex clinic presented to the Health Department of the Odesa Regional State Administration. The Department’s response to Olha Melai states that Dim Medytsyny LLC and Medical House "Odrex" LLC reported that they were unable to provide the requested documentation because it had been seized by law enforcement officers.
This raises the question: if the clinic has copies of Ihor Melai’s medical documents, why were they not provided to the Department for the inspection?
The falsification of medical documents could cost Odrex its license 07.08.26, 09:00 • 94172 views
This contradiction is particularly significant given what exactly Olha Melai asked to have investigated. In her appeal to the Ministry of Health, she pointed to discrepancies between the medical documents the family received during Ihor Melai’s treatment and the documentation the clinic subsequently submitted to the court. In particular, these concerned the type of anesthesia used during the surgery, the circumstances of the procedure itself, and the description of the postoperative period. Melai also specifically asked for the records in the electronic healthcare system to be examined and for it to be established whether any changes had been made to them.
We remind you
Ihor Melai died after nearly eight months of treatment at the private Odrex clinic. As UNN previously reported, the man was undergoing treatment for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
According to his widow, Olha Melai, Odrex doctors initially planned to conduct eight courses of immunochemotherapy. On April 26, 2025, Ihor Melai was offered the insertion of a pleural port. According to Olha, the procedure was presented to the family as a minimally invasive intervention that was to be performed under local anesthesia. However, after the surgery, the man was transferred to the intensive care unit, where he remained on mechanical ventilation for three days. During the first 24 hours after the procedure, approximately five liters of fluid were drained from his chest cavity. Treatment was subsequently continued, but Ihor Melai completed only four of the eight planned courses of immunochemotherapy.
According to Olha Melai’s statements, law enforcement officers initiated criminal proceedings concerning certain circumstances of her husband’s treatment. The court must provide the final legal assessment of the medical personnel’s actions, the authenticity of the documentation, and any possible violations.

Ukrainian company Vyriy unveils Slavic tactical reconnaissance UAV – photos
Ukrainian company Vyriy Industries is launching its new Slavic tactical reconnaissance drone.
Source: Vyriy Industries
Quote: "The drone was developed as a Ukrainian alternative to Chinese commercial copters. It allows reconnaissance crews to operate at a safer distance from the line of contact and remain airborne for longer, while retaining the DJI Mavic control logic familiar to operators."
Details: The Slavic is equipped with a 40,000 mAh solid-state battery, providing up to 1.5 hours of flight time. Its tactical range is up to 30 km, allowing reconnaissance of the front line while keeping the crew at a safer distance from the engagement zone.
The drone can operate without GPS, using optical positioning for navigation. Its communications system operates across a wide range of channels, allowing operators to select channels with less interference and maintain better connectivity in challenging terrain.
The manufacturer says the Slavic is equipped for surveillance with a 2K digital daylight camera (2560×1440) mounted on a three-axis stabilised gimbal, offering 10× optical zoom and 30× hybrid zoom.
The system is supplied ready to use out of the box, with all the equipment required for operation without additional modifications in the field. The supplied controller supports integration with the Delta and Kropyva situational awareness systems, as well as video streaming directly from the controller to the Vezha app.
Oleksii Babenko, founder and CEO of Vyriy Industries, said, "The war has changed, and so have the conditions in which crews operate. The kill zone has expanded, while available commercial drones have a limited tactical range. The main task now is to provide the military with a specialised platform that can fly for longer and farther, allowing crews to operate farther from the line of contact. That is precisely why we began developing the Slavic."
The company said its new drone had successfully completed initial combat trials with seven units of the Ukrainian defence forces and was now being prepared for scaling up.
The manufacturer added that the team was simultaneously working on new Slavic configurations, testing thermal imaging modules for night-time reconnaissance and the use of the platform as a communications relay carrier. The company is also preparing to scale up production and deliveries to the Ukrainian defence forces.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that Vyriy had unveiled the first prototype of its Slavic copter-type reconnaissance UAV and disclosed the platform's initial specifications.

PRESS REVIEW – Monday, September 28: Papers discuss the Orange Order parade standoff in Northern Ireland. Also, who are the suspects in the RAF base terror plot? Finally, we look at some of the latest data on relationships.
Amid a standoff in Northern Ireland over a Protestant parade, the headline of The Irish News reads "We don't want this. We just want to live in peace". It's a quote by a mother of a Catholic child who died during the Drumcree parading dispute 30 years ago. The height of that dispute came in the 1990s, when several Catholic children died in a petrol bomb attack on their home by the Ulster Volunteer Force. The mother says she feels "traumatised" and as if history is repeating itself.
The BBC explains that the "Orange Order march row goes to the heart of the ongoing divisions in Northern Ireland". The article says that chamber disputes between unionists and nationalists happen almost every week. But ground-level arguments like this one are rare. The Orange Order is a Protestant, pro-British organisation and the area where it wants to march is mostly Catholic and has pro-Irish nationalists. The article reminds us that in the 1990s, the dispute spread to other places and "almost derailed the peace process". But while it was never resolved, it slowly faded.
But The Guardian writes that the "Drumcree stand-off shows Northern Ireland's troubled past still threatens its peace". The paper says the conflict reminds us "how easily history can undermine the present – if imperfect – peace and stability". The Guardian says that today's Northern Ireland is very different from that of three decades ago: there is no longer a unionist majority and First Minister Michelle O'Neill is from Sinn Féin, a party focused on achieving a united Ireland.
Next, an analysis piece in The Times says that the "RAF bases have long been targets of terror attacks". Counterterrorism police haven't ruled out the possibility that Islamists are behind Sunday's foiled plot. But British bases have also been on alert since this summer, when Iran said that anyone assisting the United States air strikes in the Middle East was a "legitimate target". This means that Iran is a suspect. The Times concludes that "any involvement of Tehran would prove a major escalation".
Finally, we look at articles discussing some new relationship data. The Guardian explains that marriages that end in divorce today last longer than at any point since records began. One hypothesis says that couples may be delaying the legal end until they can afford what comes next. There are other hypotheses, like delaying divorce because of Covid-19 or also overall external uncertainty, like the environment, politics, etc. The Guardian also reminds us that women are mostly the ones who ask for divorce.
But what about couples who are doing well? It turns out that regular churchgoers – married men and women – have more sex than secular couples, The Atlantic reports. Mostly Christians were interviewed, but there were some Muslim and Jewish people too. Those surveyed live in the United States and attend religious services at least twice a month. So according to this study, it seems like religious couples have avoided the "sex recession". Could this be just wives feeling obliged to sleep with their husbands? According to the data, they actually describe their sex life as "excellent" or "very good".
However, we should take all this data with a pinch of salt as the survey in question was conducted by the Institute for Family Studies, a conservative think tank that aims to strengthen marriage and promote traditional family structures. Also, we don't know if gay couples were even surveyed.

Immigrants help ease labor shortages in critical sectors in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:15:50 UTC
18:15:50 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Some 27% of all dependent employees in Germany had a migration background in 2025, according to Destatis on Monday.
In key shortage occupations, workers with a migration background are heavily represented, led by cooks at 56% and food manufacturing workers at 55%.
They also account for more than half of the workforce in floor laying at 54%, scaffolding at 51% and meat processing at 51%.
Among bus and tram drivers as well as food service staff, the proportion stands at 47%.
One-third of employees in nursing occupations have a migration background, while the share reaches 44% in plastics manufacturing and 41% in freight transport.
The lowest proportions in shortage occupations are found in emergency rescue services at 7%, meat sales at 13% and agriculture at 15%.
Outside shortage occupations, people with a migration background are underrepresented in police services at 8%, as well as in public administration and the judiciary at 9% each.
According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), labor market integration varies depending on region of origin and length of stay.
EU-born men aged 25 to 59 living in Germany for less than five years had an employment rate of 89%, while the rate for EU-born women stood at 73%.
While employment rates for immigrants from Africa and the Middle East are lower during the early years, they converge after 20 to 25 years toward the general employment rates of 88% for men and 81% for women.

Sweden faces political deadlock after election-winning center-left bloc fails to form government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

Sweden's center-left bloc fails to form government
September 28, 2026
The leader of Sweden's center-left Social Democratic Party, Magdalena Andersson, on Monday said her talks with other parties had failed to form a government after her bloc's narrow election victory.
The breakdown leaves Sweden without a new government more than two weeks after the election and opens the door for the outgoing right-wing bloc to try to remain in power despite losing the vote.
Why did Sweden's government talks fail?
Andersson had been trying to bring together the Social Democrats, Greens, Center Party and Left Party, which together won 176 of parliament's 349 seats.
But talks foundered on deep divisions between the centrist Center Party and socialist Left Party.
"Based on the discussions I have had, I can conclude that, as things currently stand, it is not possible for me to form a government," Andersson told reporters.
The four-party bloc won 176 seats in the September 13 election, compared with 173 for the outgoing right-wing alliance. The popular vote difference was around 50,000.
What happens next?
The speaker of parliament is now expected to ask another party leader to try to form a government, with outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson of the center-right Moderate Party the likely next choice.
Kristersson continues to lead a caretaker government. His bloc, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats, has also failed to secure a majority and would probably need support from the Center Party.
Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has ruled out supporting a government that gives influence to either the Sweden Democrats or the Left Party.
Protracted government formation is not unusual in Sweden. It took 37 days to establish a government following the 2022 election and 134 days after the vote in 2018.

Russia under Putin lost nearly half its schools — war propaganda fills the rest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:12:41 UTC
18:12:41 KST

Closures driven by per-pupil funding that made smaller rural schools unviable far outpaced demographic decline. Since 2022, all remaining schools hold mandatory weekly classes on Russian "traditional values" and the Kremlin's version of events surrounding Russia's war in Ukraine.
The number of schools in Russia has fallen by 45% since the start of the century, with rural communities losing the most, according to a report by the Higher School of Economics published this month.
Russia's secondary school network has shrunk from 68,800 institutions in 2000 to just under 38,000 in 2026, the report says. The school-age population has fallen by around 13.5% over the same period, from 20.5 million to 17.7 million children.
Russia now has fewer schools than Germany, even though its population is roughly half the size. Germany has more than 40,000 schools in 2026.
Closures have been most severe in rural areas, where the number of state schools has fallen from more than 45,000 to around 21,000, a reduction of more than half.
Urban schools have also declined, from 22,700 in 2000 to 16,300 today. The number of pupils each school serves has grown substantially over the same period: from around 300 pupils per school 15 years ago to around 470 today.
Private schools have increased in number, from 635 in 2000 to 982 in 2026, but account for only 2.5% of total provision.
Is bigger always better?
The closures stem from an optimisation programme launched in 2001 that remains ongoing.
A shift to per-pupil funding made smaller schools financially unviable: the fewer children a school enrolled, the less state money it received. Schools were merged with neighbouring institutions or closed outright.
By 2010, 26% of Russia's schools had shut. Around 10,000 more closed in the 2010s, and a further 2,300 since the early 2020s.
Teachers and parents protested the mergers. They argued that large consolidated institutions were harder to manage, that neighbourhood schools with distinct characters were being lost, and that overcrowded classes would reduce educational quality.
Sociologists have also linked school closures to village depopulation, according to a 2026 study published in the Russian magazine Nozh.
The study found that when a village school closes, families typically split — one parent relocates to a town with the children while the other stays to work — and the separation becomes permanent.
"By saving on the costs of a single classroom and teacher, you can wipe out a whole thriving local economy," the study said.
The village of Atary in Kirov region's Lebyazhsky district is one example: after the local school was declared unprofitable, young people left, and the settlement is now largely abandoned.
Communist Party MP Dmitry Novikov has called for rural schools to be funded as strategic social infrastructure rather than on a per-pupil basis.
He has proposed a moratorium on closing upper secondary classes in villages and, where closures go ahead, guaranteed year-round transport to schools in neighbouring areas.
'Loyal state ideology'
Since September 2022, all Russian schools have held a mandatory weekly class called "Conversations about What Matters," with lesson plans supplied directly by the Ministry of Education.
Topics include Russian traditional values, Russia's global role and Moscow's war in Ukraine — referred to in official lesson materials as a "special military operation," the Kremlin's only legally allowed term minimising its all-out invasion — along with themes such as "service to the Motherland" and "self-sacrifice".
New unified history textbooks were introduced for senior pupils in 2023 and for middle-school years from 2024-2025.
The 2023 unified history textbook describes Ukraine as an "aggressive anti-Russian bridgehead," presents Moscow's 2014 invasion, occupation and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea as the rectification of a "historical injustice," while Western sanctions are portrayed as an attempt to destroy Russia's economy.
Anna Wright, Amnesty International's researcher for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, said that the books "hide the truth and distort the facts about serious human rights violations and crimes under international law committed by Russian troops against Ukrainians."
Wright described the indoctrination of children as "a cynical attempt to eradicate Ukrainian culture, Ukrainian cultural heritage and identity."
The textbooks instruct pupils not to trust information found online. They were updated this summer: chapters on the war were expanded, and a section on the Trump-Putin Alaska meeting was added.
The books were edited in part by Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Putin, former culture minister and head of Russia's delegation in ceasefire talks with Ukraine.
After he moved directly to the Kremlin as a presidential aide, he was appointed chairman of the Interdepartmental Commission on Historical Education, established in 2021 to counter what Russia terms historical "falsification”.
Mendinsky's approach has been described as pseudo-historical rhetoric deployed to construct "loyal state ideology". He is under sanctions from the EU, the US and Canada.

What is known about arrests at US airbase in Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:12:34 UTC
18:12:34 KST

What to know about suspected plot to attack UK RAF base used by US?
LONDON, Sept 28 - Iran denied involvement on Monday in a suspected plot to attack a British airbase used by the US to strike Iranian sites, and police said five men arrested over explosives and terrorism offences were British nationals.
Below is what is known so far about the incident at RAF Fairford:
WHAT HAPPENED AT FAIRFORD?
Police were called to the airbase, 90 miles (145 km) west of London, early on Sunday morning by a local farmer who said she had seen three large white vans parked near the base and a group of "hooded and masked men" running into a field nearby.
Armed officers from the local force, Gloucestershire Police, responded and arrested five men in the Whelford area, about a mile from the base.
The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of offences under the explosives act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act after counter-terrorism police took over the investigation.
About 85 households were evacuated from properties near where the three vehicles were found and a 400-metre cordon was put in place around them.
WHAT DO WE KNOW ABOUT THE MEN WHO WERE ARRESTED?
Counter Terrorism Police said in a statement on Monday that the five men detained were all British nationals aged between 23 and 25 who lived in London.
An image on social media purported to show some of the suspects, seated shirtless with hands behind their backs, after their arrest. Reuters was unable to independently locate and verify the source of the photograph.
WHY WOULD FAIRFORD BE A TARGET?
Fairford, which opened in 1944 and was used by allied troops for the D-Day invasion of Normandy, has this year been used by US forces for strikes on Iran.
It is one of the US Air Force's only European airfields suitable for heavy bombers, and played a key role in both the first Gulf War in 1991 and the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect Fairford after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow US bombers to fly from the base. The Guards said any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.
Over the last six weeks there has been increased surveillance in the area after a specific threat from the Iranians, according to a local councillor.
WHAT HAVE PEOPLE SAID SO FAR ABOUT THE INCIDENT?
The farmer, who has not been named, told British media she saw eight to 10 men running from the vans with their faces covered and that they got within about 100 metres of the perimeter fence of the airbase.
"I just can't process how that base was on such high alert, and that the men were even there," she said, adding that a blockade had focused only on the main entrance.
"I'm really glad they ran away."
British defence minister Wes Streeting told BBC TV he was grateful to the witness but that she only had a "partial picture" of what had happened after she said she was "staggered" it had been left to a member of the public to report them despite the heightened threat.
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday the group had been under investigation as part of a long-running investigation. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding that the suspects intended "big damage" to the base.
Iran's embassy in London said in a statement on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" about Tehran's possible involvement in the incident. REUTERS

Boss of Beaverbrooks urges government to give businesses ‘a bit of a break’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:12:20 UTC
18:12:20 KST

The boss of the family-owned jeweller Beaverbrooks has called on the government to give business “a bit of a break” by halting cost increases amid flat sales and falling profits.
The retailer, founded in 1919, revealed a 9% fall in underlying operating profit to £7.8m last year after an increase in employer national insurance contributions (NICs) and the legal minimum wage introduced by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves.
Anna Blackburn, the managing director of Beaverbrooks, said she was positive about the performance against the backdrop of a challenging retail market: “Everything we hear in the jewellery industry [suggests] this is a pretty strong performance,” she said.
Total sales slipped 0.1% to £217m at the group, which operates 56 Beaverbrooks and four Loupe stores as well as 22 outlets for specific brands including watchmakers Omega, Breitling, Tudor and TAG Heuer.
Blackburn said she wanted to see the government help boost consumer confidence and provide stability by tackling unemployment and inflation and not adding new taxes in next month’s budget as retailers prepare for Christmas.
She said: “[The government] can’t increase business costs much more. Give business a bit of a break and stimulate some growth and confidence. A long-term, joined-up strategy is critical.”
Blackburn said Beaverbrooks was outperforming its rivals in tough conditions as it continued to invest in its stores and staff, modernising its online operation and developing new products.
“Our business has remained strong for 107 years because we believe in the high street and the importance of exceptional products and customer service.”
The group has just opened its fourth Loupe watch boutique, in Sheffield, and is investing in revamping its outlets in Manchester’s Trafford Centre and Lakeside in Essex in the year ahead.
Blackburn’s comments come after the since-departed boss of the John Lewis department store chain, Peter Ruis, said the chancellor’s budget would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates.
The boss of fellow retailer JD Sports has also said Reeves’s move to increase employer NICs at the same time as a chunky rise in the legal minimum wage had been “really a wrong movement” and pushed retailers to use more technology and hire fewer young people.
The government faces a tricky budget as the high price of oil and government borrowing put the squeeze on its finances – and on household bills.
The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly considering shifting more green subsidies from energy bills into general taxation, examining fuel duty and targeting help at the poorest households.

Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi liberates 3 more settlements, inflicts 2,000 Russian losses, 3rd Army Corps announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:11:47 UTC
18:11:47 KST

Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi liberates 3 more settlements, inflicts 2,000 Russian losses, 3rd Army Corps announces
Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps have liberated three more villages in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of the ongoing Operation Vivaldi, corps commander, Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi said on Sept 28.
The villages of Ridkodub, Nove, and Katerynivka were liberated, while full Ukrainian control was restored over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka.
The latest official update from the offensive operation, which has been covered by strict operational security measures for most of its duration, marks 51 square kilometers newly liberated, bringing the total so far of territory officially retaken to 176 square kilometers.
This phase, described as the "third season" of Operation Vivaldi, inflicted over 2,000 Russian losses and saw over 250 Russian soldiers taken prisoner, according to Biletskyi.
"The idea that 'Russians don’t surrender' from movies in practice turned into entire units surrendering in full — including officers, pilots and artillerymen," the general said.
"We hope to exchange them for Ukrainian soldiers currently in captivity in the near future."
Operation Vivaldi, the corps' offensive operation around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, was only made public on Sept. 15, although Russian pro-war Telegram channels and independent open-source intelligence (OSINT) researchers on social media had been tracking Ukrainian attacks in the area since late spring 2026.
The operation has sought to eliminate a large Russian salient that had built up over the previous year of fighting, one of two major pincers designed to encircle the remaining Ukrainian presence in the region.
The recent updates bring the officially-reported gains closer to those circulated by OSINT analysts and pro-war Russian Telegram channels, that reported Ukrainian forces pushing all the way east to the Zherebets River.
"One of the most important components of our success was our deception operations," Biletskyi said, "as a result, the enemy was convinced that the main direction of our attack was the Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna axis."
"This forced them to pointlessly burn through their reserves in counterattacks in that direction; in reality, the enemy slept through the main strike, which was aimed at capturing Nove."
The two previous "seasons" of Operation Vivaldi were each announced in similar updates, first on Sept. 15 when the offensive was given its name, and then on Sept. 20, when the liberation of the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove were announced.
The operation is a rare example of offensive success on the Ukrainian side, achieved despite a major disadvantage in manpower and the domination of the drone-based "kill zone" above the front line.
According to the 3rd Corps, success has been enabled by the repression of Russian drone assets and logistics, and the creative use of technology, including ground drones.
In the Sept. 28 update, Biletskyi reported the use of modified Soviet-era armored personnel carriers as "kamikaze" ground drones during the offensive.

Expanding Turkey-Libya agreement threatens Israeli shipping far from Turkish borders - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:09:50 UTC
18:09:50 KST

The IDF Intelligence Directorate has begun focusing on the "Libya corridor" and Turkey's growing military and diplomatic influence in the region, based on a maritime economic agreement signed in 2019 between the Turkish government and Libya's politically and militarily divided government, and has expanded over the past two years.
The agreement creates an artificial corridor stretching from Turkey's coast to Libya's, while completely disregarding the chain of Greek islands between them, including Crete and Rhodes.
The move includes armed Turkish activity in the area and effectively divides the Mediterranean Sea in two.
In return for Turkey's military support for Libya, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan secured a presence in Libyan ports, an aerial presence, and rights to search for energy resources in Libyan territory.
Such a security reality allows Turkey to establish military infrastructure in the region and disrupt military and civilian activity, including civilian shipping, far beyond its internationally recognized borders.
How does the process affect Israel?
The Turkish-Libyan agreement and its implications are intended to block, or at least disrupt, the construction of a gas pipeline from Israel to Cyprus, through Greece, and onward to Europe.
Turkey argues that any such project would require the pipeline to pass through Turkish territory and receive the Turkish government's approval.
Another area affected by tensions between the countries is the deployment of undersea communications infrastructure and electricity cables in areas where there are clear concerns that they could be damaged.
Israeli defense officials stressed that the Intelligence Directorate has not ignored developments in the region and must examine any development that could affect the interests of Israel and its allies. The developments come against the backdrop of Israeli energy agreements with Greece, Cyprus, and Egypt.
At the same time, there are concerns over possible harm to Israel's freedom of navigation, with 98% of Israeli imports arriving by sea.
Israel defense organizations concerned over Turkish threats
Israel's defense establishment, particularly the IDF Intelligence Directorate, the Mossad, and the Israel Navy's intelligence branch, is concerned by Turkey's moves in the region, as senior officials view them as attempts to constrain and isolate Israel, in addition to what they see as clear and direct threats from Erdogan.
According to Israeli sources, Turkey already maintains a military presence in Libya, both in the air and at sea. This includes the presence of Turkish advisers and frequent visits by senior commanders.
The defense establishment is particularly sensitive to movements and changes along maritime trade routes amid tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the Red Sea, due to the potential impact on Israel's economy and its security interests.
Israel's intelligence community is also monitoring Hamas's attempts to establish infrastructure in the region, primarily logistical infrastructure, that would serve the terrorist organization's interests.

Lithuanian students retrace Holocaust history on memorial day, confront country's role in massacres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:09:34 UTC
18:09:34 KST

Hundreds of Lithuanian teenagers marched last week to sites where Jews from their towns were murdered, confronting their country’s history of collaboration during the Holocaust while honoring those who risked their lives to save Jews.
Over the course of two days, on September 22 and 23, 2026, around 600 non-Jewish Lithuanian high school students took part in the March of the Living commemorations in Vilnius and Ponary, Lithuania, to honor 70,000 people, most of them Lithuanian Jews, who were murdered at Ponary and to learn about the choices made by Lithuanians who risked their lives to save their Jewish neighbors.
Here, they retraced the history of Jewish communities destroyed during the Holocaust and marched to sites where Lithuanian Jews were murdered 85 years ago.
 
The commemoration events were organized by the International Commission for the Investigation of Nazi Crimes in Lithuania and the European March of the Living as part of Lithuania's National Memorial Day for the Genocide of Lithuanian Jews, observed on September 23, the anniversary of the liquidation of the Vilnius Ghetto in 1943. 
The events brought together students and teachers for marches, testimony readings, and memorial ceremonies at Holocaust killing sites.
The family that hid a future judge
As part of the educational program, students learned the story of the Rakevičius family, recognized as Righteous Among the Nations for risking their lives to rescue Jews during the Holocaust.
 
Jaroslavas and Teklė Rakevičius and their four sons, Juozas, Zenonas, Česlovas, and Algimantas, helped Jews escape from the Kaunas Ghetto and hid them on their farm. 
The four young brothers kept watch day and night and sought out neighbors willing to provide additional hiding places, knowing that discovery would put the lives of the entire family at risk.
 
“The Rakevičius brothers were young people just like the students marching today. Their example reminds us that when we see hatred, we have a choice. At a time when antisemitism is again rising across Europe, young people must not remain indifferent. They must recognize hatred, confront it and choose to act,” said Michel Gourary, Executive Director of the European March of the Living.
Among those the brothers helped save was Aharon Barak, then an eight-year-old Jewish boy who was smuggled out of the Kaunas Ghetto in a sack. Barak survived the Holocaust and later became President of the Supreme Court of Israel and a Justice of the Supreme Court of Israel. Years later, Algimantas Rakevičius described the motivation behind his family’s actions simply: “We could not allow innocent people to be killed.”
A march in the rain
On the second day, 150 high school students from Radviliškis, a town in north-central Lithuania, marched three kilometers from the center of town to a forest clearing where 300 Jewish men were murdered by Nazis and their collaborators in July 1941.
  
At the Radviliškis killing site, the students held a memorial ceremony, read excerpts from testimonies, and placed stones of remembrance at the monument commemorating the Jewish victims. The students made the journey in the rain, retracing the route from the town to the site where members of their community were murdered in the Holocaust.
Radviliškis was one of hundreds of Lithuanian towns and villages whose centuries-old Jewish communities were destroyed during the Holocaust.
Before the war, Jewish life spanned 297 shtetls throughout Lithuania. Following the Nazi invasion in June 1941, mass shootings rapidly spread across the country, with Jewish communities murdered at killing sites in forests and fields near the towns in which they had lived.
Marches bring younger generations to sites connected to destruction of Jewish communities
According to the organizers, the marches sought to confront students with nuanced perspectives of Holocaust history, including the role played by Lithuanian collaborators in the murder of their Jewish neighbors, alongside the comparatively few Lithuanians who risked their own lives to rescue Jews and were later recognized as Righteous Among the Nations.
“To see 600 young non-Jewish Lithuanians walk with their teachers to the places where Jewish communities were murdered 85 years ago carries enormous meaning,” said Gourary.
March of the Living is an educational program that holds commemorative and educational events throughout Europe during the year, alongside its annual March from Auschwitz to Birkenau. The local marches bring younger generations to sites connected to the destruction of Jewish communities, combining remembrance of the victims with education about the consequences of antisemitism, hatred and indifference.
Mass shootings known as ‘holocaust of bullets’
Between July 1941 and August 1944, approximately 70,000 people, most of them Lithuanian Jews, were murdered by the Nazis and their local collaborators at Ponary, today known as Paneriai, outside Vilnius. The site became one of the most prominent symbols of the mass murder of Eastern European Jews during the Holocaust.
 
The destruction at Ponary formed part of a much broader campaign of mass murder across Lithuania. Following the Nazi invasion in June 1941, Jewish communities were systematically targeted in mass shootings carried out by German forces and Lithuanian collaborators. Within months, communities that had existed for generations had been almost entirely erased.
 
Before the Holocaust, approximately 200,000 Jews lived in Lithuania, including around 70,000 in Vilnius. The mass shootings carried out across Lithuania and elsewhere in Eastern Europe became known as the “Holocaust by Bullets,” in which Jews were taken from their homes and communities and murdered in nearby forests, fields, and mass graves.
 
The Vilnius Ghetto, established by the Nazis in 1941, was liquidated on September 23–24, 1943. Thousands of its remaining Jewish prisoners were deported to concentration and labor camps or murdered.
“Lithuania’s history includes the painful reality of collaboration in the murder of its Jewish population, but also points of light in those who refused to remain indifferent and risked everything to save Jews,” concluded Gourary.

Jammu and Kashmir has remained a Union Territory since the BJP-led Centre abrogated Article 370 in August 2019 and reorganised the erstwhile state into two Union Territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
The BJP opposed the resolution, questioning the manner in which it was allowed by Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather. BJP legislators said the Speaker had permitted the resolution to be taken up in relaxation of the assembly rules.
As soon as the assembly proceedings began on Monday, BJP members stood up and protested against the resolution.The opposition party also moved a motion seeking the removal of Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather, alleging that he had allowed the chief minister's resolution in violation of the rules.

Palestinians condemn Israeli minister’s death threat against detainee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:07:37 UTC

Qais Omar Darwesh, Nour Mahd Abuaisha, and Lina Altawell
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
The Palestinian Commission of Detainees’ Affairs on Monday condemned Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s threat to execute a prisoner inside his cell, describing conditions inside Israeli prisons as “organized terrorism.”
Ben-Gvir posted a video Sunday on US social media platform X showing him inside the cell of Palestinian prisoner Hassan Salameh, telling him: “I want to kill you. I want to execute you.”
“The footage published by Ben-Gvir shows that degradation and depravity have reached their highest levels,” commission head Raed Abu al-Hummus said in a statement, terming conditions inside Israeli prisons as “organized terrorism.”
He questioned the position of the international community and its institutions toward prison conditions in Israel, warning that allowing such practices to continue without international action “encourages further violations.”
According to Palestinian prisoner institutions, Salameh, from the Gaza Strip, has been imprisoned since 1996 and slapped with multiple life sentences. Israel refused to release him as part of a 2011 prisoner exchange deal.
Ben-Gvir said in a post on X after publishing the video that if he becomes defense minister in the next government, he would work to implement death sentences against Palestinian prisoners.
In late March 2026, the Israeli Knesset passed a law allowing the death penalty to be imposed on Palestinian prisoners by a vote of 62-48, amid support from Israeli right-wing parties.
The law allows a death sentence to be issued without a request from the prosecution and does not require a unanimous decision.
The legislation drew widespread criticism and protests in several Arab and regional countries, amid calls for its repeal and for Israel to be held accountable over violations of the rights of Palestinian prisoners.
Palestinian group Hamas said Ben-Gvir’s threat to kill Salameh “signals new crimes” against Palestinian detainees, while pledging to continue efforts to secure their release.
It said Ben-Gvir’s threat is part of an Israeli policy “that turned prisons into arenas of direct physical liquidation, in blatant violation of all international laws.”
The group said it continues to make “every possible effort at all levels and by all means to secure the release of prisoners in the occupation’s prisons.”
“We will remain committed to this until prisoners gain their freedom,” it added.
Ben-Gvir’s remarks come as political competition intensifies ahead of Israel’s general election scheduled for Oct. 27, as opinion polls indicate declining support for the governing coalition of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and gains for the opposition.

Swift won Video of the Year for “The Fate of Ophelia,” along with the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors and Best Direction for “Opalite.” The three awards lifted her career total to 33 VMAs, moving her ahead of Beyonce as the most-awarded artist in the history of the awards.
Swift dedicated her Video of the Year award to late country music icon Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80. Calling Parton “the ultimate showgirl,” Swift said audiences were fortunate to have shared the world with her. Earlier in the ceremony, she also premiered the music video for “Patient Zero,” featuring actors Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell.
Madonna, meanwhile, led the night with seven awards, including Artist of the Year, Best Collaboration with Sabrina Carpenter for “Bring Your Love,” and Best Dance for “Confessions II – The Film.” She also opened the ceremony with her first VMA performance in 23 years, performing with Carpenter and Charli XCX.
The 68-year-old singer, who performed at the first VMAs in 1984, reflected on her decades-long career while accepting Artist of the Year award. She also spoke about her latest album, “Confessions II,” saying she had spent the past 18 months finding herself and making the music she wanted to make.
K-pop group BTS was also among the major winners. The South Korean group won Song of the Year and Best K-pop for “Swim,” as well as Best Group, taking three awards in total.
BLACKPINK member Lisa won Best Pop for her solo song “Dream,” featuring Japanese actor Kentaro Sakaguchi, while British singer Sienna Spiro was named Best New Artist.
Elsewhere, Bad Bunny won Best Latin for “NUEVAYoL,” Olivia Rodrigo took Best Alternative for “the cure,” Bruno Mars won Best R&B for “I Just Might,” and Cardi B and Kehlani took Best Hip-Hop for “Safe.”
The ceremony also honored influential artists from earlier generations. Nirvana received the Michael Jackson Video Vanguard Award for the band’s impact on music videos, with surviving members Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear accepting the honor.
Kacey Musgraves paid tribute to Parton by performing “I Will Always Love You,” while Sombr, Raye, Teddy Swims and Adam Lambert joined a tribute to British singer George Michael.
Hosted by Snoop Dogg, the 2026 VMAs were held at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles. The ceremony was broadcast on CBS and MTV and streamed on Paramount+, with winners in major categories selected through fan voting.

Plymouth-built uncrewed boat armed with Sea Venom missile
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:05:09 BST
18:05:09 KST

A twelve-metre armed uncrewed surface vessel built near Plymouth has been launched carrying MBDA’s Sea Venom anti-ship missile alongside loitering munitions, jammers and surveillance equipment, according to STARK, the defence technology company behind it.
Vanta 12 is described by the company as an AI-enabled modular platform able to integrate missiles, loitering munitions, anti-submarine effectors and electronic warfare systems alongside intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance equipment, and it has been designed from the outset for mass production rather than small batch build. The boat can undertake patrols of 1,200 miles, sprint at more than 40 knots and remain continuously at sea for weeks, which STARK says brings the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap, the Baltic and European territorial waters within reach of a single vessel while reducing the number of personnel exposed to danger.
Sea Venom is already in Royal Navy service aboard the Wildcat helicopter, where it is used against fast attack craft and larger surface targets, and MBDA is now working on a version fired from the surface. Andrew Blackburn of MBDA said: “MBDA is developing a surface-launched variant of Sea Venom to meet the growing demand for precision maritime strike in complex littoral environments, to both deter and defeat a wide range of threats. This collaboration with Stark has showcased a potent new capability that is made possible through the integration of a precision weapon system such as Sea Venom onto autonomous maritime platforms such as Vanta 12. Participation in REPMUS 26 is giving both MBDA and Stark a wealth of learning that we can feed forward into the battle-winning capabilities that are needed for future Hybrid Navies.”
The missile is designed to engage targets up to the size of larger warships as well as coastal and land-based targets, including in congested waters where precision matters. Putting it on a boat of this size gives a vessel with no crew aboard the sort of strike capability that until now has come from a helicopter or a frigate.
Vanta 12 spent this week at REPMUS, the NATO exercise in Portugal that serves as the alliance’s largest event for robotics and uncrewed maritime systems, taking part in simulated combat missions and working alongside conventional vessels and other uncrewed boats.
Mike Armstrong, managing director of STARK UK, said: “Vanta 12 is the first unmanned vessel to bring together missiles, loitering munitions and surveillance to help NATO countries face down the threat.
“Vanta is an export success story for British defence, giving our NATO allies capability that can be produced at scale, deployed rapidly and adapted quickly.
“Industrial deterrence is what modern warfare increasingly demands, and what Vanta 12 has been designed to deliver.”
Fred Thomas, the MP for Plymouth Moor View, welcomed the launch in his constituency city. “It is exciting for European security, and also locally for Plymouth as a city, to see STARK launch this uncrewed boat today,” he said, adding: “Built right here in Plymouth, it will be a highly capable addition to Europe’s maritime capabilities. I am particularly excited to see anti-ship missiles, usually fired from helicopters, launch from the boat.”
The company sets the vessel against the pattern of activity now familiar in the North Atlantic and the approaches to European waters, where shadow fleet ships mask their ownership to move sanctioned cargo, transponders are switched off, undersea cables and pipelines are interfered with, and civilian-flagged vessels loiter near critical infrastructure. Around 300 shadow fleet vessels transited British waters in the first quarter of this year, and the Royal Navy interdicted the sanctioned tanker Smyrtos in the Channel in June. Vessels capable of deploying deep-sea submersibles have been sighted repeatedly near the cables carrying Britain’s data and energy.
STARK argues that answering this at scale requires lower cost uncrewed systems rather than warships, an approach it calls the Hybrid Navy and which it says is being taken up by the British, Norwegian and German armed forces. Readers will know the Royal Navy has been moving in that direction for some time, with uncrewed systems trialled for mine countermeasures and seabed monitoring and a hybrid fleet concept running through recent planning.
The company was founded in 2024 in response to operational demands from Ukraine and is headquartered in Berlin, with a presence in Germany, Ukraine, Britain, Sweden and Greece. Its first British manufacturing facility opened at Swindon in November 2025 and employs more than 100 people, and Vanta vessels have already been exported from the United Kingdom to other NATO allies. The maritime division that built and tested Vanta 12 is based in the south west of England.

The neutrality initiative’s defeat on Sunday came as little surprise to much of the Swiss media. The clear rejection strengthens the Federal Council’s position and marks a setback for Swiss People's Party's billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative.
The 70% of votes against the initiative is “a final verdict for those who were aiming for strict neutrality as an end in itself”, said the Corriere del Ticino in an editorial. The clear result also represents “an endorsement of the policy” of parliament and the government. The initiative, it says, “was a total defeat, which precludes any serious chance of a revival”.
“A verdict with no appeal,” is how the La Regione described Sunday’s resounding result. On Sunday, 70.2% rejected the “neutrality initiative”. The Ticino-based newspaper said the result “averts the risk of dogmatising what remains, after all, a mere – albeit important – instrument of Swiss foreign policy: a means, not an end, which as such must be able to continue to be used with the necessary flexibility, depending on the circumstances that arise around the world”.

The United States and its allies have withdrawn their troops from Iraq as part of the conclusion of the international military mission against the terrorist organization ISIS.
964media reported on this.
Iraqi authorities said the international coalition has already handed over to Iraq all military bases and headquarters used by its mission.
After September 30, no combat or training units from the coalition are expected to remain in Iraq.
The troop withdrawal is taking place under an agreement reached between the United States and Iraq in 2024. The agreement called for the gradual end of the coalition’s military mission in the country.
Some U.S. troops have already left Iraq, although certain units continued to operate in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.
The U.S. military presence in Iraq began after the invasion on March 20, 2003. At the time, U.S.-led coalition forces launched an operation against Saddam Hussein’s regime and captured Baghdad on April 9.
The main U.S. combat forces left Iraq in 2011. However, in 2014, the United States sent troops back to the country following the rapid advance of ISIS.
The Iraqi government asked the United States and other countries for assistance in fighting the group.
In September 2024, Washington and Baghdad agreed to gradually end the international coalition’s military mission in Iraq and transition to bilateral security cooperation.
Since then, the coalition has gradually withdrawn from its facilities in Iraq. In January 2026, U.S. forces completed their withdrawal from Ain al-Asad Air Base, after which control of the base was transferred to the Iraqi military.

A total of 72% Ukrainians believe Zelenskyy is responsible for corrupt actions of his entourage – KIIS
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:02:00 EEST
18:02:00 KST

A total of 72% Ukrainians believe Zelenskyy is responsible for corrupt actions of his entourage – KIIS
According to the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS), 72% of surveyed Ukrainians believe that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy bears personal responsibility for the corrupt actions of his entourage. Nearly 25% of respondents disagree with this statement.
Source: survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, conducted on 12-21 September 2026.
Details: According to the survey results, 72% of respondents stated that Zelenskyy bears personal responsibility for the corrupt actions of his entourage. 25% believe the president does not bear such responsibility, while another 3% were undecided.
KIIS urges caution when interpreting the concept of "personal responsibility". According to KIIS's assessment, this refers primarily to political responsibility.
Quote: "Respondents were also asked whether President Volodymyr Zelenskyy bears personal responsibility for the corrupt actions of his entourage. Before moving on to the results, we should note a cautious interpretation of 'personal responsibility'.
The broader context of KIIS (and other companies') surveys shows that 'responsibility' in the minds of citizens is not the same as 'personal involvement'. This is now perceived more as a political responsibility rather than a personal accusation of involvement in corrupt actions."
Details: Sociologists also analysed the responses based on the level of trust in the president.
Among those who fully trust Zelenskyy, 3% hold him responsible for the corrupt actions of his entourage, 81% do not and 16% were undecided.
Among those who rather trust the president, 17% place responsibility on him, 60% do not and 23% were undecided.
Among respondents who rather distrust Zelenskyy, 57% hold him responsible for the corrupt actions of his entourage, 19% do not and 23% were undecided.
Among those who do not trust the president at all, 85% hold him responsible, 5% do not and 10% were undecided.
For reference: The KIIS survey was conducted between 12 and 21 September 2026 via telephone interviews across all government-controlled regions of Ukraine. A total of 1,002 respondents were surveyed. The poll sampled adult citizens of Ukraine aged 18 and older residing in Ukrainian-controlled territories at the time of the survey.
Formally, under normal circumstances, the statistical margin of error for such a sample (with a probability of 0.95 and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) did not exceed 4.1% for indicators close to 50%, 3.5% for indicators close to 25%, 2.5% for indicators close to 10% and 1.8% for indicators close to 5%.
In wartime conditions, a certain degree of systematic bias should be considered in addition to the stated statistical margin of error.

18:00:27 KST

Russia’s government is suspending routine state inspections of companies whose property has been damaged in Ukrainian attacks, Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Grigorenko said Monday, describing the temporary measure as a way to reduce bureaucratic red tape during recovery efforts.
The moratorium, which takes effect Monday and will remain in place until Oct. 1, 2027, is “aimed at reducing the administrative burden on businesses and supporting firms that are currently restoring facilities targeted in strikes,” Interfax quoted Grigorenko as saying.
Russian companies are subject to regular and often intrusive inspections from various government agencies, including fire safety, labor, consumer protection and tax authorities.
Under the new rules, companies rebuilding after attacks remain exempt from planned inspections, though emergency audits can still be triggered by an executive order, prosecutorial requests or concerns based on national security and public health.
The move follows comments from President Vladimir Putin earlier this month, who criticized subjecting businesses receiving emergency government support to aggressive regulatory oversight as “harmful and pointless.” It also builds on a one-year tax deferral granted last month to Russia’s largest online retailer Wildberries and sellers who use the platform.
However, the administrative reprieve also comes alongside growing state pressure on companies. In August, Putin signed an executive order allowing the government to seize companies and critical infrastructure if owners fail to properly protect their properties against drone attacks or delay repairs.
Over the weekend, the Russian government reportedly moved to invoke that authority to place one of Moscow’s largest gas station chains under temporary state control.
