They filmed it and shared the video, after which the situation began to be widely discussed on social media. Later, according to the environmental protection project Biologicamente, the tourists were stopped at the airport, reports UNN.
Details
According to information from the Italian environmental protection project Biologicamente, the video showing the cruel treatment of turtles was posted by a user named Vadym Oliinyk. The post also said that the tourists were allegedly in Oman as part of an environmental protection mission.
"These images speak for themselves. The photographs were published on a profile with 200,000 followers. Obviously, the author has already received a generous dose of abuse and was forced to disable the comments section. But he immediately defended himself, claiming that he had done nothing wrong, had broken no laws and had not behaved improperly. (...) And do you know why they are so convinced that they helped the poor turtle? Because they were together with volunteers from a fake environmental organization that monitors turtles coming to Oman", the project’s post said.
It also added that a serious and professional association accompanied by a scientific committee would never allow its volunteers to sit on turtles in order to take selfies. "It is disgusting and unpleasant. This is exploitation, mistreatment and abuse—nothing resembling volunteering", the post said.
After the situation gained publicity and Vadym Oliinyk, who posted the video showing the cruel treatment of the turtle, received a wave of criticism, he posted another video on Instagram—this time with an apology. The man addressed the Oman Environment Authority and the organization involved in protecting green sea turtles and apologized. At the same time, according to him, he "did not pay attention to the rules for handling turtles" and "made a mistake".
After the video was shared, the situation was also discussed by Ukrainian users on Threads. One user wrote: "First you show what a tough guy you are, that you can climb onto a turtle. Your companion does the same. Then you record an apology and say that you were misled and did not see the rules", the network user wrote.
"There are instructions on all the beaches. The staff also mention it. And during the egg-laying season, controls are strengthened in general, and they make sure that no one damages the nest… They knew and understood perfectly well what they were doing", another user added.
"I would not be surprised if I were you. Very many parents tolerate this kind of attitude by their children toward animals. And these are adults who pass on such values", another user noted.
"I can’t watch the poor turtle trying to escape", another network user wrote indignantly.
Later, according to information from the Italian environmental protection project Biologicamente, the "heroes" of the video were stopped at the airport.
"An update regarding the two tourists who sat on the shell of a female turtle while holding her newly hatched babies: my post went viral in Oman, especially thanks to you sharing it… The two tourists were stopped by police at the airport! This time, reporting to the competent authorities worked. Thank you for publishing it. Thank you", the project’s post said.
The author of the post thanked everyone concerned about the situation and also promised to keep people informed about further developments related to the incident. "The fake guides involved in this episode were also fined", the post said.

Trump offered to sell arms to Xi: US ambassador to Fox News

2026-09-28

Breadcrumb
Trump offered to sell arms to Xi, US ambassador to China tells Fox News
US President Donald Trump offered to sell arms to his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in response to concern over weapons sales to Taiwan, the US ambassador to China said in a Fox News interview that aired Sunday.
US arms sales to the self-ruled island, which China claims is part of its territory and has threatened to seize by force, have long been a thorny issue between Washington and Beijing.
The United States is required by law to supply Taiwan, which has a democratically elected president and legislature, with weapons for its defense.
US Ambassador to China David Perdue said the issue was raised again when Xi visited the United States last week.
"President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world.' He actually asked President Xi—would he like to buy some?—at one point," Perdue said in the interview.
"There are continuing conversations about other sales, (Trump) and President Xi talk about that every time they get together," Perdue said, adding that the US position has not changed.
The White House did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.
White House officials said that the US had no plans to sell arms to China, according to the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal.
The US State Department said in a statement to the New York Times that "US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China."
The Chinese foreign ministry did not directly answer when asked about the comments on Monday, but said China has "always strengthened its national defense capabilities based on its own needs, and remains committed to maintaining world peace and stability."
Beijing warned Taiwan in June that seeking independence "by relying on the United States or through military means is a dead end."
Washington approved a $11.1 billion arms sale to Taiwan in December, which Perdue said was a sale of "more arms to Taiwan than any other president since 1979."
The US paused a $14 billion weapons purchase by Taiwan in May, with Trump calling it a "very good negotiating chip" in dealings with China, raising fears that Taiwan's security could be traded away.
During his Washington trip, Xi repeated his warning that Trump should show "prudence" over Taiwan, and went further to urge the United States to oppose Taiwan independence explicitly.
Both leaders confirmed they would meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November and the G20 forum at Trump's Doral resort in Miami in December.

Taiwan builds drone industry park to shed Chinese supply chain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:20:09 UTC
17:20:09 KST

- Taiwan broke ground on an aerospace and drone industrial park in Chiayi on Sept. 28 and opened a new NCSIST drone research campus.
- The park aims to build a drone supply chain free of Chinese components and is planned to host about 100 companies.
Taiwan broke ground Monday on an aerospace and drone industrial park in the southern county of Chiayi, where the island’s main military research institute wants to build a drone supply chain free of Chinese parts.
President Lai Ching-te led the Sept. 28 ceremony, which also opened a new Minxiong campus for the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, known as NCSIST, the state-run institute that develops most of Taiwan’s homegrown missiles and military drones. The institute did not say at the ceremony how much the new park will cost, how many companies have signed up or when it will open.
The Minxiong campus took three years to build. It includes a research building, hangars, laboratories and facilities for integration testing, and NCSIST says engineers there can work on every stage of a drone’s development, from designing the airframe to building the propulsion and flight-control systems and testing the finished aircraft. The campus also uses digital twin technology, which creates a virtual copy of an aircraft that can be tested in simulation before a real one flies, along with artificial intelligence and virtual reality tools.
The industrial park going up next door is meant to bring manufacturers, government agencies, universities and researchers together around shared computing power and digital engineering tools. NCSIST describes the goal as a “non-red supply chain,” the term Taiwan uses for components and systems that do not come from China. Chiayi County Magistrate Weng Chang-liang said in August that the park is planned to hold about 100 companies.
Taiwan’s push for its own drones picked up after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, where both sides used drones on a massive scale and Ukraine initially relied heavily on Chinese-made DJI models. Concerns that Chinese drones and parts could be tracked or cut off have pushed Taiwan to require that drones bought by public agencies come from non-Chinese supply chains.
The new park builds on the Asia UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center, which opened in August 2022 in Puzi City, also in Chiayi County, on a site that had sat empty for years. The center now hosts more than 50 drone companies and institutions, and Weng said in August that demand has outgrown its space, with another 40 to 50 firms waiting to move in.
The industry has grown quickly. Taiwan’s drone output reached NT$12.9 billion ($407 million) in 2025, about 2.5 times the 2024 figure, and exports totaled NT$2.95 billion ($93 million), according to the Ministry of Economic Affairs. In October 2025, the Executive Yuan, Taiwan’s cabinet, launched a six-year, NT$44.2 billion ($1.39 billion) program to develop the uncrewed vehicle industry, with a goal of pushing annual drone output above NT$40 billion ($1.26 billion) by 2030.
That spending has faced political resistance. In July, the Ministry of Economic Affairs warned that cuts proposed by the opposition Kuomintang, which controls the legislature, would hurt the industry. Weng has also pressed lawmakers to approve more than NT$40 billion ($1.26 billion) in drone-related procurement funding.
Taiwan’s drone strategy relies on three tiers: buying larger military drones from the United States, having NCSIST develop mid-size military drones, and buying small dual-use drones from Taiwan’s private sector. The Minxiong site is designed to link the institute’s military work with those private companies.

Thai downpours shift north-westwards after Bangkok declared a disaster zone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:18:24 UTC
17:18:24 KST

Bangkok was declared a disaster zone by its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions.
The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average 585mm a year). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall.
Out in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away from Hawaii where it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status.
Meanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.

India: LPU suspends classes after unrest over alleged rape

Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passes resolution seeking urgent restoration of full statehood
The regional assembly of India-administered Kashmir on Monday passed a resolution seeking the urgent restoration of full statehood from its current status of a Union Territory, which is federally administered.
The resolution was introduced by Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and was passed in the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly amid chaos as legislators of the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) staged a walkout calling the non-binding resolution "unconstitutional" and "anti-national".
The resolution calls on Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government in New Delhi to ensure "the immediate and urgent restoration of full (federal) statehood to Jammu and Kashmir".
In 2019, a contentious decision by the Modi government stripped Jammu and Kashmir of its semiautonomous status.
The region was divided into two federally administered territories, bringing it directly under New Delhi's control.
In 2024, the region elected its first government since being recategorized as a Union Territory with Abdullah's Jammu and Kashmir National Conference party at its helm.
But the local government's powers are limited.
The Modi government has consistently said that statehood for the territory would be granted at an "appropriate time".
On Monday, Abdullah, who said that statehood was the territory's "right," sought a clarification on the timeline and questioned what "appropriate time" means, local Kashmir outlets reported.
The text of Monday's resolution also referred to the constitutionally non-binding resolutions demanding federal autonomy, passed in 2000 and 2024.
Modi's BJP, which is the largest opposition party in the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly, strongly opposed the resolution with protests and sloganeering as Abdullah spoke ahead of the vote. BJP legislators also tore up copies of the resolution, reports said.
Muslim-majority Kashmir has long been a bone of contention for India and Pakistan, both of whom lay claim to the restive, strategically important Himalayan region.
Chhattisgarh floods: Air Force personnel rescue 12 people stranded on hut roof
Heavy rains have wreaked havoc in the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh, causing rivers and streams to swell up and leading to flood-like conditions in some parts.
Over 5,000 people were rescued over the weekend from the inundated areas and taken to relief camps and safer locations, according to reports.
The districts of Bastar, Dhamtari, Bilaspur, Durg, Raipur, Balodabazar-Bhatapara and Narayanpur are among the regions affected by the heavy downpour.
On Monday, the Indian Air Force (IAF) rescued 12 people stranded in a village on the northern bank of the Indravati river, which was flowing above the danger mark, news agency ANI quoted a Defense Ministry statement as saying.
The group of people, which included women and children, were reportedly stuck on the roof of a hut which was at risk of collapsing due to the force of the floodwaters.
An IAF commando was lowered on the roof from a helicopter, which hovered above as the people were pulled up, according to the ministry.
India's Supreme Court takes note of recent Delhi-NCR rape cases
The Supreme Court of India said on Monday that the recent slew of rape cases in the Indian capital of New Delhi and its neighboring districts "starkly underline a systematic failure" by law enforcement and public administrative authorities, legal news websites reported.
The top court made the statement as it opened a "suo motu cognizance" legal review of the latest cases of rape in Delhi-National Capital Region (NCR), LiveLaw and Bar and Bench reported.
In Indian law, a suo motu cognizance refers to a court taking notice of a matter on its own initiative, without a formal petition or complaint being filed.
The two-judge bench expressed its distress over the news reports of the recurring sexual violence and underpinned the need to fix accountability, LiveLaw reported.
"These incidents considered alongside other recent reports of sexual offences across Delhi-NCR starkly underline a systematic failure on the part of the law enforcement and the public administrative authorities to guarantee basic public safety," LiveLaw quoted the bench as saying.
Last week, Delhi saw hundreds of students protesting and expressing their outrage over the safety of women after a teenage girl was allegedly gang raped by three men at a public park in the capital.
In August, media reports said that a 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang raped in a bus moving from Noida, a staellite city of the Indian capital, to Delhi by the vehicle's driver and conductor.
The court on Monday said that public spaces, including parks, roads, buses, metro stations, subways and footbridges, cannot be allowed to become "high-risk zones" over inadequate illumination or surveillance, lack of patrolling, or other preventable administrative inadequacies, Bar and Bench reported.
Supreme court says need to fix accountability
The judges drew parallels with the 2012 fatal Delhi gang rape on a bus that came to be known as the Nirbhaya case.
"One cannot help but draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012," LiveLaw reported the bench as saying.
The court also observed whether the systematic law enforcement apparatus has made any meaningful advancement since the Nirbhaya case, according to LiveLaw.
The court stressed that "expressions of solidarity" were not a solution to the offences it called "social evil," adding that a "measurable response" was required with fixing "responsibility and accountability" upon the authorities entrusted with crime prevention, maintenance of public order and protection of vulnerable persons, according to local outlets.
India's badminton star Sindhu 'hurting' after hectic Asian Games schedule
Indian badminton star PV Sindhu has voiced her disappointment at losing her Asian Games quarterfinal, also questioning her gruelling schedule that saw her play three matches in less than 24 hours over the weekend.
"My Asian Games campaign is over, and I'm hurting," Sindhu wrote to her roughly 3 million followers on social media. "I had my chance. Letting it slip hurts."
The 31-year-old lost to China's Chen Yufei on Sunday, having played both her second and third round matches on Saturday.
"Three matches in 18 hours. Back at 3 a.m. [on Saturday night], out again at 8:30 a.m. [on Sunday morning]. It took a toll," the former world champion and two-time Olympic medalist wrote.
Sindhu thanked fans who had stayed up to cheer her on and said she also felt a sense of pride at competing her fourth Asian Games, concluding the post by saying, "I'll go again."
Sindhu's India teammate H.S. Prannoy had similarly criticized both the packed schedule and other conditions for players like accommodation and logisticts in the province of Aichi and main city of Nagoya in Japan.
"It's cruel beacuse everybody is aiming for a good Asian Games, which comes once in four years," Prannoy said. "To have two singles games in a day, I haven't seen it like that in ages."
Lovely Professional University protest: Classes suspended after violence during protests over suspected assault
Punjab's Lovely Professional University (LPU) has suspended classes starting Monday and postponed mid-term examinations after a protest over an alleged rape turned violent on Sunday with protesters clashing with the police and vandalism being reported.
The private university located in the city of Phagwara witnessed massive student unrest after claims spread on social media that a female university student was allegedly raped within the campus premises by an outsider and had later died by suicide.
The protests grew to be violent when the protesters clashed with the police, pelted stones at the security personnel, smashed windows and set fire to some objects within the university complex, reports said.
Some students later claimed in social media posts that the vandals were not students, but outsiders.
Heavy police deployment
The university has suspended regular classes for 10 days, news agency ANI cited a statement from LPU as saying.
The statement said students could travel to their hometowns during the suspension of classes and advised those who stay back to remain in their hostels or places of accommodation and avoid any unnecessary movement. The statement also called on students to avoid involvement in the unrest.
Over 2,000 police personnel were deployed to ensure security on the campus, reports quoted the Additional Director General of Police Fayaz Farooqui as saying.
The protesters also blocked the national highway between Jalandhar and Phagwara highway early Sunday, leading to traffic disruptions.
On Monday, police said that the situation had been brought under control and traffic movement on the highway had been restored.
Claims of rape remain unverified
Meanwhile, the police are yet to confirm whether a student was raped within LPU's campus. They have launched an investigation to examine the facts of the incident.
Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann has taken note of the situation and has directed the Director General of Police to visit the campus, reports said on Monday.
Meanwhile, the Punjab State Women Commision is seeking a detailed report on the alleged rape, ANi reported.
What has LPU said?
The LPU has denied that the alleged rape took place, calling the claims "false, baseless and fabricated rumors".
The university on Sunday posted a video with three female students who it said reside in the girls' hostel room where the alleged incident is claimed to have taken place.
The video purportedly shows the girls denying that there had been a rape, with one of them asking the police to stop visiting the room repeatedly.
However, media reports on Monday said that the same girls later appear in a separate purported video, claiming that they were instructed on what to say in the statement. They then allegedly claim that their clips were "trimmed" and used without their consent.

Purchasing power splits in two: down for the poor, up for the rich
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:17:33 EEST
17:17:33 KST

The recovery in household purchasing power is unfolding unevenly across Finland, according to Labore, the Labour Institute for Economic Research.
Purchasing power is still falling for the bottom tenth on the income scale this year, while it is rising for the top decile.
Labore's latest analysis estimates that purchasing power in the bottom income decile will decline by 3.5 percent this year, while that of the top decile will increase by 2.2 percent.
The gap is bigger over a longer period. Between 2023 and 2026, the difference in purchasing power growth will exceed 16 percentage points. The outlook is particularly weak for renters and single parents.
"Purchasing power among the lowest income households has deteriorated for several years, and that trend won't reverse in 2026," explained Milla Nyyssölä, a senior researcher at Labore, in a statement. "The gap is not explained by prices, but by different income trajectories."
Labore described the development as unusual by historical standards. During the years of growth that followed Finland’s recession in the 1990s, differences in income growth between groups were substantial. But even then, purchasing power among the lowest decile did not decline.
Consumer confidence drops
Consumer confidence meanwhile weakened again in September from the previous month, with views of both household finances and the wider economy deteriorating slightly, according to Statistics Finland.
While expectations for Finland's economy over the next year remained around their long-term average, consumers were notably less optimistic about their own finances with continued concern about the risk of job loss.

bottega veneta crumples cardboard boxes into sculptural stools for summer 2027 show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:17:09 UTC
17:17:09 KST

Illya Goldman Gubin shapes cardboard through an embrace
For Bottega Veneta’s Summer 2027 show, Ukrainian artist Illya Goldman Gubin turns cardboard boxes into stools through an unusually physical process, embracing and crumpling each box with his body before reinforcing it with resin and fiberglass. Each stool begins as an individual box, with its folds and interlocking flaps retained in the final form, recalling the interwoven leather fettucce of Bottega Veneta’s Intreccio. Goldman Gubin uses his own body to give each piece its final form, leaving the marks of that encounter visible on the finished seats.
images courtesy of Bottega Veneta, unless stated otherwise
Bottega Veneta’s Intreccio inspires the folded structure
Cardboard has been a recurring material in Goldman Gubin’s work, from sculptures and installations to furniture. For these stools, he starts with the box as it is, folding and crumpling it by hand so that each form develops through the pressure of his body. The resulting creases, dents, and uneven surfaces remain visible once the cardboard is reinforced with resin and fiberglass, making each stool slightly different from the next.
A cardboard box is made to carry something before it is usually thrown away, but Goldman Gubin gives the same material another purpose by turning it into a seat. The box that once carried an object can now carry a person, while its folded flaps are worked into one another to recall the interwoven leather fettucce of Bottega Veneta’s Intreccio. Goldman Gubin uses the existing structure of the box to create the interlocking effect. The process leaves the making visible in the finished stools, with the original material still legible beneath the hardened surface. What begins as an ordinary cardboard container is reshaped through direct physical contact into a piece of furniture, retaining the folds and irregularities produced along the way.

WATCH: Tens of thousands of Jewish worshipers gather for Birkat Kohanim at Western Wall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:16:52 UTC
17:16:52 KST

Over 50,000 Jewish worshipers gathered at the Western Wall plaza for a joint Birkat Kohanim (priestly blessing) prayer on Monday, during the Hol Hamoed days of Sukkot and the High Holy Days.
The tradition of conducting a mass event for the blessing has been a highlight of the week-long Sukkot and Passover holidays for over 50 years, with most gatherings attended by tens of thousands of people in a huge blanket of white tallitot.
"This year, we added an additional Birkat Kohanim event to alleviate the crowds and enable anyone who wishes to participate in this emotional tradition to do so," the Western Wall Heritage Foundation said. "This is a prayer that we all carry in our hearts to our Father in Heaven, asking Him to remove baseless hatred from us and to spread the sukkah of peace over us," the Western Wall rabbi added.
What are the priestly blessings?
The priestly blessing is a blessing recited by the descendants of the Cohen tribe (usually surnamed Cohen, Katz etc.) at every morning minyan of Shacharit.
During holidays, there is an additional Mussaf prayer after the morning services, and therefore, a second Priestly Blessing every day.
The Sukkot ceremonies also involve the practice of netilat lulav, the blessing of the Arba Minim, or Four Species: Aravot, etrog, hadassim, and lulav.

Ex-Mossad diplomacy official says he was unaware of Egypt, UAE warning Netanyahu before Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:16:45 UTC
17:16:45 KST

Eyal Tsir Cohen, a former head of international diplomacy at the Mossad, told Army Radio on Monday that, contrary to recent reports, he hadn't heard about any warnings from Egypt or the United Arab Emirates to Israel or Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu before or after October 7, 2023.
"I do not recall any reports regarding a warning from MBZ [Emirati President Mohammed bin Zayed] and Sufian Abu Zaida [a former senior Fatah official], nor do I recall a visit by Abbas Kamel [the Egyptian intelligence chief]," Cohen said.
He added that, while Kamel could theoretically have secretly visited Israel without going through the Mossad's international diplomacy division, he had held numerous meetings with Kamel and his team since October 7, with no mention of the visit or any warning ever raised.
Another former Mossad head, Danny Yatom, also told Army Radio on Monday that Netanyahu's recent trip to the UAE to meet with Zayed had likely concerned the reported warnings that he had received ahead of October 7.
"We're talking about two or three different sources that warned," Yatom said. "You can't ignore that."
Egyptian intelligence chief, former Fatah leader, reportedly warned about Oct. 7
Numerous reports of alleged warnings made to Israel and Netanyahu ahead of October 7 have circulated throughout Israeli media.
On Saturday, The Atlantic reported that Kamel secretly visited Israel 11 days before the October 7 attack and delivered a warning that Hamas was preparing for a significant attack and that time to prevent further escalation was running out.
The investigation found that on September 26, 2023, as senior Israeli officials gathered in Jerusalem to mark the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, a chartered Cessna aircraft linked to Egyptian intelligence services landed at Ben-Gurion Airport, with Kamel on board.
Last week, Zaida disclosed information about a message from Hamas leader in the Gaza Strip, Yahya Sinwar, that he had relayed to Israel three weeks before the October 7 attack in a documentary aired on Al-Ghad.
In the documentary, Zaida said that he had met with Sinwar in Gaza on September 14, 2023, and that during the meeting Sinwar asked him to relay a message to Israel that before the end of that month, Hamas would place “cards” on the negotiating table that would cause an “earthquake,” and that Israel should prepare for the “emptying of the prisons.”
Zaida said he transmitted the message to the Israeli side in both Hebrew and Arabic.
UAE president warned Netanyahu about October 7, 'Haaretz' reports
Haaretz reported earlier this month that Zayed had warned Netanyahu a week and a half before October 7 that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel. The warning was not passed to Israeli intelligence agencies or the military, Haaretz reported.
The UAE has declined to comment on the Haaretz report but has said that the UAE and Israel have maintained "open and direct lines of communication" since establishing diplomatic relations in 2020.
Jerusalem Post Staff, Amichai Stein, Idan Kweller, and Walla contributed to this report.

Morocco-Israel ties deepen as protesters demand ‘no ambassador, no embassy’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:16:14 UTC
17:16:14 KST

Moroccan opponents of normalization with Israel were wrapping up three days of protests Sunday against the kingdom’s decision to upgrade relations to full embassies, even as Rabat moved forward with plans to exchange ambassadors and deepen economic ties with Israel.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The demonstrations followed a Sept. 16 announcement in New York by Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz that the two countries would elevate their liaison offices to embassies and appoint ambassadors. They also agreed to conclude investment-protection and double-taxation agreements by the end of the year.
“There are always demonstrations against normalization,” Yasmine Hasnaoui, a political scientist at Hassan First University in Settat, told The Media Line. “Morocco does not stop those things. Has Morocco changed its course? Morocco did not stop its relations with Israel, because Morocco sees itself as a mediator in the Palestinian and Israeli cause.”
The upgrade builds on the 2020 agreement under which Morocco restored formal relations with Israel and US President Donald Trump, during his first term, recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Morocco also hosts African Lion, the largest US military exercise in Africa.
The Moroccan Front for Supporting Palestine and Opposing Normalization announced the protest campaign on Sept. 17, calling the embassy upgrade a further deepening of relations with Israel. Another coalition, the Moroccan Commission for Supporting the Nation’s Causes, said it organized 76 events in 45 cities on Friday.
Protestors demand 'fall of normalization' with Israel
In Rabat, demonstrators gathered outside Parliament chanting, “The people want the fall of normalization,” according to Moroccan media. Protesters in Marrakech shouted, “No ambassador, no embassy.” No serious disturbances were reported.
Moaz al-Hajri, national coordinator of the Front, also criticized the Israeli liaison office’s move to Mehdi Ben Barka Avenue in Rabat, calling the location “a provocation to the Moroccan people and to the memory of the martyr Mehdi Ben Barka.”
Ben Barka, a prominent independence-era opposition leader, advocated constitutional limits on royal power, land reform and state-led development before disappearing in Paris in 1965. Israeli journalists have reported that Mossad assisted Moroccan agents in tracking him.
Those long-running questions about political power and the distribution of economic gains also surfaced during Morocco’s parliamentary election Wednesday.
Final results issued Friday gave the palace-aligned Authenticity and Modernity Party 97 of the 395 seats in parliament. The National Rally of Independents won 66, Istiqlal 65 and the Islamist Justice and Development Party, known as the PJD, 54, up sharply from 13 in 2021. Turnout fell to about 38% from about 50% five years ago.
At a party council Saturday, PJD leader Abdelilah Benkirane credited the result to “great success from God” and said the public once again viewed the party as “a truly serious party.” He did not attribute its gains to the anti-normalization campaign.
The PJD itself headed Morocco’s government when relations with Israel were restored in 2020.
“They are against normalization, and they have demonstrated that on several occasions, except when they were in government,” Hasnaoui said. “They will take to the streets against what Morocco has done recently in upgrading the status of relations and establishing embassies. But I do not think it will touch the sovereignty of the country when it comes to the Western Sahara.”
Einat Levi, an expert on Morocco and Israeli-Moroccan relations who previously headed economic and academic affairs at Israel’s mission in Morocco, said ties between the two countries have deeper foundations than electoral politics.
“Morocco-Israel relations are anchored in something broader than party politics,” she told The Media Line. “They reflect a strategic direction led by the king and the highest levels of the Moroccan state, built on long-standing ties, shared interests and a common heritage.”
Western Sahara remains central to that strategy.
Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara
Morocco claims sovereignty over the former Spanish colony, while the Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks independence. UN Security Council Resolution 2797, adopted in October 2025, called for negotiations using Morocco’s 2007 autonomy proposal as a basis while reaffirming the goal of a mutually acceptable settlement consistent with the principle of self-determination. The mandate of the UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara expires Oct. 31.
Morocco has simultaneously maintained a public commitment to the Palestinian cause.
Speaking at the United Nations last week, Bourita defended the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), criticized Israeli annexation proposals in the West Bank and condemned settler violence.
UNRWA has become a major point of contention between Israel and many of its regional partners. Israel accuses the agency of allowing Hamas infiltration and says its treatment of Palestinian refugee status perpetuates the conflict. A UN investigation found that nine UNRWA employees may have participated in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack, and Israel subsequently barred the agency from operating on its territory. UNRWA rejects claims that recognizing descendants of Palestinian refugees is unique to the agency, noting that multigenerational refugee status also exists in other prolonged refugee situations.
Morocco has also pledged to deploy a military field hospital to Gaza. King Mohammed VI chairs the Organization of Islamic Cooperation’s Al-Quds Committee, which focuses on Jerusalem and Palestinian issues.
“The king is head of the Al-Quds Committee,” Hasnaoui said. “That does not mean they are with Israel. Morocco is there to mediate.”
The committee’s operational arm, the Bayt Mal Al-Quds Acharif Agency, spent part of the protest week holding consultations in Ramallah and Jerusalem. Mohamed Salem Echarkaoui, the agency’s acting director, met Palestinian officials, Muslim and Christian religious figures, universities, hospitals and business representatives as the organization develops its 2027-2030 plan.
The agency says it wants to move gradually from direct assistance toward employment, entrepreneurship and longer-term economic support in Jerusalem.
Israel’s diplomatic presence in Morocco has also faced complications. Israel recalled its first envoy in Rabat, David Govrin, in 2022 during a misconduct investigation. He was later cleared and returned. Israeli personnel were withdrawn for about 10 months after the Oct. 7 attacks.
The current head of mission, Yossi Ben-David, a Likud member and former mayor of Tiberias, was appointed in 2024. Israel has not yet named the ambassador who would head the newly upgraded embassy, and with Israeli elections scheduled for Oct. 27, the appointment could fall to the next government.
Eli Bar-On, a former senior Israeli official and head of the regional development organization MENA2050, said the United States has been integral to the relationship from the beginning.
“In many ways, it has been a trilateral relationship: Israel, Morocco and the United States,” he told The Media Line. “Both Israel and Morocco have very strong alliances with the US, and that was a key pillar of this relationship.”
Since the Gaza war began, Bar-On said, visits by Israeli ministers and officials “have not stopped, but they have been kept quiet, and that was for the benefit of the relationship.”
He also pointed to security cooperation. Israel accepted Moroccan participation in the US-backed stabilization force in Gaza, he said, and Israeli-owned BlueBird Aero Systems has been linked in Israeli and Moroccan media to drone production in Morocco.
Levi said the diplomatic upgrade could create new economic opportunities, but only if the two governments translate agreements into practical arrangements.
“Diplomatic momentum does not last forever,” she said. “The task now is to build on what has already been achieved and, above all, to give real substance to the many agreements signed since relations were renewed. The burden of proof is now on us.”
The embassy upgrade means “for the first time, an Israeli ambassador will be formally accredited to Morocco,” she said. Yet without agreements covering double taxation, customs and other trade issues, “doing business between Israel and Morocco remains less competitive compared with other markets.”
People-to-people ties have endured even through the political tension. Pilgrimages by Israelis of Moroccan descent to Jewish holy sites “never really stopped,” Levi said, and restored direct flights are heavily booked.
Nearly one million Israeli Jews trace their family roots to Morocco, making them one of Israel’s largest communities with origins in Arab and Muslim countries.
“Finally,” Levi said of the diplomatic upgrade. “The hope is that Morocco can become not only a place of nostalgia and heritage, but an integral part of their future as well.”
The next Moroccan government will face pressures extending far beyond foreign policy.
Under the constitution, King Mohammed VI appoints the head of government from the party that wins the most parliamentary seats, while retaining control over foreign policy, defense and religious affairs. He has not yet named a new head of government from the Authenticity and Modernity Party.
Hasnaoui said the election result comes against a backdrop of youth frustration, social protest and sharp disparities between Morocco’s infrastructure ambitions and everyday living conditions.
“We do not want to have another Ceuta or another Gen Z movement,” she said, referring to this summer’s attempted mass crossings into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and last year’s youth protests.
Those protests began in Agadir after eight women died following cesarean sections at a public hospital. Weeks later, the king opened a new university hospital there, while the 2026 budget increased spending on health and education and provided tens of thousands of new public-sector positions.
“It does not make sense that Morocco is going at two speeds,” Hasnaoui said, “one where you have the infrastructure, the high-speed train, the biggest projects, and another where human development is way behind.”
The contrast is visible in the automobile industry. Morocco has become a major vehicle manufacturing and export center, with annual production capacity above 500,000 vehicles, yet a 2025 survey found that about 70% of Moroccan households did not own a car.
“The success of the next phase of Morocco’s development should be measured not only in kilometers of railway, or the size of the ports, or the beautiful buildings in Rabat,” Hasnaoui said, “but in whether a young Moroccan in Dakhla, in Errachidia, in Fez or in the Atlas region can say that this economic transformation has created an opportunity for me.”
That tension between modernization, identity and political continuity will also be on display next month in Fez.
The Museum of Moroccan Jewish Culture is scheduled to open Oct. 12 in the city’s historic Jewish quarter on land donated by the local Jewish community. The state-funded museum, launched by King Mohammed VI in 2019, will trace more than 2,500 years of Jewish life in Morocco. Moroccan media describe it as the first publicly funded museum devoted entirely to Jewish culture in an Arab or Muslim country.
At Casablanca’s Beth El synagogue on Yom Kippur last week, Serge Berdugo, secretary-general of the Council of Jewish Communities of Morocco, prayed that the new year would bring “a peaceful and just resolution to the fratricidal conflicts that are bringing grief to the Middle East.”
Bar-On said Rabat is also watching Israel’s upcoming Oct. 27 election.
“In Morocco they will also want to see what kind of government Israel has after the elections,” he said.

Serbia's President Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime minister in snap elections

The ballot in October will be held against a backdrop of high political tensions as Vučić’s populists seek to remain in office despite widespread popular discontent.
Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vučić resigned on Sunday to pursue a bid to become prime minister in upcoming snap parliamentary elections that will test his rule in the Balkan country, which was rattled by nearly two years of protests.
Vučić’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term and said he was resigning to lead his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party in the 25 October vote.
The governing populists face a major challenge at the ballot box from a youth-backed movement that led protests triggered by the 1 November 2024 train station canopy collapse in the northern city of Novi Said that killed 16 people.
University students demanded accountability for the tragedy. Their struggle for justice and against corruption has grown into a strong movement that will attempt to oust Vučić’s government after 14 years in power.
Vučić himself has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years.
“I am resigning the duty of the President of the Republic,” Vučić said, reading the text of his resignation.
Presidential vote to be held later
After Vučić’s resignation, the acting president will be close ally and former prime minister, Ana Brnabić, who is the outgoing speaker of Serbia’s 250-member Parliament.
Vučić said the first round of the early presidential election must be held by the end of this year because of a 90-day deadline.
Vučić and his party have been accused of rampant corruption, organised crime links and a clampdown on democratic freedoms, including the critical media.
The SNS party has gradually taken control over all state institutions since coming to power in 2012, while denying abuse of office and repeatedly pledging to fight graft.
The student-backed election list includes little-known experts, professors, teachers, athletes and other individuals from all walks of life.
Groups of students have been touring the country on bicycles as part of their campaign calling for the rule of law and an end to corruption.
Analysts say the student group and Vučić are polling close, heralding a tight race and a referendum-like atmosphere.
Also running are Vučić’s allies, the Socialist Party, a pro-EU opposition alliance and several smaller groups.
Vučić said that as of Monday, he will be “everywhere in Serbia to listen to the people.” While praising his government's achievements, Vučić contended that “I have made mistakes but I have worked diligently like hardly anyone in this position.”
Vučić also said he had pardoned 49 people before leaving the office, including 23 who have been prosecuted for alleged offences during the protests. They include a group of anti-government activists who fled Serbia after being accused of anti-state activities.
Authorities have pushed hard against protesters with police violence and detentions as Vučić, without offering evidence, accused his opponents and critical media of intending to “destroy the state” under unspecified foreign influence.
He told Serbia’s state-run RTS Television earlier on Sunday that foreign powers and unidentified people in the country plan to stir unrest on election night.
Serbia’s efforts to join the European Union have stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and a refusal to join sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.

Britain seeks compromise over blocked Orange Order march in Northern Ireland
BELFAST, Sept 28 - Britain's Northern Ireland minister will on Monday meet residents who blocked a Protestant parade from marching through a Catholic area of a Northern Irish town, and hopes to find a compromise to reduce tension.
A local lawmaker warned of "profound" consequences if the parade did not proceed in the next two days.
About 2,000 protesters including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill and Claire Hanna, the leader of Irish nationalist party SDLP, blocked the route on Sunday. This led to a standoff, with both sides declining to disperse and police between them.
The attempt to hold the parade from Portadown to the nearby hamlet of Drumcree followed Friday's lifting of an almost 30-year ban on the route. The parade had triggered unrest across British-run Northern Ireland in the run-up to a 1998 peace deal.
The head of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition told protesters late on Sunday that he would meet Northern Ireland Minister Chris Bryant and the chief of police after receiving commitments that the march would not proceed overnight.
He asked that a small number of volunteers remain on the road through the night to ensure the commitments were not broken, the BBC reported.
"We've stopped them once, the process now is to stop them permanently," Breandán Mac Cionnaith told the protesters.
Northern Ireland's Parades Commission, set up during the original Drumcree dispute to regulate marches, permitted a smaller-than-usual parade after its initial decision to continue the ban was quashed by the High Court in August over a procedural error.
EFFORTS TO REDUCE TENSION
Bryant has the power to revoke the Parades Commission's ruling at the request of Northern Ireland's police, but said he had received no such request.
"I've made it very clear that I think it's important that we get to a resolution and we need to find some kind of compromise. Nobody wants to perpetuate this tension and this anger," Bryant told reporters after meeting political parties on Sunday night.
The dispute has created new tension in Northern Ireland's compulsory power-sharing devolved government led by Sinn Fein and pro-British rivals, the Democratic Unionist Party. The DUP says the parade must go ahead.
"He (Bryant) has 24 to 48 hours to ensure the rule of law is upheld and the parade proceeds," DUP lawmaker Carla Lockhart wrote on social media after the party met the minister.
"If that does not happen, the consequences will be profound. Mob rule cannot defeat the rule of law." REUTERS

Zurich voters back stricter skyscraper regulations

Zurich voters back stricter skyscraper regulations
Voters in Zurich have backed stricter regulations for high-rise buildings and a reduction in the areas designated for tower developments. The measures form part of a partial revision of the city’s building and zoning code (BZO) approved on Sunday.
There are currently around 300 buildings in the city that are over 25 metres tall. The city council’s initial proposal was to keep the total area allocated to residential towers virtually unchanged. However, it intended to reduce the zones for buildings up to 80 metres and introduce new areas for those up to 60 metres, as well as expanding those for buildings between 25 and 40 metres.
More
A 260-metre skyscraper in Zermatt?
The council, however, made significant changes to the plan, further restricting the areas designated for taller buildings. Those up to 80 metres will only be permitted along the railway lines and in the centre of Oerlikon, whilst several zones earmarked for buildings up to 40 metres have been removed. For left-wing parties the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, this revised plan helps prevent a wave of demolitions and provides greater protection for residents against the risk of being forced out of their neighbourhoods.
More
Office towers go higher, bigger, greener – but what’s the point?
The aim of the revision, for both variants, was to better integrate high-rise buildings into the urban fabric, creating added value for the population through more vibrant ground floors, greater spaces for public and community use, and the enhancement of green spaces.
In the vote, 62.6% of residents backed the council’s more restrictive amendment, whilst the one proposed by the city administration – presented as a counter-proposal – was rejected by the same percentage. Voter turnout was 45.8%.

Live: Pope Leo XIV arrives in Metz for final stop of France visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28

Live: Pope Leo leads Mass in France's Metz after speech on Europe's roots and future
Pope Leo XIV urged Europe to remember its Christian history and appealed for peace and unity in a speech delivered in France's northeastern city of Metz on Monday, the fourth and final day of his visit. After touring the city in his popemobile, the pontiff later led a Mass at Saint-Etienne Cathedral attended by French President Emmanuel Macron. Follow our liveblog for all the latest.
Pope leads Mass in Metz cathedral
In his final event in France, Leo is celebrating Mass in the cathedral of Saint-Etienne (St. Stephen) in Metz, a city with a long history of conflict that was part of Nazi Germany during the war.
The cathedral, finished in 1522, is one of the greatest examples of French Gothic style, with its soaring vaults and stained-glass windows, some of which were later designed by Marc Chagall, a 20th-century Jewish artist.
In his homily, Leo said that Metz and its surroundings experienced evil, but now “bear witness to the whole world that reconciliation is only possible when one has the courage to break the chains of resentment.”
The cathedral’s stained-glass windows, designed by a Jew, are “an extraordinary symbol of ecumenism and interreligious dialogue,” where God’s light unites “different histories and cultures into a single marvelous mosaic of peace.”
French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte attend the Mass in Metz. Credit: Christian Hartmann, Reuters
“As we contemplate these stained-glass windows, we learn that Europe’s future does not lie in uniformity, but in the harmony of differences, where the wounds of the past become openings through which light shines,” he said.
The colored glass has given the cathedral the nickname the “Lanterne du Bon Dieu,” or “The Good Lord’s Lantern.
Pope Leo blessed Rafale pilots after joining Air France cockpit crew
Pope Leo spent half an hour in the cockpit of a plane earlier todayy, chatting with the pilots and speaking by radio to the crews of the Rafale fighter jets escorting his aircraft, Air France said.
"The Holy Father came into the cockpit for the entire Lourdes-Metz cruise phase," said Eric Marguerite, the flight's co-pilot.
"We had informal conversations with him. He is passionate about aviation, cars and mechanics in general," he added, after landing in Metz.
The flight, commanded by Captain Clemence Coussonneau, was escorted by two Rafale jets flying about 50 metres (yards) from the pope's plane.
"We handed the microphone to the Holy Father, who spoke to the Rafale pilots," said Marguerite.
"He offered his blessing to them and to all military personnel working to protect people and promote peace around the world."
Macron invokes Europe’s Judeo-Christian foundation as Leo visits
In his speech alongside the pope a short while ago, Macron said Europe was built on a "Greco-Roman and Judeo-Christian foundation", invoking the continent's religious heritage.
The remarks were notable from the leader of a constitutionally secular state, in a country that regularly agonises over national identity, religion and the place of faith in public life, notes Reuters.
Macron, who attended Leo's last mass in Metz on Monday after skipping other religious services, said Europe's heritage had helped crystallise "the primacy of the person" and later "the free and rational individual".
"Our Europe ... is above all a civilisation," Macron said. "This Europe of our cities and villages, schools and universities, cafes and public squares, was built on a Greco-Roman and Judeo-Christian foundation."

Pope urges Europe to help battle 'lies and deceit' in international ties
Pope Leo warned that relations between nations were becoming "increasingly uncivilised" with people boasting of "lies and deceit", and urged Europe to help "break this cycle".
"Relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilised. The value of keeping one's word is dismissed. Instead, people boast of lies and deceit," he said. "Europe can help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learned to cultivate and preserve."
Pope Leo urges negotiations as Ukraine war drags on
Pope Leo said that negotiators seeking to end war in Europe must be willing to sacrifice some of their positions to achieve peace, as efforts to end the bloody, four-year conflict between Russia and Ukraine continue to fail.
The first US pope, speaking in Metz, a city central to the European Union founding, lamented that "war has returned, even to Europe: a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day".
Offering his clearest political vision yet for Europe, Leo also spoke in favour of European integration and multiculturalism at a time the far right is gaining strength across the region.
The pontiff called on Europe to integrate migrants "as if they were part of one's own family".
Pope urges Europe to remember Christian history, strengthen democratic ideals
Pope Leo urged Europe to remember its Christian history in a speech delivered in Metz, the hometown of Robert Schuman, a founding father of the European Union, during his four-day visit to France.
"One cannot speak of Europe without mentioning Christianity," he said.
The pontiff praised European integration and multiculturalism, adding that dialogue with others was a "social and political necessity" and urging EU leaders to give "real substance" to words such as freedom, democracy and unity.
"Europe has flourished and progressed when it has been able to draw on the best aspects of its past and reinvent them in new and creative ways through encounters with others," the pope said.
President of the Conference of Bishops of France Cardinal Jean-Marc Avelines speaks

France's President Emmanuel Macron said Europe should return to the "courage of its founders" to become a force for peace in the face of resurgent nationalism.
Europe "must rediscover the courage of its founders – yes, courage – in order to become the force for peace, independence, and democracy that it is meant to be," he said in the presence of Pope Leo XIV in the northeastern city of Metz near the German border.
"The courage not to give in to withdrawal, to hatred of others, to the return of nationalisms that divide," he said.

“Religious discourse must constantly call for the disarmament of hearts and words. This is the direct responsibility of each of us, as guardians of our respective traditions,” continued Léon XIV. He spoke after the reading of the “Metz Appeal,” a joint declaration by representatives of religious communities in France calling for interreligious dialogue and peace.
🎥 Leo building on Francis's legacy while reincorporating 'more traditional elements of papal activity'
FRANCE 24's Erin Ogunkeye speaks with Miles Pattenden, historian of the Catholic Church at the University of Oxford.
For Pattenden, Pope Leo XIV’s visit to France is part of a broader recalibration of the papacy. While Pope Francis placed particular emphasis on the Catholic Church’s peripheries and the needs of the Global South, Leo is subtly bringing the Church’s historic European heartlands back into focus.
France is especially significant in this regard, given its deep historical relationship with Catholicism and its evolving relationship with Christianity, European identity, secularism and contemporary geopolitical debates.

7-year sentence handed down to Oleg Bessedin for anti-Estonia activities
A court has found a pro-Kremlin propagandist guilty of crimes against Estonia's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The first-tier Harju County Court on Monday found Oleg Bessedin guilty, and also convicted him of repeated violations of international sanctions, under a plea agreement made last week.
The court found that the plea agreement complied with the law and had been entered into voluntarily, and approved it. Under the ruling, the state will confiscate €77,104.32 worth of assets owned by Bessedin. Procedural costs totaling €3,195.80 will also be covered from these seized funds.
The ruling follows a plea bargain reached with the Office of the Prosecutor General on the first day of Bessedin's trial, last Tuesday, September 22. He was arrested in November 2025 and has been detained in custody since then.
Bessedin, 52, was charged with activities against Estonia's national security, including spreading pro-Kremlin propaganda and distributing sanctioned Russian content, dating back to May 2022 and in coordination with Russian state organs and individuals involved in influence operations.
The activities entailed producing and disseminating narratives justifying Russia's war of aggression, false claims and fear-mongering rhetoric, primarily via a YouTube channel, with the aim of dividing Estonian society, reducing trust in state institutions and undermining support for NATO and the EU.
Bessedin was also found guilty of repeatedly violating sanctions imposed under Council of the European Union Regulation No. 269/2014 by allowing the TV channel TVN, which he controlled, to broadcast a program from a sanctioned Russian media outlet; publishing content linked to a sanctioned media outlet on his social media platform; transferring the screening rights to three of his films to a sanctioned Russian state media agency; and helping to launch a television channel through which content from Russian television channels under EU sanctions was broadcast.
Initially, under the plea agreement, he was to forfeit more than €73,000 in assets and serve seven years in prison. The court's ruling on Monday approved this agreement. The Harju County Court ruling has not yet entered into force.

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Flash floods triggered by heavy rainfall have affected 44,889 families across Cambodia, forcing 3,685 families to evacuate to higher ground, a disaster control spokesperson said on Monday.
Soth Kim Kolmony, spokesperson for the National Committee for Disaster Management, said that 10 provinces have been hit by the deluge. Kolmony noted that the current flooding is driven primarily by local heavy rainfall. The Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology reported that Cambodia is experiencing widespread rain, thunderstorms, and strong winds from Sept. 24 to 30, triggered by the peripheral systems of Typhoon Surigae. ■

China's deep-sea drilling capacity reaches 5,000-meter level
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:00:39 CST
17:00:39 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on July 28, 2026 shows China's ocean drilling vessel Mengxiang conducting an operation at night. China's Mengxiang ocean drilling vessel has set a national record for deep-sea drilling, elevating its capability to the 5,000-meter level, after obtaining basalt samples from the South China Sea basin, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Monday. This marks China's entry into international advanced ranks in deep-sea drilling operation capacity, according to the ministry. (Photo by Zhang Fatao/Xinhua)
GUANGZHOU, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's Mengxiang, meaning Dream, ocean drilling vessel has set a national record for deep-sea drilling, elevating its capability to the 5,000-meter level, after obtaining basalt samples from the South China Sea basin, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Monday.
This marks China's entry into international advanced ranks in deep-sea drilling operation capacity, according to the ministry.
A 4.27-meter basalt sample was extracted during the voyage via a self-developed drill, which made China the third country after the United States and Japan to obtain hard rock samples from a deep ocean basin using drilling vessels.
The research team conducted a long-term and high-intensity operation of shipborne remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), deploying two ROVs to operate for over 358 hours in total at a depth of 4,000 meters, with a single continuous operation lasting up to 103 hours, reaching internationally advanced levels, said Sun Zhen, a researcher at the Guangzhou Marine Geological Survey (GMGS) in south China.
Following the standards of the International Ocean Discovery Program for the first time, researchers also completed on-site multi-parameter processing and analysis of the samples, including cataloging, cutting, scanning, testing and storage, thereby mastering full-process operational capabilities for ultra-deep water ocean scientific drilling.
The samples and data obtained during the voyage provide crucial empirical evidence for addressing core scientific issues such as the expansion of the South China Sea. They are also of great significance for studying the evolution of the ancient marine environment in the sea and for the exploration and development of ultra-deep water energy resources, researchers noted.
A total of 170 researchers from nine institutions participated in the voyage, which was organized by the China Geological Survey and implemented by the GMGS.
China's first domestically-built ocean drilling vessel, Mengxiang, was officially commissioned in 2024. ■

SINGAPORE, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's manufacturing output rose 15.4 percent year on year in August, driven by broad-based growth across most clusters, official data showed on Monday.
On a seasonally adjusted month-on-month basis, manufacturing output fell 0.5 percent in August, the Singapore Economic Development Board said in a statement.
All clusters except chemicals recorded year-on-year growth in August.

Biomedical manufacturing output edged up 0.4 percent, with the medical technology segment recording higher production of medical devices amid stronger export demand.
Chemicals were the only cluster to record a decline, with output falling 12.7 percent, weighed down by the petroleum and petrochemicals segments. ■

Exile has not broken young Rohingya people. But survival cost us more than our homes | Ajas Khan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:00:28 UTC
17:00:28 KST

Nine years ago, I was forced to flee my home in Maungdaw township, Rakhine state, Myanmar. I was 13 years old. I remember how quickly an average day turned into a day when life felt extinguished, leaving behind the place where I grew up with my family.
Even now, when I go to sleep, what comes into my mind is the memory of that journey, the fear of not knowing what awaited me. It took three days to reach refuge.
With so many others, my family and I crossed the Naf River into Bangladesh. But survival came at a high price: the price of my home, my liberty, my life.
I am Ajas Khan, a climate activist, youth leader and Rohingya genocide survivor.
Nine years is a long time for a child to grow up, to feel at home, or not to feel at home if the place you are staying in is not your country.
It is a long time for the whole family to wait, in exile, seeing another generation grow up in the camps. The people of Bangladesh have given us a safe place to stay, which we are incredibly grateful for and can never forget. Humanitarian organisations have saved many lives. However, a plastic shelter is not a permanent solution. It can provide a place to sleep, but little else in the way of home, citizenship, freedom or dignity.
But the exile has not broken us. Young Rohingya people are studying, caring for each other, and survivors are telling their stories. We are not just victims; we have a history, a culture, a home and dreams for the future.
When we speak of justice, we do not seek revenge. Survivors want the truth to come out about those who have committed genocide against the Rohingya people, and for the international community to continue to provide all possible support. Those responsible for these crimes must be brought to justice, which will allow us a future away from the brutality of the past.
It makes no difference if the perpetrators are soldiers or politicians, state actors or non-state actors. If they destroy homes, expel people, take away their lives and nothing happens to them, they will do the same again.
Nine years is more than enough. Time must never become an excuse for impunity.
I’ve never for one second let go of the hope of returning to my home. Going home doesn’t mean just crossing back over the Naf River. It means going home with full human rights in our motherland, without fear, with our citizenship, security, equality, land and livelihood restored. Our healthcare and education.
There is no choice between being rendered stateless and living in the camps, or repatriation without rights. Return without citizenship is no solution at all.
On this ninth anniversary, I would like to raise the point that decisions over the fate of the Rohingya people must no longer be made by any entity other than the Rohingya themselves.
The government of Bangladesh and NGOs have made immense sacrifices to care for Rohingya refugees, navigating the immense humanitarian and economic implications of hosting more than a million Rohingya in Bangladesh. It is understandable that the government of Bangladesh might want to make concessions in its negotiations to ensure solutions can be brokered, and to engage with anyone claiming authority in Myanmar who could contribute to this goal. But such concessions should not come at our expense.
The Rohingya are not a footnote; we are a people with a history, and our future can no longer be dictated either by governments or armed groups. Should the governments of Bangladesh or Myanmar, or the Arakan Army in Rakhine, or any other interlocutor, make decisions, then Rohingya representatives must be at the table.
We give our breath to our future. And through all these years of fighting, our identity is still there and our dreams have not gone away, despite the pain.
I remember all the people who were lost during the 2017 massacres, and those who survived but are still being chased and hated. I think about the people whose families are broken, who have injuries, and those whose childhood was taken away.
Rohingya children should grow up with different stories – not of loss, but tales of returning home. We need justice; we need to be recognised as humans; we need our citizenship; we need accountability. And we need to go home.
I want our next generation to hold their lives in their own hands and not in those of strangers. I want them to see our land, not just hear stories.
For me, I have spent nine years in a foreign refugee camp without a future, in an open jail, and I’m still waiting for hope to return.

Column: A miner's leave slip that debunks Japan's "benevolent colonialism"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:00:23 CST
17:00:23 KST

by Zhou Yaxin
In the winter of 1943, at the Xi'an Coal Mine in what was then the Japanese puppet regime of "Manchukuo" in China's northeast, a miner named Li Xingyu submitted a leave application.
Written in simple, broken words, the slip reads: "My name is Li Xingyu. My three sons are all dead. I am heartbroken ... My mother is over seventy and blind ... I have nowhere else to turn. I beg the director to have mercy and give me a certificate so that I may return home to visit my mother. I worked shifts with my sons, never missing a single day ... Of my five children, four are dead. I have no heart left to work ..."
This leave application was never approved.
Today, it is preserved at the Exhibition Hall of the Liaoyuan Miners' Tomb from the Period of Japanese Occupation in Northeast China. Also on display are the largely intact remains of 197 miners, along with more than 20 sets of scattered remains. Some skulls bear knife marks, and some leg bones are severed. The youngest victim was merely 12 years old. A local ballad from the era captured the horror: "Electric fences stretch high, watchtowers stand tall; miners are locked up like prisoners in a cell. Entering the mine was like stepping through hell's gate; to stay alive was harder than death itself."
These are stark reminders of the colonial expansion and resource plundering carried out by Japanese militarism in northeast China, deeply rooted in history and etched in memories that remain searing to this day.
After the Meiji Restoration, Japan embarked on a path of military expansion in Asia. China's northeast, with its abundant resources and unique geostrategic position, became a primary target.
On Sept. 18, 1931, the Japanese Kwantung Army deliberately staged the September 18th Incident. Within less than half a year, China's three northeastern provinces fell under Japanese occupation.
The crimes committed by Japanese militarism during its 14-year colonial rule in the region will never be forgotten. The lie of "benevolent colonialism" repeatedly peddled by Japan's right wing will collapse under its own weight.
Plundering resources and monopolizing the economy -- Japan pursued a colonial economic model of "Japan being the industrial hub and China's northeast the raw material base." It set up over 200 entities, including major railway, power and coal companies, and used them to seize control of northeast China's economic lifelines. According to incomplete statistics, between 1932 and 1945, Japan extracted 223 million tons of coal and 120 million tons of grain, along with other resources, from northeast China to fuel its war machine. Japan also profited enormously from opium smuggling in the region.
Enslaving education and colonial indoctrination -- The Japanese invaders adhered to the principle that "To subjugate a nation, first erase its history." After the establishment of the puppet "Manchukuo" in 1932, Japan started to replace Chinese language with Japanese in schools, attempting to make Chinese children forget their own history and identity. The puppet regime revised middle school textbooks, removing content on traditional Chinese culture and history to promote the narrative that "Manchukuo" was an "independent state."
Brutal exploitation and disregard for human life -- Across coal mines, the Japanese military enforced a policy that treated human lives as expendable in the pursuit of coal. Countless laborers starved, died from disease, were beaten to death or burned alive in mines where basic safety measures were virtually nonexistent. According to the Japanese puppet regime's coal production cost data, Chinese laborers were listed alongside explosives and detonators, treated as little more than inputs in the production process.
During the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, Japan forcibly recruited over 10 million Chinese laborers across the country. In northeast China alone, 2 million died from abuse. Unit 731 of the Kwantung Army built the world's largest germ warfare base in Harbin, where it experimented on imprisoned civilians and prisoners of war -- subjecting them to frostbite, poison gas and low-pressure tests, and deliberately infecting them with plague, anthrax and cholera. During Japan's invasion of China, an estimated 650,000 Chinese died as a result of Japanese biological warfare.
Yet even today, some right-wing forces in Japan not only refuse to reflect on their history of colonial aggression, but also deliberately distort historical facts.
They portray the war of aggression as an effort to "liberate Asia from Western colonial rule," and claim that Japan accelerated the "modernization" of some Asian countries and regions through infrastructure construction and "good governance" during its colonial rule.
The historical record tells a different story.
The infrastructure built by Japan in occupied territories was designed primarily to serve its own war needs. The systematic extraction of resources and the atrocities committed under Japanese militarism left local people in abject poverty, severely disrupted the economic and social development of Asian nations, and impeded the progress of colonized countries. The so-called "good governance" practices are in fact evidence of crimes, scars of suffering, and engines of death. The much-vaunted "Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere" was in reality a "Greater East Asia Aggression Sphere." Tens of millions of soldiers and civilians died under Japanese militarism -- hardly a record of "co-prosperity."
Ninety-five years on, some right-wing forces in Japan still show no remorse or repentance for the September 18th Incident. They even attempt to tamper with historical facts and whitewash their record, seeking to turn the page on all their crimes of aggression and colonization in Asia. The Chinese people will never accept this, nor will the peoples of other Asian countries that suffered Japanese aggression.
History cannot be falsified. Conscience and justice will endure. Miner Li Xingyu's leave application is an irrefutable evidence, as are the miners' remains on display and the records left behind by the puppet regime.
The alarm bell of the September 18th continues to ring -- not to perpetuate hatred, but to ensure that these pieces of evidence are seen, remembered and passed on from one generation to the next.
As long as these records endure, the historical truth will endure, and the Japanese right wing's plot to peddle the myth of "benevolent colonialism" will never succeed.
Editor's note: The author is an international affairs observer.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Concerned expedition companies said several of their staff members who were at the base camp of the 7,126-meter-tall mountain to fix ropes and set up tents ahead of the autumn climbing season remained missing.

 among young newcomers at 53.1%, followed by Utrecht and Leiden at 49.5% each.
The Hague was the exception: 65.4% of the young people who moved there were not students.
Just under a third of those leaving home were students, and half of them (49.9%) moved into privately rented housing. The rest went into social housing or owner-occupied homes. Non-students were most likely to move into an owner-occupied home (42.6%).
The figures only cover young people registered as living with their parents in the Netherlands at the start of 2024. They exclude anyone who moved to the country from abroad that year, such as newly arrived international students.
