A year’s study at uni now costs a student living in digs at least 18,000 euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:59:00 UTC
16:59:00 KST

A year’s study at a Flemish university or polytechnic has become almost 50% more expensive than 10 years ago. That is according to calculations by the Thomas More University of Applied Sciences. A student living in digs without a grant now has to fork out at least 18,000 euros. Expenditure for students who commute from home has risen to almost 12,000 euros per year.
A year’s study at uni now costs a student living in digs at least 18,000 euros
Studying at a university or polytechnic has become significantly more expensive. The annual calculations by the Centre of Expertise on Budget and Financial Well-being (CEBUD) at Thomas More University show that costs have risen by almost half over the past 10 years.
A student living in digs without a grant faces costs of at least 18,229 euros this academic year. Compared with last year, this represents an increase of 601 euros, or 3.4 per cent. Ten years ago, the cost was 12,334 euros.
For commuting students, the costs this academic year amount to at least 11,803 euros. That is 314 euros, or 2.7 per cent, more than last academic year and also represents an increase of almost half over the past 10 years.
Impact of cost of living rise
‘The fact that the figure is so high is largely down to the cost of living that has been included in the calculation,’ says Nele Peeters of CEBUD. ‘These are the costs of food, clothing and leisure, for example. Every family incurs these costs, whether you’re a student or not.’
The cost of living is estimated at just under 10,000 euros for an academic year. That is around 230 euros more than last academic year and about 25 per cent more than five years ago. Leisure, at 3,209 euros, accounts for the largest share of living costs, followed by food (2,947 euros for students living in digs and 2,582 euros for commuting students).
In addition, there are costs that are entirely related to studying, such as enrolment fees, course and book fees, a laptop, study trips and work placements.
These so-called ‘strict study costs’ amount to an average of 1,980 euros this academic year for a student not receiving a grant, 1,422 euros for a student eligible for a grant but not currently receiving one, and 938 euros for a grant recipient. This, too, is 25% higher than five years ago.
The centre of expertise does emphasise, however, that costs can vary significantly depending on the chosen field of study.
Accommodation and transport
Finally, there are also the ‘broader study costs’, such as transport costs and rent for student accommodation.
Students living in student accommodation can expect to pay a total of 5,963 euros for rent and room costs – almost 5 per cent more than last year (+274 euros) – and 271 euros in transport costs.
For commuting students, transport costs amount to 255 euros, but CEBUD only takes into account students who travel by train. “Anyone who drives to campus in their own car needs an additional budget of 4,142 euros per year,” it has calculated.
Student grants
“More and more families are struggling to make ends meet and, consequently, to pay for higher education,” says Katrien Beeusaert of the families’ association Gezinsbond. “For single-parent families in particular, it is becoming almost impossible to allow their child to study at uni.”
“We’re seeing more and more students combining their studies with part-time work to help pay for their studies and student life. But combining studying and working is, of course, no easy task.”
The Gezinsbond singles out student grants. “All too often, these still end up with people who don’t need them,” says Beeusaert.
“Too much emphasis is still placed on household income alone as a condition for a student grant. Other sources of income or assets are not taken into account. If we want to avoid higher education becoming something reserved solely for the ‘happy few’, we will have to make some changes to the eligibility criteria for student grants.”
The Gezinsbond says it is particularly concerned now that the Flemish Government is considering cuts to allowances.
“I think teachers and schools need to think even more carefully about how they can reduce certain costs even further. Parents should really only need to buy the absolute essentials.”

“I don’t think this exchange rate is good enough,” “Magyar” said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Brovdi, commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces, stated that among the challenges Ukraine will face in the near future is an escalation of Russian strikes using missiles and jet-powered drones.

Swedish opposition leader Andersson says she cannot form government in current situation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:57:51 UTC
16:57:51 KST

Sweden faces political deadlock after Andersson gives up attempt to form government
STOCKHOLM, Sept 28 - Attempts to form a new government in Sweden hit the buffers on Monday after Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson said she was unable to secure enough support, despite the centre-left bloc winning a narrow majority in this month's election.
"I can conclude that there is currently no possibility for me to form a government," Andersson said at a press conference, saying she had lost the support of Sweden's Left Party.
The speaker of Sweden's parliament is now likely to turn to Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson to see if he can form a government. Kristersson's Moderates are the next biggest party after the Social Democrats.
The general election on September 13 saw the centre-left opposition winning a narrow majority, taking 176 seats in parliament to the centre-right's 173.
The result was driven by a decline in support for the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats in the Nordic nation of 10.6 million people, bucking a Europe-wide trend of gains for the far right.
Despite the centre-left's victory, the vote, widely seen as a referendum on Kristersson's promise to bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into a ruling coalition, has left forming a stable government fraught with difficulties.
Andersson said she had given up trying to form a government after the Left Party, one of the parties she needed to form a majority, said it would support a candidate from the centre-right as speaker of parliament.
The Left Party has said previously it will only support Andersson as prime minister.
Andersson would likely get another shot at trying to form a government if any centre-right attempt fails.
The speaker can put four candidates forward to parliament for approval, but if each is rejected, Sweden will hold a new election.
Casting a further cloud over the process, police said on Friday they had started preliminary investigations into five complaints of election fraud around Stockholm.
The probes come days after prosecutors opened a separate investigation into suspected fraud in the central Swedish town of Borlange, a case that could put 11 parliamentary seats in play if the Election Review Board orders a re-run of the vote there.
In 2018, Social Democrat Stefan Lofven took 134 days to form a new government. REUTERS

Volcanic ash halts Italy's Catania airport for third day in a row
MILAN, Sept 28 - Flights at Italy's Catania airport will remain suspended on Monday for a third consecutive day after volcanic ash emissions from Mount Etna disrupted operations, the Sicilian airport's operator said.
All flight operations at the airport, Italy's fifth-busiest by passenger traffic, have been suspended until 2159 GMT on Monday, according to an updated notice from operator SAC.
Passengers were advised to check the status of their flights with their airlines before traveling to the airport. The operator said further updates would follow.
Mount Etna, Europe's highest and most-active volcano, frequently disrupts flights at Catania, and ash emissions have been particularly intense this summer, affecting thousands of travelers during the peak holiday season this summer. REUTERS

Finland bound to defense cooperation with Israel ‘whether we like it or not’: Defense minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:57:31 UTC
16:57:31 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Finland must maintain long-term defense cooperation with Israel, Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen said Monday, as arms trade with the country faces criticism and restrictions elsewhere in Europe.
In a statement by the Defense Ministry, Hakkanen said Israeli weapons systems acquired in recent years were central to Finland’s defense capability, citing the David’s Sling air defense system, Gabriel 5 missiles and Spike anti-tank missiles.
His remarks come amid a wider European debate over military ties with Israel. Human rights groups have urged governments to halt arms transfers to Israel, warning that continued supplies risk enabling violations of international law in Gaza. Spain has tightened restrictions on arms trade with Israel, while Italy suspended automatic renewal of a defense cooperation agreement earlier this year.
Hakkanen said purchasing the systems also entails a long-term relationship with Israeli suppliers for spare parts, software updates, training and technical support.
“This fact binds us to cooperation with Israel, whether we like it or not,” he said.
He also said Israel was named alongside the US and South Korea as a key defense materiel partner in Finland’s 2024 Defense Report. Of Finland’s parliamentary parties, only the Left Alliance opposed cooperation with Israel, he said.

The exhibition “Italy and Romania Told Through Data” has opened in Bucharest
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:57:18 CEST
16:57:18 KST

The exhibition “Among Us – Italy and Romania Told Through Data” was inaugurated in Bucharest at the Ion Mincu University of Architecture and Urbanism. The initiative is part of the “Italian Design Day in the World 2026” program, promoted and organized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Culture, as part of the Italy-Romania Cultural Year, coordinated by the Italian Embassy in Bucharest, the Italian Cultural Institute, and the ICE Agency Office.
                                    
                                       
				“Tra noi · Între noi” is a cultural diplomacy project that describes the relationship between Italy and Romania through data. The ties between the two countries are among the strongest in Europe. Over one million Romanian citizens reside in Italy, where they form the largest community of any other nationality; Italy ranks first in terms of the number of companies registered in Romania and is Romania’s second-largest trading partner; every year, thousands of people travel between the two countries for study, work, or family ties. Using  data, a map, and a European comparison, the exhibition explores the scale of this phenomenon, its trends over time, and its multidimensional nature. The goal is to provide both countries with a common ground of shared and verifiable information, which is essential for an accurate comparison between them. Data is the starting point for reasoning; it serves to spark reflection and help us understand the complexity of the world. In some cases, it helps us reexamine certain stereotypes that are reinforced in traditional media.

U.S. Navy’s newest destroyer arrives in Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:56:20 UTC
16:56:20 KST

- The future USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), a Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, arrived in Whittier, Alaska, on Sept. 27, 2026.
- The U.S. Navy will commission the ship there on Oct. 3, the first Navy commissioning in Alaska since 2013.
The U.S. Navy’s newest destroyer, the future USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), arrived in Whittier, Alaska, on Sept. 27, less than a week before it is due to be formally commissioned there in a ceremony the state has not hosted in more than a decade.
The Flight III Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer will be commissioned Oct. 3, 2026, in the small port town on Prince William Sound, the U.S. Navy said. Commissioning is the ceremony at which a ship officially joins the fleet and the crew takes charge of it. The last Navy ship commissioned in Alaska was the amphibious transport dock USS Anchorage (LPD 23), in Anchorage on May 4, 2013.
The ship is named for Ted Stevens, a decorated World War II Army Air Corps pilot who went on to represent Alaska in the U.S. Senate for four decades and became a leading voice on defense spending. It is the first Navy warship to carry his name. Alaska’s congressional delegation and state officials pushed to hold the ceremony in the state, and then-Secretary of the Navy John Phelan approved Whittier as the location in March.
After the ceremony, the destroyer will not stay in Alaska. Its homeport is Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia, where it arrived in May after delivery trials.
Ted Stevens was built by Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Ingalls Shipbuilding division in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and delivered to the U.S. Navy in December 2025. It is one of the Flight III ships, the latest version of the Arleigh Burke design, which has been in production since the 1980s and makes up the backbone of the U.S. Navy’s surface fleet.
The main change in Flight III is the AN/SPY-6(V)1 air and missile defense radar, which can detect and track aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles at longer range than the SPY-1 radar on earlier Arleigh Burke destroyers. The ship also carries the Aegis Baseline 10 combat system and has more electrical power and cooling capacity to run its newer sensors and weapons. The destroyer displaces about 9,700 tons and can carry out air defense, ballistic missile defense, anti-submarine and surface warfare missions.
Holding the ceremony in Alaska ties the ship to the U.S. Navy’s growing presence in the far north. The Navy said it maintains a persistent operational presence in Alaska, including high-latitude maritime security operations, and the state sits along the northern Pacific and Arctic sea lanes that link North America with Asia.
Ted Stevens is part of a steady stream of new Flight III destroyers entering the fleet from Ingalls and from General Dynamics’ Bath Iron Works in Maine. The U.S. Navy has not said where the ship will make its first deployment or when it will join a carrier strike group.
The commissioning ceremony is scheduled for Oct. 3 in Whittier.

&quot;We need to prepare for the worst-case scenario&quot;: Prime Minister responded to whether the internet is under threat

"We need to prepare for the worst-case scenario": Prime Minister responded to whether the internet is under threat
Kyiv • UNN
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that internet systems are being distributed among the cloud, foreign platforms, and various locations.
Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhii Koretskyi spoke about preparations for possible threats to the country’s internet due to attacks by the russian federation. He said this in an interview during the telethon on September 27, UNN reports.
Details
Answering a question about the threat of the country losing internet access and the protection of the relevant facilities, the Prime Minister noted that the systems should be distributed among different locations.
"Something should be in the cloud, something should be abroad, something should be a mix, and something should be all three simultaneously. But the fact that we need to proceed from the worst-case scenario, think that way, and prepare ourselves accordingly is a fact," Serhii Koretskyi noted.
Addendum
Expert Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov stated that distributed networks would protect Ukraine from a complete loss of internet access. Local disruptions and higher service costs are possible.

Pope Leo to address Europe’s role in world on final day of France visit – Europe live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:52:57 UTC
16:52:57 KST

'This is an attack on science,' director of Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences says after Russian drone strike
Pjotr Sauer
in Kyiv
Anatoly Zagorodny, director of Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside the building.
Standing outside the burning academy, he said he feared some of his colleagues might still be inside. Officials have confirmed that one person was killed.
Zagorodny said he did not know why Russia had targeted the academy, a leading Ukrainian centre for research.
“We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said.
Pope Leo says negotiators must be willing to sacrifices 'some positions' to achieve war
Angelique Chrisafis
in Paris
Pope Leo has said negotiators seeking to end war in Europe must be willing to sacrifice “some positions” to achieve peace, as efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine continue to fail.
“Today sadly war has returned, even to Europe: a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day,” the pontiff told an audience in Metz at the end of a four-day visit to France.
Without directly mentioning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, he said:
“We need to commit ourselves to patient dialogue, to show courage in negotiation and to be willing to give up some positions for the greater good of peace.”
He invoked a similar 1917 appeal from Pope Benedict XV amid the carnage of the first world war.
Leo, the first US-born pope, also reiterated his opposition to rising European military spending, which grew last year by the highest amount since the end of the cold war, while under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump, and the threat from Russia.
“We must also guard against the illusion that rearmament is the answer,” he said.
“Today we must ask whether we are truly making creative efforts to advance world peace, or whether we are simply seeking to ‘stem the tide of war’ and better prepare ourselves for wars that we assume are still to come.”
Leo also praised integration and multiculturalism at a time when anti-immigration parties are gaining strength across the region.
Speaking in French, he urged Europeans to recall the founding values of the EU, including the rule of law and the equality of all people without distinction of race, colour, class or profession.
Leo urged European leaders to integrate people arriving on the continent who are fleeing “war, persecution and misery” and to offer them opportunities as if they were family members.
The pope, who has frequently urged world leaders to treat migrants more humanely, repeated his call for “legal and safe pathways” for immigration, and international cooperation to fight human trafficking.
“To welcome a person means to integrate them as if they were part of one’s own family, offering them the opportunity to develop their gifts, abilities and sensibilities,” he said.
“Today, relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilised. The value of keeping one’s word is dismissed; instead, people boast of lies and deceit. Europe can help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learned to cultivate and preserve.”
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy offered a further response to today’s strikes on Kyiv.
On his social media channels, he said:
“Every Russian act of terror results in casualties that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total.
Pressure on everything that finances and produces Russia’s weapons of terror, and on everyone who uses them.
The world must understand that terrorists will keep going if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine. And such brutal strikes must not be ignored.
There must be a response – with global resolve and strength. We are counting on the strength of Europe, America, and our other partners who can help protect lives.”
Global security 'unsettled' and 'likely to become more so' in coming years, top Nato commander in Europe warns
Jakub Krupa
Nato’s supreme allied commander Alexus G. Grynkewich warned the global security environment is “unsettled,” “complex” and “likely to become even more so over the next several years.”
“We were reminded of this again this past weekend in the United Kingdom, where five men were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act in preparation of a terrorist act near RAF Fairford,” he said.
He said the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East showed “not only a changing character of warfare, but also a sobering preview of how future simultaneous and potentially protracted conflicts might look: multi-theater conflicts, multi-domain conflicts, and highly autonomous conflicts.”
He repeated his recent warning that as a result “we are all eastern flank nations now.” “Those drones can go 1000s of miles, 1000s of kilometres, and so if one gets through, it’s not just a threat on the eastern flank; it’s a threat to the entire alliance, including all the way in North America,” he said.
Grynkewich also acknowledged “growing instability across Nato’s periphery” and “an increase … in hybrid activity targeting our critical infrastructure, our societies, and our resolve,” as “state-directed sabotage is growing increasingly brazen.”
“It isn’t working, as evidenced by the Danish response when they fast-tracked a major military aid package worth 1.8bn kroner to Ukraine following the flare incident,” he said.
“The goal of the Russian activity right now is primarily to break our will to continue supporting Ukraine, and … the logic of this is if we make the security situation seem dire enough, populations will want nations to withhold from Ukraine for their own protection. ...
The Danish response is one that I would commend to everyone. If there is a hybrid attack on your country, reinforcing the will to support Ukraine will show the Russians that their strategy isn’t working, and maybe have them back off that strategy.”
He also said as a result of Nato’s Eastern Sentry mission, Russia appears to be “much more careful to avoid coming across the border with drones in the Baltics or into Poland.”
But Grynkewich said Nato was “detecting, attributing and responding as these hybrid threads arise,” acknowledging they get “more blatant” and grow both in numbers and severity.
He told lawmakers that “it is really important that we share intelligence and information about these threats so we all have the same, common operating picture.”
The Nato commander said that countries should not shy away from naming who they think is responsible for these incidents:
“Once we have confidence in the attribution, we do need to make that public … bringing that attribution out publicly will let state sponsors know that we understand what they’re doing, and that increases costs on them. They will realise that their networks are ineffective and that they have to modify their behaviour, and that in of itself has some deterrent effect.”
He also spoke about the broader need to keep reforming and investing in European defence to meet the growing challenges.
“Industry must not only produce the capabilities we need to seize the initiative, but it must be ready to sustain the fight in the event it goes on longer than we would like. Meanwhile, our societies must build the resilience needed to withstand manipulation designed to weaken our resolve from within,” he added.
In comments likely intended to dismiss Russia’s criticism of the alliance, the commander stressed that Nato remains “a defensive alliance,” and has “no ambitions, no plans and no intentions beyond the defence of our territory.”
“But our defensive nature should not be mistaken for a lack of will or a lack of resolve. While we do not seek conflict, we will meet any attack against our alliance with overwhelming combat power, ensuring any attack will fail,” he stressed.
France’s far-right National Rally surges in partial Senate elections
in Paris
In other European news, the French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has said her 2027 presidential campaign will be boosted after her anti-immigration party, the National Rally (RN), and its allies secured a record 14 seats in partial senate elections this weekend.
Le Pen called the results a “historic victory” and “major milestone” after her party cleared the 10-seat threshold to be able to form a senate group for the first time, following an indirect vote by local officials including mayors and councillors.
The party’s progress in the senate will allow them higher visibility and more funding in the second house of parliament ahead next spring’s presidential election. Le Pen is currently polling high as Emmanuel Macron prepares to step down after ten years in office.
The RN MP Sébastien Chenu called the gains “a boost for the presidential campaign” and said there was “no more glass ceiling” for the party. Edwige Diaz, who secured a large senate win for the RN in Gironde outside Bordeaux, told Le Parisien: “This will be very useful for us before the presidential election.”
The 348-seat senate is France’s second chamber of parliament alongside the national assembly. Final results on Monday morning showed the senate remained dominated by the traditional right and centre-right.
The upper chamber’s president of more than a decade, Gerard Larcher, 77, from the rightwing party Les Républicains is expected to be re-elected next week.
Although the RN is currently the biggest single opposition party in the national assembly, and has the largest number of French members of the European parliament, it has until now never had a grouping in the senate, where its presence has been small.
AP is carrying an updated casualty toll, stating that Russia’s round-the-clock bombardment of targets in Ukraine killed at least seven people and wounded more than 53 others from Sunday to Monday.
'This is an attack on science,' director of Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences says after Russian drone strike
Pjotr Sauer
in Kyiv
Anatoly Zagorodny, director of Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside the building.
Standing outside the burning academy, he said he feared some of his colleagues might still be inside. Officials have confirmed that one person was killed.
Zagorodny said he did not know why Russia had targeted the academy, a leading Ukrainian centre for research.
“We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said.
'Several' workers feared missing after drone strikes Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv

in Kyiv
Meanwhile, the Guardian’s Pjotr Sauer is in Kyiv near the building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, which was hit by a Russian drone today.
He reports:
“Director of the academy Anatoly Zagorodny told me they still haven’t been able to reach several workers that remain missing.
Rescue operations were temporarily paused as firefighters had to evacuate after another drone in the area.
Poland to change rules to allow fighter pilots to shoot down foreign aircraft detected by radar
Neighbouring Poland will allow its fighter planes and helicopters to shoot down foreign aircraft detected by radar under special wartime defence measures, its deputy defence minister said, AFP reported.
Such a change will allow “the pilot or the operational commander to make a decision to shoot down a foreign aircraft on the basis of radar readings or other information that enters the system”, minister Cezary Tomczyk said.
This will replace “the standard in peacetime”, where opening fire requires visual identification, rather than on the basis of radar readings or other relevant information, AFP said.
It is the latest step to raise the Nato and EU member state’s defences as the war in neighbouring Ukraine drags on into its fifth winter and allies warn of a rising threat of Russian drones.
One night last September some 20 Russian drones violated Poland’s airspace in one of the most dangerous incidents of this type in recent years.
'Russia will face a response to this,' Zelenskyy says, after strike on Kyiv kills at least one person
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has just responded to the strike on Kyiv.
In a post on X, he said:
“A Russian strike against the building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. A rescue operation is underway: crews are putting out the fire and searching for people who may have been trapped inside. All services are deployed.
Today in Kyiv, a pharmaceutical company and gas stations were also attacked; in Dnipro, a business center; and in other cities and regions, civilian facilities, businesses, and communications infrastructure were targeted as well. Sadly, people have been killed… My condolences to their families and loved ones.
Russia will definitely face a response to this.
And every one of Ukraine’s partners must see from this terror, from these strikes, that supporting Ukraine means truly supporting people’s lives – supporting the principle that terror must never be normalised, anywhere. Russia must be held accountable for all of this and face real consequences. I thank everyone who helps Ukraine!”
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said one person was killed and at least three were injured in the strike.
'Loud explosion' in central Kyiv after Russian drone alert
Just as Kallas was speaking, Reuters snapped on “a loud explosion” in the central part of Ukraine’s capital Kyiv, which the city administration said was caused by a Russian drone.
AFP identified the building hit as the National Academy of Sciences, stressing it was “the latest in a series of escalating attacks on the Ukrainian capital.”
“The site is in the very centre of Kyiv – usually well protected from Russian attacks – close to the German embassy, a famed cathedral, the national opera and government buildings.”
EU needs to 'rearm more quickly' to meet its targets as Russia 'not interested in peace at all,' Kallas says - summary
EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned that“Europe needs to rearm more quickly and more effectively to meet our target of 2030,” with a “decisive change” in its approach to defence (12:55).
Briefing reporters after talks with EU defence ministers, Kallas also said they started having discussions on a new “emergency security protocol” which could help coordinate response to any incident falling below the Article 5 of Nato, amid growing concerns about acts of sabotage or aggression from Russia (12:58, 13:02, 13:16).
Kallas also said that Russia’s behaviour following talks with German foreign minister last week shows that “Russia is really not interested in peace at all.” (13:07).
Kallas also gets asked about what the new proposed “emergency protocol” would actually mean or do that isn’t already covered by the EU’s Article 42.7 or Nato’s provisions in Articles 4 and 5.
She says that she is in touch with Nato’s Mark Rutte to make sure there is “no duplication.”
She explains that Nato’s Article 4 (where countries can request a discussion “whenever, in the opinion of any of them, the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened”) is “just consultations” with no specific actions, while Article 5 (“an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all”) is “very clear” on its military implications.
The new protocol would focus instead on “what tools can be used at the moment of aggression that is not armed aggression, and is under the threshold of Article 5,” she says.
Kallas also gets asked about the dire situation in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
She says:
“It clearly shows what happens to the people in the occupied territories.”
She says the EU is “trying to get the humanitarian aid in,” and working to “help Ukraine to defend itself and its people,” including through work on “the largest listing of sanctions” to date.
'These talks show that Russia is really not interested in peace at all,' Kallas says
EU’s Kallas also responds to German foreign minister Johann Wadephul’s talks with Russia’s chief diplomat, Sergei Lavrov on the margins of the UN week.
She says there was many countries outside Europe that seem to believe that simply talking to Russia would resolve all problems.
“These talks show that Russia is really not interested in peace, at all. Otherwise you don’t treat your negotiation partner … this way,” she says in response to Lavrov’s comments ridiculing Germany after the meeting.
She continues:
“Russia needs to show, by stopping the attacks on civilians, that they are interested in peace, which they are not.
And then they need to talk to Ukraine because it’s between, Ukraine and Russia. Everybody else can facilitate this process, but in the end, they need to agree.”
Asked about the details of the new protocol, Kallas says it was “the first discussion on it, very initial,” with further talks needed.
“So, clearly, there were some who were saying that, that we need some kind of mechanism for anything under the armed aggression threshold, which is Article 42.7 [of EU treaties], but many stressed that it has to be absolutely complimentary with Nato, so we do not create anything additional; this has to work hand in hand.”

Latin America, the new 'laboratory' of Israeli military-technological complex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:52:50 UTC
16:52:50 KST

The announced shift by Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella's government toward Israel is not limited to a diplomatic readjustment.
The promise to build a bilateral relationship "like never before," the reopening of the Colombian embassy in occupied East Jerusalem, the "recognition of Israeli sovereignty” over the occupied Golan Heights, and the reactivation of economic and trade ties all point to a broader transformation of Colombian foreign policy.
Specifically, it is expected that some 30 Israeli companies will visit Colombia in the coming months to explore investment opportunities, as confirmed after a meeting between the Minister of Commerce, Mauricio Gomez, and Betsy Berns Korn, president of the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations.
Behind this shift lies a broader issue: the possible reactivation and expansion of a security architecture that includes military technology, surveillance, intelligence, cooperation with Washington, and increasing private-sector participation in strategic state functions.
The official website of De la Espriella's political party, Defenders for the Homeland, states that "greater collaboration with Israeli defence industries opens up opportunities for technology transfer, creation of specialised jobs and strengthening of sectors such as cybersecurity and military intelligence."
This technological boost, presented as part of a strategy to combat what the party calls organised crime, could become a cornerstone of the new relationship with Israel.
For some experts in Tel Aviv, security cooperation could also expand significantly. “Everything related to national security will involve extensive collaboration with Israel,” says political scientist Alberto Spektorowski. “Colombia will request it, Israel will provide it, and that relationship will be strengthened,” he added.
Ultimately, according to an analysis published in The Times of Israel, “this is not merely diplomatic protocol: it is a calculated message directed at the entire region, at a time when Israel is seeking to rebuild alliances in Latin America after years of deterioration.”
The security dimension could therefore become a key point of convergence in this new phase, linking foreign policy with military technology, intelligence, and surveillance capabilities.
Israel's technological tentacles in Latin America
This process, however, did not begin with the current government. Its origins lie in decades of military and intelligence cooperation between Colombia and Israel.
During the administration of former President Virgilio Barco (1986-1990), journalistic investigations revealed the presence and advisory role of Israeli agent Rafi Eitan, who was allegedly consulted on matters of presidential security and protection.
Subsequent investigations also raised questions about a possible link between his presence in Colombia and the escalation of violence against members of the leftist Patriotic Union (UP) party.
The accusation generated controversy, and some of its aspects were later denied or questioned. The journalistic investigation itself indicates that there is no evidence of a connection between Eitan and the murders of UP members, although it highlights that his presence in Colombia coincided with the sharp increase in these homicides beginning in 1987.
Years later, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights recognised the responsibility of the Colombian State for the extermination and political violence against members of that party.
During the administration of former President Alvaro Uribe (2002-2010), the military relationship between Colombia and Israel deepened, focusing on security policy and strengthening the capabilities of the Colombian Armed Forces.
The Galil, an Israeli-made assault rifle, became one of its symbols, accompanied by technology transfer and cooperation in aircraft, intelligence, surveillance, and other military systems.
Subsequently, INDUMIL, a company attached to the Colombian Ministry of Defense, developed national versions of the Galil through technology transfer agreements with Israel, showing how an initial dependency could also become local industrial capacity.
The political and diplomatic break with Israel during the government of former President Gustavo Petro (2022-2026) marked a turning point in this trajectory.
In October 2023, Israel suspended military cooperation and exports to Colombia. Then, in February 2024, Petro announced the suspension of new arms purchases from Israel, and on May 1, he announced the severing of diplomatic relations.
In parallel, Colombia advanced a strategy of industrial autonomy for defence. The Jaguar rifle project— described as a symbol of "technological, industrial, and strategic sovereignty"—was initiated by INDUMIL in 2020.
Its name honours the animal that represents "strength, intelligence, adaptability, precision, territorial dominance, and a connection with the jungle and American nature," and which for centuries has been "an ancestral symbol of the indigenous peoples of the Americas."
The rifle was officially unveiled in May 2026 as a domestically developed weapon intended to strengthen the country's sovereignty. The Jaguar incorporates significant improvements over the Galil system currently used by Colombian forces.
Elbit Systems and its footprint in the region
The business dimension makes the potential scope of this relationship clearer.
In December 2021, the Colombian Army contracted with Elbit Systems—one of the leading Israeli companies in the defence and technology sector—for a border surveillance and reconnaissance system and a command-and-control centre for the border with Venezuela for approximately $30 million.
The contract was executed under a bilateral Colombia-Israel agreement. It was not simply a matter of acquiring equipment: it involved incorporating technological capabilities developed by an Israeli company into the security management of a strategic territory.
Elbit and other Israeli companies have expanded across Latin America.
Academic research has documented the regional use of Hermes 450 and Hermes 900 drones, systems developed by Elbit that integrate intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition, and reconnaissance capabilities.
Brazil, Chile, and Mexico are among the Latin American countries that have operated platforms of this type.
The company itself acknowledges contracts to modernise Hermes 900 systems used by Latin American clients.
The issue takes on a particularly sensitive dimension when military technology intersects with digital surveillance.
In 2024, the Colombian Attorney General's Office opened an investigation into the alleged purchase and use of Pegasus software, developed by the Israeli company NSO Group, whose distribution is controlled by the Israeli Ministry of Defense.
The complaint alleged a transaction for approximately $11 million and a supposed cash payment. The investigation was to determine, among other things, whether the acquisition actually took place and how the software was used.
Ecuador offers another significant case. In December 2024, the National Assembly approved an investigation into the alleged use of the Pegasus software against journalists, opposition members, and activists.
The resolution ordered the appearance of the director of the Strategic Intelligence Center and requested information from the Israeli Embassy regarding the program's alleged use on Ecuadorian territory.
Again, the relevance lies in the institutional question: who acquires these technologies, under what controls, against whom can they be used, and what mechanisms exist to guarantee fundamental rights?
This process coincides with a broader transformation of regional security: the increasing participation of private companies in functions traditionally reserved for the state.
In this respect, Haiti's case is illustrative.
Vectus Global, a private security company linked to Erik Prince, founder of the controversial Blackwater company, has been operating in Haiti since 2025, using drones to target armed groups.
Prince also said he had reached a long-term agreement with the Haitian government that would include, once the situation stabilises, participation in restoring the tax collection system.
In 2026, Reuters reported that US officials were considering closer cooperation with the company, while human rights organisations expressed concern about civilian deaths associated with drone strikes.
The privatisation of security functions
Meanwhile, the privatisation of security functions raises questions about sovereignty, accountability, and legal responsibility.
The debate is not unique to Latin America: the United Nations Human Rights Council has established a working group to develop an international framework to regulate, monitor, and control the activities of private military and security companies.
The central problem is that outsourcing coercive functions can complicate identifying responsibility when abuses occur.
In this context, the political role that Israel has acquired for the “new right” must also be analysed. Journalist Pablo Stefanoni has studied how the defence of Israel has become, for sectors of the extreme right, a means of legitimising themselves after 1945, when antisemitism had been a historical hallmark of much of the radical European right.
In his analysis, Stefanoni points out that “anti-antisemitism” can operate simultaneously as a legitimising mechanism and as an instrument of confrontation against groups such as Muslims, Palestinians, and progressive sectors.
This interpretation helps explain why the relationship with Israel today extends beyond the strictly military or commercial sphere.
Against this backdrop, Colombia presents a particularly relevant case. The new government of De la Espriella has proposed reviving military cooperation with Israel and strengthening the strategic alliance with Washington.
Analysts cited by TRT World have linked this project to a potential deepening of Israeli technological cooperation in security, intelligence, and the fight against drug trafficking, in a framework some are calling “Plan Colombia 2.0.”
Security for whom and sovereignty for what?
The fundamental issue is not simply what weapons, platforms, or software each state purchases, but what kind of security infrastructure is built when intelligence, surveillance, drones, cybersecurity, and military capabilities begin to integrate with private companies and international alliances.
In this context, greater technological dependence can also translate into greater strategic dependence, particularly when critical capabilities become tied to external providers.
The Latin American experience compels us to ask questions that go beyond simply purchasing equipment.
Who defines the threats? Who manages the data? Which companies are involved? What controls are in place? And, above all, what economic and geopolitical interests lie behind these new security architectures?
The question becomes especially relevant when technology, security, and infrastructure become linked to strategic territories and assets.
In Colombia, the approach to the Israeli state-owned company Mekorot and its potential involvement in water management issues related to the Sumapaz Paramo area reopen the debate over who decides on water and strategic ecosystems.
Thus, it is worth asking: could dependence on defence and surveillance open new doors to corporate intervention in territories, water, minerals, biodiversity, and critical infrastructure?
What businesses operate behind these alliances, and who captures the value of our strategic assets?
The dispute is not only technological or military: it is also a dispute over sovereignty and the future of territories.
In a Latin America rich in water, minerals, biodiversity, and energy, turning security into a gateway to new dependencies can limit the decision-making power of states and communities over their common resources.
The sovereignty of peoples over their territories cannot be the hidden cost of any alliance.
(This article was first published on TRT Español)

UK Arrests Multiple Men Over Explosives Near Base Used by US Nuclear-Capable Bombers
British police arrested several men over suspected explosives offenses near RAF Fairford, a UK military air base used by US forces and capable of supporting deployments of American nuclear-capable strategic bombers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on September 27, Gloucestershire Police declared a major incident in the Welford area near the base, while a specialist military explosive ordnance disposal team was deployed to inspect several vehicles.
Police said a number of homes in Welford were evacuated following the arrests. Evacuated residents were taken to a local leisure center while emergency services worked at the scene.
Around 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines, were reported in the area, Reuters said. Armed officers also restricted access to RAF Fairford’s main gates as security around the facility was increased.
The men were detained on suspicion of offenses under Britain’s explosives legislation. Police said the situation was considered contained, while military bomb disposal specialists continued examining vehicles near the base.
The US Air Force declined to disclose specific measures being taken to protect personnel and facilities, citing operational security.
“The 501st Combat Support Wing and other UK-based units remain vigilant and will take appropriate measures to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors and their families,” a US Air Force spokesperson said, according to Reuters.
RAF Fairford is operated by the Royal Air Force and serves as a key European location for US bomber deployments. The base has previously hosted US strategic aircraft, including nuclear-capable B-52H Stratofortress and B-2 Spirit bombers.
Reuters reported that Britain had also authorized the United States to use RAF Fairford for strikes against Iranian missile sites linked to attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
Police had not disclosed the identities of those arrested or provided further details about the suspected explosives offenses as of September 27.
Earlier, German investigators found suspected explosives meters from a crashed drone near Wunstorf Air Base, which hosts the Bundeswehr’s A400M transport fleet, and began examining a possible link to the suspected Russian sabotage plot at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Madrid housing protests enter third day after pensioner's eviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28

Protesters demand Spanish government limit evictions after pensioner forced out
MADRID, Sept 28 - Protesters camped outside the Madrid regional government's headquarters for a third day on Monday to object to the eviction of an octogenarian and demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.
Protests boiled over last week after police evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal on a stretcher from her Madrid home of more than seven decades because of an eviction order secured by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Hundreds of people outside her building clashed with police, while the Socialist-led central government condemned the centre-right regional administration for not preventing the eviction.
By Monday, hundreds of tents filled the central Puerta del Sol square, echoing the protests of 2011 when it was occupied for a month by activists demonstrating against austerity measures adopted during the global financial crisis.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Sunday the government was working to enact a housing decree in parliament by Tuesday that would bring immediate relief for tenants.
Unlike in the financial crisis, when many evictions were linked to mortgage defaults after a property bubble burst, a growing share are now related to rent disputes, reflecting a shortage of properties. Rents have on average doubled over the past decade, far outpacing salaries.
TENS OF THOUSANDS MARCH THROUGH MADRID
On Saturday, some 30,000 people marched through Madrid to object to the treatment of Abascal and others forced from their homes by investment funds.
Marchers shook keys and bore banners with slogans including "Speculators go home" and "Housing is for living".
As night fell on Puerta del Sol, home to the office of Isabel Diaz Ayuso, centre-right president of the Madrid region, dozens of activists put up tents, and their number has steadily grown since.
Blanca, a student, said young Spaniards were struggling to move out of their parents' homes.
"Politicians not only do nothing but make it worse," she said. "We've decided to put our foot down, so let’s hope they hear us."
Further protests were set to take place across Spain on Monday, according to the Tenants' Union, which has been co-ordinating the protests.
From her hospital bed in Madrid, Abascal said she could not join the demonstration and urged protesters to keep fighting.
"Be brave, fight, defend what is yours and, please, take care of yourselves; keep camping there for as long as your bodies can hold out and as long as you wish to. Let’s hope all this comes to a successful conclusion tomorrow," she said in a video distributed by the Tenants' Union.
Spain has a deficit of 750,000 homes, according to the central bank, which has said that figure could rise to over 1 million by 2028. Only about 120,000 are built each year, a sixth of the rate before the 2008 financial crisis.
Ayuso said the protests were an attempt to "change the rules of the game" on existing contracts and asked whether the activists thought there should be age limit for paying rent. REUTERS

Ukraine's women's tennis team won silver medals at the Billie Jean King Cup. UNN reports, citing the National Olympic Committee of Ukraine.
Details
Ukraine's women's tennis team played in the final stage of the Billie Jean King Cup for the first time in its history — the largest international team competition in women's tennis.

In the next match, Elina Svitolina played against Linda Noskova, the world's sixth-ranked player. In a tense contest, the Czech tennis player celebrated victory — 0:2 (3:6, 6:7).
Thus, the final score of the tie was 0:2 in favor of the Czech Republic: the Ukrainian team finished the tournament with the best result in the history of its appearances, winning the "silver" at the Billie Jean King Cup
What’s next

How successful is Europe at closing the gender gap between men and women?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:47:59 UTC
16:47:59 KST

Europe continues to be a global leader when it comes to what is possible for men and women, but huge gaps exist between European countries, and full equality remains a very distant reality.
It is widely known that a gap remains between men and women in the world, not only when it comes to equal pay, but also to access to the labour market, education and health. This difference in opportunities is referred to as the gender gap.
Europe has regained its position as the global leader in closing this divide, according to new data from the World Economic Forum (WEF), which has measured this gap since 2006.
The continent closed 75.7% of its overall gender gap this year. This leaves a 24.3% gap to achieve equal representation. It narrowly overtook North America, which ranked first last year.
Since 2006, Europe's gender parity has improved by 7 percentage points. It is not expected to reach full parity — meaning there is no difference in the opportunities for men and women, or a zero percent gender gap — in 70 years.
The report looked at education, health, economic participation and politics. Europe is the champion in the latter category with a score of 37%. It is closely followed by Latin America and the Caribbean (34.2%). Other regions trail behind by ten percentage points or more.
Europe continues to maintain near parity in the categories of Educational Attainment (99.5%) and Health and Survival (96.9%). Still, it is in third and fourth place in these indexes compared to other regions.
When it comes to Economic Participation and Opportunity, it ranks in fifth position (69.5%), almost eight percentage points below the table's leader, North America (77.1%).
Uneven growth
Of all regions in the world, Europe accounts for the most countries in the top ten. "Since the index was launched in 2006, Europe has occupied 69% of all top 10," the WEF report noted. "Continuing the trend established in prior editions, this year’s top performers include seven European economies."
These countries are Iceland, Finland, Norway and Sweden (which have featured in every top ten for the past two decades), as well as the United Kingdom, Germany and Ireland.
Only Iceland has closed more than 90% of the gender gap (93%).
"Iceland has demonstrated a consistently positive trajectory towards gender parity over the past two decades, remaining in the global top 10 throughout the period and holding the top position since the 2009 edition," the WEF report read.
It scores particularly well when it comes to Political Empowerment (95.4%). This is driven by the country's intentional public policies promoting gender balance and its history of female representation in top positions of power: Iceland was the first country in the world to democratically elect a woman, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, as president in 1980.
Despite Europe's top position, a deep divide remains within the continent. The countries topping the region’s ranking are mainly located in Northern Europe, while many of the states trailing behind are located in the East.
The bottom three performers, Türkiye (0.649%), Romania (0.698%) and Hungary (0.707%), stand more than 20 percentage points below Iceland.
In Romania, this low score is largely due to its low score in the Political Empowerment category (0.145%), placing it in 104th place for this category. This is driven by a lack of mandatory quotas and closed internal party systems.
This category is also the driving factor for Hungary's low score (0.132% in Political Empowerment). It has no women in ministerial positions, giving it a score of 0% in this particular category of this subindex.
The European Union wants to close the broader gender gap through a range of policies and measures, ranging from EU Pay Transparency Rules requiring companies to share information on salaries in a bid to bring down the pay gap, to rules on parental leave and flexible working hours to help divide care and work duties.

At least two people were killed in a Russian attack on Ukraine’s Kyiv region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, as both countries accused each other of overnight strikes.
 
One of those killed was an Azerbaijani citizen, Zelenskyy said in a statement on Telegram.
 
Separately, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said 35 people were injured in a strike, and search and rescue operations had been completed and no one was found under the rubble.
 
Meanwhile, four people, including three children, were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Voronezh region, regional Gov. Alexander Gusev said.

In Russia’s Bryansk region, part of a railway bridge collapsed after a drone strike, causing 10 railcars to derail, regional Gov. Alexander Kovalchuk said. He said Ukrainian drones had targeted railway infrastructure in several parts of the region.
 
Eighteen empty freight cars also derailed in the Unechsky district, while railway tracks were damaged in the Navlinsky district, according to Kovalchuk. No one was injured in the attacks, he said, adding that train traffic was not disrupted in Navlinsky.
 
In a separate statement, the Russian Defense Ministry said its forces struck Ukrainian logistics and communications facilities, port infrastructure and vessels it said were used to support the Ukrainian armed forces.
 
The ministry said the targets included data centers and fuel infrastructure in Kyiv, facilities at the Vasylkiv military airfield in the Kyiv region, a logistics center in Odesa, infrastructure at the Izmail port and a shipbuilding and repair facility.
 
It added that two dry cargo vessels carrying military or dual-use supplies had been hit.
 
The ministry separately said its Northern Group of Forces had taken control of Ulanovo in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, while the Central Group of Forces had taken control of Novovodyane in the Donetsk region.
 
Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces struck a Pantsir-S2 surface-to-air missile and gun system near the settlement of Seltso in Bryansk.
 
Neither side's claims could be independently verified.

WSJ: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Says Washington Influenced Government Changes in Europe

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle made the remarks during a private meeting in Athens while discussing the resignation of Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan.
The Wall Street Journal reported the comments in its investigation into the U.S. diplomat’s activities and her efforts to advance American energy projects in Southeastern Europe.
According to the newspaper, Guilfoyle attended a dinner in Athens in March 2026 with Greek and U.S. officials. During the discussion, she clashed with Greek Environment and Energy Minister Stavros Papastavrou.
Speaking about the expected resignation of the Romanian prime minister, Guilfoyle reportedly said, according to one of the meeting’s participants:
“We can do this to any country we want. We can do it here, too.”
According to The Wall Street Journal, Papastavrou responded that the United States could not change the Greek government, which the country’s citizens elected.
Guilfoyle’s attorney, however, disputed the newspaper’s account of the conversation. No independent evidence currently confirms that the United States was involved in the change of Romania’s government.
The government of Ilie Bolojan was dismissed on May 5, 2026, after the Romanian Parliament approved a vote of no confidence. A total of 281 lawmakers voted in favor, exceeding the 233 votes required.
Romanian outlet G4Media links the Wall Street Journal report to disputes surrounding U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG) and the so-called Vertical Gas Corridor.
The route is intended to transport natural gas from Greece through Bulgaria and Romania to countries in Central and Eastern Europe, as well as Moldova and Ukraine.
According to G4Media, former Romanian Energy Minister Bogdan Ivan approached President Nicușor Dan and Prime Minister Bolojan in January with a proposal to begin negotiations on an intergovernmental agreement with the United States to purchase American natural gas.
The media claims the presidential administration and Bolojan’s government responded cautiously to the proposal because of concerns about the gas’s cost and economic viability.
The U.S. administration pushed countries on Europe’s eastern flank to increase purchases of American natural gas. Guilfoyle was actively involved in these negotiations and promoted Greece’s Aktor Group, which, together with its partners, is working to supply gas to the region.
Representatives of Romanian political parties denied that Guilfoyle was involved in actions that led to the Bolojan government’s fall.
Romania, meanwhile, remains one of the United States’ key allies on NATO’s eastern flank. In May, Bucharest said it was ready to host up to 5,000 U.S. troops reportedly planned to be redeployed from Germany.

Vietnamese embassy in Iran holds Vietnam–Iran business networking event in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:46:51 UTC
16:46:51 KST

Vietnamese embassy in Iran holds Vietnam–Iran business networking event in Tehran
From coffee to connectivity: Vietnam and Iran build practical business bridges
TEHRAN — The Vietnamese Embassy in Iran on the evening of September 27 hosted a Vietnam–Iran Business Networking Event at its embassy in Tehran, bringing together more than 50 businessmen active in different fields.
In the opening remarks of the event, it was said: Vietnam should be seen not only as a market but as a strategic platform. It can serve as a bridge between Iranian businesses and ASEAN, while Iran can offer Vietnamese firms access to its market and the wider region. Vietnam is now embedded in global manufacturing and supply chains, with geographic advantages, ASEAN links, and extensive maritime access. Its trade combines manufacturing strength with competitive agriculture and food processing. This creates complementarity: Vietnamese goods for Iran, and Iranian raw materials, petrochemicals, agricultural products, and other goods for Vietnam. Existing bilateral trade is limited relative to potential, so the goal is not merely to increase volume but to build new channels, direct company contacts, and practical solutions for logistics, standards, payment, and market access. Agriculture offers immediate opportunities—coffee, cashew, pistachios, dried fruits, petrochemicals, fertilizers, minerals, and handicrafts.
In these remarks, a focused, results-oriented business mission to Vietnam with pre-arranged B2B meetings, meetings with VCCI and Iran’s embassy, cooperation with Vietnam Persian Market, and visits to Cai Lan port/Ha Long and Ho Chi Minh City was proposed, stressing that regional connectivity, matters as much as individual markets.
‘Concrete results’ are foundation for sustainable Vietnam–Iran trade: Ambassador Nguyen Luong Ngoc
Then came the speech by H.E. Nguyen Luong Ngoc, Ambassador of Vietnam to Iran, its full text appears below:
Distinguished Guests,
Representatives of Iranian business associations and the business community,
First of all, on behalf of the Embassy of Viet Nam in Iran, I would like to warmly welcome and thank all of you for taking the time to attend today’s business networking event.
I am particularly pleased to see that many of you here today already have business relations with Viet Nam, have imported and distributed Vietnamese products, or are actively exploring new opportunities for cooperation with Vietnamese companies.
Therefore, today I do not wish merely to introduce Viet Nam’s potential. I would like us to look together at what Viet Nam has achieved, at the trade activities that are actually taking place between our two countries, and, at the same time, to have a frank exchange on the current difficulties and on what both sides can do together to maintain and further develop our business relations.
Dear friends,
First, allow me to share a few highlights regarding Viet Nam’s economic development. Despite considerable volatility in the global economy in recent years, Viet Nam has maintained macroeconomic stability and achieved relatively high economic growth.
In 2025, Viet Nam’s GDP grew by 8.02%. The size of the economy reached approximately USD 514 billion, an increase of around USD 38 billion compared with 2024. GDP per capita exceeded USD 5,000. Notably, growth was recorded across all three major sectors of the economy. Industry and construction grew by nearly 9%, with manufacturing and processing continuing to serve as one of the important drivers of growth. The services sector expanded by more than 8.6%.
International trade continues to be one of the major strengths of the Vietnamese economy. Total merchandise import-export turnover in 2025 reached approximately USD 930 billion, an increase of more than 18% over the previous year. Viet Nam continued to record a trade surplus, marking ten consecutive years of trade surpluses. This achievement is partly attributable to Viet Nam’s network of 17 Free Trade Agreements, which provide preferential tariff access to 60 economies, including most of the world’s major economies.
Also within last year, total registered foreign investment in Viet Nam reached approximately USD 38.4 billion; and there were 21.2 million international visitors coming to our country. In particular, disbursed FDI reached approximately USD 27.6 billion, up 9% from the previous year and the highest level recorded in the past five years.
These figures demonstrate that Viet Nam is not only a market of more than 100 million people, but is also continuing to strengthen its position as a manufacturing and export hub and an important link in regional supply chains. Viet Nam aims to become a high-income developed country by 2045. To achieve this goal, Viet Nam is targeting annual economic growth of 10% or higher.
Alongside manufacturing and processing, agriculture and the food industry remain among Viet Nam’s key strengths. Viet Nam is currently one of the world’s major producers and exporters of a wide range of products, including coffee, pepper, cashew nuts, rice, tea, seafood, fruits and vegetables, and processed food products. These are also areas in which I believe Viet Nam and Iran still have considerable room to expand cooperation.
Distinguished Guests,
Viet Nam and Iran enjoy a long-standing traditional friendship. The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1973 and, for more than half a century, have maintained good relations across many fields. In the economic and trade sectors, exchanges of goods between the two countries have continued despite the difficulties arising from the regional and international situation.
According to customs statistics, in 2025, total direct merchandise trade between Viet Nam and Iran reached approximately $170 million, of which Viet Nam’s exports to Iran amounted to around USD 150 million, while imports from Iran stood at approximately $20 million. However, when assessing these figures, we should also take into account an important characteristic of bilateral trade.
Customs statistics on direct trade between Viet Nam and Iran do not fully reflect the actual scale of transactions and flows of goods between the two economies. This is also one of the reasons why we believe that the actual potential for bilateral trade is considerably greater than what is reflected in official statistics.
Vietnamese products that have been and are currently traded in the Iranian market include coffee, pepper, cashew nuts, tea, seafood, certain food products and consumer goods. In the other direction, Viet Nam also has demand for products in which Iran has strengths, including chemicals, petroleum products, plastics and raw materials, metals, pharmaceuticals, as well as certain distinctive Iranian agricultural products.
Among Vietnamese products, I would particularly like to highlight coffee. Viet Nam is the world’s second-largest coffee producer and exporter and has a particularly strong position in Robusta coffee. In addition to green coffee beans, Vietnamese companies are increasingly developing higher value-added products such as roasted and ground coffee, instant coffee, packaged coffee and private-label products for their customers.
Iran has a well-developed beverage culture, and demand for coffee is continuing to grow. I therefore believe that this is a highly promising area in which businesses from our two countries can build long-term partnerships rather than limiting cooperation to individual transactions.
In addition to coffee, Vietnamese pepper, cashew nuts and tea – products in which Viet Nam ranks among the world’s leading exporters – are already present in the Iranian market and still have considerable potential for further growth.
Importantly, we should not limit ourselves to simply buying and selling raw materials. The two sides can go further by cooperating in processing, roasting, packaging, branding, distribution and the development of products tailored to the preferences of Iranian consumers.
Another area of great importance to bilateral relations is air connectivity and tourism.
Geographical distance has always been one of the obstacles to exchanges between Viet Nam and Iran. Therefore, efforts to promote direct air connectivity between the two countries are important not only for tourism but also for trade, investment and people-to-people exchanges.
Viet Nam is becoming an increasingly well-known tourism destination in Asia. Meanwhile, Iran possesses an ancient civilization, a rich cultural heritage and many unique destinations that Vietnamese people have not yet had many opportunities to explore.
If we can strengthen and maintain more convenient air connectivity between our two countries, I believe that the number of tourists, businesspeople and trade delegations travelling in both directions will increase significantly. When people are able to meet more frequently, trade and investment will certainly have greater opportunities to develop.
Dear friends,
Alongside these opportunities, we must also frankly acknowledge that trade between Viet Nam and Iran currently faces a number of difficulties.
First is payment. This remains one of the greatest obstacles for businesses in both countries. The lack of direct banking payment channels makes many transactions more complicated, more costly and more exposed to risk.
Second is transportation and logistics. The geographical distance is already considerable, while recent developments in the region have significantly affected shipping routes, vessel schedules, delivery times and logistics costs. These issues directly affect the competitiveness of goods.
Third are procedures and technical requirements applicable to goods, particularly agricultural and food products. Businesses on both sides need clearer information on standards, quarantine and sanitary requirements, product registration, labelling and import procedures in order to avoid additional costs and delays after goods have already arrived at the port.
Fourth are commercial risks and the verification of business partners. When transactions face difficulties related to payment and transportation, choosing the right partners, clearly defining responsibilities in contracts, and maintaining direct communication between buyers and sellers become even more important.
In my view, these are not issues that can be resolved through a single meeting or trade promotion event. However, we can certainly address them step by step if businesses and relevant authorities of both countries work together in a practical and effective manner.
For its part, the Embassy of Viet Nam in Iran would like to focus on several concrete areas.
First, we will continue to directly connect businesses in the two countries that have genuine commercial needs, particularly in coffee, tea, pepper, cashew nuts, food products and other agricultural commodities.
Second, we stand ready to assist Iranian businesses in identifying and verifying suitable suppliers in Viet Nam, while also supporting Vietnamese businesses in identifying and selecting capable partners in Iran.
Third, both sides should promote the exchange of information on import regulations, quarantine requirements, quality standards, logistics and payment methods, enabling businesses to fully assess potential risks before signing contracts. For products that already have established trade flows, such as coffee, pepper, cashew nuts and tea, we would like to gradually move from individual transactions towards stable and long-term supply relationships, while encouraging cooperation in processing, packaging and brand development in the Iranian market.
Fifth, Viet Nam offers a promising destination for direct investment by Iranian businesses to manufacture products that can be exported to markets across 60 economies. The Government of Viet Nam welcomes foreign investors and is committed to creating favorable conditions for their investment and business activities. The consideration and issuance of investment licenses generally takes between 5 and 15 working days, except for certain special projects for which the approval process may take longer.
Finally, we hope that the authorities and business communities of both countries will continue to promote air connectivity and tourism and facilitate visa issuance, as these constitute an important foundation for expanding economic exchanges between Viet Nam and Iran.
Dear friends,
I believe that, under the current circumstances, the most important thing is not to set overly ambitious targets, but rather to maintain existing trade flows, address the specific difficulties faced by businesses, and gradually build trust between partners in our two countries.
A container of coffee successfully delivered, a pepper contract safely completed, an Iranian company finding a reliable supplier in Viet Nam, or a Vietnamese company finding a good distributor in Iran – concrete results such as these are the foundation upon which sustainable bilateral trade relations can be built.
I hope that today’s event will not only be an opportunity for us to meet and enjoy Vietnamese coffee and other Vietnamese products, but, more importantly, that it will lead to direct discussions, new connections and concrete business opportunities between companies from our two countries.
The Embassy of Viet Nam in Iran will continue to accompany and serve as a bridge in support of these efforts.
I wish all of you good health and success, and I wish for the continued development of the friendship, economic cooperation and trade relations between Viet Nam and Iran.
Thank you very much.
Vietnam has risen like a Phoenix: ICCIMA vice chairman
Ghadir Qiafeh, vice chairman of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA), was the next speaker. He said that when he visited Vietnam several years ago, he was astonished by the country’s development and progress, and by the efforts of its people.
“I saw that Vietnam, like a phoenix, has risen from the ashes of war, spreading its wings, emerging, and soaring into flight,” he said.
There are many fields for cooperation between the two countries, he noted, and through joint investment they can take significant steps together.
Looking into Vietnam’s trade statistics, he found that the country’s eight-month trade had reached $770 billion. “It is a very big figure for a South Asian country,” he said.
Despite the economic capabilities of Iran and Vietnam, bilateral trade remains very low, he said. The figure stands at $170 million, of which $140 million is Vietnam’s exports to Iran and $20 million is Iran’s exports to Vietnam.
Iran enjoys huge sources of energy and a special strategic location, Qiafeh said, and it could have been the hub for Vietnamese products in the region. Vietnam, meanwhile, enjoys a vast trade network and export market, and both sides should benefit from this by playing a key role in Asia’s value chain. The cooperation approach, he stressed, should be win-win.
The private sector can play a significant role in expanding relations between the two countries, he added.
Transportation and logistics are very important in bilateral trade ties, Qiafeh said. The establishment of a database for traders and businessmen is also very important, to provide knowledge about the other country’s market.
He called for strengthening ties between ICCIMA and the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI).
“I wish we see a noticeable leap in the expansion of economic relations between Iran and Vietnam,” he concluded.
25 years of friendship, and a direct flight at last
Meysam Sadri, from the Iran–Vietnam Friendship Association, was the next speaker. He said the association has been active for over 25 years and has offices in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City.
The association is multipurpose and active in different areas, including cultural, social and economic fields, he noted.
After 15 years of follow-up, he said, the association finally achieved the establishment of a direct flight between Iran and Vietnam.
Business dialogue and dinner
After the speeches, several participating businessmen addressed the gathering, and a question-and-answer session followed.
A dinner was then served, during which businessmen had the opportunity to become better acquainted and explore new partnerships.

Biletsky: 3rd Army Corps liberates Nove, Ridkodub and Katerynivka in Operation “Vivaldi”

Biletsky: 3rd Army Corps liberates Nove, Ridkodub and Katerynivka in Operation “Vivaldi”
According to Ukrinform, the press service of the Third Army Corps reported this on Facebook.
“The 3rd Army Corps liberated Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka and regained control of Karpivka and Novomykhailivka. Enemy losses totaled 2,000 troops, and more than 250 Russians were taken prisoner. This marks the end of the third phase of ‘Vivaldi,’ a turning point for the entire operation,” the statement reads.
The corps noted that during the third phase of the operation, an additional 51 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory were recaptured, bringing the total reclaimed since the start of offensive operations to 176 square kilometers. The main target of the third season was Nove—a key enemy hub on the bridgehead.
According to Andrii Biletsky, commander of the Third Army Corps, control over the high ground surrounding this settlement allows for maintaining the initiative on the bridgehead.
“The enemy was convinced that the main direction of the attack was Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna. This forced them to pointlessly burn through their reserves in counterattacks specifically in that direction. The Russians missed the real strike, which was focused on capturing Novoye,” Biletsky stated.
To break through the enemy’s defenses, the Third Army Corps deployed Soviet BTR-60 armored personnel carriers, converted into robotic kamikaze systems. These were used to blow up the enemy’s strongest fortifications. Entire Russian units, including officers, pilots, and artillerymen, surrendered.
Soldiers of the Third Assault Brigade played a key role in the third season of “Vivaldi”; according to the corps, they demonstrated high morale and professionalism. The 3rd Border Guard Detachment named after Hero of Ukraine Colonel Yevhen Pikus regained full control of Ridkodub and quickly established defenses along the new front lines. The 10th Mobile Border Guard Detachment “DOZOR” took an active part in the assault operations.
