Pentagon creates permanent team to hunt down waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:44:40 UTC
16:44:40 KST

- Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg created a permanent team in the Pentagon comptroller's office to find wasteful, inefficient and duplicative programs.
- The Force Agility and Streamlining Team will recommend cuts, consolidations and changes, but its director, size and savings goals have not been disclosed.
The U.S. Department of War is setting up a permanent team inside the Pentagon comptroller’s office to find programs and processes it considers wasteful, inefficient or duplicative and recommend cutting, merging or reshaping them, under a memo signed by Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg.
The new Force Agility and Streamlining Team, or FAST, will serve as the “foundation of an enduring institutional mechanism” to eliminate waste across the department, Feinberg wrote. The department announced the team on Sept. 25. It has not named the team’s director, said how many people it will employ or set a savings target.
FAST will be led by a director who reports directly to Jules W. Hurst III, the under secretary of war who serves as comptroller and chief financial officer. The team will work with the military departments, the Joint Staff, defense agencies and field activities to look for duplicative programs, unnecessary paperwork and approval steps, inefficient spending and offices that no longer contribute to the department’s mission. It will recommend eliminating, realigning, consolidating or modifying them, and department leaders will make the final decisions, the Department of War said.
“Success will be measured by results, not by another layer of process,” said Under Secretary of War Jules W. Hurst III. “If a program is duplicative, we should eliminate it. If a process can be streamlined, we should streamline it. And if resources can be put to better use supporting the warfighter, we have an obligation to make that happen.”
Placing the team in the comptroller’s office puts it next to the budget process, where program money is requested and allocated. The team’s first review and first recommendations have not been scheduled publicly.
FAST is the latest in a series of efficiency moves Feinberg has directed. In April 2025, he ordered a department-wide organizational review under the Workforce Acceleration and Recapitalization Initiative to cut layers of management and realign civilian jobs. This month, he signed a memo titled “Fostering One Strong Industrial Base” that directs the department to drop government-unique cost accounting standards in favor of the commercial accounting rules most companies already use, and to reduce audit and compliance demands on contractors.
The team’s creation came days before the start of fiscal 2027 on Oct. 1.

Counter-terrorism police in the UK are investigating whether there is a link to Iran after police found explosives on three vans near an RAF base in Gloucestershire on Sunday.
Speaking to the BBC on Monday morning, the Defence Secretary Wes Streeting cautioned that it would be "irresponsible to speculate."
"As soon as we can keep the public informed, we will. I would just ask people for a bit of forbearance to give the police and security services the time and space to do their job," he said.
Since March, RAF Fairford has been used by the US military to launch air strikes on Iran as the war in the Middle East rumbles on.
In July, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it was aware that the base was being used by US bombers and warned the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces.”
Armed officers detained a group of five men on Sunday after a call to emergency services about three "suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the air base," London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
Counter-terror police said on Monday that all the men are British nationals in their mid-20s.
US President Donald Trump told reporters they had been "looking to do big damage" at the base in southwest England.
"We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding the US and UK had been working together on the incident.
A local resident who said it was known locally that the base was on lockdown due to a "terror threat" alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking the road and a large group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas.
She told the PA news agency she found it "astonishing" it had been effectively down to a "plucky amateur" spotting unusual activity to raise the alarm.
Some 85 households in the nearby village of Whelford were advised to evacuate and army bomb disposal experts called in to examine three large white vans stopped on a rural road.
Incident 'contained'
"Counter Terrorism Policing can now confirm they are leading an investigation into an incident which took place overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire," the Met statement added.
Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot moving around the vans, two of which had their rear doors open.
Police believed the incident had been "contained" and a 400 metre cordon had been put in place.
Armed officers could be seen guarding the entrance to the base.
In March, then prime minister Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases including Fairford.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being kept updated on the incident, a government spokesperson said.
Burnham, who was in the northwestern city of Liverpool along with other senior ministers for his Labour Party's annual conference, thanked the police, armed forces and residents who had been asked to leave their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out."
Attacks by proxies
Fairford is the UK base of the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US air force administrative support wing, which said in a statement that no US air force personnel had been involved in the incident.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," it said.
"We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities," it added.
The incident comes amid concerns about the actions of hostile foreign states.
Interior Minister Shabana Mahmood has accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on UK territory.
Earlier this month, reports said British military sites had been targeted by drones more than 300 times over the past year.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Morocco has resumed accepting tourist visa confirmation letter applications from Taiwan passport holders after suspending the service in July, the foreign ministry said Monday.
CNA reported that the ministry said applications resumed on Sept. 21 after it received verbal confirmation from the Moroccan Embassy in Tokyo. Morocco has not formally announced the change, and the reopening currently applies only to tourists.
Taiwanese travel agency Lifetour said it also confirmed the change with the Moroccan Embassy in Tokyo. The agency has resumed helping Taiwan travelers apply for the confirmation letters needed for tourist visas.
Taiwan has not yet decided whether to resume accepting visa applications from Moroccan nationals. The foreign ministry said it would first confirm how the restored process works for Taiwan passport holders before reviewing its restrictions on Moroccan applicants.
Morocco instructed its diplomatic missions worldwide in July to stop accepting visa confirmation letter applications, affecting Taiwan passport holders seeking to visit the country. Taiwan responded by suspending visa applications from Moroccan nationals under the principle of reciprocity, except in specially approved cases.

Prime Minister: Arctic Security is Closely Linked to the Security of Europe as a Whole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:41:10 UTC
16:41:10 KST

On 13–14 September, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs attended the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi (Finland), where leaders of the European Union (EU) Member States and institutions discussed the importance of the Arctic for European security and stability, the geopolitical situation in the region, as well as the need to strengthen cooperation, security and resilience in the Arctic.
The Prime Minister participated in the summit sessions devoted to security and the European Union’s role in the Arctic. The discussions focused on the challenges the region is facing, the development of defence capabilities, societal resilience and strengthening the EU’s role in the Arctic. The Arctic is undergoing rapid and far-reaching changes that have an increasing impact on European security and stability. Intensified competition between major powers, the consequences of Russia’s war against Ukraine, China’s growing interest in security issues, and climate change are reshaping the region’s strategic environment.
The Prime Minister underscored that closer cooperation between European countries on security and defence matters is essential to strengthening the resilience of both the Arctic and Europe as a whole.
“Developments in the Arctic have a direct impact on Europe’s security. As the situation in the Arctic changes and competition between the world’s major powers intensifies, Europe must be more united and ready to defend its interests. At the same time, we cannot view the Arctic and the Eastern Flank as two separate regions. Our security is interlinked,” emphasised Andris Kulbergs.
The Prime Minister also pointed out that Russia poses a long-term threat to both the Arctic and the Eastern Flank. Latvia faces this threat on a daily basis in the form of provocations, hybrid attacks and disinformation campaigns; therefore, Europe must invest more in security.
“We are living on borrowed time that Ukraine has brought for us. We must use this time to strengthen Europe’s security. Europe has the financial resources, the technology and the strength. We must stand united and act in a coordinated manner,” stressed the Prime Minister.
At the summit, he also reiterated that the countries on the Eastern Flank play a significant role in defending Europe’s external borders and therefore need additional funding under the EU’s multiannual budget.
At the conclusion of the summit, a joint statement was adopted, in which the leaders of Latvia, Finland, Denmark, Estonia, Italy, France, Greece, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden emphasized the growing strategic role of the Arctic for European security and stability. In view of geopolitical changes, Russia’s aggressive behaviour and growing competition between major powers, the Arctic is increasingly becoming part of European security policy. The joint statement expresses a commitment to preserving the Arctic as a region of peace, stability and constructive cooperation, based on international law.
Latvia, together with its partners, calls on the EU to strengthen its strategic and proactive engagement in the Arctic by increasing investment in security, military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure. Particular attention should be paid to strengthening capabilities to counter hybrid threats, maritime situational awareness, space and satellite technologies, and safe navigation under Arctic conditions. These issues are also important for the security of Latvia and the Baltic region as a whole, and contribute to strengthening Europe’s resilience and defence capabilities.
At the same time, the joint statement emphasises the protection of the rights and interests of Indigenous Peoples, as well as the need to strengthen coordination and cooperation between the EU, its Member States, NATO and like-minded partners in order to promote security, resilience, stability and rules-based governance in the region. The European Commission is expected to put forward a proposal for a new EU Arctic strategy and an action plan for its implementation this autumn.
During the visit, the Prime Minister also visited the Finnish Air Force’s Lapland Air Wing, where he learned about the country’s defence capabilities and watched demonstrations of aircraft and armoured vehicles manufactured by the Finnish company Patria.
The aim of the summit was to strengthen the EU’s common strategic approach to the Arctic region, given its growing geopolitical significance. The summit was hosted by Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo and was also attended by President of the European Council António Costa, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas, Commissioner for International Partnerships Josef Síkela, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Mihal, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda and Romanian President Nicușor Dan.

Israel strips Dutch diplomats’ status over settlement goods ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:39:13 UTC
16:39:13 KST

Israel strips Dutch diplomats’ status over settlement goods ban
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Israel is revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats in the West Bank city of Ramallah in the latest pushback against the Netherlands’ ban on goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in occupied territories.
In a statement on social media, Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar said the diplomats must return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documents within seven days, after which their diplomatic privileges and immunities will expire. He said the move was intended as a response to the ban that came into force last week.
“If the Netherlands wishes to continue representing its interests with the Palestinians, it may do so from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the State of Israel,” he said.
Dutch foreign minister Berendsen said in response that the move was “unnecessary” and that he “deeply regrets” it, adding that the ban on settlement goods “is not directed at Israel” but rather an obligation to comply with international law.
Last month, Israel expelled two Dutch officials from the US-backed centre in Kiryat Gat that coordinates the Gaza ceasefire.
Settlement ban
 The Netherlands is the main EU import hub for goods produced in settlements in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights – all of which are considered occupied under international law.
The cabinet agreed to the ban in May. It covers imports of and trade in settlement goods, and also applies to Dutch companies operating abroad.
Saar said that “Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it. Any country that acts in a hostile and unilateral manner against Israel will lose influence and relevance in the region.”
He also spoke of “growing antisemitism and incitement openly seen on the streets of the Netherlands. Not only are this antisemitism and incitement not being seriously addressed, but the anti-Israel policies of the Dutch Government are fueling them.”
Saar did not specify what he was referring to. This spring there were four attacks on Jewish and pro-Israel targets in the Netherlands, which Dutch investigators believe were coordinated by an Iraqi man arrested in the US. Experts have said the attacks were very likely directed by Iran.
Economic ties
 Despite the dispute over settlement goods, the Netherlands is the biggest destination for Israeli capital in the world, holding €44.9 billion in investment in 2024 – nearly four times as much as the US, according to research by Amsterdam-based corporate watchdog SOMO.
It is also the world’s second biggest investor into Israel, with €27.3 billion invested there in 2024 alone.
Earlier this month, more than 230 former Dutch ministers, ambassadors, diplomats and civil servants called on the cabinet to take tougher measures against Israel, including a full arms embargo and the suspension of the European Union’s trade agreement with the country.

Floods kill at least eight in Thailand, up to 10 feared dead in Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:38:32 UTC
16:38:32 KST

Rescuers in Myanmar were battling on Monday to reach flood-hit areas where up to 10 people are feared dead and dozens missing, as neighbouring Thailand grapples with widespread flooding that has affected more than 1.7 million people and killed eight since mid-September.
Myanmar's southernmost Tanintharyi region has been hit by heavy rains since Friday night, part of an intense weather system also hitting neighbouring Thailand and flooding Bangkok over the weekend.
Myo Min, chairman of the volunteer Dawei Zabuthiri Emergency Medical Service, told AFP several townships in Tanintharyi were badly affected by flooding and landslides.
Some villages had become only accessible by foot, and aid teams have found hundreds of residents displaced from their homes to monastery shelters, he said.
There are "no confirmed figures" of casualties yet, but preliminary information suggests a death toll between seven and 10 people, with 20 to 30 missing, he added.
"Rescue workers have not yet been able to fully manage the entire disaster area," he said.
Authorities have not yet released any official toll in a country whose civil war complicates aid efforts.
The conflict often makes even the scale of natural disasters hard for humanitarian organisations to judge.
Myanmar, a nation of 51 million people, ranks among the 10 nations most vulnerable to climate crisis, according to non-profit Germanwatch.
In Thailand, the capital Bangkok declared a flood disaster over the weekend after almost 48 hours of heavy rain left homes, shops and roads waterlogged.
Nearly 4,900 people were evacuated to shelters, with around 52,000 households affected, according to the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration.
Eight dead in Thailand floods since mid-September
Eight people have died in flooding in Thailand since September 16, although none in the capital, Bangkok, which declared a disaster this weekend following heavy rains, the government said on Monday.
The eight died in eastern provinces, five in Sa Kaeo, two in Chanthaburi and one in Saraburi, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), which did not give further details.
Not including Bangkok, more than 500,000 households and 1.7 million people across 27 provinces in the Southeast Asian country have been affected by flooding, the DDPM said.
A further 52,000 households were impacted in the capital, which on Saturday declared a city-wide disaster after almost 48 hours of heavy rain swelled canals and flooded roads. Thousands sheltered on Monday in evacuation centres in the Thai capital, parts of it still flooded.
No deaths have been officially reported in Bangkok, and the DDPM said water levels had stabilised.
Entire neighbourhoods were inundated and the drainage network swamped after 320 mm (12.6 inches) of rain fell during two or three days last week, or nearly as much as the sprawling low-lying city usually gets in all of September.
Schools have been closed and people urged to work from home, a call that many heeded, with streets and public transport networks noticeably quieter on Monday morning.
"Some areas in Bangkok are still facing high water levels," government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises told a news briefing.
Drainage systems had reduced water levels to the point that more people could travel, he added.
Thailand is used to wet weather and September is the peak of the rainy season, but many residents said this year seemed worse than previous ones.
The floods could cause economic damage of at least 11 billion baht ($327 million) nationwide, with the losses likely to rise unless the situation improves, said Aat Pisanwanich of Rangsit University's economics department.
Bangkok and the eastern region are likely to take the brunt of the impact, particularly wholesale and retail businesses, while industry and agriculture will suffer elsewhere, Aat added.
Last year's catastrophic southern floods, triggered by 630 mm (25 inches) of rain over three days, killed at least 145, inundated more than 33,000 homes and damaged critical facilities such as schools, hospitals and highways.

The world’s most valuable company said that it had approved a $150bn increase to its buyback programme, beating Apple’s previous record of $110bn in 2024.
The company’s shares have surged by almost 1,000% in the past five years alone thanks to huge demand for its chips, which help power large language models.
Matt Britzman, an equity analyst at the investment broker Hargreaves Lansdown, noted that Nvidia is now authorised to spend $235bn on share buybacks over the next six quarters. He said:
That’s well ahead of the roughly $165bn the market had pencilled in over the same period. We’ve said for a while that cash flow is becoming the real flex here. With free cash flow heading toward $200bn this financial year, Nvidia can keep investing heavily in its lead across chips, networking, software and full data centre systems while still handing a huge amount back to shareholders.
Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, said in a statement:
Nvidia’s growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing.
Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders. This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead.”
Shares in Nvidia are up by about 2% in pre-market trading.
Businesses are now sharing their reaction to chancellor John Healey’s speech at the Labour party conference:
Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said the speech set out a “strong vision for how a politics of hope can translate into stronger business confidence and, ultimately, higher living standards.”
He said:
His commitment to fiscal discipline and recognition that it is a precondition for sustainable growth should provide reassurance to markets that the government is prepared to take difficult decisions to secure stable public finances.
Just as important was the recognition that business needs breathing space. Firms cannot invest, hire and grow if rising costs continue to absorb the headroom they need to do so. By linking the cost pressures facing business to the wider challenge of raising living standards, the chancellor showed an appreciation that a stronger economy depends on giving firms the confidence and capacity to create jobs, raise wages and invest.
…The speech sent many of the right signals. The budget now needs to turn them into action if we are to fundamentally change firms’ willingness to invest, take a chance on a young person, and scale a business here in the UK.”
Tina McKenzie, national chair of the FederationofSmallBusinesses, said he was “tight to put the cost of doing business at the centre of his address today”. She said:
The broad theme of hope needs to be followed up with concrete pro-business, pro-growth changes that help small businesses. As well as tax changes on costs, including fuel, late payment reforms must be fast-tracked and proposals for expanded regulation from Companies House should be turned around.
She also called for an increase in small business rates relief from £12,000 to £25,000, a reduction in employment taxes on small firms, a statutory sick pay rebate for small employers, an increase in the VAT registration threshold to £100,000 and a reversal in the rise in business asset disposal relief.
Shevaun Haviland, director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, also called for more help on the everyday cost of doing business.
Firms are being asked to invest while facing a tsunami of rising costs from employment, energy and business rates.
For a typical SME their policy related operating costs have increased by more than 70 per cent in 10 years. The budget must give them breathing space, avoid any further tax rises and cut some of these costs.
…He must go further on youth unemployment, a cut in employer National Insurance contributions for under-25s, will help firms create more opportunities for them.
He should also consider reducing energy bills for firms, by cutting the Renewables Obligation by 75 per cent, and lowering business rates multipliers.

Alex Daniel
The chairman of JCB, LordBamford, has appointed his youngest son to serve alongside him as co-chair of the yellow digger manufacturer.
GeorgeBamford, who founded his own watch making firm in 2009, will take the role from the start of October, JCB announced on Monday as it revealed turnover fell to £5.7bn last year from £5.8bn the year before.
The Staffordshire-based company, which has 23 factories and 20,000 employees across the world, said the drop was because of 5.2% fall in machine sales last year, to 113,498 units.
Profit fell 6.6% to £642m, but the group said it increased its global market share despite “challenging year with mixed market conditions”.
JosephCyrilBamford founded the group in 1945 before his son, Anthony, became chairman in 1975. More recently, LordBamford, who retired as a Conservative peer in 2024, has become a prominent donor to the Reform party, giving £200,000 last year and funding an £8,000 trip for NigelFarage to visit his Rocester factory in 2024.
The company said it would invest £100m in its Staffordshire factory last year and is planning to open a new factory in Texas next month.
LordBamford said:
From the day my grandfather founded JCB in 1945, innovation and investment in Great Britain have been at the heart of everything we do.
While JCB has expanded globally over the years, our home has always been here, and the record investment we are making in our facilities and in new products is good news for Britain and good news for JCB.”

All eyes are on the bond market now as investors watch UK chancellor John Healey’s speech at the Labour party conference.
Bond yields are rising broadly across the world today, led by US Treasuries, with the cost of government borrowing rising in response to higher oil prices.

Russian language study falls, German rises in Lithuanian schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:35:00 UTC
16:35:00 KST

The number of Lithuanian school students learning Russian as a second foreign language has fallen by more than 40 percent since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while the number studying German has risen by 50 percent.
During the 2021–2022 academic year, more than 110,000 students studied Russian as a second foreign language, compared with 65,700 this year. Meanwhile, 39,000 students are learning German as a second foreign language this year, up from 25,000 at the start of the war.
The number of French language learners rose from 10,000 to 15,000, while the largest increase was recorded for Spanish, from 766 to about 15,000 students. About 1,000 more students chose English this year, while 279 chose Polish. The ministry emphasised that the data from the beginning of the school year are preliminary.
Education, Science and Sport Minister Raminta Popovienė said the ministry is currently focusing heavily on strengthening German language teaching. She said the popularity of Russian will likely continue to decline, but it is not yet possible to abandon it completely due to a shortage of teachers for other foreign languages. The minister predicted that the process should settle over the next five to six years.
Starting this September, schools have allowed Spanish to be chosen as a first foreign language, alongside English, French and German. The ministry has also created more opportunities for native speakers and individuals highly proficient in a foreign language to work as European Union language teachers, provided they obtain pedagogical qualifications within two years.
The ministry said some schools have already stopped teaching Russian, with 51 schools dropping it during the last academic year. However, municipalities still face a shortage of foreign language teachers, especially in smaller district schools.
The ministry has included French and German among priority pedagogical specialisations. Students in these specialisations are eligible for monthly scholarships of 481 euros, while those who sign a contract with a school and commit to working there under set conditions receive 814 euros.
Opportunities are also available for those who already have pedagogical qualifications to acquire competencies in another subject. In the 2023–2024 academic year, 48 Russian language teachers participated in a European Union-funded project for free retraining. Half of them chose European Union foreign languages, mostly German.

Escapism from the Streets: How Air-Conditioning Reshaped the Asian City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

In many Asian cities, the summer climate can increasingly be experienced from a distance. In Hong Kong, it is possible to move from an apartment tower through a podium mall, enter the Mass-Transit-Railway system (MTR), arrive beneath another commercial complex, and continue through enclosed footbridges or underground passages while encountering remarkably little of the atmosphere outside. Heat, humidity, rain, and seasonal variation remain present, but they can be largely bypassed through a continuous network of conditioned interiors.
Over several decades, air-conditioning has expanded from a technology for cooling individual rooms into an infrastructure capable of producing an alternative urban environment. This has been particularly visible in parts of East Asia and South East Asia, where transit-oriented development frequently combines railway stations, shopping centres, housing, offices, and other everyday services within interconnected complexes. The Railway plus Property model has helped institutionalize this relationship between transport and development, creating districts where movement through the city is often inseparable from movement through privately managed interiors.
There is much to admire in these systems. They allow dense populations to move efficiently, concentrate daily activities around public transport, and provide relief from heat, humidity, heavy rainfall, and other climatic extremes. In many cases, the shopping mall has become far more than a destination for consumption; it functions as part of the city's circulation network and everyday infrastructure. The success of these environments lies precisely in how seamlessly they make urban life more comfortable and convenient.
Related Article
Digital Worlds and the Limits of Frictionless Space: Rethinking Scale and Materiality
Yet that success also raises a more uncomfortable question. At what point does adapting to climate become escaping from it? As conditioned environments become larger, more interconnected, and more continuous, the exterior city can begin to register primarily as the uncomfortable interval between controlled interiors. What begins as climatic relief may gradually become a form of climatic withdrawal, reshaping not only how cities are built, but how inhabitants understand and expect to experience the climate of the places in which they live.
When the Mall Becomes the City
The contemporary Asian mega-mall differs considerably from the familiar image of the suburban shopping centre as an isolated destination surrounded by parking. In Hong Kong, the mall often functions as circulation infrastructure. One passes through it to reach a railway station, executes most of their vertical circulation within the city, collects groceries on the way home, eats, meets friends, and eventually reaches a residential or office tower above. In everyday use, what is technically a commercial interior begins to perform many of the functions traditionally associated with streets, squares, and other parts of the public city.
This condition makes the mall difficult to dismiss simply as an architectural expression of consumerism. Its success lies precisely in its usefulness. By combining transport, commerce, services, and circulation into compact developments, Hong Kong has produced an extraordinarily convenient model of dense urban life. The mall has not withdrawn from the city so much as absorbed substantial parts of it. Walking, waiting, meeting, eating, moving between transit modes, and passing from work to home can all occur within a sequence of managed interiors.
Elsewhere in the region, similar networks have become explicit planning tools. Singapore's Urban Redevelopment Authority supports covered, elevated, and underground pedestrian connections between developments and rapid-transit stations, with some districts planned around comprehensive multi-level networks intended to provide comfortable, seamless, all-weather movement. In Bangkok, One Bangkok combines shaded outdoor routes with enclosed air-conditioned spaces as parallel responses to pedestrian comfort in the city's climate. The result is not simply a collection of climate-controlled buildings, but an increasingly continuous interiorized urban landscape.
The environmental cost of maintaining such interiors is not insignificant. In Hong Kong, air-conditioning alone accounted for around 30 percent of total electricity consumption in 2023, according to the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department. As a rough order-of-magnitude exercise, and depending on assumptions about system efficiency and how that electricity is ultimately dissipated, this level of consumption can be thought of as producing a comparable quantity of waste heat over time. Averaged across the year, that would be on the order of the heat output from nearly 800,000 two-kilowatt electric heaters running continuously. The comparison is necessarily approximate, but it helps convey the scale of the energy involved in keeping the city's interiors cool.
But energy consumption is only part of the architectural question. As conditioned interiors become larger and better connected, they also begin to alter expectations of what urban comfort should mean. A comfortable city is no longer necessarily one that makes its outdoor spaces inhabitable; it can increasingly become one that makes exposure to those spaces optional.
Escaping the Street
This shift creates a subtle feedback loop. As more daily activities migrate into conditioned interiors, investment and attention naturally follow them. The mall becomes cleaner, cooler, more convenient, and more densely programmed, while the exterior street is increasingly experienced as the interval one crosses to reach the next controlled environment. The less comfortable that interval feels by comparison, the more attractive the interior becomes. Climatic escape can therefore reinforce the very conditions that make further escape desirable.
The difference is important. Air-conditioning was initially a means of improving particular interiors; it can now participate in reorganizing the city around them. If heat can be solved by moving indoors, there is less pressure to make an exposed pedestrian route comfortable. If heavy rain can be avoided through a tunnel or enclosed bridge, the street edge no longer needs to carry the same burden of shelter. As circulation migrates above, below, and through buildings, the architectural threshold between inside and outside can become increasingly abrupt. One environment is controlled; the other is something to pass through.
This does not mean the answer is to return nostalgically to a city before mechanical cooling. Nor is complete climatic exposure inherently more authentic. In increasingly hot and humid cities, air-conditioning can be essential to health and everyday comfort. The more relevant question is whether conditioned space remains one form of urban experience among many, or becomes the assumed destination of urban life itself. Singapore offers an instructive counterpoint in this respect: alongside underground and elevated networks, its planning guidelines continue to require and incentivize open-sided covered walkways, sheltered public routes, landscaping, and at-grade connections that provide climatic protection without necessarily enclosing pedestrians from the outside environment altogether.
The distinction may become most apparent across generations. For those who experienced tropical Asian cities before widespread air-conditioning, entering a cooled interior represented a conscious form of relief: one knew exactly what was being escaped. For subsequent generations, the conditioned environment increasingly forms the ordinary background of urban life. Moving from an air-conditioned home into a lift lobby, through a podium, onto a railway, and into another mall or office no longer necessarily feels like retreating from the city. It simply feels like the city. Escapism becomes most complete when the alternative environment ceases to register as alternative at all—a possibility for younger generations who have known the air-conditioned city less as an exception than as the default.
This normalization can also change what inhabitants expect architecture to provide. Seasonal variation becomes an inconvenience to be eliminated rather than a condition around which everyday habits might adjust. A comfortable environment is expected to remain relatively constant regardless of what is happening outside. At their most extreme, mega-developments begin to resemble urban-scale refrigerators: enormous interiors capable of maintaining preferred atmospheric conditions while the weather, season, and climate continue beyond their envelopes. The accomplishment is technologically impressive, but it also produces a particular relationship to place—one in which environmental differences can increasingly be suspended rather than encountered.
Returning to the Climate
The challenge is therefore not to reject the air-conditioned city, whose convenience has become fundamental to contemporary urban life. Nor should mega-malls and transit-oriented developments be dismissed simply because they are enclosed or privately managed. In cities such as Hong Kong, their density and integration with public transport have produced real urban efficiencies, while protected circulation can make cities significantly more usable during extreme heat and rainfall. The question is what happens when this model becomes so successful that the world outside begins to matter less.
Between the sealed mall and the exposed street lies a much broader architectural territory. Covered walkways, shaded public rooms, planting, open-sided arcades, breezeways, semi-conditioned thresholds, and spaces capable of changing with weather can offer protection without requiring complete environmental separation. The objective is not to remove air-conditioning, but to prevent mechanical conditioning from becoming the only imaginable definition of comfort.
Escapism becomes problematic not when architecture offers relief from an uncomfortable climate, but when the relief becomes so complete that the climate outside ceases to register at all. As cities face hotter temperatures and greater climatic uncertainty, architecture will undoubtedly need cooling. But it will also need to retain the knowledge required to make streets, thresholds, and public spaces inhabitable without enclosing all of them within a single artificial atmosphere. The question may therefore be less about how successfully Asian cities can escape their climates than how architecture can allow people to remain within them. If architecture makes it possible to live without encountering the climate, eventually it may also become possible to forget how to design for it.

Almost half those suspected of LGBT hate crimes are under-18s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:29:38 UTC
16:29:38 KST

Almost half of the people suspected of hate crimes against LGBT persons are aged under 18 according to daily Het Laatste Nieuws that makes the claim based on figures requested by MP Alexander Van Hoecke (far right Vlaams Belang). Last year, a total of 600 hate crimes against LGBT people were recorded.
The figures come from the federal police. Since April 2024, the police have been recording incidents with homophobic and transphobic motives separately.
The highest number of reports came from Brussels, Antwerp and Ghent. These involved physical violence, theft, extortion and damage to property.
Of the 600 offences, 498 were homophobic in nature, and 102 were transphobic.
Highest number in Molenbeek
For 2025, Brussels leads the tally with more than one in six reports (107). Almost a quarter took place in the municipality of Sint-Jans-Molenbeek.
Antwerp comes second with 78 recorded incidents, whilst Ghent takes third place with 49 reports.
Suspects' heritage not recorded
The vast majority of suspects are Belgian, but Vlaams Belang wants the origin of offenders to be recorded as well, says lawmaker Van Hoecke.
“These nationality figures tell us very little. To tackle a problem, we need to be able to identify it. We can only do that if we have a clear picture, if we know which communities are over-represented in these figures.”
Federal Equal Opportunities Minister Rob Beenders (Flemish socialist Vooruit) says that the problem of hate crimes is present in all sections of the population. For him, the origin of the perpetrators is not a priority.
Beenders describes it as a societal debate in which parents must also talk openly at home. “Supporting young people in their search for identity is still best achieved through a personal conversation. The algorithms on the internet push people in a certain direction; we must counteract that,” explains the minister. He promises an action plan.
How should we tackle this?
The LGBTQI+ umbrella organisation Çavaria has noticed the trend in society.
“Recent research in the Netherlands and Flanders shows that acceptance among young people is falling sharply. That is a new development. Young people themselves say that they hear nothing about gender diversity or sexual orientation at school, but that they are inundated with negative messages on social media,” says spokesperson Thomas Jans.
Çavaria is calling on all schools to make this a structural priority. “Schools that talk about it can make a difference,” it says.

Canton Graubünden rejects lowering voting age to 16

Canton Graubünden rejects lowering voting age to 16
Voters in canton Graubünden in southeastern Switzerland on Sunday rejected a proposal to lower the voting age to 16. Overall, 67% of residents were against the idea.
Glarus therefore remains the only canton where 16- and 17-year-olds can vote at the cantonal level. In Graubünden, the voting age remains fixed at 18.
Voters in all Graubünden municipalities rejected the proposal to lower the voting age. The strongest ‘no’ vote came from Buseno in Val Calanca, where almost 90% rejected the proposal. This negative trend was confirmed across the Moesa region, which, with almost 78% voting ‘no’, led the way at regional level, followed by the Bernina region, with almost 76% against. Turnout on Sunday was 45%.
More
Swiss canton sets out proposal to let 16‑year‑olds vote
Political parties
The Centre Party, the Social Democrats, the Greens, the Protestant Party and the youth wings of the Centre Party and the Liberal Greens had supported the initiative. The centre-right Radical-Liberal Party had abstained, whilst the right-wing Swiss People’s Party and the Young Radical-Liberals had campaigned against it.
Had the proposal been approved, as many as 3,000 young people would have been able to cast their votes in cantonal referendums and elections from next year. The number of eligible voters would thus have risen to 146,000. As regards municipal referendums, local authorities would have been able to continue deciding independently whether to allow 16- and 17-year-olds to take part as well.
In the information leaflet sent to voters, those opposed argued that young people under the age of 18 lacked the necessary political maturity and were at greater risk of being influenced, for example by social media. Furthermore, they believed that setting the voting age at 16 was not in line with the responsibilities laid down in civil and constitutional law.
More
Voting at 16: more than just a symbolic gesture?
The majority in the Graubünden parliament, however, saw the proposal as an opportunity to counter the ageing of society and to enable young people to participate in decision-making processes at an earlier stage. They added that the public was to be asked to decide on this “important matter of constitutional law”, which is why even some lawmakers critical of the bill had voted in favour.
‘A heavy defeat’
The initiative committee said Sunday’s result was “a disappointment, but not a surprise”. Andrin Ehrler, a member of the committee, told the Keystone-ATS news agency: “Based on experiences in other cantons, we should have expected this.” Although the result was less decisive than in other parts of Switzerland, it must still be described as a “heavy defeat”.
Ehrler attributes the rejection to a lack of trust in young people, but also to the fact that young people themselves have little confidence in their own abilities. “For this reason, the traditional right-left voting pattern did not even emerge in this vote.” The canton has thus missed an opportunity to take on a pioneering role. Although the proposal has been shelved for the time being, Ehrler believes it is still important to continue reflecting on how to promote young people’s political participation. “A strong youth assembly remains essential,” said Ehrler.

The purest democracy? Visiting one of Switzerland’s historic open-air assemblies
‘No surprise’
The president of the Graubünden government, Martin Bühler, who was oversaw this issue, takes a similar view on the referendum result. He told Keystone-ATS that the result came as no surprise. The proposal was discussed in a very practical and substantive manner, he said. The government had supported lowering the voting age to 16, given that the proposal had originated from the Youth Session and had secured a large majority in parliament.
But the government had also raised certain critical points, such as the risk of a disparity between the right to vote and the right to stand for election. According to Bühler, it is now important to continue promoting young people’s political participation, “so that it is not just others who decide the canton’s future”.
Sunday’s result in canton Graubünden mirrors attitudes to lowering the voting age across the country. In 2024, a similar initiative was also rejected at national level by the federal parliament. Last year, 80% of voters in canton Lucerne rejected a proposal to lower the voting age. Attempts in other cantons, on the other hand, have failed either in parliament or in referendums.

France actively working to combat child malnutrition in Sudan, in cooperation…
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:26:07 CEST
16:26:07 KST

France actively working to combat child malnutrition in Sudan, in cooperation with UNICEF's child Sudan Food security Statement On : September 25th 2026 On 24 September 2026, at an event held by UNICEF on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly to mobilize the international community around the prevention of nutritional crises and famine, France announced its support for UNICEF’s Child Nutrition Fund. The conflict in Sudan has sparked a famine, confirmed in 2025, and the situation there remains disastrous: 35% of the population – 19.1 million individuals – are suffering from acute food insecurity. The situation is especially critical for children under five: 825,000 of them are facing severe acute malnutrition, which is putting their lives in danger. French support for the Child Nutrition Fund will allow a malnutrition prevention and treatment programme to be implemented in the Darfur and Kordofan regions, affected by armed conflicts. It will benefit 100,000 people, with the aim of caring for 80,000 children under five and 20,000 pregnant women and mothers of children under two. It will emphasize the importance of providing the nutritional intake essential for children in the first 1,000 days, the decisive window in their lives. This French aid will be matched by an equivalent amount of funding from other donors committed to UNICEF, thus doubling the impact of France’s commitment to Sudan’s most vulnerable children. By contributing to UNICEF’s Child Nutrition Fund, France is reaffirming its determination to act, in Sudan and throughout the world, to combat malnutrition and protect child victims of conflict. The fight against food insecurity and malnutrition is a priority of France’s foreign policy. In the spirit of the Nutrition for Growth Summit (N4G), hosted in Paris in March 2025, France reaffirms that investment in this area is decisive for human development.

Pop sensation Taylor Swift won three prizes at the MTV VMAs, including the top honour - video of the year - cementing her status as the most decorated solo artist.
Taylor Swift has broken yet another record by becoming the most-awarded artist in MTV VMA history.
The mega popstar picked up the inaugural Artist Director Honors on Sunday night in recognition of artists "whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling."
“I got to start making music videos and being a part of music videos 20 years ago,” Swift said in her speech, adding that she's been involved in making roughly 60 music videos, 18 of which she wrote and directed.
Swift also debuted the music video she directed for her latest song 'Patient Zero' which stars actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson.
Swift, who was previously tied with Beyoncé for titles with 30 VMAs each, also went home with the top prize of the night - video of the year - for 'The Fate of Ophelia' from her album 'The Life of a Showgirl.'
Madonna wins big
The other major winner of the night was Madonna who kicked off the proceedings by performing her single 'Bring Your Love' alongside Sabrina Carpenter. The pair won the award for best collaboration for the song.
If her aim was to bring the dance floor to the award show stage, Madonna did exactly that in her opening number — and then some, when Charli xcx emerged from a club bathroom to perform their reworked version of 'Danceteria.' Around them? A trove of dancers and various famous friends, including actor Debi Mazar, Sombr and Julia Garner.
Madonna also won the coveted artist of the year award and completed her hat-trick with the best dance honour.
“First of all, I would like to thank my fingers because I can always count on them,” she said on collecting the artist of the year trophy.
Dolly dedication
Picking up the award, Swift heaped praise on the late, great country singer Dolly Parton whom she described as the "ultimate showgirl."
Parton, whose soaring vibrato vocals, emotive songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, died in Nashville of cancer last month. She was 80.
“I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time," Swift said.
Other stars also paid tribute to Parton with a string of performances and covers of her most well known tracks. Kacey Musgraves sang 'I Will Always Love You' while Raye delivered a medley of her throwback soul, including 'I Will Overcome' and 'Where Is My Husband!'
Bruno Mars slowed things down with 'Dance With Me.' Shaboozey launched into his saloon single 'Cowgirl,' before being joined by Gunna for some hybrid country-rap with their crossover track, 'High Noon.'
Night of Nirvana
One of the most coveted prizes, the Video Vanguard Award, went to legendary grunge band, Nirvana.
The honour was presented to surviving members Krist Novoselic, Dave Grohl and Pat Smear. Frontman Kurt Cobain died in 1994.
“They were completely original and always fearless at a time when the status quo kind of got to the point of being formulaic,” Public Enemy rapper Chuck D said when presenting the award.
“Kurt was one of one,” Novoselic said in their acceptance speech, adding that the band never imagined its sound and aesthetic would resonate with so many people. He said the music continues to endure because people are still hungry for “something real, something uncompromising” and a message that “it’s just OK to come as you are.”

'I'm responsible for hell': Ben-Gvir threatens Hamas terrorist behind 1996 bus bombings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:24:58 UTC
16:24:58 KST

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir threatened imprisoned Hamas terrorist Hassan Salameh in a video published late Sunday night, telling him, “I want to kill you. I want to put you to death.”
In the video, which Ben-Gvir said was recorded during a prison visit about two weeks earlier, he told Salameh, who orchestrated the deadly 1996 Line 18 suicide bus bombings, that he would go to hell in the afterlife. “But here, I’m responsible for hell,” the minister added.
Salameh is serving multiple life sentences for orchestrating three suicide bombings in 1996. The two Line 18 bus bombings, carried out on February 25 and March 3, killed 45 people. A third bombing at Ashkelon Junction on February 25 killed IDF soldier Hofit Aish.
Salameh was arrested that year, convicted and sentenced to 46 consecutive life terms plus 30 years.
“You killed 48 people,” Ben-Gvir said. “Children, women, men and soldiers” - people he said he regarded as his own children.
“When I was a kid, I protested that they need to take care of people like you,” he said. “Today, I’m closing that circle.
Ben-Gvir pushes to worsen conditions for security prisoners
Ben-Gvir, whose ministry oversees the Israel Prison Service, has made worsening conditions for security prisoners a central part of his policy.
Since the October 7, 2023, attacks, the prison service has barred security prisoners from purchasing food at prison canteens or preparing it themselves, while Ben-Gvir has repeatedly said they should receive only the minimum conditions required by law.
In September 2025, the High Court ruled that the service was not ensuring prisoners received food sufficient to meet basic legal requirements and ordered it to take steps to do so and monitor implementation
The Israel Prison Service said, in response to a query by The Jerusalem Post, that all prisoners receive food in accordance with the law and court rulings, and that the service operates under binding directives and the oversight of the relevant authorities.
In March 2026, the Knesset passed the Death Penalty for Terrorists Law by a vote of 62-48. The law makes execution by hanging the default sentence for West Bank residents who are neither Israeli citizens nor residents and are convicted by military courts of intentionally killing someone in a terrorist attack, unless special circumstances justify life imprisonment. In civilian courts, it allows either death or life imprisonment for anyone convicted of intentionally killing another person with the aim of denying Israel’s existence.
Because harsher criminal penalties cannot be imposed retroactively, the law cannot apply to Salameh’s 1996 offenses. Israel has not carried out an execution since Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann was hanged in 1962.
“As National Security Minister, I led a policy that turned his life into hell,” Ben-Gvir wrote. “And with God’s help, as Defense Minister, I will act to ensure that murderer terrorists like him are put to death, and I will advance the emigration policy from Gaza and from Judea and Samaria.”
Hamas claims not to be intimidated by Ben-Gvir
Hamas said in response that neither it nor Palestinian prisoners were intimidated.
“Our heroic people will remain loyal to their national causes, foremost among them the issue of the prisoners,” Hamas stated. It said prisoners “will not be intimidated by the criminal minister Ben-Gvir or other extremist, terrorist leaders of the occupation,” and accused him of “further crimes” against prisoners.
Ben-Gvir responded that Hamas’s condemnation showed he was “on the right path” and said he would continue pursuing harsher treatment of security prisoners and implementation of the death penalty law.
“They will receive the minimum required by law - and not one millimeter more,” he said. “If Hamas is crying out, it means they understand very well that the rules have changed and the boss has gone mad.”
The Gaza-based Waed Association for Prisoners and Released Persons said Ben-Gvir’s direct threat to kill Salameh represented an unprecedented level of hostility.
The US Treasury designated Waed as a specially designated global terrorist entity in January 2026, saying it was integrated into Hamas’s military wing and had provided material support to the organization.
Waed said the incident was not merely a media stunt, but reflected how the minister responsible for the prison system viewed inmates and what he considered permissible treatment.
Khaled Abu Toameh contributed to this report.

Ireland defeats Israel 3-0 amid pre-game controversy, plenty of pressure

2026-09-28
07:24:53 UTC
16:24:53 KST

Israel’s national soccer team returned Sunday to the Nagyerdei Stadium in Debrecen, Hungary, for its UEFA European Nations League “home” game against the Republic of Ireland.
The match came three days after Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria and amid controversy after Maccabi Tel Aviv’s Sayed Abu Farchi, after scoring a goal, made a celebratory gesture involving a corner flag that led to his sending-off.
On Saturday, however, the focus was almost entirely off the pitch.
Major internal drama within the Irish team raised questions over whether Ireland would refuse to play and boycott both Sunday’s match in Debrecen and its “home” match against Israel, scheduled for next Sunday behind closed doors in Serbia.
The Irish team did not participate in a scheduled training session and postponed a planned press conference before holding a closed-door crisis meeting involving the players, manager and Irish football officials. The meeting resulted in a significant majority of the squad voting to proceed with the game.
Subsequently, Irish goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the team and said that, as “a man of strong faith” trying his “best” to be a “man of character and principle,” he believed it was wrong “to participate” in the game.
Bazunu was one of Ireland’s reserve goalkeepers and was unlikely to have played. He cited as his reason a “personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong.”
Irish groups unsuccessfully push for Israel's removal from UEFA
The statement was subsequently embraced by Irish groups campaigning against Israel. For the previous seven months, these groups had unsuccessfully campaigned for Israel to be expelled from UEFA and for Ireland to boycott the matches.
Multiple protest marches, public meetings, demands from opposition politicians that the Irish government intervene to stop the games, and incessant social media pressure on Irish players had clearly contributed to internal divisions within the team.
The campaign also gained the support of a majority of Irish sports journalists and broadcasters, RTE, Ireland’s public-service broadcaster, Irish trade unions, human rights groups and all of Ireland’s opposition parties.
The same campaign continued in the background over the weekend, with efforts to prevent the Irish Wheelchair Association from participating in a European women’s wheelchair basketball tournament in which Israeli wheelchair athletes are competing.
Bazunu was subsequently praised by many of the groups campaigning against Israel. His decision was based, he said, on his opposition to the killing of innocent people. The campaigners’ response, however, came amid the continuing debate surrounding the October 7 massacre, the Nova Music Festival, where the dismembered body of 22-year-old Irish citizen Kim Damti was found, Hamas’s stated commitment to repeating October 7, and the thousands of missiles fired at Israel throughout the Israel-Gaza conflict.
Despite the controversy, the Irish team took to the field with determination after having lost 1-0 to Kosovo last Thursday.
As it became increasingly clear over the weekend that the game would take place, the groups campaigning against the match reacted angrily on social media and in public statements.
Prior to the game, the Irish team agreed to wear black armbands “for all lives lost in the conflict” and also agreed not to shake hands with Israel’s players.
At the team’s Saturday press conference, Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson, who had previously stated under pressure from campaigners that Ireland was “not playing with genocide, but was playing against genocide,” acknowledged that his reference to genocide was wrong. He also explicitly referred to the pressure being imposed on the team, describing it as having reached a near-breaking point.
Israel Football Association head of communications Sholomi Barzel welcomed the decision for the game to take place, saying that football had won. He also invited members of the Irish team to visit Israel as a learning experience.
Not everyone among the two teams was a stranger to the other side.
Most of Ireland’s players play for English Championship teams, and many have played against Manor Solomon, who previously played for Leeds United and this season plays for West Ham United.
Israel captain and goalkeeper Daniel Peretz is a teammate of Irish internationals Finn Azaz and Brian Manning at Southampton. Ireland assistant coach Paddy McCarthy works with Anan Khalaili, who recently transferred to Premier League club Crystal Palace.
Interestingly, Bazunu was Southampton’s Premier League goalkeeper last season before the team was relegated to the Championship, and he was subsequently transferred to Bolton Wanderers in League One.
The Nagyerdei Stadium in Debrecen was a dismal venue on Sunday night.
Debrecen's Nagyerdei Stadium nearly empty for Israel-Ireland match
A fine stadium with a capacity of 20,340, it was virtually empty, with approximately 200 Israeli supporters and about 20 Irish supporters in attendance. No tickets were acquired or sold by the Irish FA because of fears that anti-Israel protesters would disrupt the game. For the same reason, next week’s Ireland “home” game will be played without any spectators.
The small group of Irish supporters cheered on their team, while the much larger and considerably noisier group of Israeli supporters cheered on Israel.
As announced, the Irish players wore black armbands, and there were no handshakes either before or after the match. Israel’s players stood respectfully as Ireland’s national anthem was played. The Irish players bowed their heads and stared at their feet as Hatikvah was played.
Within 17 minutes of the game starting, Ireland led 2-0. After 25 minutes, it was 3-0.
Goals by Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan reflected Ireland’s dominance, which continued throughout the first half.
The opening 20 minutes of the second half saw a significant improvement in Israel’s play, but it did not show on the scoreboard. The final score remained 3-0 as both teams made substitutions and the game gradually petered out.
In the dying minutes, Israel’s supporters repeatedly chanted “IDF, IDF.”
Meanwhile, back in Ireland, those campaigning against Israel took to social media to denigrate and vilify both the Irish team, despite its excellent first-half performance, and its Israeli opponents.
As this writer tweeted developments during the match, my X/Twitter feed was hit by a deluge of antisemitic hate originating from Ireland.
The campaigners will spend the coming week attempting to stir further hostility in the hope that Ireland’s team can be intimidated into boycotting next Sunday’s rematch.
They will not succeed.
Perhaps sanity and decency will ultimately prevail, with the Irish team shaking hands with their Israeli opponents both before and after the game and showing Israel’s national anthem the same respect that the Israeli team showed Ireland’s.

Liberman further predicted that the US would recognize a Palestinian state within two and a half years and support a UN Security Council resolution to that effect. He offered no evidence for the prediction, and it represents his assessment rather than an announced US policy.
The planned elections come 20 years after the last Palestinian legislative vote, in which Hamas defeated Fatah. Hamas won 74 of the Palestinian Legislative Council's 132 seats, compared with Fatah's 45. A power struggle followed, culminating in Hamas's takeover of the Gaza Strip in 2007.

Iraq said Saturday that it had reached an agreement with the United States to continue shipments of physical US dollars to Baghdad, with another delivery expected within days, after Washington disrupted the flow earlier this year as it pressed the Iraqi government over Iran-backed armed groups and illicit dollar transfers.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Iraqi government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi said the understanding was reached during Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States and would help Iraq meet legitimate demand for foreign currency.
“A new shipment will arrive in the coming days,” al-Aboudi said.
He said the agreement followed Iraqi steps to tighten oversight of dollar distribution, regulate the use of foreign currency, reduce misuse of the financial system and expand electronic payments.
The United States halted an expected shipment of roughly $450 million to $500 million in physical currency in April as part of pressure on Baghdad over attacks by Iran-backed armed groups. At the time, an Iraqi central bank official said an April shipment had not arrived, and the status of another expected in May was unclear. Electronic dollar transfers used for imports and trade were not affected.
Limited US dollar shipments to Iraq resume in July
Some cash deliveries resumed by early July. Reuters reported on July 2, citing The New York Times, that limited air shipments of US dollars had restarted after the several-month pause. Reuters said at the time that it had not independently verified the resumption.
The latest Iraqi announcement goes further, presenting the continuation of cash shipments as an agreement reached with Washington and saying another shipment is expected within days.
The currency comes from Iraqi oil revenues held through the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Iraq keeps more than $100 billion in reserves in the United States, giving Washington substantial influence over Baghdad’s access to physical dollars.
The US has also sanctioned Iraqi banks accused of facilitating transactions benefiting Iran, while Iraqi authorities have introduced tighter financial controls intended to curb illicit dollar flows.
Iraq remains closely tied economically to neighboring Iran, with bilateral trade worth more than $10 billion annually.
The value of the next cash shipment and its precise delivery date were not disclosed.

Avanti West Coast will be renationalised in spring, as Andy Burnham declares “enough is enough” for passengers who have put up with a rail service “that has failed them time and time again”.
The rail operator, which is one of the worst in the country for train delays and cancellations, will come under public ownership from 7 March when its contract ends.
The Labour government has been nationalising passenger rail services across the country as their contracts have expired, as the public body Great British Railways prepares to take full oversight in 2027.
Avanti had among the highest proportion of train cancellations in Britain, at 7.1% from April to June this year.
The company connects the north and south of England, with its service running from London to Manchester and Liverpool. It also runs services through the north-west of England and on to Wales, Glasgow and Edinburgh.
The prime minister has previously complained about high prices on Avanti, with tickets for peak-time returns from Manchester to London as high as £300.
Burnham wrote on social media that “for years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again”.
“So my Labour government is bringing Avanti West Coast into public ownership at the earliest opportunity in March next year. That means passengers, not shareholders, will come first.
“More investment, fewer delays, and a renewed focus on getting the basics right. We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.”
Avanti has the worst punctuality rating for any large rail company in the UK.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, – who will formally announce the decision in her speech at Labour conference on Tuesday afternoon – added that “for years, we’ve heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price”.
She added that the Labour government “is committed to putting essential services back in public hands, connecting people to opportunity and delivering growth in every postcode and this move reflects that commitment”.
Andy Mellors, managing director at Avanti West Coast, said: “We’re proud of what we’ve achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before.”
He said the improvements had given “customers greater choice, more capacity and better connectivity, while we’ve continued to innovate to shape the future of the west coast and wider rail industry”.
Earlier this month, Chiltern Railways became the latest train operator to enter public ownership, becoming the sixth to be nationalised under Labour, with the remaining four to follow by the end of 2027. Who writes the code of the new world? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:24:19 UTC
16:24:19 KST

For decades we thought of code as something hidden behind the screen -- a technical language, a sequence of instructions written by engineers and executed by machines. That definition no longer holds. Code now governs financial systems, biometric identification, telecommunications, energy grids, intelligence platforms, satellites, autonomous weapons and artificial intelligence. It is no longer merely running civilization; it has become part of civilization's strategic architecture. That shift raises one of the defining security questions of our time: who writes this code, who controls it, and what values are being embedded within it?
Much of the architecture of modern computing emerged from American universities, laboratories and defense programs. But the American technological model was never ethnically homogeneous. Its strength came precisely from its ability to absorb talent from everywhere – European scientists, Jewish refugees fleeing persecution, engineers from Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America, all folded into a single technological ecosystem. Other centers of power have since emerged alongside it. China built an enormous computational and industrial base. Israel developed one of the world's most sophisticated concentrations of cybersecurity and defense technology. Iran, despite decades of sanctions, built substantial indigenous cyber capabilities. North Korea proved that even an isolated, impoverished state can project cyber power far beyond its borders. Strategic influence today depends as much on software, data and computational infrastructure as on armies, territory and industrial capacity.
This distinction is critical: code has no ethnicity, but it is not strategically neutral. A Boolean operation behaves identically in Boston, Tehran or Beijing. What differs is the institutional environment surrounding the engineer – who sets the requirements, who defines the threat, who controls the data, who decides when an autonomous system may act, and who has the authority to shut it down when it fails. Those questions, not the passport or ancestry of the person at the keyboard, are what turn software engineering into a matter of national and international security.
Modern geopolitical competition is increasingly a competition over architecture: who manufactures the semiconductor, who controls the cloud, who owns the satellite constellation, who trains the AI model, who holds the cryptographic keys – and ultimately, who teaches the machine what should count as normal, suspicious or dangerous. NATO's January 2026 Alliance Digital Strategy explicitly places secure digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, Zero Trust architecture, post-quantum cryptography and human-machine collaboration at the center of the alliance's future defense posture, describing digital transformation not as mere modernization but as a source of operational advantage. The 21st century's strategic contest will be decided in part by who can collect, protect, interpret and act on information faster and more securely than an adversary.
For open societies, this produces a genuine paradox. Innovation depends on scientific openness, international cooperation and the free movement of talent. Yet many of the same technologies are dual-use: artificial intelligence can detect cancer or sharpen a targeting system; computer vision can authenticate a citizen or enable mass surveillance; cryptography can protect a population or conceal a hostile operation. The challenge for democratic states is not simply producing more technology – it is preserving openness while shielding the systems that matter most.
The threat is no longer theoretical. The US intelligence community's 2026 Annual Threat Assessment finds that China, Russia, Iran, North Korea and non-state ransomware actors continue to seek access to American government, private-sector and critical-infrastructure networks for espionage, disruption or profit. It describes North Korea's cyber program as sophisticated and agile, funding weapons development in part through cryptocurrency theft that reached roughly $2 billion in 2025 alone, and it flags Iranian cyber capabilities as a persistent concern alongside Tehran's missile and drone programs. These are American assessments, shaped by an American vantage point – but they illustrate why Washington and its allies now treat software supply chains, AI systems and telecommunications infrastructure as strategic assets rather than ordinary commercial products. A small group of programmers can now produce effects that once required a conventional military. That changes the arithmetic of international security.
Israel's approach illustrates the defensive mirror of the same logic. Its national cybersecurity strategy treats digital defense as requiring coordinated action across government, the security establishment, the private economy and international partners – cybersecurity as an extension of national infrastructure rather than an IT function. Across technologically advanced states, that boundary between digital security and national security is dissolving, drawing in energy, finance, biometric identity, space systems and civilian resilience alike. It extends even into orbit: software written in one country can now govern a satellite operating over another continent, giving code strategic reach without physical territory – and giving any failure or malicious instruction inside an autonomous, nuclear-warning or space-control system consequences that are no longer merely technical.
The emerging Western answer is not simply more code, but trusted code: auditable systems, secure development environments, verified supply chains, Zero Trust infrastructure, human oversight of consequential AI decisions, continuous red-teaming and intelligence sharing among allies. NATO's digital strategy already leans in this direction. But the balance is delicate – too little oversight invites exploitation by hostile actors; too much invites the suppression of the innovation, privacy and scientific openness that made Western technology strong in the first place. Managing that tension will be one of the central governance problems of the AI era.
There is, however, a line democratic systems must not cross. The security question can never become a question of the programmer's ethnicity – that would be both scientifically meaningless and institutionally corrosive. The relevant questions are about control, not ancestry: who owns the organization, what jurisdiction governs it, where the data travels, who can access the source code, what dependencies exist, whether the system can be independently audited, and whether a human can override it. This distinction matters most for the United States and its allies, whose technological edge has always depended on attracting talent from every part of the world.
That diversity is itself a security asset, not merely a social virtue. An engineer sees architecture; a cybersecurity specialist sees attack surfaces; an intelligence analyst sees hostile intent; a privacy lawyer sees surveillance risk. Someone who has lived under authoritarian rule, or under terrorism, or under sustained cyber warfare, will often recognize a danger that a colleague without that history simply cannot see. The goal, then, is not ethnic uniformity but institutional trust paired with intellectual diversity – a combination that makes systems harder to manipulate and easier to correct before an error becomes a catastrophe.
For thousands of years, civilizations encoded their values in constitutions, religious texts, laws and institutions. The 21st century has added another repository: source code. Future historians may study our algorithms the way today's historians study ancient legal codes, asking what we optimized, whom we trusted, whom we monitored, and what authority we surrendered to machines before we built the safeguards to control it. The threats catalogued by Western intelligence agencies make that reckoning immediate rather than theoretical. But preserving openness, civil liberties, and scientific collaboration remains part of the security equation too – because we are no longer simply teaching machines to operate inside our civilization. We are encoding pieces of that civilization into them. The defining strategic question of the coming decades is who will write that code, who will control it, and under whose rules the new digital world will operate.
The author is a cybersecurity strategist and AI & data governance expert.

British police said on Sept 28 that the five men who were detained were all British nationals who live in London, and were all in their mid-twenties. But they have not linked Iran to the arrests, and an investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing was under way.

Terrorism threat severe
Britain in April raised its national terrorism threat level to “severe” from “substantial” after a series of anti-Semitic incidents in north London, indicating a terrorist attack within the six months is considered highly likely.
Police said they were investigating Iran links to many of the incidents in which properties connected to the Jewish community or Iranian dissidents were targeted.
In May, Britain sanctioned 12 individuals and entities linked to Iran, accusing them of involvement in hostile activity including plotting attacks and providing financial services to groups seeking to destabilise Britain and other countries.
Iran has repeatedly denied involvement in attacks or plots in Britain and elsewhere.

“US-associated facilities, gatherings, and organisations may be at heightened risk,” the statement said.
