In Fairford, police have imposed a 400m cordon around the base and evacuated residents from 85 homes.

‘They thought we were police’: Farmer’s emergency call leads to RAF Fairford terror arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:19:23 UTC
16:19:23 KST

A farmer driving home from a party in the middle of the night had no reason to expect anything unusual on the quiet country roads around her Gloucestershire village. Then her headlights swept across three white vans blocking the road near RAF Fairford, and a group of hooded and masked men suddenly scattered into the darkness.
Some ran into the fields and trees. Others, she said, appeared to head toward the airbase, a Royal Air Force facility heavily used by the U.S. military. The woman, who has asked British media not to identify her for security reasons, drove away and called the emergency number 999. She then warned neighbors in a village WhatsApp group to lock their doors.
“They would have seen the bright headlights,” she told the Press Association. “They probably thought we were the police and panicked.”
Police arrived around 15 minutes after her call. Five men were subsequently arrested, initially on suspicion of offenses under Britain’s Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Three vans were left at the scene, where bomb disposal specialists deployed a robot to examine them.
The woman believes the accidental encounter may itself have disrupted whatever the men were doing. “It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they were planning,” she said.
The farmer’s account also appears to challenge Trump’s description of how the suspects were caught. President Donald Trump said Sunday that the operation was “fantastic,” praised cooperation between the United States and Britain and claimed the suspects had been watched for some time.
British reporting, however, indicated that the police operation itself was not intelligence-led and that officers responded after receiving the call about the suspicious vehicles. At the same time, residents said security around the base had visibly tightened in the days before the arrests, suggesting authorities had broader concerns about a possible threat even if they had not identified the men or vans in advance.
‘Thank God we spotted them’
The farmer said she first assumed the vans might have been abandoned. Their appearance quickly made her suspicious: they carried commercial branding that appeared false, and a phone number displayed on at least one vehicle was missing a digit. Fuel2U, the company whose name appeared on a van, said the vehicles had no connection to the business.
When she turned around, her headlights revealed the men nearby. She told The Telegraph that the realization of what might have happened only fully struck her afterward, saying it was “pretty incredible” to think she may have come face to face with potential terrorists and helped foil a plot.
“It was clear they had just got there. Thank God we spotted them,” she said.
At the time, her instinct was simpler. She saw masked men running through the countryside in the early hours near a heavily secured military installation and immediately concluded something was badly wrong.
The encounter also left her thinking about how vulnerable she had been. Had the group attempted to stop her from leaving, she told British media, the outcome could have been very different.
Her unease was heightened by what villagers had already noticed around Fairford. She said B-1 bombers that had been stationed there were moved earlier in the week, entrances were blocked with heavy machinery and civilian personnel had been sent home by Friday. Residents had also begun noticing unfamiliar people around the small village who they suspected were plainclothes police.
Those signs made what she saw on the road even harder to dismiss.
“A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the air base is on high alert,” she said. “I think it’s absolutely astonishing.”
Five suspects remain at center of terror investigation
British counterterrorism police took over the investigation after the five arrests. Authorities imposed a 400-meter cordon around the vehicles and evacuated about 85 nearby households while military explosive ordnance specialists examined the scene.
Investigators are examining several possible motives. British media reported that one line of inquiry is whether Iran was connected to the suspected plot, though police have not publicly identified the suspects, disclosed their nationalities or established a motive.
RAF Fairford has particular strategic significance because it serves as a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force and has been used by American aircraft for missions against Iran. Tehran had previously warned that bases used to launch attacks on Iranian territory could be considered targets.
Security around Fairford had already been strengthened during the conflict. Residents described barriers and heavy equipment appearing at entrances, while reports said the base had recently been placed on the highest U.S. force-protection alert level.
But for all the security measures surrounding one of the most sensitive military facilities in Britain, the moment that brought armed officers racing to the scene began with something far less sophisticated: a farmer, driving home late at night, wondering why three vans were blocking her road.

Bangkok streets turn to canals as days of heavy rain bring citywide flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:16:11 UTC
16:16:11 KST

Parts of Bangkok remained under water on Monday after days of heavy rain overwhelmed the city's drainage system.
In Bang Kapi, residents waded through knee- and waist-deep water to collect essential supplies, while small boats helped people reach shops. Some areas recorded more than 30 centimetres of rain, with around 300 millimetres falling in 48 hours in parts of the capital.
The flooding disrupted roads, businesses and public transport, with some cars partly submerged. Authorities declared a disaster across all 50 districts and made Monday and Tuesday public holidays to reduce traffic and help emergency services respond. Bangkok Metropolitan Administration schools were also closed.
More than 200 temporary shelters were opened, with around 3,000 people staying in them on Sunday. Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said drainage systems were working at full capacity, but warned that high canal levels could prolong flooding in some communities.
Officials said two to three rain-free days could be needed to drain the remaining water.
Flooding has also affected more than 545,000 people in 25 provinces outside Bangkok. At least eight people have died since 16 September, according to disaster officials. No deaths had been reported in Bangkok at the latest update.

Almost all forms of heating to become more expensive for Estonians this winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:16:00 UTC
16:16:00 KST

Almost all forms of heating to become more expensive for Estonians this winter
Prices for nearly all types of heating will rise as the heating season gets underway. The increase will be particularly steep for those who heat with natural gas, as its price on the global market has more than doubled.
Most homes in Estonia are heated by central heating, but wood-burning stoves, gas heating and heat pumps are also used. Global fuel prices have risen because of ongoing crises and this could have an impact on the cost of heating homes this winter.
Merike Kaljula, a longtime music teacher in Türi, still heats the more than 100-year-old house where she was born with firewood. Although firewood became more expensive this year, she believes switching to another type of heating would cost even more.
"I've been offered electric heating, like the heat pumps and everything they have now, but I don't want it. I bought my firewood at the beginning of May and it was €80 per cubic meter, and I bought 15 cubic meters. It is more expensive, but since I'm happy with Toosikannu, I'm not complaining," Kaljula said.
Mart Liivak, head of firewood sellers Harju Puu, said the increase in firewood prices over the past year has nevertheless been small because raw material prices have remained stable. There is a significant price difference between wet and dry firewood.
"The price of dry firewood may rise by 5 to 10 percent at most. When producing kiln-dried firewood, wood chips — which we use to heat the drying chamber — are a fairly significant expense for us. Electricity costs are also considerably higher. The lowest cost is for fresh, loose firewood, which explains the large price difference," Liivak said.
Wood pellets, however, are reaching record-high prices. They did not see their usual summer price decline because Estonia's pellet exports to Poland have increased by half.
"They had this Clean Air program, which helped quite a large proportion of people replace their wood-fired boilers, coal-fired boilers and old heating systems with more modern ones," Liivak said.
Central heating can be used to heat a row house or several apartment buildings at once. More than half of Estonia's residents, however, use district heating, through which heat producers supply large heating areas.
"We have eight district heating areas, including Tallinn and Maardu. Unfortunately, prices are indeed rising in five of the eight, with an average increase of around 10 percent. We've seen a relatively large increase in fuel prices. As for Tallinn specifically, the Iru waste-to-energy unit supplies heat to Tallinn residents and it raised its price by 6 percent this spring. Wood chips have risen by around 20 percent, by our estimate," said Robert Kitt, head of Utilitas Estonia.
The main culprit behind the price increases, however, is natural gas, which district heating companies use to produce between one-third and one-half of their heat. Compared with the previous heating season, the market price of natural gas has risen two and a half times because of the Hormuz crisis. Elenger is trying to keep its price increases smaller.
"The average price during the previous heating season was €0.54 per cubic meter and today it is €0.96. That's not a doubling," said Elenger Commercial Director Armen Kasparov.
Elenger has 15,000 customers who heat their homes with gas. Most live in detached houses, while 25 percent are apartment associations with their own boilers. The size of their price increase depends on the gas plan they use.
"If you've been on a market-price plan, that's the fairest comparison. You can expect an increase of 35 to 40 percent compared with the previous heating season, while district heating providers will also see some percentage increase," Kasparov said.
Narva is in the worst situation because the city's district heating system depends predominantly on gas. In a city where heating was inexpensive until recently, heating prices have now risen to the highest level in Estonia.
"There is one municipality in Latvia where it is even more expensive. They're at €150, while we're at €137 per megawatt-hour. And what's the reason? The price of gas," Narva Mayor Jaan Toots said.
Natural gas is currently more expensive than shale oil. Narva is asking the state for a special permit to use shale oil for heating this winter, saying residents could otherwise become unable to pay their bills.
"Thirty percent are pensioners and 13 percent are unemployed and both figures are considerably higher than in Estonia as a whole. And that hurts. Worst of all, of course, we have Khrushchev-era apartment buildings that, partly because of the residents themselves, have not been insulated or weatherproofed and have old windows, so the costs are enormous. Heating now eats up half the money pensioners receive. So this is a very serious problem for me as mayor and we hope the Environmental Board grants the exemption," Toots said.
The Environmental Board will issue Narva a special heating permit next week. Utilitas is also considering applying for one.
"As a provider of an essential service, continuity is naturally one of the most important things for us and we are seriously considering applying for permission to use other reserve fuels, including shale oil, should the need arise," Kitt said.
Utilitas will be able to reduce its dependence on gas to below 10 percent during the next heating season as a large-scale wastewater and seawater heat pump plant in Paljassaare nears completion.

Source: "AK. Nädal"

DRC Ebola cases surpass 8,000 for the first time in the outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:12:50 UTC
16:12:50 KST

The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has risen above 8,000 for the first time in the Central African country's ongoing outbreak, government data showed on Monday.
The latest situation report from the public health institute put the number of cases at 8,067 and deaths at 3,901.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, became the largest and deadliest in DRC's history after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is second only to the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Near $3 billion mobilised for Ebola response
Last week, the World Health Organization said the outbreak remains uncontrolled despite improvement in some areas, as cases surge in North Kivu province.
Children under 5 remain especially vulnerable, the agency says, with a case fatality rate above 60% versus about 40% for adults.
Africa's public health agency, Africa CDC, said Thursday $2.9 billion has been mobilised for the Ebola response, as cases climb in DRC.
Director General Jean Kaseya announced the funding after a US-convened G20+ meeting of foreign ministers in New York on Wednesday.
Held on the margins of the UN General Assembly, the talks brought together DRC, Uganda, G20 members, partner countries and international organisations.
US contributions total $886 million, while the EU mobilised €500 million ($568 million) in emergency aid, vaccines and treatment, Africa CDC said.
"Pledges alone will not stop Ebola," Kaseya said, urging that every dollar be traced from commitment to services reaching affected communities.
Africa CDC pledged to strengthen financial tracking with DRC and partners so funds reach the frontline faster and gaps become visible.
Prime Minister Judith Suminwa called the outbreak a "major test" and said fighting it is "an absolute priority" for DRC.

At least 10 people have been rescued from Mount Himlung, a 7,126-metre (23,380-foot) peak in north-central Nepal after the avalanche hit on Sunday.

According to NDRRMA, 5,500 people were still missing and 13,795 had been rescued.
Researchers from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) group said in a report released last week that the disaster was not caused by a single extreme weather event but rather a “compound crisis” shaped by long-term warming, glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and geological instability.

French far right gains ground in Senate months before presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:08:52 UTC
16:08:52 KST

France's National Rally (RN) party and its allies secured a record 14 seats in France's 348-seat Senate after Sept. 27 elections, for the first time crossing the threshold to form a caucus.
RN co-leader Marine Le Pen hailed the result as a "historic victory," mere months before France's presidential race in which she is a front-runner.
While the right-wing-dominated Senate is less influential than the French parliament's lower chamber — the National Assembly — the results underscore the growing popularity of the far right in France and elsewhere in Europe.
Local elected officials vote for half of the Senate every three years, with each senator serving a six-year term. The Senate shares legislative powers and represents France's local territorial communities.
The far-right party first entered the parliament's upper chamber in 2014. In the Sept. 27 vote, the RN won nine seats, adding to the three won in 2023.
Two seats were won by the Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR) party, an RN ally that split from the conservative Republicans in 2024.
The RN leadership said their senators would form a parliamentary group with UDR representatives.
Commenting on the results, Le Pen declared that the party's "senators will play an essential role in the presidential campaign, carrying and defending the voice of local communities."
The anti-immigration, nationalist RN is France's most popular party and the strongest opposition force. Polling consistently shows Le Pen beating all rivals in the April 2027 presidential election.
Incumbent centrist President Emmanuel Macron will not run, as he is concluding his constitutionally permitted two consecutive terms.
The RN has long faced criticism over a favorable attitude toward Russia, an image the RN tried to shed after Moscow's all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Le Pen and RN co-leader Jordan Bardella recently lashed out at Moscow after its seizure of French and other European business assets in Russia. Both also said France should continue supporting Kyiv militarily but that Paris must scale back its financial support.

The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
“We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.”
He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies.
Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign and rapidly moved south-west, seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast.
The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed over Yemen, with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022.
The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles.
Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air.
He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation.
“Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.”
His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day.
“What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said.
Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students.
“On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said.
The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic.
“The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour.
The resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses.
Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people.
“It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods.
The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen.
“This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.”

Eighth round of China-U.S. economic and trade consultations yields positive consensus: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
15:06:17 CST
16:06:17 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China and the United States held the eighth round of their economic and trade consultations in New York and Washington, D.C., the United States, from Sept. 20 to 23, reaching positive consensus that contributes to the economic and trade outcomes of the meeting of the two heads of state, China's Ministry of Commerce said on Monday.
The two sides agreed to establish the Board of Trade under the China-U.S. economic and trade consultation mechanism, with the primary target of optimizing bilateral trade, the ministry noted in a statement.
The ministry said the Board of Trade will provide an important platform and institutional guarantee for the two countries to continuously expand the list of cooperation and shorten the list of problems in economic and trade affairs.
To implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, China and the United States have held multiple rounds of consultations under the Board of Trade framework on an arrangement for a 30-billion-U.S. dollar reciprocal tariff reduction, and have reached consensus, the ministry said.
The two sides agreed to reduce tariffs on about 30 billion U.S. dollars' worth of goods imported from each other on a reciprocal basis, with tariffs on around 90 percent of the covered products to be lowered to most-favored-nation rates. These reductions will be implemented simultaneously after each side completes domestic legal procedures, according to the ministry.
The economic and trade teams of the two sides agreed to include Chinese coal imports from the United States in the reciprocal tariff reduction framework, which is expected to facilitate Chinese coal imports from the United States in 2027 and 2028, the ministry revealed.
Importing U.S. coal will complement China's domestic coal market while providing stable revenue and employment for the U.S. coal industry, helping to stabilize and expand bilateral trade, the ministry explained.
The two sides also agreed on lists of products subject to the 30-billion-U.S. dollar reciprocal tariff reductions, based on their respective market needs and industrial interests. The United States will reduce tariffs on Chinese imports including toys, home appliances, baby products, kitchen and bathroom goods, and holiday gifts, while China will lower tariffs on U.S. imports including agricultural products, personal care products, medical devices and coal, according to the ministry.
The two sides will jointly release their respective lists of products covered by the tariff reductions, the ministry added.
This arrangement is expected to help stabilize bilateral trade and create more favorable conditions for Chinese exports to the U.S. market, while meeting domestic market demand and strengthening trade cooperation in agricultural products, energy, manufactured goods and consumer goods, the ministry noted.
In the consultations, China and the United States also agreed to establish the Board of Investment under the China-U.S. economic and trade consultation mechanism. It will provide an institutionalized communication platform for both sides, with the two countries' economic and trade teams conducting regular dialogue on potential investment opportunities and barriers, the ministry said.
The two sides further agreed to establish an agricultural working group under the Board of Trade, to be co-chaired by China's Ministry of Commerce and the Office of the United States Trade Representative, with participation from relevant regulatory agencies of both countries, said the ministry.
The working group will discuss issues including two-way market access and regulatory matters for agricultural products. Both sides agreed to hold the working group's first meeting before the end of 2026, the ministry said.
The two sides reached a consensus in principle on financial services. China will examine and approve applications from financial service institutions of all countries, including those with U.S. capital, to conduct business and establish branches in China.
China hopes the United States will also provide a fair, transparent and stable policy environment for Chinese financial institutions, said the ministry.
As the two sides' lead negotiators under the China-U.S. economic and trade consultation mechanism, Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent established a dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI) and held their first discussion on AI-related risks and benefits. The two sides agreed to hold the next dialogue before the end of November this year and to set up a communication channel for AI incidents.
On the basis of extending the joint arrangements of economic and trade consultations in Kuala Lumpur through Jan. 10, 2027, China and the United States agreed to continue actively discussing the issue, with a view to reaching a mutually agreed solution.
Such an arrangement, on the one hand, gives both sides room to take stock of and assess the implementation of the joint arrangements and consider how to move China-U.S. economic and trade relations forward. On the other hand, by combining a time-bound extension with continued active discussions, it provides a relatively stable and predictable policy environment for cooperation between businesses of the two countries, according to the ministry.
It is believed that the two sides will continue their efforts and seek a positive solution on a further extension through high-level economic and trade interactions before the end of the year, the ministry noted.
The two sides also exchanged views on increasing direct passenger flights between the two countries, agreeing to maintain communication on increasing China-U.S. flights and related matters.
Since last year, China and the United States have held eight rounds of economic and trade consultations. During the latest consultations, the two sides reaffirmed and renewed their commitment to fully implementing the consensus reached in previous rounds of economic and trade talks, which will help create favorable conditions and a stable environment for bilateral economic and trade cooperation, while also contributing to global economic growth, said the ministry. ■

Russia Revives Secret Nuclear Bunker Built to Launch Retaliatory Strike. Here’s What We Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:04:32 UTC
16:04:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Revives Secret Nuclear Bunker Built to Launch Retaliatory Strike. Here’s What We Know
Russia has carried out a major modernization of a secret underground command complex in the Ural Mountains linked to Perimetr, the Cold War-era nuclear command system known in the West as “Dead Hand.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a joint investigation by Danwatch, The Sunday Times, and the Dossier Center published on September 26, thousands of Russian military procurement records indicate that large-scale work at Object 1335, buried inside Mount Kosvinsky in the Sverdlovsk region, began in 2018.
The investigators reviewed more than two million Russian military procurement documents and found orders for construction materials, excavation equipment, ventilation systems, electrical infrastructure, and protective equipment associated with the facility.
The purchases included around 22,000 tons of steel, more than 56,000 tons of cement, roughly 600 kilometers of electrical cables, as well as specialized filtration systems designed to protect against chemical, biological, and radioactive contamination.
The Sunday Times separately reported that procurement documents refer to at least 24 underground chambers and show that the distance between the facility’s main and emergency exits is approximately 2.5 kilometers. Satellite imagery also shows extensive excavation and new construction around the mountain.
Object 1335 is believed to serve as a protected command center for Russia’s Strategic Missile Forces. Former personnel described the underground network as extensive enough for buses to move between different sections of the complex.
The facility has long been associated with Perimetr, a Soviet-designed backup nuclear command system intended to preserve Russia’s ability to order a retaliatory strike if its senior leadership and normal communications channels were destroyed in a nuclear attack.
Pavel Podvig, a nuclear disarmament expert and head of the Russian Nuclear Forces project, told The Sunday Times that “Perimeter is actually a communication system,” designed to ensure that a retaliatory order can still be transmitted after an attack.
Details of Perimetr’s current operation remain classified. However, Russian military publications uncovered by the investigators indicate that the system has undergone further modernization.
Retired Major General V. G. Khalin, who participated in its development, wrote that its automation system and technical capabilities had been upgraded, including through mobile command posts and space-based communications.
Another Russian military veteran wrote that Object 1335 was placed on combat duty in 2023, while Khalin later referred to the facility as having the technical capability for an automatic retaliatory strike.
Danwatch said the expansion of Object 1335 forms part of a broader modernization of Russia’s nuclear forces and command infrastructure. The Kremlin and presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not respond to requests for comment from the investigative outlets.
Russia has also continued exercising other parts of its strategic nuclear forces. On April 2, Russia conducted drills in Siberia involving mobile RS-24 Yars intercontinental ballistic missile systems, with crews practicing dispersal, combat duty, protection from simulated air attacks, and operations under conditions of radioactive contamination.
The Yars is one of the core systems in Russia’s nuclear arsenal, with a reported range of up to 11,000 kilometers and the ability to carry multiple independently targetable warheads.

Dutch river cruise stranded as Rhine falls to new record levels
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The river Rhine dropped to a new record low level at the weekend at the Dutch-German border, with no sign of fresh rainfall in the days ahead.
The river measured 6.1m at Lobith, the point where it flows into the Netherlands, on Sunday, below the previous record of 6.12m set in August.
Further upstream in Cologne, a Dutch cruise ship became stuck in mid-river as water levels dropped to just 40 centimetres on the gauge, leaving around 1.5 metres of navigable depth.
The Dutch Melody, which carries 140 passengers, was able to continue downriver after being assisted by another ship, German river police said. The four-deck vessel is due to arrive in Nijmegen later on Monday.
River levels are expected to drop further this week due to low rainfall in the Alps. At Lobith the flow of water has fallen below 600 cubic metres per second for the first time on record.
Dutch water authorities have had to impose restrictions on river traffic as channels became narrower and shallower during the summer drought.
Vessels using the IJssel to travel from Arnhem to Zutphen are having to take a 300km detour after Rijkswaterstaat imposed a one-way system.
Some ferries across the rivers have been cancelled and river cruises have had to cancel trips or shorten their itineraries because sections of the Rhine have become impassable.

Why is the EU looking for associate members? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot

The EU Commission opened the door for Canada to become its first-ever “associate member” as both parties want to reduce dependence on the US. But what's behind the proposal? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Canada might become Europe’s first "associate member” during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France, on 16 September.
It’s the first time the EU has offered this status to a third country. If all 27 member states agree, the EU would have to create a new legal framework, including rights and obligations, since current EU treaties do not include “associate membership”.
The proposal does not mean Canada will join the EU. It would establish a deeper EU-Canada partnership that goes beyond existing cooperation, including the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and the military mobility and logistics projects under Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO).
The aim is to build an “Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space”, said President von der Leyen. While not yet finalised, the partnership would cover critical policies across manufacturing, energy, minerals, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity, the Arctic, as well as a tech alliance and integrated defence industrial bases.
The push comes as both partners’ relationship with the US grows more uncertain, and dependence becomes riskier.
Stronger ties with Canada could help the EU reduce its reliance on the US for energy, technology, and defence. At the same time, the partnership could give Canada a like-minded ally as it seeks to reduce its economic dependence while caught up in a tariff dispute with the US, which, as of August 2026, is imposing up to 50% duties on some Canadian goods.

====================================================================================================

Forget the famous names. Here is who actually deserves this year’s Nobel peace prize | Haakon Gjerløw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:00:28 UTC
16:00:28 KST

The Nobel peace prize is not a contest determined by fame. Yet the betting markets consistently gravitate towards the biggest names in global politics – among them this year, Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
That misses what the prize is for. The real work of building peace is often done far from the headlines: by courts that uphold international law, journalists who document atrocities, and humanitarian organisations that protect communities. With the 2026 prize due to be announced on 9 October, the Nobel committee has an opportunity to remind the world that peace is built through institutions and cooperation, not just diplomatic grandstanding.
Despite the favourable odds, Trump will not win. A sitting president waging a war against Iran is an impossible candidate for a prize intended to advance peace. Whatever Trump’s diplomatic efforts elsewhere, the Nobel committee will consider the totality of a candidate’s contribution – a record that now includes allegations of US war crimes.
The Ukrainian president is also unlikely to win. Awarding the Nobel peace prize to the serving commander-in-chief of a country fighting a major war would risk turning the prize into an endorsement of one side in the conflict, regardless of Ukraine’s right to defend itself. It would also sit uneasily with Alfred Nobel’s will, which called for efforts to promote “fraternity between nations”, reduce standing armies and advance peace.
Look past the headline-grabbing names, and Save the Children, Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms and the international court of justice all feature near the top of Polymarket’s rankings, with a current combined 28% chance of winning. On these candidates, the markets may well be closer to calling the result. But they are also missing several of the world’s most deserving peace-builders.
As head of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, an independent body that conducts research on the conditions for peaceful relations between nations, groups and individuals, I am regularly asked whether the prize should be awarded at all, given the scale of conflict today. The wars in Ukraine and Sudan continue to exact a massive human toll, while the war involving Iran has added another dangerous front to an unstable international landscape. Our latest conflict trends report recorded 65 state-based armed conflicts in 2025 – the highest number since records began in 1946.
Such a backdrop only strengthens my belief that the more war there is, the more the Nobel peace prize matters.
There is no shortage of worthy people and organisations the prize should honour. Each year, I publish a list of candidates I believe deserve the prize. Several who have featured on past lists have subsequently become Nobel laureates.
This year, my list includes the international court of justice and the international criminal court (ICC). Rules matter only if they can be enforced, and these courts uphold a principle increasingly under pressure: that international law applies even to the powerful. At a time when the US administration is placing sanctions on ICC officials, awarding the courts the prize would affirm the importance of the international legal order.
International law also depends on knowing when it has been broken. Journalists provide the evidence, often at enormous personal risk. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) recorded 132 journalists and media workers killed in 2025, the deadliest year in its records. It attributed two-thirds of those deaths to Israel. Protecting journalism protects our ability to establish what happens in war – essential for accountability and peace. The CPJ would be a fitting laureate.
Protecting civilians, particularly children, is another fundamental task. Save the Children works globally to prevent and respond to grave violations against children in conflict. In Ukraine, Mykola Kuleba’s Save Ukraine has returned more than 1,700 children from Russia and occupied territories. In Sudan, the Emergency Response Rooms have built community-led networks providing food, medical care and other lifesaving services amid war.
International cooperation creates predictability and reduces the risk of conflict. The International Space Station (ISS) is an extraordinary example: for more than 25 years, geopolitical rivals have sustained a peaceful scientific partnership even as relations on Earth have deteriorated. As the ISS approaches decommissioning and space becomes more crowded, commercialised and weaponised, a Nobel peace prize for the partnership would celebrate what sustained cooperation can achieve – and underscore the continuing importance of keeping space governed by common rules and peaceful collaboration.
Peace is something we construct: it is achieved through cooperation that reduces uncertainty, humanitarian rules that restrain cruelty, courts that impose consequences and journalists who ensure violations cannot simply be erased.
The Nobel committee has an opportunity to turn the world’s attention towards some of the essential tools for securing international peace. In a world breaking records for conflict, it should look past the big names and bet on those doing the painstaking work of building peace.
- 
  Haakon Gjerløw is the acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo

Israeli occupiers on Monday attacked the towns of Ras Karkar and Deir Abu Mashal in the central West Bank and set Palestinian vehicles on fire, according to local sources.
A group of occupiers attacked the Al-Shaab al-Ghuwait area in Ras Karkar north of Ramallah and set fire to an agricultural tractor and a truck, the sources told Anadolu.
In the village of Deir Abu Mashal west of Ramallah, occupiers attacked a Palestinian home and set fire to a vehicle parked in its courtyard, the same sources said.
The attacks came amid escalating occupier violence in the West Bank, particularly as the olive harvest season approaches, a period that usually sees an increase in attacks on farmers, their land and property.
In June, 14 UN experts warned that the sharp rise in occupier violence backed by the state posed an existential threat to Palestinian communities.
According to figures from the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli occupiers carried out 628 attacks in the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, in August.
Palestinians estimate that around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in the West Bank across 194 illegal settlements and 400 settlement outposts.
Since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip on Oct. 8, 2023, the Israeli army and occupiers have intensified attacks across the occupied territory, killing 1,206 Palestinians, including 254 children, injuring around 13,350 others, and leading to the arrest of more than 24,600 people, according to Palestinian figures.

Does Europe need new global partners? Take our poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:00:08 UTC
16:00:08 KST

Could Canada become a test case for a wider EU partnership model? Relations reached a historic turning point when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested making Canada the EU’s first-ever "associate member”.
The concept of an "associate member" is a new political framework that does not currently exist in EU treaties, which mandate that only geographically European states can apply for full membership.
But the EU wants Canada to join forces in an "Alliance for the Future" that expands cooperation well beyond standard trade agreements. This includes integrating defence industrial bases, securing critical raw materials and energy supplies, aligning on advanced technology (like artificial intelligence and quantum computing), and introducing shared mobility programs for young citizens to live and study across the Atlantic.
Following the breakdown in bilateral negotiations, U.S. President Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billions of Canadian goods, triggering an economic dispute and matching dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.
So, faced with this economic coercion, and repeated suggestions from U.S. President Donald Trump regarding Canada becoming the 51st state, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has championed a strategy to reduce reliance on Washington, actively building global alliances.
Will the new alliance between the EU and Canada strengthen them both? Or will it bring unnecessary pressure from threatening international actors? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across XL's EU-wide coverage, including videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

When hospital patients swelter, is it time for Switzerland to turn to air-conditioning?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

When hospital patients swelter, is it time for Switzerland to turn to air-conditioning?
The long hot summer is over, but debates on how to keep buildings cool during heatwaves continue. In Switzerland, questions remain about the role of air-conditioning and restrictions on its use.
The question came up time and again during the stifling summer of 2026. Social media usersExternal link, foreign tourists at hotel receptions and hospital patients all wondered: why is air-conditioning so rare in Switzerland?
Indeed, air-conditioning systems are an exception in the country. In many cantons, installing split-system air-conditioning – made up of an indoor and an outdoor unit – means complying with some strict energy, environmental and town-planning regulations. Surveys across EuropeExternal link and in Switzerland show however that most people are in favour of relaxing any restrictions.
“In Switzerland, heat already claims more lives than road traffic accidents,” saysExternal link Arno Schlüter, professor of architecture and building systems at the federal technology institute ETH Zurich. Air-conditioning is sure to become more important, in particular to protect the most vulnerable people in hospitals, care homes and schools. However, the expert cautions, a future in which every apartment and every office is air-conditioned is not the solution.
Like in France and Germany, air-conditioning has become a hot political issue in Switzerland, prompting several parliamentary motions at both cantonal and national levels. The federal parliament is due to discuss the matter, along with other questions related to heat and drought, in a special session on September 30.
>>Switzerland was built for winter; now it has to equip itself to cope with increasingly hot summers:
More
Switzerland’s new energy challenge: keeping cool in a warming climate
More air-conditioning to protect the vulnerable
The right-wing Swiss People’s Party wants current restrictions in Switzerland to be eased. In a parliamentary initiativeExternal link, Thomas Burgherr has proposed changing the legal framework so that a permit is no longer required to install split-system air-conditioning.
For the People’s Party parliamentarian, a lack of air-conditioning also has negative economic consequences. People arrive at work less refreshed, hotel guests are left disappointed, and high temperatures in industrial plants increase the risk of accidents.
Modern air-conditioning systems, Burgherr notes, have a much lower environmental impact than in the past. In summer, they can be powered by solar electricity, of which there is ample supply.
The centre-right Radical-Liberal Party also stresses that installing air-conditioning to protect the population must be a top priority. A motionExternal link tabled in mid-September calls for a simplified notification procedure, similar to that already in place for fitting solar panels.
The aim is also to limit reliance on portable air-conditioning units. These do not require special permission, but are generally less efficient and consume more electricity than fixed systems.
Even left-wing political parties – which are traditionally skeptical of artificial cooling – no longer rule out its use in certain situations, such as hospitals, care homes for the elderly and schools, as reportedExternal link by the Swiss public broadcaster RTS.
Air-conditioning increases comfort on the hottest days of the year and reduces the health risks associated with heatwaves. However, its use leads to higher electricity consumption and exacerbates the climate crisisExternal link. Worldwide, air-conditioning systems consume around 7% of electricity and produce 3% of CO₂ emissions.
Medical certificate needed
In Switzerland, fewer than one in ten homes is fitted with a fixed air-conditioning system, which is below the European average of around 20%. In the US and Japan, some 90% have artificial air-cooling.
Installing a fixed air-conditioning system in Switzerland can also be more complicated than in neighbouring countries. There is, in fact, no single federal law; instead, the rules depend on cantonal laws and various energy and environmental regulations.
In most cantons, a building permit or energy authorisation must first be obtained. Geneva is one of the most restrictive cantons in this respect. Those aiming to install a permanent system may have to demonstrate a genuine need by providing a medical certificate. In Fribourg and Neuchâtel, the energy used for air-conditioning must be offset by locally produced renewable sources.
Despite the restrictions, the market for split-system installations is growing in Switzerland, albeit slowly. Sales are rising by around 2% a year, according to GebäudeKlima Schweiz, the Swiss Association for Heating, Ventilation and Air-Conditioning Systems.
A rarity in Swiss hospitals
Air-conditioning is also rare in facilities which care for particularly vulnerable people. An investigation published in June by the news portal Schweiz HeuteExternal link shows that in the major Swiss hospitals, air-conditioned rooms and wards remain the exception. At Geneva University Hospital, indoor temperatures soared above 30°C this summer.
It is not just the patients who suffer the consequences; healthcare staff are impacted too. Some facilities have taken action by installing portable air-conditioners and fans and setting up air-conditioned spaces for the most vulnerable patients.
Overheating is a particular problem in older or protected buildings. Tomas Honegger, a spokesman for Bern’s Inselspital, told Swissinfo that before installing air-conditioning systems, various building regulations, health and hygiene requirements and patient safety must be taken into account. Meanwhile air-conditioning can, for instance, lead to an increased risk of bacterial proliferation.
In newly built hospital buildings, by contrast, air-conditioning is standard across many departments, Honegger said. “Patient areas in newer buildings are largely, if not entirely, air-conditioned.” Inselspital has renovated most of its facilities in recent years, and around 75% of the buildings are now air-conditioned.
Protecting the elderly in care homes
The situation is similar in care homes. “Most residents do not have air-conditioning in their rooms,” says Christina Zweifel of Curaviva, the umbrella association for the country’s elderly care institutions. Many facilities opt instead for organisational adjustments, sun-shading systems and other passive cooling measures.
Care homes are well able to assess which architectural, technical or organisational solutions best suit their specific circumstances, Zweifel adds. However, they must be given the necessary leeway, and permission, to implement the most effective measures to protect vulnerable people during heatwaves.
A much broader debate than just air-conditioning
The Swiss Energy Foundation, a non-profit organisation which advocates for ecological energy policies, acknowledges that air-conditioning can be a sensible – and sometimes even essential – solution for coping with the heat. However, the foundation stressesExternal link, it should only be considered after trying out passive cooling measures.
According to Schlüter of ETH Zurich, with the climate as it is in Switzerland, much can already be achieved by simple yet effective measures – such as shading systems, night-time ventilation and fans to improve air circulation – and by changing daily habits.
Protection from heat is a broader societal challenge that requires a coordinated approach based on climate-adapted urban planning, appropriate infrastructure and green spaces. As such, for Schlüter, the debate should not overly focus on air-conditioning, but also on the different ways to ensure the well-being of people inside buildings. “This calls for a shift in mindset,” he concludes.

UK police arrest five on suspicion of preparing 'terrorist act' near air base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:59:13 UTC
15:59:13 KST

A US Air Force B-1 Lancer bomber is pictured on the tarmac at RAF Fairford base on Sept. 27, 2026 in Fairford, England. (Photo by Leon Neal/Getty Images)
British police arrested five men near an air base used by the U.S. Air Force on Sept. 27 on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, prompting the evacuation of about 85 households.
Armed officers detained the men in Whelford, near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, after an emergency call about three suspicious vehicles apparently heading toward the base, London’s Metropolitan Police said.
The men were initially arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act before being further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Counterterrorism officers took over the investigation.
Police said they believed the incident had been contained. A 400-meter cordon was placed around three white vans while army bomb disposal experts examined them. A nearby leisure center was opened to accommodate evacuated residents.
U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been “looking to do big damage” at the base and that U.S. and British authorities had worked together on the case.
“We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he told reporters.
A resident told the PA news agency she had alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking a road and a group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, attending the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool, thanked police, the armed forces and residents who had left their homes while precautionary checks were carried out.
Defense Minister Wes Streeting said he had spoken with his U.S. counterpart, Pete Hegseth, and that the two countries were working closely. Asked about possible Iranian involvement, he declined to speculate.
In March, then Prime Minister Keir Starmer authorized the use of Fairford and another U.K. base for what he described as defensive U.S. operations against Iranian missile sites.
The U.S. Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing, based at Fairford, said no U.S. Air Force personnel had been involved in the incident. It said it was coordinating with British authorities to ensure the safety of military personnel and local communities.

Late-September heat sets records across Switzerland

Late-September heat sets records across Switzerland
Record temperatures were registered north of the Alps over the final weekend of September, with many locations reporting unprecedented highs. In Basel-Binningen, in northwestern Switzerland, temperatures reached 30.1°C.
“Never before has a hot day been recorded so late in the year on the northern side of the Alps,” said the weather service Meteonews on the social media platform X.
In Basel-Binningen, the highest temperature of this summer – 39.7°C – had already been recorded on July 30. The weather station therefore equalled the record for the northern side of the Alps set by Geneva-Cointrin in July 2015.
More
Switzerland’s record-breaking summer by numbers
Elsewhere, Delémont, in canton Jura, recorded 29.6°C on Sunday. The Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology (MeteoSwiss), also reported temperatures of up to 30°C.
It will remain warm for the next few days, with temperatures of 25°C to 29°C expected, according to the weather services.

Wife of Malaysia’s former Premier Mahathir dies at 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:58:28 UTC
15:58:28 KST

Faisal Mahmud
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali, wife of Malaysia’s former Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, died on Monday at the age of 100, the veteran leader's office said.
Siti Hasmah died at the National Heart Institute (IJN) in Kuala Lumpur on Monday morning, state news agency Bernama reported, citing her son Mokhzani Mahathir.
She is survived by Mahathir, 101, and their seven children.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim expressed condolences to Mahathir and his family, saying Malaysia would remember Siti Hasmah’s contributions to the country.
“I express our deepest condolences and sympathies on the passing of the late Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali,” Anwar said on US social media platform X. “The nation will forever remember her maternal figure and cherish her contributions.”
Anwar said he directed officials to accord Siti Hasmah a funeral with full state honors.
Born in Klang, Selangor, in 1926, Siti Hasmah was among the first Malay women to become a doctor in Malaya. She graduated from the King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore in 1955 and later worked extensively in maternal and child health and rural public health.
She married Mahathir in 1956, and the couple marked their 70th wedding anniversary in August.
Mahathir served as Malaysia’s prime minister from 1981 to 2003 and again from 2018 to 2020.

Mediators press Iran for nuclear concession to revive ceasefire talks with US: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:58:25 UTC
15:58:25 KST

Merve Berker
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Mediators are pressing Iran to make concessions on its nuclear program in an effort to revive ceasefire negotiations with the US, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The initiative follows US President Donald Trump's rejection of an Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz and ended the US blockade of Iranian ports, according to the Journal.
Mediators described the effort as a long-shot attempt to secure movement from Tehran on its nuclear program, while Iran has so far given little indication that it is prepared to discuss the issue.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran remained open to negotiations but would respond to renewed military action.
"We are fully prepared for the war to resume," Araghchi told NBC News when asked about the Journal report.
"We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. But at the same time we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he added.
Arab mediators said Iran had made no concessions since Trump rejected its ceasefire proposal, while Gulf officials said Tehran wants Washington to offer concessions before negotiations advance.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, whose country is relaying messages between Washington and Tehran, said the conflict was becoming increasingly difficult to resolve.
"This conflict is very complex," he said, earlier in New York at a special UN General Assembly edition of the Qatar Economic Forum.
Iran wants Washington to return to a memorandum of understanding reached in June that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz and eventually beginning nuclear negotiations in exchange for measures including sanctions relief, the unfreezing of billions of dollars in Iranian funds held overseas and an end to the US blockade.
US officials, however, said Trump no longer wants to return to that agreement, while Washington has tightened sanctions and maintained its blockade.
A senior Middle Eastern official involved in the talks said Iran could compromise on its nuclear program but would require explicit assurances that Israel would not attack again after any US-Iran agreement.

South African tavern shooting death toll rises to 18 after one more victim dies
JOHANNESBURG, Sept 28 - The death toll from a tavern shooting over the weekend near Johannesburg has risen to 18 after another victim died in hospital, South African police said on Monday.
The shooting happened late on Saturday when suspects armed with AK-47 rifles opened fire at the tavern in Wedela township, about 80 km (50 miles) west of Johannesburg.
Police said in a statement that four of those killed had so far been identified: two South Africans and two nationals of Lesotho.
Violent crime remains a major challenge in South Africa despite efforts to curb one of the world's highest per-capita murder rates.
Police are still searching for the perpetrators of the shooting but said they managed to get clear pictures of them. One line of inquiry is that the incident was part of a turf war between the heavily armed gangs that control the illegal gold-mining trade in the area.
Authorities are also investigating another weekend shooting near Cape Town in which 10 people were killed. REUTERS

DPP’s Lai Jui-lung proposes smaller classes, lighter teacher workloads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:51:59 UTC
15:51:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) of the Democratic Progressive Party unveiled seven education pledges aimed at reducing class sizes and teacher workloads while improving student learning and support, CNA reported Sunday.
The plan, called “Kaohsiung Education for the Future,” would gradually reduce class sizes and review student-teacher ratios in preschools. It would also expand support for students with diverse learning needs.
Lai proposed adding counselors, social workers, special education staff, and school safety personnel. The plan also calls for improving the safety, nutrition, and quality of school lunches, per Newtalk.
For teachers, Lai proposed reducing administrative duties and gradually assigning non-teaching work to professional staff. Teachers with administrative roles would teach fewer hours, while a new support center would provide legal, psychological, and mediation services for school-related disputes.
The plan would encourage schools to develop programs based on their strengths and local characteristics. These could include reading, arts, sports, technology, and marine education, per UDN.
Lai also proposed age-appropriate artificial intelligence education and greater use of technology to reduce teachers’ workloads. Schools would strengthen digital literacy education and track students’ progress in core academic skills, per Liberty Times.
For international education, Lai proposed doubling the bilingual education budget without increasing teachers’ workloads. His plan would expand partnerships with overseas schools and opportunities for students to study abroad.
The plan would also provide international training for teachers and strengthen bilingual education in rural areas. Support for local languages would continue alongside bilingual education.
Lai also proposed expanding career education, partnerships between schools and businesses, internships, and employment opportunities. The plan would provide programs to help residents develop additional skills and a second area of expertise.
Lai said he would hold education roundtables with teachers, principals, parents, students, and representatives from preschool, special education, and vocational education. He also proposed a public dashboard to regularly report progress on the seven pledges.

SpaceX to attempt putting Starship rocket into Earth orbit for first time

SpaceX's supersized Starship rocket reaches Earth's orbit for the first time
SpaceX launched its enormous Starship into orbit for the first time on Monday, aiming for six full laps around Earth to prove its readiness for NASA’s Artemis moon programme. The 10-hour flight, which involves the deployment of 26 Starlink satellites, represents a milestone in the development of the massive launch vehicle.
Three years after its first test flight, SpaceX's supersized Starship rocket entered Earth's orbit for the first time on Monday, a key step in the development of the massive launch vehicle designed for future missions to the Moon and Mars.
The spacecraft almost failed to achieve the long-desired goal after one of its engines shut down too soon. But with everything else working well and the bad engine no longer needed, flight controllers decided after several tense minutes to proceed as planned.
“Starship is orbital,” Mission Control announced to cheers. Multiple previous tests had ended in spectacular explosions.
Read moreSpaceX: Why Chinese investors are banned from the biggest IPO in history
The test, expected to last about 10 hours, will involve the upper stage of the experimental rocket deploying 26 next-generation Starlink satellites in Earth's orbit.
After several years of development and testing in Texas, SpaceX began flying the rocket in its full configuration in 2023, deliberately following suborbital trajectories, which are safer and less challenging.
Watch moreWhose space is it? Europe scrambles as US rules satellite race
Numerous modifications have been made to the black-and-silver behemoth, the largest and most powerful object ever to have flown.
But immense technical challenges remain before Starship – which Musk hopes to make fully reusable – can be considered ready for commercial flights or to reach the Moon or Mars.
28,000km/h
With this new test, SpaceX hopes to usher in an "exciting new phase" of development that will include, among other things, tests of refuelling the rocket in orbit.
The spacecraft was launched Monday on a suborbital trajectory and then performed a second burn to reach orbit.
"That's the hardest part," requiring "more forces and more complex calculations", explained Kathleen Curlee, a senior analyst at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
Read moreSpaceX to build $100 billion rocket launch facility in southern Louisiana
To reach the necessary altitude and speed, "the rocket has to do different things when it's experiencing different levels of gravity", she told AFP.
On this flight, SpaceX is aiming for a circular orbit about 275km (171 miles) above the Earth, requiring a speed of about 28,000km/hour.
The spacecraft will then attempt to deploy satellites designed to expand the company's already massive satellite internet constellation.
Public expectations
The plan calls for the rocket to finish its journey in the Pacific Ocean after orbiting the Earth six times.
The huge first-stage booster, called "Super Heavy", was due to fall shortly after launch into waters of the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX does not plan to catch it this time using huge mechanical arms.

AI threat ‘not a hoax’ – Bill Gates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:48:52 UTC
15:48:52 KST

AI threat ‘not a hoax’ – Bill Gates
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has rejected US President Donald Trump’s dismissal of artificial intelligence safety concerns, arguing that Washington should impose mandatory safeguards on the rapidly advancing technology.
Trump has resisted calls to slow AI development, arguing that restrictions could allow China to overtake the US and dismissing fears surrounding the technology as a “hoax.”
Gates, however, has criticized what he described as a “nationalistic” approach to the issue and said safeguards would not undermine Washington’s technological advantage.
“No. It’s not a hoax at all,” Gates said when asked about Trump’s position in an interview with NBC News’ Meet the Press aired on Sunday.
Earlier this month, Trump dismissed warnings that AI could escape human control and destroy humanity. “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” he wrote, adding that the US is leading China and other countries.
Gates argued that treating the technology primarily as a geopolitical competition was encouraging a potentially dangerous rush to develop increasingly powerful systems.
“Because it’s cast in this nationalistic, you know, us-versus-them type thing, you have people who are saying, ‘Well, let’s just go full-speed ahead,’” he said, calling it “completely irresponsible” not to require AI systems to have safeguards and monitoring capabilities.
Gates acknowledged that the US government has “so little expertise” regarding some of the capabilities recently developed by private AI companies, but nevertheless insisted that government involvement is necessary.
“No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said, calling for legislation and mandatory monitoring of advanced models.
Gates also predicted Trump could ultimately change his position once convinced that such measures would not damage Washington’s standing against Beijing.
“I think after he hears from me and other people, including that this does not handicap us in whatever he thinks the nation-state race is, that, you know, we will come to a consensus,” Gates said.
Trump, however, doubled down on his position on Sunday. Asked about reports of rogue AI agents, he told Fox News: “I don’t worry about it.” The president argued that slowing development could sacrifice Washington’s technological advantage, which he estimated at around 18 months.
“We’re about maybe a year and a half up on China,” Trump said. “We’re leading... And why should we give that up?” He also confirmed plans to have dinner with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, one of the leading advocates of slowing development of increasingly capable AI systems.
Gates, meanwhile, disputed suggestions that Beijing would reject safeguards, arguing that China itself has an interest in preventing attacks involving advanced AI.
“Certainly, all countries should want the safeguards in place,” he said. “So anyone that says, ‘Well, you know, China won’t put these safeguards in place’ – I totally disagree with that.”
He nevertheless acknowledged that reaching an international agreement could prove more difficult than Cold War negotiations on nuclear weapons. Asked whether US-Soviet arms-control talks could serve as a model for Washington and Beijing, Gates replied: “Yeah, absolutely. This is more difficult than that was.”
The US and China have recently taken initial steps toward cooperation on AI risks, agreeing following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington to launch a bilateral dialogue on the technology.

Trump asked Xi Jinping whether China would like to buy American weapons - U.S. ambassador
Kyiv • UNN
Ambassador David Perdue said that Trump asked Xi Jinping about purchasing weapons. The White House and the State Department denied plans for such sales.
U.S. President Donald Trump proposed selling weapons to China while hosting its leader Xi Jinping last week, U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue said on Sunday. UNN reports this, citing The Guardian.
Details
"President Trump keeps saying: 'Hey, we sell weapons to other people all over the world.' He even asked President Xi whether he would like to buy some weapons," David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday, September 27.
The unusual statement, the publication writes, came during an interview about U.S. policy toward Taiwan, which had been waiting for months for Trump's approval of a new $14 billion arms-sale package after a record multibillion-dollar deal was unveiled last December.
Taiwan expresses "cautious optimism" regarding US weapons supplies19.05.26, 13:31 • 3719 views
Trump's level of commitment to defending Taiwan, it is noted, had previously been called into question. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was postponing the $14 billion arms-sale package for Taiwan, calling it "a very good bargaining chip" in relations with China.
Washington, the publication writes, has long maintained a position of strategic ambiguity on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the longstanding U.S. Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taiwan with sufficient military equipment for self-defense.
Beijing has repeatedly stated that it "firmly opposes" Washington's arms sales to the island democracy, which it considers a separatist province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to achieve this. During their meeting in Washington last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose "Taiwan independence," according to a report by China's official news agency Xinhua.
After Perdue's interview, the White House told The New York Times that the U.S. did not plan to sell weapons to China, while the State Department said: "U.S. law prohibits arms sales to China, and there is no proposal or plan to sell weapons to China."
What Taiwan says
Before the interview, Taiwan's Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi spoke about the serious military threat posed by China.
"Taiwan is facing a serious situation in the Taiwan Strait. Even though China's economy is declining, it continues to invest more resources in building up its military capabilities. In this context, the United States understands our defense needs very well," he told reporters in Taipei.
Trump did not mention the sale at last week's summit, saying only on Saturday that Xi understood his position on Taiwan.
Perdue himself told CNBC on Friday that Trump's policy toward Taiwan, including on arms sales, had not changed.
