Top French literary prize drops novel over AI allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:17:42 UTC
15:17:42 KST

AFP Photo
Organizers of France’s top literary prize, the Prix Goncourt, have removed a best-selling debut novel by Canadian-Haitian writer Thelyson Orelien from its longlist following online allegations that it was written with artificial intelligence.
The Goncourt Academy said on Sept. 25 the decision was made to preserve the integrity of the prize and the academy, whose role is to promote and honor literature written by humans.
Orelien, 38, has denied using AI to write his novel, “It Was Either That or Die,” and said the campaign against him was racially motivated and an attempt to silence his voice. He has also promised to produce a file that will prove he wrote the book himself.
The academy said “several credible researchers and journalists” had concluded that the novel was “in all likelihood very largely” produced by AI. However, AI use has not been conclusively established, with different detection tools producing different results.
The controversy has also been compounded by evidence of alleged plagiarism in Orelien’s earlier work. Montreal-based La Presse reported Wednesday that a newspaper column he wrote in 2013 was almost entirely a lightly edited translation of an article published several days earlier by The Philippine Star.
Radio-Canada also found that an Orelien novella that won an audience prize in 2010 contained phrases taken from “Le matin des magiciens,” a French-language book by Louis Pauwels and Jacques Bergier published in 1960.
“It Was Either That or Die” is a fictionalized account inspired by Orelien’s life. It follows a protagonist who leaves gang-ridden Haiti and undertakes an arduous journey through several countries before arriving in Canada.
The novel has been sold in more than 20 countries, including the United States. Paris-based publisher Grasset reportedly paid 300,000 euros for its French rights.
The controversy has highlighted the growing challenge of distinguishing AI-generated writing from human work and the disruption AI is causing in creative industries.
“This case is unprecedented in France, but it’s certainly not the last,” Alexandre Gefen, a researcher at France’s CNRS and co-author of a recent book on AI in the cultural sector, told AFP.
Orelien’s Canadian publisher Boreal suspended his promotional tour Friday but said it continued to stand by his work. Grasset also expressed its “absolute trust” and admiration for the author’s writing.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,531,060 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:17:17 UTC
15:17:17 KST

Russia has lost around 1,531,060 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Sept. 28.
The number includes 2,090 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,385 tanks, 25,450 armored combat vehicles, 154,735 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,477 artillery systems, 2,165 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,679 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,774 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."

bomb cloud sculpture takes shape in soil, straw and water inside abandoned lisbon school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

earth, straw, sand, water, and wood form The Weight of the Soil
The Weight of the Soil is a large-scale sculpturalinstallation by Iranian-born, Brooklyn-based artists Saman & Sasan Oskouei, installed inside an abandoned school in Lisbon. The work gives physical form to the fleeting image of a bomb cloud, using adobe, soil, straw, sand, water, and wood to slow down a moment of destruction and give it material weight.
Constructed in situ, the sculpture uses a minimal wood structure covered with layers of adobe made from soil, sand, straw, and water. The earthen material was built up by hand into irregular, cloud-like masses, leaving the texture and character of the soil visible across the surface. Rather than depicting the explosion itself, the installation focuses on what follows: dust settling, material hardening, and the transformation of destruction into landscape.
the installation is constructed in situ inside abandoned school
The use of earth introduces a central contrast within the work by artists Saman & Sasan Oskouei. A material traditionally associated with shelter, home, and permanence is shaped into an image of destruction. The installation’s earthen construction also connects the bomb cloud to the physical ground, turning an image usually encountered for only a few seconds through photographs, videos, and screens into a lasting spatial presence.
The work occupies an abandoned school that had been unused for approximately 15 years. Its worn architecture, tiled walls, damaged ceiling, and traces of former use become part of the installation. A building associated with learning and the future provides the setting for a form associated with destruction and its aftermath.
As the dust settles and the adobe hardens, the bomb cloud becomes a landscape. The work considers how violence extends beyond the moment of impact, becoming embedded in memory, architecture, landscapes, and the ground itself.

Behind Nasrallah’s elimination: The intelligence, pager attack and 83-ton strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:14:43 UTC
15:14:43 KST

Two years after the dramatic elimination of Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah, new details are emerging from the closed-door deliberations of the IDF Intelligence Directorate and the Israeli Air Force.
Two of the key figures who led the operation — Maj. G., who headed the Intelligence Directorate’s Lebanon target section at the time of the assassination, and Maj. (res.) R., operations officer in the Air Force’s targeted assassination cell — recount the behind-the-scenes drama, from a decade of painstaking intelligence surveillance and the Hezbollah leader’s deeply entrenched assumptions to the tense hours in which the decision was made to drop 83 tons of bombs on the bunker where he was staying.
“I commanded the Intelligence Directorate team, which included everyone involved in this — Unit 8200, Unit 9900 and others,” Maj. G. says. “In the two years before the strike, this team studied the man to understand his lifestyle and what he was doing at all times. The investigation went down to the most intimate and precise details of his daily routine: when he went to sleep, what he liked to eat, who he usually traveled with. Once you have that amount of knowledge, there is nothing more powerful.”
At the outset, it turns out, Nasrallah enjoyed a false sense of security based on a fundamentally mistaken assumption.
“We knew where he was even before Oct. 7,” Maj. (res.) R. says. “This was not a small compound. Eighty-three tons of bombs were dropped there, primarily because of the challenging underground layout. It was professional, precise work.”
According to R., “On Oct. 8, Nasrallah felt comfortable because he understood that Israel’s attention was focused on Gaza. He operated relatively routinely. He was careful to move covertly, but not as though he were in a full-scale war.”
G. adds: “On the one hand, Nasrallah created the impression that he was constantly operating in secrecy. On the other hand, he was deeply involved and made public appearances. He was involved in everything, from situation assessments to decisions on budgets and force buildup. He decided whether to invest in the Radwan Force or in missiles. He was very involved.”
The dramatic turning point was the pager attack, which plunged the organization into unprecedented chaos.
“From the pager operation onward, the organization understood that it had control over nothing,” R. says. “It shook their confidence in everything, from communications devices to people. They had to relearn everything they had been doing up to that point.”
Despite the severe blow, Nasrallah did not flee.
“He had difficulty grasping the scale of the events and obtaining a complete picture of the situation,” G. explains. “We expected him to move to a new location, but he remained at the site we knew. We assess that this happened because he misjudged what was happening on the ground. The location was comfortable and familiar to him, and he failed to properly analyze the sequence of events. He did not understand that he needed to leave.
“He froze, perhaps because of a mistaken assumption. He did not think Israel would go all the way. I think he categorized the pager attack and the assassinations of senior figures as an exchange of blows. He did not see that we were escalating it into a war. As a team, our mission was to push the assassination up through the senior ranks so they would approve it before he moved, before he realized what was happening.”
‘No blind spots’
The degree of intelligence control in those days was comprehensive.
“We had no blind spots when it came to him. We knew where he was every minute,” G. says.
When new intelligence emerged that could have prompted Nasrallah to flee, the team approached decision-makers and pressed hard for the strike to be carried out.
G. recalls the critical hours at the Kirya, the IDF’s Tel Aviv headquarters: “The main thing we felt was that we were in the best possible situation. Both in terms of the nature of the collateral damage and the target location, it was optimal. Any change could have worked against us because we did not know where his next location would be.
“We were very aggressive with the senior offices. We made sure it reached the prime minister so that the right decision could be made.”
He adds: “During those hours, I was constantly on top of the team, checking every piece of intelligence that came in and making sure nothing had changed. There was tremendous excitement. When I took the position and we told people we were going to assassinate Nasrallah, they told me we were dreaming.
“In terms of my confidence in the operation’s chances of success, I felt very certain. I wasn’t worried about a mistake. I was worried the decision-makers might change their minds, that someone would want to postpone it.”
‘Collateral damage: 30’
When it came to collateral damage, decision-makers demanded maximum precision even during the planning approval stages.
“I’ll say candidly that the question of collateral damage was always part of the plan-approval process, even though Nasrallah was such a senior figure,” G. says. “For an intelligence assessment of collateral damage, you are required to provide substantiated information on how many people are in every room, in every home in the building.
“We provided the answer, and in the end the damage was far lower than we had estimated. In practice, the collateral damage from the entire strike was 30 uninvolved civilians. If you compare the collateral damage with the number of Hezbollah operatives killed alongside Nasrallah, it comes out to one-to-one. There was nothing disproportionate about it. It is important to note that one of the things that helped was that once we began striking Beirut, many families left.”
According to R., the assassination of the Hezbollah leader marked the decisive turning point in the campaign on the Lebanese front.
“The organization — and this is already well known and clear — is not the same without Nasrallah,” he says. “Hezbollah is not even close to the capabilities it had on Oct. 8. Its force-building capabilities no longer exist and its ability to exert influence has been dramatically damaged. It is an ostracized organization.”
He adds: “Any leader who sets out to destroy the State of Israel — we will come after him. Naim Qassem, Nasrallah’s successor, understood that nothing is safe. You can see it in him. You can see it in Khamenei’s son as well. His turn will come too.”
For G., it is important that credit be shared.
“Behind every final target approval I signed stood an entire team that sat with me in the room during the most critical hours: active-duty and reserve intelligence researchers who made up the operation’s intelligence team throughout.
“They included Lt. L., the head of my cell; N., a researcher in the cell; Z., a reserve researcher who began as the target officer; and reserve researchers R., Y., Y. and T., who studied Nasrallah’s underground facilities, along with other senior commanders who had regularly reported for reserve duty in the unit even before the war.
“From Oct. 7 onward, they left everything behind and were with me around the clock, working continuous shifts. They possess years of accumulated knowledge and were central to carrying out the operation. Without them, without the partnership and friendship that bind us to this day, it simply would not have happened.”

German security agencies face dilemma after victories for far-right, far-left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:11:45 UTC
15:11:45 KST

This month's victories for far-right and far-left parties in German state elections have intensified official debate over whether security authorities can restrict secret information that might be shared with Russia or criminal groups.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which came close to winning an absolute majority in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, and the far-left Left Party, which came first in the capital Berlin on September 20, could both pose risks, senior figures in the ruling coalition say.
In Germany's federal system, states have their own domestic intelligence agencies under local government control, which share information with each other and operate with the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV).
Politicians from rival parties and former security officials have expressed fears that if the agencies come under the authority of ministers from the far right or far left, confidential information could leak either to Moscow or, in the case of Berlin, to groups investigated over suspicions of organized crime links.
"This concerns information relating to organized crime – that would be an issue in Berlin," said Alexander Hoffmann, head of the parliamentary group of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU). "And it's about issues concerning Russia – that would be Saxony-Anhalt," he said.
The AfD rejects accusations from rival parties that it is effectively allied to Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying that it seeks only to avoid war and opposes Germany providing military support for Ukraine.
An AfD spokesperson said the government was "clutching at straws in an attempt to discredit us in the eyes of the electorate."
"It is telling that we have been confronted with such speculation and accusations for many years, yet the other side has failed to produce a single piece of evidence," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
The Left Party did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But party leaders have previously said they consider unacceptable any association with what German police identify as clan structures within the Kurdish, Lebanese and Palestinian communities in Berlin involved in organized crime.
The accusations of links to such groups are often intertwined with accusations of antisemitism, which the party also says it firmly rejects.
Security services drawing up plans, source says
The discussion over restricting confidential information has been underway ever since opinion polls pointed to a possible victory for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, where the local branch of the party is designated as right-wing extremist by the local office of the domestic intelligence agency.
Hendrik Wuest, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, earlier this month called for a special federal and state committee to be set up to consider how to deal with the issue of information-sharing with an AfD-led government.
"Of course, preparations are under way – but people are still waiting to see what happens, because it isn't even clear whether the AfD and The Left will form governments at all," said one security official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Despite coming first in the election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell short of the absolute majority it would need to govern alone, and its coalition options are restricted because the other main parties have all ruled out cooperating with it.
The Left Party is, however, likely to try to form a coalition with the center-left Social Democrats and the environmental Greens, but both parties have demanded that it take action to eliminate antisemitism from its ranks.
Several of the AfD's state party branches have been designated as far-right extremist groups by domestic security authorities, prompting the AfD in turn to accuse the intelligence services of political interference.
Officials are also concerned that security officials involved in investigating the AfD could be targeted by a future AfD-led administration.
Tensions between political parties and the security services have surfaced from time to time in recent decades - but the idea of systematic exclusion from information sharing underlines the gravity of the division.
Along with the main domestic security agency, the BfV, other security services and state governments are now considering restrictions, although security officials say they would not want to cut off all information-sharing, citing issues including indications of potential terrorist attacks.
Left Party representatives say terms such as "clan-related crime" often stigmatize entire ethnic communities and say that contacts with local residents do not imply support for criminal activity.
Left Party, AfD suspicious of BfV
Like the AfD, it has long been suspicious of the BfV. The Left Party's Berlin campaign program called for the Berlin state agency to be abolished and replaced with "a transparent, democratically controlled body that is close to the people."
However, one Left Party member of the federal parliament has acknowledged social media contacts with a member of an extended family in Berlin accused of involvement with criminal groups and said he would "take the time to dispel any doubts" and "review my communication style."
"There is absolutely no justification for elected representatives having contacts with individuals associated with organized crime," Ferat Kocak said in a post on X/Twitter.

Roads and villages in the surrounding area are not always safe, and residents have reported movement restrictions, arrests, gunfire, and harm to civilians. Last week, seven armed groups in Ethiopia, including the Fano movement in Amhara and the Tigray People's Liberation Front, announced an alliance against the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
"They are afraid. They can't move around freely," Ababa said. "There is a war now between the government and the forces and militias. Yesterday, they told me about a neighbor of theirs who was killed, and they sent me pictures of a house that was completely damaged by gunfire."
Ababa, who has relatives in Gondar and in a village in the Amhara region, said the security situation was affecting large areas. "The Tigray region and parts of Amhara, there's nothing to talk about. There are concerns in Gondar too," he said.
Relatives have been kidnapped, ransomed, Ababa says
For Ababa, the concern is not merely from afar. He said his relatives had previously been kidnapped and that family members were forced to collect money and pay a ransom to secure their release.
"My relatives were kidnapped, and we had to pay a ransom from the whole family," he said. "We are very worried about them."
Ababa immigrated to Israel 25 years ago and has not returned to Ethiopia since. "I'm a village person, and if I travel, I want to get to my village. But there is no public transportation there, and people are stopped on the way. Especially if they know you are coming from Israel or suspect that you support Fano," he said.
He said he still has extended relatives in Ethiopia, including his relative Estaol Agen, whose parents are already in Israel and who is the only member of his immediate family left behind.
"He has been left alone for more than 25 years, and because of the fear of kidnappings, they move him from place to place."
No aliyah made from Ethiopia in four years
Ababa said the family has sought to advance the aliyah of additional relatives but has encountered prolonged difficulties. "There has been no aliyah for four years. We have a group, and we work day and night, but we don't get a response," he said.
Ababa, who lives in Lod and works to promote aliyah for members of the community, said many families in Israel remain deeply concerned about relatives living in areas affected by the fighting.
"People here are worried, and the people there are still waiting."

Syria says sending imported petrol to Iraq
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:10:28 UTC
15:10:28 KST

This aerial picture shows cars and trucks loaded with goods waiting to cross over into Syria at the al-Rabia border crossing on April 20, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Syria has begun delivering imported petrol to Iraq, months after Baghdad began exporting its oil via Syria when the Middle East war disrupted the Strait of Hormuz.
"The Syrian Petroleum Company has begun transporting petrol imported for Iraq through the Banias oil terminal" on Syria's Mediterranean coast, state news agency SANA reported on Sept. 27.
The move is part of "a renewable three-month agreement to secure energy supplies amid disruptions to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz", it added.
The report cited Syrian Petroleum Company official Ahmed Qubbaji as saying that operations began on Sept. 24 with a first batch of 57 tankers, with work underway to increase the number of trucks crossing the Al-Tanf land border to Iraq to 200 per day.
The Qatari firm UCC was responsible for purchasing the petrol "from various global sources," with Syria then transporting it for a fee, Qubbaji said according to the report.
The operations support "Syria's role as a corridor for importing, exporting and transporting materials and energy between regional countries," he said.
The closure of Hormuz has hit Iraqi oil exports hard, and in April Baghdad said it had begun shipping crude through Syria by truck to circumvent the strait, though the amounts are far below what used to travel by sea.
Qubbaji said that up to 1,200 Iraqi oil tankers transited Syria daily.

Can you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:10:25 UTC
15:10:25 KST

Today’s puzzle played a pivotal role in the birth of classical physics.
The tower drop
An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land?
- 
  slightly to the west
- 
  slightly to the east
- 
  exactly at the bottom
The answer is counter-intuitive. Or, in the words of Isaac Newton, who posed the problem in a letter he wrote to Robert Hooke in 1679, the answer is “quite contrary to ye opinion of ye vulgar.”
Some hints. Think about how the spin of the Earth might affect the downwards trajectory. Also think about what happens when a spinning figure skater pulls in their arms.
I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solution.
PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Instead discuss your favourite seventeenth century scientists.
Today’s puzzle was suggested by David Acheson, emeritus professor of maths at Oxford and the author of several excellent popular maths books. His latest is Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics, a beautifully accessible introduction to the science of motion.
Acheson’s book includes more background about the tower drop puzzle. Hooke’s correspondence with Newton rekindled Newton’s interest in gravity and motion, which ultimately led to his formulation of the mathematical foundations of classical physics in the Principia.
Wonders of Motion by David Acheson is on sale at the Guardian Bookshop.

South Korea Demands Apology From Ukraine Over Disclosure of North Korean POW Transfer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:07:48 UTC
15:07:48 KST

South Korea has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine over Kyiv’s public disclosure that two North Korean prisoners of war had been transferred to South Korea, escalating a diplomatic dispute over whether the move was covered by a confidentiality agreement.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung first criticized President Volodymyr Zelensky for revealing the transfer during his address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Writing on X on Thursday during a visit to Mexico, Lee said publicly disclosing the transfer could create serious diplomatic and security problems.
“The repatriation of North Korean prisoners is an extremely sensitive issue with serious implications for diplomacy, national security and the situation on the Korean Peninsula,” Lee said.
“It was appropriate in every aspect not to disclose, considering many problems it may cause when disclosed, and [we] had agreed to do so,” he added.
On Sunday, South Korea’s presidential office went further, demanding an official explanation and apology from Kyiv.
“The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” Seong Ghi-hong, a senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement.
What Matters More to Putin? Russian Refineries or Striking Ukraine?
Seong said Seoul was reviewing additional measures over the dispute if necessary, adding that Ukraine’s denial of the confidentiality arrangement had seriously damaged trust between the two governments and could affect bilateral relations.
Seoul says transfer was meant to stay secret
On Thursday, Lee said the South Korean government had faced calls from both within the administration and from opposition politicians to disclose the return of the two soldiers.
He defended the decision to keep the transfer private, saying the issue could affect inter-Korean relations, national security, and the safety of the prisoners and their families in North Korea.
“I do not know the specific circumstances that prompted the Ukrainian side to breach the agreement and make the information public, but this is deeply regrettable,” Lee said.
South Korean officials have said Kyiv had repeatedly discussed the transfer with Seoul through diplomatic channels and had requested that it remain confidential because of the potential risks.
Seoul had previously declined to confirm that the two North Korean soldiers had arrived in the country, citing concerns over their safety and that of their families.
Ukraine disputes confidentiality claim
Kyiv has disputed Seoul’s characterization of the arrangement.
In response to South Korean media inquiries, a Ukrainian presidential official said Seoul had been informed in advance that Zelensky might mention the transfer during his UN speech.
The official said Ukraine had disclosed only the fact that the two soldiers had been transferred to South Korea, without revealing details about how or when the operation took place.
Kyiv also said it would have been strange to keep the transfer entirely secret, particularly because South Korean authorities later confirmed that the handover had taken place following direct discussions between the two governments.
A senior South Korean official similarly confirmed that Seoul had been told beforehand that Zelensky might mention the prisoners, but said South Korea had asked that their destination not be disclosed.
The disagreement therefore centers on what exactly Kyiv and Seoul agreed to keep confidential: South Korea says there was an understanding not to disclose the prisoners’ transfer to the country, while Ukraine says it did not agree to conceal the fact that the transfer had taken place.
Two North Korean soldiers captured in Kursk
The two soldiers were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025 after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
They were the first North Korean soldiers known to have been captured alive since Pyongyang began sending troops to support Moscow.
The soldiers later expressed a desire to go to South Korea rather than return to North Korea. Seoul and Kyiv subsequently held discussions over their transfer on humanitarian grounds.

The defendants will return to Kowloon City Court on November 2 to deal with documentation for the court transfer. They are expected to enter their pleas at the District Court at a later stage.

Jetten’s D66 conference speech interrupted by Gaza hecklers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prime minister Rob Jetten’s speech to his D66 party’s weekend conference was interrupted by hecklers protesting against Israel’s military intervention in Gaza.
Jetten was briefly led from the stage by security guards after demonstrators twice shouted out at the start of the speech in the Amsterdam RAI arena on Sunday.
The prime minister initially said the protesters could stay in the conference hall if they sat down “so you don’t bother those sitting behind you”, but after the second interruption a handful of demonstrators were escorted out of the hall.
The demonstrators wore T-shirts with slogans such as Bloedcoalitie (“blood coalition”) and Liberaal/Neutraal/Genocidaal (“liberal, neutral, genocidal”).
Jetten said: “I see that you want to highlight the situation in Gaza and I understand that very much.”
Afterwards he told RTL Nieuws that the protest had been respectful. “The right to demonstrate and have your say is one of the strengths of our democracy, as long as it’s done respectfully, and that’s what we saw here in the hall.”
Budget delays
The conference marked the 60th anniversary of the foundation of D66 and the first time a prime minister had addressed the autumn gathering.
Jetten said his cabinet had made progress in several areas, such as drawing up plans to cut nitrogen pollution and preventing the online government services portal DigiD being sold to an American company.
But he admitted it had taken longer than hoped for his government to make a deal with opposition parties to pass next year’s budget. The minority coalition of D66, CDA and VVD needs the support of at least two other parties in both houses of parliament.
Jetten said he had seen signs during talks last week that parties “from left to right” were prepared to negotiate, proving that “broad co-operation is possible with this generation of politicians”.
The prime minister also insisted he would not give in to the “anti-Dutch forces that want to destroy our democracy from within”, referring to the violent demonstrations in The Hague a week ago that featured “appalling extreme right-wing slogans and even Nazi salutes”.
Jetten vowed that the “wave of optimism” would ultimately triumph over the loudest voices, echoing his predecessor Mark Rutte, who called on people to vote for “doers, not yellers”.
“They might shout louder, but we get more done,” Jetten said.

Where are salaries and job opportunities highest in Portugal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:02:42 UTC
15:02:42 KST

Information technology remains one of the most attractive fields in the Portuguese job market, offering high average salaries and strong job creation, according to Randstad's latest Salary Trends Study.
Portugal’s technology sector is adding jobs fast and paying some of the country’s highest salaries. Employment in information and communication rose by 27,600 year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, while annual salaries for the IT roles surveyed range from €40,000 to €55,000, according to Randstad’s 2026/2027 Salary Trends Study.
According to the report, which cross-references Randstad’s recruitment database with official statistics from INE and Eurostat, the number of people employed in the information and communication sector in the second quarter of 2026 stood at 237,200, representing around 4.4% of the total workforce in Portugal.
Year-on-year, there was an increase of 27,600 jobs (+13.2%). According to Randstad, the five areas most in demand by companies in this sector are cloud and security, data analytics, BI and AI, software development, business applications (CRM/ERP) and IT management and strategy.
Close behind is the life sciences and healthcare sector, which, according to data from INE’s Employment Survey for the second quarter of 2026, cited in a Randstad press release, employs 567,700 people in human health and social care, representing around 10.5% of the total workforce in Portugal.
Year-on-year, there was an increase of 43,200 jobs (+8.2%), “consolidating healthcare as one of the biggest drivers of skilled job creation in the country”, Randstad said in the same press release.
In pharmaceuticals and research, the average gross annual salary ranges from €35,000 to €60,000, according to Randstad’s survey, “with strong demand for sales representatives, quality assurance roles, regulatory affairs, market access and medical affairs”.
In healthcare, the average stands at between €30,000 and €46,000 gross per annum, with organisations focusing on recruiting nurses, doctors, multi-therapy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacists.
Another sector emerging as a driving force for change in the Portuguese market, according to Randstad, is engineering and industry, “a highly skilled sector characterised by a high level of job stability in the Portuguese market”.
According to data from INE for the second quarter of 2026, cited by the Dutch human resources firm, the workforce in the industrial sector (which includes extractive industries, manufacturing, electricity, gas, water and construction) stood at 1,333,700 people, representing around 24.7% of the total workforce in Portugal.
Year-on-year, there was an increase of 43,000 jobs (+3.3%). With average salaries estimated by Randstad at between €33,500 and €49,500 gross per annum, “companies are actively seeking site managers, automation and robotics engineers, product development engineers, production supervisors and supply chain or logistics technicians.”
In banking and insurance, where average salaries range from €35,000 to €50,000 gross per annum, the workforce stood at 118,700 people in the second quarter of 2026, representing around 2.2% of the total workforce in Portugal.
Year-on-year, there was an increase of 8,400 jobs (+7.6%), which, according to Randstad, reflects “an ongoing restructuring of branches and gains in operational efficiency through digitalisation in traditional banking”. “With an ever-increasing focus on risk and compliance, the most in-demand roles are business manager, compliance officer, corporate finance analyst, underwriter and private banker,” the company said.
As regards marketing and sales, sales roles have average salaries of between €23,000 and €39,500, whilst marketing roles range from €26,000 to €36,500 gross per annum.
“Demand is centred on roles such as CRM specialist, performance marketing manager, customer experience manager, technical sales representative and sales engineer.”
INE does not break down figures for marketing and sales, but according to Eurostat, the number of people employed in marketing totalled 37,200 in the first quarter of 2026 (0.7% of total employment in the country). Compared with the previous quarter, there was a decrease of 13.3% (a loss of 5,700 jobs); however, year-on-year there was an increase of 1,400 people (+3.9%).
Finally, in the broad sector of finance, HR and legal services, according to data from INE, the number of people employed stood at 488,100, representing around 9% of the national total.
Year-on-year, there was an increase of 6,800 jobs (+1.4%). With an average gross annual salary ranging from €24,000 to €33,500, this sector “leads the demand for controllers, reporting/statutory specialists, chartered accountants, talent specialising in HR analytics and compliance officers”.

Bailiffs turned up at my home to seize goods over four unpaid Ulez fines issued by Transport for London (TfL) that have nothing to do with me.
The saga began two months ago when I received four enforcement notices from CDER Group relating to a vehicle I have never owned.
I was told my address had been obtained from the DVLA, but the DVLA confirmed that the vehicle has never been registered to me or my address. I sent this confirmation to CDER, but they nevertheless ordered bailiffs to come to my house and told me enforcement could not be stopped.
I complained to TfL, which referred me back to CDER. CDER then informed me that TfL had rejected the evidence I had supplied.
For more than 25 years I have been repeatedly mistaken for another individual with the same name, resulting in debt collection activity by numerous organisations. I have spent years proving my identity and correcting mistakes, only for the same problems to happen again.
CW, Blackpool
It seems that the original penalty charge notices (PCNs) were sent to the address of the offending driver and, when they ignored them, tracing agents trawled citizens with the same name and decided you were a good fit.
Your labours to prevent bailiffs confiscating your belongings, including sending CDER 13 years of payslips and eight years of bills, took such a toll that you had to be signed off work.
Most gobsmacking of all is an email from TfL to CDER rejecting the DVLA’s written confirmation that the offending vehicle has never belonged to you.
“We cannot consider the evidence as valid,” TfL wrote, and it instructed CEDR to continue enforcement action.
In the meantime, you discovered that the credit reference agency TransUnion had incorrectly merged a stranger’s credit report with yours. This, it turned out, was the third time in three years that it had done so.
That explains why tracing agents came to your address because of a debt owed by a man with the same name in Yorkshire. You have now established that your address has, over the years, been given to tracing agents acting for more than 20 creditors, a few of whom have pursued you for debts accrued by your Yorkshire namesake.
This blunder by TransUnion does not excuse either CDER or TfL for failing legal obligations to ensure they had the right person before contacting you, and for failing to accept the evidence proving your innocence.
TfL, responding also for CDER, belatedly apologised when I intervened.
“Our contracted enforcement agents use credit searches to track down the person liable [for unpaid PCNs],” a spokesperson says. “From this search, it wrongly concluded that CW was the owner of this vehicle.”
TfL has now cancelled enforcement action, and CDER has paid you £500 in compensation for the “anguish” it now recognises it has caused.
TransUnion declined to comment while the Financial Ombudsman Service investigates a complaint you have lodged about its conduct.

Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject to our terms and conditions.

‘The champagne of pale ales’: my search for the perfect kölsch beer in Cologne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:00:26 UTC
15:00:26 KST

There’s a saying in Cologne, repeated with the mild smugness of people who know they’re right: kölsch is the only culture you can drink. It sounds like a line lifted straight from the tourist board’s brochure. Then you spend a day working your way around the city’s traditional brewhouses and realise it’s a statement of fact.
Since 1997, kölsch has held a protected geographical indication within the EU, guaranteeing that any beer bearing the name is brewed within 50km of the city and made strictly to the Kölsch-Konvention. That agreement, signed in 1986, defined the style as “a light, highly attenuated, hop-accentuated, clear, top-fermenting ‘vollbier’ [full-beer]”, restricting production exclusively to the local area. It is, in effect, the champagne of pale ales: locally adored and tied to a city that has always insisted on doing things its own way.
The delivery is as ritualised as the brewing itself. You sit. A köbes – the traditionally deadpan, blue-aproned brewhouse waiter – arrives carrying a kranz (a circular tray) holding a ring of stangen, narrow 200ml glasses designed to keep the beer cold and effervescent long enough for you to drain one before the next takes its place. You drink. He marks a tally on your beer mat with a stub of pencil. You never order a second; you never need to. The conveyor belt only stops when you place your beer mat on top of your glass.
Ten hours, seven brewhouses and an inadvisable number of tally marks later, I had formed some very firm opinions about Cologne’s legendary liquid culture.
Brauhaus Früh am Dom
The twin spires of Cologne cathedral are visible from the doorway of this brewhouse. So, unfortunately, is the gift shop and a tour group from Ohio. Früh am Dom, arguably the most internationally recognisable kölsch brand, is housed in a sprawling warren of vaulted dining rooms, cellars and long oak bars. It is enormous and boisterous, yet the kölsch, poured at speed to a rotating cast of daytrippers, lacks the crisp clarity found elsewhere. Being on the cathedral’s doorstep makes this prime real estate, but the footfall turns the room into something closer to a transit lounge, where most visitors drop in for a quick photo with their stange before rushing off.
4.5/10, €2.50
Brauhaus Sion
Founded in 1912 and heavily renovated since, Sion merges a contemporary interior with old-world charm. The result is the slickest room on this list: warm mood lighting, clean lines and a menu that reaches beyond the usual brewhouse staples of fried pork and potatoes. The kölsch itself is technically flawless and refreshing, though it lacks the rustic bite of the city’s smaller producers. It’s a fine spot for a proper sit-down dinner rather than a session – and even the köbes here shows genuine warmth, a demeanour that feels either refreshing or faintly suspicious depending on how strictly you hold to Rhenish brusqueness.
6/10, €2.60
Brauhaus Päffgen
Beyond the tourist centre, in the lively and historic Friesenviertel district, is the hallowed Päffgen. Operating on Friesenstraße since 1883, this is one of the last hausbrauereien (brew pubs) that refuses to bottle for supermarket shelves; if you want Päffgen, you come here or haul a wooden keg home yourself. The beer is tapped straight from wooden barrels on the counter, giving a pour with a floral, grassy hop aroma, a hint of stone fruit and a crisp bitter finish. The room feels untouched by time – look out for the old wooden beichtstuhl (“confessional”), the elevated booth where the innkeeper once oversaw the floor and counted the day’s takings. One of the köbesse, sliding a fresh stange across the counter without breaking stride, put it more bluntly than any brochure could: “Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion. And this is the church.” With its gruff, lightning-fast staff and a leafy beer garden out the back, Päffgen is the gold standard of kölsch culture. 
9.5/10, €2.60
Peters Brauhaus
Tucked into the historic old town, Peters is what the cathedral-adjacent halls wish they were. It strikes the finest balance in central Cologne, fiercely popular with local people while remaining welcoming to passing travellers. The interior is gorgeous – stained-glass skylights throwing amber light across scrubbed, decades-old wooden tables, dark wainscoting framing the chatter of the room. The kölsch is beautifully balanced: smooth, clean and poured properly cold. We might have come at a bad time, though, as it wasn’t particularly busy and lacked atmosphere.
7/10, €2.50
Brauerei zur Malzmühle
Sitting on the edge of the historic Heumarkt, Malzmühle is the second-oldest brewery in Cologne, operating on this spot since 1858. Destroyed almost entirely in the second world war, only the stone portal survived; you now pass through that same archway into a sprawling hall of rustic brickwork and heavy oak benches. Malzmühle brews Mühlen Kölsch, a pour favoured by the former US president Bill Clinton, who declared “Ich bin ein Kölsch” on a visit in 1999. It is slightly darker and maltier than its peers, with a gentle honey note against a solid bitter backbone. The atmosphere is unapologetically noisy and authentic – a meeting ground where workers in hi-vis vests share benches with executives in suits. We spoke to one of the köbesse, Carl, who told us he’d worked here for 38 years: “This is the place to be. These walls have seen so much and heard so many conversations. I wouldn’t work anywhere else.”
8.5/10, €2.50
Gaffel am Dom
Gaffel is a heavy hitter among local people, distributed widely across the city’s bars and football stadiums. Its flagship hall, opposite the central station, is handsome and impeccably run, with high ceilings and sweeping arches giving it real metropolitan energy. The kölsch is consistently good – bright, sharply carbonated and noticeably hop-forward, exactly as the Konvention prescribes. Knowing this same beer is sold at the gate in Cologne Bonn airport slightly undercuts the local romance, though; it’s reliable in a high-volume, commercial way. The kitchen redeems it somewhat with a stellar himmel un ääd – crispy black pudding with smooth mash and stewed apples – comfort food good enough to justify the visit alone.
6.5/10, €2.50
Brauhaus Sünner im Walfisch
Down a cobbled alley in the old town, Sünner im Walfisch is pure historical theatre. Housed in a striking 17th-century step-gabled building, dismantled and rebuilt brick by brick on its current site, it serves as the old town outpost for Sünner, Cologne’s oldest operating kölsch brewery. Inside, narrow timber-framed rooms and low ceilings transport you back to medieval Rhineland. The beer is fantastic – crisp and dry with a peppery hop finish that makes it dangerously easy to drink – and it’s quieter and more intimate than the echoing halls near the station, its köbesse still delivering drinks with a wink of humour. A favourite for decor and character, if not quite for atmosphere.
8/10, €2.50
Scott Antcliffe’s travel to Cologne was provided by Viking as part of its 8-day Rhine Getaway, from £1,695

I’ve been unemployed for four years. But I do have an important job – to act as a warning to others | Antimony Deor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:00:26 UTC
15:00:26 KST

Every Friday I write a little essay about how great I am and send it off to a stranger. Sometimes I receive a generic rejection two or 12 weeks later, but usually they never reply.
I used to apply for jobs more often, but after a few hundred applications and increasingly worse mental health, I found I got exactly the same response whether I sent a thoroughly researched and edited cover letter or a picture of my cat, so I gave up trying so hard. I used to obsess about what was wrong with me. Everyone told me that it was them, not me; that it was business, not personal; that doing the same thing over and over while expecting a different outcome was extremely sane. But still, every rejection fed the little worm in my brain that said I was useless. I don’t think the worm is entirely in the wrong. I think it’s normal to feel like a reject after being repeatedly rejected, to feel worthless when your bank balance is zero, to feel lost after losing.
Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads
It strikes me that my life is very different to most people my age, and the rickety rope bridge spanning that chasm is only getting more frayed. I live a “student lifestyle” at twice the age of a typical student (I just turned 40). I shop exclusively at discount grocers and secondhand shops – except when I don’t, and feel incredibly guilty. I don’t have a car, and public transport is stressful because I’m always looking out for inspectors, so I ride an old bike. Unless my parents die right now or I become CEO of Incredible Profits Industries tomorrow, I’ll never own a house, and won’t be able to build enough superannuation to retire comfortably. When I imagine the future, I can only imagine being in the same precarious position I’m in now, but fatter, wrinklier and even more fed up with my old, cold share house.
Unemployment gives you the time to ask all sizes of existential questions, without the resources to answer any. “What is a good life?” is on the same level as “How am I going to afford to take Mum out for her birthday in October?”
“How do I live life as a failed person?” I think to myself in the shower. “Is it actually cool and anti-capitalist that I’m incomprehensible to HR managers and don’t fit in to neoliberal society?” I wonder while buttering my toast. “If I get my act together, maybe I could start a thriving micro-business selling sarcastic animal key chains at small country markets,” I fantasise during my jog. “I love animals; could I do a Tafe course in vet nursing? No, I hate people yelling at me,” I think while peering at birds for signs of imminent ecological collapse. Variations of these thoughts kaleidoscope constantly, but since I had the bad career judgment to do a PhD in the arts, I don’t trust myself to make any decisions.
Like a lot of other unemployed people I know, I have an interesting health history, but not interesting enough to be classed as disabled. My 20s were lost to depression, but after trying a dozen or so medications, gender transition and a few decades of talk therapy, I’m overjoyed to say that I’m now just an ordinary sad person. However, having a chronic disease takes time and money to manage, and means I have to be careful with stress. I think of it as a type of chronic pain; if there was a big pile of jobs 100 metres away, and everyone had to quickly run over and grab one, the people with bad knees would be left behind. I just have bad knees of the brain.
It’s true I’ve also had lots of advantages – supportive parents, a great education, and the accent and misplaced faith in institutions that come with a middle-class upbringing. I’m very lucky to have some lovely little writing jobs that pay about $500 a month, and I get $780 a fortnight from Centrelink. Life is not as hard for me as it is for other people on the dole.
I’ve been unemployed for about four years, since I graduated from my humanities PhD. When they gave me the scroll and silly hat I thought, “Thanks goodness that’s over. Now the hardest part of my life is done and everything will be much easier. I can look for a nice little research job that finishes at 5pm! Maybe four days a week! Maybe work from home!” After a few months of looking for this fictional job, I switched to applying for graduate programs. Then entry-level government roles. Last year I applied to be a cleaner, lollipop laddy and person who arranges the chairs at an event centre. This year I just gave up on traditional job applications.
I wrote this from my catsitting job in rural Victoria. I may enrol in a medical trial, do market research, be a mystery shopper or pick up a little graphic design work (sorry, real graphic designers). These, combined with my multiple freelance writing gigs and volunteering work, add up to about the same hours as a full-time job. For a long time I saw volunteering as like licking a bakery window – all of the work with none of the reward. But hearing “good job Antimony!” after years of “unfortunately on this occasion” almost brought me to tears.
Forgive me. I always find myself needing to explain to myself and others how I came to be this way. I’m performing my essential economic function as a warning to others.
I do have an important job. It’s to act as a cautionary tale. If you lose your job, terrible things could happen. You could end up unemployed like me.
Antimony Deor is a freelance writer, illustrator, graphic designer, garden volunteer, podcast presenter, community health volunteer and unemployed person from Naarm/Melbourne

The endangered native ponies of Eriskay in the Outer Hebrides – a photo essay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

On the slopes of Beinn Sciathan, a rocky outcrop in the Outer Hebrides, white and grey ponies roam freely. Eriskay ponies, one of the rarest native breeds in the world, are critically endangered.
They have often been mixed with the Highland pony and other breeds, giving the false impression of higher population numbers. Only about 300 to 400 Eriskay ponies are thought to remain.
Efforts have been made to boost their numbers since the 1970s, both on their small homeland, Eriskay Island, and on the mainland. The island’s ponies have a lifestyle fascinating enough to draw tourists. They are neither wild nor kept enclosed. For half of the year, including winter, they are free to roam the island and its village. Each pony has an owner who can easily identify their own despite them looking nearly identical to the average observer.
About 150 people live on Eriskay, many of whom speak Gaelic. It is a close-knit community, but over time the island has become a tourist destination known for stunning beaches with clear blue water, the grounding of the SS Politician, and even a Fifa-recognised football pitch. But its history of fishing, crofting and Catholicism, and of course its ponies, are integral to its culture.
“It all makes Eriskay what it is today,” says Sandra MacInnes, the chair of Comann Each nan Eilean, the island’s pony society, who owns several of the animals.
In the 1850s, thousands of families in the Outer Hebrides were forced from Barra and South Uist during the Highland clearances. For many, Eriskay became a crowded refuge. MacInnes says: “[The landlords] thought it’s rubbish for grazing so they sent them here thinking they’ll never survive. They came here and made their houses … They were cleared from crofting communities and had to learn fishing, but then they thrived.”
Once the Eriskay community was established, the ponies thrived because of their role in the region’s social fabric. Originally used for crofting, they would be fitted with creels to bring peat up the hill and move seaweed as fertiliser for crops.
In the 1970s, however, their population shrank to a low of about 20 purebreds. Mechanisation was one of the main reasons for their decline, and Comann Each nan Eilean was founded in 1972 to restore the breed.
Community members also note that the climate crisis has begun to affect their island. Recent winters have hit hard, and the beaches are starting to erode. But the ponies adapt well to harsh and fluctuating winters with their hardy coats and their ability to navigate the island to stay out of the wind.
Triona MacKinnon owns two ponies on Eriskay and a few others on South Uist. “Winters are getting longer and wetter,” she says, noting that the community is having to help more in feeding the ponies – but at the same time that milder weather encourages ticks, which affect the animals.
“This winter’s been particularly long,” she says. “You can get loads of rain. Some ponies can get rain scald, and you’re not used to seeing that.”
The ponies have shaped the town’s culture over time. Local people quote the former parish priest Father Calum MacLellan, who once said: “Without the people of Eriskay there would be no pony, but without the pony there would have been no people on Eriskay.”
Or as MacInnes says: “They both needed each other.”
The ponies’ population has increased in the last 60 years, but there is still work to do. Comann Each nan Eilean is developing a breeding programme, and it manages the herd numbers to ensure the the grazing land can sustain the animals without them overrunning the community.
One foal was born on the island this year, and the community hopes for a few more next year. When first born, the ponies are almost black and then become lighter as they age. Most turn white, but some actually develop a brown coat.
In the winter months, the ponies need extra food and their owners feed them with support from the island’s pony society. In the summer, the ponies are kept up on Beinn Sciathan to allow the soil on lower slopes to recover so it can be used for farming.
Owners hike up and down whenever they can to check on their ponies. Some tend to their own ponies’ hooves, but many need to pay for a farrier, as well as veterinary care when needed. The work is financially demanding and time-consuming, but many islanders see a life alongside the ponies as something beautiful and part of their heritage.
Although MacInnes married into the community caring for ponies, she has since become attached to them.
“You get to know how docile they are. They all have their own personalities, they all have names, they all have little characters,” she says. “It’s nice to see herd dynamics as families. They are families.”

Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026: Headline speakers, key topics and how to watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit on 29 September brings together policymakers and industry experts to debate the biggest issues shaping the future of travel.
Europe’s travel industry will take centre stage as political leaders and industry experts gather for the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit.
Live on Tuesday 29 September from the Albert Hall in Brussels, the one-day summit will examine how the industry is changing amid shifting traveller expectations, economic pressures and a complex geopolitical landscape.
It comes after an eventful year for global tourism. Conflict in the Middle East has disrupted air routes, pushed up fuel costs and influenced where people travel, while extreme weather, overtourism and the rollout of new border controls have presented further challenges for the industry.
Despite the disruption, demand has proved resilient. Europe recorded its busiest-ever summer for air traffic in 2026, averaging 35,959 flights a day across July and August. Those developments will provide an important backdrop to the summit.
Live on Euronews.com, the Euronews app and on YouTube, doors open at 9am, with sessions running throughout the day.
Programmes and speakers
Bringing together policymakers and senior figures from the tourism, aviation and hospitality sectors, discussions will range from managing overtourism and creating more sustainable destinations to improving connectivity between Europe and Asia.
Two of Euronews’ flagship programmes – The Ring and The Big Question – will also be part of the agenda, bringing their popular formats to some of the industry's biggest debates.
Among the headline speakers is Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, who will sit down with Maria Tadeo for a one-on-one interview. Albania has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing travel destinations, with international arrivals reaching 11.9 million in 2025 – up 93.6% compared with 2019, according to UN Tourism. Improved air connectivity, affordable prices and growing interest in the Albanian Riviera, Tirana and the country’s mountains have all helped fuel the tourism boom.
Other confirmed guests include Bill White, the US Ambassador to Belgium; Eduardo Santander, Chief Executive Officer and Executive Director of the European Travel Commission (ETC); and Florian Sengstschmid, the Chief Executive Officer of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board (ATB).
What are the big topics on the agenda?
One of the opening conversations at the summit will look back at the European summer travel season, with Santander examining the trends, challenges and successes that have defined 2026, before looking ahead to the industry's prospects.
Sustainability will be another major theme with panellists discussing how Europe can reduce tourism's environmental impact without compromising accessibility, affordability and mobility.
Overtourism will also be high on the agenda and the summit will explore how popular destinations can cope with growing visitor numbers, including the potential of “second cities” and strategies to encourage travellers towards less-visited neighbourhoods and regions.
Meanwhile, The Big Question will turn its attention to the blue economy. MSC Cruises CEO Gianni Onorato will discuss whether Europe's cruise industry can chart a greener course, looking at cleaner fuels, next-generation ships, smarter ports and emerging “blue corridors”.
Later in the day, The Ring, hosted by Euronews' Méabh Mc Mahon, will bring its head-to-head political debate format to the summit.
Follow the latest stories on Euronews Travel via the website, newsletter and social media platforms.

Unlike proprietary software from top US labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, open-weight models allow their trained parameters – essentially the AI’s “brains” – to be freely downloaded, modified, fine-tuned and run independently by anyone online.

Republicans are pouring money into more than three dozen US House races previously considered “safe” after internal polling showed they could be vulnerable in the November 3 election, according to three Republican operatives familiar with the party’s thinking.
The shift is already starting to show in advertising reservations and campaign finance filings. Since September 1, major Republican groups and megadonors have begun spending in at least 39 congressional races where they haven’t previously deployed money this cycle, a Reuters review of spending by some of the largest Republican political groups shows.
Many of the candidates receiving new support sit in Republican strongholds and are still running ahead of Democratic opponents in public polls, these people said, indicating rising worry among party leaders over whether voters will use the November 3 election to air dissatisfaction over US President Donald Trump’s policies.
House Republican leaders recently warned dozens of campaigns that the party’s internal data shows that they cannot assume they will win, even if they are currently ahead in public polls and represent districts Trump won by double digits, two of the people said.

EU is preparing &quot;road maps&quot; for accession for Ukraine and three other countries — Politico
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
08:59:27 EEST
14:59:27 KST

EU is preparing "road maps" for accession for Ukraine and three other countries — Politico
Kyiv • UNN
The European Commission is planning clear schedules for reforms and negotiations for Ukraine, Montenegro, Moldova and Albania. They will not be offered to other candidates for now.
The EU is drawing up proposals that would give the four countries closest to joining the bloc, including Ukraine, a clear, step-by-step path to membership, while others are lagging behind. Politico reports this, citing sources, writes UNN.
Details
Targeted "road maps" are being considered for Montenegro, Ukraine, Moldova and Albania, two senior European Commission officials working on the draft proposals said, as part of efforts to speed up the years-long process.
These four countries are viewed as leaders in the EU accession process, but they still face slow progress and unclear timelines as to when they may be formally admitted.
Although Brussels has long supported their membership applications, the "road maps" would mark the first time they are given guarantees that, if they continue the necessary reforms, they will be admitted, as well as indicative deadlines for completing the negotiations, the publication writes.
According to one official, the "road maps" will more clearly define what is expected of each candidate country, while also creating obligations for current members, who must give their blessing for the process to continue. The plans also set approximate dates for the formal completion of groups of reforms known as negotiating "clusters" — important milestones on the path to membership.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised targeted support for candidate countries "that have made the most progress" during her State of the Union address in early September.
However, officials confirmed that other candidate countries at earlier stages of the process, such as Kosovo, North Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, will not be offered "road maps" at this stage. Nor will they be offered to Georgia, Turkey or Serbia, whose applications have stalled due to concerns about democratic backsliding and the judiciary.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed that the new "road maps" will "provide a path toward completing the accession negotiations. They will set out a clear list of priorities: timelines and outcomes, to help the most advanced candidates complete the necessary reforms."
"A geopolitical imperative"
The move comes against the backdrop of a separate review of the EU's "pre-enlargement" policy. Candidate countries need to be offered a better path toward "gradual integration" into the bloc, officials believe, one that would use economic benefits and access to joint projects to reward them for progress. This policy review, led by von der Leyen's close adviser Alexander Adam, is due to be presented to senior officials on October 6; it is intended to keep them on the path to the EU while their applications are being considered.
"Enlargement … remains a geopolitical imperative. However, accession takes time," says a draft of the "pre-enlargement" policy review. "Candidate countries must undergo a rigorous, merit-based process and carry out far-reaching and lasting reforms. This time should be used fully and strategically both to prepare the Union for enlargement and to deepen gradual integration in areas of mutual interest," the document states.
As part of this review, von der Leyen and EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos will propose changes to the bloc's internal operations to ensure that safeguards are in place to prevent new members from disrupting key policies or reneging on their commitments. The changes may include provisions for emergency clauses and transitional periods before certain membership rights are fully granted.
"The policy reviews show that the Union can accept more members through targeted adaptation, largely within the existing treaties," the draft says, arguing that the EU's foundational laws do not need to be changed to allay concerns about enlargement.
The governments of the bloc’s countries are cautious about admitting new members, some of which have only a few decades of democratic governance, after Hungary backslid on the principles of the rule of law under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and used its veto power to block key policy decisions, such as sanctions against Russia and support for Ukraine. The support of current members must be unanimous for candidate countries to advance through the EU accession process.
EU leaders will discuss how and how quickly new members can be brought in during a two-day summit in Brussels starting on October 15; in turn, the European Commission will ask them to provide political support for accelerating the pace. The European Council will hold a "strategic discussion on enlargement and internal reforms," according to the draft agenda.
Kallas said earlier this month that she hoped the proposed changes and talks with leaders would lead to an "autumn of enlargement" after many years of slow progress.

Iran says ready for diplomacy as Trump expects more talks

14:59:17 KST

Iran said it was ready for diplomacy but prepared for renewed U.S. attacks, as President Donald Trump said he expected more talks this week after rejecting Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sept. 27 that Iran was “fully prepared” for fighting to resume but remained willing to negotiate.
In a subsequent post on X, he said he and President Masoud Pezeshkian had come to New York “to forge peace.”
Iran would stand firm against any aggression, even an “apocalyptic war,” while remaining ready for “real diplomacy,” he added.
Araghchi said Tehran had heard Trump’s rejection but was still awaiting an official response through mediators before deciding its next step.
He outlined a seven-day plan under which Washington would first take steps including ending the war, lifting its naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and allowing Iranian oil sales. Iran would then reopen the strait on day six, followed by negotiations on a final agreement on day seven.
Trump, who rejected the proposal on Sept. 26, told Axios the following day that he expected U.S. negotiators to hold further talks with Iran this week.
“They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” he said.
Asked whether he was considering resuming strikes against Iran, Trump replied: “I am always thinking about it.”
Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations, but the sides remain divided over their scope.
Tehran wants to focus on the strait and the U.S. naval blockade, while Washington is demanding nuclear concessions.
Trump also said more than 20 million barrels of oil had passed through Hormuz over the weekend, crediting the U.S. military with facilitating the shipments.
Oil prices rose in early Asian trading on Sept. 28 following Trump’s rejection of the Iranian proposal. Brent crude futures gained 1.27 percent to $105.64 a barrel by 00:36 GMT, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 0.76 percent to $93.11,
Preliminary data from maritime intelligence firm Kpler, cited by Reuters, put crude exports from major Middle Eastern producers at 12.8 million barrels a day in September, their highest level since the war began but still below February’s 18.8 million.
Shipments through Hormuz were on track to reach about 7.4 million barrels a day this month, as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates increased exports.

Mecca alliance could help stabilize region: Academic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:57:07 UTC
14:57:07 KST

The Mecca Defense Alliance could help stabilize the region, Danish researcher Niels Hahn has said, arguing that Türkiye stands to gain from closer economic integration across Eurasia.
Speaking to daily Milliyet, Hahn assessed the alliance between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan against what he described as a longstanding U.S. interest in keeping Eurasia divided.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on Aug. 7.
Hahn, whose research focuses on U.S. military interventions, cited the 1988 National Security Strategy issued under President Ronald Reagan as a basis for his interpretation.
The document warned that U.S. national security interests would be endangered if a hostile state or group of states dominated the Eurasian landmass, which it described as the world’s heartland.
“We fought two world wars to prevent this from occurring,” the report stated.
It also outlined U.S. efforts since 1945 to prevent Soviet domination of neighboring regions and a shift in the global balance of power against Washington.
Hahn linked that objective to what he viewed as a continuing U.S. strategy of preventing political and economic integration across Eurasia.
Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East serve that interest by disrupting infrastructure, trade, investment, energy networks and transport corridors, he argued.
They also separate countries that might otherwise develop closer economic and political relations.
Discussing Israel’s ties with Greece and Greek Cyprus, Hahn suggested that Israel and Greece could help Washington put pressure on Türkiye and destabilize its surrounding region.
He described the Mecca alliance as a potentially stabilizing development through its support for peace and development.
Türkiye’s position between Europe and Asia gives it particular importance in this wider contest, Hahn said.
Peaceful economic integration across Eurasia could bring the country substantial economic and strategic benefits, he added.
He warned that a conflict between Türkiye and Israel would further divide an area capable of connecting Europe, Asia and Africa.
Syria, he said, had become an increasingly important arena for competing Turkish and Israeli interests.
Hahn also pointed to Iran’s position along potential Eurasian trade, transport and energy routes.
He argued that the conflict there should be understood as part of the broader struggle over Eurasia’s future.

US, China agree to reciprocal tariff cuts on $30bn of goods after Trump-Xi summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:54:38 UTC
14:54:38 KST

China and the US have agreed to reciprocally reduce tariffs on about $30 billion worth of imports from each other, with around 90 percent of the products covered to face most-favoured-nation (MFN) tariff rates, China’s commerce ministry confirmed on Monday.
The agreement was among the outcomes of economic and trade consultations held by Chinese and US teams in New York and Washington from September 20-23, the ministry, known as MOFCOM, said in a statement on Monday.
The two sides will implement the tariff reductions simultaneously after completing procedures required under their respective domestic laws, it said.
China and the US also agreed to establish a bilateral trade council under their economic and trade consultation mechanism, with facilitating bilateral trade as its primary task.
Tariffs on US coal exports to China will be included in the reciprocal $30 billion tariff-reduction framework, which MOFCOM said would facilitate Chinese imports of US coal in 2027 and 2028.
The two countries also agreed to establish an investment council and an agricultural working group jointly led by MOFCOM and the Office of the US Trade Representative. The agricultural working group is expected to hold its first meeting before the end of 2026.
The ministry said the two sides also reached an agreement in principle on financial services and established an artificial intelligence dialogue led by Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The next AI dialogue is expected before the end of November, while the two sides also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents.
Trump hails ‘tremendous progress’ after meeting Xi
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, hailed the “tremendous progress” made during his summit last week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“Our nation is winning,” Trump said while speaking to reporters aboard Marine One, describing his meeting with Xi as “incredible” and noting that “it lasted for a long time.”
He added that “the last three days has been very amazing,” saying “a lot of good things are happening” following the talks.
Xi concluded the three-day US visit after talks with Trump, during which the two leaders agreed to build “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, according to the White House.
They discussed global issues including Russia, North Korea and Iran, agreeing that Iran “can never have a nuclear weapon” and that no country or institution should be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways.
The two countries also agreed to establish a US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue to discuss the risks and benefits of emerging technologies, while Trump advocated trilateral arms control talks involving the US, Russia and China.

Undetonated mine spotted near site of DMZ blast that injured 3 South Korean troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:53:41 UTC
14:53:41 KST

Faisal Mahmud
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
An undetonated land mine was spotted near the site of last week’s explosions inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that wounded three South Korean soldiers, Yonhap News Agency reported on Monday, citing military sources.
The South Korean military is investigating the cause of two explosions last Monday south of the Military Demarcation Line separating the two Koreas. Two soldiers were severely wounded and another sustained minor injuries.
A Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) official said troops reported seeing an object resembling a North Korean wooden-box mine near the blast site.
“We received testimony that (what the troops witnessed) was similar to a wooden-box land mine,” the official said.
Some witnesses described the object as resembling a wooden-box mine but appearing to be made of plastic, while another believed it was a different type, according to the JCS.
South Korea’s military and the UN Command, which oversees the border area, launched a joint investigation on Sunday but were unable to reach the blast site before operations ended at sunset.
The National Forensic Service is analyzing mine fragments and explosive residue collected from the soldiers’ protective equipment.
Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said investigators did not yet have enough evidence to determine the type of mine involved.
If the mines are confirmed to be North Korean, investigators will seek to establish whether they were washed south by rain or deliberately planted. The latter would constitute a violation of the armistice agreement that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
North Korean wooden-box mines exploded on the South Korean side of the DMZ in 2015, seriously injuring two soldiers.
