Why the EU is unlikely to slash its diplomatic delegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The EU is unlikely to cut its diplomatic delegations despite budget pressure. The network, already being restructured, is vital for smaller member states and European companies.
Sensitive budget talks are eyeing the EU's administrative machinery and global funding as the most likely targets for deep cuts. But the delegation network is already being reorganised, and small European countries, as well as companies, rely on it heavily.
European governments are locked in tense negotiations over the bloc's next long-term budget, with the administrative costs of EU institutions abroad and the global programme the most likely casualties. But small countries have much to lose if the EU's global diplomatic network shrinks.
A coalition of so-called "frugal" countries, including Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, is pushing to cut the proposed size of the next Multiannual Financial Framework, the EU's budget for 2028-2034, by several hundred billion euros.
According to the ongoing discussions, there is broad consensus among member states on cutting spending dedicated to the EU institutions, while the Global Europe Fund also faces significant reductions from the levels the European Commission proposed.
These cuts are raising the prospect of scaling back the network of EU delegations worldwide, which would be highly problematic for small EU countries, according to four EU officials who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity.
"Small member states with few embassies rely heavily on the network of EU delegations," an EU diplomat from one of the smaller member states concerned said, speaking anonymously to discuss sensitive issues freely.
Global diplomatic network
According to the European External Action Service's (EEAS) 2025 report, the EU's diplomatic arm, the bloc runs 145 delegations and offices, employing almost 6,000 people for a budget of around €1bn a year.
The delegations aren't staffed by the EEAS alone: they also work with the Commission departments for international partnerships and for civil protection and humanitarian aid, while hosting seconded diplomats from national ministries and employing local agents.
Supporters of the network point out that its cost is relatively modest given the global reach it offers smaller EU member states that have no diplomatic presence of their own in many countries.
"Most costs for delegations do not come from staff but from security and facilities, which is the same reason why some member states cannot afford a diplomatic presence there," a second EU official told Euronews.
According to this official, the idea that the next budget might cut the delegations, politically unlikely, stems from an ongoing power play by the Commission to take fuller control of the EU's diplomatic service.
All the more so since the delegations are already undergoing a "modernisation" drive.
Ongoing modernisation
Since 1 September, the delegations have been undergoing a modernisation reform that has already brought significant cuts to administrative staff, prompting opposition from several EU civil service unions.
The plan centralises administrative tasks, finance management and contracts at headquarters and at regional hubs overseeing clusters of countries. The hub in South Africa, for instance, also covers Botswana, Mauritius, Madagascar and Comoros.
Local delegations, meanwhile, have been left with smaller, sometimes minimal, diplomatic representation to maintain political dialogue with local authorities, companies and stakeholders.
"The result has been a centralisation of power, weakening delegations that in the past, especially when headed by a diplomat from a large member state, could act far more independently from Brussels," a third EU official said.
At the same time, officials point out that EU countries with their own diplomatic presence often duplicate the delegations' work, and are not always aligned with how Brussels is now engaging with third countries.
From development to partnerships
During Ursula von der Leyen's first term, the Commission renamed its directorate-general for international cooperation and development (DG DEVCO) as the directorate-general for international partnerships (DG INTPA).
The change was far more than a rebrand: it marked a wholesale shift in the bloc's engagement with third countries, away from development aid and towards backing European companies on major infrastructure projects in strategic areas such as critical raw materials, connectivity and energy.
The Australian mining company Viridis, for example, signed a letter of intent with the Belgian chemical company Solvay to supply Brazilian rare earths for processing at Solvay's plant in France.
In other words, in line with von der Leyen's "geopolitical" approach, the Commission has all but dropped development projects in favour of initiatives that help European companies compete abroad with their Chinese and American rivals.
According to EU officials, when these projects are successful, they manage to help Europe's private sector win contracts far larger than the EU's own contribution, to the point that several European companies have started collaborating with the Commission much more closely.
In the new budget, the intent is also to make global funding allocation more flexible, earmarking it by macro-region, such as Latin America and Africa, rather than by individual country, so the EU can better seize opportunities such as commercial contracts or trade agreements.
"The delegations are key to managing projects with local partners; there are certain tasks that simply cannot be moved to headquarters," a fourth EU official said.

MPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix it | Jane Turner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

The UK government is discussing the country’s biggest challenges at the Labour party conference. But amid the speeches, announcements and headlines, it should not forget one of the clearest messages to emerge from parliament just two weeks ago – our palliative care system is not working for far too many people.
Throughout the assisted dying debate, MPs who disagreed deeply on the core issue, often agreed on one thing – our palliative care system urgently needs fixing. Some spoke from personal experience where they had seen relatives forced to wait hours in pain, or those who had to go to hospital instead of staying in their own homes because the right support wasn’t available.
They raised concerns that those from poorer backgrounds were more likely to struggle to access good quality palliative care and described the system as a “postcode lottery”, with some areas offering 24-hour specialist support in people’s homes, while in the next town over, A&E is the only option.
As attention turns to conference season and the next set of political priorities – including a new system of adult social care free at the point of delivery – there is a danger these concerns are forgotten. That must not happen. MPs were right to say palliative care needs urgent reform during the assisted dying debate; that urgency can’t disappear now the vote is over.
At Sue Ryder, we have a neutral stance on assisted dying. But we are clear that everyone deserves access to good palliative care when they need it. Too often, the debate is framed as a stark choice between unbearable suffering on one side and an assisted death on the other. The reality is rarely that simple.
Of course, dying is not easy. Some people experience pain, breathlessness, restlessness or other distressing symptoms. When that happens, our responsibility is to respond – bringing all the skill, expertise and compassion we have to relieve suffering as best we can. But one troubling thing about the debate around assisted dying is that the most difficult deaths are often presented as if they are the norm.
When good care is available, dying can be a calmer, more peaceful experience: families gathering around bedsides, holding hands, sharing stories, laughing through tears and making the most of whatever time remains. We see people becoming increasingly tired. They sleep more and eat less, gradually becoming less aware of the world around them as their bodies begin the natural process of dying. We sometimes see fear, but it is not always fear of pain. More often, it is the fear of leaving loved ones behind. We see people who need honest conversations about what lies ahead. People who need dignity, compassion, expert care and the confidence that someone will be there to support them and those they love.
I understand why stories of suffering have such a powerful impact. They should. Nobody wants to see another human being in pain or distress. And even with the best quality care, some deaths can be difficult. But in truth, some of the greatest suffering we witness is not physical. It is uncertainty. It can be loneliness. It is spending precious final days in a crowded hospital ward because the support needed to get someone home has not been arranged in time. It is families exhausted from navigating a complex system when they should be focused on time together.
That is why the conversation about assisted dying must now be matched by an equally urgent conversation about how people live in their final weeks and months. A good death is rarely defined by one final act, but by whether someone feels safe, comfortable and listened to. It is about having the right care, in the right place, which is often at home, and ensuring nobody faces the end of life feeling frightened, unsupported or alone.
Whatever your view on assisted dying, decent palliative care should be non-negotiable.
My perspective comes from standing at the bedsides of dying people for years, and supporting the families who love them. Working with our partners within healthcare, we want to build a palliative and end-of-life care system that can keep pace with growing demand and give everyone access the care they deserve.
We need to invest in palliative and end-of-life care where people need it most. That means better palliative care in hospitals. We also need the right expertise in the community to avoid unnecessary and distressing hospital admissions. And that means expanding care in the community with increased hospice-at-home services so more people can be cared for in their own homes, surrounded by the people they love. And it means making sure specialist support is available when people need it, not determined by their postcode or the time of day they become unwell.
These are not optional extras at the end of life. They are essential components of healthcare, and they should be available to everyone.
As Labour MPs gather at conference, ministers have an opportunity to show that improving palliative care is more than a talking point raised during a contentious debate. The responsibility to tackle the inequalities the debate brought into sharp focus has only just begun. The assisted dying vote may be over. The palliative care crisis is not.
- 
  Jane Turner is chief nurse at the palliative support charity Sue Ryder

Starwatch: Tracking down the faint stars of Pisces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars.
The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen.
Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location.
The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars.
Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.
From the southern hemisphere, Pisces is also well placed in the evening, appearing higher in the sky.

Should you lock into a fixed-rate savings account paying 5.25%?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

Returns on the top fixed-rate savings accounts are at their highest level in years and still climbing, with some now paying up to 5.25%.
It leaves those with money to put away facing a choice: lock into some of the best interest rates on offer in several years or hold your nerve in the hope they get even better?
While new fixed mortgage rates have jumped in recent months – dealing a blow to many homebuyers and those aiming to remortgage – their pain has been savers’ gain.
This month, the data provider Moneyfacts said fixed savings rates were at “multiyear highs”, fuelled by strong competition, and this trend has continued: on Thursday the average new one-year fixed savings bond rate was 4.41%.
With a fixed-rate savings bond, you typically have to tie up your money for between six months and five years, and they provide a clear, guaranteed return. The one-year version tends to be popular as many people do not want to tie up cash for long periods.
The top-paying accounts are offering a fair bit more than that average: at the time of writing, GB Bank had a one-year fixed-rate bond paying 5.05%. Meanwhile, Kent Reliance had a 13-month account offering 5.06%. (With both, the minimum deposit is £1,000.)
The best-buy rates are even higher if you tie up cash for longer. This week, GB Bank, Shawbrook Bank and Vanquis were among those paying 5.25% on a five-year fixed bond.
However, some savers will recall that as recently as late 2023 there were fixed bonds paying 6%, and if and when the Bank of England base rate goes up, that could push returns on savings higher than they are now.
Many economists predict the Bank will lift the base rate before the end of this year, with further rises thought likely next year.
Rachel Springall at Moneyfacts expects the deals on offer to savers “to get even better”. However, she cautions that we do not know the path interest rates will follow, and that anything could happen in the next few months or so.
Those with cash to stash may want to hedge their bets by putting some into a competitive fixed-rate bond now and keeping another chunk in a high-paying easy access account. There are easy access accounts paying up to 5%.
Some fixed-rate savings bonds will let you “drip-feed” cash in – for example, some will let you add money while the account is still open to new customers, while others have a specific “funding window”, which might be a few weeks but can be just a few days.
The cost of living is still a big issue, with many worried about the prospect of higher energy bills this winter – so it could be a mistake to put all your savings cash out of reach. Springall suggests spreading your money across fixed-rate products and accounts that are accessible, plus also making use of tax-free cash Isas.
If you are aiming to put some money into savings or switch providers and are not using your Isa allowance at all, you are missing out on valuable tax benefits.
Rates on fixed cash Isas are often slightly lower than for similar non-Isa accounts, although not always: Shawbrook Bank’s five-year fixed savings bond and five-year fixed cash Isa pay 5.25%.
Every tax year you can save up to £20,000 in Isas, but from April 2027, the rules will change for anyone under 65. Instead of being able to put all of the money into a cash Isa, that element will be capped at £12,000. If you are 65 or over, all £20,000 can still be put into a cash Isa.

Rice ‘polenta’ with sausage sauce and rice with pork, lemon and saffron: Pasta Grannies’ Italian rice recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

If I were to say “Italian rice”, you might well think “risotto” and “the Po Valley”. However, these two recipes come from Sardinia and the Marche, mainly because I wanted to share a few easy, not-laden-with-rules Italian rice dishes.
Maria’s riso con maiale e zafferano (rice with pork and saffron)
Eighty-three-year-old Maria was widowed young and, to make ends meet, set up an agriturismo dining space in her home near Oristano in Sardinia’s rice-growing heartland. This rustic risotto with a wonderful combination of flavours was one of her customers’ favourites, and it’s a great recipe if you are nervous about making a classic risotto with all its rules.
Prep 20 min
Stock 2 hr+ (optional)
Cook 1 hr 20 min
Serves 4
For the stock (optional)
1kg pork bones
  1 sun-dried tomato, or ½ tsp tomato puree
1 onion, peeled
  2 celery sticks
  1 carrot
For the rice
Extra-virgin olive oil
  1 carrot, diced
Sea salt and black pepper
500g pork shoulder steak, or other stewing pork, cut into 1cm chunks
1 onion, peeled and chopped
1 sprig fresh rosemary
  1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed
1 sun-dried tomato, minced (optional; see method)
3½ tbsp white wine (vernaccia, if you can find it, otherwise any dry white wine)
100g passata
750ml hot meat stock, homemade (see above and method) or bought in
250g arborio rice
  Zest of 1 lemon, ½ finely grated, the rest pared off in strips and julienned
2 0.1g sachets saffron powder, or 1 pinch saffron threads soaked in hot water or stock
50g pecorino, grated, plus extra to serve
If you’re making your own stock, simmer the pork bones in plenty of water with the tomato, onion, celery and carrot for several hours, until deeply flavoured. Strain and keep hot if you are going to use it immediately.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pan, then fry the diced carrot with a pinch of salt until it starts to soften. Add the diced pork, fry, stirring, until browned all over, then add the onion, rosemary and garlic, season well and cook for five or so minutes, until the onion is translucent.
If you didn’t use a sun-dried tomato in your stock, add the minced one now – it’s Maria’s secret for boosting umami. Pour in the wine, let the liquid evaporate, then stir in the passata. Add a ladle of hot stock and simmer gently for anything between 20 and 40 minutes, depending on your cut of pork: you want the stew to have cooked properly before making a risotto with it. Indeed, you can make it the day before to improve its flavour; just reheat first.
When the stew is ready and bubbling and the stock is keeping hot in another pot next door, add the rice to the stew, stirring to coat it in the sauce. Add more hot stock a ladleful at a time, stirring frequently until absorbed. Tasteand add salt if necessary. When the rice is about halfway cooked, stir in the grated lemon zest and julienned peel.
Dissolve the saffron in a little hot stock, then stir it through the rice. Keep cooking, stirring and adding stock as needed, until the rice is tender but still has some bite; the finished dish should be more like a pilaf than a creamy northern Italian risotto, and the whole process will take about 20 minutes.
To finish, stir through the grated pecorino and serve with extra cheese at the table.
Rita’s frascarelli con sugo di finocchietto e salsiccia (rice “polenta” with wild fennel and sausage sauce)
Rita, Adriana and Brunhilde are the bustling heart of my home town, Cingoli in Le Marche, where they organise a sagra, or food festival, at which they serve this rice “polenta” that has sustained families in the region for centuries. Frascarelli was traditionally served plain to invalids and new mothers, because it was considered nourishing and easy to digest, but when dressed with a spicy, robust sauce, it becomes a hearty meal for the whole family. It was originally served on a communal polenta board, because in the old days people didn’t have individual crockery, and our Instagram post of the three friends demonstrating this went viral (some viewers were horrified); of course, these days, everyone uses plates or bowls.
Prep 10 min
Cook 45 min
Serves 6
For the sauce
1 bunch wild fennel fronds, or 1 tsp freshly ground fennel seeds
Extra-virgin olive oil
  ½ tsp dried chilli flakes, or to taste
  1 splash white wine
  3 large, meaty Italian sausages
  1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed (optional; see method)
400ml passata
  1 tsp caster sugar
  Salt, to taste
For the frascarelli
400g arborio rice
50g plain flour
  1 generous pinch salt
Begin by making the sauce. Pick through the fennel fronds for the tenderest pieces and wash thoroughly; otherwise, use freshly ground fennel seeds, or substitute with chervil or parsley. Heat a generous amount of oil in a large pan on a medium heat. Add the fennel, chilli flakes and white wine, and cook gently for a few minutes, to release the aromatics. (Adriana says the older the herb, the longer it will need to simmer, and that you should cook it for at least 10 minutes.)
Skin the sausages, crumble the meat into the pan and cook, stirring frequently, until it begins to brown and release its fat (if your sausages aren’t Italian, add the crushed garlic clove at this point and fry for an extra minute). Add the passata, rinse out the jar with a little water to capture every drop, and add that, too. Stir in the sugar to balance the acidity of the tomatoes, then simmer gently for at least 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Check the seasoning and keep warm.
For the frascarelli, bring two litres of water to a gentle simmer in a large, heavy-based saucepan. Add the rice, stir well and season with a good pinch of salt. Keep the heat moderate, to prevent the rice boiling over – Rita is vigilant about this – and cook, stirring regularly to prevent the rice sticking to the bottom of the pan. After about 10 minutes, when the rice is nearly tender, the mix will still be liquid. Gradually whisk in the flour to thicken it to a soft, polenta-like consistency; the texture should be creamy but not too thick.
Spoon the frascarelli into warmed bowls, top generously with the fennel and sausage sauce and serve immediately.
- 
  These recipes are edited extracts from Pasta Grannies: Eat Everything – Pasta and Beyond for the Good Life, by Vicky Bennison, published by Rizzoli at £29.95. To order a copy for £26.95, go to guardianbookshop.com

Tokyo vs Seoul: Which trendy capital should you visit on an Asian adventure?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

Tourism in both Tokyo and Seoul has been booming for a while now and there’s no sign of this slowing down just yet. Here we take a look at two of Asia's trending capital cities.
What’s the answer to the question in the headline above? It’s an easy one, really. If you are planning a trip to the Far East, then of course you should visit both Tokyo and Seoul.
The capitals of Japan and South Korea have emerged as two of the world’s most in-demand destinations – not just for the trendy jet-setters, but for travellers of all ages and interests.
As someone who’s been to both – and is genuinely fascinated by both – Tokyo and Seoul offer very different vibes for a city break in Asia.
But the one thing they do have in common is the sheer amount of things to see and do, especially for first-time visitors.
Tokyo: A big-city experience
Few cities can match Tokyo for sheer scale or energy. And the numbers don’t lie as in 2025 Japan’s capital welcomed a record 28.65 million international visitors.
According to the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO), the country’s travel sector is “booming” and for many first-time visitors classic destinations like Tokyo and Kyoto remain a major draw with their temples and historic neighbourhoods.
Tokyo really does have everything and is so big that it can sometimes feel like there are cities within a city, with each area and district having their own personality.
When I arrived my first port of call was the gigantic Shinjuku train station – a memorable experience in itself. Not only is it the world’s busiest station, serving more than 2.7 million passengers every day, but there are also more than 200 exits. Yes, 200. So, first things first, if you arrive at Shinjuku carefully check where to exit or you could soon get lost…
Once you have managed to leave the station and make it to street level, you’ll really feel like you’ve arrived. Shinjuku is home to towering skyscrapers, wide shopping streets and plenty of cafes, bars and restaurants – many of which are open around the clock.
Another introduction to modern Tokyo is Shibuya with its famous crossing, shops and observation decks. For fashion and creativity head to Harajuku, a close walk from Shibuya, where you’ll see street fashion and youth culture on display from stylish Tokyoites.
Akihabara is Tokyo’s go-to district for pop culture, electronics, anime and manga. Other cool areas to see include Roppongi and the Roppongi Hills Mori Tower, which boasts the Tokyo City View observation deck, and Ginza, which offers luxury shopping and high-end restaurants.
While modern Tokyo is neon-lit and bustling at all hours, centuries of culture and heritage reveal a much slower side to the Japanese capital.
Located in the historic district of Asakusa, Sensō-ji is Tokyo’s oldest Buddhist temple and definitely worth a visit. As is Meiji Jingu Shrine next to Yoyogi Park in Shibuya. Don’t forget your camera here as there’s an Insta-worthy shot of a wall of decorated saké barrels on the path leading towards the shrine. Honestly, your camera roll will soon be full…
For foodies, Tokyo has more Michelin-starred restaurants than any other city in the world, including 11 three-star and 26 two-star. However, it’s not all about fine dining as some of the most memorable meals can be found on the streets and are quite affordable.
A few days is not nearly enough to truly discover what makes Tokyo one of the world’s best capitals. With temples, traditional gardens, anime culture and a brilliant nightlife to explore, even a week would barely scratch the surface here.
If you do have a day or two to spare though, don’t miss out on Mount Fuji and the Fuji Five Lakes region. We stayed by Lake Kawaguchi and here you can enjoy lakeside walks, hot springs and panoramic viewpoints of Japan’s iconic peak.
Seoul: K-culture sparks tourism boom
While Tokyo has long been one of Asia’s tourism heavyweights, Seoul is experiencing a remarkable rise of its own – thanks in part to all things “K-culture”.
In South Korea’s capital, K-pop, K-dramas, Korean food, fashion and beauty have helped create one of the world’s hottest city break destinations. Need proof? Just look at some of the trends and stats.
Described by Time Out as “a master of all trades”, Seoul jumped 33 places to rank ninth in the magazine’s 50 Best Cities in the World for 2026. The trendy Jongno 3-ga was also named by Time Out as officially the coolest neighbourhood on Earth. High praise indeed. Head to Jongno 3-ga and explore a “maze of alleys, late-night food stalls and rivers of makgeolli”.
With the rise of K-culture, Seoul was also named the favourite worldwide city among Gen Z and Millennial travellers in the Trazees awards for the fifth consecutive year.
International arrivals are booming, too: a record 8.23 million overseas visitors came to the city during the first half of 2026, up 21.3% year on year, according to the Seoul Metropolitan Government.
Like Tokyo, one of Seoul’s biggest attractions is the contrast between old and new.
Start at Gyeongbokgung Palace, the largest of Seoul’s five grand palaces. Time your visit for the colourful changing of the guard ceremony before exploring its courtyards, pavilions and gardens. You can easily spend a few hours here.
From Gyeongbokgung Palace, walk to nearby Bukchon Hanok Village and explore the narrow streets lined with traditional Korean “hanok” houses. Personally, the village was one of the highlights from my trip.
After the palaces and traditional side of Seoul, it’s time to hit the skyscrapers, shops and nightlife of Gangnam, made globally famous by Psy’s 2012 smash hit “Gangnam Style”. Please, don’t do the dance…
As well as a trip to trendy Jongno 3-ga, other neighbourhoods to put on your list include Myeong-dong, a major destination for shopping and street food, and Hongdae, which is known for its nightlife and music scene. Meanwhile, Seongsu has emerged as one of Seoul’s coolest districts for cafés, fashion and pop-ups.
Foodies should not miss out on the classics like Korean barbecue, soju, and “chimaek” – a hugely popular combination of fried chicken and beer. What a pairing. For fine dining, Seoul has 42 restaurants that have been awarded a Michelin star.
While Seoul is undoubtedly a megacity, there’s also plenty of nature to enjoy. The Han River cuts through the heart of Seoul and its waterfront parks can be explored on foot or by bike. Another nice option is a river cruise, especially at night. For hiking trails and mountain views, Bukhansan National Park is a good choice and easily accessible from the city.
Make time for N Seoul Tower and its views of the South Korean capital. Another attraction you’ll certainly see is Cheonggyecheon, an 11km-long restored stream and public park running through the centre of downtown Seoul.
For an easy day trip from Seoul, book a tour to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between North and South Korea. It’s a strange experience, but worth seeing. Depending on the tour, you can visit the Dora Observatory for views across the border and Dorasan Station, a symbolic railway station built with the hope of connecting the two Koreas.
Tokyo or Seoul? Why not both?
So, which one will it be, Tokyo or Seoul? Tokyo wins for sheer scale and endless exploration, while Seoul offers an exciting mix of K-culture, historic sights and cool neighbourhoods. But there’s little reason to choose.
Direct flights between Tokyo and Seoul take around 2.5 hours, with multiple services every day. If time and budget allow, combining a trip gives you two very different sides of an Asian city break.
Faced with the difficult choice between them, I decided to visit both cities on the same trip. And I’d definitely do the same again.

Amid warnings over possible attack, Europe mulls contingency plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs disagrees with the mounting calls and reports that Russia may attack NATO or the European Union in the coming months in an attempt to weaken their support for Ukraine. He says they've already started.
"We are not talking about a conventional war. We are talking about all kinds of provocations, all kinds of acts of sabotage, all kinds of tests, and definitely this is something that is already happening as we speak," the Latvian leader told RFE/RL in an interview at United Nations headquarters on September 21.
European intelligence officials, the CIA, and even French President Emmanuel Macron and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk have all warned in recent days of assessments that Moscow may go as far as to launch an air attack in some form on NATO territory in the coming months to show the military alliance's Article 5 common defence pledge is little more than a few words on a piece of paper.
Instances of attacks in recent months attributed to Russia – what the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) calls a "coordinated series of kinetic campaigns" – include arson, assassination plans, and the sabotage of infrastructure, such as railway vandalism and electronic interference.
Moscow consistently denies any involvement in the sabotage operations attributed to it by European governments, but officials from NATO and EU capitals have ramped up efforts to draw up contingency plans and measures to counteract.
The Narva scenario
One such scenario is the so-called Narva scenario, which describes a hypothetical military scenario in which Russia would attack a NATO country using hybrid warfare tactics similar to the initial phase of the actual 2014 Russian invasion of Ukraine's Crimea.
Narva is a small city with a sizeable Russian population on the Estonian side of the border with Russia. Analysts have said that such a move from Russia could be taken as a means to test NATO's willingness to risk a direct confrontation over strategically insignificant territory.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna warned of growing Russian hybrid attacks across Europe in an interview with RFE/RL this week, saying there are lots of rumours that Putin is going to wage a full-scale military operation against the Baltic states or Poland.
But, he added, "our intelligence doesn’t see any serious military movements on the other side of our borders because Russia is stuck in Ukraine".
Analysts at the ISW, however, said on September 21 that while Estonia and Latvia have both said that they have yet to observe any evidence of a buildup of Russian forces near their borders that would be necessary for a full-scale invasion of their countries, "scenarios for Russian action have not received the detailed analysis they deserve and require".
RFE/RL contacted several diplomats with knowledge of EU and NATO preparedness planning, but none would give concrete examples of what is in the works saying the information was classified.
One Central European official acknowledged that there are informal discussions on a working level on what to do logistically in case the Baltics and Poland are attacked, but added there are no official guidelines and real preparations in place.
A NATO official said the alliance has the national defence plans of members, "which are top secret but essentially spell out what we do in all types of war scenarios".
Rinkēvičs said calling the current wave of Russian attacks "hybrid" may also be stifling the urgency needed among European officials to address the situation.
"I think that when we use the word "hybrid," then it somehow sounds less, let's say, dangerous, kind of more innocent terminology than actually those acts per se," he said.
"I think that the most dangerous scenario would be if Russia gets reckless, if we do not respond in an efficient manner and there are real casualties happening. [...] Our part of Europe is trying to be as ready as possible. But look, if Russia launches a missile attack, then it is absolutely clear this is Article 5, and then it's absolutely clear that there is going to be a response."
A permanent US base In Poland?
The increased tensions have caught the attention of Washington, which has been looking at its European troop deployments, basing arrangements, status-of-forces agreements, and general host-nation negotiations.
Last week, US President Donald Trump says Washington and Warsaw are making "major progress" toward establishing a permanent US Army base in Poland, potentially expanding the American military presence on NATO's eastern flank.
The move came a day after Polish authorities temporarily closed airports in Lublin and Rzeszów as Russian strikes targeted parts of Ukraine near the Polish border, according to Polish officials.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also warned that Russia could seek to conduct drone or missile attacks against NATO countries supporting Ukraine while presenting them as accidents.
He too said such incidents could be intended to test NATO's response and undermine allied unity. The assessment was based on intelligence from NATO, Ukraine, and the United States, according to Tusk.
Similarly, the Baltics were rattled last year when three Russian jet fighters violated Estonia’s airspace for 12 minutes.
According to Estonian officials, the Russian pilots acknowledged but disregarded communication from two Italian pilots in F-35 fighter jets, which had been scrambled from NATO’s Baltic Air Policing Mission in Ämari Air Base in Estonia, before ultimately being escorted into international skies.
Tsahkna pointed out in his interview with RFE/RL that Russia is already attacking Europe.
In response to the incursion, which Russia denies, Estonian called for Article 4 consultations under NATO's constitution, which are just below invoking the collective defence clause in Article 5.
"We must be ready to act united," Tsahkna said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is showing no signs that he "really would like to have a meaningful peace and a just and lasting peace" with Ukraine after more than five years of war and is watching how Europe reacts to provocations.
"But if he is going to have Ukraine, it’s just one step, and we’ll see further aggression in Europe," the Estonian minister warned.
This story was originally published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), partners of LRT English.

Stories as a Resource: How Narrative Design Builds Resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

This article is part of "Thresholds", a special edition printed newspaper by Cobe Notes x ArchDaily.
There are two unique things about being human that made us survive the early years and spread over the whole planet: sweating and storytelling. Sweating helps cool down the body when running long distances. Stories help us collaborate in big numbers and share knowledge across groups and generations. As architects, we still rely on the same tools to make visions become reality.
As professor of stories Angus Fletcher points out in his book Primal Intelligence, there is a common misconception about the role of stories: when our "rational" brain has developed an idea that we fail to explain to a wider group, we pack it into a story, and suddenly everybody understands. Fletcher argues that it actually works the other way around: ideas come from stories, our brain works in stories, and stories form reality. Architects have a derogatory term for turning that process the wrong side up: "post-rationalisation", for example when diagrams are made to explain a design that is already decided.

The sea full of diclofenac — how researchers are trying to cut pharmaceutical pollution in the Baltic Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:57:43 UTC
13:57:43 KST

Paracetamol, ibuprofen, carbamazepine, diclofenac, and other pharmaceuticals are being found in the Baltic Sea. Researchers say changing how some medicines are prescribed, used and disposed of could help reduce the flow.
The Baltic Sea — an inland sea surrounded by nine countries in the northeast of Europe — is one of the most polluted seas in the world.
It carries the legacy of decades of pollution: thousands of tonnes of chemical munitions and other war material were dumped into its waters after the Second World War.
Today, microplastics, industrial chemicals and agricultural runoff are adding to the pressure on an ecosystem that is particularly vulnerable because of its semi-enclosed nature.
The pharmaceutical pollution is what researchers from four different countries — Sweden, Finland, Lithuania and Latvia — are after, arguing that the Baltic's pharmaceutical problem cannot be solved entirely at the shoreline.
“It's not only about wastewater treatment,” Marmar Nekoro, a researcher at the faculty of pharmacy at Uppsala University in Sweden, told Euronews. “We have to look across the rest of the life cycle.”
Some of the pharmaceutical pollution may be preventable much earlier — when a medicine is prescribed, when a patient decides whether and how to take it, and when an unused packet is returned to a pharmacy rather than discarded.
The approach does not mean asking patients to stop taking medicines they need. Instead, researchers say doctors could consider the environmental impact when choosing between medicines, while patients and health systems could do more to prevent unused drugs from entering the environment.
One of the medicines researchers are watching is diclofenac, a widely used anti-inflammatory painkiller that has been detected in aquatic environments. According to Kristina Garuolienė, a researcher at Vilnius University, there can be circumstances in which alternative medicines could be considered.
“That is turning to rational prescribing; when doctors are prescribing medicine, they have to also think about which medicine is not dangerous to the environment,” she told Euronews.
The issue is particularly relevant in the Baltic Sea, an inland sea surrounded by nine countries in northeastern Europe. It is one of the most polluted seas in the world and is particularly vulnerable because of its semi-enclosed nature.
The toll of pollution
Pharmaceuticals enter the Baltic Sea through multiple pathways, including wastewater from households and hospitals, discharges from pharmaceutical production sites, and runoff from agriculture and other land-based sources. Companion animals can also contribute when their faeces are not properly collected and disposed of.
Wastewater treatment plants alone are estimated to release around 1,800 tonnes of pharmaceuticals into the Baltic each year, according to a decade-old report by UNESCO and the Baltic Marine Environment Protection Commission. Most wastewater treatment plants are yet to be equipped with a fourth treatment stage specifically designed to remove pharmaceutical pollutants.
“Whenever you ingest pharmaceuticals, you take it as a patient, your whole body or the whole medicine is not taken up by your body; part of it or quite a large part of it is excreted,” Marmar Nekoro, a researcher at the faculty of pharmacy at Uppsala University in Sweden, told Euronews.
Once pharmaceuticals reach the sea, they can persist in the environment for long periods. Carbamazepine, a prescription medication used to treat epilepsy, nerve pain and bipolar disorder, has been repeatedly detected across the Baltic.
“It takes almost three and a half years for it to break down into half,” Nekoro said. “So the breakdown is very, very slow,” which leads to accumulation of the substance.
The main concern is not that people will be harmed simply by swimming in the water, according to Björn Wettermark, professor of pharmacoepidemiology at Uppsala University who leads the project, aside from the risk of antibiotic or antimicrobial resistance.
Instead, researchers are concerned about the effects on non-target organisms living in the sea. Pharmaceuticals can affect wildlife and contribute to the broader problem of antimicrobial resistance.
Fish, frogs and other species can experience feminisation due to synthetic oestrogens, potentially affecting entire populations. The Baltic blue mussel, Mytilus edulis — a key species in the ecosystem because it filters water — can have less energy available for normal metabolism and growth when exposed to some painkillers.
Changes to mussel populations could create additional pressure on an ecosystem already affected by pharmaceuticals and other pollutants, as well as eutrophication — the process by which a body of water becomes overly enriched with nutrients, leading to rapid plant and algae growth that depletes dissolved oxygen.
Prescribing the right medicines
Therefore, researchers are looking at improving how medicines are prescribed and used as one of the ways to cut pollution.
That does not mean asking patients to stop taking medicines they need. Rather, researchers say that when several clinically appropriate options are available, environmental impact could become another factor in the choice.
“We know for several studies for a long time that not the best drugs are being prescribed, neither from the clinical effect of it, or we have an overuse which is unnecessary,” Wettermark said.
“So there are lots of win-wins here through improving the prescribing and the use of medicines first, but both are probably needed to get an impact on the environment.”
But changing prescribing practices is not simply a matter of telling doctors to choose “greener” medicines.
A recent study of environmentally responsible prescribing in Sweden found that doctors need more targeted education and better access to environmental information about pharmaceuticals.
Returning unused medicines
Unused medicines can also find their way into the environment if they are thrown into household waste, poured down sinks or flushed down toilets.
In Lithuania, Garuolienė said, awareness of returning unused medicines to pharmacies has been increasing.
“Every year, people are returning more and more medicine to pharmacies,” she said, adding that Lithuania has rules governing how medicines should be returned.
That is a positive development, she said, because it means people are less likely to throw medicines away or flush them down the toilet.
But it also raises another question: why were the medicines unused in the first place?
“Probably they are not using [them] as prescribed, or maybe our doctors are prescribing too many medicines and some of them are not necessary,” she said.
The researchers’ aim is ultimately to move beyond individual prescribing decisions and build a broader picture of how pharmaceutical pollution can be reduced across the Baltic region.

US FDA approves Mirum’s drug for rare bone disorder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:56:00 UTC
13:56:00 KST

US FDA approves Mirum’s drug for rare bone disorder
WASHINGTON - The US FDA on Sept 25 approved Mirum Pharmaceuticals’ pill for a rare bone disorder, offering patients a new treatment option that can help slow the disease’s progression.
The once-daily drug zilurgisertib, branded as Atebrioz, is approved for patients aged 12 years and older with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), which causes muscles, tendons and ligaments to gradually transform into bone, restricting movement and leading to severe disability.
Atebrioz blocks ALK2, a protein that is abnormally active in most patients with FOP and drives bone formation outside the skeleton. The recommended dose is 100 milligrams.
FOP is typically diagnosed in early childhood. About 300 people in the US and 900 worldwide, according to Mirum, have the condition.
Mirum expects to launch the drug in October and plans to announce its price at the launch, chief executive officer Chris Peetz told Reuters.
“It is a game changer for patients to have a medicine like this that can really stop that progressive, endless accumulation of bone,” Peetz said.
Citizens analyst Jonathan Wolleben estimates Atebrioz could cost about US$750,000 (S$958,410) annually and generate roughly US$150 million in peak worldwide sales.
Mirum had licensed the drug from Incyte earlier in 2026 for US$16 million upfront, along with potential milestone payments and sales royalties.
The approval by the US Food and Drug Administration was based on a 63-patient study, in which Atebrioz significantly cut new bone formation compared to placebo at week 24.
Current treatment options for FOP include Ipsen’s oral drug Sohonos and Regeneron’s Pasatru, a monthly infusion. Sohonos is approved for certain children and adults, while Pasatru is approved for adults.
Wolleben said Atebrioz could become a preferred treatment because it combines oral dosing with strong efficacy and a favorable safety profile, offering greater convenience than Regeneron’s monthly infusion and potentially fewer safety concerns than Ipsen’s Sohonos. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Asbestos Emergency: War Debris Poses Hazardous Waste Challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:52:00 UTC
13:52:00 KST

Ukraine lacks services or landfills to handle asbestos-contaminated rubble emerging from its war-damaged buildings, a United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) official has warned, raising fresh concerns for workers and communities as reconstruction gathers pace
More than 70% of roofs on residential and public buildings in Ukraine are covered with corrugated asbestos-cement sheets, according to a UN Environment Programme article published on May 7, 2025. The material also appears in fencing and pipes used for water supply and heat removal systems.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Asbestos, which severely damages the lungs and can cause fatal diseases even decades after exposure, has been banned throughout Europe since 2005 (in Italy since 1992).
The scale of destruction caused by Russian land operations and bombing compounds the challenge. According to KSE Institute’s count, published on 17 August 2026, there are nearly 416,000 damaged or destroyed buildings as of February 2026. That figure measures building damage; it does not establish how many affected structures contained asbestos. However, it gives an idea of the size of the problem.
EU-supported research involving Kyiv School of Economics (KSE) Institute and Open Environmental University Plus wrote a local study European Green Dimensions: Fundamental, Applied, and Industrial Aspects (2025), which provides more specific evidence. Researchers surveying demolition waste across seven communities in Mykolaiv region, covering 33 hectares, reported 713.82 tons of building materials containing asbestos. These data refer to a single Ukrainian region.
Taiwan Cement Backs Ukraine’s Recovery With IFCEM Investment
The study warns that improper handling of demolition waste can contaminate soil, air and water. Its discussion of recovering concrete, brick, wood and metals illustrates the wider reconstruction challenge: retrieving useful materials while managing hazardous components.
First announced in 2025, UNEP launched a Japan-funded initiative to strengthen hazardous waste management. The initiative was designed to examine handling methods, costs, disposal space and public health considerations, alongside material testing, worker safety and site trials. Together, the sources document an urgent waste-management problem. They urge urgent investments in safe handling and disposal capacity.
On Sept. 24, at the Odesa Region Recovery Conference, the Senior Programme Officer of UNEP in Kyiv, Pier Carlo Sandei, confirmed that Ukraine has no services and suitable landfills to dispose asbestos-contaminated debris or dangerous waste.
All the rubble is piled up in open fields without any hazardous waste separation, much less a recycling system. Therefore, both waste collection workers and residents near the dumps are exposed to serious health risks.
The 2022 Law of Ukraine on Public Health banned the use of asbestos in the construction of new buildings, but did not provide regulations for its removal from old buildings.
Yet, this sector represents a major business opportunity for international companies specializing in collection and storage, which could benefit from funds raised by an international program.

Treasurer defends inflation record as 15-year interest rate high looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:36:42 UTC
13:36:42 KST

Treasurer Jim Chalmers defends inflation record as 15-year interest rate high looms
In short:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has defended the government's track record on inflation on the eve of an anticipated rate hike.
The government has celebrated a deficit $6 billion lower than the May forecast but warned there are tough times ahead for households.
What's next?
The Reserve Bank is anticipated to increase the cash rate to its highest level since 2011 on Tuesday.
On the eve of a widely anticipated rate hike that would push interest rates to their highest level in 15 years, the treasurer has defended the government's track record on inflation, saying high petrol prices are to blame rather than government spending.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers confirmed the budget deficit for last financial year was $6 billion better than the $28.3 billion forecast in May.
He said that showed the government had been "limiting spending growth" and doing the work to curb inflation ahead of the Reserve Bank's looming decision on Tuesday whether to again hikes the official cash rate to a possible 4.6 per cent.
The last time the cash rate was around this level was October to November 2011, meaning anyone who has purchased their first home since that time has never had to service a higher borrowing level on their loan.
Mr Chalmers revealed the projected national debt was lower than forecast in the May budget, with health costs and other payments down $1.4 billion and revenue up $4.6 billion more than expected.
The increased tax was driven by better-than-expected returns on superannuation and other investments, rather than a higher take from wage earners or mining revenue, the latter which came in short on budget forecasts.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher credited the budget savings to less spending across aged care, childcare and the pharmaceutical benefits scheme (PBS).
Households brace for interest rate hike
The treasurer pushed back on suggestions the government could do more to help households, pointing to global economic pressure and the Iran-US war as "absolutely disastrous" for family budgets in Australia.
While Mr Chalmers celebrated an improvement for the budget, he conceded that there would be "difficult months" ahead.
He insisted other countries were in a "far worse position" than Australia, and said anybody who had watched recent developments in global debt and bond markets would understand they were having a "very serious pressure" on borrowing costs.
The figures released on Monday showed government spending had risen from 26.6 per cent to 26.9 per cent of GDP, largely reflecting the weaker economic growth of the Australian economy.
Mr Chalmers insisted the war in the Middle East, not government spending, was to blame for increasing inflation.
"Any objective observer of what's happening in our economy and particularly what's happening with inflation, will conclude that a big driver of the inflation we're seeing in our economy right now comes from the Middle East,"
But Opposition Leader Angus Taylor pointed the finger back at Mr Chalmers, saying the government was wrong to put the blame on international factors.
"He's just terribly unlucky, isn't he? Every day he wakes up and it's someone else's fault … The link between inflation and high interest rates that we've seen for the last four-and-a-half years is with this government," he said.
Loading...
Pushed on whether the government could do more to meet the inflation challenge, Mr Chalmers conceded it had existed before the war in the Middle East.
"The best way to describe the inflation challenge right now is that we have an inflation challenge in our economy, made much worse by the war," he said.
He said while the government was committed to working on productivity gains, the benefits would "unfortunately" be felt in the "coming years, not necessarily the coming days and weeks".
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also blamed global inflation as the primary issue driving up interest rates, and acknowledged some people were "doing it tough".
"We'll continue to take work such as the $6 billion deficit compared with what was anticipated in our May budget," he said.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics is due to release the inflation figures for August on Wednesday.

The energy supply shock was also driving up inflation fears, while interest rate differentials and a weaker New Zealand dollar could add to the impact of higher petrol prices, Kiwibank said. ■

Observers say stable China-U.S. ties benefit world, underpin steady global trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:32:30 CST
13:32:30 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Observers worldwide have said that a stable China-U.S. relationship serves not only the interests of the two countries but also those of the world, providing greater predictability for global trade.
Chinese President Xi Jinping's just-concluded U.S. state visit has led to new progress toward building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.
In his talks with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House on Thursday, Xi also called for translating the new vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability into action and finding the right way for the two major countries to get along with each other.
"It aligns with the common aspirations of the international community yearning for stability, as stable Sino-U.S. relations will help anchor global peace and stability. It stands to disprove the inevitability of the Thucydides Trap myth in managing Sino-U.S. relations," said Ong Tee Keat, president of the Belt and Road Initiative Caucus for Asia Pacific.
As reality has time and again dawned upon the two major countries of the world that they have to accommodate each other in the current dynamics, peaceful co-existence is therefore the common denominator they need to cherish, said the Malaysian scholar.
Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at Malaysian think-tank Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, concurred, saying a good relationship between China and the United States will not only benefit these two major countries but the world.
"This is not only within trade but also in geopolitical terms, where both sides, and the whole world, can take advantage," he added.
"I believe it is critically important that the U.S. and China be on a trajectory in a positive direction as partners, and not on a trajectory of the adversaries," said Kenneth Quinn, president emeritus of the World Food Prize Foundation and a former U.S. ambassador to Cambodia.
Quinn, 84, who has led exchanges between the U.S. state of Iowa and China for decades, said his "number one goal" is that the China-U.S. relationship would continue its "constructive strategic stability" and "won't have that volatility, that up and down and huge increases in tariffs and planned tariffs."
"President Xi is absolutely right that stabilizing the China-U.S. relationship is critical. Creating a constructive relationship would be even better," said Bruce McLaughlin, CEO of Sinogie Consulting Group in Australia.
"Both sides benefit from a constructive, stable, well-regulated relationship that nurtures further trade and investment," McLaughlin said.
"What is vital here is that the U.S. administration stops seeing trade as a zero-sum game, and instead recognizes that it is possible to work toward mutual benefit," he added.
The leaders of the world's two largest economies meeting and talking directly is welcome news for business everywhere, said Rhys Roberts, national president of the Australia China Business Council. "What business values most is predictability."
"Commitments made at leaders' level matter most when they flow through into consistent, practical arrangements that companies can plan around. That is where business will be watching," he added. ■

Macao reports slight rise in local resident unemployment rate for June-August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:32:14 CST
13:32:14 KST

MACAO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's Macao Special Administrative Region saw a slight uptick in the unemployment rate for local residents during the June-August period, official statistics showed, as fresh graduates entered the labor market.
The local resident unemployment rate edged up 0.1 percentage point compared with the May-July period to 2.5 percent in June-August, while the local resident underemployment rate fell 0.2 percentage point to 2.0 percent, according to an official employment survey by Macao's Statistics and Census Service (DSEC).
Of the 7,500 unemployed local residents, most previously worked in gaming as well as wholesale and retail trade. New labor-market entrants hunting for their first job accounted for 18.9 percent of unemployed residents, up 6.7 percentage points, as recent graduates entered the workforce. Most of the 5,900 underemployed residents were engaged in business activities and construction.
Macao's general unemployment rate stood at 2.0 percent, a 0.1-percentage-point rise from the May-July period. The overall underemployment rate dropped 0.2 percentage point to 1.5 percent. ■

Column: Committed to China since 1979 -- on 20th anniversary of World Economic Forum's Beijing Office
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:32:12 CST
13:32:12 KST

by Klaus Schwab
The twentieth anniversary of the World Economic Forum's Beijing office is a deeply personal milestone for me. The office has been present in Beijing since 2006, but my own journey with China -- and the Forum's engagement with China -- began much earlier, in 1979.
In the autumn of 1978, I followed with great interest the first signs of China's reform and opening-up. Deng Xiaoping had emerged as the driving force behind a new course, based on modernization, pragmatism and greater engagement with the world. I was convinced that something of historic importance was beginning. I invited Deng Xiaoping to the 1979 Davos Symposium. He did not attend personally, but China sent a distinguished delegation of economists, led by Professor Qian Junrui of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. It was the first official Chinese participation in Davos.
A few months later, I travelled to China for the first time and subsequently led a delegation of 20 European chief executives. China was then very different from the country the world knows today. Its economy was still largely separated from global markets, its international business links were limited, and few outside China anticipated the magnitude of the transformation ahead.
I did.
My belief was not based on economic statistics. It came from what I encountered: the determination to modernize, the enormous human potential of the Chinese people, the importance attached to education and development, and a willingness to learn from the outside world while finding a distinct Chinese path.
Before China had become a global economic power, we decided to build a relationship for the long term. Over the following decades, the Forum became a bridge connecting Chinese leaders, entrepreneurs and scholars with counterparts from around the world. In 2006, we gave this relationship a permanent institutional home by opening our Beijing office. A year later, we launched the Annual Meeting of the New Champions -- the Summer Davos -- in China.
The transformation I have witnessed since my first visit is extraordinary. China has become the world's second-largest economy, a central part of global manufacturing and trade, and an increasingly important source of technological and scientific innovation. More than 800 million people have been lifted out of extreme poverty. Whatever challenges remain, the scale and speed of this development are among the defining developments of our era.
I remember especially President Xi Jinping's participation in Davos in January 2017, the first by a Chinese head of state. At a moment of growing doubts about globalization, he warned: "Pursuing protectionism is like locking oneself in a dark room ... that dark room will also block light and air." It was a striking message about the importance of openness and interdependence.
Today, China's international role is entering another phase. China is no longer only adapting to the institutions of the global system; it is increasingly seeking to contribute ideas and initiatives to the debate about how that system should evolve. In May, Foreign Minister Wang Yi announced that China would host the Xiong'an World Governance Forum this autumn. He linked the initiative to themes including sovereignty equality, international rule of law, multilateralism, a people-centered approach, and real actions.
One need not agree with every proposal advanced by any country to recognize the significance of this development. The great global challenges of the Intelligent Age -- artificial intelligence, climate change, economic fragmentation, security and technological transformation -- cannot be addressed by one nation or one political system. They require mechanisms of cooperation that are more inclusive, more responsive and capable of translating dialogue into action.
China will inevitably have an important voice in shaping that future, just as other major powers, emerging economies, international organizations, business and civil society must have theirs. A responsible global governance system cannot be built through confrontation or exclusion. It must be created through dialogue among different perspectives and interests.
Looking back over almost half a century, I am proud that the Forum recognized China's potential early, long before the scale of its rise had become conventional wisdom internationally. But I am even more convinced that the essential lesson of those years is about the future, not the past.
The bridges that matter most are the ones built before they become indispensable.
That was my conviction when I first travelled to China in 1979. It remains my conviction today.
Editor's note: The author is the founder and builder of the Geneva-based World Economic Forum, a non-governmental international organization dedicated to studying and discussing issues concerning the world economy and promoting international economic cooperation and exchanges.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

During the night of September 28, a fire broke out at the Edelweiss-95 oil depot in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai following a drone attack. ASTRA reported this based on an OSINT analysis of eyewitness videos, UNN writes.

Country diary: A young shieldbug has found a safe place to hide – or so it hopes | Nic Wilson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:30:23 UTC
13:30:23 KST

Looking across a swathe of golden oat grass to the Apple House, it seems almost inconceivable that the M25 and M1 motorways are just beyond the treeline. I’m exploring the Serge Hill Project for Gardening, Creativity and Health: a therapeutic resource for local schools, community groups and charities, founded three years ago by Tom and Sue Stuart-Smith.
All around me, a diverse collection of drought-tolerant plants is thriving in a six-inch layer of sharp sand in the uppermost section of the Plant Library, despite not having been watered once during our sweltering summer.
Among the many plants I’ve not met before, Crete scabious is the epitome of autumn glory. Its pale lilac flowers have transformed into globular seed heads that quiver in the breeze. Each sphere is a fanfare of tiny trumpets, their flared funnels marked with brown stripes. On closer inspection, I can see that some of these papery alcoves harbour hairy shieldbug nymphs, Dolycoris baccarum.
Elsewhere in the garden, troops of adults and juveniles cluster on sunflower stems and wine-red dahlias, but nowhere is the nymphs’ camouflage as successful as on the scabious seed heads. While the adults invite attention with their black and white striped antennae and connexivum (edge of the abdomen), and reddish-brown forewing bases and pronotum (a hardened plate covering the front of the body), the young bugs’ markings shield them from sight. Golden-brown bands on their abdomens and along the connexivum break up their oval outlines, and the colour match between plant and insect helps them sink into sepia obscurity.
Their sanctuary – Crete scabious – is one of many Mediterranean species planted in the garden as part of the project’s research into climate-resilient landscapes, so it’s encouraging to see the shieldbugs making themselves at home. So far, almost 350 invertebrates (including five species of shieldbug) have been recorded across more than 2,500 herbaceous perennials, low shrubs and bulbs in the Plant Library.
Like the children and adults who come to this inclusive garden to connect with nature, the Serge Hill Project provides wildlife with a safe space to shelter and develop. And all within a mile of the London orbital, Britain’s busiest motorway.

The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.

“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Three years since Oct. 7: families plan silence, protests and public testimony across Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:23:05 UTC
13:23:05 KST

Israel will mark three years since the Oct. 7 massacre with a week of remembrance and protest events led by bereaved families and former hostages, beginning with a nationwide moment of silence at 6:29 a.m., the time Hamas launched its attack.
The Oct. 7 Council announced Sunday that the anniversary program will include memorial ceremonies, protest convoys, public testimony and demonstrations across the country, culminating in a central families’ ceremony at Ganei Yehoshua Park in Tel Aviv. The event will be hosted by former hostage Eli Sharabi, who lost his wife and daughters in the attack, and will be screened at several locations, including Hostages Square.
The commemorations will begin Saturday night, Oct. 3, after Simchat Torah, with the opening of “The Space Left Behind,” a memorial exhibition at the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation in Jaffa.
On Wednesday, Oct. 7, families and civil society groups will hold events throughout the day. A minute of silence at 6:29 a.m. will be followed by remarks from Oct. 7 Council families, memorial installations and protests in Caesarea, Jerusalem, the Gaza border region and dozens of other locations.
At 7 a.m., council members and activists plan to gather outside the homes of ministers who were serving in the government on Oct. 7 for what organizers have called a “wake-up call.” Ten minutes later, a protest convoy dubbed the “Path of Abandonment” will leave Caesarea for Tel Aviv, followed at 8:30 a.m. by a women’s protest and installation at Trumpeldor Beach.
Additional convoys will leave northern, central and southern Israel at 10 a.m. for a ceremony at Ben Shemen Forest. From 11 a.m., families will take part in memorial services in Gaza border communities and elsewhere around the country.
At noon, organizers are calling for another one-minute nationwide pause at hospitals, high-tech companies, restaurants and other workplaces. The memorial exhibition at the Peres Center will also open that day, displaying personal belongings of dozens of people murdered or killed on Oct. 7, hostages who died in captivity and residents of communities near the Gaza border.
Evening protests are scheduled from 6 p.m. in Haifa, Afula, Tzemach Junction, Rosh Pina Junction and other locations. At 7:30 p.m., an open stage for testimony will begin in the Sha’ar HaNegev area, leading into the main families’ memorial ceremony at 9 p.m. in Tel Aviv.
‘It must not become just another date on the calendar’
“Three years after Oct. 7, this day must not become just another date on the calendar,” the Oct. 7 Council said. “Behind the numbers are people, families and entire lives that were cut short, and behind the disaster there are still questions the Israeli public deserves answers to.”
The council said the week was intended not only to commemorate those killed and harmed, but also to keep demands for accountability and a state commission of inquiry on the public agenda. It called on Israelis to “stop, come, listen” and join the demand for an inquiry to be established after the next government is formed.
“The Space Left Behind” exhibition will open to the public on Oct. 4 and feature personal objects that tell the stories of those killed, abducted or otherwise affected by Oct. 7. Among them are Ariel Bibas’ balance bike, IDF observer Roni Eshel’s beret, paramedic Amit Mann’s stethoscope, Yagev Buchshtab’s musical instruments and the camera of ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth photographer Roy Edan.
The exhibition will begin with an Israeli flag from Oct. 7, burned and torn during the fighting, and end with flags carried by former hostages Matan Zangauker and Matan Angrest when they returned from captivity. Visitors will also be invited to write questions they believe should be investigated by a future state commission of inquiry.
A separate social media project, “Don’t Forget Them,” will pair 14 actors and cultural figures with 14 bereaved families. Led by Hila Avir, whose brother Lotan Avir was murdered at the Nova music festival, the project will focus not only on how the victims died, but on who they were in life.
Participants include Ania Bukstein, Yuval Scharf, Lucy Ayoub, Liraz Charhi, Yael Goldman, Shani Cohen, Naomi Levov and Yedidya Vital. The videos will be released in the days before the anniversary, with organizers saying the project is aimed especially at younger audiences and at returning the victims’ personal stories to the center of public attention.

Lung cancer deaths down 16% with low-dose CT screening: IARC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:22:22 UTC
13:22:22 KST

Lung cancer deaths can be reduced through low-dose CT screening, which can also help detect the disease before it reaches advanced stages in people at high risk, according to an IARC assessment.
NEW DELHI: Low-dose computed tomography (CT) screening can cut the risk of dying from lung cancer by 16% in high-risk people, while also reducing the incidence of advanced stage III or IV disease, an International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has found.Published in The New England Journal of Medicine, the assessment found established evidence that low-dose CT reduces lung cancer mortality when used in people at high risk based mainly on age and smoking history.IARC convened a working group of 23 clinicians and scientists from 17 countries, including Dr Abhishek Shankar of All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, to assess the benefits and harms of lung cancer screening.The evidence mainly applies to people aged 50 to 80 with a substantial smoking history, typically at least 20 to 30 pack-years. Studies involving former smokers generally included those who had quit within the previous 10 to 15 years, with screening usually performed annually.In India, people aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years of smoking who are current smokers or quit within the past 15 years can contact the Indian Lung Screening Trial, led by Dr Abhishek Shankar at AIIMS, New Delhi, about screening.
Dr Shankar has invited eligible people to contact him for screening under the trial.The evidence behind the finding came mainly from randomised trials. In the US National Lung Screening Trial, people screened with low-dose CT had a 16% lower relative risk of dying from lung cancer than those screened with chest X-rays at seven years. The European NELSON trial also found lower lung cancer mortality among men screened with low-dose CT at 10 years.Based on this evidence, the IARC group classified low-dose CT as Group A, indicating established evidence that it reduces lung cancer mortality and the incidence of stage III or IV disease. Chest X-rays, with or without sputum examination, were classified as Group C, as their ability to reduce lung cancer mortality could not be established.However, the review cautioned that low-dose CT screening is not meant for everyone. False-positive results ranged from 1% to 42% across studies, depending on the screening protocol. Among those with false-positive results, 5% to 32% underwent at least one invasive procedure, with complications occurring in 10% to 22% of such procedures.
The review also estimated that 3% to 26% of lung cancers detected in randomised trials involving high-risk people could represent overdiagnosis, meaning cancers that might not have caused harm during the person's lifetime.The working group said effective lung cancer screening needs more than CT scanners, including systems for identifying eligible people, assessing risk, monitoring nodules, providing treatment and follow-up, along with smoking-cessation support. Organised programmes also require trained staff, quality assurance, adequate healthcare capacity and equitable access.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.
