====================================================================================================

Taipei Confucius Temple holds annual Teachers’ Day ceremony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:19:23 UTC
13:19:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Confucius Temple on Monday held its annual ceremony honoring Confucius on the 2,576th anniversary of his birth, an event that coincides with Teachers’ Day in Taiwan.
The ceremony began at 6 a.m. at the plaza in front of Dacheng Hall and followed traditional rites honoring Confucius, who is revered as the Great Sage and Teacher. The annual ceremony consists of a series of traditional ritual procedures and is held each year on Sept. 28, Teachers’ Day in Taiwan, per a press release.
Taipei Deputy Mayor Lin Yi-hua (林奕華) served as chief officiant, while Kong Chui-chang (孔垂長), the 79th-generation direct descendant of Confucius, served as the temple's sacrificial official. City councilors, municipal advisers, outstanding teachers, and distinguished citizens also participated as ceremonial officials, joining the traditional rites to pay tribute to Confucius.
Students from Minglun Senior High School and Lishan Senior High School served as ceremonial attendants, while students from Chongqing Junior High School provided the ceremonial music.
Students from Dalong Elementary School performed the eight-row Yi dance, a traditional ritual dance accompanying Confucian ceremonies. Teachers and students from Kaiping Culinary School prepared the ceremonial food offerings.
Student participation from different schools has become an important part of the annual ceremony. Taipei Confucius Temple has previously highlighted the roles of students serving as ritual attendants, musicians, and dancers in preserving the ceremony's traditional forms.
Taiwan-Okinawa Confucian exchange
This year's ceremony also highlighted historical exchanges between Taipei Confucius Temple and the Kume Soseikai Association in Okinawa, Japan. A delegation from the association visited Taipei Confucius Temple and presented a certificate of appreciation, recalling exchanges that date back more than five decades, per the press release.
Historical research documents that representatives of the Kume Soseikai Association visited Taipei Confucius Temple in 1973 to study its Confucian ceremony and ritual practices as the group worked toward rebuilding the Confucius temple in Naha. Taiwan subsequently assisted, including Confucian tablets and ritual implements, during the reconstruction of the Kume Confucius Temple.
The historical exchanges continued through the 1970s and included Taiwanese participation in ceremonies in Okinawa. Academic research records that Taipei Confucius Temple and other Taiwanese organizations provided ritual objects and other assistance for the reconstruction of the Okinawa temple, which was completed in the mid-1970s.
More than five decades later, the renewed exchange at Taipei Confucius Temple highlighted the longstanding cultural links between Taiwan and Okinawa surrounding Confucian ritual traditions. The ceremony also featured the sounds of bells, drums, and traditional music, with teachers, students, and volunteers working together to conduct the rites.
Taipei Confucius Temple also prepared commemorative gift bags featuring an illustration of Confucius. The temple said the design was intended to convey the Confucian ideal of broadening one's horizons through learning and travel.
The annual ceremony is part of Taipei's effort to preserve traditional Confucian ritual and music culture while introducing those traditions to younger generations. The Taipei Confucius Temple has held Confucian ceremonies since the early 20th century, with the current temple complex's Dacheng Hall completed in 1929.

A Polish priest injured in a deadly knife attack at the Benedictine Sisters' Abbey in Jaroslaw, Poland on Sept. 24, urged people not to blame Ukrainians for the actions of the suspected attacker, Polish media reported on Sept. 26.
Father Adrian, who was wounded in the attack, returned to celebrate Mass two days later with bandages on his head and hand and bruising on his face, according to Polish outlet Onet.
"I would also like to ask you not to blame the nation from which the perpetrator comes," Adrian said during the service, according to Onet.
"The evil was committed by a specific person who is responsible for his actions," he said, urging those gathered to respond with "love, support, and understanding."
Adrian also said that he forgave the suspected attacker, 31-year-old Ukrainian citizen Ihor M., and asked worshippers to pray for him so that he "may receive the grace of conversion."
The priest recalled that Ukrainians came to the monastery following the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 and received support from local residents. He urged the community to continue showing that support.
A Ukrainian man attacked five people with a knife at the Benedictine Sisters' Abbey in Jaroslaw on Sept. 24, killing Catholic priest Stanislaw Zbojnowicz and injuring four others.
Three of those attacked were members of the clergy.
Polish prosecutors have charged Ihor M. with murder, attempted murder, and causing grievous bodily harm. Psychiatric experts who examined him said he was experiencing symptoms of an acute psychotic disorder and was unable to participate in legal proceedings at the time of the examination, according to Polish media.
A Polish court subsequently ordered the suspect held in custody, Onet reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the attack on Sept. 24 as a "horrific crime," saying the perpetrator must "bear full responsibility in accordance with the law."
Ukraine's Ambassador to Poland Vasyl Bodnar also said he believed the attack was not nationally motivated.
The attack came amid growing anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland and strains in relations between Warsaw and Kyiv. Polish officials and church leaders have warned against assigning collective blame to Ukrainians over the attack.
On Sept. 25, Polish Bishop Krzysztof Zadarko also warned against blaming Ukrainians collectively for the attack during a press conference in Warsaw ahead of the 112th World Day of Migrants and Refugees. “We don't know all the details,” he said, “but shifting the blame from one person onto an entire society, an entire ethnic or national group, is an abuse.”

Ukraine reserves 79.5% of minimum amount of natural gas required for heating period
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:05:34 UTC
13:05:34 KST

MOSCOW, September 28. /TASS/. Ukraine had accumulated only about 10.5 billion cubic meters of natural gas in its underground storage facilities by late September, and it is approximately 79.5% of the minimum volume required to get through the cold weather season and about 72% of the planned level of 14.6 billion cubic meters by December 1, according to TASS calculations.
Earlier, Ukraine virtually refused European gas imports citing high prices and gas shortages in EU countries, and it is now replenishing its storage facilities resorting to domestic production, but these volumes will be insufficient for the country’s preparations for the winter season.
If the storage capacity is brought to the level of the minimum required volumes, the country needs to purchase natural gas worth about $1 billion, while the planned level of 14.6 billion cubic meters amounts to about $2.5 billion. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s budget recently faced serious problems.
The heating season in Ukraine officially starts on October 15, but the heating is usually supplied to social infrastructure facilities before that date. Therefore, Ukraine will have to start using up gas reserves in the days to come from storage facilities that have not been filled to the required level.

Ed Miliband will tell campaigners and party members who raised the plight of Palestinians they were right that Labour’s approach had not been enough, saying he was heeding the calls of millions of people by imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements.
The foreign secretary will tell the Labour party conference that the government will take more explicitly progressive foreign policy positions under Andy Burnham, and that the UK will be a leader among like-minded countries in a new age of diplomacy.
He will say there is a “fundamental and wider lesson from Israel and Palestine about how we have changed our approach as a party”, saying Labour will succeed “because of, not in spite of, our progressive values”.
He will talk of the start of a new and more muscular foreign policy. “We are not here to accept the status quo but to change it at home and abroad,” he will say.
The party’s conference hall was often the scene of fierce opposition to Keir Starmer’s stance on Israel and Palestine in Labour’s final year of opposition and early in government.
Since becoming foreign secretary, Miliband has announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 countries – including France and Canada – announcing they would also impose sanctions.
The Guardian understands Miliband will say in his speech that the sanctions marked a definitive change in how Labour will approach the situation in the Middle East.
“I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right,” he will say.
“And under Andy’s leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with actions.
“We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government, says ‘we will not let you succeed’.”
Miliband will pay tribute to those who have campaigned against the Israeli onslaught in Gaza, though his warm words are likely to raise questions about whether the government will review the proscription of Palestine Action. Police arrested a number of demonstrators outside the conference hall on Sunday.
“The bonds of solidarity between the British people and those who yearn for peace in Israel and Palestine are too strong to be broken,” Miliband will say.
“Our decision to act mobilised the international community, country after country. This is how to make change happen in today’s world. Doing what is right and galvanising others to act too.”
Miliband will say in his first speech to the party conference as foreign secretary that cooperation in imposing sanctions will be the beginning of a new bond with “likeminded countries” such as France and Canada, though it is also likely to be interpreted as being more willing to sideline the US.
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has made an explicit argument for middle powers to do more to build alliances with each other outside traditional structures, and was direct in his desire to forge closer ties with and among European countries in a speech in Brussels earlier this month.
A source close to Miliband said that would be a key theme of his time in office. “Britain’s interests are served by standing up for our values on the world stage. Our ability to build coalitions on big global issues depends on our ability to bring countries with us,” he will say.
“This Israel/Palestine reset is a sign of how we want to do business. We are going to be propositional in bringing countries with us on the issues we really care about.”

Switzerland’s love of referendums keeps the far right at bay | Joseph de Weck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:00:24 UTC
13:00:24 KST

Fascism rests on a two-part confidence trick. First, a leader claims to embody the will of the people. Then they argue that only by being granted sweeping powers can that be realised. Having grown up in Switzerland, I find it easy to see through this trick. That is because the policies championed by the far right rarely pass the referendum test.
Dismantling publicly funded media? In March, 62% of Swiss voters rejected a far-right initiative to halve funding for the country’s public broadcaster. Corporate tax cuts? In 2017, 59% struck down such plans of the Swiss government. Immigration police hunting down migrants? Again, 59% rejected a far-right proposal to automatically deport foreign nationals convicted of crimes without judicial review. Or this week’s resounding 70% “No” vote on a far-right proposal to tighten Switzerland’s neutrality to the point that Bern would have been forced to drop sanctions on Russia over Ukraine.
Switzerland is hardly a nation of progressives. Leftwing parties won just 29% of the vote in the most recent national elections. Women gained the right to vote only in 1971. The asylum law is one of Europe’s toughest. That, too, is the legacy of direct democracy.
Yet, most often, the country’s tradition of putting decisions out to referendum exposes how, despite dominating social media and the press amplifying its positions, the far right thrives on imagined majorities.
Direct democracy also frustrates the second part of the authoritarian project: the power grab. From Donald Trump to Giorgia Meloni, the right seeks to centralise power. Direct democracy disperses it. History shows that parliamentarians can be pressed into surrendering their prerogatives. Good luck trying to persuade millions of voters to do the same.
Enter Hannah Arendt. Having fled Nazi Germany in 1933, the philosopher and political theorist spent much of her life trying to understand why democracies abolish themselves, why the Weimar Republic failed.
Part of her answer was that parliamentary democracy could drift towards the rule of party elites and bureaucracy. Autocrats exploit the feeling of loss that happens when citizens feel disenfranchised.
The central question, therefore, is how to maintain the link between demos and kratos – between people and power? Arendt’s answer was citizens’ participation. She pointed to the town hall meetings of the American revolution or soviet councils of the Russian revolution as possible models.
Indeed, deeper citizen involvement is one of the great unmet desires of European politics. Take the gilets jaunes movement in France in 2018. The protesters’ demands went well beyond better public services or lower taxes. At its heart was a plea to be seen and heard, embodied in the call for citizens’ referendums.
A 2017 poll found that 74% of German, French and Spanish people think that public referendums would be a good way to govern their country. Yet, whenever I argue for more direct democracy abroad, there is the same reaction: curiosity from ordinary people, eye-rolling from political and economic elites. But aren’t referendums a high-risk way of governing, they ask? Brexit, anyone?
There are risks. In June, Swiss voters narrowly rejected (55%) a far-right proposal to cap the population at 10 million and terminate EU-Swiss economic agreements. But unlike the Brexit referendum in the UK, a vote is never a final decision for the Swiss. Since 2000, the Swiss have voted on relations with Brussels more than a dozen times. Unlike politicians, the demos has little difficulty in admitting that yesterday’s answer may not be right for today.
But wouldn’t voters, if given the chance, blow a massive hole in the budget deficit? As every parent knows, responsibility breeds responsibility. Two-thirds of Swiss voters rejected a proposal to extend annual holidays by two weeks. A tragic case of excessive responsibility.
It seems that many in Europe have forgotten that we want to live in republics not only because they “deliver” in terms of rubbish collection or maximising individual freedom. Democracy’s most powerful idea is the promise of self-government: a political order that recognises we humans not merely as consumers or subjects of politics, but as the authors of our common future.
When that promise is broken, when people feel their votes have little impact and elites always get their way, the difference between democracy and authoritarianism begins to blur. It is then that things become truly dangerous.
To put a lock on the far right and breathe new life into that republican promise, we need a transfer of power from the nation state to its citizens. But here is the crux. If we really want to reestablish the primacy of democracy, the transfer of power to citizens needs to be accompanied by a transfer of power from the nation state to Europe.
Let’s not fool ourselves: today, nation states often cosplay sovereignty more than they exercise it. To claw back power from Silicon Valley, Washington and Beijing, we must organise as Europeans. And this is where another of direct democracy’s secret superpowers comes in.
In Switzerland, with its four linguistic communities, referendums are what create a joint public sphere and a sense of national community. In a multicultural country, being governed together is not enough. A shared identity is built above all through the experience of debating and governing together.
For Europe to become a real political community, it must find a way to both connect and empower its citizens. Direct democracy delivers on both. Giving up some national sovereignty in return for more individual power is an attractive offer. It could open a new chapter in the continent’s coming together, one capable of inspiring genuine excitement.
Imagine Europeans debating and voting together on such things as migration policy, the 2035 ban on new petrol and diesel cars, or taxing the big digital corporations. Utopian? Perhaps. But every democratic advance once was.
- 
  Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zürich and Paris

‘I sleep with all my clothes on to protect my privacy’: a glimpse into life inside a child prison in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:00:23 UTC
13:00:23 KST

The cells of the children were difficult places for me to photograph because they are impersonal and intimate at the same time. Once inside, you quickly find yourself going in circles, with nowhere to go. Your gaze settles on the very few elements that make up the space: a window, cell bars, a rudimentary bed, a plank serving as a desk, and sometimes a book or a few drawings.
Sometimes, due to staff shortages, a young person may spend as much as 23 hours a day in their cell. This and the low levels of access to educational and sports activities have been criticised by Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture.
‘It’s worse at night’
“We’re locked in our cells every day. Even though it can become our quiet corner, it’s hard. Because of the way the buildings are laid out, the quiet corner is never really quiet. All the cells are connected to each other, and this is a place that invites outside intrusion. We are constantly being called out. The windows look on to the yard, and we hear screaming all day long. It’s even worse at night.”
For all prisoners, minors and adults, the prison yard is a mandatory one-hour stop each day. The cell windows overlook the yard, so it’s almost impossible not to be watched. Every movement, every word takes place under the eye of fellow prisoners and guards. They talked to me about boredom in prison and an altered, artificial sense of time.
‘I’d rather go back to my cell’
“I feel like being here is making me stupid. I feel like an idiot. I forget things. I’ve lost what I knew. I don’t see anything new any more. In my cell, my vision gets blurry from staring at the same walls, especially on weekends, which feel like three whole weeks. [There are no classes on weekends and almost no activities.] I’m losing it here. TV drives me crazy, so I draw to keep myself occupied. It takes mental strength. Some people go crazy; they don’t care about anything any more, as if they had nothing left to lose. I don’t like being around the other kids, the ones from the other units. I’d rather go back to my cell to avoid trouble.”
Out in the courtyard, one boy told me about his love of nature. He wanted to photograph birds, sleep outdoors and wash in rivers. It was the day before his court hearing. He just wanted to talk – sharing everything that was crossing his mind: his mother and her drug addictions; his fear of the hearing; his lawyer; heroin; the desire to end it all; to stay here, to go elsewhere, the river.
In France, only three of the six juvenile detention centres are authorised to accommodate girls. They are housed in a separate unit but take part in the same activities and classes as the boys. In her cell, a girl talked to me about the difficulties of being in detention, and the paradox of feeling unsafe in a space entirely built around security and surveillance.
‘I hide my sadness to protect myself’
“I’m always self-conscious when I’m in bed, afraid that someone might be watching me through the peephole. I no longer sleep in whatever position I want. Before, I didn’t like wearing pants to sleep, but here, I sleep with all my clothes on. I don’t know how else to protect my privacy. I don’t show that I’m sad, so I hide my sadness. I don’t talk about it with the other girls either, to protect myself. Girls are like that: the slightest argument, and the whole prison knows about it. Being a girl in detention isn’t easy. When we scream, we really scream.”
I am able to photograph the disciplinary unit, where children are confined alone, when the cells are empty. Inside, there is a tiny concrete yard and almost completely bare cells, with no privacy. The windows are locked and cannot be opened. The narrow, grey yard exists only to allow the daily mandatory hour of outdoor exercise. On the walls, there are phrases written with faeces, as detainees are not allowed to have pens or personal belongings.
For minors, confinement in the disciplinary unit can last up to five days, or seven days in cases involving violence. Under the law, children are meant to be given activities and occupied, but that is not always respected and can result in situations of de facto isolation. A few days earlier, a young person had told me what it was like for them.
‘You can’t come out of there normal’
“I got a saw to cut through my bars, and because of that, I’m going back to confinement. In the hole, you’re there, you stay there, that’s it. You lose it – you just have to talk to the wall; there’s nothing else to do. Honestly, some people want to kill themselves in there. It’s too horrible. They call it the disciplinary unit, but you can’t come out of there normal. It’s not possible. You can’t open the window. You can’t turn the light on or off yourself. You have to call the guard to do it. They tell us it’s a place to rest, but that’s not true. You end up thinking about doing even worse things after going through all this.”
I met one boy drawing lines in a notebook, crossing off the days, keeping track of time: a seemingly mundane act in prison. In his cell, he didn’t want to talk about it, but a few weeks later he spoke to me.
‘I stopped counting the days’
“When I arrived, I took a notebook they gave me and drew lines to count the days I had left. I felt like doing it. And one day, I stopped. It wasn’t making the days go by any faster. The hardest part is staying in the cell all day. The days pass more slowly than the nights. There’s only a TV in the cell, and after a while I get tired of it, so I sleep.
“I try not to overthink things. I’d rather go see the social worker, as it gets me out of the cell and makes me feel better. I don’t really care about meeting people, but the activities and classes help take my mind off things. [If I get out] I want to continue my studies and find an employer for a work-study programme. It might be this summer, or maybe next summer. Trials can take a long time. I think you can go crazy in prison, but I’m not worried about myself.”
The reason why they are in prison is very often the same here: drug trafficking. I encounter a boy outside in the garden, standing among flowers the same colour as his sneakers and cap. He quickly tells me his story.
‘I’m inventing a life for myself’
“I started at 10am, in a small park, with a shoulder bag. Inside, there was a really big package: 50 baggies, droppers and heroin. It was a lot of money. I had clients, and at one point I saw a BAC [Anti-Criminal police] team. I still had the bag on me when they grabbed me.” 
At times I feel his account is embellished, or perhaps more glamorous than the reality. I then think back to what an educator once told me about another young person here, who talked to her about his path in drug dealing. Knowing his judicial file, she told him, “But you weren’t really in it.” And he answered, “I know, I’m inventing a life for myself.”
In the gym, a young person is playing football. He looks very young; his gaze is tired. We talk briefly, and I learn that he is an unaccompanied migrant.
‘It’s my first time in prison’
“I took an inflatable boat with 18 people on board. I arrived in Spain. Then in France 10 months ago, and I’ve been here for almost three months now. This is my first time in prison. I wanted to play football, so I came to Europe for that, and also for freedom. The stadium isn’t far away, so I can hear the games from my prison cell. I love Lionel Messi, he’s my model; he’s the best player in history. I’m going to be a player.”
In the shared space of the prison, another boy is having his hair cut. It is a special moment. The barber is well known on social media for the haircuts he gives in working-class neighbourhoods. His hairstyles are very different from those cut by the guards, which are often simpler and more uniform. The young people can choose the style they want. They trust him; he knows how to talk to them. One of the young people tells us about a 17-year-old friend of his who was murdered a few days after his release from prison. A settling of scores linked to drug trafficking.
‘It’s another death that will be forgotten’
“The guys were on scooters. They pulled up next to him, pulled out a ‘guitar’ [a rifle], and shot him. He had a huge debt, and they took him out a few days after he got out. They did some crazy stuff to him – they kidnapped his older brother because he had changed the password to the Telegram account to keep his clients.”
When a risk of suicide is identified, the young person is placed in a special cell called an emergency protection cell. Then a “single-use kit”, made up of tearable clothing intended to prevent hanging, is given to them. While suicides here can be counted on one hand, there are more attempts. And then there are those who do not appear in any statistics, because they died some time after their release, outside the prison system. A member of the prison educational and medical team confided how difficult it is to face such situations.
“It’s the suicides that hurt me the most. One boy killed himself here, a week and a half before his release. It destroyed me. Another girl had been released and went to a specialised hospital unit, where she took her own life a few weeks later. We undergo training on ‘identifying suicidal crises’, but with little Jonathan, we never would have suspected it. To kill yourself just days before your release. These are moments we live through here, pains. But afterwards, what do we do with them? It’s another death that will be forgotten.”

‘You can taste the land’: the Somerset farmer bringing wildflowers back to cheddar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:00:23 UTC
13:00:23 KST

In the rolling hills of Somerset, hundreds of thousands of cows placidly munch lush green grass to produce milk for cheddar.
But six fields stand out. Rather than uniform grass, they have technicolour wildflowers sprouting across the meadows. Farmer Tom Calver said that to allow the flowers to grow he has to keep fewer cows and leave some fields ungrazed as they mature.
“Other farmers thought we were nuts for doing this,” said Calver, who runs the Westcombe dairy in the eponymous hamlet in Somerset.
He is pioneering emerging research that suggests that when cows are fed in an organic way, their microbiome is healthier and more complex than when they are given modern feed. It is thought that feeding cattle a wide range of plants creates a healthier gut microbiome still.
“We have actually lost milk production in what we’re doing,” Calver said, but added the cheese tasted better than ever as it is “meadow flavoured”.
Cheddar has been made in the county for over 850 years, and cows once grazed more varied pasture, much like Calver’s black-and-white herd do now.
Calver believes his Westcombe cheddar, which is raw and unpasteurised, has a much more complex taste than the average supermarket block and this is because of its microbiome.
“If you look at the diversity of what cows have been eating before, we were growing lots of maize and Italian rye grasses,” Calver said.
“Now, actually, the cows are out into 19 different species of plants in our paddocks. What’s living on those plants is a huge, diverse range of microbiome, and I think you’ve probably heard a lot about how the microbiome is actually helping our guts and minds and everything else like that. It also actually has a massive input in the flavour profile.”
Calver, a trained chef, said he didn’t understand why cheese couldn’t have a “terroir” – a taste of the land where it was created, just like wine does. “You talk to viticulturists, winemakers, and they talk about terroir, and I think that’s amazing. It’s what we can actually use to improve diversity in our landscapes and in the flavour of our foods.”
The drawback is that his way of farming is “much more expensive”.
But Calver believes it’s worth it. He said that growing wildflowers rather than just maize and grass has boosted nature on his farm, and he also prefers the taste of the cheese now: “You can actually like taste the land. You can taste everything around it.”
Calver said it had been hard to market the cheddar as it tasted different every time due to the diversity of the plants the cows are fed.
“One of the things that we are very bad at, I think, is wanting to have the same thing every single day. When you’re working with nature and you’re actually trying to farm in that particular way, you have to embrace diversity, even of the actual flavour profiles that you’re actually creating as well, which makes it very difficult for a retailer to actually market that. It is quite a challenge.”
Growing deep-rooted wildflowers in the meadows helped the farm during this year’s drought, too. “We’ve got lots of chicory that’s actually going down and accessing water from subsoil and actually bringing that up. So we’ve done rather well.”
Farmers trying to graze their cattle on parched fields looked at Calver’s comparatively greener land with envy. “I think there’s been a lot of other farmers locally who have been, hopefully, maybe inspired by taking a slightly different approach,” he said.

By observing matter at the atomic scale, the Hefei Advanced Light Facility could drive breakthroughs in microchips
2-MIN READ2-MIN
1
 Listen
Zhang Tongin Beijing
China has produced an electron beam using a cutting-edge electron gun, taking a step towards building a “super microscope” that could help drive breakthroughs in everything from Alzheimer’s research to advanced microchips.
The Hefei Advanced Light Facility (HALF) in central China’s Anhui province fired its first electron beam on September 20.
Bunches of electrons generated by the gun were accelerated by a 192-metre (630-foot) linear accelerator until they reached 2.2 billion electron volts, marking a milestone for the fourth-generation light source project.

Amman Architecture City Guide: 11 Projects in a Capital Shaped by Migration and Stone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Built across several hills, Amman has grown at a pace few Middle Eastern capitals have matched. The city has received successive waves of migration — Circassians in the late 19th century, Palestinian refugees in 1948 and 1967, the Iraqi population after 1990, and Syrians since 2011 — each reshaping its density and social profile. Locally quarried limestone, extracted from quarries across Jordan and required by law for façades since the 1970s, has become the city's only common visual denominator. Behind this material uniformity, however, lies a continuous dialogue between vernacular tradition and international ambition.
This condition has taken concrete architectural form over the past decades. The monumental scale of the Al-Iskan (Housing Bank Center), built in Shmeisani between 1980 and 1984, consolidated large-scale architecture as a symbol of the country's emerging financial capital. At the same time, prominent Jordanian architects, including Jafar Tukan and Ammar Khammash, developed a distinct architectural vocabulary that reinterprets stone masonry, topography, and the natural landscape in contemporary terms, producing museums, conservation centers, and environmentally responsive buildings of remarkable local sensitivity. More recently, international firms and technologies have expanded this urban infrastructure through new geometries and bioclimatic solutions.

Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, wife of Malaysia's Mahathir Mohamad, dies aged 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:54:16 UTC
12:54:16 KST

Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, the wife of Malaysia's longest-serving prime minister, Mahathir Mohamad, has died at age 100, the veteran statesman's office confirmed.
She passed away at the National Heart Institute in Kuala Lumpur, state news agency Bernama reported, citing the couple's son Mokhzani Mahathir.
A popular and respected figure in her own right, Siti Hasmah was widely recognised for her unassuming personality, warmth, and good humour, which often contrasted with her husband's blunt political style.
Throughout her decades as a prominent political spouse, she actively championed public health programmes, family planning initiatives, and numerous social causes across the nation.
A seven-decade partnership
The couple first met whilst studying at medical school in Singapore in the late 1940s.
Celebrating 70 years of marriage in August, they raised seven children, including businessman Mokhzani, social activist Marina Mahathir, and prominent politician Mukhriz Mahathir.
Mahathir, 101, frequently described his wife as the essential backbone of his political career and success, expressing profound admiration for her early determination to attain a university degree at a time when tertiary education was an exceptional rarity among ethnic Malay women.

17 injured as minibus hits truck on Hong Kong highway during morning rush
Accident temporarily blocked part of Fanling Highway, causing traffic to back up near Kwu Tung
Seventeen people have been injured in Hong Kong after a minibus collided with a truck on Fanling Highway in the New Territories during the peak-hour commute.
Emergency services were called to the scene at around 9am on Monday after the minibus, which was travelling in the direction of Tai Po, struck the truck near Choi Yuen Estate in Sheung Shui, police said.
The truck had slowed down on the highway when the minibus failed to brake in time and crashed into it, the force said.

Seoul seeks apology after Ukraine 'breached' confidentiality agreement over transfer of North Korean POWs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:49:15 UTC
12:49:15 KST

North Korean soldiers were among the foreign contingent conscripted to fight alongside Russian troops on various frontlines in the war on Ukraine, after the Kremlin sought assistance from its close allies to bolster its deployments amid struggles with domestic conscription.
South Korea's President’s Lee Jae Myung’s office demanded an apology from Ukraine for denying an agreement to keep the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war from its territory to Seoul confidential.
The row was ignited by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's disclosure last week that his country had sent two North Korean soldiers to the South, adding that they were "not easy to capture alive".
The intensifying dispute risks complicating Kyiv's efforts to obtain weapons from allies, including South Korea, to fight off bombardments from Russia.
Hours after Zelenskyy's disclosure, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung criticised the action.
"I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing," he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy's aide Dmytro Lytvyn sought to play down the disclosure, saying that the president had only made public the fact that the soldiers were handed to South Korea. Ukraine is an "open country", noted Lytvyn, saying that it would be “unusual” to hand over the soldiers in secret.
But Seoul condemned it as a breach of trust.
Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement late on Sunday that South Korea was "considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter".
"It is in itself a very serious matter that the Ukrainian side violated the confidentiality agreement between the two countries and made the disclosure unilaterally,” he said.
"But the Ukrainian presidential press office's false statement that there had been no confidentiality agreement, seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries," he added.
The South Korean Presidential office demands "an official explanation and apology," said Seong.
Ukraine captured early last year two North Korean soldiers among Pyongyang's troops fighting for Moscow. One of them said he served in a reconnaissance unit and while some North Korean soldiers had been trained to use Russian military equipment, he had not.
The soldier said he was conscripted to the military aged 17 and had been serving since then. A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South of the Peninsula.
Analysts believe Lee Jae Myung’s angry reaction to the confidentiality agreement risks sparking intense feuds with the nuclear-armed north, which could translate into further hostility towards Seoul.
"North Korea has been using the deployed soldiers to create a heroic narrative for regime propaganda, and the South Korean government appears concerned that confirming the prisoners' return to the South and publicising it could further fuel hostility towards Seoul," said Park Won-gon, a professor at Ewha Womans University.
Beyond the ramifications within South Korea, the row also risks complicating Kyiv's requests to the ally for armaments supplies.
South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war. Nevertheless, it had been considering requests for defensive weapons, especially since North Korea deployed troops to support Russia.

The High Court has discharged a recently empanelled jury from the murder trial of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s former relatives after one member asked to be excused for health reasons, leading to a delay in proceedings.

Source: State Emergency Service of Ukraine
Details: The Russians damaged a non-residential building in the Podilskyi district. A fire broke out there and part of the roof was also destroyed.
The blast wave from a subsequent strike then damaged windows in a nearby residential building. State Emergency Service workers found three injured people at the scene.
A Russian drone struck a two-storey residential building in the Holosiivskyi district. One person was injured in the attack.
Fires broke out in office buildings in the Pecherskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts as a result of the Russian attack.
Background:
- An air-raid warning was issued in Kyiv on 27 September at 15:46 due to a large-scale Russian drone attack.
- The threat to the capital continued uninterrupted for 9 hours and 10 minutes. The all-clear was given on 28 September at 00:56. Explosions were heard throughout the city and its outskirts during this time, while air defence forces were responding.
- At 05:46, an air-raid warning was issued in Kyiv for the second time that night due to a drone threat. In the morning, the Russians struck a petrol station in Kyiv's Obolonskyi district with a drone.

Macao's composite CPI up 1.29 pct in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
11:42:25 CST
12:42:25 KST

MACAO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Macao's composite consumer price index (CPI) rose by 1.29 percent year on year and 0.28 percent month on month in August, the special administrative region's Statistics and Census Service (DSEC) has said.
The service noted on Friday that the food and non-alcoholic beverages index increased by 1.37 percent year on year in August, driven by higher eating-out and takeaway charges. The transport index grew by 3.08 percent due to rising gasoline prices.
For the first eight months of 2026, the average composite CPI grew by 1.13 percent year on year, while the average composite CPI for the 12 months ended August rose by 0.96 percent from the previous period. ■

US tech firm charged over secret Russian ownership sold tools to European police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:40:43 UTC
12:40:43 KST

BRUSSELS — A U.S.-based data-extraction firm accused of being secretly run from Russia has worked on EU-backed projects and sold its services to European law enforcement agencies, according to documents seen by POLITICO.
The U.S. Justice Department last week charged Oxygen Forensics — officially headquartered in Virginia — of concealing that it was actually owned and operated by Russians. The company develops and sells powerful software capable of extracting and analyzing information from smartphones and computers, a process known as "digital forensics."
According to public records reviewed by POLITICO, Oxygen was used in at least two EU-funded projects aimed at improving how electronic evidence is collected, processed and shared in criminal investigations.
Advertisement
The first project, EVIDENCE, (European Informatics Data Exchange Framework for Courts and Evidence), which received more than €1.9 million in EU funding between 2014 and 2016, listed Oxygen Forensics among the companies consulted on how Europe could better handle and exchange digital criminal evidence. That placed the company in a wider network that included EU police agency Europol, judicial cooperation agency Eurojust and the European Anti-Fraud Office's digital forensics unit.
The second project, INSPECTr, backed under Horizon 2020, an EU research and innovation funding arm, was designed to help European police bring together and analyze digital evidence collected using different tools. It built software that could take evidence extracted with Oxygen Forensics and make it easier for investigators using other systems to access and analyze it.
Although both of those EU-backed projects were launched well before Russia’s February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine and subsequent European sanctions, INSEPCTr continued to operate until 2023. Oxygen also currently remains listed on the websites of both projects. On its own now-defunct website, Oxygen Forensics had listed the European Commission as a client.
A Commission spokesperson stressed that Oxygen Forensics was not a member of either consortium, "and hence did not receive funding under these projects from the Commission." The spokesperson, who was granted anonymity to speak freely about a sensitive topic, said EU-funded projects are subject to strict eligibility and ethics standards, and "since the beginning of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine, Russian-based entities cannot participate in Horizon Europe projects in any capacity."
Sister company's FSB link
More recently, after its involvement with the EU-backed projects, Oxygen's products have been accredited and purchased by multiple national police agencies across Europe, including those in Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland, according to notices in the EU tender database.
A statement published Wednesday by the U.S. Justice Department found Oxygen Forensic's software was developed and managed by a team in Russia under the direction of Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, but purported to be led by Lee Reiber, a 55-year-old native of Boise, Idaho. An affidavit filed with the complaint says Oxygen Forensics was in contact with the U.S. Department of War and several parts of the Department of Homeland Security, including the Secret Service, its digital-forensics training institute, Homeland Security Investigations and the department's internal watchdog.
Advertisement
Reiber has since been arrested in the U.S. Davydov was arrested Sunday at London's Heathrow Airport as he prepared to board a flight to Istanbul, according to a statement by the Justice Department. Lawyers for the two men did not respond to POLITICO's request for comment.
Representatives for Oxygen Forensics did not respond to requests for comment either. In the meantime, the company's website has been seized by the U.S. government.
Prosecutors allege that after Washington imposed sanctions on Russia in 2022, Oxygen's Russian owners concealed both their ownership and the continued development of the company's software in Russia. The five Russians behind Oxygen Forensics also controlled a Russian sister company, MKO Systems, that sold the same underlying technology to the Russian Security Service (FSB) and the country's Interior Ministry.
The Justice Department complaint does not allege that Oxygen's software contained malicious code or that the company used it to gain unauthorized access to customers' systems or data. U.S. investigators did, however, seize corporate bank accounts, 57 domains and other cyber infrastructure they said was "used in furtherance of the alleged acts."
Used across Europe
Oxygen's footprint extends beyond the Commission-backed research projects. The French investigative news organization, Disclose, found its surveillance software was supplied to Moroccan authorities under an EU-funded border-management program for the Maghreb. As well as financing the purchase of the software, the EU also funded training courses led by employees of Oxygen Forensics for Moroccan police.
The company has listed major European law-enforcement bodies among its customers.
Advertisement
In Hungary, a government procurement document shows that the Hungarian police signed an IT contract in Dec. 2024 with Oxygen Forensics worth 10.14 million Hungarian forints (€27,000) which ran through Dec. 2025.
In Italy, an April 2026 technical brief issued by the Public Prosecutor's Office in the Sardinian city of Sassari explicitly lists Oxygen Forensics among the recognized systems that judicial police can use to extract and analyze data from mobile devices.
And in Spain, a 2026 study on digital analysis of WhatsApp on Android and Apple smartphones was produced by a National Police inspector accredited by Oxygen Forensics and involved in training police investigators in digital analysis.
Law enforcement agencies in Romania and Latvia also bought its software, as recently as September.
None of the national police agencies involved responded to requests for comment.
Natalia Krapiva, senior legal counsel at digital rights group Access Now, said civil society organizations had warned for years about Oxygen Forensics' Russian ownership and development links, which she said have now been corroborated by the U.S. case.
"If in fact Russian-made software designed for the FSB and Investigative Committee was used for handling EU Commission criminal evidence database, it raises a serious possibility of sensitive information being compromised and accessed by Russian authorities," Krapiva said.
"We call on the EU and every government using these tools to suspend them and fully investigate how a Russian-owned company spent a decade inside Western law enforcement."

Malaysian durian industry eyes China market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:33:56 UTC
12:33:56 KST

Malaysia is pushing to take durian, whose powerful smell delights its lovers and repels its haters, beyond its roadside stalls and family orchards, particularly targeting the Chinese market.
Devotees savour durian like wine. 
For the Malaysian ones, the taste of their rich and creamy flesh varies widely across types. 
Some are prized for their sweet custard and fruity notes, others for a hint of bitterness, an alcohol tinge or even a peanut butter flavour.
Malaysians' efforts to elevate the industry can be found in the capital, Kuala Lumpur, at a centre devoted exclusively to the fruit and the growing variety of products made from it.
At the Kuala Lumpur Durian Experience Centre, near the landmark Petronas Twin Towers, visitors venture into a replica durian orchard to discover the fruit’s culture and history. 
In another room, a theatre show draws laughter. 
Downstairs, visitors enjoy platters and egg tarts crafted from it.
Launched this summer after an investment of nearly US$2 million, the two-story centre spans about 1,900 square metres and is open daily. 
Its durian shop welcomes guests from morning to midnight.
Its founder, Edison Ang, said the centre targets both local customers and tourists, especially those from China, the world's biggest durian importer. 
He said Chinese palates have long been influenced by Thai durian culture.
“What we actually hope for now is not to get people who don’t eat durian to start eating durian," he said. 
“Instead, we hope consumers who are already eating durian from other countries will switch to Malaysian durian.”
In 2025, China imported 1.87 million tonnes of fresh durian worth US$7.5 billion, with volume jumping over six times in the past decade.
Thailand’s earlier entry helped it secure over half that market by value in 2025. 
Malaysia, which began exporting fresh durian to China in 2024, was dwarfed. 
But for the first half of 2026, the value of China's fresh durian imports from Malaysia quadrupled compared with the same period last year, pointing to rapid growth.
Unlike their rivals, Malaysian growers typically do not harvest early, instead collecting only naturally ripened fruit caught in nets or ropes as they fall.
That’s the industry’s biggest advantage and also its biggest weakness, Ang said, as sellers have to race against time because the fruit’s shelf life is at most two to three days. (AP)

Taiwan ends 60-year men's athletics gold drought at Asian Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:30:49 UTC
12:30:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — High jumper Fu Chao-hsuan (傅兆玄) ended a 60-year wait for a men's athletics gold medal at the Asian Games on Sunday, clearing 2.25 meters to win the men's high jump.
The 23-year-old matched his season-best mark in a rain-soaked final in Nagoya. Fu and India's Sarvesh Kushare both cleared 2.25 meters, but Fu won the gold after clearing the height on his first attempt. Kushare needed two attempts, while South Korea's Woo Sang-hyeok (禹相赫) took bronze with 2.22 meters, per LTN.
Fu and Kushare subsequently failed three times at 2.28 meters, leaving Fu atop the standings. Fu said he had initially expected to finish second or third and was surprised to win gold. “I thought I might get third, and if I was lucky, second. I never expected to win the gold medal,” he said.
Fu also said he was deeply moved. “I hope I can go around the track and stay on the field longer,” he said.
The victory marked Taiwan's first Asian Games medal in men's high jump since Liao Hsueh-sung (廖學松) won bronze at the 1990 Beijing Games. It was also Taiwan's first Asian Games gold in a men's athletics event since Wu Ah-min (吳阿民) won the decathlon at the 1966 Bangkok Asian Games, per CNA.
Fu said his progress had been slow at times as he watched teammates improve and set national records while he struggled to improve his own performances. He credited his family and friends with helping him stay focused.
His mother was in Japan for the competition, marking the first time she had watched him compete at an international event in person. Fu said he felt he performed better when his family was in the stands.
Fu is set to receive NT$4.5 million under the National Glory Award system. He will also receive a bonus of NT$63,000 (US$2,000) from Taiwan Olympic Committee President Tsai Chia-fu (蔡家福) and NT$300,000 from Taiwan Athletics Association Chair Yeh Cheng-yen (葉政彥), per LTN.
Fu said he planned to share a significant portion of the prize money with his family as a way of thanking them for their support.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers touts stronger budget amid darkening economic outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:29:23 UTC
12:29:23 KST

In brief
- Australia’s 2025-26 budget deficit came in about $6 billion better than forecast, driven by stronger investment and super income.
- The improved result was overshadowed by expectations of a fresh RBA rate rise as oil prices fuel inflation fears.
Australia's budget has finished about $6 billion better off in the 2025/26 financial year, the government has revealed, as it braces for a damaging interest rate rise.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher touted their fiscal credentials when they released the final budget outcome on Monday, but also face difficult questions about an increasingly gloomy economic outlook.
Chalmers noted that today's improvements did not come from higher taxes on wages or commodities.
"Mining profits came in lower than what was anticipated," he said.
"It is overwhelmingly from higher super and investor income than what we anticipated in the Treasury's forecasts in May."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Though he readily welcomed the government's improved bottom line, he conceded there are "difficult months" to come, acknowledging that interest rates are expected to rise when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) meets on Tuesday.
Gallagher confirmed the improvement to the underlying deficit, which was projected to be $28.3 billion in the May budget.
It's still a good deal worse than the previous year's final budget outcome, which put the deficit at just under $10 billion for 2024/25.
With deficits projected for another decade, and mortgage holders bracing for another Reserve Bank rate hike on Tuesday, Gallagher was forced to defend the role of government spending on inflation.
"We've found savings, including savings in an ongoing sense, to make sure that where government investment is happening, that it's not adding to the inflation challenge in our economy," she told ABC Radio National.
"But there is a war in the Middle East, and that war is having impacts not just at the petrol bowser, but across the board. The sooner that war ends, the better."
With inflation stubbornly above the RBA's 2-3 per cent target band, the Middle East oil shock is set to keep price pressures elevated for longer.
Brent oil futures lifted to US$106 a barrel as peace talks between the US and Iran hit another snag.
The shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, higher Chinese imports and softer exports from non-OPEC countries have further weakened the supply picture, said the Commonwealth Bank's head of commodities Vivek Dhar.
"If global oil and refined product inventories do deplete, Brent oil futures risk surging as high as US$150 a barrel to induce uncontrolled demand destruction (i.e. where high prices reduce demand) in emerging and developing Asian economies," he said.
Each US$1 increase in the Brent oil price roughly translates to a 1c increase in fuel prices at the bowser.
Those higher service station costs will likely nudge headline inflation from 3.5 to 4 per cent by the time the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports on Wednesday.
The US, Europe and Japan have all hiked interest rates due to rising fuel prices since the RBA met in August.
Hawkish comments from governor Michele Bullock and other top RBA officials in recent weeks have emphasised that the bank is losing patience with inflation and is likely to follow.
The bank's board is widely expected to lift the cash rate to 4.6 per cent when it wraps up its two-day meeting on Tuesday — the highest level in 15 years.
Liberal MP Zoe McKenzie sought to pin the inflation spike on government spending, despite growth in public demand moderating in recent years.
"The rest of the world is not experiencing the inflation that we are experiencing here at home," she told News24.
While drivers despair at the pump, auction clearance rates, a leading house price indicator, slumped to a 10-week preliminary low of 50.3 per cent on Sunday, according to housing data firm Cotality.
Median property prices nationwide have slumped 3.6 per cent since March's cyclical peak as the removal of tax concessions in May's budget combines with three consecutive rate hikes to cripple buyer confidence.
While Bullock has stressed interest rate decisions are not designed to target house prices, economists have linked lower house prices to consumers spending less across the board, tugging inflation down.

Eight US Marines were injured two weeks ago when an Iranian anti-ship cruise missile struck a vessel they were operating on in the Strait of Hormuz, NBC News reported Sunday, citing three US officials.
The report said the Marines were not seriously injured but suffered smoke inhalation and possible traumatic brain injuries after experiencing concussion-like symptoms, including headaches.
Seven of the Marines were enlisted personnel, while the eighth was an officer. All eight returned to duty shortly after the Sept. 14 attack, according to the officials.
The Marines were operating as part of a battalion landing team when the Iranian missile struck the vessel, they said.
The officials said the vessel was not a US Navy ship but declined to specify its type, referring to it only as a maritime vessel.
The Pentagon has faced growing scrutiny over casualty figures since the US-Israel war with Iran began in February, with the number of injured and killed troops subject to changes in reporting and classification.
As of Wednesday, the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) had recorded 861 US service members as injured in the conflict.
The eight Marines were added to the database nearly 10 days after the Sept. 14 attack, while a US official attributed delays in reporting to symptoms that may appear later and the system’s lack of real-time updates.

US releases product lists for US$30 billion China tariff deal

US releases product lists for $38 billion China tariff deal
- The US and China agreed to cut tariffs on about US$30 billion of imports each, focusing on non-sensitive goods like household products, toys, meat, and agricultural items to stabilise trade relations.
- The tariff relief covers US$60 billion in bilateral trade, with about 90% of products seeing reductions to most-favoured-nation rates, benefiting US agricultural exports and Chinese consumer goods.
- Both countries extended their trade truce to January 2026 and will set up a new Agricultural Working Group to boost US agricultural purchases, aiming to meet annual targets through 2028.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US and China detailed a plan to cut tariffs on about US$30 billion (S$38 billion) of imports from each country, as the superpower rivals take steps to steady ties following a summit between leaders Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The list for goods entering the US contains 77 entries, including fireworks, household products, sporting equipment and toys, according to documents published by both governments.
They also listed 1,619 goods set to potentially enter China, such as meat, seafood, dairy products, grains, coal, timber and medical equipment.
The expected tariff relief for US$60 billion in bilateral trade was one of the most tangible outcomes of Xi’s state visit to Washington last week, even though the amount is a fraction of the US$415 billion in total goods exchanged between the world’s largest economies in 2025.
The two sides extended their trade truce until January as they pursue a broader agreement ahead of two more expected meetings between Trump and Xi in 2026.
With major disputes over export controls and Taiwan unresolved, non-sensitive trade has emerged as one area where agreements remain possible.
Shares of some Chinese appliance makers rose after details of the tariff cuts emerged, with Joyoung Co jumping by the 10 per cent limit in Shenzhen and Bear Electric Appliance up as much as 9.5 per cent.
China said the tariff reductions would take place simultaneously after fulfilling procedures required in domestic law.
“This arrangement will help to further stabilise China-US economic and trade relations and create favourable conditions for China’s exports of relevant products to the US,” the Chinese Commerce Ministry said.
About 90 per cent of the products covered by the reciprocal arrangement would have their tariffs reduced to most-favoured-nation rates, according to the statement.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer described the selected products as non-sensitive goods that could qualify for more favourable tariff treatment.
He said the recommendations would improve access for US agricultural products and medical devices while lowering barriers on Chinese household goods and toys.
“President Trump is unlocking improved market access for about 30 percent of US exports to China, while benefiting consumers with imports from China of household goods, toys, and other products that the United States generally does not import from other countries,” Greer said.
Beijing said tariffs on coal imported from the US would be included in the framework, a step it said would support Chinese purchases in 2027 and 2028.
The White House had previously said China agreed to import at least 10 million tonnes of coal from the US in 2027 and again in 2028.
Key grains including wheat, corn and sorghum are among the agricultural exports destined for a tariff cut.
That could help China make progress toward a goal to buy at least US$17 billion in US agricultural products annually through 2028, in addition to a commitment to buy 25 million tons of soybeans per year.
Progress towards the US$17 billion goal has been slow since it was announced by the Trump administration after the last leaders’ summit in May, with traders looking to potential tariff cuts from the meeting in Washington DC to spark a wave of new buying.
Agricultural purchases are often seen as the low hanging fruit of any trade deal between the US and China, less complicated than more sensitive issues such as chip technology or artificial intelligence.
A new Agricultural Working Group will be established between the two countries following the summit, according to China’s Commerce Ministry, with an inaugural meeting set to take place by the end of 2026. BLOOMBERG

The atmosphere here is completely calm, and the university students are also cooperating with us in restoring peace...,” he said.Jalandhar Police Commissioner Satinder Singh said reports of disturbances in the hostels were rumours and that all hostels had been checked.“First of all, reports of disturbances in the hostels were merely rumours. All hostels have been checked, and there are no issues. Traffic has resumed, and the situation is normal. Other matters will be resolved through discussions with the students... Overall, the atmosphere is fine, and any minor issues will be addressed... Please inform the families that all students are safe and there is no cause for concern,” Singh said.DIG (Jalandhar Range) Naveen Singla also said the situation had been brought under control and that traffic movement on NH-44 would soon be restored.Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann has directed strict action against those responsible for the unrest at Lovely Professional University (LPU), the Chief Minister’s Office said.Mann also directed Director General of Police Gaurav Yadav to visit the spot and assess the situation.Clashes, arson and highway blockadeThe protest began near Girls' Hostel-3 around 1 am on Sunday after students alleged that a female student had been raped by a plumber three days earlier. They also claimed the hostel warden had been informed but no action was taken.The protesters blocked NH-44 outside the university from around 8 am, causing long queues of stranded vehicles. Police later attempted to clear the blockade, but students allegedly threw water bottles at them and clashed with personnel.Police resorted to a mild lathi charge, following which students moved towards the campus and continued to pelt stones at police vehicles. Two police vehicles were set on fire, while four to five vehicles were damaged, according to Jalandhar Rural SSP Harvinder Singh Virk.Viral videos showed damaged property, vehicles and an ATM kiosk on the campus. Some students were also seen climbing onto a decommissioned MiG-23UM aircraft and a military tank installed on the premises.A truck driver, Vikas Yadav, said, “We have been stranded since 7 AM; there is no sign of things opening up yet... We are extremely distressed... We have had to abandon our vehicles and flee...”Rape case registered, SIT formedPolice said an FIR had been registered against an unknown person based on a complaint by the students and a special investigation team had been formed.Singla said the girl was staying in Hostel No. 3 and had returned to her home after students alleged that no action had been taken on the matter. He said the investigation would involve student representatives.“We will analyse forensic samples, CCTV camera footage, call records, etc., before reaching a conclusion,” Singla said.The DIG also said students had demanded that the hostel staff comprise only women, adding that the management would address the demand.Asked about another death, Singla said a female student from Telangana studying at LPU had died by suicide 15 days earlier. “If the students say that there was foul play, action will be taken,” he said.LPU Vice Chancellor Jaspal Singh Sandhu said the university was not aware of any such rape incident but would cooperate with the investigation.LPU denies rape claim, releases students' videoLPU management has denied the rape allegations, with Registrar Monica Gulati saying certain “anti-social elements” were spreading “false, baseless and fabricated” claims.The university released a video featuring three female students identified as residents of Room No. 504 of the hostel. In the video, the students said no rape had taken place in their room and asked police and other students not to disturb them.Gulati introduced the video by saying, “I would like you to hear what the girls residing in room number 504 of GH3 told us.”The first student said, “So, we are the residents of room number 504. Nothing of that sort happened in our room; we have been living here for the past two months. Please, police and students, do not bother us. Nothing like that happened in our room, and we are not involved in this at all.”The second student said, “We have been extremely distressed today, and if we face further trouble, we will involve our parents. Please do not harass us.”
The third added, “And the police should also stop coming to our room repeatedly; otherwise, we will call our parents.”Gulati later said, “The only conclusion to be drawn from all this is that anti-social elements and individuals with vested interests are behind this.”Congress attacks Punjab governmentThe opposition Congress criticised the AAP government over the law and order situation in Punjab.“What is happening at LPU is deeply concerning. If students have serious questions or concerns about any incident, they deserve transparent, impartial and time-bound answers, not rumours or suppression. The violence is a testament to the failed law and order situation in Punjab,” state Congress chief Amrinder Singh Raja Warring said.“NH-44 has been blocked since the morning, yet not a single representative from the AAP government has bothered to meet the students and hear their grievances,” Warring said.

Is the universe infinite? The answer gets weird fast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:18:42 UTC
12:18:42 KST

Is the universe infinite? The answer gets weird fast
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- Universe Today
- Summary:
- Measurements of ancient light from the cosmic microwave background suggest that the universe is remarkably flat. But that does not prove it is infinite, because the observable cosmos could be only a small patch of a much larger curved universe. Space could even be flat while wrapping around on itself in exotic ways.
- Share:
Earth has a finite surface. We can measure it, and if the planet itself were expanding, that surface area would increase over time. Surprisingly, our familiar planet also offers a useful way to think about something far harder to understand: what the universe might be like beyond the region we can observe.
The simplest assumption is that beyond our cosmic horizon, there is simply more universe. More stars. More galaxies. More AI-generated cat videos. It is similar to standing somewhere on Earth and assuming that beyond your visible horizon, there is still more Earth.
But how large is the entire universe, including everything beyond what we can see?
The frustrating answer is that we may never know.
The Limits of the Observable Universe
The boundary of the observable universe is not merely the farthest distance our telescopes can currently reach. It represents a deeper limit on what information can ever reach us. The universe contains a finite amount of information that can become accessible to us, even if we waited for an arbitrarily long time.
Beyond that boundary, we are left to infer and speculate.
One possibility is straightforward: the universe is infinite. Space simply continues forever with no endpoint.
But another possibility is that the universe is finite.
That immediately raises an obvious question. How can something be finite without having an edge?
Earth provides the answer.
The surface of our planet has a finite area, yet someone traveling along that surface never encounters a boundary where the ground suddenly ends. Yes, Earth has an edge if you leave its surface in the third dimension and head into outer space, but that misses the point. The two-dimensional surface itself is finite and has no border because it curves back around.
How Geometry Reveals Curvature
We do not need to leave Earth to prove that its surface is curved. Mathematics gives us several ways to detect curvature while remaining entirely on the surface.
Triangles provide one example. On a perfectly flat plane, the three interior angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. Thank you, Euclid.
But imagine drawing enormous lines between three widely separated cities on Earth. The resulting triangle would not behave like one drawn on a sheet of paper. Its interior angles would add up to more than 180 degrees because the surface beneath it is curved.
Parallel lines offer another clue. On a flat plane, parallel lines never meet. On a curved surface, however, lines that begin parallel can eventually converge.
Imagine that you and I begin at different points along the equator and travel straight north. Eventually, our paths meet at the North Pole. Neither of us turned toward the other. The surface of Earth curved beneath us.
Astronomers can perform similar geometric tests on the universe itself.
Ancient Light Tests the Shape of Space
One of the most powerful tools comes from the cosmic microwave background, or CMB.
This ancient radiation was released when the early universe cooled enough for light to travel freely through what had previously been a hot, dense plasma. Scientists understand much of the relevant plasma physics (we have a decent understanding of plasmas here on Earth), which allows them to predict what patterns should appear in this ancient glow.
Those predictions include tiny temperature variations scattered across the CMB.
And those variations are exactly what astronomers observe.
More importantly, scientists can calculate how large those temperature patches should appear. If space were strongly curved, the light traveling toward us across billions of light years would follow altered paths. That distortion would change the apparent size of the patterns.
Astronomers can therefore compare the observed size of the CMB features with the size predicted for different cosmic geometries.
The features appear at essentially the expected scale for flat space.
That is why scientists say the universe appears to be geometrically flat.
So is the mystery solved? Does a flat universe automatically mean an infinite universe?
Not quite.
Flat Does Not Necessarily Mean Infinite
Imagine trying to measure the curvature of Earth while confined to your own neighborhood. The area would look nearly flat. Small triangles would behave almost exactly as Euclid predicted, and short parallel paths would not noticeably converge.
The problem would not be that Earth is actually flat. Your measuring area would simply be too small compared with the size of the planet.
Something similar could be true of the universe.
Our measurements are limited to the observable cosmos. Within that enormous region, space appears extremely flat. But the universe outside our observable patch could be vastly larger.
It is therefore possible that the universe has curvature that becomes apparent only on scales much larger than we can access (I know that tens of billions of light-years isn't exactly tiny, but it is compared to how big the universe COULD be.)
If so, space might eventually curve back around itself.
In principle, that could mean traveling continuously in one direction would eventually return you to where you started, much as traveling around Earth can bring you back to your starting point.
In practice, the expansion of the universe places regions beyond our cosmic horizon permanently out of reach, so such a journey remains a theoretical thought experiment.
But things can get even stranger.
The Universe Could Be Flat and Still Wrap Around
A universe can be geometrically flat without being infinite in every direction.
To understand how, picture a flat sheet of paper. Draw triangles and parallel lines on it. Now bend the paper into a cylinder without stretching or tearing it.
Locally, the geometry remains flat. The triangles still behave like ordinary triangles, and the parallel lines still behave like parallel lines. Yet one direction now loops around.
This highlights the difference between geometry and topology.
Geometry describes properties such as curvature. Topology describes the broader way a space is connected.
The observable universe appears geometrically flat. But that does not automatically tell us whether one or more dimensions might wrap around and connect back to themselves while remaining locally flat.
Topology allows for some very strange possibilities.
A Mobius strip can be created by connecting the ends of a strip after introducing a twist. A Klein bottle can be thought of as another unusual connected surface. Cylinders, donuts, Mobius strips, and Klein bottles can all illustrate how spaces with locally flat geometry can have very different overall structures.
In three dimensions, mathematicians have identified 17 distinct topologies that can all remain geometrically flat. One particularly interesting example is Hantzsche Wendt space, which involves repeating structures related to hexagonal patterns.
Scientists Have Looked for Cosmic Loops
Astronomers have searched for evidence that the universe has a closed topology.
One strategy is to look for repeated patterns in the cosmic microwave background. Another is to search for galaxies that might appear in different places on opposite sides of the sky because their light has traveled through a universe that wraps around itself.
So far, researchers have found no convincing evidence that this happens.
Based on everything we can currently observe, the universe appears both geometrically flat and topologically simple. In other words, there is no detected sign that its dimensions loop back on themselves.
But once again, our cosmic horizon creates a fundamental limitation. If the scale of any such looping is larger than the observable universe, we may never be able to detect it.
That means we may never know with certainty whether the entire universe is infinite, finite, curved, or connected in some larger and stranger way.
And then there is the multiverse.
In some cosmological ideas, everything we call the universe, including regions far beyond our observable horizon, might be only one bubble among potentially countless others. Those bubbles could expand away from one another while new regions undergo their own Big Bang-like beginnings.
But that is probably enough cosmic geometry for one day.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universe Today. Original written by Paul Sutter. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
