La Rábida monastery: where Columbus persuaded Castile to discover America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:17:22 UTC
12:17:22 KST

The discovery of America remains one of history's great feats, when two cultures met. Before sailing, Columbus gained vital backing at La Rábida from Franciscan friars and the Pinzón brothers.
On a low hill outside Huelva, at the point where the Río Tinto meets the Odiel before they flow into the Atlantic, stands one of the most decisive sites in world history: the monastery of Santa María de La Rábida. Without its walls, its friars and the faith invested there, it is quite possible that Christopher Columbus's great enterprise would never have set sail from the nearby shores of Palos de la Frontera bound for the New World.
The Franciscan presence here dates back to the early 13th century, when the first friars settled in this early hermitage on the Huelva estuary. For decades, La Rábida was a place of retreat and prayer, far from the bustle, until destiny – and the persistence of a navigator – turned it into the epicentre of one of the most momentous episodes in history: the encounter between two worlds that until then were strangers to one another.
Today we can walk on the very ground the navigator trod and pass through the doorway that determined his fate. Here at La Rábida, the friars welcome visitors just as they welcomed Christopher Columbus more than 500 years ago.
A refuge for a navigator down on his luck
When Columbus reached these shores, he had spent years trying to persuade a European crown to trust his project: a westward trading route to the Indies which, without his knowing, would lead him to an unknown continent for Europeans. Before arriving in Huelva, the navigator had sought backing in Portugal, France and Italy, without success. He had also tried to strike a deal with Castile and Aragon, but the monarchs at the time were focused on the Granada campaign, to reconquer the last Muslim stronghold on the Iberian Peninsula after more than 770 years of Reconquista.
It was in the convent of La Rábida that he found more than a bed for the night: he found allies willing to believe in him and support him before Queen Isabella I of Castile, the great patron of Columbus's project and a defender of the Indigenous peoples who lived in the newly discovered lands. She asked that they be treated as Castilian citizens, free subjects protected from all abuse and slavery. Even in death she did not forget these new Castilian citizens: the will of Isabella of Castile is regarded as a key legal milestone that anticipated the modern concept of human rights, by guaranteeing the protection and freedom of Indigenous Americans.
The Franciscan friars, especially Fray Juan Pérez, who had been the queen's confessor, listened to Columbus's proposal and decided to intercede at the court of the Catholic Monarchs. Thanks to that mediation, the pioneering navigator finally obtained an audience that would lead to the backing of Isabella I of Castile, the visionary queen who agreed to fund the expedition that would change the course of history.
The Virgin who 'witnessed' the start of the voyage
Within the walls of this hermitage the image of Santa María de La Rábida, also known as Our Lady of the Miracles, is still kept today. According to tradition, it was before this statue that Columbus himself prayed moments before departing for the unknown, on a voyage many considered madness and which would ultimately redraw the map of the world.
Visiting the chapel where this image is kept today is, in a way, to stand at the very spot where the journey was forged: a place where silence is almost tangible, a point that bore direct witness to a decision that would shape the destiny of two continents.
The Pinzón brothers, the key to setting sail for the New World
Convincing the Crown was not enough: Columbus needed a crew willing to embark on a voyage into the unknown, which many sailors of the time saw as a one-way journey. That was when one of the most influential families in the seafaring world of Palos de la Frontera came into play: the Pinzón brothers.
Martín Alonso Pinzón, an experienced navigator and a highly respected figure in the town, put his reputation at the service of the venture and helped recruit much of the crew, overcoming the misgivings of those who doubted the navigator's plan. His involvement was so crucial that he ended up commanding the caravel La Pinta, while his brother Vicente Yáñez Pinzón took charge of La Niña. The third brother, Francisco Martín Pinzón, sailed as master, the second-in-command, on La Pinta, completing a family presence that proved decisive across the three ships of the expedition, alongside the carrack Santa María, captained by Columbus himself.
Without the human and nautical support of the Pinzón family, it is doubtful that the project would ever have left the port of Palos on that 3 August 1492.
Today, replicas of these three vessels can be visited at the Muelle de las Carabelas. There, the three ships offer a glimpse into the exploratory past of what was then Castile.
A legacy of light and shadow
The discovery of America, launched from this small monastery in Huelva, led to the greatest cultural, economic and biological exchange in modern history. That encounter brought to Europe foods that are now staples, such as the potato – crucial, centuries later, for example during the Irish famine – the tomato, sugar cane and coveted cocoa. At the same time, that epic was marked by episodes of violence and subjugation against Indigenous peoples, a reality that today is examined through a critical lens, though one that is hard to apply to the 15th century.
La Rábida is more than a religious building: it is the symbolic starting point of a complex historical process, capable of explaining both the flowering of a new relationship between cultures and the darker aspects that process carried with it.
Today, the Franciscan convent of Santa María de La Rábida has become a cultural and tourist landmark for those who want to retrace the steps that led up to the discovery of America. Its rooms preserve documents, models and objects that recreate convent life in the 15th century, as well as the atmosphere in which Columbus worked out the final details of his expedition.
Walking through its cloister under the sky lit by the moon that inspired the navigator to venture beyond the seas, contemplating the image of Our Lady of the Miracles or looking out over the same landscape from which the caravels set off, is a way of travelling straight back to the origins of modern history. It is a place of pilgrimage not only religious but also historical, for anyone wishing to understand how a small monastery in Huelva ended up changing the course of the world.

Over 258,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine identified by media investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:13:18 UTC
12:13:18 KST

Over 258,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine identified by media investigation
Russian independent media outlet Mediazona, in collaboration with the BBC Russian service, has confirmed the identities of 258,989 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine.
More than 10,000 names were added to the list in less than two weeks, roughly double the usual rate, according to Mediazona. The outlet said the increase was largely due to a leaked list of bodies exchanged between Russia and Ukraine, with names added only after their identities could be independently confirmed through official registries.
The journalists note that the actual number of deaths is likely significantly higher, as their verified information comes from public sources such as obituaries, posts by relatives, regional media reports, and statements from local authorities.
As of Sept. 21, Mediazona had confirmed the deaths of 7,692 officers of the Russian military and other security agencies. The list also includes around 20,500 mobilized soldiers, though Mediazona said that figure is a significant underestimate because recruitment details are increasingly omitted from recent obituaries.
The date of death is known in 241,600 cases. Mediazona cautioned that data for the most recent months remains incomplete and is likely to change as additional deaths are verified.
The Kyiv Independent cannot independently verify the reporting.
The latest update comes as Russia continues to suffer heavy battlefield casualties in Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 27 that Ukrainian forces had killed or wounded 10,660 Russian troops over the previous week, citing a report from Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi. The losses came as Ukrainian forces continued offensive operations in the Lyman sector of Donetsk Oblast.
Ukraine's General Staff estimated on Sept. 27 that Russia had suffered 1,528,970 personnel losses since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. The figure does not distinguish between troops killed, wounded, missing, or captured.
Casualty estimates vary widely, and neither Russia nor Ukraine publishes comprehensive independently verifiable figures for military losses.

Russia offers US$20 million reward for information on Unmanned Systems Forces commander Magyar – WSJ
Russia has offered a US$20 million reward through post-Soviet criminal networks for information that could help locate Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces.
Source: The Wall Street Journal
Details: The Unmanned Systems Forces said that, due to the high effectiveness of Ukrainian drones, the Kremlin has made Magyar one of its main targets for assassination. In addition, Russian courts have convicted the Ukrainian serviceman in absentia on fabricated terrorism charges and sentenced him to decades in prison.
Due to the serious threat to his life, the commander and his subordinates are forced to follow strict security measures.
The journalists said that before visiting a secret command post, they were asked to put their phones into flight mode and then place them into Faraday cases that block Wi-Fi, mobile, Bluetooth and GPS signals. They were driven to the secret location in cars with tinted windows to conceal the route to a site which, according to the journalists, is located somewhere in Ukraine's south-east.
Brovdi himself attributes the Russian focus on him to the scale of Russian military losses. He stated that the Unmanned Systems Forces account for just 2.5% of the total strength of the Ukrainian Armed Forces but are responsible for around a third of all Russian losses over the past year.
He also noted that the Russians had killed 79 members of Magyar's Birds since the beginning of the full-scale war. Their names are engraved on a wall near the entrance to the command centre. On the day of the interview, the Unmanned Systems Forces had killed or wounded 656 Russian soldiers for every one of their own fallen troops.
"I don't think this exchange rate is good enough," Magyar said.

Huckabee announces groundbreaking for permanent US Embassy in Jerusalem to be soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:09:35 UTC
12:09:35 KST

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said Sunday that the United States will soon break ground on a permanent embassy complex in Jerusalem, announcing the next step in the project during a Sukkot reception for foreign diplomats hosted by Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion at Safra Square.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
“We will soon be breaking ground on our property to begin the construction of the US embassy that will be our permanent home rather than being spread out all over the country,” Huckabee told the gathering.
Israel and the United States signed an agreement July 1 allocating the Allenby Compound in southern Jerusalem for the permanent embassy. Israel had approved the site in March. The project follows President Donald Trump’s 2017 recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and the opening of the US Embassy there in 2018.
Huckabee acknowledged that construction could take years but described the project as a long-term American commitment to the city.
“It is our commitment as the United States of America and a partner of Israel to say that we are going to put a permanent imprint in this city,” he said.
Lion and his wife, Stavit, hosted the diplomatic corps in the municipality’s 800-square-meter sukkah, which can accommodate about 650 people at a time and which the city bills as the world’s largest. According to organizers, 46 ambassadors were invited and 32 attended.
Among them was British Ambassador to Israel Simon Walters. His attendance was noteworthy because the British Embassy remains in Tel Aviv and the UK does not recognize Israeli sovereignty over Jerusalem pending a negotiated settlement of the city’s status.
Lion used the traditional Sukkot theme of welcoming ushpizin, or guests, to address the diplomats.
“Tonight, you are our ushpizin,” he said, describing Jerusalem as “open, welcoming, and diverse.”
Lion urges more countries to move embassies to Jerusalem
Lion also urged more countries to move their embassies to Jerusalem, saying nine currently have missions there and Colombia is expected to become the 10th in the coming weeks. Colombia’s new government agreed earlier this year to relocate its embassy to Jerusalem as part of the restoration of full diplomatic relations with Israel.
Huckabee praised the city’s development and said the permanent embassy would make the American presence in Jerusalem harder to reverse.
“There is no way that in the future someone would ever come and try to move us out of Jerusalem, where we belong,” he said.

Israel must resist election economics, vote buying ahead of October 27 - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:09:22 UTC
12:09:22 KST

Back in the Great Depression era of the 1920s in the United States, the Republican Party campaigned on assuring voters of a “chicken in every pot and a car in every garage.”
The longstanding cynical political ploy of promising constituents just about anything to get elected should be recalled with caution as Israel enters its final 30 days before its fateful October 27 election.
In a functioning government, regardless of elections, legislation is passed, allocations are approved, and programs are launched and implemented all the time, as they should be.
A country needs to run, decisions must be made, and budgets must be disbursed. During election season, however, every move is suspect. What are the motives? Who is the initiator, and who benefits?
Current government holds all cards
Call it election economics, and in this case, the government holds all the cards. That’s why it’s ever so important that every bill and every allocation must be circumspect and vetted extra carefully by the opposition, the media, and the general public to ensure that decisions are not being made simply to garner favor and secure voting loyalty.
Some ministry decisions should be beyond reproach. For instance, last week, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced a NIS 35 million pilot program that will compensate uninsured businesses for direct property damage caused by protection-money extortion.
As The Jerusalem Post reported, the program will provide an economic safety net that will help businesses maintain operational continuity and encourage them to cooperate with law-enforcement authorities, thereby assisting the effort to reduce the phenomenon.
This program benefits everyone, and it would be difficult to construe its implementation as an election ploy to buy votes.
On the other hand, this past summer, Smotrich also announced a roughly NIS 2.4 billion funding package for neighborhoods and access roads in West Bank settlements. Coming as it did, with the full knowledge that an election was in the offing, the move can be seen as a blatant attempt by Smotrich to bolster his electoral base.
Sometimes, efforts to discern the difference between electioneering and legitimate decisions become blurry.
A-G postpones E1 proposal deadline over electioneering concerns
On Sunday, the Attorney-General’s Office ordered a monthlong delay of the deadline for submitting proposals for a tender to build 1,200 housing units in the controversial E1 expansion near Ma’aleh Adumim, citing concerns that the project could be used for electioneering.
The delay would move the deadline until after the election. Ma’aleh Adumim Mayor Guy Yifrach, however, argued that the attorney-general’s decision itself constituted a form of reverse electioneering.
“The diplomatic decision to advance the tender was made months before the election, and since then, it has progressed via a professional process that by its nature takes time,” he told Hebrew media outlets. “If the claim is that continuing the tender is ‘political,’ I say exactly the opposite: Stopping it now is, in fact, an intervention with political implications.”
There is a thin line separating allocations and legislation that are a normative outcome of a functioning society that is responsible for millions of people’s safety and services, and thinly veiled bribery to lock in support, party loyalty, and votes.
As we enter the final month before the October 27 election, it’s incumbent on all elected officials from the government, its ministries, and the Knesset to display the utmost responsibility and rein in the instincts to cozy up to constituents with financial incentives and benefits disguised as legislation.
Past elections have shown that those instincts are usually impossible to tamp down. This time, the stakes are too high to allow election economics to take hold. Vigilance is needed and demanded, and violations should be called out with vigor.
At the same time, not every government decision can be confronted with the accusation of vote buying. A country needs to keep running. We call on the government to refrain from election economics and the opposition to refrain from calling every government decision made in the next month to be all about the election.
There are more than enough vital issues facing the country, and the parties running should be articulating how they intend to address them if they gain Knesset seats or join the government.
That’s the way to garner support and loyalty from voters – not by buying their ballot with sectarian favoritism.

Eight US Marines were injured in an Iranian attack on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz on September 14, NBC reported Sunday evening, citing three US sources.

Pentagon accused of misrepresenting casualty count

The Defense Department has also been accused of downplaying injuries by wounded soldiers who spoke to CBS News.
One soldier described suffering severe shrapnel wounds and undergoing multiple emergency surgeries in Kuwait. A US Army official told his wife that his injuries were "minor."
The US military has strongly disputed this claim, telling CBS that military designations, including “not seriously injured” and “combat casualty,” have specific definitions that have been misconstrued.
"The care and well-being of our soldiers is of the highest priority," CBS cited an army spokesperson as writing. "Any assertion that the army seeks to downplay a soldier's injuries is simply not true."

Putin is testing NATO on Norway’s remote Arctic islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:07:39 UTC
12:07:39 KST

BARENTSBURG, Norway — For the best part of a century, the biggest threat to the residents of Svalbard was polar bears. Increasingly, it now comes from Russia.
Fears are growing that Moscow could use the sprawling Arctic archipelago — a part of Norway with an unusual legal status — to test NATO militarily amid growing uncertainty over the U.S. commitment to European defense.
Allies suspect Russia of probing crucial undersea cables in the waters off Svalbard and staging military-style events that test the limits of the rules governing its presence there. As Russia ramps up hybrid attacks across Europe, Oslo is racing to boost its naval and surveillance capabilities to protect its northern flank, while local authorities on Svalbard are investing in critical infrastructure — and even have an evacuation plan in place.
Advertisement
“There is more tension in the Arctic and in the north, and of course also Svalbard is a part of that,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik told POLITICO. “We know that Russia ... uses a lot of ways to try to provoke or find ways to do hybrid threats.”
Despite its status as Norwegian territory, the archipelago's main island, Spitsbergen, is home to a Russian town.
“Russian leadership is highly unpredictable and more and more risk prone,” said Kari Aga Myklebost, a Russian history professor and Svalbard expert at Norway's Arctic University. “I wouldn't close out any scenario when it comes to the Kremlin's will to confront NATO.”
High North, high tension
For decades, Svalbard symbolized the Norwegian maxim “High North, low tension,” which saw efforts to build cooperation among Arctic countries, including Russia.
Beyond its remoteness — lying over 900 kilometers from mainland Norway — and its glacial temperatures, that was down to the archipelago's unique status. Under a 1920 international treaty, countries recognized Oslo’s sovereignty over the islands and in return gained resource exploitation rights — with the Soviets buying the town of Barentsburg to mine local coal deposits soon after.
Advertisement
The treaty also forbade any nation from using Svalbard for “warlike purposes” including the construction of naval bases and fortifications, but Norway does visit the archipelago with coast guard and military vessels.
At its Cold War peak, 2,400 Soviet citizens lived on Spitsbergen, the only populated island, making up around 70% of its population.
Moscow has little incentive to upend the treaty because it could rebound against its own interests. With Russia’s northwestern Kola Peninsula — home to two-thirds of its nuclear second-strike submarines — sitting around 1,000 kilometers away, “Russia has been cautious to avoid any kind of escalation,” Myklebost said.
A Soviet-era placard in Barentsburg. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
That makes it strategic for NATO, too. “In a military conflict … this is where the Russian submarines could enter the North Atlantic and hide at greater depths and pose a threat to NATO and the U.S.,” she argued.
Yet tensions have grown following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow also began direct boat trips from Russia in 2024 and last year set up a chapter of the Russian Geographical Society, which is led by former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu.
“We call them gray zone provocations,” Myklebost said. “It’s a very cost-efficient way of asserting Russian presence and … challenging Norway's jurisdiction.”
As a result, Norway’s intelligenceservices this year warned the Kremlin “aims to increase Russian scope for action in Svalbard.”
British, American and Norwegian forces this spring reportedly caught Russian vessels testing a secret subsea cable-cutting weapon off Svalbard’s coast.
Although Barentsburg’s coal reserves are dwindling, Moscow is not abandoning the town. Moscow provided state-owned Trust Arktikugol, which administers Barentsburg, with about 1.89 billion rubles (€20 million) in federal subsidies in 2025, according to its accounts.
Russia’s ambassador to Norway, Nikolay Korchunov, told POLITICO he wanted to see a “transformation of the economic activities” from coal to services in Barentsburg, and said Arktikugol was investing in maintaining the town.
Advertisement
Cranes and scaffolding adorn many of Barentsburg’s Soviet-era buildings, which lie scattered across a jagged hill facing the imposing snow-specked Vøringen glacier — a sign of Russia’s continued interest.
But “we are not questioning any sovereignty of Norway,” Korchunov insisted. “We stress the necessity and importance of fulfilling all the Svalbard Treaty,” he said, accusing Oslo of contributing to a “negative trend towards NATO militarization of entire Baltic-Arctic region.”
On thin ice
Vice Adm. Rune Andersen, the chief of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters, said his priority was “striking that balance between deterrence but maintaining stability” on Svalbard, and remaining “calm and collected” on hybrid threats.
Svalbard Deputy Governor Katharina Rise. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
But given the “risks” of escalation, the military is investing to reinforce its surveillance capabilities, he said, including launching three new maritime mapping satellites next year — alongside “a renewal of the navy and coast guard … to have a continuous presence” nearby.
NATO countries “are more often up in our waters,” said Sandvik, the minister. Defending Svalbard is also a part of NATO’s planning process, he said.
Advertisement
Locally, the strategy is to keep a lid on tensions. Svalbard’s Deputy Governor Katharina Rise said her office meets with Russia’s local consulate four times a year. “We have good and constructive dialogue,” she said. “It's our responsibility to secure the stability and … low tension here.”
Terje Aunevik, the mayor of Longyearbyen, the main Norwegian town on Spitsbergen, said authorities had plans in place to rapidly evacuate the settlement if tensions flare.
With just two subsea internet cables, one airport, one water reservoir and one diesel-run power plant in Longyearbyen that depends on imports, Aunevik said “major investments” are underway, including the construction of two new water reservoirs by around 2029. “We are quite vulnerable in that perspective,” he said.
Out in the cold
Up close, Barentsburg doesn’t look particularly threatening. Few locals venture outside the several dozen crumbling buildings. A plume of smoke escapes the aging coal plant and a lonely hammer-and-sickle Soviet flag flaps in the wind. Barentsburg feels like an abandoned relic of a bygone era.
Some of the recent hybrid activity is also down to a local push for attention from Moscow, said Arild Moe, a research professor and Russia expert at the Fridtjof Nansen Institute think tank. “They’re playing on nationalist strengths … to get priorities and to get finance.”
But Putin’s unpredictability and Trump's repeated wavering on NATO remain wild cards.
Anxiety is also palpable on Spitsbergen. In Barentsburg, “we don’t speak about [political] topics,” said a waitress from St. Petersburg who asked that her name not be used, while acknowledging locals fear a potential NATO-Russia war. “Of course this worries us,” she said.
“There is of course this constant chatter about if the Russian government wants to push a NATO member and Svalbard is the place where they would do it,” said Jonatan Svensson, an expedition guide who has lived in Longyearbyen for five years.
Jonatan Svenssson. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
To assuage those fears, NATO should consider air patrols over Svalbard, shift defensive air assets to the north of mainland Norway and hold joint exercises nearby, the two NATO diplomats said, provided Oslo agreed and the measures complied with the Svalbard Treaty.
However, so far NATO has no public plans to boost its naval or air presence around the islands. But some worry the alliance's current posture won't be enough to deter Moscow.
In theory, it would be “really easy” for Russia to occupy Svalbard, said Ståle Ulriksen, a lecturer at the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy, if it flew in special forces from northern Russia and seized the airport. However, he argued such a scenario is unlikely.
Yet Moscow wouldn’t need to launch a full occupation. According to Myklebost, the analyst, Russia could stage an emergency affecting its local citizens and send in crisis management forces, a move that may not clearly trigger NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause.
“A worst-case scenario is a situation where Moscow sees an opportunity to test NATO cohesion,” she said. “Maybe Norway's shouting for help from allies, and then you have Donald Trump saying: ‘No — we are not risking our good deals with Russia over this tiny island.’”

Another Lao Activist Vanishes in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:02:00 UTC
12:02:00 KST

In the early hours of September 15, Khieo Lapchanh, a 26-year-old Lao content creator, finished his shift at a restaurant in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon province and vanished. The following day, he was due at the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) for his first asylum registration interview. He never arrived.
Khieo came to Thailand in 2019 and late last year began posting Facebook videos sharply critical of the Lao government. Within months, his Khiew Channel Facebook page had amassed some 159,000 followers. Among his targets was the Siphandone dynasty, whose hold on high office runs from former president Khamtay Siphandone to his son, Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone, and his daughter, Vice President Viengthong Siphandone.
The backlash was swift. Khieo was doxxed, depicted in violent AI-manipulated content and subjected to death threats, including a $8,000 bounty on his life. Fearing for his safety after Lao officials twice visited his mother’s home, he withdrew from public activism. Silence, however, offered little protection.
A Familiar Pattern
Khieo is far from the first Lao dissident to vanish or die in Thailand while seeking UNHCR protection. In August 2019, Od Sayavong, a member of the Free Lao group, disappeared in Bangkok while awaiting resettlement to a third country, and Thai police concede that their investigation has made no progress. In May 2023, the body of Bounsuan Kitiyano, a UNHCR-recognized refugee and fellow Free Lao member, was found near the Lao border in Ubon Ratchathani province with three gunshot wounds. He had been planning to move to Australia, and no one has been held accountable for his killing.
The timing of these cases suggests that Lao authorities are closely monitoring activists’ engagement with UNHCR, and that they are prepared to use violence to stop their critics from reaching the safety of a third country.
These cases also expose Thailand’s failure to protect those seeking refuge within its borders. In a 2024 report, Human Rights Watch analyzed 25 cases of transnational repression in Thailand since the 2014 military coup, finding that refugees and asylum seekers have faced surveillance, violence, abductions, enforced disappearances, and forced returns facilitated by the Thai government. The report describes a “swap mart” in which foreign dissidents sheltering in Thailand are effectively traded for critics of the Thai government living abroad.
Thailand’s legal framework compounds this vulnerability. Because the country is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, asylum seekers are treated as illegal immigrants and remain liable to deportation. In January 2022, another member of the Free Laos group, Khoukham Keomanivong, was arrested in Thailand for overstaying his visa (despite holding a UNHCR card) and only narrowly avoided deportation to Laos following intervention by civil society actors.
A Global Problem
Responsibility for Khieo’s disappearance does not rest with Laos, or Thailand, alone. On September 23, just eight days after Khieo disappeared, more than 130 U.N. human rights experts issued a joint statement urging states to prevent and combat transnational repression and calling for expedited asylum, resettlement and humanitarian visa processes for those at risk. They also warned that such repression is increasingly digital, deploying social media, spyware and malware.
The cross-border targeting of activists is part of a broader global democratic retreat in which many states are culpable. Freedom House reports that global freedom declined in 2025 for the 20th consecutive year, while CIVICUS finds that just 7 percent of the world’s population lives in countries with open or relatively open civic space. Laos fares poorly on both, scoring 13 out of 100 in Freedom House’s index and rated “closed” by CIVICUS. Nor does the threat to Lao activists end at Thailand’s borders. In June 2025, exiled activist Joseph Akaravong was stabbed in the throat and torso in Pau, France, in what the local prosecutor described as an attempted assassination.
China has long been identified as a force for authoritarian consolidation in Southeast Asia and it is the largest source of development assistance and investment in Laos. But China is not the only country with responsibility to bear. In 2025, after Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency set its sights on USAID, the Trump administration cancelled 83 percent of the agency’s programs. Human Rights Watch reports that safe houses for at-risk human rights defenders in authoritarian countries have closed as a result. Manushya, the organization supporting Khieo, had relied on U.S. government funding to run nine safe houses for activists from neighboring states, including Laos and Cambodia, and its founder warned that without that funding it could no longer protect activists facing transnational repression. The sector is now understaffed and under-resourced, leaving activists less safe. The United States must reinvest heavily in human rights protection in Southeast Asia, and other democracies must increase their funding.
The Real Story of 2026
On November 24, Laos is scheduled to graduate from least developed country status, a milestone that will no doubt be marked with much fanfare. Yet it must not be forgotten that the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party has ruled for five decades without organized opposition, independent civil society or independent media, and that since Sombath Somphone’s shocking abduction in 2012, there have been at least 10 murders or attempted murders of Lao activists. Any celebration of the country’s graduation must be accompanied by this story.
Another accompaniment to the graduation toasts is a recognition that young Laotians are no longer willing to remain silent about the lack of freedom and opportunity in their country. Each dissident killed or disappeared only deepens convictions that activism is necessary. The party may continue to silence individual critics, but others will continue to speak out – and those who do not confront the government directly are protesting with their feet. Freedom House notes that Laos’ economic crisis has prompted growing youth emigration, with Lao nationals now the largest group using Thailand’s formal labor migration channel; they now total 267,871, or 40 percent of the total, a figure that continues to rise. In one Xayaburi district, 1,039 of 5,632 high school students dropped out in a single year to find work, and the true number of young Lao leaving is considerably higher once irregular migrants are counted. Their departure is a protest against a government that is failing to offer them a future.
The final lesson of Khieo’s disappearance is one for Lao activists themselves: they must build stronger solidarity. In May, a prominent U.S.-based Lao activist posted a video stating that Khieo was alive and working at a restaurant in Thailand, and shortly before he vanished, it was circulating online once more. This is not the first time an activist has been exposed in this way. When Anousa “Jack” Luangsuphom was shot in Vientiane in 2023, his family initially reported him dead, fearing that the gunman would return if he learned Jack had survived. Within days, news that he was alive in hospital became public and was shared online by a fellow activist. Rivalries and egos among Lao activists only undermine their shared cause and leave everyone less safe. To succeed, they will need to work together.

Why the EU must stand firm on its Common Fisheries Policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

The health of the ocean is fundamental to life on Earth. It sustains food security, livelihoods, biodiversity and climate stability for billions of people. As we approach the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and pass the midpoint of the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science, global ocean governance must be strengthened, not weakened.
For the European Union, that choice is particularly significant. Through its Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), the EU has established one of the world’s most ambitious frameworks for fisheries management. At a time when the future direction of the policy is under discussion, preserving its core principles is essential, not only for Europe’s seas and fishing communities, but also for the EU’s standing as a global leader in sustainable ocean governance.
A policy that delivers results
The CFP is widely recognized as one of the world’s most ambitious and comprehensive fisheries management frameworks. Following years of overfishing and declining profitability, its reform in 2013 placed sustainability at the heart of fisheries decision-making. Progress has been neither uniform nor easy, but the overall direction has been clear: healthier fish stocks, improved management and a stronger foundation for the long-term viability of the sector.
According to the European Joint Research Centre, in 2003 only 27 percent of fish stocks in the North Atlantic were fished at levels below the maximum sustainable yield. By 2021 that figure stood at 74 percent, demonstrating the positive result of the CFP.
Progress has been neither uniform nor easy, but the overall direction has been clear: healthier fish stocks, improved management and a stronger foundation for the long-term viability of the sector.
The policy has not just contributed to positive outcomes in European waters. Its legally binding commitments to end overfishing, restore fish stocks to sustainable levels, tackle overcapacity and destructive fishing practices, and promote access for small-scale fishers to marine resources also apply to EU fleets operating outside EU waters. Moreover, the policy is fully aligned with SDG14, which is dedicated to the conservation and sustainable use of the ocean’s resources. This is no coincidence, for it reflects a deliberate effort to ensure fisheries management serves both people and nature around the globe over the long term.
Influence far beyond EU waters
The CFP’s significance extends well beyond the EU’s maritime borders. As one of the world’s largest seafood markets and fishing powers, the EU exerts considerable influence over global fisheries governance. Through its Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements with non-EU countries, participation in regional fisheries management organizations and market requirements for imported seafood, the EU has helped promote higher standards on sustainability, transparency and labor rights.
Oceana / Ángeles Sáez
At a time of geopolitical uncertainty, biodiversity loss and mounting pressure on marine resources, the EU’s leadership in ocean governance is more important than ever. International partners look to the EU as a credible advocate for science-based management that can deliver environmental, social and economic benefits simultaneously. Thus any move to weaken the EU’s own commitments would send a troubling signal globally.
A critical moment for the CFP
Today, it is widely perceived that the CFP is facing growing political pressure. It is observed that calls for reform seek greater flexibility on core sustainability provisions such as exploitation rates, fleet capacity and the discard ban. While policy frameworks should evolve in response to new evidence and changing circumstances, there is a clear difference between making constructive adjustments and undermining core principles and objectives.
International partners look to the EU as a credible advocate for science-based management that can deliver environmental, social and economic benefits simultaneously.
The central challenge facing EU fisheries is ensuring that those hard-won objectives are fully implemented, consistently applied and effectively enforced. Indeed, the European Commission’s evaluation of the CFP concluded that the policy remains broadly fit for purpose and emphasized the need for stronger implementation as the most effective way to address the challenges facing EU fisheries.
Credibility cannot be taken for granted
The EU has played an important role in shaping fisheries management and international discussions on ocean governance. Importantly, the recent release of the Food and Agriculture Organization’s State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture report shows that global fish stocks are being over-fished by 37 percent. Thus, greater effort is required, and by continuing to build on the strength of its existing framework, the EU can support global progress toward sustainable fisheries and provide a useful reference point for other countries pursuing similar objectives.
Oceana / Juan Cuetos
Weakening the CFP’s core provisions would risk undermining the long-term resilience of the fisheries sector itself. Sustainability is not a constraint on economic performance; it is its foundation. Food security, competitiveness and stable livelihoods all depend on abundant fish populations and healthy marine ecosystems.
The value of staying the course
Behind fisheries policy are people: small-scale fishers, coastal communities and future generations. They need predictable rules, sustainable resource management and a level playing field that rewards responsible practices. Strong fisheries governance is essential to meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It is about ensuring that coastal livelihoods can endure and prosper over the long term.
Sustainability is not a constraint on economic performance; it is its foundation. Food security, competitiveness and stable livelihoods all depend on abundant fish populations and healthy marine ecosystems.
The European Union has played a leading role in advancing global ocean stewardship. Its actions have contributed to progress toward international sustainability goals and encouraged others to raise their own ambitions.
It is self-evident that defending a strong, science-based CFP is an investment in the ocean’s well-being. At the same time, further elevate food security and the EU’s credibility on the global stage. In conclusion, I wish to affirm that true leadership is measured not by the willingness to lower standards when pressures arise, but by the determination to uphold them when they matter most.

The startup was sanctioned by the Trump administration after refusing in February to allow its tools to be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance.
Trump also badmouthed Amodei, saying he was trying to be “a perfect little angel” after the Anthropic chief called for a pause in AI development.
Amodei was absent from the state dinner held for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, attended by AI industry leaders, including Amodei’s rival Sam Altman of OpenAI.
Despite mounting calls to slow down AI development due to the risk of losing control of the technology, the US government believes that the sector’s major players – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta – cannot afford to slow down for fear that China will gain the upper hand.
Trump and Mike Johnson, the speaker of the House of Representatives, are set to meet with leading AI executives on Tuesday.

JERUSALEM – Israeli forces have killed a Palestinian militant who was filmed abducting a couple at a music festival during Hamas’s deadly attack on Oct 7, 2023, the military said on Sept 27.
Video footage widely circulated in the aftermath of the attack showed militants abducting Noa Argamani and her boyfriend Avinatan Or at the Nova music festival.
Argamani was rescued in June 2024 during an Israeli operation in the central Gaza Strip, while Or was released by Hamas in October 2025 as part of a ceasefire deal.
Israeli forces “struck in the Nuseirat area and eliminated the terrorist Saher Nidal Latfi Sakr, a terrorist operative affiliated with global jihadist organisations operating in the Gaza Strip”, the Israeli military said in a statement on Sept 27.
Sakr drove the motorcycle used to abduct Argamani and Or, according to the statement.
Hamas and allied factions killed at least 370 people and took 44 hostages at the Nova festival on Oct 7, 2023, according to Israeli figures. AFP

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China, home to the world's largest high-speed rail network, opened four major high-speed railway sections to traffic on Monday, improving transport links across several regions.
The new sections connect Xiong'an in Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province, Yichang with Xingshan in Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province.
Spanning northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, the new lines will facilitate travel for residents, improve regional connectivity and support economic development. ■

5 elderly residents die amid flu outbreak at southern Portugal care home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:49:45 CST
11:49:45 KST

LISBON, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Five elderly residents have died at a care home in southern Portugal following an outbreak of influenza A, local health authorities said Sunday.
The Local Health Unit of Central Alentejo (ULSAC) said that its Multipurpose Emergency Service had received nine patients from the care home since Wednesday. Among these patients, three died, with laboratory tests confirming the virus in two of the deceased. Three others had been discharged from hospital, while three remain hospitalized, it added.
The three hospital deaths brought the total number of fatalities linked to the outbreak to five, following two earlier deaths at the care home.
The ULSAC public health department visited the care home in Estremoz, in the Evora district, on Thursday and has been conducting epidemiological surveillance, including monitoring compliance with infection control measures, hygiene protocols, isolation procedures and the use of personal protective equipment.
A follow-up visit on Sunday afternoon found no new cases or clinical deterioration among the remaining residents.
Portugal's Attorney General's Office confirmed that an inquiry had been opened into the deaths, with no suspects formally identified so far. ■

Sarah Brightman mourns Liu Huan, her Beijing Olympics duet partner, as "true gentleman"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:49:36 CST
11:49:36 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Soprano Sarah Brightman has paid tribute to late Chinese singer Liu Huan, her duet partner at the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games, describing him as a "true gentleman."
Brightman said on her social media account, "I have been saddened to hear of the passing of the great Liu Huan, who I had the pleasure of singing with at the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games, performing the opening theme song, 'You and Me.'"
"He was an amazing talent and a true gentleman. He will be greatly missed."
Liu, one of China's most celebrated musicians, died of illness in Shanghai on Friday morning at the age of 63.
His most internationally recognized performance came at the opening ceremony of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, where he performed the theme song "You and Me" alongside Brightman before an audience of billions around the world.
A few years ago, Brightman told the Foreign Correspondents' Club of Japan (FCCJ) in Tokyo that it was an honor to be invited to sing with Liu before 91,000 spectators at Beijing's Bird's Nest stadium, describing the performance as "the highlight" of her career.
"It was such an honor," she said. "I think I was the only western artist to have performed on the opening show."
"In many ways, it was the highlight of my life. It was wonderful," she said.
Brightman has returned to China many times since the 2008 Olympics to hold concerts across the country. She and Liu also performed "You and Me" together again during her 2014 concert in Beijing. ■

Chinese yuan strengthens to 6.7399 against USD Monday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:49:25 CST
11:49:25 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The central parity rate of the Chinese currency renminbi, or the yuan, strengthened 90 pips to 6.7399 against the U.S. dollar Monday, according to the China Foreign Exchange Trade System.
In China's spot foreign exchange market, the yuan is allowed to rise or fall by 2 percent from the central parity rate each trading day.
The central parity rate of the yuan against the U.S. dollar is based on a weighted average of prices offered by market makers before the opening of the interbank market each business day. ■

Faulty road design can turn an everyday drive into a deadly crash.
NEW DELHI: Even seven years after a penal provision was introduced to hold road contractors, designers and road-owning agencies accountable for crashes caused by faulty road design, construction or maintenance resulting in death or disability of victims, not a single agency has been penalised so far under this provision of Motor Vehicles Act.Last week experts flagged this issue at a conference on the impact of amendments that govt made to the Motor Vehicles Act in 2019 while pointing out the need to carry out detailed and proper investigation into all serious crashes across all types of roads. However, there have been few instances where agencies and courts have pulled up road owning entities for failure on their part for serious crashes.
Only this year, govt increased the penalty for agencies found responsible in such cases by 50 times -- from earlier provision of up to Rs 1 lakh “fine” to up to Rs 50 lakh “penalty” through an amendment to Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act.While fines can be imposed by courts after trial, which is a lengthy process, penalties can be levied directly by administrative, regulatory, or governing authorities for non-compliance without a court trial. Sources said this change is likely to have its impact on govt authorities taking action against agencies responsible for poor design, construction and maintenance where these factors resulted in a serious crash.
Some officials of the state road owning agencies admitted that one of the biggest hurdles is establishing a direct causal link between a road engineering defect and a crash as in almost all cases multiple reasons contribute to accidents. This has resulted in accountability remaining confined largely to drivers, with agencies responsible for planning, constructing and maintaining roads escaping scrutiny.The MV Act amendments in 2019 specified that while imposing the fine, courts must consider the road’s design, expected traffic, applicable maintenance standards, the condition in which users could reasonably expect to find the road, whether the designated authority knew or should have known about the hazardous condition, and whether adequate warning signs had been displayed.

Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:39:28 UTC
11:39:28 KST

Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
A surprising immune pathway outside the brain may help drive Alzheimer’s-related damage, and blocking it dramatically protected mice from neurodegeneration.
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- WashU Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists found that immune cells contributing to Alzheimer’s-related brain damage may be activated in lymph nodes outside the brain before traveling into the nervous system. Blocking this pathway in mice dramatically reduced neurodegeneration and preserved cognitive abilities, pointing to a potentially more accessible treatment target.
- Share:
Immune cells that usually defend the body by attacking infected or foreign cells appear in unusually high numbers in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease and related conditions. Evidence suggests these cells contribute to neurodegeneration, but researchers have not known where they originate or what prompts them to gather in the brain.
A new study from Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis points to an unexpected source outside the brain. In experiments with mice, researchers found that T cells receive signals from lymph nodes that appear to prepare them to enter the brain and contribute to damage. When the scientists disrupted those signals, neurodegeneration was dramatically reduced.
The findings reveal a previously unrecognized immune pathway that may offer a way to slow or potentially halt damage associated with Alzheimer's disease and primary tauopathies. These disorders are marked by twisted accumulations of tau protein in the brain.
The study was published Sept. 3 in Nature Neuroscience.
An Alzheimer's Pathway Outside the Brain
David M. Holtzman, MD, the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in WashU Medicine's Department of Neurology and senior author of the study, said the discovery is especially intriguing because it identifies a disease related process that begins outside the brain. That could make it possible to target mechanisms that are easier to reach and better understood.
"One of the issues in developing treatments for neurological diseases is that you need to engineer your treatment so that it gets into the brain and past the blood-brain barrier, but we might not actually need to get the drugs into the central nervous system to mitigate neurodegeneration," Holtzman said. "There are lots of ways to manipulate T cells that have been studied extensively and that are approved treatments for other diseases, but many haven't yet been explored for neurodegenerative diseases."
Tracing T Cells Back to the Lymph Nodes
Holtzman's laboratory has played a leading role in investigating how the immune system contributes to neurodegenerative disease. In a previous study, the team showed that removing T cells from the brain prevented much of the neurodegeneration that normally develops in mice modeling the tau related damage seen in Alzheimer's disease and primary tauopathies.
The next question was where those immune cells came from and what caused them to move into the brain.
In the new study, Holtzman's team included Hao Hu, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow and the study's first author; co-senior author Jason Ulrich, PhD, a professor of neurology; and their collaborators.
Certain T cells rely on other immune cells, known as dendritic cells, to identify the molecular targets they should attack. Very few of the relevant dendritic cells, known as classical dendritic cells type 1 (cDC1), are found in the brain. Those that are present also do not appear to interact with the T cells that emerge after tau tangles develop.
That evidence suggested that both the dendritic cells and the T cell activation process were originating somewhere outside the brain.
Blocking Immune Signals Reduced Brain Damage
To test that possibility, the researchers eliminated dendritic cells from the lymph nodes and other locations in mice that would normally develop tau tangles and neurodegeneration.
The result was striking. Elevated numbers of T cells in the brain, particularly CD8 T cells, largely disappeared, along with the associated brain damage. Yet the amount of tau tangles in the brain did not change.
The mice also preserved their cognitive abilities. That finding suggests that suppressing T cell activity could potentially slow or reduce the cognitive decline associated with Alzheimer's disease, even when tau tangles remain present.
How Brain Damage May Trigger an Immune Attack
Researchers still do not know the exact signal that causes dendritic cells to activate the T cells.
Holtzman said one possibility is that damage caused by tau releases material from brain cells. That material may then travel to lymph nodes in the neck, where dendritic cells identify it and present it as a target for T cells.
The T cells could then be directed toward the brain, where their activity contributes to neurodegeneration.
A Potential New Route for Alzheimer's Treatment
Because this immune pathway operates outside the brain, it may provide several new therapeutic targets.
Holtzman's team is now testing whether interfering with dendritic cell activity in midlife, around the time tau tangles begin to emerge, can produce the same protection seen when the cells were blocked from birth in this study.
The researchers are also working to identify the specific signal that guides T cells toward the brain. If that signal can be determined, it could offer another way to prevent the immune cells from reaching brain tissue and contributing to damage.
"Until not that long ago, most people, including myself, did not think that the immune response was even involved in neurodegenerative diseases that are due to protein accumulation in the brain," Holtzman said. "That these dendritic cells are involved in neurodegenerative disease is exciting; we've shown they're important, and that they are a potential target for future therapy."
Story Source:
Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hao Hu, Peter Bor-Chian Lin, Carisa Zeng, Yongyi Li, Megan E. Bosch, Joshua T. Emmerson, Prabal Sharma, Ray A. Ohara, Wendy Dong, Tong Wu, Siling Du, Wenqing Gao, Hong Jiang, Liya Yuan, Xin Bao, Shasha Li, Anthony N. Vomund, Petra Erdmann-Gilmore, Yichen Gu, Miwei Hu, Jonathan Nulman, Timothy M. Miller, Wayne M. Yokoyama, Cheryl F. Lichti, Jeffrey Milbrandt, Richard J. Perrin, Jonathan Kipnis, Maxim N. Artyomov, Kenneth M. Murphy, Jason D. Ulrich, David M. Holtzman. Priming of CD8 T cells by peripheral dendritic cells exacerbates tau-mediated neurodegeneration. Nature Neuroscience, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02427-5

Ukraine, South Korea relations sour over North Korean POWs
September 28, 2026
South Korea has demanded an official apology from Ukraine after accusing Kyiv of breaching — and then reportedly denying the existence of — a confidentiality agreement regarding the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul.
Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer in an address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, adding that the soldiers were "not easy to capture alive."
Hours later, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung wrote on social media: "I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing."
On Sunday, the South Korean consternation was made official when Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, demanded "an official explanation and apology."
"The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine's unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement," Seong said in a statement.
"It is in itself a very serious matter that … seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries."
Seong said Seoul was "considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter," but did not specify what they might be.
Ukraine: When were the North Korean soldiers captured?
The North Korean soldiers were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025 — two of around 14,000 North Korean troops deployed to the area to help halt and push back a surprise Ukrainian incursion.
Ukrainian intelligence estimates that around 3,000 North Korean troops were killed and another 1,500 injured, with the rest still stationed on Russian territory. To date, no North Korean troops are believed to have operated on Ukrainian territory itself.
Ukrainian troops reported that North Korean soldiers who were surrounded or injured on the battlefield preferred to die by suicide than surrender — and only two were captured.
Under President Lee, who has attempted to improve relations with the North, South Korea has appeared hesitant to take custody of the pair. But, under Article 3 of the South Korean constitution, North Koreans are still considered citizens of the South and are permitted to live in the South.
South Korea is an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which has so far only provided non-lethal aid. But Kyiv has been pressing Seoul to provide advanced air defense systems.
Last month, President Zelenskyy claimed that up to 50,000 more North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia.

Does daylight saving mess with mental health? What to know before the clocks change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:31:49 UTC
11:31:49 KST

In brief
- Daylight saving time starts on Sunday.
- A new study examined how it affects mental health, amid overseas calls to end seasonal clock changes.
It's that time of year again. This weekend, millions of Australians trade an hour of sleep for more sunshine at the end of the day as daylight saving time (DST) begins.
For some, it signals the start of summery evenings in Australia and more light for after-work activities. For early risers, it could mean tougher wake-ups, with the sun rising later in the morning.
And then there's the disruption to sleep as the clocks move forward by an hour on Sunday — an adjustment often blamed for leaving people tired, irritable and out of sorts.
But new research suggests these disruptions don't necessarily translate into more serious mental health outcomes.
In an international review of existing research into a range of health and wellbeing effects associated with DST transitions, Swinburne University researchers focused specifically on outcomes including depression, bipolar disorder, dementia and seasonal affective disorder.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We found that there were no consistent or large effects on the transition to daylight saving time on these serious mental health outcomes," Ben Bullock, a senior lecturer and researcher at Swinburne University who specialises in psychology, sleep, mental health and circadian rhythms, told SBS News.
So what does that mean as the spring clock change approaches?
When does daylight saving time start, and where?
On Sunday 4 October, clocks in NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia, ACT and Norfolk Island will jump forward to 3am, costing people an hour of sleep in the process.
Queensland, Western Australia, Northern Territory, Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands do not observe daylight saving.
Daylight saving ends on Sunday 4 April at 3am, when clocks go back an hour.
Does daylight saving negatively affect your body?
Some sleep experts believe DST can negatively impact sleep, leading to other health risks.
Research suggests that sleep is crucial for mental and physical health, with chronic deprivation and disruption linked to mood changes, cardiovascular disease and impaired cognitive function.
The Sleep Health Foundation, for example, says DST can affect sleep patterns and overall wellbeing by disrupting the body's internal circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycle.
According to the organisation, the springtime change of clocks is generally harder to adjust to than the one in autumn, when you gain an hour of sleep.
Sleep science organisations in the US, UK and Europe have previously called for seasonal clock changes to be abolished. In the US, President Donald Trump is pushing legislation to make DST permanent year-round across the country.
So, does daylight saving affect our mental health or not?
Bullock stressed the findings don't mean people can't feel the effects of the clock change.
Changes to the timing and availability of light can affect circadian rhythms and sleep, which can in turn influence mood and cognitive function.
But his research found little evidence that these effects translated into more serious mental health outcomes.
The review examined studies using hospital and other official records to measure serious mental health outcomes, including presentations involving depression, substance abuse and psychosis.
Bullock said the researchers wanted to examine whether the evidence supported significant policy changes such as the one proposed by several international sleep science groups.
"There are effects on sleep and circadian rhythms from changes in the available light and the timing of that light," he said.
"If we're going to get rid of something like daylight saving ... we need a stronger evidence base, and we just didn't find that it had that effect."
He said the broader review did, however, find small effects on some other health and wellbeing outcomes, including heart attacks and road accidents.
What can you do to get through the transition?
For those who struggle with the switch to daylight saving, Bullock said there are ways to make the adjustment easier.
In the days leading up to the change, he recommends gradually bringing your bedtime forward, rather than suddenly losing an hour on Sunday.
Getting outside into natural light early on Sunday morning can also help reset the body's internal clock.
"The third thing is to plan for the change and sort of be a bit gentle on yourself," he said.
"So don't plan any big things or big events, or expect to do lots of things on the Sunday after the transition."
"If you just look after yourself on that day, you will adjust slowly over the following few days. The body's pretty good at adjusting reasonably quickly, and it's quite resilient."

A civil disobedience campaign has emerged since Palestine Action was outlawed in July 2025, with more than 3,600 people arrested for showing their support for the group, often while holding signs reading, “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”
The UK Supreme Court is now set to hear the case after London’s Court of Appeal upheld the government ban in June.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:13:00 EEST

Ukraine's PM on threat of losing internet access in Ukraine: "We must prepare for the worst-case scenario"
Ukraine's Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi has stated that due to targeted Russian strikes on data centres, there is a constant threat of losing internet access, which is why Ukraine is preparing for the worst-case scenario.
Source: Koretskyi in an interview for Ukrainian media outlet TSN.Tyzhden
Details: Commenting on recent discussions among the Staff of the Supreme Commander-In-Chief regarding Russian attacks on telecommunications facilities, the head of government emphasised that the danger to all critical infrastructure will persist until the end of the full-scale war.
According to Koretskyi, the Cabinet of Ministers is applying non-standard solutions to safeguard digital data and equipment. Part of the infrastructure is being moved underground, another part is being placed in cloud storage or physically relocated abroad. Depending on the need, these three methods can be applied simultaneously.
The prime minister stressed that there is no single universal rule for protecting such facilities, but the government is constantly building up protection based on the worst-case scenario.
Quote: "Firstly, we are protecting it. Secondly, there are non-standard solutions. Some things have to be kept underground, some things need to be in the cloud, some must be abroad, some should be a mix and some must involve all three simultaneously. Therefore, there is no single... rule, but the fact is that we must plan for the worst-case scenario, think in those terms and prepare ourselves accordingly."
Background:
- Between 23 and 25 September 2026, Russian forces launched a series of targeted attacks on Ukrainian data centres belonging to Utels, MiroHost and Datagroup, as well as communication hubs.
- As a result of the strikes, equipment belonging to a number of Kyiv internet service providers and major telecommunications companies was destroyed or damaged. Due to this, hundreds of thousands of customers in the capital, Kyiv Oblast and other regions of the country experienced temporary internet outages.
- Following these events, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, after which officials and heads of special services were instructed to implement additional solutions to protect the country's telecommunications infrastructure.

Pakistan to host SCO coordinators’ meet from Sept 28-30
India will participate in a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) national coordinators that Pakistan will host on September 28-30, official sources said. The meeting is expected to approve the calendar of events under Pakistan’s presidency, leading up to the Council of Heads of State (CHS) summit for which Islamabad will soon send out invitations to the leaders of all member-states of the Eurasian bloc, including PM Narendra Modi.After joining the China-dominated grouping in 2017 as a full member, India has participated actively in various SCO mechanisms, with Modi representing India at the heads of state summits and external affairs minister S Jaishankar joining the heads of government meetings.Unlike with SAARC, India has ringfenced its involvement in SCO from outstanding bilateral differences with Pakistan, mainly the core issue of cross-border terrorism, while consistently reminding the Organisation that one of its original mandates was to fight terrorism, extremism and separatism. Government has backed SCO connectivity initiatives too but with the rider that these must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of all States.India’s national coordinator Alok Dimri is expected to participate in the national coordinators’ meeting that will begin on Monday. Even without any substantive bilateral engagement for a decade, India and Pakistan have regularly seen their officials visiting each other’s country for SCO-related exercises and Jaishankar himself travelled to Pakistan in 2024 for the SCO heads of government meeting.
However, the key question remains – even if it’s too early to ask – whether Modi will attend the summit in Islamabad next year. The SAARC summit process remains blocked because of the PM’s reluctance to travel to Pakistan and, barring a dramatic change in the situation, the PM is unlikely to visit Islamabad.
According to Indian officials, any such change can only be effected by Islamabad through tangible and irreversible action against cross-border terrorism and UN-proscribed terror entities operating out of Pakistan. Government recently denied strongly that it is involved even in any track 2 dialogue with Islamabad.Pakistan had assumed presidency of the SCO at the Bishkek summit earlier this month. Modi said the same day in his address that countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy, providing shelter to terrorists, must be categorically told terrorism can never be a strategic asset for anyone.

Netanyahu wants to bring Erdogan to The Hague – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:06:19 UTC
11:06:19 KST

Netanyahu could target Erdogan with ICC case – media
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is preparing a potential International Criminal Court (ICC) case against Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, seeking to use it as leverage in their escalating dispute, i24NEWS has reported, citing sources.
The move follows Türkiye’s announcement last month that it had asked Interpol to issue a Red Notice for Netanyahu after a Turkish court issued a warrant for his arrest on charges including genocide over Israel’s interception of the Gaza-bound Global Sumud Flotilla earlier this year.
Netanyahu responded by lashing out at the Turkish leader, calling him “an anti-Semitic dictator” and accusing him of massacring Kurds and harboring Hamas members. He repeated his allegations in his UN General Assembly speech last week, describing Türkiye as “the latest country to become a super spreader of antisemitic lies.” Türkiye’s communications director, Burhanettin Duran, dismissed the remarks as “baseless accusations.”
Netanyahu has now reportedly instructed an Israeli interministerial team and the head of Israel’s International Law Department to prepare a dossier focused primarily on alleged attacks against Kurdish minorities. It would also address claims that Erdogan’s government funds Hamas.
The Hague-based ICC was established under the Rome Statute, which entered into force in 2002, to prosecute genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. According to i24NEWS, Israel is more likely to pursue the case through a third party, although there is also a possibility that it could file the case directly.
Israel, however, hopes to avoid taking either step and “aims to use the existence of the case as leverage against Erdogan, effectively using it as a deterrent,” according to sources cited by the outlet.
In November 2024, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu, accusing him of using “starvation as a method of warfare,” intentionally directing attacks against civilians in Gaza, and committing crimes against humanity.
Neither Israel nor Türkiye is a party to the Rome Statute, while the United States – Israel’s closest ally and a vocal opponent of the Netanyahu warrant – is likewise not a party. Washington sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye, accusing the court of exceeding its mandate. The ICC said it “strongly rejects” the designations, calling them “a flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution.”
The ICC has no means of enforcing the warrant on its own and relies on countries to carry out arrests. A July Economist/YouGov poll found that 49% of Americans thought the US should arrest Netanyahu if he entered the country.

MELBOURNE, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Three people have died and one other has been hospitalized with critical injuries following a collision between multiple vehicles northwest of Melbourne on Sunday night.
Police said that two vehicles were traveling on a highway near the small town of Ledcourt, 230 km northwest of Melbourne, when they collided around 6:45 p.m. on Sunday.
Detective Acting Sergeant Leigh Miller from the Major Collision Investigation Unit told reporters at the scene that a car had collided with a truck before crossing onto the wrong side of the road and colliding with an oncoming car.
Two people in the second car, who have not been formally identified, died at the scene.
Police said that there were four occupants in the car that crossed onto the wrong side of the road, including a 14-year-old girl who was taken to hospital in a critical condition and later died.
An 11-year-old girl was also taken to hospital in a critical condition, while the 17-year-old learner driver sustained minor injuries. A 43-year-old woman was not injured.
The truck driver was not injured and stopped at the scene.
"At this stage we don't know why the collision has occurred, but what we will be investigating is whether fatigue or distraction, whether speed is involved," Miller said.
Police asked anyone who witnessed the collision to contact investigators. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Over 1,500 people are still staying in evacuation centers two months after a powerful earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture in southwestern Japan on July 28, local media reported Monday.
The 7.1-magnitude quake registered a maximum of 7 on Japan's 0-to-7 seismic intensity scale in the hardest-hit areas, leaving 38 people dead.
As of Friday, 1,514 people remained in shelters at 32 locations across the prefecture, while many others continue to live in hotels or in their damaged homes, Jiji Press reported, citing the prefectural government.
The quake damaged 71,518 residential buildings, including 9,540 that were completely or partially destroyed.
The Kumamoto prefectural government faces the key challenge of securing safe and stable accommodation for affected residents as soon as possible and helping them rebuild their lives. ■

BERLIN, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Germany suffered its first defeat under Jurgen Klopp as Dimitrios Kourbelis's second-half strike gave Greece its first-ever victory over the four-time world champion with a 1-0 UEFA Nations League win in Augsburg on Sunday.
Four days after a 1-1 draw in the Netherlands that opened its League A Group 2 campaign, Germany dominated possession but struggled to turn that control into clear chances against a compact Greek side.
Greece, fresh from a 2-1 win over Serbia in its opener, defended deep and looked to exploit the pace of Christos Tzolis and Konstantinos Karetsas on the counterattack.
Germany began creating openings midway through the first half. Karim Adeyemi fired over from a promising position and later forced goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis into a fine save, while Younes Ebnoutalib sent a volley wide.
The host remained largely untroubled at the other end before the break, with Jan-Aurel Bisseck settling well into the back four alongside Josha Vagnoman and Nathaniel Brown.
Debutant Bambase Conte threatened again shortly after the restart, forcing Tzolakis into action, before the Greek goalkeeper tipped away a curling Joshua Kimmich free kick.
Germany was warned in the 67th minute when Kimmich lost possession to Vangelis Pavlidis, who released Fotis Ioannidis, but the forward dragged his effort narrowly wide.
Greece made the host pay seven minutes later. Tzolis switched play across the German defense and Kourbelis found space on the edge of the area. His shot took a deflection off Kimmich and beat Alexander Nubel.
Klopp introduced Florian Wirtz and Jonathan Burkardt in search of an equalizer, but Germany struggled to break down the visitor in the closing stages.
"It wasn't an easy game. To be honest, we didn't do well enough," Germany defender Jonathan Tah said. "We had our chances but didn't take them. In the end, they made the most of their moments and scored the one they needed."
The result leaves Germany on one point from its opening two Group 2 matches, while Greece tops the group with six points.
Germany will host Serbia in Munich on October 1 before traveling to face Greece in Thessaloniki on October 4. ■
