Filipina Drug Trafficker Walks Free After Receiving Presidential Pardon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:03:00 UTC
11:03:00 KST

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Friday granted a pardon to Mary Jane Veloso, who was serving a prison sentence for drug trafficking in the Philippines after her arrest in Indonesia in 2010.
According to PhilStar Global, Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr., the director general of the Bureau of Corrections, “personally handed” Veloso a copy of the pardon and her official release, completing the procedures for her discharge. Earlier on Friday, Marcos confirmed to reporters that he had signed a pardon the day before, without elaborating.
Veloso, a 41-year-old domestic worker and mother of two, was arrested in Yogyakarta in 2010 for trying to bring 2.6 kilograms of heroin into Indonesia. She was subsequently sentenced to death under Indonesia’s severe drug laws, but received a last-minute reprieve from execution in 2015 after Philippine officials asked then Indonesian President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo to let her testify against members of a prominent drug trafficking organization.
In December 2024, Indonesia agreed to repatriate Veloso after years of requests from the Philippines, where Veloso’s relatives and supporters had waged a persistent campaign for her release.
Veloso has always maintained her innocence, claiming that she was tricked into carrying the drugs by her godsister. She smiled as she left her prison cell in the Philippines on Friday, after more than 15 years behind bars. In a press conference with Catapang at the Bureau of Corrections, she held up the “absolute pardon” signed by Marcos, which removes the remaining legal consequences of her conviction, allowing her a fresh start, and offered a tearful thanks to the Philippine leader.
“I just want to tell our beloved President: Thank you so much for clearing my name and allowing me to return to my family,” she said, as per Inquirer.net. She added that she was looking forward to reuniting with her two sons, who have grown nearly to adulthood since her arrest.
“It was really hard being separated from them … I didn’t see my children grow, but I believe it’s not yet too late for me to be their guide,” Veloso said.
Veloso’s release was greeted with joy by family members and advocacy groups that have spent years campaigning for her release.
Veloso’s pardon marks a rare positive development in a story connected to Southeast Asia’s tough anti-drug regime. Indonesia is known particularly for its unforgiving approach to drug crimes, especially large-scale trafficking offenses.
Under the agreement Yusril Ihza Mahendra, then Indonesia’s senior minister for law and human rights affairs, said that the Philippines had agreed to respect the Indonesian court’s sentencing of Veloso and her status as prisoner in Indonesia.
However, Yusril also said that the Indonesian government would also respect any decision made by the Philippines once Veloso is back on Philippine soil, including the possible granting of clemency.
“This only proves that there are really second chances, and we are happy that Veloso can now enjoy her newfound freedom with her family,” Catapang said.

Europe’s divided conservatives launch 2029 plan to beat far right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Europe’s divided conservatives launch 2029 plan to beat far right
As Manfred Weber launches a task force to shape the EPP’s 2029 platform, internal records and interviews reveal the party’s defining choice: hold the center or move further right.
Europe’s biggest political family is already preparing its 2029 election strategy to win back voters from the far right — even as its own members split over whether to work with those parties and how far to follow them on policy.
The center-right European People’s Party chair, Manfred Weber, internally launched a “Win2029” task force two weeks ago. The main goal of the group will be to develop an attractive enough policy platform to take on the far right at the polls in three years’ time.
But interviews and internal meeting records reveal deepening disagreements over cooperation with far-right groups and how closely to align with them on migration, climate and social issues.
Advertisement
“The main polarization across the continent in many national elections, and certainly in the European election 2029 … will be the anti-European populists against the EPP parties,” said EPP vice-chair and Romanian prime minister nominee Siegfried Mureșan.
Anything beyond the “battle” between EPP and the far right “will be of secondary importance,” echoed the conservative group’s spokesperson Pedro López de Pablo. “Because they are not in government, they can promise the earth. Faced with that kind of rhetoric, we need to think of which alternatives we can offer to the people.”
Siegfried Mureșan participates in a meeting in Brussels on June 26, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
With the European Parliament not yet halfway through its current term, the task force marks an unusually early start to the EPP’s 2029 election preparations — and underscores the urgency party leaders feel as far-right parties gain ground across the bloc.
Led by Spanish MEP Esteban González Pons, the task force will help draft the party’s final electoral program. Talks are due to start at an October retreat in Sicily and continue through next spring’s EPP congress in Rome.
EPP lawmakers are already wrestling with the choice ahead.
“This is the political history, the historical dilemma EPP needs to decide — it needs to be clear and it needs be truthful for the voters, are we center right or are we another right-wing party?” said Finnish EPP lawmaker Sirpa Pietikäinen.
Advertisement
To deal or not to deal
The divisions reflect different political realities across the party. In some countries, governing with the far right has become a political reality; in others, those parties remain the EPP’s main rivals and cooperation is a red line.
Poles and Romanians oppose any alignment with the far right, while conservatives in Spain, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands have governed with them. German lawmakers are divided, as some in Berlin start questioning the firewall against Alternative for Germany (AfD) given its recent electoral successes. Yet most German EPP members in Brussels remain opposed.
“There has always been that discussion within the party: Whether we should put content first, or the centrist platform first,” said Finnish EPP delegation chief Mika Aaltola.
Mika Aaltola sits in the European Parliament in Brussels on July 16, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Meeting notes from the past six months show the EPP attempting to maintain its firewall in the Parliament, with lawmakers repeatedly instructed to reject the far-right Patriots’ initiatives while backing similar proposals from the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists, home to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. The EPP considers ECR an acceptable partner.
To make an example of one of its lawmakers and quell criticism, the group went as far as to expel Slovenian MEP Branko Grims after he appeared at an event organized by the AfD.
Yet the EPP cannot escape the temptation to go with far-right groups on sensitive issues where agreement with the Socialists and Democrats is harder to reach.
Advertisement
That happened recently on the EU’s long-term budget file, when a right-wing majority voted to strip green and gender criteria from spending oversight. EPP leaders had vowed to stick with the center but could not keep lawmakers in line, exposing a divide now spilling into day-to-day legislative battles.
At its last plenary, the EPP group discussed how to pass a resolution on the migration crisis in Ceuta, the Spanish territory, after negotiations with the Socialists and Democrats collapsed. Two sets of internal notes seen by POLITICO show the strategy was to make the Patriots feel part of the process and get their voteby deliberately backing one of their amendments.
A temporary migrant camp is set up at El Trampolín beach in Ceuta, Spain, where more than 2,000 migrants are estimated to be living, according to the latest figures on Sept. 24, 2026. | Manu Brabo/Getty Images
The idea came from the Spanish delegation, which wanted a political win in Madrid. EPP leaders backed the plan, urging lawmakers to support the text whether or not the Patriots’ amendments passed.
Migration tensions
The EPP’s bigger challenge may be not whether to work with the far right, but whether to fight it on its issues or shift the political agenda onto its own terrain — and, in doing so, whether to move right to win back voters or stand their ground in the center.
At the congress following the 2024 EU election, Weber made clear that he wanted to reshape the party’s “narrative” to regain support from voters tempted by far-right populists. That meant tougher migration policies, more deportations and rolling back green rules — positions that have only hardened since.
Even as the EU’s Migration Pact introduced faster asylum and border procedures in June, and negotiators agreed on bloc-wide rules to speed up deportations, the EPP pushed for tougher measures.
Advertisement
At its Vienna political assembly that month, it called for more investment in Frontex, the EU’s coast guard agency, and easier returns at the bloc’s external border. Delegates also agreed to replace “irregular migration” with “illegal migration” throughout the text, adopting language more commonly associated with the far right, according to the confidential minutes.
That migration strategy is raising eyebrows within the party.
During a heated debate on political Islam in Europe in the same assembly, EPP Vice President and former Commissioner Mairead McGuinness warned colleagues “against conflating religious faith with political extremism,” calling for “a clear commitment to freedom of religion,” the minutes read.
A French member of Frontex works at the cross-Channel terminal in Calais, France on July 25, 2024. | Bernard Barron/AFP via Getty Images
German EPP lawmaker Dennis Radtke, who leads the party’s wing in charge of relations with trade unions, told POLITICO the party should avoid blaming the far right’s rise on migration alone.
“Of course we have to ensure secure borders, no doubt about that, but to link the success of the extreme right in Europe only with the question of migration … I have doubts that this is the case,” he said. “The asylum seeker numbers are going down; the extreme right is still going up because a lot of social problems are not solved or even touched.”
Culture wars
As competitiveness and deregulation dominate the EPP’s response to Europe’s economic woes, some fear social and workers’ rights are being sidelined.
Advertisement
In February, the party’s workers’, seniors’ and women’s wings pushed a resolution calling for stronger social protections, skills and youth employment support. Austrian, Finnish, German and Swedish delegates came out against it, accusing it of being “poorly framed”, as “its focus on social justice sends the wrong signal given EPP priorities on competitiveness and productivity,” according to meeting minutes.
Other lawmakers pushed back, arguing the party could not abandon the social dimension. The leadership postponed the vote, and the resolution quietly disappeared from the next meeting’s agenda.
“It has not become easier,” said Radtke of trying to strengthen the EPP’s social focus. “If we are not willing to deliver on workers’ rights, on social issues, then we cannot claim to be Europe’s last people’s party.”
Mairead McGuinness speaks during a press conference at the EU headquarters in Brussels on June 27, 2023. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images
The far right’s culture wars are also reverberating inside the EPP, where longstanding tensions over feminism, gender and reproductive rights are shifting in favor of the conservative camp.
In Parliament, the EPP has traditionally backed strong sexual and reproductive rights while allowing national delegations a free vote on abortion, said veteran gender equality MEP Pietikäinen. Now, as some delegations harden their positions, consensus is eroding and more issues — including gender budgeting, which examines how public spending affects women and men — are left to free votes. “Now it has been more difficult,” she said.
A report on gender inequalities in health descended into pandemonium at an EPP group meeting last plenary, as Irish, Polish and Luxembourgish lawmakers urged colleagues to back it, while Spaniards called it “crazy” and Croatians denounced its “gender ideology” as “radical” and “extreme.”
Advertisement
The party’s vow to simplify EU legislation has also opened rifts, as lawmakers disagree on how far to scrap green laws. Its factions are divided over how far to weaken the combustion-engine phaseout, and how much to soften industry’s carbon emission restrictions under the Emissions Trading System, which puts a price on industrial emissions.
The disputes expose the EPP’s central dilemma ahead of 2029: whether to harden its positions to win back voters from the far right or hold the center — a choice that risks deepening divisions among its national parties.

Text description provided by the architects. Az-Boroun — Persian for "from outside" — turns the edge between house and garden into a deep spatial threshold: three overlapping volumes form a deep frame, while two voids bring landscape, daylight, air, and movement into the section. Commissioned as a weekend villa with a lush garden, the project occupies two adjoining plots in Zafaranieh, on the western outskirts of Karaj, Iran. The elongated site is bounded by gardens to the north and south, making continuity with the landscape central to the brief. Rather than placing the house as an object within the garden, the design uses the depth of the site to make the landscape part of the spatial organization.

Putin is testing NATO on Norway’s remote Arctic islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BARENTSBURG, Norway — For the best part of a century, the biggest threat to the residents of Svalbard was polar bears. Increasingly, it now comes from Russia.
Fears are growing that Moscow could use the sprawling Arctic archipelago — a part of Norway with an unusual legal status — to test NATO militarily amid growing uncertainty over the U.S. commitment to European defense.
Allies suspect Russia of probing crucial undersea cables in the waters off Svalbard and staging military-style events that test the limits of the rules governing its presence there. As Russia ramps up hybrid attacks across Europe, Oslo is racing to boost its naval and surveillance capabilities to protect its northern flank, while local authorities on Svalbard are investing in critical infrastructure — and even have an evacuation plan in place.
Advertisement
“There is more tension in the Arctic and in the north, and of course also Svalbard is a part of that,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik told POLITICO. “We know that Russia ... uses a lot of ways to try to provoke or find ways to do hybrid threats.”
Despite its status as Norwegian territory, the archipelago's main island, Spitsbergen, is home to a Russian town.
“Russian leadership is highly unpredictable and more and more risk prone,” said Kari Aga Myklebost, a Russian history professor and Svalbard expert at Norway's Arctic University. “I wouldn't close out any scenario when it comes to the Kremlin's will to confront NATO.”
High North, high tension
For decades, Svalbard symbolized the Norwegian maxim “High North, low tension,” which saw efforts to build cooperation among Arctic countries, including Russia.
Beyond its remoteness — lying over 900 kilometers from mainland Norway — and its glacial temperatures, that was down to the archipelago's unique status. Under a 1920 international treaty, countries recognized Oslo’s sovereignty over the islands and in return gained resource exploitation rights — with the Soviets buying the town of Barentsburg to mine local coal deposits soon after.
Advertisement
The treaty also forbade any nation from using Svalbard for “warlike purposes” including the construction of naval bases and fortifications, but Norway does visit the archipelago with coast guard and military vessels.
At its Cold War peak, 2,400 Soviet citizens lived on Spitsbergen, the only populated island, making up around 70% of its population.
Moscow has little incentive to upend the treaty because it could rebound against its own interests. With Russia’s northwestern Kola Peninsula — home to two-thirds of its nuclear second-strike submarines — sitting around 1,000 kilometers away, “Russia has been cautious to avoid any kind of escalation,” Myklebost said.
A Soviet-era placard in Barentsburg. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
That makes it strategic for NATO, too. “In a military conflict … this is where the Russian submarines could enter the North Atlantic and hide at greater depths and pose a threat to NATO and the U.S.,” she argued.
Yet tensions have grown following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow also began direct boat trips from Russia in 2024 and last year set up a chapter of the Russian Geographical Society, which is led by former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu.
“We call them gray zone provocations,” Myklebost said. “It’s a very cost-efficient way of asserting Russian presence and … challenging Norway's jurisdiction.”
As a result, Norway’s intelligenceservices this year warned the Kremlin “aims to increase Russian scope for action in Svalbard.”
British, American and Norwegian forces this spring reportedly caught Russian vessels testing a secret subsea cable-cutting weapon off Svalbard’s coast.
Although Barentsburg’s coal reserves are dwindling, Moscow is not abandoning the town. Moscow provided state-owned Trust Arktikugol, which administers Barentsburg, with about 1.89 billion rubles (€20 million) in federal subsidies in 2025, according to its accounts.
Russia’s ambassador to Norway, Nikolay Korchunov, told POLITICO he wanted to see a “transformation of the economic activities” from coal to services in Barentsburg, and said Arktikugol was investing in maintaining the town.
Advertisement
Cranes and scaffolding adorn many of Barentsburg’s Soviet-era buildings, which lie scattered across a jagged hill facing the imposing snow-specked Vøringen glacier — a sign of Russia’s continued interest.
But “we are not questioning any sovereignty of Norway,” Korchunov insisted. “We stress the necessity and importance of fulfilling all the Svalbard Treaty,” he said, accusing Oslo of contributing to a “negative trend towards NATO militarization of entire Baltic-Arctic region.”
On thin ice
Vice Adm. Rune Andersen, the chief of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters, said his priority was “striking that balance between deterrence but maintaining stability” on Svalbard, and remaining “calm and collected” on hybrid threats.
Svalbard Deputy Governor Katharina Rise. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
But given the “risks” of escalation, the military is investing to reinforce its surveillance capabilities, he said, including launching three new maritime mapping satellites next year — alongside “a renewal of the navy and coast guard … to have a continuous presence” nearby.
NATO countries “are more often up in our waters,” said Sandvik, the minister. Defending Svalbard is also a part of NATO’s planning process, he said.
Advertisement
Locally, the strategy is to keep a lid on tensions. Svalbard’s Deputy Governor Katharina Rise said her office meets with Russia’s local consulate four times a year. “We have good and constructive dialogue,” she said. “It's our responsibility to secure the stability and … low tension here.”
Terje Aunevik, the mayor of Longyearbyen, the main Norwegian town on Spitsbergen, said authorities had plans in place to rapidly evacuate the settlement if tensions flare.
With just two subsea internet cables, one airport, one water reservoir and one diesel-run power plant in Longyearbyen that depends on imports, Aunevik said “major investments” are underway, including the construction of two new water reservoirs by around 2029. “We are quite vulnerable in that perspective,” he said.
Out in the cold
Up close, Barentsburg doesn’t look particularly threatening. Few locals venture outside the several dozen crumbling buildings. A plume of smoke escapes the aging coal plant and a lonely hammer-and-sickle Soviet flag flaps in the wind. Barentsburg feels like an abandoned relic of a bygone era.
Some of the recent hybrid activity is also down to a local push for attention from Moscow, said Arild Moe, a research professor and Russia expert at the Fridtjof Nansen Institute think tank. “They’re playing on nationalist strengths … to get priorities and to get finance.”
But Putin’s unpredictability and Trump's repeated wavering on NATO remain wild cards.
Anxiety is also palpable on Spitsbergen. In Barentsburg, “we don’t speak about [political] topics,” said a waitress from St. Petersburg who asked that her name not be used, while acknowledging locals fear a potential NATO-Russia war. “Of course this worries us,” she said.
“There is of course this constant chatter about if the Russian government wants to push a NATO member and Svalbard is the place where they would do it,” said Jonatan Svensson, an expedition guide who has lived in Longyearbyen for five years.
Jonatan Svenssson. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
To assuage those fears, NATO should consider air patrols over Svalbard, shift defensive air assets to the north of mainland Norway and hold joint exercises nearby, the two NATO diplomats said, provided Oslo agreed and the measures complied with the Svalbard Treaty.
However, so far NATO has no public plans to boost its naval or air presence around the islands. But some worry the alliance's current posture won't be enough to deter Moscow.
In theory, it would be “really easy” for Russia to occupy Svalbard, said Ståle Ulriksen, a lecturer at the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy, if it flew in special forces from northern Russia and seized the airport. However, he argued such a scenario is unlikely.
Yet Moscow wouldn’t need to launch a full occupation. According to Myklebost, the analyst, Russia could stage an emergency affecting its local citizens and send in crisis management forces, a move that may not clearly trigger NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause.
“A worst-case scenario is a situation where Moscow sees an opportunity to test NATO cohesion,” she said. “Maybe Norway's shouting for help from allies, and then you have Donald Trump saying: ‘No — we are not risking our good deals with Russia over this tiny island.’”

Despite rainfall deficit, kharif acreage above 5-year average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:57:15 UTC
10:57:15 KST

NEW DELHI: Overall acreage of kharif (summer-sown) crops in the country declined by just over 1% this year compared with last year and while the dip was expected due to deficient monsoon rainfall this year, the sowing season still ended up recording higher than 'normal' (average of last five years) acreage. Though only marginally above the 'normal', it reflects tweaks in farmers' strategy if warning comes in advance.Latest acreage data shows total sown area at 1,107 lakh hectares (ha) as of Friday was 3 lakh ha more than 'normal' acreage (1,104 lakh ha) despite a cumulative deficit of 12% (June 1-Sept 26) in monsoon rainfall. In the same period in 2025, which recorded 8% more than normal (surplus) rainfall, total acreage was 1,121 lakh ha.The most popular kharif crop and one of the most water-intensive, paddy, reported a 3.6% decline in acreage compared with last year, but this was still 4.6% higher than the 'normal' acreage. Another guzzler, sugarcane, too reported higher acreage than its normal sown area, reflecting farmers' preference for crops which assure them of better returns, even as they had to depend on excessive use of groundwater, at the risk of high input cost.
The real test of what rainfall deficit will entail, however, may be reflected in the yield of these crops, first estimates for which will soon be released by the Union agriculture ministry. The output of pulses (mainly pigeon peas), oilseeds (mainly soybean and groundnut), cotton and coarse cereals (mainly bajra and maize) may be a real concern due to deficient and skewed distribution of rainfall in the 'monsoon core zone' - the large part of central India and Bihar which depend on seasonal rains for farming in absence of adequate irrigation coverage.
Floods in certain parts of Bihar and Assam, and drought in parts of Maharashtra and Karnataka may also negatively impact the overall output.Apprehending the impact of deficient monsoon rainfall on the rabi (winter-sown) crops due to low moisture content in the soil and shortage of water for irrigation, the agriculture ministry will discuss contingency measures at a two-day meet starting Monday.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

West violates radiation safety agreements by supporting Kiev — Russian diplomat

10:45:55 KST

MOSCOW, September 28. /TASS/. By supporting Ukrainian strikes on nuclear facilities, Western countries are violating numerous international agreements that they themselves previously signed, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told TASS.
"Just try to understand what goes on inside madmen’s mind and draw conclusions at the same time about what they are thinking about when they boldly violate a wide range of international norms, particularly those regarding peaceful nuclear energy and radiation safety," he said in an interview with TASS.
"All of this was stipulated by a number of agreements that were inked by the states that have nuclear power and possess nuclear weapons. These countries are signatories to the required conventions and are the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] active participants. But here we are," he continued.
Miroshnik cited as an example the current developments regarding the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant.
"To begin with, the Ukrainian side actually denied the chief of the largest international organization, the IAEA, Rafael Grossi, the opportunity to simply pay a visit to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant, saying ‘Sorry, we cannot provide security for you’," he noted.
"At the same time, Russia provided security guarantees, but Ukraine failed to guarantee that they would not deliver strikes. As a result, this person’s visit was simply cancelled as, according to the protocol, he cannot visit the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant under such conditions," Miroshnik added.
The Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant and the city of Energodar have repeatedly come under attack by the Ukrainian army. On July 15, Ukrainian forces attacked a Zaporozhye NPP service vehicle with a drone, killing Chief Engineer Alexander Yakovlev and the driver.

The Zaporozhye NPP is located on the shores of the Kakhovka Reservoir in Energodar. It is the largest nuclear power plant in Europe, with six power units capable of producing a combined 6 GW of electricity.

‘This is my country’: Israel-born children of Filipino migrants fight for right to join IDF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:44:57 UTC
10:44:57 KST

As the IDF fights the longest war in its history and struggles with a severe manpower shortage, a group of young people born and raised in Israel has spent months fighting a very different battle: getting permission to enlist.
John Ray Delisai, Moliv Vicente and Mariel Aya, all born in Israel to parents who legally immigrated from the Philippines, are among dozens of young adults behind a petition to the High Court of Justice seeking the right to serve in the military.
Mariel, 19, was born in Be'er Sheva and raised in Tel Aviv. Since finishing high school, she has been waiting for movement in the legal battle. John Ray, 20, also from Tel Aviv, hopes to serve in a combat role in a special unit. Moliv, 20, was born in Jerusalem, lives in Tel Aviv and has already completed a year of national service.
“The sentence that best describes our situation is, ‘A person is nothing but the landscape of their homeland,’” Mariel said. “We were born here and raised here, just like any other Israeli, with Zionist values.”
“We feel we have something meaningful to give,” she added. “When we see our friends coming home from the army, it gives us a knot in the stomach. We also want to give something back to the country.”
John Ray described military service as an expectation that surrounded him throughout childhood. “I was born and raised in a society that loves the country and wants to protect it,” he said. “All my friends, everyone around me, knows that after school you give three years or more of yourself. Not because you have to, but because you want to. That’s what I was raised on, and that’s what I want too.”
Oct. 7 made the desire stronger
The Oct. 7 massacre and the war that followed only intensified their determination to enlist.
“I was educated at school and in the Scouts on Zionism,” said Moliv, who joined the Re’im service-year program after high school. “After Oct. 7, I volunteered at Kibbutz Nirim. I saw what happened there, and I also saw what was happening in Kiryat Shmona. I told myself, ‘This is my country. There’s no way I’m not going to protect it.’”
Mariel said she felt the same pull while still in 12th grade. “I think that was the effect Oct. 7 had on most young people in Israel. Everyone saw what happened and wanted to be the ones standing on the front line and protecting the country.”
Their frustration has grown as the IDF publicly warns of a shortage of personnel.
“The head of the IDF Personnel Directorate and the chief of staff say they are short of people,” Mariel said. “It’s crazy that there is a group here ready to stand on the front line, to take part, even at the risk of our lives.”
“Are we foreign workers? We physically grew up here, with the values of this country. We even speak Hebrew better than many others. It’s absurd. The country is still at war, and we are here, ready.”
John Ray said the contradiction is difficult to accept. “There are people trying every possible way to get out of serving. When do you see a group of people saying they want to enlist even though they don’t have to?”
“I know they need me, but they don’t want to accept me. I’m disappointed. It hurts. I’m only asking them to stop for a minute and look at us for who we are, not under the label ‘children of migrant parents.’”
‘A certificate that says I’m Israeli’
Their situation stems in part from temporary government decisions adopted between 2005 and 2010. Those measures allowed some children of foreign workers who grew up in Israel and attended Israeli schools to receive permanent residency, on condition that they serve in the IDF at age 18.
But the measures were temporary and were never enshrined in permanent legislation. After a limited application period, the pathway closed.
For the current group, the distinction can feel arbitrary. Moliv described a friend from the same age group whose older sister qualified under the earlier arrangement, allowing him to regularize his own status and later enlist in the Golani Brigade.
“We’re the same age, with the same circumstances, with parents from the Philippines,” he said. “What is different between us and them?”
For John Ray and Moliv, military service is also about belonging.
“The army would give me the feeling that I’m part of something,” John Ray said. “It would give me that stamp that I’m really part of society, that people see me as an equal and not as some strange outsider.”
Moliv put it more simply: “It’s like getting a certificate that defines me as Israeli.”
‘We’re being left behind’
The three are part of a group of dozens of young men and women who have petitioned the High Court seeking permission to enlist. The petition was filed in December 2025, but the state’s response has been postponed repeatedly. It is now required to respond by Oct. 4.
“This has been a fight for years,” Moliv said. “I remember being seven years old and seeing my parents meet with lawyers and go to court hearings. Now they’ve postponed us for the sixth time.”
John Ray said the delays carry a personal cost. “We’re losing momentum, and we’re being hurt by being left behind. My vision was that six months ago I would already be at the induction center, but I didn’t understand how difficult and cumbersome the legal system could be.”
Despite the delays, all three say giving up is not an option.
“We accept the postponement, but we don’t lose hope,” Mariel said. “Because if we had lost hope, we probably wouldn’t still be in this process. We hope it happens soon.”
Attorney Zari Hazan, chairman of the Israel Bar Association’s Immigration Committee and one of the lawyers representing the petitioners, said there was no dispute that the IDF needs thousands of additional soldiers.
He accused the defense establishment of failing to respond to the petition despite an earlier court order, saying the delay was prolonging harm to the petitioners and, in his view, to national security.
The IDF said: “The petition has been received. The state’s response will be submitted as part of the legal proceedings, as customary.”
Defense Minister Israel Katz’s office said the issue had not been presented to the minister. “When it is brought before him, we will respond accordingly.”

The BBC is reviewing the inclusion of 53 terrorists on a list published by BBC Arabic of “journalists” killed in Gaza during the Israel-Hamas war, according to a Saturday report from The Telegraph.
According to the Telegraph, the 53 alleged journalists have been claimed by Hamas and other Palestinian terrorist organizations as martyrs after they were killed.
When war broke out after Hamas’s October 7 massacre, BBC Arabic published and continually updated a list of alleged journalists who were killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza. The list, which was most recently updated in August 2025, consists of over 180 Palestinian journalists, including the 53 terrorists.
Ten of the terrorists were described as journalists by both BBC Arabic and English-language BBC, and the other 43 only appeared on the BBC Arabic list.
Twelve of them have been removed from the casualty list of the US-based organization the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), which defends the rights of journalists in combat zones.
CPJ removes individuals from list after finding terror group ties
A review conducted by the CPJ found that multiple individuals on the list belonged to terror groups and some had participated in the October 7 massacre.
Abdullah Darwish, described by BBC Arabic as a cameraman for Al-Aqsa TV, was removed from the CPJ list after photos emerged of Darwish in Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigade uniform and it was revealed that he had participated in the October 7 attacks, the Telegraph wrote.
Yaqoub Al-Barsh, described by BBC Arabic as executive director of Namaa radio, was removed from the CPJ list after he too was discovered to have been a member of Hamas's Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades, which lists him as a "martyr" online, according to the report.
An additional 20 out of the 53 alleged journalists were found to have obituaries published by terrorist organizations, including Mohammed Al-Zaq, whose obituary was written by the Palestinian Islamic Jihad; Mustafa Bakir, described by Hamas as a field commander; and Abdullah Iyad Baris, described by Hamas as a "knight" in its Khan Yunis Brigade, among others, the Telegram wrote.
The remaining 21 names listed as journalists appeared in pictures online carrying weapons and wearing military uniforms, including Ahmed Samir Muhammad Washah, who appeared in a post being trained to use a grenade launcher, and Amr Abu Odeh, who was hailed as a hero of the Al-Qassam Brigades, according to the Telegram.
BBC previously accused of anti-Israel bias
The BBC has come under fire before for alleged bias against Israel.
A whistleblower report from November revealed that BBC Arabic chose to “minimize Israeli suffering” in its reporting of the war against Hamas in order to present it as the aggressor.
The whistleblower claimed that BBC Arabic gave a platform to journalists who made antisemitic comments and provided multiple examples, including one man who said Jews should be burned “as Hitler did,” who appeared as a guest on BBC Arabic 244 times in a year and a half. Another, who said Jews are “devils,” appeared 522 times during the same time period.
“It is hard to conclude anything other than that BBC Arabic’s story treatment was designed to minimize Israeli suffering and paint Israel as the aggressor,” the reporter said, according to the Telegraph.

====================================================================================================

Stephen Sondheim was unmistakably Jewish, but did he live a ‘Jewish Life?'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:33:15 UTC
10:33:15 KST

When Daniel Okrent first proposed writing a biography of Stephen Sondheim for the Yale Jewish Lives series, he had a warning for his publisher.
“I would love to write about Sondheim if you’re interested, but I have to tell you that he was not in any way, in any remote way, a practicing Jew,” Okrent recalled saying.
The people at Jewish Lives were unfazed - that is, until he turned in his manuscript.
“They said, ‘Could we have a little bit more Jewish stuff in there?’”
I can sympathize. It can be tricky to write about famous, highly assimilated Jews like Sondheim, for whom Jewishness did not seem to be a significant part of their private identity or what made them famous. In writing an obituary, for example, there’s a risk of “claiming” someone as Jewish in ways they might have rejected, or of forcing their life into a Jewish narrative in a way that seems artificial or exaggerated.
Not religious, but unequivocally Jewish
And yet, Okrent argues, Sondheim was unmistakably Jewish.
“I look at it as a form of Americanized Yiddishkeit: his nature, his worldview, his sense of humor,” said Okrent in an interview last week. “To me, also having grown up as a pretty areligious Jew, that felt very Jewish.”
Okrent, a journalist and former public editor of the New York Times whose previous books include histories of prohibition and US immigration policy, wrote “Stephen Sondheim: Art Isn’t Easy” as an unabashed fan.
“I wanted to understand the life through the work and the work through the life,” he told me. The book chronicles the friendships, rivalries and personal demons that informed Sondheim’s unmatched contribution to the American musical, from the lyrics he wrote for “West Side Story” and “Gypsy” to the scores and lyrics he composed for canonical shows like “Company,” “A Little Night Music,” “Sweeney Todd” and “Sunday in the Park with George.”
And while Sondheim, who died in 2023 at age 91, spent a lifetime denying it, Okrent concluded that his life and art were “intimately intertwined,” and that his shows were often autobiographical.
With the exception of a handful of musicals, “everything else reflects his life, his feelings, his triumphs, his failures,” said Okrent.
That includes “Sweeney Todd,” the ghoulish, operatic story of a deranged barber who kills his customers and serves them up as meat pies. When Judy Prince, wife of his longtime collaborator Hal Prince, told Sondheim that “Sweeney Todd” was the story of his life, Sondheim agreed.
“What did he see in that? Revenge,” said Okrent. Sondheim understood what it was to hold a grudge - against critics, notably, and anyone else who suggested his shows were too elitist, too cool or (and this galled him to the degree that he wrote a song about it) not “hummable.”
Sondheim described his Jewish identity as 'very deep'
What almost never appears in his shows or music, however, is a Jewish theme or character, at least explicitly so. And when they do appear - notably as theatrical producers in shows like “Gypsy” and “Merrily We Roll Along” - they reflect the main way Sondheim himself claimed his Jewishness.
When asked about his Jewish identity by the journalist Abigail Pogrebin for her 2005 book “Stars of David,” Sondheim said, “It’s very deep. It’s the fact that so many of the people that I admire in the arts are Jewish. And art is as close to a religion as I have.”
The future composer grew up on New York’s Upper West Side; his parents, Herbert and Etta, known as Foxy, were prominent in the dressmaking business. They belonged to Temple Emanu-El, the socially prominent Reform synagogue on the East Side. After their divorce when Sondheim was 10, he moved with his mother to a Pennsylvania exurb not far from the lyricist Oscar Hammerstein, who became a surrogate father and musical mentor.
Hammerstein was himself only one-quarter Jewish by ancestry but is, as Okrent notes, now included in the pantheon of Jews who helped create the Broadway musical as we know it.
Sondheim sought Hammerstein’s counsel until his mentor’s death in 1960. When an up-and-coming Sondheim balked at an offer to write the lyrics for “Gypsy,” saying he wanted to compose as well as write lyrics, Hammerstein convinced him that it was an unmissable opportunity to learn how to write for a star - in this case, the Broadway legend Ethel Merman.
Before that, there was a stint in military school, which Okrent writes that he loved, and math and music studies at the WASP-y WIlliams College, where the Jewish kid was blackballed from a fraternity. Having had no religious schooling or bar mitzvah, Sondheim once asked his Jewish roommate, “Am I even Jewish?” Okrent quotes musicologist Steven Swayne: Sondheim may have been “‘a Jew to the goyim,’ but not to himself.’”
And yet, Sondheim’s professional world would become saturated with Jewishness.
Sondheim did not seek Jewishness
He teamed up with Leonard Bernstein, Arthur Laurents and Jerome Robbins, three other gay Jewish men, on “West Side Story.” In addition to Prince, he created shows with Jule Styne, John Weidman, James Lapine and Larry Gelbart.
But Sondheim did not appear to approach his work by looking for Jewish stories, even when others were mining hits from the Jewish past (“Fiddler on the Roof”), the birth of Israel (“Milk and Honey”) and even the Holocaust (“Cabaret”).
“He never would have said, ‘I want to find a show that has, you know, a Jewish theme,’ any more than he said, ‘I want to find a show that has a cowboy theme,’” Okrent said. “It’s just not the way he went about his work.”
Instead, stories usually came to him through collaborators. “Sweeney Todd” and “Passion,” one of his last shows, were among the exceptions.
Others have attempted to locate Sondheim on the spectrum of Jewishness. Okrent mentions a course given in 2022 at the 92nd Street Y, “Sondheim and the Torah.” The theater scholar Gabrielle Hoyt, in a 2022 paper, also sees Jewish themes in many of his shows: “the line between vengeance and justice” in “Sweeney Todd”; the “boundaries of community” in “Company”; the “isolation of the prophet” in the 1960s flop “Anyone Can Whistle.”
Hoyt also compares Sondheim’s eagerness to nurture young talent to that of a rabbi. Okrent writes about the young composers and lyricists Sondheim mentored, including Jonathan Larson, Adam Guettel, Lin-Manuel Miranda and “South Park” creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone, whom he encouraged during their work on “The Book of Mormon.”
“He provided really substantive criticism for those who came to him for help and with whom he built relationships,” said Okrent.
So immersed in Jewishness that he didn't need to notice it
Okrent, who co-created the 2012 stage revue “Old Jews Telling Jokes,” chuckled when I compared Sondheim’s Jewishness to the metaphysical joke about a fish. “How’s the water?” an old fish asks a young fish. “What the hell is water?” says the young fish.
Sondheim, agreed Okrent, may have been so deeply immersed in a Jewish milieu that he rarely thought about it, or bothered to craft a carefully worked-out theory, like so many others, as to why Jews thrived on Broadway.
“I suppose if he interrogated himself about it, he probably would have. But I don’t know. I can’t say that with certainty,” Okrent acknowledged.
Sometimes, Sondheim did notice the water. Okrent recalls that he was proud of “A Little Night Music,” his hit adaptation of the Swedish director Ingmar Bergman’s film “Smiles of a Summer Night.”
“But I don’t know if I really like it,” Sondheim told the Jewish playwright Jules Feiffer. “It’s so damn goyische.”

Haifa International Film Festival opens with emotional tribute to Avi Nesher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:33:03 UTC
10:33:03 KST

The 42nd Haifa International Festival opened with an emotional tribute to director Avi Nesher, who was awarded its lifetime achievement award, and the official Israeli premiere of his latest movie, Our Loves.
The festival will continue until October 3, and Our Loves will open throughout Israel on October 15.
Our Loves received a standing ovation, and the tribute referenced Nesher’s personal and professional connections to the festival in a way that was especially meaningful. Nesher was joined after the film by the cast of his epic, multi-character drama about a group of people in the south of Israel who think they are having the worst day of their lives on October 6, 2023, and struggle to survive when Hamas attacks the next day.
As he stood on stage with most of the cast, including Shalom Michaelshwilli, Magi Azarzar, Noa Cohen, Daniel Gimpel, Yaniv Biton, Chancela “Sean” Mongoza, Hadas Yaron, Amir Banai and others, he seemed overcome at times with emotion over the audience reaction, the film’s message, the support of his cast, and his own memories.
Nesher dramatizes October 7 stories, providing closure
The last day of the 2023 Haifa International Film Festival was October 7 – of course, it had to be canceled – and there was a feeling of a kind of closure that some of the stories from that day had been dramatized by Nesher, one of Israel’s most beloved and most acclaimed directors. In this moment, Nesher – whose previous films include The Troupe, a look at an army entertainment troupe in the 70s; Rage and Glory, a story about the Lehi Underground; and Image of Victory, a drama about young Israelis and Egyptians during the Independence War -- could be seen as Israel’s national storyteller, taking us into the darkest moments of recent history and finding moments of grace amid the horror.
He was fresh from the film’s triumphant run at the Toronto International Film Festival earlier this month, where he received standing ovations at the film’s three sold-out screenings. While the audiences there were enthusiastic, he said, the security was heavier than anything he had ever experienced before when five of his previous films were shown there.
After he learned that Our Loves had been accepted by Toronto, he said, “The festival officially asked me to provide a name other than my own for the sign held by the driver meeting my wife and me at the Toronto airport. They explained that displaying the name of a well-known Israeli might attract attention and that something violent could happen. I don’t have to tell you what went through my mind.
“Throughout the festival, we had very heavy security: an armored vehicle and bodyguards. It was frightening. Then we heard that every ticket to the premiere had sold out within minutes. That should have been good news, but we were nervous about who would fill the theater. We arrived to find it packed. We were brought in under security, and … [Our Loves cast members] Noa Cohen, Daniel Gimpel, Yaniv Biton, and I stood before that large audience. Someone told us, ‘This is the moment.’ We were apprehensive. Then, suddenly, there were cheers, applause, and cries of ‘Bravo!’ Some 500 people rose to their feet and applauded an Israeli film. It was unbelievable. We were overwhelmed, looking at one another as the applause went on and on. We knew something important had happened–something that cinema can do.”
Nesher continued: “We returned to Israel a few days ago knowing another emotional moment awaited us. Tonight is the first time the film is being shown officially to an Israeli audience. It’s perhaps less frightening, but much more intimate. It’s like introducing your new girlfriend to your family. Haifa has shown many of my films, and it has always felt like a loving family here.”
The ceremony featured a musical tribute to Nesher’s work, with several well-known songs from his movies performed as clips from the movies played, including a medley from The Troupe performed by one of the film’s stars, Sassi Keshet, and an IDF quartet. “New Day Will Rise,” a song about the massacre at the Nova Music Festival, was performed by Nova survivor Yuval Raphael, who sang it in the 2025 Eurovision competition, and she was joined by the Iranian singer Gola, making it into a memorable duet.
There was also a pre-recorded interview with Nesher, in which he described being a lifelong cinema buff, and clips of some of his favorite movies were shown, including North by Northwest and High Noon, with Cary Grant and Gary Cooper’s faces replaced by images of Nesher.
“I’m very grateful for this lifetime achievement award, but I don’t think it belongs to me alone. I share it with the many people whose talent, dedication, ideas, and wisdom helped make the films I wrote and directed,” he said and thanked a number of his collaborators, including producer Moshe Edery and Edery’s late brother, Leon Edery, as well as his longtime editor, Isaac Sehayek.
Said Nesher, “Tonight, I thank the people closest to me: my wife, the wonderful artist, Iris, and my daughter, Tom [a director who made the movie, Come Closer]... Each has been part of my life and my films in her own way.”
Nesher discusses 2018 film festival
The most meaningful moment came when he recalled the last time one of his movies opened the film festival in Haifa, in 2018, with the Israeli premiere of The Other Story.
“Now comes the sad part. Today is September 26, Ari’s birthday. You know his story,” he said, referring to his late son, Ari Nesher. Following the 2018 festival opening in Haifa, Ari was injured in a hit-and-run accident in Tel Aviv and died on September 27. He was just 17.
“The fact that you know it is itself part of what makes this feel like a family: that Israeli sense of togetherness and shared responsibility. So, because we are family, I want to share this with you. At the screening of The Other Story here in Haifa, I went up at the end to thank the audience. People were standing and applauding, and there, in the tenth row, was my son Ari, with a huge smile.”
The screen behind Nesher filled up with a photo of his wife and daughter, and zoomed out to show Ari with them, and several other photographs of the family were projected on the screen. His normally confident voice wavered, and he teared up as he said, “I know he would have been proud of this award, and proud of this film. I’m sorry; I didn’t mean to bring everyone down. But families share everything–the awards and the sadness, too.”
At the end of the screening, standing with his cast and crew, Nesher looked simultaneously full of love and sorrow, knowing he was in a room filled with people who understood the story of both his own personal tragedy eight years ago and the nation’s 2023 tragedy. After the movie, dozens of well-wishers came up to thank him for the film, expressing sympathy for him and gratitude that he was able to help them make sense of the nation’s recent loss.

France’s far-right National Rally surges in partial Senate elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:31:45 UTC
10:31:45 KST

The French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has said her 2027 presidential campaign will be boosted after her anti-immigration party, the National Rally (RN), and its allies secured a record 14 seats in partial senate elections this weekend.
Le Pen called the results a “historic victory” and “major milestone” after her party cleared the 10-seat threshold to be able to form a senate group for the first time, following an indirect vote by local officials including mayors and councillors.
The party’s progress in the senate will allow them higher visibility and more funding in the second house of parliament ahead next spring’s presidential election. Le Pen is currently polling high as Emmanuel Macron prepares to step down after ten years in office.
The RN MP Sébastien Chenu called the gains “a boost for the presidential campaign” and said there was “no more glass ceiling” for the party. Edwige Diaz, who secured a large senate win for the RN in Gironde outside Bordeaux, told Le Parisien: “This will be very useful for us before the presidential election.”
The 348-seat senate is France’s second chamber of parliament alongside the national assembly. Final results on Monday morning showed the senate remained dominated by the traditional right and centre-right.
The upper chamber’s president of more than a decade, Gerard Larcher, 77, from the rightwing party Les Républicains is expected to be re-elected next week.
Although the RN is currently the biggest single opposition party in the national assembly, and has the largest number of French members of the European parliament, it has until now never had a grouping in the senate, where its presence has been small.
Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, in addition to the three who won seats in 2023. The RN ally, Eric Ciotti’s Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR) party, also won two seats.
The far-right party had entered the senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the Front National, and won three seats in 2023.
The senate has an indirect voting system, with local elected officials choosing new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term.
Sunday’s vote by local mayors and councillors reflected the RN’s growth in support in medium towns at the last local elections in March. It also showed the party has support among independent rural mayors. The RN leader Jordan Bardella called on politicians on the traditional right to join forces with his party.
The Socialist senator, Laurence Rossignol, said a crucial question would be whether the right and centre right in the senate now move closer the RN and harden their own stance on issues such as immigration and welfare benefits. She told Public Sénat TV: “Will there be a republican barrier against RN ideas? That will be key.”
The right, the centre and the left’s Socialists remained the three major forces in the upper house.
The radical left party, La France Insoumise, won a senate seat for the first time, with Gabriel Amard elected in the Rhône. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the party’s leader, who is currently the highest-polling left candidate for the presidency, said Amard’s win was a “good omen” for his own 2027 presidential campaign.

How Hong Kong is trying a new solution to its land value problem

Opinion
How Hong Kong is trying a new solution to its land value problem
After decades of lucrative land sales, can the city finally build a system in which the land itself creates economic value?
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Dr Ken Ip is an assistant professor specialising in business innovation and entrepreneurship at Saint Francis University, Hong Kong. 
When Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, announced his housing plan in 1997, the ambition was extraordinary. The government would produce at least 85,000 flats a year across the public and private sectors, and raise the home ownership rate to 70 per cent. The idea was simple. Build more homes, make housing more affordable and allow more families to own a piece of Hong Kong. Then history intervened.
The Asian financial crisis struck. Property prices collapsed. The economy weakened. The 85,000-flat target quickly became politically toxic, and the government retreated. Nearly three decades later, Hong Kong is still wrestling with the same dilemma: how much land can the government release without destabilising the value of the land already in the system? That is the uncomfortable question behind the Northern Metropolis today.
Rising land and property values can generate government revenue and household wealth, but they also make it harder for younger generations to enter the housing market. Hong Kong took this model to an extreme.

Middle East shipping recovery
Brent edged up 0.4 percent last week, whereas WTI plunged 7.9 percent on concerns that the US administration might ban diesel exports to curb record domestic fuel prices—a step that could restrain American refinery output.
Meanwhile, crude oil exports from key Middle Eastern producers rebounded in September to 12.8 million barrels per day (bpd), marking the highest volume recorded since the war erupted in February, according to preliminary shipping data from Kpler on Monday, as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates ramped up deliveries.
The recovery was driven by a restoration in shipments traversing the Strait of Hormuz, which were projected to reach approximately 7.4 million bpd this month.
The shift occurred as Saudi Arabia redirected exports away from the Red Sea port of Yanbu towards its eastern terminal at Ras Tanura following militant strikes that damaged its East-West pipeline.

To live with joy, a person’s attention needs to be open and free. When it is open and free, it becomes possible to see need and how it must be addressed, and it is by meeting need that joy is created. Conversely, attachment to particular intentions limits the range of attention, causing need to be ignored, which then produces suffering.
The experience of suffering is an indicator that attachment is present, and liberation from suffering is possible only by releasing attachment. Attachment is released through the awareness developed from open and free attention to experience, but it is attachment itself that causes attention to become limited and narrow.
The only feasible solution to this problem is to make a conscious effort to loosen attention until the awareness is developed to keep it loose. But loosening attention from the objects of attachment first requires the ability to loosen it in general. It is necessary to develop the skill of letting go of the many thoughts, feelings, memories, ideas, and so on that arise throughout ordinary life.

Pakistan's first astronaut prepares to make history in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:17:13 UTC
10:17:13 KST

Two Pakistani pilots are spinning in centrifuge drills and learning to eat, sleep and repair equipment while weightless, as a decision nears on which one will become the first foreign astronaut aboard China's Tiangong space station.
The voyage into space would be a first for the South Asian nation.
It is part of broader cooperation with Beijing that includes a joint satellite-navigation system and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on China's Chang'e 8 lunar mission around 2028.
Pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud have spent months training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Centre in Beijing for a mission the two countries conceived in 2019, said Amer Gilani, who oversees human spaceflight cooperation at Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.
China has not said which of the two will fly or when, but Gilani said a final astronaut selection decision is expected in mid-to-late October.
Whoever is chosen will not return to Pakistan before launch, setting off into space directly from training in China and returning home after a recovery period following the return to Earth, Gilani told Reuters in an interview.
Training includes intensive Chinese-language instruction, learning spacecraft systems, and adapting to both the microgravity of orbit and the g-forces of liftoff, he added.
The two men beat out roughly 20 finalists culled from an initial pool of pilots and scientists, screened for medical fitness, psychological resilience and, according to SUPARCO's director of artificial intelligence Uzair Ansari, a tolerance for g-forces that few scientists possess.
"You cannot easily find scientists who are familiar with travelling and facing high-level g-forces," he said, explaining this is why the two men with backgrounds in high-speed flying were chosen.
The details shared by Gilani and Ansari are the first insight SUPARCO has provided to foreign media since the pilots were selected and deployed to China.
China's space agency did not respond to a request for comment about the selection process.
Modest payload
Once in space, the chosen pilot will carry the title of "payload specialist", which is astronaut-speak for someone whose job in orbit is running Pakistan's science experiments rather than flying the ship, Ansari said.
Of more than 300 proposals SUPARCO fielded from universities in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad after a year-long campaign, Gilani said Chinese institutes picked four for this flight: biotechnology experiments that will help combat food insecurity and climate change.
Every experiment is built and pre-tested in SUPARCO's own labs before Chinese engineers sign off — a rare case, Ansari said, where Pakistani technology gets validated on an international platform.
The scientific payload is modest next to a station that has already hosted more than 180 experiments and produced over 500 research papers and 150 patents, Ansari added.
Tiangong's three modules — Tianhe, Wentian and Mengtian — weigh about 77 metric tons combined and house roughly 14 experiment racks spanning life sciences, materials, fluid physics, combustion and radiation exposure, Gilani said, including some mounted outside the station and exposed directly to space for materials and biotechnology payloads.
The Pakistani astronaut is due to return with two members of a Chinese crew that arrived at the space station in May because the third member is expected to stay for a year to enable the study of long-duration human physiology in space.
Since Yuri Gagarin's 1961 first flight, citizens of about 50 countries have flown in space, but only three nations — Russia, the US, and China — have launched their own crewed spacecraft.
Asked whether Islamabad had secured any promise to send an astronaut to the moon under the same partnership, Gilani said "there is no official commitment or discussion on this matter," adding that what comes next will depend on how "our maiden mission" turns out.
The Pakistani-built lunar rover that is due to fly on China's Chang'e 8 lunar mission around 2028 is a separate strand of that cooperation: it will use AI-based stereo imaging to detect obstacles, judge depth and plan its own path across the lunar surface, since Earth-based controllers cannot guide it in real time, Ansari said.
Still, Ansari was clear that the mission is a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" for Pakistani scientists.

Samples from asteroid Bennu reveal what Earth could have formed from 4.5 billion years ago
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:59:01 EEST
09:59:01 KST

Samples from asteroid Bennu reveal what Earth could have formed from 4.5 billion years ago
Kyiv • UNN
Isotopic analysis of samples from Bennu showed that it formed at the boundary between the hot and cold regions of the protoplanetary disk 4.5 billion years ago. The asteroid’s composition is close to the material from which the terrestrial planets formed.
Samples of asteroid Bennu, delivered to Earth by NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission, helped scientists determine where and from what material this space object formed. The study showed that Bennu originated at the boundary between the hot and cold regions of the protoplanetary disk about 4.5 billion years ago, reports Space.com, writes UNN.
Details
According to Maria Schönbächler, a professor of isotope geochemistry at ETH Zurich, Bennu may provide one of the best insights into the initial mixture of chemical elements from which the terrestrial planets eventually formed.
Bennu may offer us the best insight into the initial mixture of chemical elements from which the terrestrial planets were ultimately built
What scientists saw in the samples
OSIRIS-REx studied the near-Earth asteroid from 2018 to 2021, and on September 23, 2023, delivered about 120 grams of its soil to Earth. NASA provided portions of the unique sample to laboratories in various countries around the world.
Schönbächler's team studied isotopes of iron, titanium, and chromium. The analysis showed that Bennu's material was well mixed and, in composition, may be close to the average composition of the protoplanetary disk's material from which Earth and other planets formed.
Bennu's composition also turned out to be very similar to that of the asteroid Ryugu, samples of which were delivered to Earth by Japan's Hayabusa2 mission, as well as to rare meteorites — CI chondrites. According to the researchers, this similarity indicates that these celestial bodies may have formed in the same region of the early Solar System.

'Use lowest effective dose of Nsaids': Fresh advisory on kidney risks of painkiller abuse

Unknown Publisher

Health Ministry warns against misuse of painkillers, antibiotics over kidney disease risk.
NEW DELHI: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued a fresh advisory on rational consumption of painkillers and antibiotics, in view of their repeated use, without proper medical advice, putting people at the risk of kidney complications and other adverse effects.The drug regulator's circular says non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (Nsaids) and antibiotics are prescription medicines under Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and should be used only when clinically indicated, at the appropriate dose and duration and under medical supervision. It has asked people not to take Nsaids, commonly used as painkillers, repeatedly or for a prolonged period without advice.
Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation has also cautioned against self-medication with antibiotics and advised people with existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment to inform their doctor before taking Nsaids.Prof Sandeep Mahajan, nephrologist at AIIMS, said unregulated and prolonged use of painkillers can accelerate the decline in kidney function. "All prescription medicines should be taken under the supervision of a qualified physician, with the prescribed dose and duration strictly followed."CDSCO has advised doctors to use the lowest effective dose of Nsaids for the shortest appropriate duration, with extra caution in patients at risk of kidney injury. This comes against the backdrop of a substantial chronic kidney disease burden in India. A 2025 review of community-based studies estimated pooled chronic kidney disease prevalence at 13.24%, although estimates varied widely across regions and studies.

Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:52:19 UTC
09:52:19 KST

Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.
David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”
On Monday, Chinese state media praised the “extraordinary level of courtesy” that Trump had shown Xi on the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington.
The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales package worth $14bn (£10.5bn), after a record multibillion-dollar deal was announced in December last year.
Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.
Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.
Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take it. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence”, according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.
After Perdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times the US had no plans to sell arms to China, while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
China is a net exporter of weapons. Of the arms that it does import, most come from Russia, but the volume is rapidly falling thanks to advances in China’s own military manufacturing capacity. China’s arms imports fell by 72% between 2021 and 2025 compared with the previous five years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Before the interview, the Taiwanese deputy foreign minister, Chen Ming-chi, spoke of the severe military threat China posed.
“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.
On Sunday, a Taiwanese official, Shen Yu-chung, also pushed back on what he said was an attempt by Beijing to “falsely claim that the Chinese Communist party and the US were allies” in the second world war. A fact sheet released by the White House after the Trump-Xi summit had said China and the US “fought side by side to win” in the war.
China’s government during the second world war was the Republic of China led by Chiang Kai-shek. Chiang’s government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, who established the People’s Republic of China in 1949.
In recent years Taiwan has sought to emphasise its history of fighting alongside western democratic allies as it hopes to bolster international support against aggression from Beijing.
Trump has not mentioned the sale since last week’s summit, saying only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.
Perdue told CNBC on Friday that there had been no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms sales.

What is celebrated on September 28 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:52:18 EEST
09:52:18 KST

What is celebrated on September 28 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
September 28 marks the international days for the fight against rabies, access to information, the right to know, and news. The Czech Republic celebrates Statehood Day.
On September 28, the world observes World Rabies Day, the International Day for Universal Access to Information, International Right to Know Day, and World News Day, while the Czech Republic celebrates Czech Statehood Day. According to the new-style church calendar, Venerable Chariton the Confessor and Saint Blessed Prince Wenceslaus of Bohemia are commemorated, while according to the old style, Saint Martyr Nicetas the Goth is remembered, UNN writes.
World Rabies Day
An official international observance of the WHO and the Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC). The event was established to commemorate the anniversary of the death of the prominent French microbiologist Louis Pasteur (September 28, 1895), who created the first vaccine in history against this deadly viral infection. The day aims to raise awareness of rabies prevention among animals and people, promote mass vaccination of domestic and wild animals, and implement the WHO's global strategy to reduce human deaths from rabies to zero by 2030.
International Day for Universal Access to Information
An official UN observance established by the General Assembly in 2019 at UNESCO's initiative (adopted in 2015). The date emphasizes that free access to information is the foundation of transparent public administration, a guarantee of respect for human rights, a key condition for the development of independent media, and the sustainable development of society.
International Right to Know Day
Established in 2002 in Sofia, Bulgaria, during an international conference of civil society organizations advocating freedom of information. The observance promotes standards of open government, citizens' access to official documents and public data, as well as the protection of civic journalists and investigative reporters.
World News Day
A global information initiative organized by the World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) and the Canadian Association of Journalists. The day seeks to draw attention to the value of professional, verified, and independent journalism amid the mass spread of fake news, manipulation, and propaganda.
Czech Statehood Day (Saint Wenceslaus Day)
The main national and state holiday of the Czech Republic, established to commemorate September 28, 935 (or 929), when Prince Wenceslaus of Bohemia (Vyacheslav) was treacherously murdered. Saint Wenceslaus is the country's patron saint and a symbol of its national sovereignty and Christian cultural tradition.
Teachers' Day in Taiwan (Confucius' Birthday)
An official public holiday commemorating the birthday of the great ancient Chinese philosopher, educator, and thinker Confucius (551 BC). On this day, traditional ritual ceremonies are held in Confucius temples throughout the country, while teachers receive state awards for their contribution to the development of education.
The Commemoration Day of Venerable Chariton the Confessor
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Venerable Chariton the Confessor—a Christian ascetic of the 4th century who endured brutal torture for his faith during the reign of Emperor Aurelian. Later, in Palestine, he founded the renowned Faran, Jericho, and Souka lavras and composed one of the earliest monastic rules.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Saint Martyr Nicetas the Goth—a 4th-century soldier and Christian preacher from the Gothic tribe who, for openly professing his faith in Christ and opposing paganism, suffered martyrdom by burning on the orders of the ruler Athanaric.

Deadly nor'easter batters US East Coast with floods, fierce winds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:45:53 UTC
09:45:53 KST

A powerful off-season storm has lashed the heavily populated US Northeast corridor with strong winds, rain and large waves, knocking out power for thousands and killing at least one person.
Nor'easters, as storms like these are known, can cause billions of dollars in damage by bringing torrential rain, sometimes snow, strong winds, and heavy storm-surge flooding to large swaths of the US East Coast.
This one is odd because they usually come later in the year and into the spring.
The violent weather system hit cities including New York, Boston and Philadelphia, killing at least one person and knocking out power for as many as 130,000 customers.
The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Sunday evening that after causing days of havoc up and down the East Coast, the storm was weakening.
"A round of heavy rain and embedded thunderstorms associated with the meandering Nor'easter is forecast to impact southern New England to the northern Mid-Atlantic through tonight and into Monday," the NWS said.
The storm's centre swirled off the coast of New Jersey, but clouds associated with the storm stretched far north across New England.
Gusts were topping out around 45 mph (72 km/h), the weather service reported, down from the 81 mph that Montauk Point, New York saw earlier in the storm.
The storm was expected to float eastward before turning north over the coming days.
Days of misery
Several local media outlets reported that a New York City public housing authority employee was killed Saturday when a tree fell on him while he walked through a parking lot.
Misery abounded at the nation's airports, with more than 500 flights cancelled and nearly 6,000 delayed across the country, according to FlightAware.
Boston's Logan International Airport saw 172 cancellations as of Sunday evening, almost quarter of its scheduled flights, while smaller airports on Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard saw nearly a third of their flights cancelled.
North Carolina's famed Highway 12, which traces the razor-thin chain of barrier islands off its coast, was washed out this week, stranding some island residents from the mainland.
Images shared by the local transportation authority showed chunks of torn-up asphalt, reminiscent of earthquake damage, washed over by large waves.
Footage shot up and down the US East Coast showed homes battered by large waves while kayakers paddled through flooded city streets.
Nor'easters take their name from the wind that they bring, which usually comes from the northeast.
In satellite images, nor'easters can look strikingly like a hurricane, with spiralling clouds forming over the ocean that span hundreds of miles of coastline.
But these storms form differently.
Whereas hurricanes largely form during the warm late summer and early autumn months and draw energy from warm tropical water, nor'easters are more common between September and April and are fueled by the mixing of cold Arctic air blowing from Canada with the relatively warm air found over coastal Atlantic waters.
