====================================================================================================

Scientists identify an overlooked brain region that sustains fear responses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
20:00:39 UTC
05:00:39 KST

A newly detailed brain region provides the continuous alarm signal needed to keep animals on high alert during a threat. The research, published in Neuron, indicates that the amygdalostriatal transition zone bridges the gap between learning about a danger and sustaining a defensive response.
The amygdalostriatal transition zone, or ASt, is a small cluster of brain cells located between the amygdala, a center for emotion processing, and the striatum, an area involved in controlling movements. When a threat appears, the brain must rapidly detect it and maintain a defensive state until the danger passes.
A 1995 study of rats demonstrated that fear-learning neurons in the amygdala respond to threat sounds in a very brief, rapid burst lasting only milliseconds. Later, a 2002 laboratory study showed that warning signals travel rapidly from the amygdala directly into the neighboring ASt.
The disconnect between brief brain signals and long-lasting fear responses became a major question, as a 2009 study of rodents highlighted the puzzle that amygdala signals fade almost immediately even though defensive behaviors persist for tens of seconds.
The new study explores this fast pathway to determine whether the ASt provides the continuous alarm signal needed to maintain defensive behaviors over longer periods. The research was led by first author Fergil Mills, an assistant professor at the University of Utah who conducted the study as a postdoctoral fellow in the laboratory of senior author Kay M. Tye at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.
“It felt as though an important part of the neural circuitry had yet to be found,” Mills told PsyPost. “In this study, we characterized the ‘amygdalostriatal transition zone’ (ASt), a largely unexplored brain region, and discovered that it maintained responses to threat cues for the full duration that they were present.”
“This was a previously unknown role for the structure, and our work identifies the ASt as a ‘missing piece’ of the neural circuits for learning and behavior,” he added.
The scientists began by examining the genetic makeup of the ASt and surrounding brain structures. They extracted and analyzed the genetic material of 97,434 individual cell nuclei from the brains of mice. The analysis indicated that the ASt has a distinct genetic identity.
Specifically, the ASt contains an unusually high concentration of a specific type of brain cell called a Drd2-positive neuron, which carries a specific receptor for the chemical messenger dopamine. About 71 percent of the neurons in the ASt were of this type, compared to just 26 percent for a related cell type known as Drd1a-positive neurons.
Next, the team measured the electrical activity of ASt neurons in 15 live mice. The mice were trained in an environment where a 20-second auditory tone predicted a mild foot shock, while a different 20-second tone predicted a sweet liquid reward. The researchers found that ASt neurons responded strongly to the shock-predicting tone.
Unlike the brief bursts seen in the amygdala, the ASt neurons fired continuously for the entire 20-second duration of the threat cue. Trials where the mice showed the highest levels of defensive behavior, such as freezing in place, were accompanied by ASt firing rates that were over three times higher than in trials with low defensive behavior.
To see if this brain activity actually produced the defensive behavior, the researchers used optogenetics, a technique that allows scientists to control specific neurons using light. They tested 18 mice that were genetically engineered so their ASt neurons could be activated by blue light lasers. When the researchers shined light into the ASt, the mice immediately began to freeze.
In a separate test where one side of an enclosure triggered the laser, the mice actively avoided that side. The team then isolated the effects of the two different cell types by testing 35 additional mice. They found that activating only the Drd2-positive neurons produced the same freezing and avoidance behaviors, while activating the Drd1a-positive neurons had no effect on these behaviors.
A motor coordination test using a rotating rod showed that the freezing was a defensive response, not a general inability to move. The researchers also tracked the activity of these specific cell types during the tone task using miniature microscopes attached to the heads of 15 mice. By observing calcium levels, which rise when neurons are active, they saw that the Drd2-positive neurons maintained high, sustained levels of activity throughout the threat-predicting tones.
Finally, the team tested whether the ASt is strictly necessary for fear responses. They used a different optogenetic tool to silence the Drd2-positive ASt neurons in a group of 21 mice. During the tone task, blocking these neurons caused the mice to reduce their defensive behaviors, such as freezing or sudden darting, by nearly 50 percent. Blocking these cells did not change the animals’ responses to reward cues, nor did it alter their general movement in an open arena.
“The neural and behavioral results that we observed were striking,” Mills said. “Inhibiting a subpopulation of ASt neurons caused a nearly 50% reduction in fear responses – a major decrease for a structure never before established as part of the fear circuit.”
“This tells us that the ASt is not just correlated with fear responses, but makes a meaningful causal contribution to them,” he noted.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The experiments used only a single type of threat, which was a foot shock, and a single type of reward, which was a sweet drink. It is not completely settled whether the ASt specifically processes the negative nature of an experience, or if it might also respond to other intense stimuli.
Additionally, the mice did not show ASt activation when placed in a context or environment they associated with fear, only when they heard the specific warning tone.
“An interesting detail of our study was that the ASt maintains responses to specific threat cues, but not to locations where negative experiences occurred,” Mills explained. “This suggests that the ASt has a specialized role in fear triggered by sensory cues, rather than the broader environment we are in – a key new insight into how the brain organizes different kinds of fear responses.”
“Importantly, we believe that our findings complement rather than contradict the established amygdala circuits for fear learning,” he said. “We think the ASt is a key part of a much larger circuit, and that the ASt and amygdala likely work together to orchestrate responses to threats. Also, these experiments were performed in mice, so a critical next step will be to determine how these findings translate to humans.”
Scientists hope to investigate whether this pathway plays a role in conditions like anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder, where responses to external stimuli are disrupted.
“Understanding the circuits for fear learning is critical to human health, because maladaptive fear responses are a hallmark of neuropsychiatric disorders such as PTSD and anxiety,” Mills pointed out. “In these disorders, fear responses can become persistent, generalized, or spontaneous, leading to debilitating health outcomes.”
“In order to develop new treatments for these disorders, we have to understand the fundamental circuitry that the brain uses for fear learning,” he added. “That’s what makes the discovery of the ASt’s role in fear so exciting – it’s part of a larger puzzle that we need to solve to improve human health.”
Although the amygdala has been heavily researched in the context of psychiatric conditions, the ASt represents a new frontier for understanding how the brain responds to danger. Future studies will need to explore exactly how the ASt communicates with the amygdala during the initial learning of a threat.
“Now that we know the ASt has a role in fear responses, it is also a new site of interest for disorders where fear responses are disrupted,” Mills explained. “It is easy to imagine that if ASt circuits mediate sustained responses to threats, then dysfunction of these circuits could give rise to the maladaptive fear responses we see in different disorders.”
“We are now collaborating with other researchers to study the ASt’s function in humans, establishing a new translational direction for a brain region that has been almost entirely overlooked in mental health research,” he said. “I want to thank Kay Tye for her incredible mentorship, and all the members of the Tye lab and Mills lab who contributed to the study. Exploring the ASt was an amazing adventure, and we are looking forward to the new science that will stem from these discoveries.”
The study, “Amygdalostriatal transition zone neurons encode sustained cue responses to guide defensive behaviors,” was authored by Fergil Mills, Christopher R. Lee, James R. Howe, Hao Li, Maria N. Keisler, Shan Shao, Felix H. Taschbach, Mackenzie E. Lemieux, Faith Aloboudi, Jesse White, May G. Chan, Matilde Borio, Laurel R. Keyes, Hannah S. Chen, Fabiha Bushra, Gates P. Schneider, Dani P. Lemmon, Kyung J. Lee, Alexa L. Gross, Kanha Batra, Reesha R. Patel, Meenakshi M. Asokan, Jeremy Delahanty, Christian Cazares, Christopher R. Heyman, Nicholas B. Poll, Liezl Maree, Romy Wichmann, Talmo D. Pereira, Marcus K. Benna, Cory M. Root, and Kay M. Tye.

Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:54:03 UTC
04:54:03 KST

As the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump’s political agenda before the November midterm elections, Senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against such spending – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal.
Kennedy, the US president’s fellow Republican, was asked by Margaret Brennan, the CBS Face the Nation host, about the White House spending to air multiple ads featuring Trump – including one that was produced for his 2024 election campaign.
Brennan first reminded Kennedy that in March he had rebuked Kristi Noem, then Trump’s homeland security secretary, for spending millions in government funds “to bolster her public image” in a $220m series of ads she starred in. She then asked the Louisiana senator to comment on the new ads featuring Trump, which the White House calls “public service announcements”.
“Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program,” Brennan said. “It’s on all major networks – it’s on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there’s a voice praising him as ‘the toughest, most resilient person I ever met’. And at the end, it says ‘paid for by the US government’. Is that the best use of taxpayer money?”
Kennedy replied: “Well, first, as to Secretary Noem, what she did was masterclass dumb. She spent $220[m] on commercials about her, and I called her out on it.”
“This looks like a commercial about President Trump,” Brennan noted, referring to the first ad in the series, a 30-second highlight reel of Trump’s second presidency, punctuated by on-screen text driving his political agenda and suggesting Democrats are communists.
“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy replied. “Now, the White House sees it differently. But … I think there ought to be a rule that you can’t – well, there probably is a rule – you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.”
Kennedy, a lawyer with degrees from both the University of Virginia and University of Oxford, appeared to be tacitly acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman and legal scholar, that any government employees who worked on the first pro-Trump ad – “or used government resources to make it” – may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch Act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities.
According to Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates, the Trump administration used more taxpayer funds to broadcast another partisan ad featuring the president that aired nationwide on Saturday during a college football game between Ohio State and Illinois on Fox. It aired again during Fox News Sunday.
That 30-second spot shows a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024.
“This is the final battle,” Trump says in the ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state; we will expel the warmongers from our government; we will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” he continues, with cheers from a crowd. Those cheers indicate that the audio was recorded during a campaign rally and at a time before he used his power as president to start a war with Iran that has left some supporters feeling betrayed.
“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate our country from these tyrants and villains once and for all,” Trump can be heard promising in language clearly calculated to appeal to Christian supporters by echoing the biblical story of Jesus driving merchants and money changers from the temple in Jerusalem.
The newest ad, with on-screen text reading “Paid for by the US Government”, is even more obviously a partisan product than the first one. In fact, the ad was created for Trump’s 2024 election campaign. And it was posted on his Truth Social account in 2023 and 2024 with a plea for funds from supporters.
The rhetoric was written in to Trump’s standard campaign speech as early as July 2023, and then repeated by him again and again at dozens of rallies and appeals for donations.
The ad was even played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination. When it was broadcast during the convention by C-Span on 18 July 2024, the ad was identified as material “provided by the Republican National Committee”.
At the end of his interview with CBS on Sunday, Kennedy volunteered that he also opposed Trump’s drive to put his own name on public buildings.
“I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive,” Kennedy said, before adding that there was such a statute in his home state.
“Well, we’ll watch, Senator, if you introduce that,” Brennan responded.

Russian Forces Begin Using New Geran-5 Version With Autonomous Optical Navigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:46:13 UTC
04:46:13 KST

Russian forces have begun using a new modification of the Geran-5 jet-powered UAV, which features an autonomous optical navigation system and a modified fuselage design.
The monitoring channel Colonel GSh reported this, referring to the new version as the Geran-5 K5.
According to the channel, the UAV is equipped with an electro-optical correction system that allows it to navigate using images of the ground surface.
Its operating principle is similar to that of OEKС (DSMAC) systems, which use terrain image matching for navigation and allow the flight path to be corrected without satellite navigation.
The new version also has a higher speed than the standard model. As a result, it may be mistakenly identified in flight as other jet-powered strike assets, including the Dan-T.
At the same time, the K5 designation and the installation of a DSMAC-class system have not been officially confirmed by Ukrainian sources.
An indirect indication that autonomous optical navigation has appeared on Russian Geran-series drones came from a statement by Russian military correspondent Andrei Filatov. He said that Russian drones of this series already use an autonomous optical navigation system called Susanin.
Filatov claims that the system navigates using images of the underlying terrain, allowing the UAV to continue along its route without radio beacons.
However, the Russian source does not specify which Geran modification is equipped with the system and does not identify it as DSMAC.
According to official data from Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the baseline Geran-5 is 6.5 meters long, has a wingspan of 3.2 meters and a maximum takeoff weight of up to 850 kilograms.
It is equipped with a warhead weighing about 90 kilograms, has a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h, a range of about 950 kilometers and can reach an altitude of up to 6 kilometers.
The Geran-5 examined by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence was found to contain a Kometa-M12 jam-resistant satellite navigation system, an inertial navigation system, a tracker with cellular modems, a mesh modem and a Chinese TELEFLY TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine. The current public list of components maintained by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence does not include a separate DSMAC system.
Russia is known to have already modified the Geran-5’s design by moving the turbojet engine inside the fuselage from an external nacelle, reducing aerodynamic drag and potentially increasing the UAV’s speed and flight range.

‘We hear explosions’: 20 Israelis trapped in Ethiopia as fighting shuts airports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:40:28 UTC
04:40:28 KST

Israel’s Foreign Ministry is working to assist 20 Israelis stranded in northern Ethiopia as fighting between federal government forces and rebels has shut airports and made road travel dangerous.
The Israelis are currently in Lalibela along with about 30 tourists from other countries. One member of the Israeli group told ynet that they had issued an urgent appeal to the Foreign Ministry to examine safe evacuation options.
In a letter sent to the ministry, the Israelis described deteriorating conditions on the ground, including concerns over the health of some travelers and shortages of food, fuel, electricity and communications.
“Flights have been canceled indefinitely, and this is no longer a delay of just a few days,” they wrote. “Fuel, food and cash supplies in the city are extremely limited, according to local residents and hotel staff.”
The group also warned that communications could be cut entirely, as had happened a day earlier in the Tigray region.
“There is concern about a complete communications blackout, which could undermine our ability to contact both the embassy and our families in Israel,” the letter said.
Some of the Israelis and Americans currently in Lalibela are elderly, the group said, and could require medical attention if they are not evacuated soon. Among the stranded foreign tourists are also people suffering from asthma.
‘We cannot know which routes are safe’
The travelers said they have no reliable way to determine which air or land routes are currently safe.
They argued that the Israeli Embassy and government are better positioned to communicate directly with Ethiopian authorities, Ethiopian Airlines, local armed groups and other relevant parties to verify and coordinate a safe route out.
The group urged Israel to act before conditions deteriorate further or communications are completely severed.
They pointed to previous Israeli evacuation operations in Ethiopia, including efforts to rescue citizens from fighting in the Gondar and Amhara areas in August 2023, as evidence that such an operation could be mounted even under difficult conditions.
The Israelis had initially remained in a protected hotel in an area affected by rebel activity and were instructed to stay inside, where conditions were relatively calm.
But the situation changed when their guide decided Saturday to begin driving toward the capital, Addis Ababa.
Several members of the Israeli group opposed the decision, leading to a dispute. Shortly after the journey began, shells started falling nearby, according to the Israelis.
The group sought shelter at another hotel. A mortar round exploded not far away, killing a rebel fighter, they said.
“We hear lots of explosions, and we can smell gunpowder,” members of the group said.
Foreign Ministry: ‘Intensive efforts’
The Foreign Ministry said its department for Israelis abroad, situation room and embassy in Addis Ababa were conducting intensive efforts and maintaining contact with Israelis in areas affected by the security escalation.
“The Foreign Ministry, the Department for Israelis Abroad, the Situation Room and the Israeli Embassy in Addis Ababa are leading intensive efforts, closely monitoring the condition of Israelis staying in areas where the security situation in northern Ethiopia has escalated and remaining in contact with the groups and relevant authorities,” the ministry said.
Officials are continuously examining possible routes out of the area together with local parties and in accordance with developments and security conditions on the ground, the ministry added.
“The Foreign Ministry is acting and will continue to act to assist Israelis in the area as much as possible, while giving the highest priority to their safety and security,” it said.

Pope Leo pledges action on clergy abuse after meeting French survivors
LOURDES, France – Pope Leo XIV reaffirmed his commitment to ending abuse of children by Catholic priests in a meeting with French abuse survivors on Sept 27, the Vatican said, hours after the pontiff urged the Church to admit its own failings and heal its “deep wounds”.
In a two-hour meeting with seven survivors in France, where Leo is on a three-city weekend visit, the Pope met privately with each of the victims and heard proposals for how to improve the Church’s safeguarding measures, said a Vatican statement.
“He thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others,” it said.
The survivors said after the meeting that it was emotional and touching. They said they felt listened to by the pontiff, and they were impressed by his compassion and his knowledge of their individual cases, but they also hoped that the words would be accompanied by action.
“He certainly believes that the Church has done a great deal in France, but he also believes that the Church in France still has a tremendous amount left to do,” Jerome Guillement said.
Leo is on a whirlwind four-day visit to France. Local Church leaders are hoping he will help repair the Church’s standing after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.
The Pope told an estimated 150,000 people gathered for a mass in a field near the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes that the Church must have the courage to face its past.
“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope said.
Veronique Garnier, one of the survivors in the meeting with the Pope, said she had found the Mass, in which Leo referred to abuse without directly apologising for it, troubling and wondered why she had attended.
But she said she was encouraged by her meeting with Leo.
“I do indeed believe there is hope – hope that there can be change and truly listening to us at a deep level, rather than just superficially with beautiful words that are never followed by any real action,” she said.
Leo also spoke about the abuse scandals in a closed-door meeting with French bishops on Sept 27, according to a Vatican-provided text.
The Pope thanked the bishops for the “courageous measures” he said they had taken to confront the scandals and urged them to buttress their safeguarding efforts and “continue on the path undertaken, maintaining the greatest vigilance”.
Leo has drawn large crowds on his visit to France. Around 800,000 people came for an outdoor mass on the Champs-Elysees with the Pope in Paris on Sept 26. He has also again urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence.
‘Cannot ignore this issue’
Leo has previously apologised directly for abuse scandals that have damaged the Church’s credibility across the world. On a trip to Spain in June, he told bishops there that they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations.
Bishop Pierre-Antoine Bozo, the spokesperson for the French bishops, said the Pope’s desire to have the meeting “shows that we cannot ignore this issue and that it must always remain among our concerns”.
The Pope’s itinerary in France included six events in Lourdes, a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains that attracts some 3 million pilgrims a year for visits to a shrine to the Virgin Mary and purported healing spring waters.
The site is also connected to a scandal that has dogged the Vatican in recent years. The shrine’s facade has a series of mosaics by Rev Marko Rupnik, a prominent religious artist with Vatican ties, who has been accused of sexual abuse.
Rupnik, accused by more than 20 women, is not known to have commented publicly on the accusations. Five of his alleged victims wrote an open letter to the Pope on Sept 24, sharply criticising an ongoing Vatican trial of the cleric.
The mosaics, stories tall, have been covered for the Pope’s visit with large, muted yellow tarps. Arriving for the Mass on Sept 27, Leo was driven in his open-top popemobile near the facade of the shrine and the covered mosaics.
The Pope, who on Sept 25 sharply reiterated Catholic opposition to assisted dying initiatives two months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable illnesses, again mentioned the Church’s pro-life stance in Lourdes.
Meeting with volunteers who help sick pilgrims hoping to find a miracle in the shrine’s waters, Leo urged them to remember the “profound meaning” of healthcare work.
“That is to care for a suffering person, not to eliminate that person,” said the Pope. “Medicine must never become the servant of programmed death!” REUTERS

But that sense of safety in their relationship was short-lived; Stella said she started seeing red flags in his behaviour three months in.

"I got stuck in a web I couldn't leave.
"I think once you have a child with somebody who is a red flag, you're tied to them for life."
What is a red flag?
The term "red flags" has its roots in military and naval customs to signal a warning or danger, and is now often used in discussions about dating and relationships.
"It's really about a warning sign," clinical psychologist and couples therapist Phoebe Rogers told Insight.
"Any behaviour that indicates that something could go wrong, someone's behaviour is toxic, unhealthy — it's going to cause harm."
Although the Sydney-based psychologist hears the term often, she's cautious about how it is applied to certain situations.
"We've got to put it all in a context, actually, and weigh it all up.
"And rather than listening to lists or what people say or 'what my friend thinks', ask 'how am I feeling' and 'what did this mean to me'?"
Rogers said red flags in someone can be difficult to spot and it is often a case of spotting them retroactively.
"I think people can reflect and look back on their past and go, 'Ugh, I knew it then'."
She believes there are many reasons why someone may stay in a situation that might not be healthy for them.
"Sometimes it's because people have grown up with childhood trauma, so they've experienced different forms of abuse.
"And so, they actually don't know what to expect in terms of what a healthy relationship is and 'how should I be treated?'"
'I want to see the best in people'
Melissa Heir has had trouble recognising red flags in friendships — including when she moved from South Africa to Sydney at 19 and had to adjust.
"I literally had to start fresh with making friends ..." Melissa said.
"It really didn't help that with autism, it makes it more difficult to make connections."
So, when an old schoolmate who had also moved to Sydney reached out, Melissa was keen to reconnect.
They spoke over the phone and had plans to meet up but they didn't always eventuate.
"She was a little bit flaky because she'd hit me up and we'd try to organise something, and then she would bail a few times."
Melissa said the friend started asking her to borrow money for food or medications — always with the promise of repayment, which she said was never fulfilled.
A few months later, when she had no extra money to lend, Melissa tallied that her friend owed her about $500. She said she learnt a very expensive lesson from the experience.
"I was quite trusting; I want to see the best in people, and it was hard for me to really think ill of people.
"With autism ... it's sometimes hard to spot these subtle social cues that could give away someone's intention."
Being called a red flag
Zachary McGrath, who is in his 20s, said he has been on the receiving end of being called a "red flag" by some potential partners and "can understand why".
He says "yes to a lot of things" and has many passions — including his military commitments and pursuit of acting and stand-up comedy. He said his commitments keep him busy, and he often forgets to reply to messages.
"My intent's never to make someone feel like they're not important or I don't care," he said.
"But obviously when that person is experiencing unavailability every time from me, no matter what my intent is, that impact is there."
Zachary believes what he considers a red flag is a bit hypocritical as he hates being ghosted by a potential romantic partner.
Ghosting is suddenly ending all communication and avoiding contact with someone without giving any warning or explanation. And Zachary prefers when someone is upfront and honest — even if that might lead to a difficult conversation.
"The other red flag is potential partners who have a big presence with their ex. That's a big one for me," he said.
"I already feel like I'm coming into a relationship and being compared to something I'm not a part of at all."
Are red flags too trivial?
Clinical psychologist Rowan Burckhardt believes that the use of red flags in dating and relationships has become too trivial.
"I actually kind of reject the entire concept of red flags when it comes to relationships and dating," Burckhardt said.
He believes using a checklist of ideal criteria to tick boxes for what one might want in a potential partner gets in the way of listening to "chemistry".
"You could meet someone who ticks all of those boxes, and if you don't feel [the chemistry], I know from my experience working with couples that it just won't be a repairable relationship or ever a healthy one."
Heeding the health warning
Journalist Hannah Vanderheide is grateful she listened to the red flags surrounding her health in her early 20s when she had unusual symptoms.
"I had a very, suddenly very high resting heart rate, couldn't sleep, loss of appetite, weight loss, fatigue, and a real sense of constant adrenaline," she said.
When Hannah saw a GP for these symptoms, they didn't physically examine her and instead prescribed her anti-anxiety medication.
It wasn't until eight months later that another GP took her symptoms seriously, did bloodwork, and diagnosed Hannah with Graves' disease, a common autoimmune condition affecting the thyroid.
She then went straight to hospital as she was at high risk of going into a thyroid storm, a rare, life-threatening condition in which the thyroid makes and releases excess hormones too quickly.
Hannah said it was a relief when the red flags of her health finally had a diagnosis after being initially turned away.
"I had an explanation for what was going on, but there was a lot of anger, and I guess an element of grief because I'd missed a lot of time already — feeling so unwell and deteriorating so quickly.
"And then I was facing a much larger recovery time that wouldn't have been there if I'd been listened to the first time."
Rebuilding a life
After having a baby, Stella's life finally started to change when she went to the police about her husband's abuse.
In 2025, the former police officer and domestic violence investigator was sentenced to two years in prison for six counts of assault against Stella between 2013 and 2018.
"I struggled to reach out to support and just to come to terms with what my reality was," Stella said.
"I was very ashamed of my life."
Now working in advocacy and support work, Stella has rebuilt her life.
"I'm fit, I'm healthy, I have my life, and I have purpose ...
"I have my family and my friends who reflect my love and their love back to me — and I think that's what life is all about."
If you or someone you know is impacted by family and domestic violence, call 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732 or visit 1800RESPECT.org.au. In an emergency, call 000. The Men's Referral Service provides advice for men on domestic violence and can be contacted on 1300 766 491.
For crisis and mental health support, contact Lifeline (13 11 14), SANE Australia (1800 187 263) or 13Yarn (139 276), a 24/7 Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islanders crisis support line.

Bill Gates says AI without regulation is ‘completely irresponsible’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:34:42 UTC
04:34:42 KST

Bill Gates says AI without regulation is ‘completely irresponsible’
The billionaire cofounder of Microsoft says without restrictions, AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’.
Not requiring AI to have safeguards and be subject to outside monitoring is “completely irresponsible” and could lead to global harm to humanity, said tech mogul Bill Gates, in a series of media appearances where the philanthropist weighed in on global discussions concerning how to regulate the technology.
“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion of what safeguards and monitoring looks like,” Gates said in an interview with NBC’s Meet the Press, parts of which aired on Sunday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3China, US to open AI ‘communication channel’ after summit
- list 2 of 3OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs call for global AI regulation at UN
- list 3 of 3Trump rejects combining US-China AI efforts
Gates warned that the technology was “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths.” Ensuring that did not happen, he said, could be a more difficult task than other existential threats, such as slowing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The tech pioneer turned philanthropist said he was willing to speak with US President Donald Trump to convey his concerns directly and disagreed with his characterisation of recent warnings over the danger AI posed as a “hoax”.
“I hope that, given my life’s work in the field, my saying how unique and different this is and how concerned I am will add to what he’s hearing from other people,” Gates said in the interview.
In recent weeks, the heads of leading AI companies have said publicly that their industry needs frameworks and guardrails to ensure the technology does not outpace human oversight, spin out of control and prove to be catastrophic for the world.
“If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic, the company behind Claude, told members of the United Nations Security Council last week.
But Trump and senior officials in his administration have baulked at imposing regulations on the multi-trillion-dollar industry, which they say is part of a race between the US and China.
On Saturday, the day after meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss AI, Trump repeated his scepticism of the warnings and said he would not regulate the industry. He compared the apocalyptic warnings to other issues he is dismissive of, such as climate change and Russian interference in US elections. “It’s just like, everybody’s going to be dead, you’re all supposed to be dead now because of global warming. It’s like Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. All of these different hoaxes,” Trump said.
Gates told CNN that the kind of safeguards needed for AI development would not harm the industry.
“The amount of slowing down is not going to be that dramatic,” he said. “To have a monitoring or policing layer that says, is this being used for a cyberattack, is this being used for bio-terrorism, that can be done.”
The 70-year-old co-founded the software company Microsoft in 1975 and ran it during an era of widespread consumer adoption of personal computers and later the internet. He became the richest person in the world in 1995, and retained that spot throughout much of the next two decades, before giving much of his wealth away for philanthropic causes and being replaced by a new generation of tech moguls, including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg.
Earlier this month, his philanthropy, the Gates Foundation, said it was committing $1bn to expand AI access in the developing world.

France's far right gains ground in Senate elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:34:30 UTC
04:34:30 KST

France’s far-right National Rally gains ground in Senate, forms group for first time
Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally and its allies won enough seats in France's Senate to form a parliamentary group in the upper house for the first time in the party's history Sunday, securing 14 seats out of 348. Half the upper house is elected through indirect voting every three years, with senators serving for six years.
France's far-right National Rally (RN) party and its allies secured a record 14 seats in the right-wing dominated Senate in polls Sunday, effectively quadrupling its number in the 348-seat chamber just months before a presidential election.
RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen hailed a "historic victory" after the results were announced.
Local elected officials vote for new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term.
The far-right party entered the Senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the National Front, and won three seats in 2023.
Le Pen is eyeing her best chance yet at power in elections next year when centrist President Emmanuel Macron steps down.
"This is a historic victory, and a major milestone with the formation for the first time of a group in the Senate," she said on X.
Read moreFrance's far-right National Rally fires policeman from security team over racist, sexist comments
Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, according to an AFP tally of results, on top of the three who won seats in 2023.
A further two were elected from RN ally Eric Ciotti's Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR) party.
RN president Jordan Bardella said the party's senators would form a group with UDR allies.
Ciotti quit the right-wing Republicans (LR) party in 2024 after calling for an alliance with the far right.
The upper chamber's LR president of more than a decade, 77-year-old Gerard Larcher, is expected to be re-elected next week.
The right, centre and left-wing Socialists looked set to remain the three major forces in the upper house, according to initial results.
The hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party won its first-ever seat.
Le Pen's anti-immigration party emerged as the single largest party in the lower-house National Assembly after Macron called snap polls in 2024, though it fell well short of a majority.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP )

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announces resignation

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announces resignation
September 27, 2026
Serbia's long-time President Aleksandar Vucic announced on Sunday that he would resign from his post in order to run for prime minister in the upcoming October snap elections.
From the presidential palace in Belgrade, Vucic spoke to supporters: "I am resigning as president."
"Tomorrow morning I will hand over my duties to the parliament speaker," he added "This is the last evening for me in this building," Vucic declared.
"I served you faithfully. I served all of you, and our homeland Serbia, honourably and honestly throughout my presidential term," Vucic told supporters. "The fight is only beginning," he added.
Dominating Serbian politics
Vucic is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term. He was serving his second term and would have left office in May of 2027.
The 56-year-old, who has ties to Serbian nationalism and had once served as minister under the administration of Slobodan Milosevic, has dominated Serbian politics for more over a decade.
Vucic supporters praise him for his stability, stated commitment to development projects in Serbia and his patriotism, in a country long overshadowed by war in the 1990s and subsequent international isolation.
Opponents, however, have decried what they see as increasingly authoritarian tendencies and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.
Abroad, Vucic has had to juggle the competing interests of his country's European Union aspirations and its close ties to Russia.
Opposition had sought snap elections
Earlier in September, Vucic called for snap elections for October. He cited "major turbulence on the domestic political scene," as the reason.
Vucic was referring to the political movement and major setback for his government that was triggered by a tragedy in Serbia's second-largest city of Novi Sad. In November 2024, an awning of a newly reconstructed railway station in Novi Sad collapsed, killing 16 people.
The disaster triggered nationwide protests by students and the opposition. They demanded accountability for those responsible for the disaster, transparency in public procurement, an end to systemic corruption, and an early parliamentary vote.
Vucic's government repeatedly denied accusations, but still, several officials, including two ministers, were arrested or resigned after the incident. The upcoming snap election will test Vucic's popularity and political survival.

Defense Forces Manage to Deliver 4,000 Kilograms of Food to Occupied Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:31:54 UTC
04:31:54 KST

Ukraine’s Defense Forces have delivered about 4,000 kilograms of food by drone to occupied Oleshky, where people are facing hunger, at 100 designated locations across the city.
Head of the Kherson Regional State Administration Oleksandr Prokudin reported this.
According to the regional administration, Russian forces are holding as hostages about 2,000 people in occupied Oleshky, including nearly 50 children who are being forced to survive without food, electricity or water.
Since March, the Administration, together with a unit of the 11th Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine and personnel from the 34th Separate Marine Brigade Borysfen, has organized food deliveries across the Dnipro River using drones.
“Recently, we managed to carry out one of the largest such operations. In cooperation with the 30th Marine Corps, the Hrim tactical group, the 34th Marine Brigade Borysfen, the Bolharychi unit of the 11th Brigade of the National Guard, the 34th National Guard Regiment and the 79th Border Guard Detachment, we delivered about 4,000 kilograms of food to 100 designated locations across the city,” he said.
However, Russian military personnel are attempting to shoot down drones carrying food and are confiscating or reselling food intended for civilians. Occupation forces detain Oleshky residents for receiving humanitarian aid packages, hold them in basements, severely beat them and subject them to violence.
The city has been on the brink of a humanitarian disaster for almost a year, since late 2025. The last food supplies reached Oleshky in late May, when local entrepreneurs managed to enter the city in two commercial vehicles.
No subsequent attempt to deliver food was successful. During one such attempt on June 2, four vehicles hit mines, killing two people. Since then, there has been no regular food supply, and after stocks and garden produce ran out, residents found themselves on the brink of starvation.
As reported by Ukrainska Pravda, the problem is not limited to food. After the start of the occupation and the destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant, the city has been without electricity, gas and drinking water, while medicines are also in critically short supply. Although the hospital is the only facility that continues to operate to some extent, even basic medical care cannot always be provided there.
All roads and access routes to Oleshky have been mined, while active fighting continues around the city, making evacuation impossible. ATMs and banks have not operated in the city for a long time. As a result, money has effectively lost its value. Although prices can formally be set for some goods, such as sugar or potatoes, in practice they are used only for barter.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross and partner countries for help organizing the evacuation of civilians. However, none of the negotiations produced results because Russia did not agree to a humanitarian corridor.
Oleshky is not the only city on the left bank of the Dnipro River that has found itself on the brink of a humanitarian disaster. There are also problems with food, medicine and transportation in Hola Prystan, Stara Zburivka, Nova Zburivka and other settlements in the region. According to rough estimates by volunteers, up to 1,500 people, including about 40 children, still remain in the city. Another 4,000 people and approximately 150 children remain in villages across the community.

Britain to keep tariffs on Chinese EVs ‘under review,’ UK business chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:29:51 UTC
04:29:51 KST

LIVERPOOL, England — Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds is keeping tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles “under review” as the U.K. fights to be included in Brussels’ Buy European program.
The European Union has requested that the U.K. raise tariffs on Chinese EVs in order to advance talks to join the industrial program, amid fears Britain could provide a back door for Chinese vehicles to enter the single market, the Financial Times reported on Friday.
During an interview at The POLITICO Pub at Labour Party conference, Reynolds said he is keeping the issue of tariffs on Chinese EVs “under review, to be frank, more closely than lots of other issues” and that “different parts of our own sector want different things from” the government’s policy.
Advertisement
EU capitals are currently considering whether U.K. auto exports should qualify for preferential treatment under the Buy European program, as Brussels moves to protect its member economies from U.S. tariffs, China’s manufacturing might and an influx of cheap EVs subsidized by Beijing.
European Union lawmakers and officials are preparing new legislation to deny overseas manufacturers access to subsidies, tax incentives and public procurement deals. The bloc slapped double-digit tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024.
But Reynolds said the U.K. government’s calculation on whether to impose tariffs differed from that of the EU.
“We are an export-orientated sector. So clearly, you shouldn’t do anything that risks your export markets, and you always have to take heed of retaliatory action if you put tariffs in place,” he said Sunday, calling the U.K.’s position on Chinese EVs “finely balanced.”
Cutting the U.K. out of Brussels’ new industrial program “wouldn’t be to the benefit of Europe,” Reynolds added.
The Made in Europe push is supposed to be “about greater resilience, greater autonomy for European industry in the face of very significant pressures from both the U.S. and China,” Reynolds added. “Now, if that is the objective, it stands to reason that the U.K., that’s the second-biggest economy in Europe, should be a part of that.”
Advertisement
Non-U.K. goods moving from Britain to the EU must pay applicable tariffs. But Reynolds has said he’s open to Chinese EV-makers setting up in Britain. Chinese firms have been eyeing Britain as a home base, with Nissan striking an MoU for Chinese EV giant Chery to use one of its Sunderland factory lines to make EVs in June.
Excluding U.K. supply chains from Made in Europe could cost €24 billion in economic activity on the EU side alone, the British SMMT automotive lobby warned earlier this month. Britain’s chemical and energy supply chains could also face restrictions under the rules.
The tussle between London and Brussels over the degree to which the U.K. should be included in European supply chains threatens to delay a major summit to wrap up talks on a range of trade issues later this year.
Reynolds also warned that “constitutional questions” regarding Britain’s EU relationship are causing “uncertainty” for business. The senior Cabinet minister said the U.K. should be focused on “how we can improve that trade relationship,” rather than whether Labour should push for Britain to rejoin the bloc.

Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:29:24 UTC
04:29:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, despite his rejection of a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
Iranian officials brought a plan to the UN General Assembly in New York for a seven-day truce, followed by the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz shipping channel.
Trump dismissed the plan and has mused on resuming full-scale air strikes on Iranian targets, but he told the news platform Axios that he expects negotiations to resume.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
"They overplayed their hand," Trump said, in the interview published Sunday.
Citing sources familiar with the matter, Axios reported that indirect talks between Washington and Tehran could take place as early as Monday.
On Sunday, Iran was still standing by its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the Gulf front of the Middle East war locked in a stalemate, while fighting rages in Yemen.
'We will not back down'
Hormuz is a key chokepoint for the world's energy supplies and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was started nearly seven months ago when the US and Israel launched a wave of strikes against Iran.
Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and a return to the conditions in an earlier ceasefire deal that fell apart.
That agreement, which collapsed during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."
Washington's ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table.
"This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk," he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday.
"I think it's kind of common sense that the president doesn't have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago."
Iran's Revolutionary Guards meanwhile said that they seized an American submersible drone on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz.
It said the underwater vehicle was being used "for espionage purposes", adding that it was "now in the hands of the force's specialists for data recovery".
'Tool for pressure'
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war, reopening the strait and launching talks on Iran's nuclear programme.
But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.
Araghchi said at the UN that Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan, adding: "The choice now rests with the United States."
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met."
Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran's demands.

I think many people followed our social media and website. All of this was covered with videos, photos, and corresponding reports. Forty-two ministers, prime ministers, and heads of state came to the Russian room, the Russian delegation’s room, for what I would once again describe as traditional talks," the diplomat said.

That is roughly how those three days went, followed by a night on the plane," the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman added.

NATO article 5 is not what you think it is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:24:38 UTC
04:24:38 KST

NATO article 5 is not what you think it is
There are few myths as captivating and durable as that of Article 5 of the 1949 Washington Treaty. Proponents of the myth are convinced that, thanks to this provision, NATO is like Alexandre Dumas’s Three Musketeers, in which an attack against one is an attack against all, and the US would automatically come in full force to the rescue of any of the allies under attack.
It’s debatable and essentially unknowable to what extent that would have worked in the situation of the Cold War, when the US genuinely feared the Soviet/Communist threat, because the bloc was never tested to that extent. But it certainly is utterly false under present conditions and likely future circumstances, and America’s allies and partners need to pay attention and be careful.
The wording of the article itself is deliberately ambiguous. Clearly, there’s no automaticity there in the use of force, and such careful formulation was a condition for the treaty’s ratification by the US Senate because American policymakers at the time abhorred entering into entangling alliances.
So much for the automatic use of US military force.
Later, after the Soviet Union developed intercontinental ballistic missiles in the mid-to-late 1950s, American military strategy sought to avoid a direct nuclear exchange. Nuclear war, if it were to be fought, was to stay limited, confined to Europe, east and west.
So much for the US nuclear umbrella.
During the Cold War, recurrent crises around West Berlin were considered in Washington as a likely casus belli, but West Berlin was formally an occupied territory, rather than an allied country. It was safeguarded by American, British, and French military garrisons, and a move against the city (which was never attempted) would have been an attack on US military personnel. The situation along the German-German, Czechoslovak-West German, or Norway’s and Türkiye’s borders with the Soviet Union, though tense, was invariably stable. Elsewhere, NATO and the Warsaw Pact were separated by wide swaths of neutral territory.
So much for the likelihood of military conflicts which would have triggered Article 5.
The current US National Defense Strategy doesn’t view Russia as a major threat, with the Trump administration busy shifting the focus of US forces to East Asia and the Pacific. President Donald Trump has shifted the burden of NATO’s defense onto the European members themselves. If his performance in the Ukraine conflict is a gauge, he has no wish and no inclination to commit US forces to defending America’s allies and clients. Selling arms to them and sharing intelligence is the limit.
Washington also probably takes seriously Moscow’s warning that a NATO-Russia war would be different from the Ukraine conflict, and that it “would be short.” This logically means, in plain English, that it would be nuclear. Americans who studiously avoided a nuclear war with the Soviet Union when they felt genuinely threatened cannot be expected now to allow themselves to be dragged, on behalf of their European allies, into a nuclear conflict with Russia – still the only country in the world that has the capability to annihilate the US.
In his time, President Joe Biden said the US would defend Taiwan if China tried to achieve national reunification by force, but Trump is far more circumspect. To contain China, as with Russia, his administration pushes its allies to the fore, and the Philippines and Japan are the top candidates. As for Taiwan, after its semiconductor industry is safely relocated to America, the island’s significance for America will greatly diminish.
US security guarantees, though admittedly not Article 5-type, have been exposed as less than hollow in the ongoing US war against Iran. Instead of protecting the Gulf Arab countries, the American bases in the region acted like magnets, drawing Iranian drones and missiles which damaged the host countries’ infrastructure. Those in Eastern and Northern Europe who think they will be better off hosting American (or French, for that matter) nuclear facilities should think again.
Ukraine lost its way and brought untold calamities upon itself when its leaders made NATO membership their goal. They didn’t realize that Washington never intended to give them even a symbolic guarantee of protection. Security in the 21st century world can’t be delegated to foreign powers, it can only rest on one’s own resources and stable relations with neighbors. This is the lesson not just for Ukraine and Europe, but also for the Gulf Arab states and East Asia.

The snap parliamentary election next month pits Vucic's SNS and its allies against Students Win, a student-led anti-corruption movement, and European Serbia, an alliance of pro-Western opposition parties.
Students Win, European Serbia and other parties still have to nominate their presidential candidates.

Israel cannot secure the Red Sea without an African strategy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:15:41 UTC
04:15:41 KST

Israel has learned, at terrible cost, that dangers dismissed as distant do not remain distant. The same complacency that helped leave the country unprepared before October 7 now shapes its view of the Red Sea. Israel watches Yemen, intercepts Houthi missiles, and deploys naval power, yet it still lacks an African strategy for the waterway connecting Eilat to the world.
I write this as an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American who knows these societies. Africa is not a map I discovered in a security briefing. Ethiopia is where I was born. Israel is the homeland for which Ethiopian Jews prayed for centuries. America taught me how institutions, alliances, and public accountability can turn power into lasting influence. From that perspective, Israel’s approach is dangerously incomplete.
The problem is larger than the Houthis. Iranian-backed forces threaten ships near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Somali piracy is again rising in the Gulf of Aden. Eritrea remains a closed, militarized dictatorship, often called the North Korea of Africa, along a coastline. Meanwhile, Ethiopia, Africa’s second-most-populous nation and the headquarters of the African Union, depends on Djibouti for access to maritime trade.
This is not a collection of unrelated emergencies. It is one regional failure. The warning signs are no longer theoretical. Maritime authorities recorded two dozen attempted or completed incidents of piracy and armed robbery across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region in only three months this year.
Renewed Houthi advances along Yemen’s coast have increased anxiety around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while conflict has displaced families toward Djibouti. Every government concerned with free navigation should understand what is at stake.
The Red Sea carries trade between Asia, Africa, and Europe. When terrorists fire missiles, pirates seize crews, or governments weaponize ports, the cost reaches American consumers, European industries, African families, and Israeli businesses.
Warships can escort vessels and aircraft can destroy launchers. But missiles cannot build legitimate institutions, create employment, or settle disputes among nations and communities.
The deeper analysis must confront an uncomfortable Ethiopian history. The leadership of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front emerged as allied guerrilla movements and later controlled Addis Ababa and Asmara.
I regard their leadership as a revolutionary political cartel that is secretive, ethnically divisive, and self-serving. My parents and I are living witnesses to the human consequences of that war. Their policies did not create democratic peace. They left authoritarianism, disputed borders, economic dependency, and unfinished tribal war and the Amhara ethnic cleansing.
Ethiopia’s Red Sea relationship is not a recent invention. The ancient Kingdom of Aksum reached the coast through Adulis, a port linking Africa to international trade. And Eritrea’s 1993 independence referendum cannot erase the reality. But neither should the international community pretend that one ballot settled every question fairly for every affected population.
The process did not adequately resolve the security of Afar communities whose historic homeland crosses Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Djibouti, and Ethiopia’s maritime future or long-term rights. Many Ethiopians believe the TPLF leadership accepted the loss of Assab and direct Red Sea access without securing a durable national arrangement.
Afar and other dissenting voices have long argued that decisions imposed by armed movements did not represent the full complexity of local loyalties. These grievances should be investigated and heard, not converted into propaganda for another war.
Ethiopia's need for dependable, diversified, and affordable sea access is real. But that need does not justify invading Eritrea or erasing internationally recognized borders. A nation of more than 130 million people should not be economically trapped; neither should smaller states live under threat. The answer is negotiated port access and enforceable regional guarantees.
Coordinating with African nations over the Red Sea
Israel should propose a Red Sea partnership led jointly with African states. Ethiopia, Djibouti, Kenya, Somalia, and willing regional partners should coordinate maritime intelligence, anti-piracy operations, port security, and emergency response. The African Union, United States, European Union, and responsible Arab governments should support it. Somaliland’s practical role in regional security should be discussed without casually dismissing Somalia’s sovereignty.
This partnership should establish a permanent regional secretariat, joint maritime exercises, a piracy prosecution framework, and an infrastructure fund connecting inland economies to multiple ports. It should guarantee commercial access without transferring sovereignty and require transparent contracts so ports do not become trophies for foreign powers.
Local Afar and coastal representatives must hold seats at the table. Peace negotiated only by presidents, generals, and financiers will remain fragile.
The partnership must also address conditions on land. Piracy and extremism flourish where young people see no work, governments offer no justice, and outside powers arrive only with weapons. Investment in ports, railways, education, water, agriculture, and coastal employment is security policy, not charity.
Israel also has a strategic resource it continues to overlook: Ethiopian Israelis. We understand African political culture, Jewish history, and Israel’s security concerns. Qualified Ethiopian Israelis should serve in diplomacy, national security, intelligence, and African missions. We should not be displayed as evidence of diversity while decisions are made elsewhere.
Our community also answers a lie spreading internationally: that Zionism is a white colonial project. Ethiopian Jews carried Jerusalem in our prayers across generations. We are a social capital and a living evidence that the Jewish people are not one color and that the bond between Africa and Zion is ancient. Yet our value is greater than public relations. We can help Israel build relationships based on dignity rather than emergency transactions.
Leadership renewal begins by abandoning the arrogance that military superiority alone creates security. Israel must listen before the crisis becomes a catastrophe, engage Africa as a partner, and include people who know the region from within.
The Red Sea can become a corridor of shared prosperity or a battlefield controlled by terrorists, pirates, and dictators. Israel may win engagements without an African strategy. It will still lose the larger struggle for secure trade, regional legitimacy, and lasting peace.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

Smotrich, Strock demand Netanyahu reject new BoP Gaza plan, say it contradicts US-Israel agreements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:15:41 UTC
04:15:41 KST

Israel should reject the new Board of Peace (BoP) plan for the Gaza Strip because it contradicts understandings reached with the United States last month, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Missions Minister Orit Strock told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a letter on Sunday.
The BoP last week proposed a six-month Gaza recovery framework that includes a $2.45 billion package of 66 funded programs for shelter, debris clearance, water, hospitals, schools, energy, roads, and jobs, to be advanced alongside deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), and what the board described as weapons decommissioning.
In the letter, the ministers said the official proposal now advanced by the BoP is “completely contrary to the understandings that were reached between you and the US administration and the Board of Peace” after the publication of the 15-point road map, which Israel had already announced it would not accept.
Smotrich, Strock demand Gaza demilitarization come first
Those understandings, they wrote, were clear: Any reconstruction, any entry of foreign forces – including the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza and the ISF – and any IDF withdrawal “will not be carried out before the complete demilitarization of the entire Gaza Strip.”
The ministers said the latest statement by the heads of the BoP “is completely contrary to this understanding – which was reached less than a month ago.” In their view, they said, the document is “an attempt to advance the ‘road map’ again in contradiction to the understandings.”
Israel cannot remain silent, they wrote, adding: “Exactly as at the time of the publication of the ‘road map,’ these serious matters cannot be left without a formal and unequivocal Israeli clarification that completely rejects the ‘regional stages method.’”
Smotrich, Strock outline alleged contradictions to Israeli position
They then listed four additional contradictions with what they described as Israel’s agreed positions.
First, they said, the statement ignored that Hamas is not disarming. “It continues to arm itself, grow stronger, train, and carry out attacks against us every day,” they wrote. As a result, “there is no possibility of carrying out reconstruction projects in the immediate term.”
Second, they said, the statement ignores a cabinet decision authorizing the entry of only 200 ISF soldiers – “not 500, and certainly not 5,000.” That decision, they added, was based on the force’s role as the implementer of demilitarization, not on the role assigned to it in the road map as “a supervisor of IDF activity.”
Third, they said, the statement ignores the plan’s leading principle: that Gaza “must be completely demilitarized of weapons.” There is, therefore, “no place whatsoever for ‘acquisition of weapons’ for any forces that would be stationed there,” they wrote, “and certainly not as long as the law that will govern Gaza is the antisemitic Palestinian Authority law, which determines that the murder of Jews is not an offense but a ‘commandment’ that has a reward.”
Fourth, they said, the statement ignores Israel’s “basic and [agreed-upon] right to prevent reconstruction that would create a threat to its residents.” It was “unthinkable” that the entire 365 square kilometers of Gaza would be rebuilt, because “even after full demilitarization of Gaza – no reconstruction will be carried out in areas that threaten our communities,” they wrote.
The ministers concluded their letter by telling Netanyahu they expect him “to clarify in an unequivocal manner that these parts of the statement by the heads of the BoP are not acceptable to Israel and, therefore, will not be implemented.”

Iran split screen: When US, Israeli interests reach a fork in the road - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
19:15:38 UTC
04:15:38 KST

With the exception of a few years, for most of recent decades, US and Israeli interests regarding Iran’s nuclear program, as interpreted by their respective governments, have strongly converged.
Both countries want to prevent an Iranian nuclear weapon.
Israel because it could be an immediate existential danger.
The US because an Iranian nuclear weapon could make the ayatollahs (or the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which may have replaced them) the new hegemon of the region and eventually become a direct threat to the US mainland, like North Korea, which started with short-range atomic bombs and gained longer-range ones within only a few years.
One of the few exceptions was this summer, when US President Donald Trump’s administration cut a deal with Iran that was defined by both Israeli government and opposition officials as a “bad deal.”
Iran made a fateful error
They said it was bad because it reduced US military pressure on Iran, placed resolving the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz at the front of the sequencing of the deal, and pushed off resolving the nuclear issues to the end of the deal, conditionally on months of amorphous negotiations.
The Iranian ballistic-missile threat, which has devastated US military bases and harmed around a dozen countries throughout the region, was not even mentioned in the deal.
Had the deal gone forward as agreed upon, Israeli and American interests would have widely diverged on Iran.
But the Iranians made a potentially fateful error: They decided to rub Trump’s face in the deal and go for an even more humiliating deal, presuming that his readiness to make the concessions he had already made meant that they could push him further.
Trump has caved in stunning and rapid ways on a number of issues during his presidency, but he almost always does so quietly to avoid humiliation.
The Iranians’ insistence on humiliating Trump led him to walk away both from the new deal they wanted and from the concessions he had made under the old deal.
A new reality set in.
Iran had bet that he would continue to cave to try to save the Republican Party from major losses in the November 3 midterm elections.
They were right to a point, as this concern led him to cut the original “bad deal” (from Israel’s perspective).
Trump's bet to outlast the Iranians
To avoid humiliation, however, Trump shifted gears, choosing a third path. He would neither push to topple Iran’s regime with military force, nor cut a deal that would humiliate him; rather, he would try to beat it in a staring contest in which US military power would be used to harm Iran’s economy at a much worse rate than whatever harm the Islamic regime could inflict on America and its allies.
It took months for this strategy to play out, as the US had not really prepared in advance for such a scenario.
But sometime in August, Washington’s military power achieved a shift in which the harm to the West’s economy started to go down, while the harm to Iran’s economy escalated tremendously.
This time, Trump made a bet that Iran would be worn down before the US midterm elections, so he could claim victory leading into those elections and gain back some of the nuclear concessions he had negotiated away earlier.
In the constant miscalculations between the sides, however, Trump continued to project Western rationalism into how he expected Iran to act.
They had lost $200 billion to $300 billion. During the war in early 2026. Now they were losing more day by day. They would for sure finally crack under the ongoing pressure, he thought.
But the IRGC officers running Iran are a mix of religious fanatics who believe their regime is aided by messianic divine currents and are paranoid that the US will just try to topple them at some later date if they do not bring America to its knees.
They could care less when their people suffered in June 2025 and in early 2026, so they still do not care in late 2026 – not if it means giving up on their sense of victory and opens them to the possibility of another US-Israeli massive attack.
With five weeks to Election Day, there are no signs that Iran will change its tune anytime soon.
Meanwhile, Trump and his administration have alternated between saying they will immediately cut a deal with Iran after the midterms and saying they will immediately re-escalate into a full war with Iran after the midterms.
This means that the next fork in the road is set for five weeks from now.
Will Trump stick to his guns, thinking of protecting Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the region from Iranian hegemony and everyone, including the US, from an eventual Iranian nuclear weapon?
In that case, will there be a later point after the midterms when internal pressure on the IRGC forces it to return to nuclear concessions?
Or will Republican pressure from losing the midterms (almost accepted now as self-evident) compel Trump back into a bad deal with Iran to shore up short-term American interests, which will go against Israeli interests and long-term US security interests?
This monumental fork in the road is just over the horizon.

The Irish national soccer team was spotted wearing black armbands and refused to shake the Israeli players' hands on Sunday's UEFA Nations League match in Debrecen, Hungary.
Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Israel's worst ever start to an official game.
The Irish players also avoided the traditional post-match handshakes and pleasantries, choosing to leave the pitch as soon as the final whistle was blown as part of an effort to protest playing the Israeli team.
The decision follows several conflicts within the team, with players even demanding not to play the game due to the war in Gaza.
According to UEFA rules, black armbands are reserved for universally recognized tragedies, periods of national mourning, or the passing of prominent football figures, and require prior approval from the soccer association.
England, for example, wore approved black armbands in its latest game against Spain on Saturday to remember English soccer legend Kevin Keegan, who passed away in July.
It's not clear that Ireland received the approval.
The Irish side also decided to lower their heads when the Israeli anthem was being played, something that generated backlash on social media.
Ireland struck early in the game, with three successive goals in the first 25 minutes of play. On the third goal, midfielder Jack Moylan took off the black armband and kissed it to celebrate.
Irish soccer player with Israeli descent benched
Finn Azaz, who is Irish with Israeli descent, was benched for the match, following rumors that he was among the players pushing for the match to be played and reports that he is considering retiring from international football due to the conflict.
According to reports by The Irish Independent, Azaz made an "impassioned speech" during an Irish team meeting to decide what to do about the upcoming fixture, and whether the squad would forfeit the match, play it with a statement, or without one.
Azaz has not made any public statements regarding his international career or the situation with the fixture against Israel, with The 42 report mentioning that the suggestion of retirement could have been raised by the Football Association of Ireland (FAI).
Sa'ar calls out 'Irish neutrality'
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar published a statement calling out "Ireland's neutrality" by showing a picture of the Irish soccer national team doing the Nazi salute during a match against Germany in 1939.
"In order to 'honor the hosts,' the Irish players stood before kick-off and gave the Nazi salute as the German anthem 'Deutschland über alles' was played," Sa'ar wrote on Twitter/X.
"In 1945, when the world already knew full well what had happened, Irish Prime Minister Éamon de Valera saw fit to visit the German representative in Ireland to offer his condolences on Hitler’s death," he added.
"Back then, they gave the Nazi salute. This time, they stand on the side of Palestinian terrorism. Above the black armbands the Irish players will wear tonight flies the black flag of jihadism," Sa'ar concluded and wished good luck to the Israeli players.
