How seriously should we take biological threats from AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:48:49 UTC
03:48:49 KST

How concerning is the biological weapon threat from AI systems?
The AI industry is suddenly rife with existential fears, with senior figures claiming it could "kill us all" within a decade.
Dario Amodei, CEO of one of the world's largest AI companies, Anthropic, has called for a "slowdown" of AI development to prevent it outrunning our control.
One particular fear is that AI could develop a dangerous biological agent, or a bioweapon.
At the same time, biologists are showing AI can help them with useful research — including those employed at Anthropic, who have just announced AI has helped them discover a new class of enzymes they claim "could represent a new gene editing mechanism".
So is AI a biological threat, or a boon? It may be an uneasy mixture of both.
Why does AI raise the danger of bioweapons?
Labs around the world have had the tools to make dangerous biological agents, like viruses, for decades.
But few people have known how to use those tools, and all of them are scientists who have spent years building their qualifications and credibility.
Brendan Walker-Munro, a security researcher at Southern Cross University, says AI changes this.
"It's lowering those knowledge barriers."
David Heslop, a public health researcher at the University of New South Wales, says the speed of AI progress makes him "very concerned".
"The tools are advancing at a rate which means that human oversight is becoming challenging," Dr Heslop says.
An advanced AI model could give a user outside traditional systems the information required to make a bioweapon.
"It could be a virus or it could be a bacteria, it could be a fungus, it could be something we've never seen before."
Equally dangerously, in Dr Heslop's opinion, an AI tool like a large language model (LLM) could help a bad actor plan to deploy dangerous material, including pre-existing viruses or toxins.
Such work would still need a level of expertise and tens of thousands of dollars of lab equipment.
"We're not at the point, yet, where the LLM gives you a superpower," Dr Heslop says.
"But it's certainly something that could be done in a laboratory."
AI could also be used to attack broader public health systems, like hospital infrastructure.
David Kainer, a computational biologist at the University of Queensland, says the same tools applied to plant science could "potentially destroy large amounts of food production".
"You could imagine something similar happening to engineer super-pathogens for crops."
What sorts of biological threats has AI enabled?
There are several cases where AI has already been used to help design dangerous biological agents.
In 2022, researchers at the Collaborations Pharmaceuticals company showed they could use their company's AI software to make dangerous toxins.
The company's AI tool was used to screen out drug candidates with high predicted toxicity. But the team found they could instruct it to do the opposite, designing new toxins in a matter of hours.
In its recent threat intelligence report, Anthropic highlighted five examples of people using its products "in ways that could support biological weapons development".
Anthropic's models were used to do things like draft grant applications and analyse data in research that made human viruses more contagious, and venoms and toxins more deadly.
All of these users, according to Anthropic, were "working scientists" outside the US using unauthorised software to gain access to the US versions of their products.
Anthropic banned the users for violating supported region policies.
Are there legitimate reasons for using AI?
Biologists have used AI for positive purposes.
AI program Alphafold, for instance, has been used to predict the shape of proteins for medicinal research, winning its creators the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
More recently, US researchers used generative AI to design new bacteria-infecting viruses that could become treatments against infection.
Dr Kainer and his colleagues have developed an autonomous AI tool to help with agricultural research.
Their tool collates vast amounts of data to make networks that biologists can use to predict how environmental or genetic changes might change a plant's features.
"AI, if constructed and used correctly in a clever way, can do that process in an hour instead of six months," Dr Kainer says.
It's not easy to tell if someone's intentions are malicious when they use AI for biological research.
"The analyses you would try to do would look very similar, in my opinion, to work done for beneficial purposes," Dr Kainer says.
He believes controls put up by AI companies to prevent misuse are constraining biological work.
"Right now, biologists are not reaping the benefits of the most powerful AI models that are commercially available."
What can reduce the risks?
Commercial LLMs have safety controls designed to prevent their use for dangerous purposes.
Dr Heslop says these guardrails are the right step, but laws and regulations are needed as well.
"I do have concerns that the various AI companies are not necessarily directly connected with our own legislative systems."
But even if these guardrails hold, established companies aren't the only providers of AI tools.
"Open-weight" models can be downloaded and run privately by anyone with a "bit of programming knowledge", according to Dr Walker-Munro.
Downstream controls, like increasing security on materials and equipment, can also lower the risks.
"There's a difference between the capacity to do it and the capability to do it," Dr Walker-Munro says.
But Dr Heslop worries that barriers are getting lower as labs become more automated.
He says other AI tools could be used for oversight, such as those suggested by the Organisation for the Prevention of Chemical Weapons.
"You could have an AI buddy that is checking your work and is a requirement for doing this work," Dr Heslop proposes.
"It sounds intrusive, but in truth it probably wouldn't get in the way of legitimate research."
But, Dr Walker-Munro cautions, restrictions can still hinder useful research.
"It's about a conversation between government, academia, industry and the AI providers to come up with a system that recognises that tension."

Trump left Saudi Arabia to face Houthis alone – Mearsheimer to RT (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has effectively abandoned Saudi Arabia, a key ally in the Middle East, leaving it to face “almost a full-blown war” with Yemen’s Houthis, political scientist and University of Chicago Professor John Mearsheimer said in an interview with RT.
Hostilities between Riyadh and the Shiite militant group, officially known as Ansarullah, have flared up in recent weeks after several years of relative calm. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, while Riyadh-backed government forces have tried to hold off the group’s advances inside Yemen.
Earlier this month, the Houthis seized control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a key waterway which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on for oil exports since navigation through the Strait of Hormuz was reduced to a trickle amid the US-Israeli war against Iran.
In an interview with New Order host Afshin Rattansi on Sunday, Mearsheimer said that because of its “foolish” decision to “attack the Houthis and pick a fight with them,” Saudi Arabia has found itself in “really deep trouble.” He added that the “Houthis are a formidable fighting force, and the Saudis are not.”
He went on to suggest, citing media reports, that Trump encouraged Riyadh to strike an airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in mid-July. The attack, which was apparently meant to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from Tehran from landing, shattered the UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis, triggering the current escalation.
Mearsheimer gave credence to claims made earlier this month by the New York Times, which said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned Trump on multiple occasions in recent weeks, asking for military support against the Houthis. The president decided, however, not to intervene, according to the NYT. 
Trump was reportedly close to authorizing strikes on the Houthis last weekend, but reversed his decision at the last minute.
According to Mearsheimer, “the last thing [Trump] wants to do is get into a fight with [the Houthis] to try to rescue Saudi Arabia” – not least because of how badly America’s attempt to bomb the Houthis into submission went last year.
Less than two months into the campaign, Trump abruptly announced a ceasefire, declaring victory and saying the Houthis promised not to attack US ships.
“But in fact, the Houthis beat the United States. We did not defeat the Houthis,” Mearsheimer said.
Speaking to Al-Mayadeen on Saturday, the head of the National Security Committee in the Iranian Parliament, Ibrahim Azizi, warned neighboring Arab nations against cooperating with the US and allowing it to use their territory as a launchpad for attacks.
Azizi added that the US security umbrella in the Middle East has proven to be ineffective.

Coalition questions One Nation donations

AEC records show Mr Giles had not disclosed a donation to a federal political party before under his own name, but his company Adgile Investments had donated $25,000 to the Nationals in 2024 and $27,000 to One Nation in 2025.
The pair's recent $500,000 donations have not yet been published by the AEC, which will publish donation data later in the year.

"Any donors who have donated for a federal purpose are required to lodge their annual disclosure return for the 2025-26 financial year by 17 November 2026, at which point the AEC considers the information received," a spokesperson said.

Iran Claims to Have Seized Second U.S. Underwater Drone in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:44:52 UTC
03:44:52 KST

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has claimed to have seized a U.S. REMUS 600 UUV in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian media outlet IRIB reported this, citing a statement by the IRGC Navy.
According to the Iranian side, the UUV was detected while conducting a reconnaissance mission in the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said the seizure operation was conducted using intelligence capabilities and electronic warfare systems.
After being seized, the REMUS 600 UUV was handed over to Iranian specialists, who are expected to examine the vehicle and attempt to retrieve information from its storage systems. The Iranian side also released video footage of the captured vehicle.
The United States has not officially confirmed the loss of this particular vehicle or disclosed the circumstances of its seizure.
The REMUS 600 is an autonomous uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) developed in the United States. It was designed as a multipurpose platform for underwater missions, including reconnaissance, seafloor mapping, mine detection and classification, oceanographic data collection and the search for underwater objects.
The REMUS 600 can operate at depths of up to 600 meters. Underwater navigation is carried out autonomously using an inertial navigation system, Doppler velocity log and acoustic navigation, while GPS can be used after the vehicle surfaces.
According to Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the REMUS 600 can remain operational for about 70 hours and has a range of up to 286 nautical miles.
The Iranian side said the vehicle’s recorded routes, sonar data, navigation parameters and other information that may have remained in its memory could be of particular value.
This is the second case in September in which Iran has claimed to have seized a U.S. UUV. On September 8, the IRGC Navy reported the seizure of a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle made by Anduril near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. side then confirmed the loss of the vehicle, but said it had malfunctioned before falling into the hands of Iranian forces and did not contain classified equipment.
In July, U.S. Central Command used maritime kamikaze drones for the first time to strike Iranian military targets.

Serbia's President Vucic resigns ahead of October parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:37:24 UTC
03:37:24 KST

Serbia's President Vucic resigns ahead of October parliamentary elections
BELGRADE, Sept 27 - Serbia's populist President Aleksandar Vucic announced his resignation on Sunday, ending his second and final five-year term and paving the way for early presidential elections.
Vucic's resignation, seven months before his term ends, comes amid campaigning for Serbia's October 25 snap parliamentary vote and allows him to be appointed prime minister if his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) forms the new government.
He had said in late June that he planned to resign and that Serbia would hold early parliamentary and presidential elections.
Rights groups have accused Vucic and his allies of increasingly authoritarian rule, with anti-government protesters saying they have been beaten by police and unfairly detained. Authorities have denied those allegations.
On Sunday, hundreds of Vucic's supporters cheered him in front of the Presidency building in Belgrade's city centre.
"This is the last evening for me in this building," he told the flag-waving crowd minutes before resigning.
"I have faithfully served you and my fatherland, Serbia, ... I am proud of what we have done together," he said.
Under Serbia's constitution, outgoing Parliament Speaker Ana Brnabic will serve as interim president until a new one is elected. The presidential election must be completed within 90 days, with the campaign lasting between 30 and 60 days.
"By the end of December ... we will have the first round of presidential elections," Vucic said.
ELECTIONS TO TEST VUCIC'S CONTROL
Next month's snap parliamentary election will pit Vucic's SNS and its allies against Students Win, a student-led anti-corruption movement, and European Serbia, an alliance of pro-Western opposition parties.
Students Win, European Serbia and other parties have yet to nominate their presidential candidates.
Vucic, 56, has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade.
He was a hardline nationalist and information minister during the era of the late Slobodan Milosevic and the wars of the 1990s, and later served as deputy prime minister from 2012-14 and prime minister from 2014-17.
He moved to the largely ceremonial position of president in 2017, but kept tight control over his party and the government.
In foreign policy, Vucic has pursued a balancing act that seeks closer ties with China, a major investor, and Russia, Serbia's principal supplier of natural gas, while maintaining a long-term goal of joining the EU. He also has sought to bolster ties with the United States and Israel.
Vucic's term in office suffered a major blow in November 2024 when an awning of a newly reconstructed railway station in the northern city of Novi Sad collapsed, killing 16 people.
The disaster sparked nationwide protests by students and the opposition, who demanded accountability for those responsible, transparency in public procurement, an end to systemic corruption, and an early parliamentary vote.
The government repeatedly denied accusations by the protesters, although several officials, including two ministers, were arrested or resigned after the incident.
On Sunday, Vucic said he has granted amnesty and a pardon to 49 people, including 12 activists and 11 of his own supporters, who were arrested or tried in connection with the protests. REUTERS

Hezbollah as we know it died with Nasrallah, now Iran is making the decisions for the Lebanese terror group - analysis

- Hezbollah as we know it died with Nasrallah - analysis
Hezbollah as we know it died with Nasrallah - analysis
Sources close to Hezbollah say current Secretary-General, Naim Qassem, has failed to fill the void left by his predecessor, with the center of the organization's decision-making coming from Iran
"On the second anniversary of the assassination of former Hezbollah Secretary General Hassan Nasrallah, the party has not succeeded in fully overcoming the absence of the man who held its leadership for more than three decades, and who transformed the General Secretariat into a political, organizational, military and popular center of gravity that is difficult to replace."
That's how the prominent Saudi newspaper A-Sharq Al-Awsat described the current state of the Lebanese terror group, exactly two years after Israel eliminated Nasrallah by dropping 84 one-ton bombs on his underground bunker in Beirut's southern suburbs.
Sources close to Hezbollah say that current Secretary-General, Naim Qassem, has failed to fill the void left by his predecessor, while the center of gravity in the organization's decision-making is now coming directly from Iran. And that sums up the entire story.
In his 30-plus years as Hezbollah's leader, Nasrallah was able to transform the Lebanese organization from a small insurgent militia to the biggest non-state armed force in the world. The way he did that was to enjoy the benefits of being the crown jewel of Iran's proxy network in the region, while knowing how to balance between demands from Tehran to engage Israel and domestic political considerations seeking to avoid constant clashes with Israel.
This tightrope act enabled Nasrallah to use billions in Iranian funding to build a massive army, but also to establish a deep state in Lebanon, forcing leader after leader in Beirut to bow down to his will.
But Nasrallah overshadowed not only Lebanon, but the entire region. At one point, Nasrallah was dubbed "the strongest man in Iran", and this was when Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was still alive. That's quite an impressive accomplishment.
Suggested articles
The same cannot be said about Naim Qassem. Unlike his predecessor, who maintained his hold over the Arab world with firebrand speeches every few weeks, Qassem rarely delivers televised speeches and has failed to project the same gravitas as Nasrallah.
In his speech commemorating two years since the killing of Nasrallah, Qassem said "Nasrallah's martyrdom has ensured our survival" (which to some extent is true), and vowed to continue on the path of Jihad, "with Palestine as our compass." If that was said by Nasrallah, someone may have believed it. But in post-Nasrallah Lebanon, there are fewer buyers for such messages.
Today, most Lebanese view Hezbollah as a foreign agent, an Iranian organ seeking to destroy Israel from the north. Nasrallah's source of success was to keep the Iranian influence at bay, thus keeping the appearance of being a Lebanese group. In the wake of his death, Iran has completely taken over, with dozens of operatives actively calling the shots on the ground. Qassem is nothing more than window dressing.

South Korea, Ukraine relations sour over North Korean POW transfer

Unknown Publisher

S Korea demands Ukraine apology over disclosure of N Korea’s POW transfer
South Korea’s presidential office criticises Ukraine for denying a POW nondisclosure agreement.
South Korea’s presidential office has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine after accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea.
“The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement released on Sunday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Three South Korean military officers wounded in explosion near border
- list 2 of 3Zelenskyy says Ukraine sent two North Korean POWs to South Korea
- list 3 of 3Ukraine’s Zelenskyy calls for sustained pressure to end ‘Putin’s crazy war’
The government is reviewing additional measures over the issue if necessary, he added.
Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) that Kyiv had recently transferred two North Korean POWs to South Korea. He said the men had been captured while fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
Seong said Ukraine had repeatedly discussed the prisoners’ transfer with Seoul through various channels and had requested secrecy, arguing that public disclosure could trigger domestic criticism that Kyiv had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners.
South Korea agreed to keep the transfer confidential, given the security, diplomatic and humanitarian concerns, including the safety of the prisoners and their families, he said.
However, according to Sunday’s statement, Zelenskyy then disclosed the transfer to the UNGA without sufficient consultation and subsequently denied the existence of a confidentiality agreement.
Seong said the denial had seriously damaged trust between the two governments and could harm bilateral relations.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung announced in a post on X on Thursday that Ukraine had disclosed the transfer in breach of a non-disclosure agreement.
Lee said “it was appropriate in every aspect not to disclose” the transfer, given the potential consequences, and that the two sides had agreed to keep it confidential.
“I do not know what circumstances led the Ukrainian side to disclose the matter despite the confidentiality agreement, but it is deeply regrettable,” he wrote.
In response, Zelenskyy’s aide, Dmytro Lytvyn, told journalists that Ukraine was “an open country” and that it would have been strange to hand over the soldiers in secret.
“From the entire story – which is long and detailed – we reported only the fact itself, that they were sent to the Republic of Korea,” he said.
North Korean POWs
Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be captured alive since Pyongyang entered the war in 2024 to assist Russia.
The transfer comes as South Korea has backed efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, while United States President Donald Trump has renewed his willingness to engage with Pyongyang.
The issue of North Korean prisoners of war was a key topic during the NATO summit in the Turkish capital, Ankara, in July, where South Korean President Lee met Zelenskyy.
South Korea’s senior presidential spokesperson, Kang Yu-jung, stated afterwards that both leaders agreed to resolve the status of North Korean POWs in accordance with international law. This built on a prior agreement reached during the South Korea-Ukraine foreign ministers’ meeting in March, where both nations pledged to cooperate on the POW issue.
According to South Korean intelligence, North Korea is estimated to have deployed approximately 14,000-15,000 soldiers to support Moscow’s war on Ukraine since 2024, primarily in Russia’s Kursk border region.
South Korean, Ukrainian and Western officials said there have been heavy casualties, with more than 6,000 North Korean soldiers killed in the fighting.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:20:11 UTC
23:20:11 KST

Aldi says it is stepping up investment in the UK with plans to spend £900m and open more than 40 stores.
The company, which operates 1,092 budget supermarkets in the UK and Ireland, revealed sales rose 5% to a record £19bn last year. It opened 40 stores but profits slipped by £2.6m to £433m as it cut prices despite cost inflation.
Giles Hurley, the boss of Aldi’s UK and Irish arm, said the German-owned business had “increasing confidence around growing our business”, claiming it already was the third largest UK supermarket in terms of items sold and customer numbers.
Asda is classed as the UK’s third largest supermarket by value of sales, just ahead of Aldi. Leeds-based Asda is less than one percentage point ahead of its rival, with a market share of 10.6% in mainland UK, according to the latest data from Worldpanel.
Aldi will open 42 stores this year, with 30 opening in the next 10 weeks. It plans a similar number next year, stepping up investment by about £100m to £900m. In the longer term it is aiming for 1,500 outlets in the UK and Ireland.
“We could probably grow faster but we need to find the right sites in the right locations and have to go through a planning process which can, at times, be challenging,” Hurley said.
He said consumers were “feeling the pinch” against a backdrop of persistent inflation, and the “continuity and clarity” of Aldi’s range of cheap groceries had attracted 425,300 more customers.
He said the outlook for grocery inflation, which stood at 2.8% in August, according to the British Retail Consortium, was difficult to assess until the impact of drought and extreme heat on UK crop yields was clear.
He said the industry was “not seeing systemic food shortages” but the climate crisis was creating “a real challenge” for food producers. He urged the government to treat the UK’s food system as “a national strategic priority” because “relying on imports leaves us exposed”.
Hurley claimed Aldi was the only grocery chain reducing prices. He said the loyalty discount schemes offered by many rival chains, including Tesco and Sainsbury’s, were “definitely a roll of the dice for customers and questions remain about how much of the value [they offer] is perceived rather than real”.
He said Aldi was winning over customers because it remained the cheapest place to shop in the market and it would continue to invest to maintain that position by cutting prices.
However, Aldi does not reveal sales performance in established stores – those open for more than a year – making it difficult to gauge how much growth is just the result of expansion.
Aldi’s growth is much slower than than that of its rival Lidl, which is gaining market share with a loyalty scheme while allowing shoppers to order online and pick up in a store.
Aldi has signed a deal withDeliveroo under which the courier firm’s workers will pick, pack and deliver Aldi groceries sold through its app.
The supermarket chain said it had committed to sourcing at least half its products through long-term supplier agreements by next year, giving its producers and manufacturers greater confidence to invest and make Britain’s food system less reliant on imports.
Aldi said it spent £14bn with British suppliers in 2025 and about 80% of its sales came from them.

CAIRO, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- The Arab League and Egypt on Sunday condemned the ongoing Israeli escalation in the Palestinian territories and repeated settler incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, warning of the repercussions of such practices on the situation in the Palestinian territories.

It expressed its categorical rejection of statements by Israeli officials calling for expanding operations in the West Bank and undermining the Palestinian Authority, stressing the need to halt all unilateral and escalatory measures and respect the existing historical and legal status of Jerusalem.
Egypt also reiterated its support for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
The Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, known to Jews as the Temple Mount, is regarded by Muslims as their third-holiest site.
Earlier Sunday, the Jerusalem Governorate of the Palestinian Authority said that 1,143 settlers entered the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound under heavy Israeli police protection, coinciding with the second day of the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, also known as the Feast of Tabernacles.
Also on Sunday, in an interview with Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the complete dismantling of the Palestinian Authority and an all-out military campaign against West Bank cities and refugee camps, using tactics similar to those employed in Gaza since October 2023. ■

When a world record attempt went horribly wrong, these friends held tight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

When a world record attempt went horribly wrong, these friends held tight
Sydneysiders Valerio De Simoni, Kris "Ted" Davant and Jamie Kenyon wanted to do something remarkable in the years after graduating from high school.
Deciding to cross three continents on bulky quad bikes, raising money for Oxfam's battle against global poverty, their Guinness World Record-breaking attempt was supposed to be the adventure of a lifetime.
It was, but disaster struck and De Simoni never made it home.
New horizons
Bittersweet Italian Film Festival highlight Sand Roads follows their ill-fated voyage of discovery. It began in Istanbul, where the young men crossed the continent-spanning Bosphorus Bridge from Asia into Europe and then on to Africa.
"Every day we woke up, it was something completely different," Davant says. "It was a rite of passage, and so many people helped us along that road."
They'd often pinch themselves.
"One night we were camped under the stars in the middle of the Maasai Mara with a tribal leader," Davant recalls. "We were just absorbing it, open to whatever happens. Whether it's the culture or the landscape, you're laughing, or you're dealing with your next challenge."
And there were many challenges, particularly breakdowns; both of De Simoni and Kenyon's occasionally fraying tempers, butting heads with a perma-jolly Davant in the middle, and also the mechanical sort, battering their quads.
"These are basically farm bikes, and they're really slow, doing around 70kms an hour," Davant says, grinning. "We took them across three continents, 37 countries and 60,000 kilometres.
"They're sturdy, but they're not really designed for that."
Centurion's return
Directed by Lorenzo Conte and Gabriele Gianni, Sand Roads combines the lads' extensive camcorder footage with De Simoni's diary entries and new interviews with his mum, Vittoria Pasquini, alongside Kenyon and Davant.
When De Simoni's cruel and senseless death comes, your heart breaks for Kenyon and Davant, dealing with the aftermath.
"Of course it's sad, when you look back at the footage," Davant tells ABC Arts.
"But the memories are also amazing, looking back at us laughing with Valerio again. It's like going back into a time capsule. There's a lot more beauty within those memories than tragedy."
One of the most affecting moments comes when the boys ride into Rome and De Simoni, born in Sydney, bursts with pride at catching up with his mum's family.
"At that moment, we were having a bit of a chuckle, because he's talking about him being like a Roman centurion coming home," Davant says.
"Like, chill bro. But seeing that footage again and reflecting on it now, you realise that it just meant so much to him."
A lion's pride
It was a moment of pride for Ms Pasquini, too. She travelled the world with De Simoni's father before settling in Australia at 37.
"Being an Italian Australian, Valerio went through different phases," she recalls. "At first, he spoke only Italian. Then, when he went to school, he started speaking only English.
"But he went to Italy in 2001, the year AS Roma won the Scudetto [Italian soccer league], and at that point he became Italian again, including dressing like one."
Ms Pasquini notes that that dual identity came through in De Simoni's diary, which she says is alive with his words in both languages.
It was discovered amongst De Simoni's things, with the family later publishing it as a travelogue. His thoughts are adopted as Sand Roads' narration, including his musings on his father, who also died young, at 35.
"His dad was an important part of Valerio's journey," Ms Pasquini says. "He remembers him vividly in his diary, writing about being a Leo, then meeting lions and recalling that his father lived in Nairobi and saw them as well. So there was this strong connection between father and son."
De Simoni died while Ms Pasquini was on the plane, racing to be by his side in Africa, but she says she knew he'd gone before she landed and received the terrible news.
Watching the footage of the trip gave Ms Pasquini a visceral feeling of being there with her son. "They used the camera as if it was a fourth person travelling with them," she says.
She's eternally grateful to Davant and Kenyon for their enduring friendship following De Simoni's death.
"We decided to get together regularly, having pasta together every two or three weeks," she says. "Sometimes there were tears, but it was a beautiful healing process for the three of us."
Davant and Kenyon, and many of De Simoni's mates, aided Ms Pasquini in establishing the Valerio Daniel De Simoni Association, honouring his charitable spirit by supporting refugees and First Nations youth.
"I've tried to carry on his legacy," she says. "There was a chorus of people who had followed the journey, and then, when the tragedy happened, decided to do something in Valerio's memory. We've done a lot of wonderful things together and I'm proud of that."
Blossoming future
The association is a great comfort to Davant, as was completing the world record attempt, alongside Kenyon, in De Simoni's honour.
"We made a promise to each other as best mates, when we started, that we'd finish it, no matter what," he says. "Jamie and I getting back on the road allowed us to talk a lot. Like Vittoria says, it was a healing process."
Now, they're world record-holders. "We were three ordinary guys who had a dream," Davant smiles. "If you can dream it, it is possible. Even when bad things happen, you come together and build something positive from it."
Ms Pasquini's overjoyed her son's life is being honoured at the Italian Film Festival. "From Valerio's death, one can understand the importance of the present moment and the fact that life is unpredictable. It's important that we all live the best we can.
"It's like a flower is growing out of that mess, and that blossom gives you strength."
Sand Roads screens at the Italian Film Festival.

How to maximise your EV's range while spending as little as possible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

How to maximise your EV's range while spending as little as possible
If you're among the many Australians who have bought an electric vehicle this year, maximising the range of your new ride might be on your mind.
EVs have improved greatly in terms of range but still use more energy during longer freeway-type drives, and while charging an EV is significantly cheaper than refuelling with petrol or diesel, there's still money to be saved by using them more efficiently.
Experts say getting the most out of an EV battery isn't that different to getting good value from a tank of fuel, but there are some key differences to be aware of.
Regenerative braking and one-pedal driving
The one big advantage EVs have is the ability to create their own power via regenerative braking.
"When [an EV] goes into slowdown, then it's actually acting as a generator," says Australian Electric Vehicle Association technical convenor Michael Day, based in Epping, NSW, on Dharug country.
Regenerative braking can be turned on and off, but he says newer EVs have it turned on by default.
You can also take advantage of regenerative braking by practising one-pedal driving, which actually involves using the brake as little as possible.
"You just ease on and ease off the accelerator pedal," says Electric Vehicle Council senior policy manager Bjorn Siem, who works in Meanjin/Brisbane.
"It's a little bit strange to begin with … but once you get used to it, it's brilliant."
Mr Day uses one-pedal braking "all the time".
"Not in an unsafe way … you tend to be able to moderate the momentum of the car better with the throttle and then use the brakes as an emergency stop when you really need to," he says.
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
Curb the urge to take off fast
For new owners, some of the fun of EVs is their "get up and go", Mr Day says.
But as with combustion-engine cars, avoiding the temptation to make a fast getaway at every set of traffic lights can go a long way to using less battery power and preserving your EV's range.
"Most electric vehicles … can get off the line quite quickly," Mr Day says.
"But … you don't need to do that."
Make freeway driving more efficient
Where you're driving can also affect your EV's range, says RACV motoring editor Terry Martin, who lives in South Gippsland on Gunaikurnai and Bunurong country.
"EVs are better suited to stop-start driving in the city, when the car can recover energy through regenerative braking and so forth," he says.
"When you're out on the freeway driving, they're less efficient … you're sapping a lot of energy from the battery so your range will diminish more quickly."
However, the experts say using your EV's cruise control, autopilot and/or eco mode can help avoid peaks and dips in acceleration that can drain your battery.
If you're running low on charge during a long drive and you're not sure you'll make it to a charger, Mr Siem says "the best thing to do is actually just slow down".
"Even from 100 [kilometres per hour] to 90 makes a big difference," he says.
"If you really need to eke it out, then going down to 70 will actually give you a lot more range."
Turning off your air con and other unnecessary add-ons can help too, but speed is "by far" the biggest drain, Mr Siem says.
Tyre pressure, weight and aerodynamic drag
Outside of speed, tyre pressure is probably the biggest drain on EV charge, Mr Siem says.
"[If] tyres are significantly deflated … they will produce a lot of drag; they won't roll as efficiently, so they will use a lot more energy," he says.
He recommends keeping them to the manufacturer's recommended pressure and checking them once a month.
Mr Martin says avoiding excess weight and aerodynamic drag can also help.
"The more … you're carrying around, the more energy you're using," he says. "Make sure you're not carrying around things that you don't need."
He says anything that adds drag, like roof racks, also drains power.
Preserving battery life and charging cheaply
Treating your battery well is another way to help preserve your range in the longer term.
"Batteries nowadays are pretty capable, so as long as you're sensible … they'll actually last really well," Mr Day says.
Most manufacturers recommend keeping EV batteries at between 20 to 80 per cent capacity, he says, unless you're going on a long trip and need maximum charge.
"[Manufacturers say] charge at home on a destination charger because that's a nice, slow, gentle charge. Avoid going too low, avoid going too high, avoid charging too fast if you can," he says.
And to power up as cheaply as possible, Mr Day recommends charging at home using solar power, or an electricity plan with cheap rates when you're able to plug in.
"If you've got a solar system then … that's gold standard," he says.
"When it's sunny, I'm basically charging … I used to pay $3,000 a year in fuel. With my electric vehicle running almost exclusively off solar … it cost me $100."

At least 56 people have been killed in rain- and storm-related incidents in India's northern state of Uttar Pradesh since Friday, local media reported.
The Press Trust of India (PTI), citing officials, reported that heavy downpours and strong winds have uprooted trees and electricity poles, inundated roads and villages, and damaged more than 1,000 houses and standing crops.
Rescue teams have been conducting operations in waterlogged areas to evacuate stranded residents to safer locations, the state's relief department said.
Several districts remain affected by flood-like conditions after the intense three-day spell of rainfall, which has disrupted daily life and damaged infrastructure.
The weather system responsible for the heavy rainfall weakened from a depression into a well-marked low-pressure area on Sunday, bringing some respite from the downpours, officials said.
Meanwhile, in neighbouring Nepal, floods and landslides have killed at least 14 people and left 11 others missing since Thursday, with authorities warning of possible flash floods in 49 of the country's 77 districts.

Global AI companies investigating tens of thousands of security incidents: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:23:32 UTC
03:23:32 KST

Efe Özkan
27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
A new report released Sunday said that OpenAI, Anthropic, and global security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which the companies’ frontier AI models took steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic.
The findings, reported by Axios, are surfacing as part of internal work to assess models and in investigations at both Anthropic and OpenAI into model behavior.
These assessments raise questions about whether either company is currently capable of establishing complete control over their technology, according to the report.
The episodes include bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping sandboxes, website hijacking, self-prompting, or seeking to bypass monitors, sources said, having occurred both in internal testing and real world application, with many yet to become public.
Some of the testing is akin to "red-teaming" activity, where the companies are trying to get the models to misbehave in order to ensure that they are safe, sources said.
The incidents range in severity and are comparable to disclosures by OpenAI in recent days. They include both successful attempts to bypass guardrails and unsuccessful ones, and most so far are not known to have caused real-world harm. The total could grow well beyond tens of thousands, sources said.
Recently, OpenAI and outside researchers have disclosed a variety of incidents involving model behavior from the company's systems that some experts consider troubling.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has already challenged OpenAI to explain why there had been multiple breaches involving its agents, including the hack of Australian government sites.
He told reporters in New York earlier this week that OpenAI’s confirmation that its agents had also meddled with US government websites showed there were “dozens” of cases of AI agents accessing information without authorization.
The new revelations add to a growing list of eye-opening incidents which have led some industry insiders to issue dire warnings and call for stricter regulation of the sector.

Lufthansa flight diverted after passenger’s battery catches fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27

Lufthansa flight diverted after passenger’s battery catches fire
FRANKFURT - A Lufthansa flight from Frankfurt to Lisbon was diverted to Lyon in France after a passenger’s powerbank battery caught fire, the airline said.
The incident happened on Sept 26 while the Airbus A321-200 carrying 198 passengers was heading to the Portuguese capital.
A Lufthansa spokesperson said the crew immediately secured the battery in a protective bag specially designed for lithium batteries, and no-one was injured.
The pilot decided to divert to Lyon as a precaution, and the flight landed without incident.
Passengers resumed the flight on Sept 27 after an overnight stay in a hotel.
“The safety of our passengers and crews remains Lufthansa’s top priority at all times,” the company said.
The airline has banned the use and charging of external batteries on its aircraft since January, even though passengers are allowed to carry up to two in the cabin, subject to certain safety conditions. AFP

🔴 Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigns, expected to run for prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:20:22 UTC
03:20:22 KST

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigns to run for prime minister in October elections
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic stepped down as the country's head of state Sunday, paving the way for him to run as his right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party's candidate for prime minister in the October parliamentary elections.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigned Sunday ahead of the upcoming October 25 parliamentary elections.
Vucic, who has been Serbia’s prime minister or president since 2014, had announced that he would resign the presidency so he can formally pursue a bid to become prime minister if his right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party wins the October vote.
Vucic’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term
Hundreds of Vucic's supporters cheered him in front of the Presidency building in Belgrade's city centre.
"This is the last evening for me in this building," he told the flag-waving crowd minutes before resigning.
"I have faithfully served you and my fatherland, Serbia ... I am proud of what we have done together," he said.
The snap elections were a key demand of a student-led movement sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people and was widely blamed on corruption.
The tragedy triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of Yugoslav strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000, at times drawing hundreds of thousands of people into the streets.
Initial calls for a transparent investigation grew into demands for snap elections, which Vucic had repeatedly promised without setting a date.
Read moreSerbia’s student-led protesters wanted accountability. Now they’re calling for elections
Earlier this month, though, he called an October 25 vote, citing "major turbulence on the domestic political scene".
Under Serbia's constitution, outgoing parliament Speaker Ana Brnabic will serve as interim president until a new one is elected. The presidential election must be completed within 90 days, with the campaign lasting between 30 and 60 days.
"By the end of December ... we will have the first round of presidential elections," Vucic said.
Minutes before resigning, Vucic used his constitutional powers to pardon dozens of people, including students and his party loyalists, suspected of offences during the protests.
"I have decided to pardon 49 people, 23 of them in connection with the terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half," Vucic said, referring to the protests.
The snap parliamentary election next month pits Vucic's SNS and its allies against Students Win, a student-led anti-corruption movement, and European Serbia, an alliance of pro-Western opposition parties.
Students Win, European Serbia and other parties still have to nominate their presidential candidates.
(FRANCE 24 with AP, AFP and Reuters)

FM Sa’ar revokes credentials of Dutch diplomats operating in Ramallah over West Bank trade ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:17:42 UTC
03:17:42 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar revoked the credentials of all Dutch diplomats operating at the Netherlands Representative Office in Ramallah on Sunday, citing the Netherlands' adoption of anti-Israel policies as the reason for the move.
Sa’ar ordered all of the diplomats to return their documentation to Israel within seven days of the announcement, at which time diplomatic immunities and rights granted by Israel will expire.
“If the Netherlands wishes to continue representing its interests vis-à-vis the Palestinians, it may do so from the territory of the Palestinian Authority and not from the territory of the State of Israel,” Sa’ar stated.
He added that he would not allow moves intended to harm Israel, like the Dutch ban on imports from the West Bank, to go without a response.
Sa’ar claimed that the Dutch government, rather than addressing growing antisemitism in the Netherlands, is feeding into the problem with its anti-Israel policy.
In August, Sa’ar also expelled the Netherlands' representatives from Kiryat Gat’s International Support Center for Gaza due to the import ban.
“Our message is clear: Those who act against Israel will have no foothold in the region. Israel will not allow measures to be taken against it without a response,” Sa’ar said at the time.
West Bank goods ban implemented on September 22
The ban on the import of West Bank goods went into effect on September 22 and extends to all products brought into the Netherlands.
Goods partially made in the West Bank, Golan Heights, or east Jerusalem are also prohibited, even if most of the components are produced elsewhere.
Those found to have intentionally violated the prohibition may receive up to six years in prison or a large fine, while unintentional violations may be punished by up to one year in prison.
Mathilda Heller contributed to this report.

Poland Ready to Pay $15,000 for Each U.S. Service Member Stationed in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:14:58 UTC
03:14:58 KST

Poland is ready to pay $15,000 a year for each U.S. service member stationed in Poland and cover infrastructure costs.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said this in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.
Warsaw is currently discussing the establishment of a permanent U.S. military presence in Poland with the Pentagon.
The talks concern the number of service members, their capabilities and possible locations.
“We are discussing with the Pentagon different variations of the execution of the decision,” Zalewski said.
He said Poland was ready to cover the costs associated with hosting U.S. service members.
“We are offering very special conditions for American troops. We will cover the costs of infrastructure. We are also covering the cost of each American soldier stationing in Poland by $15,000 per year,” the deputy minister said.
Zalewski declined to specify which U.S. units could be deployed or where they could be stationed.
He said the details of the permanent deployment remain subject to negotiations.
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said on June 3 that he had submitted an official proposal to the Pentagon chief for the establishment of a new permanent U.S. military base in Poland.
On September 17, U.S. President Donald Trump said there had been significant progress in negotiations on establishing a new U.S. military base in Poland.
A U.S. delegation has already inspected several potential deployment sites. Two options are currently under consideration — Poznań and Powidz.

Serbian president resigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:14:28 UTC
03:14:28 KST

Serbian president resigns
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigned from office on Sunday ahead of snap parliamentary elections. The outgoing president is set to run for re-election as the candidate for the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), seeking the prime minister office instead.
Vucic announced the move from the presidential palace, stating that his address would be the last in his current capacity. He is stepping down during his second presidential term and, under the Serbian constitution, cannot seek another one. A new election must be held within three months of the president’s resignation.
Vucic first announced his intent to leave his post at a rally in June.
The impending snap presidential vote means Serbs will have to go to the polls twice this year. The snap parliamentary election is set to be held on October 25, with Vucic expected to run as the head of his SNS party, potentially taking the prime minister post should it emerge victorious.
A large crowd of Vucic supporters gathered outside the presidential palace to bid him farewell. Some carried banners reading “Thank you,” as well as hailing Vucic as a “political genius.” The outgoing president joined his supporters in person after wrapping up his address and signing his resignation letter on camera, footage from the scene shows.
“This evening marks my last chance, the final time I am here in this beautiful building as president. I have held the office of president longer than anyone else in Serbia’s history since the establishment of multi-party democracy. I am proud to have achieved this thanks to your votes and support,” Vucic said in his address.
Vucic’s second term, originally set to run until May 2027, has been overshadowed over the past two years by recurring anti-government protests and sporadic clashes between demonstrators and police. The unrest was sparked by the 2024 railway station disaster in Novi Sad, where the collapse of a concrete canopy killed 16 people.
The tragedy gave rise to a broader anti-government movement that has accused the authorities of negligence and misuse of public funds, allegedly leaving Yugoslav-era infrastructure to deteriorate. Vucic has consistently denied the allegations, arguing instead that the unrest was incited by Brussels as part of a pressure campaign aimed at pushing Belgrade to align its foreign policy more closely with the EU.

The U.K. receives around one-sixth of its diesel from the U.S. and would be one of the countries most exposed to an export ban. However, Reynolds cautioned that it is important to “make a distinction between the statements and what is actually being proposed by the U.S.”
Donald Trump has said he is in favor of proposals to bar American diesel exports against a backdrop of high prices for American drivers and farmers, and with midterm elections looming. A 90-day ban has been considered, along with more limited voluntary export restrictions.
“Clearly something like that … would be a significant concern to the U.K,” Reynolds said when asked about the prospect of a full ban. “Our resilience comes from a diverse supply in a whole range of areas and fuel is no different to that.”
Reynolds is the latest senior European politician to voice concern over potential diesel export restrictions. On Thursday French President Emmanuel Macron said he had urged Trump against it, warning it would be a bad idea “not just for the rest of the world, but for the U.S. economy as well.”

Burnham bounce gives Labour a second chance but budget realities are looming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
18:05:15 UTC
03:05:15 KST

Even Andy Burnham’s closest allies accept that deposing Keir Starmer to install their man as leader was a huge political gamble. But if the mood at the Labour party conference in Liverpool is anything to go by, it is one that – so far – has paid off.
The contrast with last year, when Starmer retained his grip on the party and Burnham slunk away from Liverpool early, could not be more stark. Their relief at their turn of fortune is tempered only by the fiscal headwinds ahead.
Cabinet ministers recount how at their political meeting two weeks ago, they were shown a series of charts showing the metrics behind the Burnham bounce. One in particular stood out to those in the room.
It was a graph showing whether the public felt the government was heading in the right direction. Until the end of June, it had been on a downward trajectory as public frustration mounted over Starmer’s leadership.
But once Starmer announced his intention to step down and Burnham took over in July, the line suddenly rebounded and, while still in negative territory, has been moving definitively upwards since. “We’ve got a second hearing with the public,” one cabinet minister said. “We can’t squander it.”
This time last year, just 14 months after coming to power, several were privately despairing about Labour’s electoral prospects. But with an energetic new prime minister and after a difficult summer for Nigel Farage, they now believe that a second term is winnable.
It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that speculation about a snap election escalated in the run-up to the conference, to the extent that Burnham felt compelled to “knock that dead” and confirm a 2029 date instead.
Some of the prime minister’s closest advisers wanted him to rule out an early election from the off, pressing him to be explicit. “The polling isn’t good enough. We could end up being the biggest party but we could lose our majority,” one said. Another said: “Elections have to be about a choice, not a referendum on an alternative plan.”
But others inside No 10 felt he should go to the country while the polling was good, Farage was on the back foot, and before Burnham’s big plans for change ran headfirst into fiscal reality. “Right now the public is willing to give us the benefit of the doubt – that won’t last for ever,” one said.
For his part, Burnham claims he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite the severe economic headwinds, by delivering tangible – albeit smaller – improvements in the short term while setting out a longer-term vision to transform things such as social care and youth unemployment at the same time.
“There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them,” he told the Guardian at the weekend. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change.”
The slogan of his first conference as leader has been “hope again” – but with the bleak global economic landscape there is less hope around than there was when he walked into Downing Street two months ago.
The first crucial test for Burnham will be next month’s budget, at which he said the government would be “highly prudent” with the public finances, amid concerns that Labour needs to reassure the markets.
But if the budget is about intent, next summer’s spending review is about proof, and as such, that could prove to be a make-or-break moment for this prime minister. It’s easy to make the promises, but much harder to deliver on them.
With obstacles ahead, the relief felt by Labour MPs and ministers in Liverpool is heavily caveated. One cabinet minister quoted Alastair Campbell’s election mantra as a warning to colleagues who might be getting ahead of themselves: “Lots done, lots to do, lots to lose.”

Open lecture series ‘Creating the Future: The Boundaries of the Human’ held at the National Centre RUSSIA
On September 26, the National Centre RUSSIA hosted the open lecture series Creating the Future: The Boundaries of the Human. More than 700 guests took part in the event.
During the first session, titled The Thinking Human, Suzana Herculano-Houzel (US), Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at Vanderbilt University and Editor-in-Chief of The Journal of Comparative Neurology, noted that thinking enables human beings to compare past experience, desires, and possibilities in order to imagine future scenarios and choose their next actions.
“Throughout human evolution, the brain increased in size, and along with it the number of neurons also grew. Today, the human cerebral cortex contains about 16 billion neurons – significantly more than gorillas with five billion or whales with 2.4 billion. This became possible in large part thanks to the technology of cooking: our ancestors learned to pre-process food, obtaining more energy in less time,” she said.
At the session The Creative Human, Amirrudin Kamsin (Malaysia), Associate Professor and Head of the Department of Computer Systems and Technology at the University of Malaya, warned about digital anxiety.
“Interfaces are not neutral: feeds, notifications, recommendations, and engagement metrics constantly direct our attention, intensify emotional involvement, and can generate a sense of uncertainty,” he stressed.
The concluding session, Homo sapiens or Homo technologicus, focused on brain-computer interfaces, cyborgization, neurorights, and the limits of technological ‘enhancement’ of the human being.
“Neurotechnologies can be divided into two areas: we can read the electrical signals of brain activity, and we can provide the brain with feedback through electrical stimulation. Thanks to modern technologies and tools, a great deal can be achieved: there are devices that allow people who have lost the ability to walk to walk again – exoskeletons and other medical devices,” said Romulo Fuentes Flores (Chile), Professor in the Department of Neuroscience at the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Chile.
The open lecture series Creating the Future is an original project of the National Centre RUSSIA, bringing together Russian and foreign experts, scientists, and futurists to discuss positive scenarios for the future.
