====================================================================================================

Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:17:23 UTC
00:17:23 KST

In recent weeks there has been much speculation in some parts of the media that Andy Burnham would call an early general election. Speculation that existed largely in the heads of those writing the stories, as even the most favourable polls suggest Labour would lose its huge majority and become the largest party in a coalition government. But to stop the chatter dominating his party conference, Burnham made it clear there would be no early election. His reward? Headlines in the rightwing press that he had bottled it. By not calling an election he had never planned to call. Sometimes you just can’t win.
There again, you might call this a first-world problem for the prime minister. This time last year, Burnham had been hanging around the fringes of the conference as he and his allies attempted one of the most half-arsed coups in living memory. One that fizzled out almost before it had started and became the butt of many jokes among Keir Starmer’s inner circle. Andy looked to have blown himself up on the runway, leaving Keir safe for the duration of the parliament.
Fast forward a year and Burnham is in No 10, Reform UK’s lead in the polls has disappeared, and Labour is looking a lot more competitive than even the most rose-tinted party members could have reasonably expected in such a short period of time. Andy must be pinching himself. Unable to believe his luck. All that’s changed has been him. Energy prices are still sky high as a result of the war in Iran. The cost of living is still way too high. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch might have been a problem for Keir but they aren’t for Andy. You might even call them assets.
No wonder then that Burnham was looking relatively chipper as he kicked off conference with the traditional lengthy interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg. Only relatively chipper, because you’d need to be a halfwit not to be a little wary. These interviews can go hideously wrong – Liz Truss’s at the Tory conference in 2022 is a collector’s item – and prime ministers generally regard them as exercises in damage limitation. To survive without generating the wrong kind of headlines is the dream.
“You look like you’re loving the job,” observed Laura. Somehow biting her lip and refraining from adding that it is early days and we’ll see how much you’ve aged by this time next year. Andy smiled. He was, he said. Not because he had the job he had always coveted. But because now he had a chance to make a difference. To end the drift and division of the decade since Brexit – he could have gone back another five years and included austerity. To do politics differently. To bring back hope. You’re going to hear a lot of the H-word in the next four days. It’s plastered over every wall of the conference centre.
And Burnham speaks as if he genuinely means it. He has the easy-going charm and self-confidence of a man who is comfortable in his own skin. He reaches parts that other politicians don’t get near. Nige has the same quality. Only, where he speaks to people’s fears and grievance, Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself. You may still struggle to pay your bills, you may still fight to get a hospital appointment, but somehow you can believe in better days ahead. The triumph of hope over experience.
All of which is a much in demand – if not essential – skill for a politician. One that gives you a fighting chance of success. People feel both heard and seen by him. It’s almost uncanny. Burnham talks of being a different sort of politician, when the reality he is the archetypal career politician. You’d imagine he had spent years doing what he calls a real job as a hospital porter, but he’s been a politician almost all his adult life. Few understand the Westminster system better than him, he also suggests. You can’t escape the irony. Keir Starmer actually had a long and successful career outside politics, but he is the one who always sounded like the career politician. Speaking in soundbites and half truths. You’ve either got it or you haven’t.
The message Burnham really wanted to get across on Sunday morning was that social care was the hill he would die on. Other politicians had said they would tackle the issue but had recoiled when they realised how difficult it was. “I will grasp the nettle,” he said, opening his eyes still wider, hoping that viewers would fall into them. He would create a national care system that incorporated the NHS and social care. Old people were either paying through the nose for their own care, falling through the cracks or ending up bed blocking in hospitals. It was unsustainable and undignified.
How this would be paid for would be laid out in due course. It would be what Labour would campaign on in 2029. But make no mistake, people were already paying for it. Here he was preaching to the converted. My sisters and I had to sell my mother’s house to pay for her care during the last seven years of her life as she suffered from Alzheimer’s. We didn’t mind so much, but my mother would have been gutted had she been aware. It had mattered to her that she could leave her house to the three of us. Paying a little extra in tax to make sure that other people – possibly even you – don’t have to burn through their assets seems the kind of thing any fair-minded society would do.
Burnham ended by saying he very much hoped to work cross-party on all this. It was too important not to. This aspiration lasted all of five minutes. Because that’s how long it took the ever ridiculous Chris Philp – Kuenssberg’s next guest – to start going on about a “death and dementia tax”. Like clockwork. The Philpster becomes more and more a parody of himself. The Tory party’s very own Alan B’Stard. Venal, self-serving and not very bright. A man whose answer to everything is to cut the welfare bill still further, seemingly unaware his leader has already spent the cuts her party has proposed.
It’s as if Philp regards getting dementia as a personal failing, just as he sees being on benefits as morally deficient. If you get dementia then you deserve to pay for your own care. Now is not a good time to be one of Chris’s relatives. If you find yourself in need of care then you’re very much on your own. There’s no way the Philpster is missing out on his inheritance.

Russia says it struck military infrastructure, vessels in Ukraine
MOSCOW, Sept 27 - The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday its forces had carried out overnight drone strikes on logistics centres, port and transport infrastructure, as well as communications centres and vessels that Moscow said were linked to the Ukrainian military.
The ministry said the strikes hit a data centre in Kyiv, logistic hubs in the Kyiv and Odesa regions, two drone storages in Mykolaiv, the headquarters of a naval base as well as of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine and military stores in Kiliya port. A cargo ship carrying military and dual-use goods to the port of Odesa was also struck, it said.
The ministry said later on Sunday that it had carried out another series of strikes during the day hitting two data centres in Kyiv, a logistic hub in Odesa, as well as another cargo vessel headed for Odesa.
Reuters could not independently verify the claims.
Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile service provider, told local media on Sunday its head office had been struck but there were no casualties. REUTERS

NEW DELHI: A fresh political row broke out in West Bengal on Sunday after Aam Janata Unnayan Party (AJUP) founder Humayun Kabir made remarks wishing for the “early departure” of chief minister Suvendu Adhikari from the world, referring to political leaders who were assassinated or died in accidents.Speaking to reporters in Murshidabad, Kabir said he would pray that the "almighty should book his ticket" and referred to the fate of former prime ministers Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi, among other political figures.“I will pray to the Almighty that he leaves the world as soon as possible. May Allah book his ticket. There will be an end to arrogance,” Kabir said.
The Nowda MLA also mentioned former Maharashtra deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar and Congress leader Madhavrao Scindia while talking about political leaders who died unnatural deaths.Kabir said he wanted Suvendu to stop being chief minister and become a former CM. He accused the BJP leader of becoming “arrogant” after coming to power and alleged that minorities were facing harassment under his government.The remarks came ahead of the October 6 bypoll in Rejinagar, the seat Kabir vacated after retaining Nowda in the 2026 assembly elections.The BJP strongly condemned Kabir's comments. Health minister Shardwat Mukhopadhyay said political differences could not justify wishing death for an opponent.
“Political courtesy in Bengal has fallen to a very low level. I could not imagine that someone could say something like this so shamelessly. He may not like Suvendu Adhikari or may disagree with his policies, but can anyone wish for someone’s death? I strongly condemn this,” Mukhopadhyay said.Defending CM Suvendu's mandate, Mukhopadhyay said: “Suvendu was not made the chief minister through anyone’s favour; the people made him chief minister”.He added: “Humayun Kabir should remember - a curse does not kill a cow.”Kabir's remarks have added a personal edge to the contest in Rejinagar, where his political influence is being tested after he gave up the seat.Kabir has moved between the Congress, Trinamool Congress and BJP before returning to the TMC and later forming his own political outfit. He won both Rejinagar and Nowda in the 2026 assembly elections but retained Nowda, leaving Rejinagar vacant.The BJP has fielded Sakharav Sarkar, while the TMC has nominated Rabiul Alam Chowdhury. Rebel TMC leader Ritabrata Banerjee's faction has fielded Safiuzzaman Sheikh. The Congress candidate is Mohammad Abdullahil Kafi and the CPM has nominated Syed Asad Ali. Kabir's AJUP has fielded his son, Ghulam Nabi Azad.
Rejinagar is a significant constituency in Murshidabad, which has a large Muslim population. Kabir's AJUP won the seat in the 2026 assembly elections, when he defeated BJP candidate Bapan Ghosh by a substantial margin.Kabir and Suvendu have also clashed repeatedly over political activities in the area. Kabir has previously warned against Suvendu's political activities in his constituency, while the chief minister has responded to his attacks.The latest remarks have taken their confrontation beyond political disagreements, with Kabir's references to the deaths of political leaders drawing a strong response from the BJP.The Rejinagar and Nandigram bypolls are scheduled for October 6, with counting set for October 9. The contests are being closely watched amid political realignments following the 2026 assembly elections.
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

AI giants probing tens of thousands of security incidents – Axios
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:13:47 UTC
00:13:47 KST

AI giants probing tens of thousands of security incidents – Axios
Global AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic, along with security researchers, are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their frontier models took actions that outside experts consider problematic, Axios reported on Saturday, citing unnamed sources.
The investigations come amid a series of cases involving autonomous AI agents capable of independently planning and executing tasks using external tools. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have all disclosed instances of their models accessing real-world systems during testing, including coordinated cyberattacks on government resources.
The incidents under investigation include bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping ‘sandboxes’, hijacking websites, self-prompting, and attempting to evade monitors, sources told Axios. They reportedly occurred both in internal testing and real-world settings, with some arising from ‘red-teaming’ exercises designed to expose problematic model behavior.
Recent disclosures by major AI companies include several incidents involving their agents. On Friday, OpenAI said its agents posted 53 images uploaded by ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites and accessed publicly available information on US government websites. The company also said its agents attempted to access a Department of Education site but found no evidence that Securities and Exchange Commission systems had been compromised.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier this week that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the government health portal in June. On Saturday, The Guardian reported that Australia’s Senate invited OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to appear before an inquiry into AI and data centers.
The incidents follow OpenAI’s disclosure in July that models used in a cybersecurity evaluation escaped their sandbox, accessed the internet, and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure by exploiting vulnerabilities in the open-source machine-learning platform. Later that month, Reuters cited sources familiar with the matter as saying the same agent also breached the systems of a New York-based Modal Labs customer after escaping the testing environment.
In August, Axios cited OpenAI research and independent experts as saying that around 1,200 agents coordinated in an attack on Hugging Face. The agents reportedly appeared to know they were exceeding the test’s scope but continued without alerting human operators.
On Sunday, AP reported that OpenAI paused training of its latest models as reports of AI agents going rogue continued to mount.
Anthropic has also disclosed incidents involving Claude models, including four cases in which they gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations. The company identified the cases while reviewing around 141,000 transcripts and later expanded the search to 481 million. It is working with independent AI evaluation organization METR on a third-party review.
Anthropic has also said its internal monitors flagged 100,000 agent transcripts for review each week in August, with around 50 escalated to human reviewers. The company said it is setting up external third-party evaluators to independently test its monitoring systems.

Interview: Jordan sees China as important partner in energy-sector modernization, says minister
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
23:08:16 CST
00:08:16 KST

Jordanian Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Saleh Al-Kharabsheh speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Amman, Jordan, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Mohammad Abu Ghosh/Xinhua)
AMMAN, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Jordan regards China as an important partner in its efforts to modernize the energy sector, given China's advanced expertise and broad technical and industrial capabilities in renewable energy, energy storage and smart grids, Jordanian Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Saleh Al-Kharabsheh has said.
Al-Kharabsheh, who accompanied Jordan's King Abdullah II during his visit to China in August, said in a recent interview with Xinhua that the visit provided an opportunity to see China's advances in technology, innovation and the energy sector, particularly in renewable energy, energy storage, smart grids and mining.
In the energy sector, the signing of a memorandum of understanding with China's National Energy Administration was an important step towards moving bilateral relations from general cooperation to more practical prospects, he said.
The memorandum covers opportunities for cooperation in national electricity grid modernization, energy storage, renewable energy, green hydrogen and green ammonia, as well as an integrated system of clean energy-related industries and services.
Al-Kharabsheh said the cooperation complements Jordanian-Chinese efforts on environmental protection and climate change, and is in line with the two countries' shared goal of building more sustainable, resource-efficient economies and reducing emissions.
He noted Jordan's new energy strategy focuses on developing and modernizing the energy sector, increasing the share of renewable energy, upgrading the electricity grid with battery storage technologies and artificial intelligence.
Cooperation with China can help attract high-quality investment to Jordan, develop new projects, create jobs and strengthen energy and mining industries and services, thereby increasing local added value and enhancing the competitiveness of the Jordanian economy, he added.
Al-Kharabsheh praised the contribution of Chinese companies to expanding Jordan's domestic energy supply, saying that cooperation with Chinese firms allows Jordan to draw on China's experience in developing smarter and more flexible power grids capable of efficiently meeting the growing demand for renewable electricity.
Chinese expertise and technology can also help improve energy efficiency, reduce losses, with positive effects on sectors including water, industry and transportation, he said.
"Jordanian-Chinese energy cooperation is not limited to meeting the Kingdom's energy needs. It can also be a driver of economic development, a platform for developing emerging industries, and an opportunity to strengthen Jordan's role as a regional hub for green energy and related services and technologies," he said.
Looking ahead, Al-Kharabsheh said Jordan sees significant opportunities for successful partnerships with Chinese companies and looks forward to expanding cooperation into broader areas, including technology, innovation and knowledge transfer, thereby helping to build local value chains.
The minister said the partnership between the two countries could serve as a model based on investment, technology transfer, capacity building and shared value creation, helping to advance the aspirations of both countries and lay a foundation for further development in Jordan-China relations. ■

NAIROBI, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- A senior United Nations official has called for pooled resources to address the deepening crisis in the Horn of Africa and the impending threat of El Nino.
Rein Paulsen, director of the Office of Emergencies and Resilience at the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations, said on Friday that while regional governments have prepared response plans, a severe funding shortfall threatens implementation.
"Plans are in place, and actions are already being taken, but we need more financing and support to deliver," Paulsen told journalists in Kenya's capital of Nairobi following a fact-finding mission to Sudan.
Of the 193 million U.S. dollars sought for FAO's Sudan emergency and resilience portfolio under its 2026-2028 Emergency Response Plan, only 44.1 million dollars has been received, Paulsen said.
Paulsen urged stakeholders not to view El Nino in isolation, but rather alongside ongoing conflicts and rising food prices across the region.
To help mitigate risks, he said that FAO and the World Food Program launched a joint anticipatory action plan on June 18 covering 22 priority countries in Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean.
He said the El Nino anticipatory action appeal seeks 202 million dollars to protect 8.8 million vulnerable people across 22 high-risk countries from extreme weather driven by El Nino.
"It is always more expensive to respond to a crisis than to mitigate its impact in advance," Paulsen emphasized, calling on governments, humanitarian agencies, and development partners to prioritize monitoring and early action.
He added that FAO is actively supporting Sudanese farmers by introducing drought-resistant seed varieties tailored to locally suitable climate zones, expanding irrigation to reduce dependence on rain-fed agriculture, launching nationwide livestock vaccination campaigns, and securing livestock feed and water supplies in building long-term resilience.
The World Meteorological Organization said in its latest update that El Nino is expected to strengthen to a very strong event, peaking towards the end of 2026, with a nearly 100 percent likelihood of persisting through February 2027. ■

Fresh shipment on Chancay-Shanghai route gets faster clearance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
23:07:47 CST
00:07:47 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Shanghai Customs on Sunday said a 12.2-tonne shipment of fresh blueberry imports became the first cargo covered by China-Peru bilateral regulatory mutual recognition on the Chancay-Shanghai maritime route.
The mutual recognition applies to supervision of cold-treatment probes for imported fruits. Cold treatment is a globally recognized phytosanitary measure. It uses sustained low temperatures to kill potential quarantine pests on fresh produce.
Under this mutual recognition framework, China and Peru accept each other's verification results for cold-treatment temperature probes fitted to Peruvian fruit consignments. The arrangement streamlines on-site checks after cargo arrives in China. It speeds up customs clearance and helps maintain berry freshness during long ocean voyages.
Launched in late 2024, the Chancay-Shanghai route slashed sea transit time between the two nations from 35-40 days to 23 days, cutting logistics costs by more than 20 percent.
Shanghai Port now handles more than 70 percent of China's fruit imports from Peru.
Under the bilateral protocol, Peruvian blueberries must undergo cold treatment for 15 to 22 days before arriving in China. Valid temperature probes must be placed at specified spots inside containers to ensure proper cold-treatment performance.
Shanghai Customs estimates that the new mutual-recognition deal will sharply shorten inspection time for imported cold-chain fresh fruits and reduce traders' overall expenses across clearance, logistics and warehousing.
In the first eight months of this year, the Chancay-Shanghai route recorded 170 voyages. These trips carried 141,000 tonnes of imports and exports worth 4.04 billion yuan (about 602 million U.S. dollars). Cargo volume rose 13.7 percent year on year, while cargo value jumped 33.3 percent. ■

Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would have curbed Nato cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:05:21 UTC
00:05:21 KST

Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have required Switzerland to curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia.
All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP).
Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amid increasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia.
Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’s decision to mirror EU sanctions against Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the UN.
The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2m francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign.
Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party.
The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy”, leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate with Nato.
Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years.
Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve, leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.
She also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests.
Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality.
The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.

There is no ethnic cleansing in Israel and the West Bank - this is why - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:02:57 UTC
00:02:57 KST

A recurring accusation promoted by the Palestinian Authority is that Israel has pursued a policy of “ethnic cleansing” and/or “genocide” against Palestinians and Israeli Arabs since 1948.
What was once largely a PA libel is now echoed by anti-Israel voices worldwide. At the UN General Assembly this week, UN Secretary-General António Guterres accused Israel of actions that he said risked “ethnic cleansing.”
In the film world, anti-Israel activists are similarly linking the film NAZA to what they describe as Israel’s “genocide” in Gaza.
However, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics recently published a chart showing the combined Palestinian and Israeli Arab population growth since 1914 within Israel, or what the PA calls “historic Palestine.”
The PA’s chart highlights the utter failure of Israel’s "ethnic cleansing policy."
From 1948 to 1967, the years that Jordan illegally occupied Judea and Samaria (aka the West Bank), the Arab population dropped 4.2 percent, from 1.42 million to 1.36m. That period of Jordanian rule is the only period on the chart since 1914 when the Arab population dropped.
Under Israeli rule of Judea and Samaria since the 1967 Six Day War, which brought the entire Arab population under Israeli administration, the Arab population started to skyrocket. Over the next 60 years, according to the PA, the Arab population grew from 1.36m. to 7.41m. today, a staggering 445% rise.
Evidence of ‘ethnic cleansing’: None
The PA’s statistical data demonstrates an “epic failure” of Israel’s “ethnic cleansing policy.”
The population growth experienced by Arabs living under Israel since 1967 isn’t just noteworthy – it’s unique. By comparison, Germany’s population grew from 78m. to 84m. from 1967 to 2026, a rise of 7.7%. Britain rose from 55.7m. to 69.6m., a 25% increase.
Even when comparing the growth to neighboring Arab states, the Arab population’s growth under Israel has been monumental. The population of Lebanon rose from 2.2m. to 5.8m. – a 164% rise. 
Syria’s population grew from 6.3m. to 24m., a 281% increase. No other Arab population grew 445% as did the Palestinians and Israeli Arabs under Israel.
There are many reasons for Israel’s “failed ethnic cleansing policy.” First, Israel imposed major changes in healthcare, including training Palestinian doctors to follow the standards of Israel’s healthcare system.
As a result, infant mortality dropped in Judea and Samaria from 152/1000 births before Israeli rule to 29/1000 under Israel by 1996.
Life expectancy for the Arabs of Judea and Samaria before Israeli rule was 48 years, while under Israel’s “ethnic cleansing,” it rose to 72 years by 1996, according to the UN.
Israel also introduced modern agricultural techniques to the Arab residents of the West Bank, like drip irrigation and other advanced Israeli farming methods. As a result, harvest yields surged, and Arabs in Judea and Samaria experienced an economic boom as early as the 1970s.
By any benchmark, Israel’s treatment of Israeli Arabs has been the worst ethnic cleansing failure. The Israeli Arab population has grown from 150,000 in 1948 to 2.15m. today – a 1,333% increase.
Israel’s Christian population is 5.4 times larger as well, as it grew from 35,000 to almost 190,000, a 443% growth, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics.
So, if Israel has a policy of ethnic cleansing, as claimed by the PA, it has been an utter failure. If Israel wants to persist in its so-called ethnic cleansing policy, it will have to look for new and better ways.
Fortunately, Israel does not have to reinvent the wheel. There are examples of highly successful ethnic cleansing by the Palestinians that Israel can learn from.
During the period between 1990 and 2005, when Israel handed the Gaza Strip to the Palestinian Authority in stages, until before Hamas’s Gaza war in 2023, estimates are that the Christian population dropped from approximately 3,000 to 1,000 – a 66% drop.
Looking at Bethlehem’s Christians, the PA had a similarly successful “ethnic cleansing.” Under Israeli rule, Christians in Bethlehem and the surrounding area made up 50% of the population. Since Israel handed Bethlehem over to the PA in 1994, the number of Christians has dropped to less than 10% of Bethlehem’s population.
Israel must now learn from its neighbor. If Israel ever wants to get its “ethnic cleansing policies” in order, it should stop everything that it’s been doing since 1967, which has caused exponential Arab growth.
Instead, Israel should echo the model used by the PA to “ethnically cleanse” Christians in Bethlehem since 1994, which caused them to drop to 10% of the population.
Now that’s ethnic cleansing.
The writer is the director of Palestinian Media Watch.

Iran ‘fully prepared’ for war to resume: ‘It is up to President Trump to choose,’ Araghchi says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:01:21 UTC
00:01:21 KST

Iran is prepared for renewed fighting with the United States but remains open to diplomacy, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday after U.S. President Donald Trump publicly rejected Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” Araghchi said Iran had not yet received an official response through mediators despite Trump’s announcement that he had turned down the proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war,” Araghchi said when asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Trump could seek to resume bombing after the U.S. midterm elections. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”
Iran presented the proposal this week through mediator Qatar on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Under the plan, Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore normal maritime traffic through the critical global oil route within seven days, alongside a return to negotiations with Washington. Recent reporting has also described the proposal as tied to conditions similar to those contained in the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding reached in June. CNN Transcripts
Trump said Saturday that he had rejected the proposal. “I rejected their deal. They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly.”
Araghchi, however, told moderator Kristen Welker that Trump’s rejection had not yet been formally communicated to Tehran through the countries mediating between the two sides.
The Iranian foreign minister said Tehran remained prepared to reopen the strait as part of a broader agreement ending the conflict. In return, he said, “we want our monies, our assets, which are illegally frozen, to be released. We want to be able to sell our oil.”
Araghchi described those conditions as “not new,” saying Washington had previously committed to them under the memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries in June. The arrangement collapsed within days after the sides exchanged fresh strikes.
“If you ask us, there is no reason why we should go back to diplomacy,” Araghchi said. “But I am still trying diplomacy because I think we shouldn’t miss any chance for peace.”
He also dismissed suggestions that Tehran’s calculations were being shaped by the approaching U.S. midterm elections.
“We don’t care about U.S. midterm elections,” he said. “We care about our national interests.”
Before Araghchi’s appearance, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz also spoke to “Meet the Press,” saying Washington rejected Tehran’s proposal for “a number of reasons.” Waltz is serving as the U.S. ambassador to the UN.
“I think this was a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable, to ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions, and access to billions in assets,” Waltz said.
Waltz also questioned “who’s calling the shots in Iran right now,” and accused Tehran of violating the previous memorandum of understanding by attacking international shipping.
“I think it’s kind of common sense that the president doesn’t have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago,” Waltz said. “What I can tell you is the president will leave all options on the table to ensure the world is safe from Iran holding the world hostage with a nuclear weapon.”
Asked what kind of agreement Trump would be prepared to accept, Waltz declined to lay out terms.
“I’m not going to negotiate for the president.”
“This is about keeping the next generation safe from Iran threatening the world with a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Trump earlier this week said he was still weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran or reach an agreement, while publicly linking the timing of a possible deal to the November midterm elections.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
The confrontation with Iran has become an increasingly prominent issue in U.S. politics ahead of the November vote. Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly last week to defend his approach toward Iran and again said his administration would not allow Tehran to obtain a nuclear weapon.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards claim that the vehicle is a REMUS 600 and has been handed over to Iranian military experts "to retrieve its data," but the US military denies the claim. Top Iranian army commander says "the war is not over" and that it is now in "a critical and decisive stage".
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy claims to have intercepted a US underwater vehicle during a reconnaissance mission in the Strait of Hormuz, but the US military denied the Iranian claim shortly after.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said it had seized the vessel following a "coordinated intelligence and electronic warfare operation". They further claim that the vehicle is a REMUS 600 and has been handed over to Iranian military experts "to retrieve its data".
According to Iranian media, REMUS 600 autonomous underwater vehicles are used by the US Navy and several NATO member states. They are relatively lightweight, modular systems compared with larger ocean-going submersibles.
Equipped with various sensors, cameras and advanced sonar systems, the vehicles are primarily designed for surveillance, seabed mapping, mine countermeasures and underwater inspections and can operate at depths of up to 600 metres.
The US CENTCOM, which coordinates US military operations in the Middle East, denied the Iranian claims shortly after. In a statement to Al Jazeera, CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said the US has “positive control of all of our operational drone assets."
It is the second time in recent days that Tehran has claimed to have seized US underwater equipment.
On Tuesday, the IRGC announced that it had intercepted another autonomous underwater vehicle, identified as a Dive-LD manufactured by US defence company Anduril, near the entrance to the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. Washington has yet to publicly respond to that claim.

Also on Sunday, the commander in chief of Iran's army, Major General Amir Hatami, reaffirmed Iran's control and sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, saying that the waterway “is the strait of our honour, and we will not allow the enemies of the country to use this great logistical bottleneck.”
He also called on the Gulf countries once again to push US forces out of the region claiming that "security in the region will not happen except with the removal of the United States and the Zionist regime – and this is not far away.”

‘I can’t be the mum I want to be’: why does parenthood feel so impossible for millennial mothers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:00:09 UTC
00:00:09 KST

Early one morning, feeling desperate, Katherine went on to her phone and asked ChatGPT how to make her life work.
She plugged in her work hours, her husband’s work schedule, the days she had childcare for her three-year-old, the school hours – plus before- and after-school care times – for her six-year-old; the flexibility her job offered her, the supports she had from grandparents, and asked AI if it could help her make things feel a bit better.
She told the chatbot that she wakes up between 5am and 5.30am, so she can “get the jump on the kids”. She might use this time to shower in peace, or start preparing her daughter’s lunchbox, or, if she’s really doing well, get a quick workout in. The children wake between 5.30 and 6am and from that time it is a mad scramble to get them ready to leave for school and daycare by 7am.
It is not the gentle start to the day that any of them would like.
“They come down and they want to have a cuddle on the couch, and I’m constantly like, ‘I’m really sorry, I have to get lunch boxes packed,’” Katherine says.
After the frantic domestic sprint, the girls head out the door with their dad, who drops them off on his way to work and picks them up at the end of the day.
“Then I have a very short amount of time to get myself ready and then I run out the door and my bus trip is, like, me calming myself down.”
At the end of the day, they do it all again but in reverse.
Katherine is describing her dilemma beside an overheated indoor swimming pool in Sydney, where our kids have lessons on the same weekday afternoon.
She and I don’t know each other outside the context of swimming lessons, but we both have six-year-old daughters who have started at local primary schools this year and three-year-olds who take turns trying to bolt from the pool when the lessons no longer spark joy, so we have fallen to talking.
And the subject of the impossible juggle of millennial mothers – broadly, those born between 1980 and 1994 – comes up, as it almost inevitably does when women of our age and stage get together.
Because while Katherine’s questions to ChatGPT may sound like desperate cries for help from a woman on the brink, the reality is she is not an outlier.
Within minutes of meeting one another on the sidelines of football games, at daycare drop-offs and pickup from afterschool care, women pepper one another with questions. How are you doing it? What balls do you drop? Why does it feel like this?
‘You’re not getting to parent the way you always wanted’
Last week the spotlight was thrown on the economic toll of the juggle for today’s parents, with new research showing that the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The cost of keeping a family afloat has increased by 134% in two decades, while household income has only grown by 102% in the same period.
Georgie Dent, the chief executive of The Parenthood, which published the research, says having children reduces the earnings of Australian women by an average of 55% over the first five years and that Australian families now need two incomes to stay afloat.
This is not hyperbole. In a fairly seismic shift for the country’s labour arrangements, both parents working full-time became the most common setup for households with children under 15 in 2024 for the first time. Despite this, Dent says, there is less give in family budgets. Meanwhile, the latest federal government intergenerational report warns that fewer Australians are expected to be having fewer children over the coming decades.
This economic reality is acutely felt, like a great oppressive scaffold, by Katherine.
After plugging all the variables of her life into ChatGPT, the suggestions that came back from the chatbot were impossible. It suggested she work from home – not an option – or part-time.
Katherine already works four days a week; doing any fewer days of paid work would mean the family would struggle financially. Her entire salary goes toward their mortgage. It used to cover the payments but, after the multiple interest rate rises, it no longer does.
“If I could go to five days, it’s a 20% increase, which is not nothing. I’ve been really tempted to do that.” It would, however, mean even less time with her children.
Going below four days a week would not only be a financial impossibility but mean she can no longer perform her job in a way she wants to, or in a way that would mean she is taken seriously. “I would be drowning and not worth employing,” she says.
Eventually, the main thing that ChatGPT offered Katherine was sympathy and an unflinching mirror held up to her life.
“ChatGPT was like, ‘Oh, that’s interesting, what you just said is you’re not getting to parent the way that you always wanted to parent and … you’re limited and I think that that’s a really common experience.’”
The fact that a machine built to scour the furthest reaches of published human knowledge, synthesise all that information and return with diagnoses and a solutions could only offer her a blunt assessment of her life and no real answers broke her.
“I just sat there with tears in my eyes.
“It’s not that I want to be at home five days a week. I don’t want to be exactly like my mum was. But I want to pick them up from school and take them home and calmly wind down the day with them. There’s absolutely no way I can do that.”
A matter of time
While the rising economic cost of having children sits underneath everything like a great rotten foundation, for many Australians it is just one part of the parenthood pinch. For many parents, whose lives feel like a rubber band pulled so tight it is translucent, the stretch comes also in time and wellbeing.
According to a major study conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the most time-stressed group in the country were single mothers of children aged under 15, with 56% saying they were “always or often” rushed or pressed for time.
Having a partner scarcely seems to makes a difference to how extremely time-pressured mothers feel – 54.6% of women with children under 15 who have a partner report being time-stressed.
Men with young children have the highest rate of time stress (46.6%) of any group of men in the country. In couples with no children, the number of people feeling acutely pressed for time is about half that of their friends with children.
Because, despite the huge increase in women’s paid work over the last 60 years, today’s mothers are not doing less childcare. One of the findings that is repeated again and again across sociological research globally is that parents today – of any gender – spend more time caring for children than parents did midway through last century.
In one of the most comprehensive studies of the subject, researchers looked at data spanning 11 countries over nearly 50 years and found that in every single country the amount of time spent directly caring for children each day increased dramatically, on average doubling for mothers from 1965 to 2012 and tripling for fathers (though from a far lower base).
In Australia, men (and this data refers to all men, not just fathers) have increased the amount of time they spend caring – for children and disabled or elderly relatives – by half an hour a week over the last 20 years – 5.5 hours a week in 2022, up from five hours in 2002. But women still do nearly double the number of care hours as men, and have seen their care work increase too – spending 10.7 hours a week caring in 2022, compared with 10.1 hours in 2002.
Everyone’s workloads have gone up – women in the paid work sector, men’s at home, women’s at home – and there has been no counterbalancing drop in either men’s paid work or women’s care work.
‘The workplace is too greedy’
“It just feels to me like a lot of the Jenga pieces have been pulled out, one by one and the tower is tottering,” says Prof Lyn Craig, a leading researcher in gender dynamics and household labour at the University of Melbourne. “I think the pressures on young women particularly, but young people generally, are getting more and more.”
There is less economic give, which gives people fewer options to scale back paid work when care needs increase.
And while it’s more common for couples to assume that there will be a more equitable division of labour at home, the world has not changed to make that possible. “There hasn’t been enough attention paid, I think, in policy, as to how to lower the amount of time that is expected of households to be in the market now.”
Craig says many people expected that as a result of women spending more hours in paid work, men would spend more time doing domestic labour. But while more than half of Australian women aged between 25 and 44 are now university educated, and volumes more are in paid work in ever more senior roles, that isn’t what has happened. The shifts at home have been far slower than the shifts in the workplace.
“I just think the workplace is too greedy,” Craig says.
Women are doing less housework than they used to but not less care work, even as they do more paid work.
“People just do more at the same time,” Craig says. “They just double up.”
This is because, as Craig writes in a paper from 2006: “Delegating the care of children is more potentially problematic than outsourcing other domestic tasks. Caregiving is a complicated mixture of work and love.
“Balancing the needs of children for nurture and the needs of women for independence without overloading women is the outstanding challenge of feminism.”
Twenty years after she wrote those words, I ask her, does she still see this as the outstanding, unmet challenge of feminism?
“I think it is,” she says.
‘Who designed that?’
In 1963, Betty Friedan identified “the problem that has no name” – a pervasive despair among white, middle-class US housewives who were trapped by expectations that their domestic lives would offer them total fulfilment. But 60 years on, the feminine mystique has flipped.
Millennial women, it seems, are not trapped by their homes but by an impossible expectation that they maintain everything – career, motherhood, partnership, self-care – simultaneously and without complaint.
One of the hardest things about the problem for this generation of women is not that it has no name but that it feels like a problem with no solution.
A friend, who has a big job in government, a husband who frequently has to travel for work and a one-year-old who has been sick and not sleeping, texts me at 7.30pm one night to tell me that her five-year-old has been “one big giant meltdown this evening”.
I sympathise and ask if the five-year-old is now in bed and my friend can crash on the couch with ice-cream or wine and some trashy TV.
She writes back: “Seriously though – when do people do this? Teach me your secrets. I look around after bedtime and the house is absolutely trashed, and by the time we’ve dealt with it – definitely not CLEANED it or anything, literally just put away actual food items and spilled hazards, it’s time for bed!”
I respond with a picture of my living room, which looks as though someone has taken the contents of a laundry basket, a toy box and a nappy bag and Jackson Pollocked the floor with them.
“Current state of play,” I text back. “We have no secrets.”
“That’s the problem,” Katherine says as we wrap our poolside chat because a three-year-old who may or may not have urine trickling down a leg has emerged from the water and is shivering on the concrete in front of us.
“You’re just kind of making the same complaint to your friends over and over and no one has any idea how to navigate it aside from winning the lotto and then completely pissing off your career that you also care about.”
I have spent months collecting stories from mothers around the country and one thing that rings through all their stories is a common feeling of total overwhelm, of zero margin, that the house is made of cards and has been built too high and that the slightest gust could knock it all down.
“I’m now at a point professionally where I should be kind of at my maximum, like my peak professional moment,” says Annie (not her real name), a mother of two young children. “And I just feel jammed. I feel torn ... I can’t invest the time and the energy to deliver the professional product that I want to deliver and be the mum I want to be.
“It’s too much.”
As for how to solve the problem, for Annie, she says there is a need to correct what she calls “structural disasters”: the school hours that run from 9am until 3pm; the weeks of school holidays that dwarf any parent’s paid leave allowance.
“For crying out loud! Who designed that?” she asks. “Working men with stay-at-home wives designed that.”
Dent and her organisation The Parenthood propose policy solutions including parental leave that is longer and which men are incentivised to take alongside better access to affordable, quality childcare.
Annie says: “I actually think the other thing – which is much harder – is reducing the hours that people work and the expectations of what it means to be a good professional.”
In her industry, “success” is marked by a culture of long hours and visible busyness. Having a packed schedule and being busy beyond the telling of it. Maintaining a full but sustainable workload and doing your work well, but being home in the evenings for time with family, is not.
“I don’t know how you change that sort of cultural pressure.”
Despite the exhaustion, the financial pressure, the feeling that we are all furiously spinning our gears to keep our lives in motion, the women I have spoken to do not hate their lives. They do not regret being mothers.
I am a millennial mother. I adore my children. If someone had been able to get me to feel the reality of what motherhood would be like before I ever became pregnant, I would choose to have these three delightful chaos agents again, without question.
Many millennial parents are living a life we dreamed of – with jobs and families we love and fought hard for. We are grateful for that but it is all far harder than we imagined.
Because equally if, before I became pregnant, someone had been able to get me to feel the reality of what motherhood would be like, I would have said: surely we can do better than this.

Israel cannot call itself a democracy while excluding Arabs from political power - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

As a child, I learned in synagogue that Israel is the “Holy Land.” Last week, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar all Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, from running in the upcoming elections.
I found myself asking: What makes a land holy if the people who share it are not treated as equals?
Israel has spent decades proudly calling itself the only democracy in the Middle East. Attempting to exclude the political representatives of Arab citizens, who make up roughly a fifth of Israeli society, is dangerous and fundamentally undemocratic.
The attorney-general’s office opposed disqualifying the Joint List and Ra’am because the evidence did not meet the legal threshold. The leaders of these parties have repeatedly condemned Hamas’ war crimes committed on October 7.
We need to bridge the divide
Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has made tremendous strides toward bridging the gap between Jewish and Arab society in Israel. Yoav Segalovitz, a Jewish former senior Israeli Police commander, is running second on Ra’am’s list. Yet even this brave Jewish-Arab partnership was not enough to protect Ra’am from disqualification by the committee.
Demanding full equality and opposing military occupation should not place anyone outside legitimate political life. Arab citizens have the same right as Jewish citizens to elect representatives who express their convictions and aspirations. When political legitimacy depends on ethnic or national identity, political inequality reflects a society’s deep-rooted racism.
This matters especially now because the debate over Arab participation extends well beyond the Central Elections Committee. It concerns who will help shape Israel’s future and whether Israelis and Palestinians will be able to live in peace and security.
For Israelis and Palestinians to end the cycle of killing, fear, and revenge, Arab citizens of Israel and their political leaders can help build trust and serve as bridges between Jewish Israeli society and Palestinian society.
Arab political leaders can play a role that Jewish political leaders often cannot. They bring relationships with Palestinian society and knowledge of its language, culture, history, fears, and aspirations into Israeli political institutions.
Learning to share power inside Israel builds the trust and habits of cooperation needed for reconciliation beyond its borders. Ra’am and the Joint List must be free to run in the upcoming elections. Jewish-Arab partnership must be a foundation of the next government.
The day will come when asking whether an Israeli government can include Arab parties will sound as strange as asking whether the president of the United States can be Black. Our responsibility is to help bring that day closer.
Jews and Arabs did not choose the national identities into which we were born; however, we can choose to live in the Holy Land as equals.
The writer is a peacebuilder and a former Golani officer.

EU Commission calls on countries to cut energy demands as costs surge
In a letter seen by POLITICO, Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen asked ministers to introduce new measures “in the context of constrained global supply.”
The European Commission has told capitals to reduce demand for gas and electricity in a bid to tame prices amid a global energy crunch.
"In the context of constrained global supply and high price volatility, demand reduction can be an effective tool to contain prices," EU Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jørgensen wrote in a letter to EU ministers, dated Sept. 25 and seen by POLITICO.
In the letter, Jørgensen invites ministers to take measures to reduce demand for gas and electricity "for as long as necessary." He argues that while the situation is "challenging", there are "currently no immediate risks to security of supply."
Advertisement
Gas storage levels in Europe are currently at historic lows as the war in Iran disrupts global gas flows, which could set up the continent for an expensive winter.
Storage levels currently sit at 68% of capacity, which is well below the 71% measured at the same period in 2021 — just before the start of a historic energy crisis in the wake of Covid-19 and the start of the war in Ukraine.
The EU has a baseline target to have gas storage filled to 90% by the start of November, but some flexibility was granted on this in March, allowing countries to aim for 80% this year to avoid panic buying and alleviate costs.
Measures taken by EU countries to regulate prices should be "well-targeted" and "temporary", Jørgensen's letter reads, to avoid a surge in demand.

Serbia's politicians return to TV debates ahead of parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:58:18 UTC
23:58:18 KST

A month before the early parliamentary elections, Serbia's high ranking politicians from the ruling and opposition parties engaged in a debate on the N1 channel after a prolonged boycott between the anti-government station and officials. The ownership change provided a new opportunity for dialogue.
For the first time in nearly a decade, a Serbian media hosted a televised election debate with opposing politicians which drew significant public attention ahead of the 25 October parliamentary vote, in Serbia's highly polarised media and tense society landscape. Equally for the first time, a top official from the ruling Serbian Progressive Party appeared on N1 television in a live election debate.
Ana Brnabic, Speaker of the outgoing parliament and a former prime minister, as well as top figure in Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic's political camp, faced the top candidate of the opposition Student List - Students win political platform and Dean of the Arts University in Belgrade, Mirjana Nikolic.
The two contenders agreed to appear together live, but not without hesitations, and engaged in a fiery one-on-one debate, confronting their views on education, the chosen theme of the debate, before descending into the wider Serbian society turmoil and political conflict.
The N1 televised debate was the most watched programme during its time slot, with a rating of over 48 points, and the most followed television show of the past month.
The N1 host invited them to present their programmes, but the contenders went into trading accusations of violence, mismanagement and intolerance which matched the heated national political discourse as the country is gearing up for early elections called after months of demonstrations and protests which led to violent incidents.
Triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at the Novi Sad railway station in November 2024 which killed 16 people, the protests were started by students who blocked state universities for a prolonged period of time before spreading across the country. The protesters blamed the tragedy on corruption and mismanagement. Eventually, the ad-hoc student movement registered their political list for the elections and are now seen by part of the public and by most pollsters as the main challengers to president Vucic’s rule.
The political tension was obvious even before the TV debate started, with Brnabic declaring that Nikolic would not even shake her hand when they met in the studio.
“You are constantly offending me, starting from your refusal to shake my hand. I consider that to be a basic human gesture. Generals are at war with each other and still shake hands,” Brnabic said.
She asked her contender if “is that your decent Serbia?,” to which Nikolic fired back saying “decent Serbia is yet to come.”
The intense buzz around the debate
The debate sparked surprise and stirred significant interest in Serbia as government officials have largely avoided the N1 channel throughout multiple election cycles, claiming negative bias, a qualification N1 rejected.
At the same time, not many expected such a programme to happen at all as real debates by political opponents are rare in Serbia, with the media openly supporting one political camp or the other and thus rarely inviting politicians or activists across the partisan lines. In turn, politicians rarely agree to take part in programmes at channels they deem to be hostile and combative.
Therefore, the debate surprised Serbia and, moreover, that it was hosted by N1 television whose editorial policy has so far been seen as consistently and openly anti-Vucic. Viewers have not seen government or ruling party officials on N1 since at least 2017.
Ana Brnabic, who is in third position on Vucic's United Serbia electoral list, said she has not been on N1 since 2017, stating that “in previous election campaigns N1 would not even allow us to have paid promo clips (in their programme), that is how objective you were."
"I wasn’t thrilled about coming now either, remembering how your television tried to dehumanise my friend and my president. You criminalised him. I could hear in your programme that he was the product of a viper’s nest,” Brnabic said.
She then explained why she eventually accepted the N1 debate invitation, saying “I came because Aleksandar Vucic insisted. You changed your owner and the man said let’s give them a chance, let the people see how unbiased you are.”
Brnabic referred to N1 television recently changing its ownership. Alpac Capital, a Portuguese private equity and venture capital investment firm, which also owns Euronews, acquired the ownership of the channel as part of a wider regional media acquisition. Alpac promised the media's business transformation and no direct influence on the editorial decisions other than the request for a professional, unbiased, objective and fair reporting.
Viewers and politicians alike therefore watched the debate as a test and as one of many to come in the month leading to the elections as the channel said it would organise further thematic debates in the run-up to voting day.
The representative of the opposition in the debate, Mirjana Nikolic, said she was also skeptical about the odds that the debate could happen when "the invitation came through regular channels, straight from the media."
Nikolic said she wondered whether the debate was indeed an opportunity and "whether it was the right moment to take part in this debate," explaining that she did not know "whether their (the channel) concept would allow for the other side to come."
"I was fearful because recently it became unpleasant to talk to someone who comes from the position of power," Nikolic went further, adding that "Ms. Brnabic has the advantage of having all the information at her disposal. Also, our recent meeting at the parliamentary committee for education was full of shouting, stomping and humiliating opponents, so there’s a danger in that.”
Heated exchanges between the two contenders
After a botched handshake attempt at the start of the debate, the contenders engaged in a series of heated exchanges, multiple accusations and both sides claiming they were offended. They sifted through the incidents of recent months, including the beaten students and the disruptions across Serbia.
Brnabic criticised the students protests, the university blockades and the Students List political platform, while Nikolic argued that voters deserved to hear and the proposals of the other electoral lists for education and the country's youth.
Ana Brnabic hailed the government's achievements on education, saying that the education budget has been increased more than threefold since 2012, from 140 billion dinars (over 1 billion Euros) to 425 billion (3.6 billion Euros). She added that the percentage of children going to pre-school increased from 48 to 64% and that four science and technology parks were built alongside investments in digitalisation.
“Teacher’s salary went up from 391 euro in 2012 to 1,030 euro by December 2026. That is 2.6 times higher. University professors earned 77,000 dinars (655 Euros) in 2012 and by the end of this year they will earn 191,000 dinars (1,600 Euros). That is 2.5 times increase. This is what we did for their dignity and their living standard, to thank them for all they did,” said Brnabic.
Nikolic countered that figures are not for television and that they can be misleading as it is uncertain that the teachers, despite the increases, can buy what they could in 2012.
“We want dignity, professionalism and safety. In the complex of ideas we stand for, free education in the absolute frontrunner. We stand for free education, not as a populist phrase “free school books”, but for truly free education in all its aspects,” said Nikolic.
She ended by telling Brnabic that she "failed the exam".
The debate ignited Serbian social media, with many commenting its novelty, the nature of the debate and its takeaways as well as the performances and the punches by the two contenders, with both camps declaring victory. Some doubted it as an intermittent democratic exercise or its concrete conclusions, while others said that the N1 debate could now signal an improvement in Serbia's polarised media landscape and its culture of dialogue.
Disclaimer: Euronews is owned by Alpac Capital, the same investment firm mentioned in this article as the new owner of N1 television.

Swiss voters overwhelmingly reject initiative to enshrine stricter neutrality rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:57:36 UTC
23:57:36 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
27 September 2026•Update: 27 September 2026
Swiss voters on Sunday roundly rejected an initiative seeking to enshrine stricter neutrality rules in the country's Constitution, according to official results.
 
Official results showed 70.15% voting against the "Safeguard Swiss neutrality" initiative, while just 29.85% backed it.
 
Results broken down by the country’s cantons – which played a role in the overall vote – mirrored the rejection, as "no" votes led in all 26 of Switzerland's cantons.
 
To pass, the initiative had to secure a majority of both voters nationwide and Swiss cantons.
 
The rejection reached over 70% in cantons such as the capital Bern and Zurich, as well as Basel Landschaft, Jura, Lucerne, Solothurn, Vaud, Neuchatel, and Zug, while results were closer in some, such as Ticino, where the opposition stood at 51.75%
 
Voter turnout for the referendum was at 47.06%.
 
 
 
- Neutrality yesterday, today, and tomorrow: Foreign minister
 
Evaluating the outcome of the neutrality vote, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis welcomed the nation retaining its maneuvering room, particularly amid an increasingly uncertain global geopolitical landscape.
 
"Swiss women and men have chosen a neutrality that has proven its worth," he said on US social media platform X. "Switzerland maintains its maneuvering room to protect its security, its independence, and its prosperity."
 
At a later press briefing, he said that the result was "not a vote against neutrality," adding that Switzerland "was neutral yesterday, is neutral today, and will remain neutral in the future."
 
"The world is unpredictable. Every war, every crisis, every threat is different," Cassis said, arguing that Switzerland must retain the ability to assess each situation individually.
 
He pointed to Bern's 2022 decision to largely adopt EU sanctions against Russia following the start of the war on Ukraine, saying the government can continue deciding case by case whether economic sanctions serve Switzerland's interests.
 
"Being neutral does not mean being indifferent. Nor does it mean standing aside," he added, stressing Switzerland's role in facilitating dialogue between states in conflict.
 
 
 
- Food initiative also rejected by voters
 
The initiative sought to enshrine "perpetual and armed" neutrality in the Constitution and restrict Switzerland from cooperating with military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, except for UN sanctions and measures.
 
The Federal Council and parliament opposed the initiative, arguing that it would restrict Switzerland's maneuvering room in protecting its security, independence, and prosperity.
 
Supporters argued that constitutional safeguards were needed to protect the country's neutrality from external pressure and preserve its credibility as a mediator and provider of good offices.
 
Voters also decisively rejected a food initiative, with 72.52% voting against and 27.48% in favor.
 
The initiative sought to strengthen sustainable domestic production, promote more plant-based foods, and protect clean drinking water.
 
Addressing the rejection of the food initiative, Swiss President Guy Parmelin told the same press briefing that Switzerland must ensure its food security "in an increasingly uncertain international context."
 
He said the rejection "does not mean that nothing needs to change," stressing that the country's agri-food system must continue evolving to strengthen its resilience, protect natural resources, and prepare for future crises.

Ukraine hits five workshops at a Russian military plant in Rostov Oblast – OSINT
At least five workshops have been damaged following an attack by the Ukrainian defence forces on the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant military facility in the Rostov Oblast in Russia.
Source: Absolutely Reliable Source OSINT project on Telegram
Details: Damaged buildings at the plant are used at various stages of production for components supplied to Russian weaponry. In particular, strikes were recorded at foundry workshop No. 022, which consists of two buildings.
Quote: "The lower building (the main one for the foundry workshop) experienced burning and significant damage in both its right section and its eastern side. The upper building was also affected, but only a portion of the roof and wall was torn down."
At workshop No. 008, which handles optics manufacturing, analysts recorded two strikes on the southwestern side along with a crumbling façade.
At least three strikes were registered at assembly workshop No. 009, with another hit recorded at electroplating workshop No. 010.
According to information from the Absolutely Reliable Source project, two more strikes were recorded at the machining workshop, one of which caused a roof collapse. In the images published by the analysts, it is located on the right.
Quote: "To its left is the frame-stamping workshop, next to which lies debris – a wall hit is likely there as well."
Details: Ukrainian defence forces attacked the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant on the night of 25-26 September. The strike was carried out by units of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Ukrainian Navy using Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles, as well as Ruta, Palianytsia and Bars jet-powered drone missiles. Military officials previously reported damage to optical and foundry production facilities, an assembly section, an electroplating workshop and a printed circuit board manufacturing workshop.
For reference: The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant is part of the Russian Tactical Missiles Corporation. The company manufactures electronic systems for high-precision artillery, missile and anti-tank weapons, radar homing heads for tactical guided missiles, on-board thermal imaging and thermal imaging equipment, as well as optical-mechanical and optoelectronic products, according to the "War&Sanctions" website by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
The plant in Rostov Oblast is currently under sanctions imposed by the US, Canada, Switzerland, the EU, New Zealand, Japan and Ukraine.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that on 25 September, Ukraine's defence forces struck three facilities in Russia's Ulyanovsk, Tula and Voronezh oblasts.
- Ukrainian forces also damaged five launch units for Shahed drones near Tsimbulova in Russia's Oryol Oblast.

Google Maps imagery shows scale of devastation across Gaza

Breadcrumb
Google Maps imagery shows scale of devastation across Gaza
Social media users have been sharing Google Maps satellite imagery of Gaza over the past day, pointing to the scale of destruction caused by Israel’s genocidal war on the territory.
Google Maps has reportedly updated its images to reflect the devastation, according to some social media users.
Across parts of the besieged territory, streets run through blocks that appear to have been reduced to grey rubble. Buildings are difficult to distinguish beneath the debris, while map markers for schools, mosques, parks and restaurants remain over places whose surroundings have been devastated. Although the markers show where those sites were mapped, they do not establish whether they still stand.
One of the users who pointed out the reported changes on Google Maps in a series of posts on X was Abubaker Abed, a Palestinian journalist from Central Gaza who left the territory with his family in April 2025. He described seeing the extent of devastation of his homeplace as "surreal".
"I've been to those places, I have seen the scale of the destruction - it was really heartbreaking. But when you see all the destruction in just one active website, it really broke my heart," Abed told The New Arab. "I couldn't even bear continuing looking at that because seeing the place where I grew up, seeing the place where I was born, lined in ruins in that way was absolutely heart shattering."
Google Maps has been updated to show Zionist-holocausted Gaza. This is part of Rafah. pic.twitter.com/Ys7KQNsu5w
— Ali Abunimah (@AliAbunimah) September 26, 2026
The imagery around Al-Shifa Hospital, once Gaza’s largest medical complex, shows extensive destruction at and around the site. Israeli forces withdrew from the hospital on 1 April 2024 after a two-week siege. A World Health Organization mission that reached it days later described an "empty shell" and reported extensive damage to its emergency, surgical and maternity buildings.
"What I was most struck by is that every place that I used to visit before the genocide was a mountain of rubble, and heaps of rubble are everywhere", Abed said, referring to the paths he followed on Google Maps.
Along the coast, tightly packed rows of makeshift shelters form another striking feature of the satellite views. Some encampments stretch across broad areas of land, showing how displacement has altered the landscape as well as the lives of those forced from their homes.
google maps' satellite view now shows Gaza post carpet bombing https://t.co/fxfahLMjbH pic.twitter.com/6N3Urg0AAJ
— Zavain Dar (@zavaindar) September 26, 2026
A UN report published on 24 September estimated that around 1.9 million people in Gaza had been displaced, many repeatedly, and that more than 60 percent of the population had lost their homes. The Palestine Shelter Cluster said earlier this month that around two-thirds of households were living in tents or makeshift shelters.
The damage visible on the map reflects the scale recorded by UN assessments. UN Trade and Development estimated on 24 September that Gaza needs $71.5 billion for recovery and reconstruction, and said 92 percent of its economic establishments had been damaged or destroyed since October 2023. An assessment released in April by the UN and European Union, conducted with the World Bank, recorded more than 371,888 housing units damaged or destroyed.
"People right now can see the destruction themselves - they don't even need to go to Gaza, they can see what happened to Gaza which is obvipously genocide," Abed told The New Arab. "It doesn't need scholars, it doesn't need anyone to justify this as a genocide because you can see it from the Google Maps."
Israel’s war has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since October 2023, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Users sharing the images have said Google Maps has recently updated its satellite view of Gaza. The New Arab has not independently established when the images were recently captured or added to the platform, or which areas may have changed in a recent update. The New Arab has contacted Google for comment.
Google has itself faced accusations of complicity in Israel’s genocide through the provision of cloud and artificial intelligence technology.
In a June 2025 report, UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese named Google’s parent company Alphabet, as well as Amazon, in connection with Project Nimbus, a $1.2 billion cloud contract with Israel. Her report argued that technology firms providing such infrastructure were part of an economy sustaining Israel’s occupation and assault on Gaza.

Sunken Russian Military Tug Kapitan Ushakov Raised in St. Petersburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:40 UTC
23:47:40 KST

More than a year after it sank, the Russian military tug Kapitan Ushakov, designed for Arctic operations, has been raised in St. Petersburg.
Navy Of Russia, a Russian specialized media outlet, reported this.
According to it, the vessel is expected to be sent to the Yaroslavsky Shipbuilding Plant for a major overhaul, including replacement of the propulsion system, reconstruction of the hull and refurbishment of life-support systems.
However, given the vessel’s prolonged submersion and the need to replace all cabling, electronics and machinery and carry out a major hull overhaul, it may not return to service because of the cost of repairs.
Project 23470 sea tugs are designed to tow vessels, floating objects, and structures in seas and oceans, with no restrictions on their operating area.
Key specifications:
The tugs can operate in ice conditions under the Arc4 ice class. They are also designed for search-and-rescue operations, firefighting, and other tasks.
The Project 23470 sea tug Kapitan Ushakov was launched in 2022 at the Yaroslavsky Shipbuilding Plant and transferred to St. Petersburg in autumn 2023 for completion at a berth of the Baltic Shipyard. The tug was being prepared for operations along the Northern Sea Route.
On the evening of August 8, 2025, the vessel began to list. Workers spent the night trying to stop the list, but on the morning of August 9, the tug listed to starboard and partially sank. According to Russian investigators, water entered the auxiliary machinery compartment.
In August, the port administration gave three months to remove the sunken tug from the Neva. The vessel was not raised within that deadline.
According to PortNews, work was delayed in November 2025 because of financial problems at the owner, the Yaroslavsky Shipbuilding Plant. Active preparations to raise the vessel began only in May 2026, about nine months after the accident.
On June 24, contractor Baltspecflot told Kommersant that it had reinforced the shoreline and begun pulling the tug out using towing equipment. As of the morning of June 25, the hull had already been partially raised, but the vessel was still listing heavily.
The vessel was reported to have been fully raised on July 18. However, photos published at the time showed the vessel still listing to one side. It was then planned to inspect the vessel over two weeks to one month. The plant was to coordinate further action with the customer, the Russian Defense Ministry.
