Swiss voters reject tighter neutrality rules that would have curbed NATO cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:33 UTC
23:47:33 KST

Swiss voters on Sunday firmly rejected a proposal to adopt a more restrictive form of neutrality that would have blocked their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO.
More than two-thirds voted against a proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be written into the Swiss constitution, according to the latest referendum projections by state broadcaster SRF.
Having failed to win the required support of the majority of Switzerland's cantonal constituencies, the initiative has effectively been rejected.
While Swiss neutrality has been internationally recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815, how the government implements it is not spelled out.
The right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) has said that Switzerland's traditional position has been eroded after Bern imposed sanctions on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.
The campaign had funded posters across the country urging people to vote "No war, yes to neutrality," featuring white peace doves, ahead of the vote.
Swiss government, most parties oppose proposal
Apart from the SVP, most parties and the Swiss government oppose the proposal, with Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis saying it would harm national security and prevent Switzerland from training with NATO.
The Green Party and the smaller Evangelical People's Party (EVP) expressed relief over Sunday's projections.
"Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on," said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green Party.
The SVP meanwhile accepted the defeat and said it currently had no plans for further action.
"I'm of course not pleased with the result," said SVP lawmaker Lukas Reimann, adding that the commitment to Swiss neutrality expressed by all sides during the campaign was encouraging.
"It is absolutely clear that neutrality belongs to Switzerland and is part of Switzerland's identity," he said. "Going forward, we will judge the opponents of the initiative by that commitment."
If the government or opponents of the initiative were to stray from neutrality, for example by adopting tougher sanctions, the party would need to become active again, Reimann said.
'Swiss voters like neutrality'
Fabio Wasserfallen, a professor of European politics at the University of Bern, said before the vote: "Swiss voters like neutrality, but they approve of how the government is implementing it at present."
"They are also generally in favor of the sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine, and don't want that to change."
The campaign wanted the constitution to stipulate that Switzerland cannot join or cooperate with any military or defense alliance unless attacked, and that it refrain from joining any sanctions unless approved by the United Nations.
It says Swiss neutrality has served the country well in the past, keeping it out of both world wars, and also helps Bern offer its 'good offices' to help negotiate peace between warring parties.
"Switzerland has not had a war for 200 years because it is permanently armed and neutral," Christoph Blocher, the billionaire businessman and backer of the SVP, said ahead of the vote.
"But neutrality has been followed less and less in recent years," he told Reuters, with Russia now seeing Switzerland as a party to the conflict because of the sanctions.

Christa Pike set to be first Tennessee woman executed in 200 years, lawyers ask Gov. Lee for mercy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:32 UTC
23:47:32 KST

Christa Pike is set to be the first woman executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years for her involvement in the murder of a 19-year-old in 1995.
Her lawyers and loved ones, however, say that if she committed the same crime today, she would not be on death row.
If her execution goes through, she will be the first woman since 1819 to be put to death in Tennessee.
Notably, only 17 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, whereas 1,663 men have been put to death under the death penalty, the BBC reported.
The murder case of Colleen Slemmer
Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and killed Colleen Slemmer, whom the pair met at a job camp for troubled teenagers.
Slemmer’s body was found on the University of Tennessee’s Agricultural campus in Knoxville with a pentagram carved into her chest and her head bludgeoned.
Court records showed that Pike and Shipp, along with their friend, Shadolla Peterson, lured Slemmer to a remote part of the campus before torturing her and beating her to death.
Pike reportedly took a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.
Pike was sentenced to death for the murder, but Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was given a life sentence without the possibility of parole.
Pike has a history of childhood sexual abuse and neglect that her lawyers claim were not considered in the initial sentencing, the BBC reported on Saturday.
"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," Sandra Babcock, a lawyer who worked on Pike’s defense and an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, told the BBC.
"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."
Christa Pike's childhood sexual assaults, abuse
Since the sentencing, Pike’s defense uncovered proof that she was sexually and physically abused by her mother’s boyfriends and husbands throughout her teenage years. In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr. Diana McCoy, who was hired by Pike’s team, found that Pike was raped when she was 11 and 17 by two of them. She was also repeatedly raped by her grandmother’s boyfriend when she was a toddler.
Her aunt testified in court that her mother routinely let her crawl through filthy, dog-feces-littered floors. Court documents showed that Pike attempted suicide when she was 12 years old.
She was later diagnosed with manic depression, also known as bipolar disorder, in 2021.
Pike’s lawyer during the trial did not call McCoy to testify or call any of the witnesses she recommended, the BBC reported. Her findings about Pike’s background came to light over 10 years later during a review of her case. A new team of lawyers argued that Pike received ineffective assistance of counsel, which the judge denied.
“If someone would have stepped in at age 5, if someone would have stepped in at age 7, if someone would have stepped in at age 11, if anyone would have done anything to help me, to get me psychological help or anything, maybe something would have been different,” Pike said in a recent documentary about her case, Dead Woman Walking: Pike Vs Tennessee.
She also said in the documentary that she regretted her actions and felt remorse.
“I’ve always felt bad for her mother, that I took someone’s child, someone’s sister, someone’s friend away,” Pike said in the documentary. “I feel remarkably remorseful for what I did.”
Still, her victim’s mother, May Martinez, says she thinks that Pike should suffer for her actions.
"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she told Knoxville station WBIR in 2021.
"I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did. My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.
"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."
She told the BBC that she stands by the statements.
Her attorneys are now asking Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life without parole, and have sought relief from the state’s Supreme Court as well as the federal court.
On Tuesday, the Tennessee Supreme Court rejected Pike’s lawyers' challenge that lethal injection would be considered cruel and unusual punishment for Pike, who has thrombocytosis, a bone marrow disorder characterized by an overproduction of blood platelets. Medical experts on the case argued that her condition would cause her to essentially drown in her own blood during her execution, Nashville’s WTVF reported.
Teen killer Christa Pike to be executed on Wednesday
Because of her trauma, Pike has requested an all-female team for her execution. She said that being held down by a team of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state has not guaranteed her request, but said that a team of female guards will transfer her to the prison where she will be executed.
On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.
"If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke,” Babcock told the BBC.
“It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable,” Babcock said.

An Ohio hospital is being sued by the US government for firing a surgeon for “being Jewish,” according a lawsuit filed last week.
The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) filed a lawsuit against Mercy Health in Youngstown, claiming a violation of federal law by subjecting a Jewish orthopedic surgeon to unfavorable terms and conditions of employment and “firing him because of his religion and race, shortly after the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel.”
The surgeon – named in other media as Dr. Ian Walton – had a successful practice with Mercy for many years and performed well, “including exceeding Mercy’s productivity goals”, the lawsuit claimed.
However, Mercy reportedly subjected Walton to antisemitic remarks throughout his employment and ultimately fired him in November 2023, advising him that he was “being terminated for a reason other than work performance.”

EEOC attempted to reach a settlement before filing the lawsuit
Lucas also said Walton was excluded from scheduled meetings and had his surgery time blocks reduced. Shortly thereafter, his contract was terminated.
“The EEOC will not hesitate to bring litigation to protect Jewish workers from unlawful discrimination and ensure they do not face adverse action simply because they are Jewish. Antisemitism has no place in the American workplace,” Lucas added.
This alleged conduct violates Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on religion and race. The EEOC filed suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Ohio after first attempting to reach a pre-litigation settlement through its administrative conciliation process.
Walton’s Jewish identity was not a secret at his workplace. The lawsuit said that he had family photographs in his office depicting relatives wearing kippot and prayer shawls.

Israeli passengers stopped, searched at Dutch airport as West Bank import crackdown begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:20 UTC
23:47:20 KST

The Netherlands has begun enforcing its strict crackdown on the import of goods from Israeli settlements, with passengers reporting thorough bag checks at Schiphol Airport.
As of September 22, 2026, the Netherlands officially enacted the sanction decision on settlements in the West Bank, the Golan Heights, and east Jerusalem.
The ban extends to all imported goods, including travelers' personal luggage and souvenirs. Those found to have adjusted origin labels will also be penalized.
The prohibition additionally applies to goods that are only partially made or produced in the settlements (i.e. if one ingredient is from the area, even if the product was predominantly made in, say, Tel Aviv).
The date of purchase of the product has no bearing on the penalty, meaning the law is effectively backdated to all purchases prior to its implementation.
Penalty for violating sanctions could result in six-year imprisonment
Under the new law, intentional violation or circumvention of the rules is punishable by up to six years' imprisonment or a significant fine.
Unintentional violations can carry a prison sentence of up to one year.
According to conservative news site Nieuwsrecht, the day after the ban came into effect, travelers arriving at Schiphol from Tel Aviv walked past customs through the “Nothing to declare” lane when a customs officer asked: “Are you coming from Tel Aviv? Yes? Everyone from Israel, come over here!”
Nieuwsrecht said all El Al passengers were made to put their luggage through a screening machine.
The news site later learned that a unit of the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee has been assigned to carry out additional checks on passengers arriving on flights from Israel at the national airport to determine whether they are carrying wine, dates, olives, or other products brought from East Jerusalem, the West Bank, and the Golan.
Posters listing prohibited items have now also been distributed.
Nieuwsrecht called it a "witch hunt."
Customs in the Netherlands did not respond to The Jerusalem Post's request for comment by the time of publication.

Ben-Gurion Airport parking lots full as holiday travel surge leaves passengers seeking alternatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
14:47:05 UTC
23:47:05 KST

Passengers planning to fly in the coming days and leave their vehicles at Ben-Gurion Airport will need to find another solution, as all airport parking lots are currently full, the Israel Airports Authority said on Sunday.
According to the authority, the number of passengers increased significantly during the High Holy Days, resulting in all airport parking facilities reaching full capacity with no available spaces. The authority asked travelers and their companions not to arrive in private vehicles and instead use public transportation. The situation will continue until further notice, IAA noted.
Parking shortage returns during peak travel periods
This is not the first time the airport’s parking lots have reached capacity. In August, on a day when around 101,000 passengers passed through Ben-Gurion Airport, the authority announced that the "Kerem" and "Pardes" parking lots were completely full and directed passengers to other lots.
That situation occurred during the peak of the summer travel season, while the current shortage comes during the peak holiday period, meaning both were times when heavy traffic was expected in advance. Despite this, passengers traveling to the airport cannot reserve a parking space in advance.
The long-term parking lot does not offer advance reservations, and vehicles can only enter if space is available. Travelers leaving home do not know whether they will find parking until they arrive at the airport.
The alternative suggested by the authority, public transportation, is also limited. The train is the fastest way to reach the airport, but its schedule changes during holidays. During Rosh Hashanah, for example, trains operated between Herzliya and Jerusalem and did not reach Ben-Gurion Airport. On weekends and holidays, train service does not operate at all.
Public transportation options remain limited
The Airports Authority said last year that exceptional congestion at the airport was mainly caused by traffic jams and the lack of train service on weekends. When trains are not operating, passengers are largely left with Egged’s 485 bus line, which runs 24 hours a day between Tel Aviv’s Central Bus Station and Ben-Gurion Airport, including on Saturdays. The line serves only one area.
Taxis have also failed to solve the problem. Passengers who landed at Ben-Gurion Airport in recent days reported long taxi lines, confrontations between travelers and drivers, and a severe shortage of available cabs. Drivers said that many prefer to work within the city rather than travel to the airport because fares and regulations have, in their view, made airport trips financially unattractive.
As a result, the authority is asking passengers to avoid private vehicles at precisely the time when alternative transportation options are most limited. Anyone who still needs to reach the airport in the coming days should check train schedules in advance and leave home with significantly more time than usual.

Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha says World Cup fame has cost him privacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:46:46 UTC
23:46:46 KST

Halis Sunnetci
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha said he preferred his life before the sudden fame brought by his standout performances at the 2026 World Cup.
The 40-year-old's profile soared after he made seven saves to help Cape Verde hold eventual champions Spain to a goalless draw in their opening match of the tournament.
Before the Spain game, Vozinha had around 56,000 Instagram followers. His following passed 1 million by full time and surged to around 14 million within days.
"A member of the team's catering staff came up to me and told me I had a billion followers," he told The Observer.
"I had no idea what he was talking about; I thought he was joking, but he insisted.
"Later, I went to do some interviews in the mixed zone and a CazeTV journalist asked me if I knew what was happening. She showed me her phone and that was when I saw that I had more than a million followers."
Vozinha said the attention that followed came at a cost.
"I've lost my peace and tranquillity," he said.
"A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality," Vozinha said.
"To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I'd choose the one I had before."
Vozinha said he also had far less privacy than before the tournament.
"I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to. Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there's always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph.
"Or, worse, someone is filming me. That's what has changed most in my life, and I don't think there's anything I can do about it."
His World Cup performances also earned him a place among the 10 nominees for the 2026 Yashin Trophy, the Ballon d'Or award for the world's best goalkeeper.
"I never imagined it could happen," Vozinha said. "It was unthinkable, but I'm grateful to those who thought of me. Just being on that list is already a great honour."

Asked earlier about the US response to Iran’s seven-point proposal, Araghchi said: “We saw the initial reaction from the US president, but the mediators have not yet conveyed anything to us.”
“We are waiting for the intermediaries to convey a definitive response, and we will decide accordingly,” he said.
“In any case, our conditions are clear. Any progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz depends on those conditions being met, and we will not back down from them.”
The new proposal lays out a roadmap to open the Strait of Hormuz to normal maritime passage within a week. It calls for the US to release frozen Iranian assets, lift oil sanctions and end the naval blockade on Iranian ports, after which the strategic waterway could be reopened and negotiations on a final deal would start.

Surprising result seen in primordial matter inside atom smasher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:50:26 UTC
23:50:26 KST

When the universe was born, space was too hot and dense for atoms to exist. Even the constituents of atoms—the protons and neutrons that make up atomic nuclei—couldn’t immediately coalesce. Instead the newborn cosmos was filled with even smaller and more fundamental building blocks, quarks and gluons, which formed a smoothly flowing soup called quark-gluon plasma.
Soon, though, the universe expanded, cooling down the soup. Gluons glued quarks together to make protons and neutrons, which floated around as a gas rather than a plasma. The change marked a phase transition, just as water can switch from vapor to liquid to solid ice. But key details of this profound primordial transition, such as its threshold energy and density, have remained deeply mysterious.
That began to change around the turn of the millennium, when physicists started smashing gold ions together at nearly the speed of light inside the giant particle accelerator at Brookhaven National Laboratory on Long Island in New York State. Those smashups were so powerful that they briefly re-created the quark-gluon plasma from the big bang. Now researchers analyzing data from those collisions have seen an unexpected signal that offers new clues about how the cosmic transition happened eons ago.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The signal comes from an experiment called the Solenoid Tracker at RHIC (Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider), or STAR. After the gold ions annihilated in collisions and produced new bits of matter, STAR tracked the paths of that debris. One measurement it made compared the particles’ momentum changes with a baseline—in particular, the so-called transverse momentum, the momentum perpendicular to the direction in which the gold ions had been traveling. The STAR data showed a surprising dip in fluctuations of this value—that is, a potential phase transition—at an energy that represents some of the densest states physicists have ever achieved in their studies of nuclear matter. The findings were reported in a paper published recently in Physical Review Letters.
“This measurement is a possible signature that, yes, a phase transition does exist here,” says Rutik Manikandhan of the University of Houston, a member of the STAR team and a co-author of the new analysis. “It hints at the existence of a critical point.”
If scientists discover a critical point—a change in how the phase transition happens at different temperatures and densities—they will better understand how the universe evolved just after it was born. They could also learn what happens to matter at its highest densities, such as within neutron stars, where the mass of an entire star is squeezed into a space about the width of a city.
“We are trying to probe the different phases of matter,” Manikandhan says. “We don’t fully understand what phase of matter is inside neutron stars. We can learn things like ‘What would be the speed of sound inside the core of neutron stars?’” Answering that question would allow astrophysicists to address other mysteries, such as the precise threshold where a neutron star will collapse to form a black hole.
But figuring out what the signal seen by STAR means isn’t easy. “The current data represent an intriguing hint, but they are insufficient to identify the origin of the phenomenon,” says Berndt Mueller, a physicist at Duke University, who wasn’t involved in the experiment. “The problem is that this is only one observable, and it is insufficient to isolate an explanation.”
For instance, instead of a critical point, the dip in momentum fluctuations glimpsed in STAR’s data could simply reflect the fact that as the energy of gold-ion collisions changes, the types of particles being created change, too. At higher energies, more mesons (pairs of quarks and their antimatter counterparts, antiquarks) are present. But at lower energies, more protons and neutrons form. “To make a substantiated claim about the QCD critical endpoint, it is important to rule out such 'trivial' effects, or at least estimate their magnitude with respect to any signals from a critical point,” says Jan Steinheimer, a physicist at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany, who studied this alternative explanation.
Researchers plan to analyze more STAR data to further unravel the mystery. RHIC operated for 25 years and shut down earlier in 2026. Yet the machine gathered reams of data that scientists haven’t been able to study yet. “We still have a lot of STAR data left to analyze,” Manikandhan says.

Trump ‘very seriously’ mulling diesel export ban

Trump ‘very seriously’ mulling diesel export ban
The White House is still “very seriously” considering a diesel export ban, US President Donald Trump has said, as fuel prices soar ahead of the November midterm elections.
Shipments being cut from the world’s largest exporter could deepen a global shortage and leave import-dependent Europe scrambling for supplies.
Diesel prices have surged amid a global supply crunch fueled by the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Russia, one of the world’s largest diesel exporters, has also restricted fuel shipments to stabilize its domestic market following Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries. US diesel production is now barely keeping pace with domestic demand, raising concerns that growing exports could further squeeze supplies at home.
Trump told a Fox News reporter on Sunday that his administration was examining the measure. “We’re looking at it very seriously – we may do it,” he said while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament near Chicago, acknowledging that the move could push gasoline prices somewhat higher.
Trump first floated the idea last week. “I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel,” he told reporters ahead of a meeting with Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky.
The potential move comes as fuel prices surge. Energy Information Administration data put the nationwide diesel average at a record $6.529 a gallon ($1.72 per liter) on September 21, up from $5.454 just five weeks earlier, as tight global supplies and elevated crude prices drive costs higher.
The idea of the world’s largest diesel exporter shutting off supplies has drawn sharp pushback from the US energy industry. The American Petroleum Institute warned that a ban could force refineries to cut production of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel, tightening supplies at home while deepening the global fuel crunch.
Diesel and natural gas price changes in the US and Europe in 2026
Change from start of period to latest reading, %
Increased exports from the US and China have partly offset lost supplies from Russia and the Middle East, according to the IEA. The agency warned that global diesel shortages are likely to persist unless Russian or Middle Eastern exports recover in the coming months or demand declines.
Russia’s diesel export restrictions, introduced after an unprecedented wave of Ukrainian drone strikes damaged refineries across the country, have added further pressure to an already strained global market, with fewer Middle Eastern barrels available to replace any potential loss of US supplies.
Trump has also repeatedly urged Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, saying the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage. “There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel. That’s hurting the world,” he said earlier this month.
A US cutoff could hit Europe particularly hard after the EU abandoned Russian energy following sweeping sanctions. Russia supplied nearly half of Europe’s diesel before the Ukraine conflict, but its share fell to around 5% by 2024 after Brussels imposed an embargo.
The US has supplied about a third of Europe’s diesel imports this year, rising to around half in August, while Middle Eastern shipments have fallen to a six-year low. The US accounted for 62-72% of diesel imports to Britain and the Netherlands that month, according to S&P Global.
Britain could be among the hardest hit. It imports around 55% of its diesel and has just four major refineries left. Analysts cited by The Telegraph warned on Sunday that a US ban could send prices from just under £2 ($2.68) to as much as £2.50-£3 ($3.35-$4.02) per liter this autumn.
The EU has also sounded the alarm over Trump’s threat, urging Washington not to proceed. “We believe this is a very bad idea,” European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said last week.
The US has supplied about a third of Europe’s diesel imports this year, with its share rising to around half in August, according to government data. Prices at the pump have already reached record highs in Germany and the Netherlands.

RAF 'terror plot' raises questions over UK's role in Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:30:39 UTC
23:30:39 KST

Breadcrumb
RAF 'terror plot' raises questions over UK's role in Iran war
A suspected terror plot targeting a British airbase used by the US to launch operations against Iran has raised questions over whether UK involvement in the conflict has increased the risk of retaliation on British soil.
Five British men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested early on Sunday after police received reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire.
They were initially detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and later arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism.
Counter-terrorism police are investigating a possible Iranian connection, but have yet to establish the motivation or whether any foreign state was involved.
Despite this, much British media coverage has focused on Iran, with some reports describing the incident as an alleged Iranian "bomb plot".
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said it would be "far too early to comment or speculate" about the motivations of those arrested.
Iran has denied involvement in a statement posted by the Iranian embassy on social media, saying it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" that it had any involvement in the suspected plot.
US President Donald Trump has claimed the suspects were planning to cause "big damage" to the base, saying US and British authorities had been watching them "for a long time".
Police said the arrests followed a call from a member of the public reporting suspicious vehicles near the base, although Streeting said the witness had only a "partial picture" of the security operation.
Why is RAF Fairford important?
RAF Fairford has become an important part of US military operations during the war with Iran.
Despite its RAF designation, the Gloucestershire base is extensively used by the US Air Force and hosts the headquarters of its 501st Combat Support Wing.
It is also the US Air Force's only bomber Forward Operating Location in Europe, designed to receive and sustain America's long-range strategic bomber force. Its infrastructure can accommodate B-1, B-2 and B-52 strategic bombers.
After initially declining to allow British bases to be used for US attacks on Iran, the UK subsequently authorised Washington to use Fairford for what it described as specific "defensive" operations. American B-1 and B-52 bombers have since operated from the base during the conflict.
London distinguishes between allowing strikes against Iranian missile facilities threatening Gulf states, shipping and British interests and participating in the wider US offensive campaign.
Iran's warning to Britain
Iran does not necessarily recognise that distinction.
In July, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned Britain over the use of RAF Fairford, saying bases used by the US to launch attacks on Iran could be regarded as legitimate military targets.
Security was subsequently increased, with a local councillor telling Reuters that authorities had responded to a specific Iranian threat against the base around six weeks before Sunday's arrests.
There is currently no public evidence establishing that those arrested were working for Tehran or that Iran ordered the alleged operation. Investigators are reportedly considering several possibilities, including an Iran-linked motive, Russian involvement and an Islamist motivation.
Even if an Iranian connection is established, it would not necessarily mean the operation was directed by the Iranian state.
Has UK policy increased the risk?
Britain maintains that it is not participating in the wider US war against Iran while allowing American forces to use British territory for some military operations against Iranian targets.
This raises questions under international law over when military assistance makes a country a participant in an armed conflict.
Traditional laws of neutrality generally prohibit neutral states from allowing their territory to be used by one belligerent for military operations against another.
The UN General Assembly's Definition of Aggression also includes allowing a state's territory to be used by another country to perpetrate aggression against a third state.
This does not automatically make Britain an aggressor or party to the wider conflict.
The UK argues that the operations constitute lawful individual and collective self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including the defence of regional states subjected to Iranian missile attacks.
International law expert Marc Weller has nevertheless argued that Britain's position has moved it closer to direct involvement and that its distinction between different categories of US operations may be difficult to sustain.
Writing for Chatham House in March, Weller noted that Iran could not know whether a US aircraft leaving a British base was conducting an operation authorised by London under collective self-defence or participating in Washington's broader campaign.
From Tehran's perspective, Fairford is therefore not simply a British military installation, but a forward base hosting US strategic bombers operating during the war against Iran.
An Iranian connection to Sunday's alleged plot remains only a possibility under investigation.
But should one be established, the incident would raise questions over whether allowing UK territory to become part of the military infrastructure used against Iran has also increased Britain's exposure to the conflict.

Hamas marks Al-Aqsa Intifada anniversary, calls for Arab, Muslim support for Palestinians

Palestinian resistance group Hamas marked the 26th anniversary of the Al-Aqsa Intifada on Monday and called on Arabs, Muslims and supporters worldwide to back the Palestinian people in regaining their rights.
“Our compass will remain firmly directed towards liberating the land and holy sites, and we call on our nation and free people around the world to support our people’s struggle and steadfastness until they secure their legitimate rights,” Hamas said in a statement marking the intifada, which erupted on Sept. 28, 2000.
It said this year’s anniversary comes amid an “unprecedented escalation” by Israel against the Palestinians and holy sites, including occupied East Jerusalem’s Al-Aqsa Mosque.
“This was accompanied by Israeli protection for extremist occupiers and efforts to Judaize Al-Aqsa, desecrate it and erase its features, as well as advance annexation and displacement plans,” it said.
“Israeli measures will not succeed in extinguishing the flame of resistance or undermining the determination and will of the Palestinian people,” the resistance group said.
It reiterated that Palestinians “will not relinquish their land, rights, national principles or holy sites,” saying Israeli government plans “are destined to fail.”
The group called for Palestinian agreement on a unified strategy, backed by sustained Arab, Muslim and international support and “effective partnership” from supporters around the world.
It called on Arab and Muslim countries and supporters worldwide to take political, diplomatic, media and popular action to support Palestinians and oppose measures targeting Al-Aqsa Mosque.
On Sept. 28, 2000, then-Israeli opposition leader Ariel Sharon raided the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem under heavy security, an event that sparked the Al-Aqsa Intifada.
The uprising lasted around five years, during which 4,412 Palestinians were killed and 48,322 others injured, according to official figures.
Israel was established in 1948 on Palestinian land seized by armed Zionist groups that carried out massacres and displaced at least 750,000 Palestinians.
Israel later occupied the remaining Palestinian territories and continues to reject withdrawal and the establishment of a Palestinian state as stipulated in UN resolutions.
